artigo.texto: Written by Eric Funderburk for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary The Texas governor has directed the state's environmental regulator to halt permits for data centers until ERCOT and state's water board have completed an audit regarding the facilities' power and water consumption as well as funding. Tightening the Reins Texas Governor Greg Abbott (R) has ordered the state's environmental agency overseeing air and water permits to halt further permits for data centers until the state's primary grid operator and the Texas Water Development Board (TWBD) complete an audit regarding power and water use. While Texas previously opened its arms widely to data center development, Abbott has thrown a temporary wrench in the works for new facilities as constituents, particularly those in his strong rural base, push back against the facilities as an upcoming election looms that could provide an outlet for their anger. An initial move came from Abbott in August when he ordered the state's primary grid operator, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), and the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) to halt power connection permits for new data centers until an audit could be performed on the facilities, ensuring they pay for their own electric infrastructure rather than existing ratepayers, reuse their water, make moves to preserve the quality of life and rely on minimal tax incentives. ERCOT serves about 75% of Texas' land area and 90% of its power load. Not long after the order for the audit, an ERCOT executive said the agency intended to make an initial filing of the audit process and results in December. However, this required ERCOT to send requests for information to hundreds of proposed data centers and have answers back by the anticipated December 10 filing. No word appears to have been made on how progress is going, but Abbott has already fired off a warning regarding a lack of responsiveness from the industry regarding its water use. Cracking Down on the Wild West In a June legislative hearing, state lawmakers learned that only 17% of the state's data centers had responded to the Texas Water Development Board's 2025 survey regarding annual water use. While this number appeared to have increased to around 28% by September, the board reported that some of the largest gaps in response came from new developments. The TWDB reported that 267 of the 329 surveyed facilities were new to the process, and only 22.5% of these had responded. The surveys are a key component in the board's formulation of its 2027 state water plan, and it now sits without this critical data as key deadlines approach. What was the penalty for the lack of response, which is listed as a Class C misdemeanor? Nothing being enforced, apparently. At least not until this week. Prior to the permitting freeze, on September 14, Abbott ordered the Water Development Board to begin enforcing penalties for past and future reporting failures, suggesting a bit of a laissez-faire attitude previously had been taken toward these legally required submissions. At the same time, Abbott also looped the water board into ERCOT's audit to gain access to information regarding future water use, but it has been unclear how this may affect the timeline of the audit's completion, so presumably the December goal still stands. The Latest Move The governor's most recent move against data centers came Monday, when he ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TECQ), which is responsible for air and water permits, to halt permitting for data centers until ERCOT and the TWDB have the info they need. Abbott's latest order will affect data centers that would have been unaffected by the ERCOT connection freeze, either because they are building their own behind-own-meter power or fall outside of ERCOT's coverage. The TWDB's jurisdiction covers the entirety of the state as does the Public Utility Commission's that oversees the entirety of the state's power. As ERCOT expects to complete its audit by December, the permitting pause will probably only be a matter of months, but will provide a better snapshot of resource use than a prior approval process that seemed to be barreling forward with a minimal view on the overall picture of resource use, setting Texas up to rival Virginia as one of the U.S.' (and the world's) biggest data center hotspots. For related information, see September 22, 2026, article - As Data Center Construction Plans Soar, U.S. Electric Utilities Race to Serve Once-in-a-Lifetime Load Growth. The Current Picture Industrial Info Resources data show more than $94 billion worth of data center projects presently under construction in Texas and an amazing $1.18 trillion worth in various stages of planning and engineering within the state. Not all of these future projects will move forward as planned, however, and with more stringent oversight taking affect in the state, the weaker projects will be weeded out. However, multiple projects are already permitted and ready to go, particularly expansions to existing facilities. Key Takeaways - Texas Governor Greg Abbott has taken further steps to pause data center permitting within the state. - ERCOT has said it aims to complete an audit regarding data center resources consumption by December. - Industrial Info Resources data show more than $94 billion worth of data center projects are presently under construction in Texas and more than $1 trillion in various stages of planning and permitting. artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich- Lately, the industry buzzword is "de-CATL-ization." Automakers are rushing to add second suppliers, invest in battery plants, and develop their own cells — creating the impression that CATL is being cast aside. Yet, viewed together, the power battery supply chain news from the first half of 2026 reveals an intriguing sense of parallelism: On one side, SAIC-GM-Wuling and BAIC Group have inked strategic partnerships with CATL, while Volkswagen Group awarded the company its annual prize. On the other, Li Auto poured 2.65 billion yuan into Sunwoda Power, and Xiaomi teamed up with CALB and Sunwoda Power to launch its Dragon Scale battery system. The truth is, no automaker has ever said, "We're done with CATL." The so-called "de-CATL-ization" is, in essence, a more sophisticated supply chain strategy — not a pivot, but a balancing act. Automakers' "Three-Pronged Strategy" Break down automakers' battery supply chain moves, and you'll find they are simultaneously advancing along three distinct tracks. For high-end core models, they continue to deepen ties with CATL. This is the visible collaboration — and the part most easily overlooked by the public narrative. Although Li Auto's L-series has incorporated Sunwoda and self-developed batteries, the core versions of its high-end models — and the orders with the strictest demands for performance and consistency — still rely on CATL as the primary supplier. For early versions of the Xiaomi SU7 and YU7, the NIO ET series, and the XPENG G9 — all positioned as premium models where quality sensitivity is highest — CATL remains the central partner. Image Source: Xiaomi EV Why? Because safety and consistency in power batteries are an automaker's lifeline. As Ni Jun, CATL's chief manufacturing officer, noted in a September interview: "Making one good battery isn't hard; making ten billion identical good batteries is." Behind that statement lies a manufacturing capability and quality control system built over more than a decade, backed by billions in R&D spending. For automakers, quality stability in premium models is the cornerstone of brand reputation. This creates an intriguing paradox: the more diversified an automaker's supply chain becomes, the more its high-end models tend to prioritize deep collaboration with CATL. It is not a contradiction, but the inevitable choice for a mature automaker managing its supply chain. For volume models, however, automakers are building multi-supplier systems. This draws the most public attention and is the source of the "de-CATL-ization" label. The refreshed Li Auto L8 brought in Sunwoda; Xiaomi's Pengcheng series adopted a dual-supplier model with CALB and Sunwoda; the AITO M6 EV version is equipped with Gotion batteries; XPENG brought CALB into its core supplier fold; and Leapmotor has built a landscape supported by a mix of Gotion, CALB, and SVOLT. Why push a multi-supplier strategy for volume models? Because high-volume models demand tighter control over costs, capacity guarantees, and delivery resilience. A multi-supplier system spreads the risk of relying on a single source while maintaining flexibility and bargaining power in a competitive market. Even more noteworthy is the depth of their involvement — no longer simple procurement and delivery, but engagement starting from the product definition stage. Li Auto poured 2.65 billion yuan into a capital increase for Sunwoda Power. In its own words, the move "centers on battery technology and manufacturing." Under Xiaomi's Dragon Scale battery system, Xiaomi handles product definition, leads pack design, participates in cell development, and manages full-process quality control. CALB custom-develops the electrochemical system and materials to Xiaomi's specifications, while Sunwoda Power provides cell manufacturing capacity — with both partners establishing dedicated production lines. Xiaomi has also deployed a "shadow factory" mechanism, installing over 8,000 quality checkpoints on production lines. Quality experts are stationed permanently at supplier facilities, exercising deep oversight over first- and second-tier suppliers. This is no longer a traditional "buyer-seller" relationship; it looks more like a deeply collaborative, joint development model. At the same time, automakers are making forward-looking moves by building reserves of self-developed battery technology. If a multi-supplier strategy is "horizontal expansion," then self-developed batteries are "vertical deepening." Li Auto has unveiled plans for a self-developed 5C battery: cells will be contract-manufactured by partners, while packs are made in-house, with a goal of eventually covering the entire lineup. Xiaomi's Dragon Scale system may not involve manufacturing its own cells, but the company is deeply involved in the underlying design of the electrochemical system, leading product definition, pack design, and quality control. NIO is advancing plans to mass-produce its own large-format cylindrical batteries. Traditional automakers like GAC, Dongfeng, and Geely are also pouring resources into in-house battery development. The core of automakers' self-research isn't manufacturing cells themselves, but seizing the right to define battery technology. The future model will likely look like this: automakers define technical standards and product requirements, while battery makers handle mass production. In this model, automakers shift from "battery buyers" to "technology definers," while battery makers transform from "technology providers" to "collaborative manufacturers." This is the deepest meaning of this supply chain reshuffle — it's not about whom you use, but who defines the standards. Why Now? Automakers' supply chain adjustments didn't happen overnight. Why is the shift intensifying specifically between 2025 and 2026? Because three underlying conditions have matured simultaneously. First, profits along the industrial chain need rebalancing. artigo.texto: City council adopts resolution regarding large-scale data centers in Lubbock, starting process for potential moratorium LUBBOCK, Texas (KCBD) - An effort to halt data centers in Lubbock, spurred by citizen petition, has culminated in compromise. As part of the ‘Save Lubbock’ group, Stephen Sanders says he’s been working with city council the last several months to see what can be done about large-scale data centers. While his 18-month moratorium ordinance proposal was not feasible under Texas law, he says a 90-day proposal by the council is a meaningful step “It gives our city time to establish guardrails, protect out resources, consider the long-term effects on our neighborhoods, and develop a clear plan, rather than rushing forward without adequate preparation,” Sanders said. The resolution to start the moratorium process was approved 5-2. While the ordinance is drafted, city planning staff is tasked with developing new guidelines on water use, power reliability, zoning, noise and lighting for any large scale center. A work session will also be scheduled within 90 days so experts can brief the council on potential data center impacts. District 6 councilman Tim Collins voted against this resolution. He says with the regular Texas legislative session set to end in May 2027, he believes now’s not the time to institute this. “We are going to receive a great deal of information,” Collins said. “A great deal of information about power requirements, a great deal about water needs, a great deal of information about what the state is going to require data centers to do. We only have one tool, and that’s this moratorium. If we exercise that tool today, come June, we’re out. We’re out of the game.” District 4 councilman Tim Green also voted not to adopt the resolution, saying he feels technology around data centers has changed and its potential for Lubbock’s economy could be significant. “If it threatens Lubbock’s water supply, we shouldn’t approve it, and we won’t approve it,” Green said. “If a company can demonstrate it can operate responsibly, then let’s look at it.” District 5 councilwoman Jennifer Wilson says she wants business to come to Lubbock, but not at any cost to our resources. “I want it to be the right project, in the right location, and in the right circumstances that it benefits us here in west Texas,” Wilson said. Mayor Mark McBrayer added that given what’s going on right now in the state, this will give the city plenty of time to assess the situation. “Given ERCOT’s situation, no one’s coming to Lubbock in the next year anyway with a data center,” McBrayer said. “We are staking a position that we want to wait for our legislators at the state level to give some direction, to give some further guidance in areas where only they can give guidance.” If the optional 90-day moratorium extension were to be approved by council, a potential large-scale data center would not be considered until June of 2027. artigo.texto: LANSING, Mich. — Michigan State University’s Institute for Public Policy and Social Research hosted a discussion Tuesday focusing on a growing topic across communities in Michigan: data centers. WATCH: Data center growth sparks environmental, community concerns among Michigan neighbors at state capital The event gave neighbors an opportunity to hear from experts and ask questions about how data centers could affect their communities. Laingsburg neighbor Ellen Link attended the Data Center Lunch and Learn looking for more information, particularly about the potential environmental impacts of data centers. “It was mostly still pro data center and economic growth, and economic growth is not going to save our planet.” During the question-and-answer portion of the event, several neighbors brought their concerns directly to MSU experts studying data centers. Meridian Township neighbor Lynn Bartley questioned the potential environmental impact. “We have to realize, what does that do to the environment?” Detroit neighbor Andria Vaughan Robinson also questioned who would ultimately benefit from data center development. “It doesn’t seem like any benefits are for the constituents.” But not everyone left the event with the same perspective. Juliann Trudell, the community engagement coordinator for Ypsilanti Township, said she was pleased by the information presented during the event. “I am very much encouraged after today’s presentation,” Trudell said. “There was a lot of research and a lot of knowledge around what is happening with construction and data centers.” While FOX 17 reporter Paige Meyer was talking with Trudell, she explained a data center has been proposed along the Huron River in Ypsilanti Township. She said the township is currently fighting the proposal. While she came to Tuesday’s event looking for more information on data centers as a whole, Trudell said she still has questions about what a data center could mean for her community. “I’m still very concerned,” Trudell said. “If there were going to be a data center coming, I think there are just a lot of unanswered questions, especially how it impacts the environment, how it impacts the surrounding community, and so we have a lot of unanswered questions still.” One of the experts on Tuesday’s panel said he expected people to have those questions. Jean Hardy, an MSU associate professor of Media & Information, said data centers can have environmental impacts, but he believes there are ways to reduce those impacts. “People should be concerned, but I think that there are solutions out there and this can be done in a way that is less impactful on the environment,” Hardy said. “There’s always trade-offs in these things so it’s about presenting all of the information that we have and ensuring that people aren’t focused only on the positive and only on the negative.” Erik Norman, director of MSU’s Institute of Public Utilities, said data centers are likely to remain part of the technology landscape as demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure grows. “They’re [data centers] serving the artificial intelligence tools that many people use and we need to develop that infrastructure in a way that’s thoughtful, that is consistent with Michigan’s clean energy laws for example, that meets the standards for quality of life in the communities, and do it in ways that everybody can benefit,” Norman said. After hearing from the experts, Tuesday’s discussion provided more information but also highlighted questions that many communities are still working to answer as data center development continues to grow. artigo.texto: CATL's Buyback Meets a Customer Rethink as Shares Sit at a 52-Week Floor Published on 09/24/2026 at 20:20 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL is putting its own cash to work in a bid to tighten the supply of stock available on its home exchanges. The battery giant picked up shares at prices as high as 294.53 yuan apiece and intends to cancel the entire tranche rather than park it in treasury. The move lands with the stock trading at 293.50 CNY, a level that leaves it clinging to a gain of just 0.2 percent over its 52-week low. That floor came into view during the current session, when the shares touched 293.00 CNY — the weakest reading of the past year. The retreat followed a soft Monday on the Shenzhen bourse, where the stock closed at 297.10 yuan, and Tuesday's dip of 2.5 percent. Automakers Rework Their Supply Maps Behind the selling pressure lies a shift in how China's carmakers buy batteries. Market watchers trace the recent weakness to efforts by vehicle manufacturers to widen their supplier bases or bring cell production in-house, moves aimed at protecting their own margins against the pricing power of the industry leader. Li Auto offered the clearest example. On September 7 the company said it would roll out self-developed batteries across its entire model lineup, with the next iteration of its Li Mega switching from CATL cells to its own designs. Li Auto also plans to sink 2.65 billion yuan into Sunwoda Electric Vehicle Battery for an 8.79 percent direct stake, a holding that climbs to 11.17 percent when affiliated entities are counted. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? Xiaomi has taken a similar path, broadening its supplier roster to four companies. Alongside CATL, it now sources components from FinDreams, CALB and Sunwoda. For its new Sky Nomad range, reports indicate Xiaomi will lean on CALB and Sunwoda cells, leaving CATL on the sidelines. CNII Pushes Back on Talk of a Deliberate Snub The suggestion that carmakers are deliberately turning away from CATL has stirred heated debate across China's industrial base. CNII, an outlet tied to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, moved to calm those fears on Tuesday. In its reading, the automakers' recent steps amount to ordinary supply-chain diversification and routine in-house production efforts. What matters most to the vehicle makers, the organ argued, is securing stable deliveries, keeping costs in check and carving out product differentiation in a crowded market. CATL is not standing still on partnerships. On September 6 it signed strategic cooperation agreements with partners including Taijin New Energy and Shenzhen Huake. Premium Demand and a Fresh SUV Launch The procurement rethink has not erased CATL's pull at the high end. For many customers the company remains the partner of choice on technically demanding premium vehicles, even as competition intensifies in the mass segment. The market launch of the AISTALAND GX7 SUV, unveiled yesterday by GAC and Huawei's Qiankun, underscores that staying power. The vehicle runs on a CATL battery and delivers 385 kilometers of range in pure electric mode. Its 800-volt architecture allows the pack to charge from 30 to 80 percent in ten minutes at fast-charging stations. CATL at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. Financially, the market leader still operates from a position of considerable earning power. CATL posted a net profit of 43.2 billion yuan in the first half of 2026. A single production line turns out roughly 10 gigawatt-hours of effective capacity, enough to equip as many as 200,000 vehicles. Management is leaning on reliability as its differentiator. Speaking at the World Power Battery Conference on September 3, CATL chief Robin Zeng stressed that top-tier manufacturing quality and trust must remain the decisive criteria for long-term supply relationships. DBS Hong Kong Puts CATL at the Top International observers also see CATL as well positioned. Analysts at DBS Hong Kong recently placed the battery maker first in their pick of favorite Chinese companies, ahead of heavyweights such as Alibaba and SMIC. In the bank's view, investor interest in China is rotating away from a distressed property sector and toward advanced manufacturing and forward-looking technology names. artigo.texto: Hitachi Energy’s battery energy storage system qualifies as NVIDIA DSX Ready BESS Features | 22.09.2026 | 3 min read Battery energy storage helps address the growing power demands of AI factories with resilient and flexible energy infrastructure Artificial intelligence is transforming industries at an unprecedented pace. Behind every AI model, data center, and digital service lies a growing challenge: access to reliable electricity. As AI factories increase in scale and complexity, battery energy storage is becoming essential for delivering the resilience, flexibility, and reliability that AI workloads demand. Hitachi Energy's battery energy storage system (BESS) has qualified as NVIDIA DSX Ready BESS as part of the inaugural DSX Ready launch, meeting the applicable reference design requirements for AI factory power infrastructure. The program helps customers identify qualified infrastructure building blocks and evaluate BESS solutions for resilient, reliable and scalable power systems. AI factories, the facilities that power the training and deployment of advanced AI models, are driving electricity demand while placing increasingly complex requirements on power systems. As these facilities grow in size and computing capacity, data center operators need energy infrastructure that can respond quickly to fluctuations in demand while maintaining continuous operations. Beyond storing energy, Hitachi Energy’s BESS serves as a flexible energy platform, supporting power continuity, power quality and operational flexibility while helping facilities respond to changing load conditions and applicable grid requirements. By rapidly absorbing or supplying power, the system supports demand response, energy cost optimization and the stabilization of dynamic AI workloads. These capabilities help data centers integrate renewable power, support grid code compliance and operate more effectively within available grid capacity. A core aspect of the NVIDIA DSX Ready program is ensuring compatibility with the NVIDIA DSX reference architecture, which helps standardize the design of power infrastructure for AI factories. The program enables customers to identify qualified technologies that can simplify deployment planning and support reliable operations across interconnected systems, including power, cooling, monitoring, and facilities management. As AI factories continue to scale, customers need power systems that can be deployed, integrated, and expanded quickly while maintaining reliability and resilience. As one of the first qualified BESS solutions in the NVIDIA DSX Ready program, this recognition reinforces Hitachi Energy's position at the forefront of AI factory electrification combining advanced technologies, power quality solutions and systems expertise to support end-to-end power infrastructure for the next generation of AI applications. Hitachi Energy's qualified solution combines energy storage, power conversion, automation, and digital technologies in an integrated architecture designed to support the dynamic energy requirements of AI-driven operations. The qualification encompasses Hitachi Energy's power converters and industry-leading power plant control capabilities that provide the responsive and reliable power conversion needed for next-generation AI data centers. By enabling precise power balancing, grid support, and energy optimization, the solution helps align BESS deployments with the performance, efficiency, and reliability objectives of the NVIDIA DSX Platform while seamlessly connecting energy storage systems with data center electrical infrastructure. The NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform brings together compute, networking, power, cooling, facilities and software to support AI factory design and operations. The DSX Ready program helps customers identify qualified power and cooling solutions that meet applicable NVIDIA DSX reference design requirements. The achievement reflects a broader trend across industries: as digitalization accelerates and AI adoption expands, energy infrastructure is becoming a critical enabler of innovation. Technologies such as Hitachi Energy’s BESS, alongside advances in grid infrastructure and digital solutions, will play an increasingly important role in ensuring that the growth of AI is supported by reliable, resilient, and sustainable power systems.

artigo.texto: EV battery prices are falling as LFP adoption, manufacturing overcapacity and intense competition reshape the global battery industry. The average lithium-ion battery pack price fell to $108 per kWh in 2025, while battery-electric vehicle packs averaged $99 per kWh and LFP packs dropped to $81 per kWh. China remains the lowest-cost manufacturing market at $84 per kWh, putting pressure on CATL, BYD, LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI and Panasonic to compete on cost, charging speed, battery life and manufacturing scale. Battery prices are one of the biggest factors determining whether electric vehicles can reach price parity with internal-combustion vehicles. In 2026, competition is increasingly shifting from simply adding battery capacity toward producing more usable energy, faster charging and longer life at a lower total cost. Global EV battery deployment reached 1.2 TWh in 2025, almost 30 percent higher than in 2024 and more than seven times the 2020 level, according to IEA analysis of global electric vehicle battery demand. How Much Does an EV Battery Cost in 2026? BloombergNEF’s latest benchmark puts the average lithium-ion battery pack at $108 per kWh, while battery-electric vehicle packs averaged $99 per kWh. At the $99 benchmark, the approximate battery value works out to: 50 kWh: $4,950 60 kWh: $5,940 75 kWh: $7,425 100 kWh: $9,900 These are manufacturing-market benchmarks rather than consumer replacement prices. Actual replacement costs can be substantially higher because they include diagnostics, labor, logistics, electronics, warranties and dealer or service margins. Average lithium-ion cell prices were around $79 per kWh, illustrating the additional cost involved in turning cells into complete battery packs with cooling, electronics and structural components. LFP Battery Packs Hit $81/kWh Versus $128 for NMC Chemistry has become one of the biggest drivers of battery economics. LFP accounted for more than 55 percent of EV batteries deployed globally in 2025, compared with nearly 50 percent in 2024. The average LFP battery pack cost approximately $81 per kWh, more than 40 percent below the $128 per kWh average for NMC packs. LFP eliminates nickel and cobalt from the cathode and offers long cycle life and strong thermal characteristics. That combination has made it increasingly attractive for mass-market EVs and energy storage. NMC and NCA remain important for premium and long-range EVs because their higher energy density can deliver more driving range without proportionally increasing battery weight. The battery-price race is therefore not simply about achieving the lowest dollars per kWh. Automakers increasingly evaluate cost per mile of range, charging performance, usable capacity, weight, degradation and lifetime. CATL Uses Scale and Fast Charging to Drive Battery Economics CATL’s strategy demonstrates how battery competition is expanding beyond cell prices. Its TECTRANS II commercial-vehicle battery platform can deliver up to 1,000 km of range, according to CATL, while offering energy density of 170 Wh/kg and charging from zero to 80 percent in 25 minutes using megawatt-level charging. CATL says its heavy-duty truck battery is engineered for a 12-year, 1.5-million-km service life with 70 percent capacity retention. The company also claims its modular architecture can shorten OEM development cycles by 50 percent and reduce R&D costs by 60-70 percent. That illustrates an important change in battery economics: a battery supplier can create value by reducing an automaker’s vehicle-development and integration expenses, not simply by supplying cheaper cells. BYD Blade Battery Strengthens LFP Cost Competition BYD has built its battery strategy around vertical integration and LFP chemistry. The company’s Blade Battery allows BYD to combine battery manufacturing, EV production and vehicle integration, potentially reducing system-level costs. In March 2026, BYD introduced Blade Battery 2.0 and FLASH Charging technology, with charging power of up to 1,500 kW. BYD says compatible vehicles can charge from 10 percent to 97 percent in nine minutes under specified conditions. The company also announced plans for 20,000 FLASH charging stations in China by the end of 2026, alongside an international rollout. Blade Battery 2.0 delivers a claimed 5 percent improvement in energy density and 2.5 percent reduction in overall capacity degradation. For consumers, improvements in degradation can be as significant as falling battery prices because longer battery life reduces total EV ownership costs. LG Energy Solution Expands North American LFP Production LG Energy Solution is responding to Chinese cost leadership through localization and manufacturing scale. Its Lansing, Michigan facility began production in 2026 and is designed for more than 35 GWh of annual capacity at full scale. LGES has invested more than $2 billion in Lansing since 2022, with around 1,700 jobs expected at full production. The company expects to have more than 50 GWh of LFP cell manufacturing capacity in North America by the end of 2026 across wholly owned plants and joint ventures. Localized manufacturing may not immediately match China’s battery prices, but it can provide automakers with shorter supply chains, regional sourcing and reduced dependence on imported batteries. Samsung SDI Bets on Solid-State Batteries and ESS Samsung SDI is pursuing a different strategy built around technology differentiation. Its R&D spending reached KRW1.4209 trillion in 2025, equivalent to 10.7 percent of revenue. The company reported approximately 1,200 U.S. patents associated with prismatic batteries and around 1,100 related to all-solid-state batteries. Samsung SDI is targeting mass production of its SolidStack all-solid-state battery technology, in the second half of 2027. It is also expanding into stationary storage. artigo.texto: Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s data center policy is noteworthy for two things it didn’t do: It didn’t call for doing away with the state’s sales tax exemption on data centers and it didn’t call for a moratorium on data center development. The governor has been adamant that the state needs to keep its word (the exemption runs through June 2035) and as manager of the state’s economy, she’s no doubt keenly aware that data centers are responsible for at least $9.1 billion in gross domestic product in Virginia. However, her executive order on data centers might come to be noteworthy for something that it does do. Section 4 sets in motion a study on where data centers should go. For a while, what we were hearing was that data centers ought to be confined to industrial/business parks, which seemed a sensible enough notion. However, lately we’re finding that even data centers headed for such places are proving controversial. See Botetourt County, where the Google complex going to the Greenfield Business Park has excited public opinion; or Franklin County, where there appears to have been a failed move to locate a data center in the Summit View Business Park, or now in Roanoke County, where a data center that’s going to the Wood Haven Technology Park is causing commotion. (Our customary disclosure: Google is one of our donors through its Google News Initiative for our New River Valley expansion; donors have no say in news decisions; see our policy. Or become a donor yourself and test that proposition.) If we can’t put data centers in industrial/business parks, where can we put them? (Those who push for a moratorium would likely say “nowhere” but, as we’ve seen, that’s off the table.) Spanberger’s study — due in 180 days, or mid-March 2027 — calls for the state’s energy department to identify possible locations “that diversify economic benefits across the Commonwealth and minimize energy, water, land-use, infrastructure, and community impacts.” Let’s parse that language in case it turns out to be meaningful. Since most data centers now are concentrated in Northern Virginia, that “diversify economic benefits” phrase clearly works out to be “somewhere other than Northern Virginia.” That potentially means data centers in whatever portions of rural Virginia qualify on the other criteria. Whether that’s a good thing or bad thing depends on how you feel about data centers. Since they have become politically toxic, the contrarian in me feels compelled to point out that data centers do generate quite a bit of tax revenue — and while they don’t generate a lot of jobs, a state study in 2024 put the workforce at the typical data center at about 50 people making six-figure salaries. That is why some localities want them, despite their energy demands and water demands. Spanberger’s executive order spells out certain places and things that should be studied. One of those is “regional diversification and development in areas with appropriate infrastructure capacity.” The first part of that phrase opens up virtually all of rural Virginia, while the reference to “appropriate infrastructure capacity” limits it. I don’t know how to draw a map showing that; maybe the state study will. However, another line in her executive order is very much mappable. The governor directs the state to “examine opportunities for brownfield redevelopment, adaptive reuse, and previously developed sites.” The two key phrases there — at least in my reading of this — are “brownfield redevelopment” and “previously developed sites.” Let’s take these in backwards order. If data centers weren’t so unpopular right now, every fiscally stressed city in the state ought to be clamoring for them as a solution to their revenue problems. Many cities these days have dead shopping malls or old factory sites that will never again see retail stores or manufacturing companies. Would data centers at some of those locations be better than paving over some farmland somewhere? The governor’s reference to “brownfield redevelopment” is more curious — and more measurable. The Virginia Department of Environmental Quality publishes an interactive map of officially defined brownfields in the state. There are multiple ways to search that map, so let’s tool around. Here are the brownfields in Virginia: Now let’s see what happens when we add in existing transmission lines. Unfortunately, those only show up when we zoom in close, which means we can only reproduce them here if we take screenshots of six different parts of Virginia. The plus side is we do get to see a closer look at some of these sites, so here goes. We’ll start in Southwest Virginia and work our way east and north. The yellow power lines are the biggest (735 kilovolts and up), the magenta is 345-500 kV, the blue 220-287 kV, the red 100-161 kV, the purple under 100 kV, the gray is listed as “not available.” OK, so that sets the general playing field. Now let’s take a closer look at some of the places that show up as brownfields. I’m not saying any of these other places should be a data center; I’m just pointing out that these are sites that could turn up on a list of recommended sites. Also note that many of these brownfields are listed as Environmental Protection Agency Repowering Sites, meaning they’ve been prescreened by the EPA as potential sites for renewable energy development. Energy generation is often as unpopular as data centers — and data centers do need energy (lots of it). Would that EPA-approved status elevate some of these brownfield sites? Former coal mines in Southwest Virginia This turns up a lot of locations, particularly in Buchanan, Dickenson and Wise counties. These locations may not match up well with other criteria — such as access to transmission lines and water — but they do survive this first search. artigo.texto: Rainha de bateria também é vitrine? O que Anitta e Virginia Fonseca mostram sobre marketing A chegada da cantora à Grande Rio, após a passagem da influenciadora pelo posto, levanta uma discussão sobre imagem pessoal, negócios e os limites da publicidade em espaços de forte identidade cultural Por O Globo — Rio de Janeiro Atualizado O posto é o mesmo, a escola também, mas a maneira de ocupar a posição de rainha de bateria da Grande Rio mudou de uma temporada para outra. A chegada de Anitta ao cargo, depois de Virginia Fonseca, colocou as duas trajetórias lado a lado nas redes sociais e abriu uma discussão que vai além de samba, figurino ou desempenho na quadra: como uma celebridade pode levar sua própria imagem e seus negócios para um espaço marcado por tradição, identidade cultural e forte vínculo com a comunidade. - De influenciadora a empresária: como famosas transformam seguidores em negócios - De criadores de conteúdo a empresários: por que o mercado de influência vive um novo momento Quando Virginia foi coroada para o carnaval de 2026, sua marca de cosméticos ganhou espaço físico na quadra da escola. Imagens da influenciadora faziam parte da decoração, enquanto um quiosque com produtos foi instalado no local como parte da divulgação. A escolha dialogava com a carreira construída por Virginia, que combina influência digital, exposição pessoal e empreendedorismo. Ao mesmo tempo, a presença comercial dentro de uma escola de samba pode ser percebida de maneiras diferentes justamente porque aquele ambiente não funciona apenas como palco para grandes eventos. Existe ali uma relação construída ao longo do ano entre integrantes, comunidade, tradição e identidade. Na coroação de Anitta, realizada no último domingo (20), a cantora seguiu outro caminho. A apresentação incorporou elementos cenográficos de sua turnê EQUILIBIVM, teve performance musical e contou com a participação do público. Antes da festa, ela também havia visitado a quadra e convocado integrantes da comunidade para o evento. A aproximação com a escola não ficou restrita à cerimônia. Anitta fez aulas de samba antes de assumir o posto e participou como compositora de um dos sambas que disputaram a final para o carnaval de 2027. São iniciativas que ajudam a construir uma presença associada não apenas à fama, mas também ao universo do carnaval. Para o especialista em marketing Pedro Marcílio, essa diferença ajuda a entender um princípio da comunicação atual: chamar atenção é apenas uma etapa na construção de uma conexão com o público. "A propaganda pode despertar curiosidade, criar desejo, gerar experimentação e levar as pessoas até uma marca. Mas, em algum momento, a promessa encontra a experiência. É nesse encontro que a marca começa a ser julgada de verdade", explica. Quando a divulgação de um produto parece natural? A questão não está simplesmente em uma celebridade divulgar ou não os próprios negócios. Anitta também transformou a coroação em uma vitrine para sua carreira musical. O que muda é a relação entre aquilo que está sendo apresentado e o ambiente escolhido para essa exposição. Música, dança, figurino e elementos de uma turnê fazem parte do universo artístico que o público já associa à cantora. Na comunicação sobre sua chegada à Grande Rio, Anitta também adotou um discurso de respeito ao carnaval e afirmou que sua presença não deveria se sobrepor à escola. Essa coerência entre mensagem, contexto e identidade é um dos pontos que, na avaliação de Pedro, devem ser considerados por uma ação de marketing. "Criatividade não deveria servir para maquiar fraquezas. Deveria servir para iluminar diferenças verdadeiras. Antes de perguntar 'como vamos comunicar?', existe uma pergunta muito mais importante: temos algo relevante para comunicar naquele contexto?", afirma. O público percebe quando a publicidade força a barra? A comparação entre duas celebridades com enorme alcance nas redes também mostra como ficaram mais tênues as fronteiras entre conteúdo espontâneo, publicidade e autopromoção. Uma ação pode ser registrada por diferentes ângulos, compartilhada e comentada em poucos minutos, enquanto a audiência também avalia se aquela presença parece coerente com o momento. Para Pedro, essa exposição tem um efeito que pode funcionar nos dois sentidos. "A propaganda amplifica. Esse é seu enorme poder e também seu enorme risco. Quando existe uma boa história por trás, ela amplifica essa história. Quando existe uma desconexão entre o discurso e aquilo que o público experimenta, ela também amplifica essa percepção", analisa. Anitta e Virginia representam modelos diferentes? As trajetórias das duas também ajudam a entender a diferença de posicionamento. Virginia construiu uma carreira em que a própria imagem está diretamente ligada ao universo do empreendedorismo e das vendas. Anitta, embora também tenha negócios e explore comercialmente sua imagem, chegou à quadra tendo a música e a performance como elementos centrais de sua identidade profissional. Isso não significa que uma forma de atuação seja necessariamente melhor do que a outra. O episódio mostra, sobretudo, como o contexto interfere na maneira como uma ação é recebida. Em uma escola de samba, a exposição acontece dentro de um ambiente que reúne símbolos, memória, tradição e vínculos construídos ao longo do tempo. A forma como uma celebridade se insere nesse espaço pode influenciar a percepção sobre sua presença, principalmente quando existe uma tentativa de estabelecer conexão com a comunidade e com a cultura da escola. "A propaganda continua sendo fundamental. Mas propaganda não faz milagre. Ela não transforma promessa em realidade. Pode conquistar a atenção inicial, mas aquilo que sustenta uma marca é a experiência que vem depois", conclui Pedro.

artigo.texto: Business · updated 2h ago · 2 min read CATL Starts Trial Production at Debrecen Battery Cell Plant in Hungary CATL began trial production at Debrecen plant on September 22, 2026 with two lines. Plant targets 100 GWh annual capacity and will be CATL's largest European base outside China. Whether nickel-exposure suspension incidents are reported. 9 of 10 outlets skipped it: temporary suspension ordered due to nickel exposure safety concerns. 10outlets compared Same story, two versions tap a side to read it in full SSource: CarNewsChina “Earlier this year, the Hajdú-Bihar County Government Office had ordered a temporary suspension of operations” SSource: PR Newswire “CATL Debrecen continues cooperating and working closely with the government and the authorities” CarNewsChina adds nickel-exposure and suspension claims, while most outlets omit those safety-incident details. Trial production begins CATL began trial production of battery cells at its newly built Debrecen plant in Hungary on September 22, 2026, after the company said it had fulfilled all preconditions required to commence the trial run. CATL said the initial trial production covers the first two cell manufacturing lines, and the trial phase is intended to set up, optimise and validate the production equipment and manufacturing processes before series production begins. CATL said the Debrecen site received its occupancy permit in August 2026, and the company later completed the requirements under its Integrated Pollution Prevention and Control (IPPC) permit before trial operations started. CATL said the Debrecen facility is expected to become its largest manufacturing site outside China once fully built out, with an annual capacity of 100 GWh. CATL said it has already been producing battery modules at the Debrecen site since autumn 2024, and it reported that 537,000 modules have been manufactured there to date. Permits, inspections, and priorities CATL said the Hajdú-Bihar County Government Office carried out repeated inspections before the occupancy permit was issued, following previously identified deficiencies that had raised concerns among local residents. CATL said government representatives confirmed that the issues had since been resolved, and CATL described the trial phase as a step toward full-scale battery cell manufacturing in Hungary. CATL said it would continue working closely with the Hungarian government and local authorities throughout the trial period, with particular attention to environmental protection, employee health and workplace safety. CATL said it would monitor environmental, occupational health and safety indicators during trial operations and proactively submit the results to regulators. CATL said it remains committed to transparency and welcomes inspections by government and regulatory authorities at the Debrecen site. What the expansion targets CATL said the Debrecen plant is intended primarily to supply European automakers, and the company described the facility as a strategic hub within Hungary’s automotive and electric mobility manufacturing network. CATL said the transition to cell production adds another manufacturing stage after module production began in autumn 2024, and the company said the Debrecen site is expected to become its largest manufacturing base outside China with a capacity of 100 GWh. CATL said it announced the Debrecen project in August 2022 as its second European battery plant after its facility in Germany, and it said construction of the first cell manufacturing building began in summer 2023. CarNewsChina said Hajdú-Bihar County Government Office ordered a temporary suspension of operations in certain areas of the plant earlier this year due to occupational safety concerns regarding nickel exposure, and it said the incidents affected nine employees. CarNewsChina said Hungarian authorities confirmed that CATL had resolved all previously identified deficiencies, allowing the project to proceed to trial production.

artigo.texto: Liberia has unveiled an ambitious vision to transform more than $30 billion in estimated natural capital—including forests, mangroves, biodiversity and renewable-energy potential—into a foundation for sustainable economic growth, climate resilience and peace. The initiative was placed at the center of Liberia’s engagement at the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly, where the government convened a high-level discussion on the links between climate change, natural resources, conflict and sustainable development. Organized by Liberia’s Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), with support from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the event brought together senior Liberian officials and international climate and development experts to examine how natural resources can become engines of inclusive development rather than sources of conflict. For Liberia, the centerpiece was the emerging natural-capital strategy being advanced under President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, with Presidential Envoy on Climate Action and Chief Executive Officer of the Liberian Carbon Market Authority, Hon. Janine Cooper, outlining efforts to measure, value and monetize environmental assets while ensuring communities benefit. Cooper said Liberia’s natural abundance provides an economic opportunity extending far beyond traditional extraction of timber and minerals. With more than 5,000 millimeters of annual rainfall, 15 rivers, extensive forests and biodiversity, significant sunshine and a 579-kilometer coastline, Liberia possesses natural assets that can support climate financing, sustainable agriculture, conservation, renewable energy and other emerging economic sectors. Under the Boakai administration, Cooper said, Liberia is working to bring these resources under an integrated natural-capital framework estimated at more than $30 billion. The initiative represents a shift in how Liberia presents its environmental assets—not simply as resources to be protected, but as measurable national wealth capable of generating investment, livelihoods and long-term development. Weeks before the UNGA gathering, the Liberian Carbon Market Authority presented Liberia’s first National Carbon Policy to President Boakai after approximately a year of work establishing digital infrastructure and valuation systems to determine the carbon value associated with specific land parcels. Cooper said Liberia wants to position itself as a supplier of high-integrity, nature-based climate solutions, allowing the country to attract financing while maintaining the environmental integrity of its forests and ecosystems. But she emphasized that natural capital must translate into tangible benefits for communities. Her presentation linked the strategy directly to peacebuilding, arguing that environmental investments can prevent local conflicts even before carbon credits or other climate-financing instruments generate revenue. Mangrove restoration, she explained, can reduce flooding and prevent families from being displaced to areas where competition for land could generate new disputes. Climate-smart agriculture can similarly improve productivity and reduce pressure on farmers to expand into neighboring community forests. “Peace, in Liberia, is often local before it is national,” Cooper said. Opening the event, EPA Executive Director Dr. Emmanuel K. Urey Yarkpawolo said Liberia’s experience of peacebuilding provides an important foundation for addressing environmental pressures that could deepen social and economic tensions. He warned that climate pressures can exacerbate existing vulnerabilities where institutions are weak and communities are excluded from decisions over natural resources. Liberia’s forests, minerals, rivers, fisheries and coastal ecosystems, he said, can drive national development if managed through strong governance systems and in ways that provide meaningful benefits to communities. UNDP Associate Administrator Haoliang Xu argued that climate change, peace, development and natural-resource governance are increasingly inseparable. Xu cited the World Meteorological Organization’s confirmation that 2024 was the warmest year on record and said climate impacts are compounding pressures involving displacement, land access and unresolved grievances globally. He highlighted Liberia’s climate commitments, noting that the country contributes approximately 0.03 percent of global emissions but has committed under its NDC 3.0 to cutting economy-wide emissions by 64 percent by 2040, with adaptation targets covering seven sectors. Xu also noted that peace and security considerations now feature in 41 percent of third-generation national climate plans globally, rising to 70 percent in fragile states. “Climate change need not be a narrative of conflict and instability,” Xu said. “With the right choices, climate action can strengthen livelihoods, improve natural resource governance, and sustain peace.” Kenya’s Special Envoy on Climate Change, Ambassador Ali D. Mohamed, described how environmental pressures can contribute to competition over land and water. With approximately 80 percent of Kenya classified as arid land, Mohamed said conflict between farmers and herders can intensify around rainfall, grazing areas and water availability. He cited the Dadaab refugee complex, which has existed for more than three decades, as an example of how prolonged humanitarian crises can place sustained pressure on local resources and host communities. Naquetta Ricks, President of the African Chamber of Commerce and an advocate for Liberia through the Liberian Surfing Association, urged Liberia to broaden its forest economy. artigo.texto: Mercedes-Benz has secured priority access to Taiwanese battery maker ProLogium’s latest fourth-generation all-solid-state battery cells and will begin verifying next-generation electric-vehicle (EV) battery technology. The two companies will assess whether the fourth-generation battery can be applied to vehicles, based on cooperation that has continued for about 10 years. On Sept. 24 (local time), EV-focused outlet Electrek and ProLogium said Mercedes-Benz and ProLogium signed a joint test agreement. Under the agreement, Mercedes-Benz secured the right to test ProLogium’s fourth-generation “superfluidized inorganic lithium ceramic battery” cells with priority access. Mercedes-Benz plans comprehensive tests of the battery cells’ electrical performance, thermal characteristics and safety at dedicated facilities and external specialist testing institutions. The test results will be used to assess whether the technology can be applied to future vehicles. ProLogium explained that the fourth-generation battery platform was designed with mass production and cost competitiveness in mind, which it said are challenges in commercialising all-solid-state batteries. It said the platform applies a non-flammable inorganic electrolyte, a ceramic separator and its own active safety mechanism to improve safety, while supporting fast charging, high output and performance in low-temperature environments. Mercedes-Benz and ProLogium have worked together since 2016. The companies have verified multiple lithium ceramic battery technologies, including pouch cells, next-generation prismatic cells and bipolar technology. ProLogium said it expanded cooperation from the early battery development stage to reviewing whether the latest fourth-generation technology can be applied to vehicles. ProLogium is also pushing to expand battery production facilities. It opened its first GWh-scale gigafactory in Taiwan in May 2024, and in February 2026 held a groundbreaking ceremony for phase one construction of a second battery gigafactory in Dunkirk, France. The Dunkirk plant is designed to secure annual production capacity of 4 GWh in phase one, with that capacity to be achieved in stages by 2030. Total designed production capacity is up to 44 GWh. ProLogium said its fourth-generation all-solid-state battery cells provide up to 400 Wh/kg energy density and can charge from 5 percent to 80 percent in 6.4 minutes. A report by third-party testing institution TUV showed ProLogium’s 185.4 Ah large-format 3.5-generation cell recorded an energy density of 381 Wh/kg by mass. ProLogium said it has been mass-producing that 3.5-generation battery at its Taiwan production facility since September 2026. ProLogium said in May it signed a business combination agreement with special purpose acquisition company Translational Development Acquisition and would pursue a Nasdaq listing. If the transaction is completed and the company meets relevant approvals and listing requirements, it plans to list on Nasdaq in the fourth quarter of 2026 under the ticker symbol “PRLG.” Mercedes-Benz is also working with U.S. all-solid-state battery company Factorial Energy in addition to ProLogium. Mercedes-Benz announced last year that a modified EQS fitted with 106 of Factorial’s all-solid-state battery cells drove more than 1,200 km on a single charge. Mercedes-Benz has set a goal of launching its first mass-produced EV equipped with all-solid-state batteries by 2030. The agreement with ProLogium can be seen as part of Mercedes-Benz’s process of expanding the scope of verification needed to apply all-solid-state battery technology to actual vehicles. The agreement itself does not confirm the launch of a mass-produced car equipped with ProLogium’s fourth-generation battery, and Mercedes-Benz plans to assess potential vehicle application based on test results.

artigo.texto: FOLLY BEACH — A home on this island where the renowned folk opera “Porgy and Bess” was penned will receive a historical placard today. Nicknamed the Porgy House, the two-story home on West Ashley Avenue is where author DuBose Heyward and his wife, Dorothy, spent their summers. In 1934, the home is where George Gershwin and Heyward collaborated to create “Porgy and Bess,” inspired by Heyward’s novel “Porgy.” Gershwin also drew inspiration from the Lowcountry’s Gullah culture during his time on Folly Beach. To recognize the home’s place in the Lowcountry’s literary and cultural history, the Folly Beach Exchange Club, the city’s Tourism and Visitor Promotion Committee and the island’s Historical Society will install a historical marker in front of the home at 712 W. Ashley Ave. on at 10:30 a.m. Community leaders will give a short address as the marker is unveiled. Members of Samuel Smalls’ family, the man on whom the titular character of Porgy was based, are expected to be in attendence. Heyward’s Porgy was inspired by Smalls, an oarsman on Charleston’s docks. Smalls was a disabled beggar who toted around a goat and a cart, earning him the nickname Samuel “Goat” Smalls. Heyward had seen Smalls in passing around the city. A blurb about Smalls appeared in The News and Courier in 1924 that caught the novelist’s eye. Smalls, described in the blotter as a man “familiar to King street pedestrians with his goat and cart” was being held on an aggravated assault charge, alleged to have attempted to shoot a woman on Romney Street after suspecting her of taking his watch. Heyward kept the blurb and a year later had published “Porgy,” a novel set in Charleston that follows the lives of African Americans in Catfish Row, a fictitious Charleston tenement. Porgy, a disabled beggar, is the main character. Smalls died in 1924. He is buried at the James Island Presbyterian Church Cemetery. The two-story, three-bedroom home where DuBose and Dorothy Heyward summered on Folly Beach still features its original wood interiors and a writer’s booth used by the Heywards and Gershwin as a workspace. The home has been on and off the market over the last several years. The last time it was listed for sale was in 2024, for around $3.4 million. That figure was reduced to $2.6 million in 2025 just before it was taken off the market. Former owners Myles Glick, a local architect, and his wife Kathy worked to preserve the home and restore the interior. The Folly Beach Historical Society currently has a companion exhibit about the Porgy House on display at the Folly Beach Museum. The installation, titled “The Porgy House: A Cottage on an Island in a Culture,” features photographs, artifacts and personal correspondence between Heyward and Gershwin.

artigo.texto: Mercado digere pesquisa eleitoral AtlasIntel e bateria de PMIs hoje; Ibovespa em dólar cai nesta quarta-feira (23) O mercado local acompanha a divulgação da pesquisa AtlasIntel nesta quarta-feira (23), que deve conformar a disputa cada vez mais acirrada entre o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL). Com a agenda nacional de indicadores relativamente mais esvaziada, as atenções se voltam para o panorama eleitoral. Candidatos ao Senado por São Paulo participam de debate no Estadão nesta quarta-feira, às 19h. Já às 20h, os candidatos à presidência Augusto Cury (Avante), Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) e Romeu Zema (Novo) realizam debate na Veja. No panorama internacional, uma bateria de indicadores de atividade econômica será divulgada nesta manhã, com os PMIs de França, Alemanha, Zona do Euro e Reino Unido como destaque. Por fim, a OCDE divulga o relatório interino de perspectivas econômicas globais. Mercado brasileiro Ibovespa: O Ibovespa (IBOV) conseguiu se recuperar na reta final do pregão e fechou no terreno positivo, impulsionado pelo otimismo no exterior com as falas do presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, sobre um avanço nas conversas com o Irã. Nesta terça-feira (22), o principal índice da bolsa brasileira terminou as negociações com alta de 0,44%, aos 187.422,92 pontos. Já o dólar à vista encerrou as negociações a R$ 5,1029, em queda de 0,11%. O iShares MSCI Brazil (EWZ) — principal ETF brasileiro negociado em Nova York — cai 0,24%, cotado a US$ 38,17. Mercados internacionais As bolsas asiáticas fecharam em queda hoje. artigo.texto: Oracle invoca "força maior" em projeto de data center nos EUA, diz fonte A Oracle invocou "força maior" devido a possíveis atrasos no fornecimento de energia para o Projeto Júpiter, um grande data center de inteligência artificial no Novo México avaliado com a Blue Owl. A medida visa adiar pagamentos contratuais mais altos caso a operação atrase além de 2028. O complexo, voltado a atender a OpenAI na iniciativa Stargate, enfrenta gargalos em gasodutos e disputas ambientais, refletindo os crescentes desafios de infraestrutura e energia do setor de IA nos EUA. A Oracle emitiu uma notificação de "força maior" a uma unidade da Blue Owl, desenvolvedora de um grande data center no estado norte-americano do Novo México, citando possíveis atrasos no fornecimento de energia para o projeto, informou uma fonte a par do assunto à Reuters nesta quinta-feira. As ações da Oracle caíam 3,3%. A fonte afirmou que garantir o fornecimento de energia para o local é de responsabilidade da Oracle, conforme previsto no contrato. A Oracle não pode rescindir o contrato de locação sob nenhuma circunstância, disse a fonte, acrescentando que a gestora de ativos alternativos Blue Owl possui cerca de US$3 bilhões em capital próprio no projeto, sendo a Oracle responsável pelo pagamento dos custos da dívida. As empresas costumam invocar força maior para se isentar de obrigações contratuais quando surgem problemas fora de seu controle, uma medida que pode gerar preocupações entre credores e investidores. Em vez de sair como locatária principal, a Oracle está tentando adiar os pagamentos caso o data center, chamado de Projeto Júpiter, sofra atrasos e não entre em operação em 2028, conforme planejado, de acordo com uma reportagem da Bloomberg. A Oracle não respondeu imediatamente a um pedido de comentário da Reuters. "O Projeto Júpiter continua dentro do cronograma planejado", afirmou a empresa no início do dia. A Blue Owl, proprietária da Stack Infrastructure, desenvolvedora da central de processamento de dados, afirmou que a notificação não altera os compromissos financeiros com esse projeto plurianual. Durante a fase de desenvolvimento, a Blue Owl obtém um rendimento de 9% sobre seu capital próprio, disse a fonte, acrescentando que, após a conclusão do projeto, o rendimento alavancado deverá ficar em torno de 11%. Ao invocar força maior, a Oracle prorroga o período durante o qual paga à Blue Owl o aluguel mais baixo da fase de desenvolvimento. A Blue Owl ainda receberá o aluguel mais alto pelo prazo originalmente planejado, mas o início desse pagamento será adiado, segundo a fonte. O campus do Projeto Júpiter, com cerca de 570 hectares e que garantiu US$18 bilhões em empréstimos de um consórcio de bancos, segundo reportagens da mídia, faz parte de um acordo mais amplo da Oracle com a OpenAI para fornecer capacidade de computação em IA. O campus do data center enfrenta vários contratempos de infraestrutura, incluindo atrasos na construção de um gasoduto e contestação judicial em relação a licenças relacionadas à água e à qualidade do ar. O projeto faz parte do Stargate, uma iniciativa para construir infraestrutura de IA nos EUA sob um compromisso de investimento de US$500 bilhões envolvendo OpenAI, SoftBank Group e parceiros, incluindo a Oracle. A construção dessa infraestrutura de IA em grande escala tem enfrentado desafios crescentes, à medida que os desenvolvedores correm para garantir energia e outros recursos, ao mesmo tempo em que gerenciam os enormes custos da implantação de capacidade computacional para parceiros como a OpenAI. A crescente oposição do público norte-americano transformou os data centers em um ponto nevrálgico político, com comunidades próximas aos projetos de centrais de processamento de dados manifestando preocupações quanto ao impacto sobre o abastecimento local de energia, água e outros recursos naturais. A corretora William Blair afirmou que, embora essa notícia intensifique as preocupações com atrasos regulatórios e relacionados ao fornecimento de energia que afetam as implantações de IA, ela espera um impacto mínimo no curto prazo para a Oracle. "Na prática, o ano fiscal de 2027 não deve ser afetado, já que o Jupiter não gera receita neste ano."

artigo.texto: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE: September 23, 2026 CONTACT: [email protected] Dr. Amy Acton Calls for Statehouse To Pass Immediate Conditional Data Center Moratorium Legislation As They Reconvene COLUMBUS, OH– Today, one week after Dr. Amy Acton called on Vivek Ramaswamy to sell his individual stocks and divest from data centers, Dr. Acton released the following statement calling for the Statehouse to pass immediate, bipartisan legislation to enact her conditional moratorium on data centers when they reconvene next week: “Ohioans have been clear; we need to lower costs, which is why I am calling on our Statehouse to pass a conditional moratorium on data centers when they return to session next week,” said Dr. Amy Acton. “My opponent is seconding my call to deliver Ohioans emergency relief at the gas pump, but we can’t stop there. While billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy has millions of dollars personally invested in data centers, I am calling on lawmakers from across the aisle to come together and fight against the unchecked development of data centers driving up costs in our communities. I will always put the needs of working families over the wants of billionaires, corporations and special interests.” Dr. Acton was the first candidate in Ohio’s race for governor to call for a conditional moratorium on data centers to ensure: - Data centers cannot pass any additional costs on to ratepayers. All costs for gas, water and electricity need to be covered by data centers and their investors, not Ohio taxpayers or our communities. Data centers must invest in their own energy generation options and prove the project will not increase our electricity prices or negatively impact regional reliability. - Data centers cannot use NDAs. No more secret deals. Ohioans must know who is coming into our communities, and at what cost and risk; transparency and accountability are not negotiable. - Data centers cannot be built without union labor. Any data center development must be built with union labor. The jobs to build, maintain, operate and upgrade data centers must be good-paying, union jobs operated by Ohioans who are trained in Ohio. - Data centers cannot violate environmental standards. Data centers must maintain zero environmental impact and use responsible and modern water-management systems that protect local waterways, groundwater, and air and meet rigorous environmental and quality of life standards. - Prioritizing brownfields. Data center development must prioritize brownfields and previously developed industrial sites, not farms or the hearts of our communities. Vivek Ramaswamy, who invested millions of dollars in data centers, is THE pro data center candidate in this race. - Ramaswamy refuses to sell his data center stocks. - Ramaswamy has repeatedly said he wants more data centers in Ohio and called them “good,” even praising data centers 10 times in one month. - While running for governor, Ramaswamy even flew to Utah for a “data center energy conference.” - Ramaswamy’s running mate voted for legislation that made Ohio more attractive to data centers and said, “it’s to Ohio’s benefit to have data centers.” ###

artigo.texto: The Structural Transition from Policy to Economics In the initial phases of the clean energy transition, institutional capital was largely tethered to state support mechanismsâsuch as feed-in tariffs in Europe, federal production tax credits in the United States, and national utility off-take guarantees. These vehicles provided bond-like predictability to balance the high capital expenditure of nascent hardware. Over the past decade, technological maturation and manufacturing scale have reshaped project unit economics. According to Lazardâs Levelized Cost of Energy Analysis (LCOE+) and tracking by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), the unsubsidized levelized cost of energy for utility-scale solar PV and onshore wind has declined to levels competitive with or below marginal fossil generation across key wholesale power markets. Concurrently, rising demand for firm, decarbonized baseload powerâdriven by broader industrial electrification and the energy requirements of modern data center infrastructureâhas expanded the market for multi-decade corporate Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs). Nevertheless, project economics are not uniformly self-sustaining across all geographies. Net margins and internal rates of return (IRRs) remain sensitive to capital expenditure fluctuations, regional interest rates, local permitting frameworks, and the availability of creditworthy off-takers. Where these economic conditions align, renewables increasingly exhibit the profile of core infrastructure assets: long operational lives, inflation-hedging capabilities, and established contractual counterparties. The Cannibalization Dilemma in Power Markets As wind and solar achieve double-digit market share across regional grids, wholesale power markets face a structural financial phenomenon known as price cannibalization. Because unhedged renewable generators within a single geographic and climatic zone produce electricity simultaneously during peak irradiance or wind events, wholesale spot prices can decline sharply when generation peaks: - European Power Markets: Market monitoring reports from the European Union Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators (ACER) document a notable increase in the frequency of zero and negative hourly day-ahead settlement prices during periods of elevated renewable output, particularly in markets like Germany and Spain. - ERCOT (Texas): Settlement records from the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) highlight recurrent pricing depressions and negative real-time settlement intervals, particularly across West Texas nodes characterized by concentrated renewable capacity alongside localized transmission bottlenecks. For developers holding merchant exposure, this dynamic erodes realized asset yields and can depress return on equity (ROE) if not addressed through contractual hedging or storage solutions. "Institutional investors have moved well past the initial trial phase with grid storage," says Stefano Endrizzi, a financial professional active in the Investment Banking and M&A Department of American MergersCorp. "What attracts private infrastructure funds to Renewable Energy infrastructure and BESS is the potential asymmetry of the cash flows. By locking in floor contracts and capacity remuneration for debt service, funds can freely hunt peak merchant spreads on the upsideâcreating an infrastructure asset that helps manage downside risk while still capturing energy market volatility." BESS as an Asset Class: The Mechanics of Revenue Stacking Utility-scale battery installations operate as dynamic grid instruments rather than simple physical backup units. In modern power finance, their returns hinge on revenue stackingâthe attempt to monetize asset availability and flexibility across several potential channels: - Wholesale Energy Arbitrage: Storing low-cost (or negatively priced) surplus power during peak generation troughs and dispatching it into wholesale markets during high-demand evening intervals. Realized margins depend on wholesale price volatility and round-trip efficiency losses. - Ancillary & Balancing Services: Contracting with Transmission System Operators (TSOs) to provide millisecond-response frequency regulation (such as FCR or aFRR in Continental Europe, or Dynamic Containment in the UK) to maintain grid stability. - Capacity Remuneration: Securing periodic availability payments through capacity markets in exchange for committed standby availability during extreme system stress events. These revenue streams represent dynamic commercial opportunities rather than fixed, guaranteed income. Ancillary market values fluctuate based on grid supply, and regulatory rule changes can alter revenue eligibility over an asset's lifecycle. Contractual De-risking: Floors, Tolls, and Corporate Off-takers The primary hurdle for pension managers and debt syndicates deploying capital into storage has been merchant power volatility. To manage these risks and establish compliant Debt Service Coverage Ratios (DSCR), the market utilizes specific risk-transfer structures: - Tolling Agreements: A third-party utility, energy trader, or aggregator pays a fixed periodic fee for the operational right to charge and discharge the battery. While this structure insulates the asset owner from wholesale price risk, it caps merchant upside and introduces counterparty credit risk. - Cap-and-Floor Frameworks: Operating structures that guarantee a baseline revenue floor to support debt obligations, while allowing equity investors to share in windfall trading spikes above a specified revenue ceiling. - Hybrid Co-location PPAs: Bundling battery facilities directly behind the same meter as solar or wind farms allows project sponsors to deliver firm, dispatchable power blocks rather than intermittent generation, thereby mitigating imbalance penalties and capturing premium PPA terms. artigo.texto: ORANGE CITY—Sioux County officials have made the next step on a data center ordinance, as the board of supervisors is set to vote on a drafted ordinance at their meeting on Sept. 29. Data centers have remained a point of discussion since the supervisors learned about a proposed project in June. The Sioux County Board of Supervisors passed a one-year moratorium on the construction of data centers and industrial battery storage facilities at its June 16 meeting. County zoning director Shane Walter said the moratorium would give the county time to draft an ordinance related to data centers. A draft of the ordinance was brought before the planning and zoning board on Sept. 10. Speaking at a board of supervisors meeting Tuesday morning, Walter said the zoning board voted to recommend the draft be brought to the supervisors. “We revised the language for the amendment to the ordinance regarding the data centers,” he said. “The commission considered it thoughtful and they’re recommending approval to this board.” After being recommended by the planning and zoning board, supervisors will have the chance to vote on the drafted ordinance at three separate meetings. “I want to be able to get on the agenda for your next meeting Sept. 29,“ Walter said. “I would recommend you do the full three readings on that. You certainly could waive the subsequent readings, but I wouldn’t recommend that on this one.” County attorney Tom Kunstle agreed that it would be better to hold all three hearings on the ordinance. “You want to get the people and the public as much opportunity to appear and make the comments,” Kunstle said. If approved by the supervisors, the new ordinance would take effect and the county moratorium on data centers would be lifted. “The whole point was to make sure we had something in our ordinance that we could utilize to govern that application process,” Walter said. “The moratorium is in place until you formally adopt the amendment.” The zoning director said he felt confident in the amendment’s language. “They’re good, they address everything that needs to be addressed, incredibly thoughtful,” he said. “Maybe even overregulation, but we’re holding them to an incredibly high standard. The onus is on them.” Supervisor Craig Hoftyzer asked what opportunity the public will have to review the ordinance. “It’ll be in our office and we’ll supply a copy for Joe so it’ll be there in the auditor’s office,” Walter said. The supervisors collectively requested that Walters and the auditor’s office post the full ordinance to the county website beforehand as well. “I’ve always been advocating for transparency and I just want people to be able to access it,” Hoftyzer said. “I realize we can’t print all 10 pages in the paper.” Kunstle recommended that the printed announcements include a link to the county’s website on where to find the proposed ordinance. Supervisors such as Hoftyzer agreed with the recommendation. “I would do that too because I want people to know where to go to find it,” Hoftyzer said. County auditor Joe Van Tol said he would post the drafted ordinance online to the county’s website. “Ample opportunities for the public to weigh in on this,” Walter said. “They’ll be able to weigh in here at your three readings, they’ll be able to weigh in once an application is submitted.”
