artigo.texto: A Comissão Europeia propôs um sistema comum de classificação para data centers com mais de 500 kW de capacidade, que deverá reunir informações sobre o uso de recursos e a contribuição de cada unidade para o sistema energético. A iniciativa ocorre em meio à previsão de forte crescimento da infraestrutura digital na região. A União Europeia pretende triplicar a capacidade de seus data centers nos próximos cinco a sete anos, movimento associado à expansão da computação e da inteligência artificial. O aumento, porém, também amplia a pressão sobre as redes elétricas e o consumo de recursos naturais, especialmente água, além de poder elevar as emissões de carbono. Flexibilidade e eficiência ganham peso na avaliação A proposta europeia busca criar uma referência comum para que seja possível comparar o desempenho ambiental e energético dos empreendimentos. O esquema deverá considerar o consumo efetivo de energia e água dos grandes empreendimentos. A avaliação também pretende incorporar a relação dessas instalações com o sistema elétrico. Entre os elementos considerados estão o reaproveitamento do calor residual, a instalação de capacidade de geração de energia limpa e a flexibilidade no consumo de eletricidade. Esse último ponto ganha relevância à medida que os data centers passam a representar uma parcela maior da demanda. Segundo a Comissão Europeia, instalações capazes de adaptar seu consumo às condições da rede podem contribuir para reduzir custos do sistema, melhorar sua estabilidade e facilitar a incorporação de fontes renováveis. Um dos exemplos apresentados pela Comissão é justamente o aproveitamento do calor produzido pelos equipamentos. Segundo a estimativas, a reutilização de aproximadamente metade de todo o calor residual gerado pelos data centers europeus poderia equivaler à demanda de aquecimento de 4 milhões de residências no continente. Escalada da IA A pressão sobre infraestrutura e recursos não é apenas uma projeção distante. Os data centers consumiram cerca de 68 TWh de eletricidade na União Europeia em 2024. Com a expansão impulsionada pela inteligência artificial, a estimativa é que esse volume praticamente dobre, chegando a 114 TWh em 2030, o equivalente a mais de 3% da demanda total de eletricidade da região. Por isso, a estratégia europeia associa a expansão da capacidade computacional a requisitos de eficiência e maior transparência sobre a chamada pegada ambiental dos empreendimentos. A Comissão também abriu uma consulta pública e uma chamada para discutir padrões mínimos de desempenho aplicáveis aos data centers em operação. O regulamento que cria o sistema de classificação ainda passará por dois meses de escrutínio do Parlamento Europeu e do Conselho. A expectativa é que os primeiros selos de sustentabilidade de data centers individuais sejam apresentados em 2027. Uma primeira revisão do modelo está prevista para o fim de 2028. Brasil cria incentivo, mas Ceará expõe desafios O debate europeu ocorre paralelamente à tentativa brasileira de atrair grandes investimentos em infraestrutura digital.Em 15 de setembro, o governo federal sancionou a Lei 15.504/2026, que instituiu o Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter). A medida concede incentivos tributários para equipamentos destinados à implantação, modernização e ampliação de data centers, mas estabelece contrapartidas ambientais, energéticas e tecnológicas. Entre as exigências previstas estão o atendimento a critérios de sustentabilidade, o suprimento integral da demanda de eletricidade por fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão, índice de eficiência hídrica de até 0,05 litro por kWh e aplicação de 2% do valor dos produtos beneficiados em projetos de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação. Um caso em andamento no Ceará, contudo, mostra que a expansão desse mercado também tende a enfrentar questionamentos socioambientais. O data center do Complexo do Pecém, em Caucaia, associado ao TikTok, da ByteDance, tem investimento anunciado superior a R$ 200 bilhões e previsão inicial de operação para 2027. Em setembro, o MPF (Ministério Público Federal) e a DPU (Defensoria Pública da União) recorreram à Justiça para impedir o início da operação até que sejam realizadas consulta livre, prévia e informada ao povo indígena Anacé e um Estudo de Impacto Ambiental e Relatório de Impacto Ambiental (EIA/Rima). A ação também coloca a necessidade de monitoramento dos recursos hídricos, sistema elétrico, ruído e comunidades do entorno. O empreendimento prevê 300 MW de potência instalada, cerca de 70 hectares, 120 geradores a diesel e captação de água subterrânea para resfriamento. Ainda no caso cearense, MPF e DPU afirmam que o empreendimento fica próximo à área de proteção ambiental do Lagamar do Cauípe, que coincide parcialmente com a Terra Indígena Anacé, ainda em estudo pela Funai. Todo o conteúdo do Canal Solar é resguardado pela lei de direitos autorais, e fica expressamente proibida a reprodução parcial ou total deste site em qualquer meio. Caso tenha interesse em colaborar ou reutilizar parte do nosso material, solicitamos que entre em contato através do e-mail: redacao@canalsolar.com.br.

artigo.texto: Multiple residents sought answers and raised concerns over a proposed data center during a 2nd Ward meeting Tuesday night. A zoning analysis application has been submitted for 1265 Hartrey Ave. to determine whether a “computer processing center” would be a permitted use for the site. Ald. Krissie Harris (2nd), said during the ward meeting she had not seen a formal proposal for the data center, and would not make a decision on it until she had more information about the proposal and discussed it with the property owner. “I don’t have an opinion yet because I have not heard what it is, I know circumstantially about data systems and data centers, but I don’t know firsthand, and I always try to get my information before I make a decision,” she said. Harris clarified that while she had previously met with the building’s owner to discuss a separate proposal for an energy storage facility, she had not discussed the proposed data center with them yet. A 4th Ward resident said she had “extreme concerns” about the environmental, economic and sociological impacts of having a data center in Evanston, and she expected the city to be a “leader in the nation” in ensuring these centers would not impact the community. Meanwhile resident Michael Courier expressed concerns over data centers disproportionately using more energy and water than other technologies, as well as opposition to artificial intelligence since he saw it harming workers and people’s way of life. “Evanston should not be complicit in the technologies that destroy what we hold dear and everything we love about this city,” he said. Prior to the ward meeting, Courier was outside the Robert Crown Center distributing leaflets expressing opposition against data centers. Reed Beidler of Lark Management, told Evanston Now the proposed facility would be a “rowboat” compared to the massive data centers that have faced fierce opposition throughout the country. According to a memo provided by Beidler, the proposed data center, which would have between four to eight full-time employees, would be contained entirely within the existing building envelope, and the existing utility infrastructure would be able to support the new facility.

artigo.texto: TEXAS — Mason McCallister said it was an act of God that sent him down a gravel road near his home in Bells, Texas, one Sunday last December. It wasn't the normal route he and his family take back from church, but he decided to detour so his daughters could shout hello to their grandmother as they drove by her home. What he saw that day catapulted him into a debate playing out around the country — and especially in Texas — over data centers. It's one that may now affect the outcome of key elections in the Lone Star State. As they rolled past, flashes of red caught McCallister's eye among the lush green of the area's gentle hills. "Driving down that road, I just see survey markers everywhere," McCallister, a real estate agent, told CNBC. "And I knew at that time what was happening. I could feel it" — a data center is coming, he said. McCallister's home is less than a mile from the survey markers, in a rural stretch between Dallas and the Oklahoma border. He and his wife, Heather, built the house on 26 acres, where they keep three horses and a donkey and host frequent family gatherings at a long farmhouse table on their spacious back patio. The outcry over data centers — warehouses that contain the hardware for powering artificial intelligence and other technology — was only a faint murmur when McCallister first saw the survey markers. In the months since, it's become a dull roar, as increasingly more projects are proposed and built, and general anxiety over AI and its potentially humanity-ending powers grows. Across Texas and the country, people have flooded local meetings to protest proposed projects, citing concerns about the use of water and other resources, noise and light pollution, rising utility costs and falling property values. Some towns and cities have moved to block their development, as anti-data center advocacy groups and social media pages proliferate. Polling shows the economy and cost of living are top of mind for voters in the runup to the 2026 midterm elections. But some political strategists say data centers are a potent enough issue that they could shift the balance of power in Texas, potentially paving the way for Democrats to win statewide for the first time since 1994. Democrats have their sights set on the governor's mansion, as well as an open U.S. Senate seat, and the outcome of the Senate race could determine control of Congress. Populists on both the left and the right — including Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Josh Hawley, R-Mo. — were quick to try to rein in data centers and protect consumers against associated utility cost increases. But Democrats have broadly staked out a clear position against data centers, as President Donald Trump cheers development of new facilities. That dynamic has left Republicans — including Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who is running for reelection, and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is running for Senate — playing defense as public opinion turns against the facilities. "I don't think Republicans have a clear, standard message on data centers and AI at this moment," said Brendan Steinhauser, a GOP strategist and CEO of The Alliance for Secure AI Action, who has called data centers a "sleeper issue" of this election cycle. The survey markers set McCallister on a hunt for answers that included knocking on neighbors' doors, approaching surveyors in fields near his house, chasing down local officials and eventually cornering Rhett Bennett, the CEO of Black Mountain, a Fort Worth-based energy and natural resources development company he discerned had designs on the land. Black Mountain did not respond to multiple requests for comment from CNBC about the potential project. But McCallister said Bennett — whom he confronted at a public meeting, with a Texas Tribune reporter in tow — confirmed the company was exploring a data center near his house. McCallister fears that if it is completed, it could effectively envelop his property. McCallister said he and his wife never planned to sell their house, so any potential hit to their property value isn't particularly worrying. He says his primary concerns are water and power usage. Other data center opponents CNBC spoke with in Texas said they were concerned about noise and light pollution as well as the long-term economic and job displacement impacts of AI, which some of the facilities power. More than anything, the ordeal has made McCallister — who said he's a lifelong Republican and voted for Trump three times — question his political leanings. The GOP, he said, has been too slow to react. "I'm definitely frustrated with the Republican Party. I have gone literally out of my way to warn them, to tell them what's happening," he said. "Y'all should have picked up on this much earlier than y'all did." 'Let Data Reign' Trump's outright dismissal of data center concerns and his reluctance to regulate rapidly evolving AI have complicated the issue for Republican leaders such as Abbott and Paxton, who are fighting for their political lives in one of the most closely watched states in the 2026 election. "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign," Trump posted on Truth Social on Aug. 31. With Trump's unyielding stance on the issue, Abbott and Paxton face a dilemma: Either they defy Trump, the de facto head of the Republican Party, and their donors with tech and data center-industry connections. Or they anger a sizable bloc of data center opponents that has emerged within their base. Fifty-seven percent of Texas voters polled by the Texas Politics Project said they opposed a data center being built in their community, including 43% of Republicans, 54% of independents and 60% of rural voters. artigo.texto: asharkyu/Shutterstock Save for later Print Download Share LinkedIn Twitter The Middle East’s renewable energy story has largely been defined by record-breaking solar projects. Yet, the next decade of the energy transition may depend less on how much renewable electricity is generated and more on how effectively it is stored. Without large-scale energy storage, even the most ambitious solar and wind programs will struggle to deliver reliable, around-the-clock power.Innovation in renewable energy has transformed how the Middle East powers its cities, opening new frontiers of development for a region long associated with oil and gas. Industry estimates suggest the Middle East’s installed renewable energy capacity could expand from 54.85 gigawatts in 2026 to 102.40 GW by 2031, registering a compound annual growth rate of 13.3% during the forecast period. Factors such as strong national decarbonization targets, steep solar-and-wind cost declines, and green-hydrogen export ambitions are all steering resources toward utility-scale clean energy projects.However, generation is only one part of the challenge. The next phase of the energy transition will increasingly depend on what happens after that energy is produced.Energy Storage as Core InfrastructureSolar panels generate power when sunlight is available rather than necessarily when electricity demand is highest. Wind power faces a similar challenge. Electricity systems, however, must continuously balance generation and consumption, since even relatively small mismatches can affect grid stability.This is why energy storage is shifting from a supporting technology to a core part of future electricity infrastructure. It not only lets power systems store excess electricity for later use but also helps manage sudden fluctuations in supply and demand.The industry faces a significant challenge. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), global energy storage capacity would need to increase sixfold to around 1,500 GW by 2030 to support the expansion of renewable energy required under its Net Zero Emissions by 2050 Scenario. Batteries would account for approximately 90% of this increase.Batteries EvolveLithium-ion batteries currently dominate the battery storage market. The same broad family of technologies that powers phones and electric vehicles (EVs) can also be installed in systems large enough to support electricity grids.Their growing adoption is driven by several advantages: they can react extremely quickly, can be built at different scales and can often be installed considerably faster than traditional power infrastructure. The economics of lithium-ion batteries have also changed dramatically. The IEA estimates that average battery costs have fallen by around 90% since 2010 due to improvements in chemistry, manufacturing and economies of scale.Battery technology itself continues to evolve. Lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, batteries have gained importance because they can offer a longer cycle life, good thermal stability and less reliance on nickel and cobalt than some other lithium-ion chemistries. Researchers and manufacturers are also developing sodium-ion batteries, which replace lithium with the much more abundant element of sodium.Of course, no single chemistry will necessarily dominate every application. An EV, a household battery and a storage facility connected to a major power grid have very different requirements. Cost, safety, energy density, lifespan and the number of hours for which energy must be stored all influence which technology is most appropriate.Storage Scales Up in the GulfFor the countries of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) — Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE — this is becoming a practical infrastructure question rather than a distant technological discussion. Saudi Arabia is rapidly emerging as a major energy-storage market, with 26 gigawatt hours of battery storage projects tendered or under development and a target of 48 GWh by 2030. In August 2026, agreements were also signed for four additional projects providing a combined 2,000 megawatts of power capacity and 8,000 megawatt hours of energy storage — equivalent to four hours at full output — representing an investment of more than $1.16 billion. These projects support the Kingdom’s wider goal of having renewables account for around 50% of its electricity generation mix by 2030.The UAE provides another indication of where the technology is heading. In Abu Dhabi, Masdar and Emirates Water and Electricity Co. are developing a project combining 5.2 GW of solar photovoltaic capacity with 19 GWh of battery storage. The project is designed to deliver up to 1 GW of renewable power around the clock. Renewable energy is therefore moving closer to being schedulable and dispatchable, rather than simply accepted whenever nature makes it available.For utilities across the GCC, the implications extend beyond renewable integration. Storage can defer costly network upgrades, enhance grid resilience during peak demand periods and provide ancillary services that have traditionally been supplied by conventional thermal generation. As renewable penetration increases, battery energy storage systems are increasingly being viewed not as standalone assets but as integral components of modern power system planning.Storage Beyond BatteriesBatteries, however, cannot solve every storage challenge. Most large lithium-ion systems today are best suited to storing electricity for several hours. As renewable penetration increases, electricity systems may increasingly need storage that can operate for much longer periods, including overnight, across several days or potentially even seasonally.This has increased interest in long-duration energy storage, with pumped-storage hydropower as one established example. artigo.texto: La Verne lithium battery storage fire forces evacuations near water district facility LOS ANGELES - Evacuation orders were issued after a fire broke out at an outdoor lithium battery storage unit near a solar panel field at a Metropolitan Water District facility in La Verne Tuesday. What we know: The fire was reported around 11:40 a.m. at the facility in the 3200 block of Wheeler Avenue. According to the La Verne Fire Department, a small explosion occurred in the battery unit which stored lithium batteries. Hazmat crews were brought in, and fire crews were mainly spraying the area with water to prevent the flames from spreading. Metropolitan said the water supply was not affected. Nearby neighborhoods evacuated Due to the hazardous nature of lithium batteries, evacuation orders were issued in the areas around the facility. La Verne police said shopping centers along Wheeler north of Foothill Boulevard were evacuated as a precaution. Shelter-in-place orders were issued for Grace Elementary School and Bonita High School. An evacuation center was established at the La Verne Community Center on 3680 D St. By 2:30 p.m., the fire was mainly out. The fire department said one civilian was injured and taken to a hospital. No additional details were released. A short time after that, some evacuation orders were downgraded to warnings, while others were reduced to advisories. An evacuation order remained in place in the immediate vicinity of the facility. The Source: Information for this story came from the La Verne Fire Department. A statement was given by the Metropolitan Water District.

artigo.texto: ARCATA – The City Council last week set a 45-day moratorium on new data center applications while it develops a formal policy on such facilities. The urgency ordinance is based on “a current and immediate threat to public health, safety or welfare.” On Day 35, Oct. 21, city staff report on the study process. By Day 45, Nov. 2, the council could extend the moratorium for up to 10 months, 15 days. After that, it could be extended another year, for a total two-year lockout on new data center apps. The city currently has no regulatory framework on data centers, and many have objected to the lack of process involved in the 2020 approval of the current facility on 11th Street. The moratorium follows adoption of similar freezes in Eureka and other California towns. Concerns center around noise, water and air quality and energy use and other impacts. The council also adopted a new Economic Strategic Plan, which This Plan works alongside the city’s housing, Reconnect Arcata effort, parks and trail expansion and climate action to foster sustainable, value-driven growth through 2031. The plan emphasizes quality of life, supporting business, job creation, strengthening Arcata’s brand and more. cityofarcata.org/189/Economic-Strategic-Plan The council also endorsed issuance of liquor licenses for the Alibi bar on the Plaza and Alchemy Distillery on South G Street.

artigo.texto: Os Estados-Membros da União Europeia (UE) concordaram em suspender temporariamente o cancelamento das quotas de emissões de CO2 excedentes detidas no mercado de carbono até 2030, a fim de aumentar a sua capacidade de resposta caso a oferta de quotas se torne escassa. UE flexibiliza regulamentações sobre armazenamento de carbono. A UE concordou em flexibilizar as regulamentações sobre o armazenamento de carbono, mantendo uma parte da oferta até 2030 para mitigar o risco de escassez e volatilidade de preços no mercado. A decisão foi adotada pelos embaixadores da UE em 23 de setembro, como parte de alterações específicas ao mecanismo da Reserva de Estabilização do Mercado (MSR, na sigla em inglês) no âmbito do Sistema de Comércio de Emissões (SCE) da UE. A MSR regula a quantidade de quotas em circulação, retirando-as quando o mercado está com excesso de oferta e reintegrando-as quando a oferta é insuficiente. Segundo o acordo, até o final de 2030, as quotas no âmbito do MSR que excedam 400 milhões de unidades serão mantidas em vez de serem canceladas, como está estipulado atualmente. Essas quotas podem funcionar como uma "reserva" caso o mercado de carbono sofra uma escassez de oferta. A partir de 1º de janeiro de 2031, o limite para cancelamento será elevado para 800 milhões de quotas, o dobro do nível atual, antes de diminuir gradualmente nos anos subsequentes. O método de ajuste dessa redução será considerado em uma revisão mais ampla do Sistema de Comércio de Emissões (SCE). O mecanismo de cancelamento de quotas, que teve início em 2023, já retirou mais de 3 mil milhões de quotas do mercado, ajudando a resolver a persistente situação de sobreoferta. No entanto, a UE considera que as condições de mercado poderão mudar nos próximos anos, aumentando o risco de escassez de quotas e de volatilidade de preços. A Comissão Europeia propôs a alteração em abril como parte de um conjunto de medidas de curto prazo para lidar com os preços elevados e voláteis da energia. O aumento dos preços dos combustíveis na sequência do conflito com o Irão aumentou a pressão sobre os governos europeus para controlarem os custos da energia. O Sistema de Comércio de Emissões (SCE) não é a principal causa do aumento dos preços da energia na Europa, mas o custo da aquisição de quotas de carbono reflete-se parcialmente nos preços da eletricidade. Em média, os custos do SCE representam cerca de 11% das faturas de eletricidade da indústria na UE, sendo o impacto variável entre os países, dependendo da sua matriz energética. Em países com forte dependência de combustíveis fósseis, como a Polônia , o impacto dos preços do carbono é maior do que em países com alta proporção de energia nuclear e renovável. A Polônia, a Itália e vários outros membros já solicitaram à UE que ajuste os mecanismos para limitar o impacto dos preços do carbono nos custos da eletricidade. Após chegar a um consenso, o Conselho da UE iniciará negociações com o Parlamento Europeu para finalizar o texto, com o objetivo de concluir o processo até o final de 2026. Esta é a primeira vez que a UE realiza uma alteração separada ao MSR. Alterações mais abrangentes ao mecanismo continuarão a ser consideradas no âmbito da revisão abrangente do ETS. artigo.texto: CBTS acquires Recovery Point Systems, adding disaster recovery services and data center space The Cincinnati technology services company is adding managed disaster recovery, ransomware recovery, and a Tier III data center in Maryland through the deal, which follows a new chief technology officer and the launch of its Forge Agents AI platform earlier this month. CBTS has acquired Recovery Point Systems, a Maryland-based disaster recovery provider. The deal adds managed recovery services and company-owned data center space to the Cincinnati company's infrastructure, cloud and security business. CBTS announced the acquisition Sept. 10. Terms were not disclosed. Bank Street Group LLC was Recovery Point's exclusive financial adviser on the transaction. By the numbers - 1994: Year CBTS was founded in Cincinnati - 3,000+: Clients served by CBTS and its OnX Canada division - 30+: Years Recovery Point has provided data protection and colocation services - 115,000: Square feet at Recovery Point's Germantown, Maryland, data center - 6: Consecutive years Recovery Point has appeared in the Gartner Market Guide for Disaster Recovery as a Service What Recovery Point brings Recovery Point provides fully managed Disaster Recovery as a Service (DRaaS) and cyber resiliency services for enterprise IT environments. Its clients range from Fortune 500 companies to small and midsize businesses, along with federal, state and local governments. The company manages recovery across complex, multi-platform environments, including legacy and mainframe systems, and handles plan development, testing and governance. The deal also gives CBTS Tier III data centers that Recovery Point owns and operates. The announcement describes them as fiber-dense and ready for expansion. The same facilities run Recovery Point's colocation business, which lets clients use one provider for hosting, resilience and recovery. Recovery Point's flagship facility is in Germantown, Maryland, about 25 miles from Washington, D.C. The company has described the site as a 115,000-square-foot Tier III data center certified by the Uptime Institute, with direct connections to Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. With the acquisition, CBTS now offers: - Fully managed DRaaS with orchestrated execution and measurable service-level agreements - Ransomware Recovery as a Service (RRaaS), with AI-powered backup validation - Cyber resiliency across hybrid, multi-cloud and legacy environments - Recovery testing and performance assurance as standard practice Why CBTS made the deal CBTS tied the acquisition to AI. As AI workloads drive up data volume and infrastructure demand, the company noted, enterprises need resilient, scalable environments they control, without the cost of building their own. The announcement also cited a Palo Alto Networks report finding that nearly 30% of security teams take more than a full day to resolve a single incident. "Resilience is now a board-level obligation, not an IT project. With Recovery Point, CBTS delivers what enterprises increasingly demand: a trusted partner who can modernize their infrastructure, secure it, and recover it end-to-end, under pressure, with measurable outcomes," CBTS CEO Kristin Russell said in the announcement. Recovery Point CEO Jack Dziak described the deal as a gain for both client bases. "With CBTS, our clients gain access to a full range of enterprise technology platforms, and CBTS gains a proven partner in cyber resilience," Dziak said. A busy stretch for CBTS The acquisition capped a run of announcements from CBTS. On Aug. 31, the company named Mark Giles chief technology officer. Giles is a 10-year CBTS veteran and former U.S. Marine Corps data systems chief who previously led the company's AI adoption as vice president of AI. The new role brings AI, product management and emerging technology under one strategy. The next day, CBTS launched Forge Agents, a platform that builds AI agents from a plain-language description of a task. It is aimed at midmarket and regulated organizations and draws on a library of 187 prebuilt components and 34 cross-industry blueprints. Forge Agents builds on Forge AI, the company's AI advisory and engineering offering launched in March. CBTS told trade outlet Channel Dive that the Recovery Point facilities strengthen its ability to host AI infrastructure in environments customers can control. About the company CBTS designs, builds and operates technology infrastructure for midmarket and enterprise organizations across North America, with expertise in AI, data, applications, platforms and security. The company has been named to the CRN Tech Elite 250 for seven consecutive years and ranks No. 49 on the CRN Solution Provider 500.

The situation is simply this: It is early in the process. We’ve heard the community, right? There’s a desire for transparency. We simply can’t be more transparent than this.” There is a lot that still remains unknown, and many questions were met with a redirection to submit a formal Freedom of Information Act request. Stay with 10 News as this breaking news story continues to develop.

artigo.texto: Virginia is home to about one-third of the world’s data centers, and a new executive order from Gov. Abigail Spanberger is not stopping that development. Instead, Executive Order 22 establishes a broad framework for changing how data centers are developed and regulated, with an emphasis on transparency, environmental protections, energy costs, clean energy and workforce development. The order says future data center development should balance economic growth with protections for communities, natural resources and the electric grid. “The policies put forth in this framework are the highest standards in America, and they’re organized around five core requirements,” Spanberger said. “Increasing transparency, strengthening environmental protections, lowering energy costs, bolstering our clean energy economy, and delivering a better deal for Virginia workers.” Transparency and local input One of the most immediate changes involves nondisclosure agreements. Executive Order 22 prohibits state executive branch agencies, boards, commissions and other entities under the governor’s supervision from entering into or requiring new nondisclosure agreements that prevent public disclosure of material information about proposed commercial data center projects, including public incentives, anticipated resource demands and community impacts. The prohibition does not currently extend to local governments. Former U.S. Attorney John Fishwick said that distinction is significant because localities are often directly involved in negotiations with data center developers. “The most immediate impact from Governor Spanberger’s executive order is that she has banned state officials from entering into non-disclosure agreements with data center companies,” Fishwick said. “That does not apply to local officials, but it does apply to state officials immediately.” The order also directs the governor’s Office of the Chief Energy Officer to develop a Data Center Planning and Community Engagement Toolkit within 120 days. The toolkit is intended to give local governments and communities model questions and information requests involving electricity demand, water and wastewater use, backup generation, air emissions, noise, traffic, public services and community benefit agreements. Restrictions on some new projects The order also immediately restricts certain state economic development assistance. Under the order, the Virginia Economic Development Partnership cannot provide assistance through the Virginia Business Ready Sites Program, expedited permitting or similar discretionary state economic development, site-readiness or expedited-review programs for a new data center project with an anticipated peak electrical demand of at least 25 megawatts. The distinction between new and existing projects is important. The executive order does not expressly cancel existing data center approvals or development agreements. Fishwick said questions about whether future laws or regulations could affect projects already underway will depend on the language lawmakers ultimately approve. “I think we’ll have to wait and see what the legislation says, whether it’s retroactive or whether it’s prospective,” Fishwick said. “That will, I think, determine whether it applies to data centers and where they are as far as being built out versus future data centers.” Environmental and water protections Executive Order 22 also directs state agencies to develop and evaluate additional environmental protections. The order calls for accelerated development of state noise regulations for data centers and directs the Department of Environmental Quality, Virginia Department of Health and Virginia Energy to review the cumulative impacts of diesel and other backup generators. That review is expected to consider the number and capacity of generators, fuel types, operating hours, geographic concentration, cumulative emissions and air quality. It also calls for consideration of cleaner technologies and potential permitting, monitoring, reporting, enforcement and public-disclosure requirements. Water use is another major part of the order. Virginia Energy is directed to develop criteria for identifying areas where cooling-water supplies may be scarce. The Eastern Virginia Groundwater Management Area is designated as a cooling-water scarcity area under the order. The framework also directs state agencies to explore ways to reduce water consumption and consider opportunities such as reclaimed water and using waste heat from data centers. Who pays for the infrastructure? The order also focuses on the costs associated with connecting large data centers to the electric grid. The framework says data centers should pay their fair share of generation, transmission and distribution costs and other public investments associated with their development. The governor’s chief energy officer is directed to work with utilities, the State Corporation Commission and PJM Interconnection on ways to shield households from data-center-driven infrastructure costs and promote more equitable cost allocation. The framework also calls for exploring ways to make data centers contribute to clean energy and grid reliability, including potential requirements involving on-site generation and sudden changes in electricity demand. Workforce and local businesses The order also includes workforce and economic-development goals. It directs state agencies to develop standards and reporting related to workforce development and local procurement, including efforts to prioritize Virginia businesses and local hiring. The framework also calls for responsible contractor standards, apprenticeship programs and consideration of project labor agreements for new developments. What happens to existing projects? artigo.texto: CATL Plunges 25% in a Month as Chinese Automakers Accelerate Supply Chain Diversification Shares of CATL (Ningde Times), the world's largest EV battery maker, have taken a direct hit from supply chain diversification moves by Chinese automaker customers. On the Shenzhen Stock Exchange, CATL closed at CNY 297.10 (approximately $44) on September 21, down 1.61% from the previous session, barely holding above its 52-week low of CNY 295.55 (approximately $44). The stock has fallen 24.04% in September alone and is down 36.5% from its early May high this year. The decline was equally steep on the Hong Kong exchange. CATL's H-shares plunged 6.01% on September 15 to close at HK$516 (approximately $66), the lowest level since March this year. The following day, shares fell as low as HK$486.4 (approximately $62) intraday, marking a roughly 38% decline from the June peak of HK$792.87 (approximately $101). A-shares also tumbled 6.16% in a single day on September 15, erasing approximately CNY 91.4 billion (approximately $13.6 billion) in market capitalization, and on September 16 the CNY 300 (approximately $45) level was breached intraday. Compared with the year-to-date high of CNY 467.34 (approximately $70) recorded on May 7, more than CNY 700 billion (approximately $104.4 billion) in combined A-share and H-share market value has evaporated. The direct catalyst behind the stock plunge is a series of "de-CATL" moves by major automaker customers. Li Auto recently invested CNY 2.65 billion (approximately $395.2 million) to become Sunwoda's second-largest shareholder. The new L8 model launched in June this year is equipped with Sunwoda batteries across all trims, replacing CATL batteries. Li Auto's management has characterized the relationship with Sunwoda not as a simple supply contract but as a "long-term interest community," pledging to strengthen joint R&D and manufacturing cooperation. Xiaomi's moves have also heightened market wariness. On September 4, Xiaomi unveiled its in-house "Dragon Armor" battery brand, announcing that its new EV lineup would feature cells from CALB and Sunwoda. Given that CATL was the primary supplier for the previously launched SU7 and YU7 models, this represents a clear strategic pivot. Xpeng has also increased the supply share from EVE Energy, while Huawei's smart car brand Aito has moved away from a CATL-exclusive supply arrangement by adding CALB and Gotion High-Tech. According to industry estimates, Li Auto and Xiaomi account for approximately 13.6% of CATL's installed capacity in China. While this figure alone is not immediately fatal, what concerns the market is not the number but the direction. China Retreats, Japan Expands While Chinese automakers are diversifying their supply chains, CATL's customer base is also shifting in other directions. The breakdown by customer is as follows: The moves by four Japanese automakers are particularly notable. Toyota, which formed a comprehensive partnership with CATL in 2019, announced in April 2026 that its Indonesian production subsidiary TMMIN would enter an EV business alliance with CATL. This marks the first time Toyota has sourced CATL batteries outside China. The CATL plant being built in West Java is targeted to begin operations in late 2026, with Toyota establishing a dedicated line inside the facility to receive batteries for locally produced hybrid vehicles. The batteries are expected to be nickel-based ternary lithium-ion cells. Honda acquired approximately 1% of CATL in 2020 and subsequently signed a 123 GWh long-term procurement agreement covering 2024–2030, while Nissan agreed in May 2025 to supply batteries for Dongfeng Nissan passenger vehicles. Daihatsu plans to launch a kei EV co-developed with CATL in Japan as early as 2026. The fact that overseas customers, led by Japan, are filling the gap left by shrinking Chinese demand demonstrates that the "diversified customer base" cited as a counterargument is more than rhetoric. The quality of overseas revenue is also higher than domestic. Overseas sales accounted for 31.48% of CATL's first-half 2026 revenue, but overseas gross margin was 29.97%, significantly exceeding the 21.16% achieved in China's domestic market. Profitability Gap Drives Supply Chain Restructuring The reason automakers are willing to absorb the costs and risks of supply chain transition to reduce CATL dependency stems from profitability pressure. CATL posted net profit of CNY 43.284 billion (approximately $6.5 billion) in the first half of this year—more than double the combined net profit of 15 major listed Chinese automakers (CNY 21.048 billion) over the same period. CATL's first-half consolidated gross margin reached 23.93%, while Li Auto's second-quarter automotive segment gross margin was 9.4%, down 10 percentage points year-over-year. Batteries, which account for 30–40% of EV costs, are the single most expensive component. Amid weak domestic demand in China and ongoing price wars, total profits across the Chinese auto industry fell 20% in the first seven months of this year. Meanwhile, CATL has maintained pricing power leverage backed by its mid-40% share of China's power battery market. A battle over product definition rights is also at play. Li Auto's new L8 is a prime example. The performance specifications, system design, software, and pack integration are led by Li Auto, with Sunwoda handling only cell manufacturing. This represents a new supply chain model in which control over battery solutions shifts from suppliers to automakers. The attitude of second-tier battery makers has also encouraged this transition. Unlike CATL, companies like CALB and Sunwoda are desperate for each individual customer and can respond far more flexibly on pricing and development timelines. Li Auto's acquisition of a Sunwoda stake is likewise interpreted not as a purely financial investment but as a strategic move to strengthen supply chain control. artigo.texto: O mercado de data centers do eixo São Paulo-Campinas acelerou em 2026 e chegou a 661 megawatts (MW) de capacidade operacional. Na comparação anual, a expansão foi de aproximadamente 91%, segundo dados da Cushman & Wakefield. O tamanho atual, porém, mostra apenas parte da corrida por infraestrutura digital. Outros 250 MW estão em construção e há 2.066 MW em projetos planejados para o corredor paulista. A combinação de computação em nuvem, digitalização das empresas e maior demanda por aplicações de inteligência artificial ajuda a explicar a pressão sobre esse mercado. São Paulo concentra o maior mercado da América Latina Com 661 MW operacionais, São Paulo permanece como o principal mercado de data centers da América Latina. A vacância está em apenas 4,1%, enquanto a absorção líquida alcançou 38 MW no primeiro semestre de 2026. Para efeito de comparação, o volume de projetos planejados equivale a mais de três vezes toda a capacidade que já está funcionando atualmente no corredor São Paulo-Campinas. Isso não significa, no entanto, que todos os projetos anunciados serão necessariamente construídos. Data centers dependem de fatores como disponibilidade de energia, conexão à rede elétrica, acesso a terrenos, licenciamento e demanda contratada. IA aumenta a necessidade de infraestrutura A expansão das aplicações de IA acrescentou uma nova camada à procura por capacidade computacional. O treinamento e a operação de modelos de inteligência artificial exigem grandes volumes de processamento, armazenamento e energia. Ao mesmo tempo, empresas continuam migrando aplicações para a nuvem e ampliando a digitalização de processos, aumentando a demanda estrutural por infraestrutura. Redata muda a equação dos novos projetos O avanço do setor coincide com a entrada em vigor do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter, o Redata. Sancionado em setembro, o regime prevê benefícios tributários para equipamentos elegíveis utilizados por empresas habilitadas, mediante o cumprimento das condições previstas na legislação. Na prática, o incentivo pode alterar parte da estrutura de custos de novos projetos, mas não elimina os principais gargalos físicos do setor. Energia, conectividade, licenciamento e velocidade de execução continuam determinantes para transformar os mais de 2 GW planejados em capacidade efetivamente disponível.

artigo.texto: Overview: - A new survey finds that fewer than 20% of local officials believe data centers are worth the cost. - Data centers are least popular among rural leaders, where the projects are typically built. - Leaders worry the project may do environmental harm and boost utility costs. This story was originally published by Bridge Michigan, a nonprofit and nonpartisan news organization. To get regular coverage from Bridge Michigan, sign up for a free Bridge Michigan newsletter here. by Ron French, Bridge Michigan September 22, 2026 Less than 1 in 5 Michigan local government officials believe large-scale data centers are worth their costs, and a majority want tighter statewide regulations, according to a survey released Tuesday. Most skeptical are leaders in rural Michigan, where the centers are typically built, according to the survey by the University of Michigan’s Center for Local, State, and Urban Policy. Among officials from rural communities, only 12% agree that data centers’ benefits outweigh their costs, compared with 40% of officials from urban areas. Those sentiments reflect a backlash to the mega projects originally hailed as economic boons. At least 18 local governments around Michigan have voted or have proposed temporary halts to new data centers. Laws against exclusionary zoning, however, make it difficult to ban data centers altogether. Rural Michigan communities “are more likely to be targets for large-scale data center development because they typically have more inexpensive available land,” said Stephanie Leiser, director of the U-M center that conducted the survey of 1,328 jurisdictions across the state. “While they acknowledge the potential benefits of data centers in terms of economic competitiveness, they don’t believe it’s fair that they will bear a disproportionate share of the costs of hosting them in their communities.” Data centers have become a major, bipartisan issue in Michigan and nationwide in the midterm elections. More than 16% of respondents singled it out as a top issue in Bridge Listens, Bridge Michigan’s election-year survey. The U- M survey indicated that nearly 6 in 10 local government leaders believe regulation of hyperscale data centers by Michigan’s state and local governments should be a very high priority. Both candidates for governor, Republican John James and Democrat Jocelyn Benson, have called for a moratorium on the centers, as have the major party candidates for Senate, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and the GOP’s Mike Rogers. A recent poll found nearly two-thirds of Michigan residents opposed the building of data centers in the state. “Data centers are polling about as well as herpes right now,” said Eric Paul Dennis, research associate at Citizens Research Council of Michigan. “We’ve got an election coming up, and there’s a lot of tough talk. It’ll be interesting to see what happens after the election.” Two years ago, lawmakers in Lansing narrowly agreed to exempt large data centers from sales and use taxes in an effort to lure the industry to Michigan. But with backlash growing, lawmakers now are considering a flurry of new bipartisan proposals, tax-break rollbacks, and potential moratoriums. Rep. Joey Andrews, D-St. Joseph, authored the bill to provide tax breaks to data centers two years ago and remains a proponent of the projects. He said he’s not surprised that local officials have soured on the centers, likening sentiment to a backlash against about battery plants and wind energy projects. “No one wants a room full of activists showing up and yelling at them,” Andrews told Bridge. “(But) this mood we’re in where we’re rejecting growth is not healthy for the state. We have to figure out how to get back to being pro-growth.” The U-M’s Leiser said local officials “feel like they’re between a rock and a hard place.” “On one hand, they’re facing vocal opposition or outright revolt from their residents who are demanding they stop any data centers from being built. On the other, they’re facing the daunting prospect of fighting expensive and protracted legal battles with deep-pocketed data center developers.” Among the U-M survey’s findings: - Metro Detroit officials are the most likely to have a positive view of data centers, with 27% saying they are worth the cost. Northern Michigan (10%) and the Upper Peninsula (13%) are the least likely to have positive views of the projects. - Local leaders believe residents are even more opposed to data centers. Statewide, just 2% thought that the majority of the people they represent favored data centers, while 13% said that they themselves held a favorable view. - A majority of local leaders believe that development of data centers in their communities would have a negative impact on water supply (60%), utility costs (57%), public health (55%) and overall quality of life (53%). This article first appeared on Bridge Michigan and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License. Debbie Dingell calls for pause on the University of Michigan’s planned $1.25-billion computing facility in Ypsilanti Township, citing lack of transparency. Plus: Warren and Dearborn advance data center moratoriums, a poll shows nearly two-thirds of Michigan voters oppose the facilities, and Oracle posts six-figure jobs for its Saline Township project. artigo.texto: New York awarded eight projects energy storage and 13 renewable energy facilities that, together, will mobilize more than $3.7 billion in private investment. The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) it awarded contracts to develop eight large-scale energy storage projects and 13 onshore renewable energy projects. Together, these facilities will add approximately 1.7 gigawatts (GW) of new energy resources to the state, the portfolio includes 950 megawatts (MW) of storage and more than 719 MW of renewable capacity. In addition, NYSERDA estimates that the projects will generate more than $3.700 million in private investment and create more than 1,000 jobs. New York adds 950 MW of energy storage The eight storage projects will add 950 MW of capacity once they are operational, the facilities will be distributed across western New York, the Finger Lakes, the Hudson Valley, New York City, and Long Island. The selection was made through a competitive process in which proposals were received for 46 projects, with a combined capacity of approximately 6 GW. The awarded systems will have a discharge duration of between four and eight hours, allowing electricity to be stored during periods of lower demand and used later when the grid requires additional resources. The selected projects are Lighthouse Energy Storage and Zenobe Burns, in western New York; Eastwater Energy Storage, in the Finger Lakes; KCE NY 5, in the Hudson Valley; Blue Spruce Storage and Palladium Storage, in the Bronx; and Holtsville Energy Storage and KCE NY 37, on Long Island. Lithium-ion batteries to reinforce the electrical grid The eight projects will use technology from lithium-ion batteries and must comply with the safety codes for energy storage systems in effect in New York as of January 1, 2026. The standards include requirements related to the safe location of facilities, the training of first responders, and the preparation of comprehensive plans to address potential emergencies. Payments under the contracts will begin once the facilities are commercially operational, after obtaining the necessary permits and local approvals. According to the projected schedule, all storage projects should be operational by the end of 2030. NYSERDA also plans to launch a second call for large-scale storage projects before the end of the year, the program aims to contract a total of 3 GW of capacity through three bidding processes. Thirteen renewable projects will contribute more than 719 MW In parallel, NYSERDA awarded 13 onshore projects renewable energy which will add more than 719 MW of new capacity. According to the agency’s estimates, these facilities could produce enough electricity annually to power more than 230,000 New York City homes. The portfolio combines solar, onshore wind, and hydroelectric projects distributed across various regions of the state. Selected developments include Flint Mine Solar, Hecate Energy Greene 1 and 2, Spier Falls, High Dam Hydroelectric Facility, Wethersfield Windpark, Chateaugay Windpark, and Diamond Island Hydroelectric Facility. The list also includes Ellenburg Windpark, Greens Corners Solar Park, Rich Road Solar Energy Center, Theresa Hydroelectric Project and Canisteo Wind Energy Center. Several of these projects have already begun construction activities, and according to the announced schedule, all 13 renewable energy facilities should be operational by 2030. Energy investment exceeding $3.700 million The awards will also have a significant economic impact, NYSERDA estimates that the 21 projects will mobilize more than $3.7 billion in private investment and create more than 1,000 jobs. In addition, more than $127 million in economic benefits are expected for disadvantaged communities identified by the Climate Justice Working Group. The new capacity will be added to a state portfolio that currently includes 95 solar, onshore wind, hydroelectric, and offshore wind projects in operation or under development. Together, these represent approximately 10.5 GW of clean energy capacity. With these new awards, New York seeks to advance simultaneously in renewable energy generation and energy storage. Batteries will allow for more flexible management of available electricity, while new solar, wind, and hydroelectric projects will expand the state’s generation capacity. artigo.texto: Oregon’s data centers use almost 25% of the state’s power, report reveals If you're not sure how you feel about the AI data center debate yet, seeing news like this may just convince you that those anti-data center folks have a point. In the first study of its kind since the AI-driven data center discourse began, researchers in Oregon have released a new report detailing the size of the data center industry in the state. In doing so, the researchers have also uncovered just how much energy data centers use up in the state. According to the report, there are 111 operational data centers in the state of Oregon, which take up 22.1 million square feet of building space. Those data centers account for a whopping 23 percent of the state's entire retail energy sales in 2025. You May Also Like The report also details that there are 32 additional data centers under construction or in the planning stages, which will take up an additional 6.9 million square feet. The researchers behind the report believe that data center energy consumption in Oregon will rise to nearly 25 terawatt hours by 2030. That's around 31 to 32 percent of all electricity demand in the state and the same energy consumption as 2.5 million homes. "Data center electricity demand is increasing substantially, and regional as well as state-level planning eﬀorts…indicate that accommodating large-load growth will require new electricity resources, transmission capacity, and coordinated infrastructure planning," the report says. The report also found that these data centers directly employ 2,630 workers. This new report was released on Thursday by ECOnorthwest and the University of Virginia. It was funded by the entrepreneurship and environmentalist nonprofit Lemelson Foundation, which is based in Portland. Topics Artificial Intelligence

artigo.texto: Paraguay and Taiwan are negotiating an agreement that could create a minimum market of 5 million carbon credits for climate projects in Paraguay. The two countries are working on an international transfer agreement that they expect to complete this year, according to Paraguay’s Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development (MADES) official, Victor Gonzalez. The first phase would target demand from Asian companies. The 5 million-credit figure is a negotiated floor, not a confirmed purchase order. Projects would still need to be developed, approved, verified, and authorized before credits could be transferred. The talks matter because Paraguay is developing its carbon market. At the same time, Asian companies seek more international carbon credits under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Paraguay Builds Its Article 6 Carbon Market The talks build on a Memorandum of Understanding signed in October 2025 between Paraguay and Taiwan to explore carbon market cooperation. The proposed Implementation Agreement would set rules for projects that cut emissions in Paraguay. It would also transfer the resulting mitigation outcomes to Taiwan. Paraguay has also been building its domestic carbon market system. Law No. 7190/2023 established a legal framework for carbon markets and created the National Carbon Credit Registry. MADES is responsible for regulating and developing the sector. The government is now working with the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) on a national carbon market strategy. In September 2026, MADES hosted a second national consultation on the strategy. About 80 representatives from government, finance, business, civil society, and international organizations attended. The goal is to create clearer rules for projects, improve transparency, and build Paraguay’s ability to take part in international carbon markets. Five Million Credits Would Create a Large Pipeline The proposed 5 million credit floor would give the Paraguay-Taiwan partnership significant potential scale. However, these credits do not exist yet. Projects must first be identified and developed. They need to measure their emissions reductions. Then, they must pass validation and verification. Finally, they should get the necessary government approvals. Only authorized mitigation outcomes can be transferred under the Article 6 framework. This is important because Paraguay is still strengthening the systems needed to support a larger international carbon market. MADES said its national strategy will focus on stricter rules, transparency, and systems for monitoring, reporting, and verification. Recent government work with Taiwanese officials has also focused on sharing knowledge about Paraguay’s carbon market rules and institutions. The 5 million-ton floor should thus be viewed as a potential future supply target, rather than credits already available to buyers. Taiwan’s Carbon Fee Creates New Credit Demand Taiwan has a clear reason to secure international carbon credits. The country introduced its carbon fee system in 2025. The standard carbon fee is NT$300 per tonne of CO2e. However, companies that meet approved emissions reduction targets can get lower rates of NT$50 or NT$100 per tonne. The fee applies to large electricity and manufacturing facilities with annual emissions of at least 25,000 tonnes of CO2e. Taiwan allows eligible companies to use approved international carbon credits. They can cover up to 5% of their chargeable emissions, following the country’s rules. This creates potential demand for credits generated in Paraguay. However, not every carbon credit will qualify. Projects must meet Taiwan’s requirements as well as Paraguay’s rules for international transfers. That could favor projects with strong measurement systems, clear carbon ownership, and credible verification. Article 6 Rules Prevent Double Counting The proposed deal would operate through Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement. It allows countries to transfer emissions reductions across borders. These transferred outcomes are known as Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes, or ITMOs. A major safeguard is the corresponding adjustment. Suppose a project in Paraguay creates an authorized emissions reduction and transfers it to a Taiwanese company. Paraguay must adjust its national emissions accounting so it does not also count that same reduction toward its own climate target. This prevents the same climate benefit from being counted twice. That makes Article 6 transactions different from many voluntary carbon credit purchases. Voluntary credits do not automatically receive a corresponding adjustment or government authorization. Paraguay already has experience with this system. It signed an Article 6 Implementation Agreement with Singapore in May 2025. This agreement sets up procedures for project approval, ITMO transfers, and necessary adjustments. A Taiwan agreement would add another international route for Paraguayan projects. Forestry and Land Projects Could Lead Forestry is likely to be an important part of Paraguay’s future carbon market. The country has large areas suitable for forest conservation, restoration, and plantation projects. Taiwan has also expressed interest in working with Paraguayan companies on forestry-related carbon projects. Paraguay’s reforestation sector has expanded quickly. IMF data show that reforested land reached about 339,866 hectares in 2024, up 66% from 2022. Paraguay’s forestry institute estimates that over 5 million hectares have a high or very high potential for plantation forestry. Not all this land will become carbon projects. Still, the figures show the scale of Paraguay’s potential forestry investment market. The country’s opportunities also extend beyond forests. Article 6 projects could cover renewable energy, agriculture, green transport, and other emissions-reduction activities. artigo.texto: EU countries back carbon market changes to curb price spikes, diplomats say By Kate Abnett BRUSSELS, Sept 23 (Reuters) - European Union countries agreed on Wednesday to keep more spare CO2 permits in the bloc's emissions trading system (ETS), to try and avoid spikes in carbon prices, according to EU diplomats and a document seen by Reuters. The plan, first proposed by the European Commission in April, is part of the EU response to a surge in fuel prices triggered by the Iran conflict, which has left governments scrambling for ways to curb energy bills. The ETS is the bloc's main climate change policy, and is not the main reason for Europe's rising energy prices – but the changes agreed on Wednesday respond to requests from governments including Poland and Italy to curb the ETS's contribution to electricity costs. EU countries' ambassadors agreed in a closed-door meeting to stop removing excess CO2 permits from the market, as is currently done, two EU diplomats told Reuters. Instead, spare CO2 permits would be retained in a special "market stability reserve" as a supply buffer that could be released into the ETS market to counter price spikes. Advertisement The ETS obliges big polluters like power plants and factories in Europe to buy permits to cover their CO2 emissions, and trades spare carbon permits in a market where their price fluctuates daily. At present, if there are more than 400 million CO2 permits in the market's stability reserve (MSR), the excess is deleted. The MSR is designed to release 75 million extra permits into the ETS, if the EU carbon price more than doubles. Countries agreed that no spare CO2 permits will be cancelled until 2030, according to a draft of their agreement seen by Reuters. From 2031, if there are more than 800 million permits in the MSR, the excess will be cancelled. This threshold will then decrease each year. EU countries will now negotiate the final rules with the European Parliament, before they take effect. On average, the ETS contributes 11% to EU industries' electricity bills, although in countries with fossil fuel-heavy power mixes like Poland it is far higher. It is lower in countries with large amounts of low-carbon nuclear and renewable energy, like Sweden. (Reporting by Kate Abnett; Editing by Andrew Cawthorne)

artigo.texto: What we know about Delaware County’s potential data center plan, ‘Project Trainer’ Link Logistics is testing the waters for a data center that would sit around 100 feet from homes in Trainer, Pennsylvania. This story is part of the WHYY News Climate Desk, bringing you news and solutions for our changing region. From the Poconos to the Jersey Shore to the mouth of the Delaware Bay, what do you want to know about climate change? What would you like us to cover? Get in touch. Delaware County residents are organizing in response to a potential data center proposal. Trainer Borough, with a population of less than 2,000, is located about 10 miles south of Philadelphia International Airport along the Delaware River and is also home to the Monroe Energy oil refinery. Borough officials gave preliminary zoning approval last month for a data center to be built in an industrial and residential area along Ridge Road at the borough’s border with Lower Chichester Township. But the property owner’s lawyer says no formal proposal has been made. Here’s what we know. Is a data center coming to Trainer, Pa.? It’s too soon to say. There is currently “no formal application” for a data center in Trainer Borough, according to a statement posted on the borough’s website. Link Logistics is currently advertising the roughly 24-acre site as a build-to-suit warehouse called the Juniper Pointe Logistics Center. But in August, Link Logistics’ lawyer requested a preliminary zoning determination from the borough for a “proposed data center” at the site. WHYY News obtained a copy of the correspondence through a public records request. What do we know about the possible data center proposal? Link Logistics’ request, signed by lawyer Leonard B. Altieri III, included a “preliminary test fit” drawing showing a two-story data center labeled “Project Trainer.” The data center would use 120 megawatts of electricity and would likely include a 3-acre electrical substation to connect the data center to the electric utility’s infrastructure and backup gas or diesel-powered generators, according to Altieri’s letter. The development would also likely include a security building. Cooling of the data center equipment would be done using a closed-loop system, Altieri said in an interview. It would not require a supply of process water, according to his letter. Altieri said that none of these details are final because his client has not yet decided whether to pursue the data center project. “No application has been submitted and no plans have been designed,” he said in an interview. “We’re purely at the due diligence phase of this.” Asked whether PECO had received any request for service at the site, a spokesperson said the company cannot discuss potential customers or prospective customer projects for privacy and confidentiality reasons. Where would the data center be located? The site where Link Logistics is considering building a data center is located at 4001 Ridge Road, mostly in Trainer. A small portion on the southwest edge of the site is located in Lower Chichester Township. The site sits between Congoleum, a vinyl floor manufacturing facility, a small self-storage facility and a construction equipment supplier. Rows of homes sit roughly 100 feet away from the site across Ridge Road to the northwest and about 200 feet away across a set of train tracks to the southeast of the site. What happens next? Trainer Borough’s zoning officer, Charles Remaley, confirmed to Altieri in August that the property’s industrial zoning allows for development of a data center “by-right.” “The proposed development is therefore permitted with respect to use,” Remaley wrote. “Any Required site plan, subdivision, building, engineering, environmental, or other Governmental approvals shall be obtained separately as applicable.” If Link Logistics chooses to pursue the data center project, it will need to submit a site plan for approval by the Trainer Borough Planning Commission and Borough Council. The project would also likely need environmental permits from the state of Pennsylvania, including stormwater and erosion control permits and air pollution permits for backup generators. Gov. Josh Shapiro recently signed an executive order reserving a more efficient process of environmental permit review for data center proposals that commit to meeting the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development, or GRID, standards and have already received local approval. Link Logistics also sought preliminary zoning approval from Lower Chichester Township, for the portion of the site that lies within that municipality. In a letter dated July 22, Frank E. Hendron, Lower Chichester Township zoning officer, said a data center is not a permitted use under the site’s current zoning. The preliminary test fit drawing included in Altieri’s August letter to Trainer Borough shows the data center building located only within the portion of the site located in Trainer. A Link Logistics spokesperson said in a written statement provided by Altieri on Monday that the company is “pleased to have received a favorable Preliminary Opinion from Trainer Borough.” “This is not a building permit; any project, should we decide to pursue, will require an application and Borough approvals,” the spokesperson wrote. The environmental advocacy group Chester Residents Concerned for Quality Living is hosting a community meeting about the possible proposal Sept. 23 in Boothwyn. artigo.texto: EU Backs Carbon Market Changes to Curb Price Spikes - EU countries agreed to retain surplus carbon permits until 2030, creating a larger buffer that could help contain sharp price increases in the Emissions Trading System. - The changes follow pressure from Poland, Italy and other governments seeking to limit carbon costs as Europe contends with higher energy prices linked to the Iran conflict. - The ETS contributes about 11% of industrial electricity bills on average, although the impact varies sharply depending on national power mixes. European Union countries have backed changes to the bloc’s carbon market that would preserve surplus emissions permits as protection against future price spikes. EU ambassadors agreed on Wednesday to stop cancelling excess CO2 allowances held in the Emissions Trading System’s Market Stability Reserve, according to diplomats and a draft agreement seen by Reuters. Instead, the permits would remain available as a supply buffer. The EU could release allowances into the market when carbon prices rise sharply. The European Commission proposed the changes in April as governments sought ways to contain energy costs following a surge in fuel prices linked to the Iran conflict. The decision now sets up negotiations with the European Parliament over the final rules. Building a larger carbon market buffer The ETS requires major emitters, including power plants and industrial facilities, to buy permits covering their CO2 emissions. Companies can trade allowances, creating a carbon price that fluctuates with market conditions. The Market Stability Reserve, or MSR, manages excess supply within that system. Under existing rules, allowances above a specified level in the reserve can be permanently removed. If the MSR contains more than 400 million permits, excess allowances are currently cancelled. The mechanism also provides protection against rapid price increases. It can release 75 million additional allowances if the EU carbon price more than doubles. Under the agreement reached by member states, no surplus CO2 permits would be cancelled until 2030. From 2031, cancellation would resume if the reserve contains more than 800 million allowances. That threshold would then decline each year. The shift effectively gives policymakers a larger stock of permits that could become available during periods of market stress. Energy costs put pressure on climate policy The proposal comes as European governments confront renewed concern over energy affordability and industrial competitiveness. The ETS is not the primary driver of Europe’s recent energy price increases. However, carbon costs feed into electricity prices, particularly in markets that remain heavily dependent on fossil fuels. On average, the ETS accounts for about 11% of electricity bills for EU industry. The burden varies considerably across member states. RELATED ARTICLE: EU Deforestation Law Could Reshape Global Coffee Trade Countries with fossil fuel-heavy electricity systems, including Poland, face a substantially larger impact. Nations with significant nuclear and renewable generation, such as Sweden, experience a smaller effect. That disparity has sharpened debate over how the EU should balance carbon pricing with competitiveness and energy security. Poland and Italy have been among the governments pressing Brussels to limit the ETS contribution to electricity costs. EU faces a carbon pricing balancing act For policymakers, the challenge is to introduce greater flexibility without weakening the price incentive at the heart of European climate policy. The ETS remains the EU’s flagship tool for reducing emissions from power generation and energy-intensive industry. A meaningful carbon price raises the cost of pollution and strengthens the economics of lower-carbon alternatives. At the same time, volatile prices can create uncertainty for companies making long-term investment decisions. High carbon costs can also compound pressure on manufacturers already exposed to elevated electricity and fuel prices. Retaining allowances rather than permanently cancelling them gives policymakers another potential tool for managing that volatility. It also changes expectations about future permit supply, an important consideration for carbon traders and regulated companies. For corporate leaders and investors, the negotiations with Parliament will therefore matter beyond short-term carbon prices. The final design will influence compliance costs, hedging strategies and expectations for future allowance scarcity. The debate also reflects a wider challenge facing European climate policy. Brussels is trying to maintain credible decarbonisation incentives while protecting industrial competitiveness during another period of energy market disruption. Member states have now established their negotiating position. The European Parliament will help determine how much flexibility ultimately enters the system, and how the EU balances carbon market stability with its longer-term emissions goals.
