artigo.texto: Este é o quinto artigo da série sobre a imersão que realizamos no setor elétrico australiano em maio de 2026. Nos textos anteriores, tratei de alguns dos temas que mais chamaram minha atenção ao longo da missão: a necessidade de uma visão sistêmica da transição energética, a evolução institucional e regulatória, a transformação da rede e, mais recentemente, o papel crescente dos recursos energéticos distribuídos. Neste artigo, avanço para outro tema que esteve presente em praticamente todas as nossas conversas na Austrália: o armazenamento de energia em baterias. O momento é particularmente oportuno para trazer essa discussão ao Brasil. Em dezembro de 2026, o país dará um passo importante para a inserção do armazenamento de energia em larga escala no SIN (Sistema Interligado Nacional). Estão previstos para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro os primeiros leilões brasileiros dedicados à contratação de sistemas de armazenamento em baterias. O desenho adotado é o de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência: serão contratados sistemas autônomos de armazenamento para disponibilização de potência ao sistema, com contratos de 15 anos e início de suprimento em agosto de 2028. A resposta inicial do mercado chama atenção. Segundo a EPE (Empresa de Pesquisa Energética), foram cadastrados 6.091 projetos, totalizando 296.807 MW de potência. Evidentemente, cadastramento não significa habilitação, contratação ou mesmo que todos esses projetos tenham o mesmo grau de maturidade. Ainda assim, a dimensão dos números demonstra o interesse existente no desenvolvimento desse novo mercado no Brasil. É um avanço relevante. Mas uma das principais conclusões que trouxe da experiência australiana é que a contratação de potência pode ser apenas o começo da história. Ao longo das reuniões com universidades, governo, empresas de energia, investidores e agentes de mercado, ficou claro que uma bateria pode desempenhar um papel econômico muito mais amplo. Mais do que um equipamento que armazena energia para devolvê-la algumas horas depois, o BESS pode ser um ativo capaz de responder a diferentes necessidades do sistema e capturar diferentes fontes de valor. Essa talvez seja uma das discussões que o Brasil precisará enfrentar depois de colocar de pé seus primeiros projetos de grande escala. Da bateria ao ativo Na Austrália, nossa discussão sobre armazenamento apareceu em praticamente todas as etapas da missão, mas sob perspectivas diferentes. Na UNSW e no CEEM (Centre for Energy and Environmental Markets) a discussão ajudou a colocar o armazenamento dentro de uma visão mais ampla do sistema. O ponto não é simplesmente adicionar baterias à rede, mas entender qual serviço determinado recurso pode prestar e como ele interage com geração, consumo, rede e mercado. Essa diferença parece conceitual, mas tem consequências econômicas importantes. Uma bateria pode deslocar energia no tempo. Pode carregar em momentos de abundância de geração e descarregar quando o sistema precisa de energia. Pode responder rapidamente a variações de frequência. Pode contribuir para a integração de fontes renováveis. Pode estar associada a uma planta solar ou eólica. E, dependendo das regras existentes, pode participar de diferentes mercados. Foi justamente essa dimensão econômica que apareceu com força na conversa com a Aurora Energy Research. Ao discutirmos a evolução do mercado australiano, ficou evidente a importância da volatilidade de preços para a economia do armazenamento. Períodos de preços muito baixos – inclusive negativos – alternados com períodos de preços elevados criam oportunidades para ativos capazes de deslocar energia no tempo. Nesse ambiente, a bateria não possui necessariamente uma única fonte de receita. Arbitragem de preços, serviços ancilares e diferentes estruturas contratuais podem se combinar na formação da receita do ativo. É o chamado revenue stacking: a possibilidade de extrair valor de diferentes aplicações utilizando a mesma infraestrutura. A experiência australiana oferece exemplos concretos dessa lógica. Projetos de armazenamento naquele mercado combinam receitas de arbitragem com a prestação de serviços de FCAS (controle de frequência) mostrando que o valor do ativo pode decorrer de diferentes serviços e não apenas da compra e venda de energia. Esse ponto é particularmente relevante para o Brasil. O valor da bateria depende também do mercado Durante nossa reunião com a Samsung C&T, o armazenamento apareceu associado ao desenvolvimento de projetos de energia e às dificuldades criadas por uma rede que precisa acompanhar a transformação acelerada da matriz australiana. Também discutimos projetos híbridos, combinando geração renovável e BESS. Essa combinação é importante porque muda a forma como enxergamos a bateria. Ela deixa de ser apenas uma resposta emergencial à falta de potência e passa a integrar a própria estratégia de desenvolvimento e operação dos projetos. Em nossa conversa com a Aurora Energy Research, surgiu uma provocação semelhante: um portfólio integrado de geração solar e armazenamento pode ter capacidade de monetização diferente daquela obtida pelos ativos analisados isoladamente. Isso também nos levou a discutir um problema muito conhecido hoje no Brasil: o curtailment. Baterias evidentemente não eliminam, sozinhas, as restrições estruturais de transmissão nem constituem solução universal para cortes de geração. Mas a possibilidade de armazenar energia em determinados momentos e deslocar sua entrega no tempo adiciona uma nova variável à gestão desses ativos e do próprio sistema. A conclusão que extraio dessas conversas é que o valor econômico de uma bateria não está apenas na bateria. Está também no desenho do mercado no qual ela opera. Software, dados e trading também fazem parte do ativo Outro aprendizado da Austrália foi perceber o quanto a digitalização está associada ao armazenamento. artigo.texto: The local government saga over a massive data center planned just northwest of Billings continues. In a letter signed this week, Yellowstone County commissioners asked local legislators to review a new law they said is stopping them from regulating the 5,000-acre project near Broadview by developer Quantica Infrastructure. The letter, approved Tuesday by Commissioners Mark Morse, Mike Waters and Chris White, is addressed to the “Members of the Yellowstone County Legislative Delegation” and asks them to “refine” a 2025 law called the Right to Compute Act. The act passed the House 61-38 and the Senate 50-0. It says any government action that hampers the freedom to own and use software, algorithms and other technologies must be “narrowly tailored” to protect the public, and that the government can’t enact those restrictions if there are “less restrictive means” available. Commissioners described the law as overly broad and said it “meaningfully limits the County’s ability to regulate data center development within its jurisdiction.” Large-scale data centers, they wrote, use a lot of electricity and water, create noise and strain public infrastructure and emergency services. “Counties have traditionally addressed such impacts through ordinary land use, zoning, permitting, and public health and safety regulation,” the letter said. As written, commissioners pointed out, the Right to Compute Act sets a high legal standard for any county action that would affect the data center. “That standard is difficult to meet and creates real uncertainty about whether the County may continue to exercise its customary regulatory authority over these developments,” commissioners wrote. “This creates a corresponding chilling effect on the County’s ability to protect its residents, infrastructure, and natural resources.” Commissioners asked the local legislative delegation to amend the law in 2027 to make clear it doesn’t change counties’ or cities’ legal authority to regulate siting, construction and other operations of data centers “through zoning, permitting, and public health and safety measures.” The Montana Legislature next meets in January. Meanwhile, local opponents of the Quantica data center are forging ahead with efforts to allow voters to weigh in on the project. Broadview resident Kassi Solberg is again leading efforts to create a ballot initiative that would require approval from two-thirds of voters participating in the county election before data centers could start or resume operations in Yellowstone County. That effort failed this summer. Solberg and others collected more than 14,000 signatures — the requirement was 16,560 — ahead of an August deadline before being told by county officials that local election administrators had calculated the deadline incorrectly. Officials determined that the new, accurate deadline was July 13 — a date that had already passed. Now Solberg aims to have an initiative approved for the local election slated for May 4, 2027. Solberg and her attorney, Democratic Eastern District Congressional candidate Brian Miller, expect more legal challenges to their effort. In a Thursday interview, Miller told Montana Free Press that he had revised the initiative language and that he thought the new version has a better chance at surviving legal scrutiny. “But I think they’re going to take a shot at it,” he said. Solberg’s first ballot initiative was challenged in court by county officials, who asked a judge to clarify whether the initiative could appear on the ballot. The county cited possible legal complications from the Right to Compute Act, which sparked this week’s letter to lawmakers, and a recent Montana Supreme Court ruling, Treasure County v. Edlund, dealing with regulations for wind energy development. After the regular discussion meeting Thursday, commissioners met with staff from the county attorney’s office in a closed-door session. According to the public meeting agenda, the topic for discussion was “Data Center Initiative.” During public comment, local resident Jack Hanson noted that closed meetings of public bodies are allowed only in limited circumstances. “As a member of the public I ask that you be perfectly clear about the specific topic of the meeting,” Hanson said. In response, Chief Civil County Attorney Steve Williams specified that the group would discuss “litigation” in the private session, one of the allowable reasons for closing meetings to the public. artigo.texto: Chinese battery manufacturer CATL has unveiled its latest commercial vehicle battery platform, with the new Tectrans II designed to deliver up to 1,000 km of range for heavy-duty trucks. The battery was unveiled at IAA Transportation 2026 in Hanover, Germany, and has been developed as a modular platform for different commercial vehicle applications and operating requirements. CATL says the platform supports different battery configurations to meet varying energy capacity and payload requirements, while being compatible with both e-axle and central-drive architectures. Designed for different truck applications Tectrans II can also switch between charging and battery swapping, giving operators greater flexibility depending on their operating requirements. CATL has standardised the battery’s external dimensions, electrical interfaces and communication protocols. According to the company, this allows battery technologies and pack designs to evolve without requiring major changes to the vehicle platform. The modular approach is also intended to reduce vehicle development times for manufacturers. CATL says it can shorten development cycles by up to 50per cent and reduce research and development costs by 60–70per cent. Up to 1,000 km of range The maximum configuration of the Tectrans II is claimed to provide up to 1,000 km of driving range, while megawatt-level fast charging can take the battery to 80per cent in 25 minutes. The battery has a gravimetric energy density of 170 Wh/kg, which CATL says is around 13per cent above the industry average. At the same battery capacity, the higher energy density can allow a vehicle to carry approximately 0.6 tonnes of additional payload. CATL has also incorporated a full-tab low-impedance design, which it says delivers 96per cent system round-trip efficiency. The company says this can reduce charging losses and increase the amount of usable energy available during operations. Built for long-term operation Tectrans II has been engineered for a 12-year, 1.5-million-kilometre service life while retaining 70per cent of its capacity, according to CATL. The battery incorporates physical protection against impacts and corrosion, alongside a maintenance-focused design. CATL says the system incorporates architecture redundancy, precise fault diagnosis and cybersecurity protection. Independent battery management system control can isolate a failed branch while allowing the remaining branches to continue supplying power. The battery also uses insulation fault-location technology to distinguish whether an insulation issue originates in the battery or another part of the vehicle, which CATL says can help speed up troubleshooting. Targeting commercial vehicle electrification CATL Executive President of Overseas Business Akin Li said commercial vehicle electrification represented a new phase of the global energy transition. “Commercial vehicle electrification is emerging as the third wave of the global energy transition,” Mr Li said. “Across products, energy, services and ecosystem, CATL is poised to work with partners around the world to catch this third wave.” The company also signed a memorandum of understanding with DHL Group at IAA Transportation 2026 to explore the development of green freight corridors across Europe, combining DHL’s logistics expertise with CATL’s battery and electrification technologies. artigo.texto: A new company has a plan to make the dirty gas turbines powering data centers more efficient: liquid carbon dioxide. American Supercritical came out of stealth Wednesday, announcing $8 million in funding. It wants to retrofit inefficient gas turbines that many data centers rely on for power with units that can generate more power, without adding more emissions (though the gas-fired turbines will continue to emit carbon pollution). The technology can also theoretically be used on a wide variety of energy sources at a time when power demand is skyrocketing. “We want to start with gas turbines but eventually expand beyond that,” says cofounder Simon Shuham. Most large gas-fired power plants in the United States use an array of heat engines in what’s known as a combined-cycle process: First, turbines generate electricity from burning compressed air and natural gas, then a separate engine uses the hot exhaust to make steam and create additional energy. But for a variety of reasons, data centers across the US have opted to power their operations with what are known as simple-cycle turbines, and exclude the steam component. These turbines are much less efficient than combined-cycle plants. Usually, only about 35 percent of the energy from simple-cycle turbines is converted to electricity, while the rest escapes as exhaust. (In combined-cycle plants, that figure hovers closer to 60 to 65 percent.) That exhaust includes greenhouse gases, making plants that run on simple-cycle turbines a much worse choice for the environment than combined-cycle plants. The size of some of these plants combined with their inefficiency is a recipe for climate disaster. A massive data-center power plant in Texas that Amazon is building with just simple-cycle turbines, for instance, is permitted to emit more than 33 million tons of greenhouse gases per year—more than the annual total of some small countries. But all these small, inefficient turbines could be a great match for supercritical CO2 technology, American Supercritical’s founders say. Carbon dioxide becomes supercritical when it’s pressurized and held at a certain temperature. In this state, it gets the density of liquid but still behaves like a gas, meaning it can move energy more efficiently through much smaller amounts of equipment. American Supercritical wants to attach its units to small gas turbines and help generate more energy. While the turbines themselves would still use gas, the supercritical CO2 unit can use the hot exhaust generated from those turbines to create additional electricity. Instead of using that heat to boil water and create steam, the heat is transferred directly by the pressurized CO2 to generate additional energy with no additional emissions. “We’re essentially building miniature combined-cycle plants,” says Shuham. Using supercritical CO2 also can eliminate or greatly reduce water use in the power generation process—something that’s drawn intense scrutiny when it comes to data centers. Importantly, the CO2 involved operates in a closed-loop system, meaning that it doesn’t have to be refilled. Cofounder Matthew Carlson, who researched supercritical CO2 for more than a decade, likens it to refrigeration systems that circulate CO2 to facilitate cooling. The company plans to initially sell a 10-megawatt unit—relatively small by gas plant standards. By American Supercritical’s math, adding supercritical CO2 units could increase turbines’ efficiency by up to 50 percent without adding any more greenhouse gas emissions or water use. But retrofitting all of the country’s inefficient gas turbines powering data centers with supercritical CO2 units won’t reduce emissions to zero. Natural gas production and use, even with efficient turbines, warms the planet. Data centers also represent a massive new source of pollution—right at a time when the world needs to be scaling back on its use. Using supercritical CO2 for power has been studied for more than 50 years in US national labs. Over the past two decades, research has moved away from theory toward trying out practical applications, assisted by technological breakthroughs that help with the pressurization process. Doug Hofer, an adviser to American Supercritical who spent two decades at GE as a turbine engineer, says that one important innovation has been the development of more compact and more affordable heat exchangers—devices that help both heat and cool the CO2. American Supercritical isn’t the only company trying to bring this technology to market, says Subith Vasu, a professor of engineering at the University of Central Florida, who runs a lab at the school’s Center for Advanced Turbomachinery and Energy Research. The companies still have hurdles to overcome to achieve commercial success. “Whenever you are venturing into new technologies, you need to have all the associated components, the supply chain,” in place, he says. Technical challenges also abound, he adds, “and cost has been a huge issue.” Hofer says that part of the delay has also simply been because larger companies are satisfied with the performance of traditional power plants and unwilling to invest in different technologies—and turbine makers are not interested in funding potential competitors. “It’s the innovator’s dilemma, right?” he says. “Getting this [technology] out there needs to have an outside influence.” The $7 trillion set to be invested in data centers globally by 2030 has helped open up a whole new potential market, especially for an industry racing to get as much power on the grid as it possibly can to come out ahead in the AI race. “There’s this incredible willingness to pay [for power], but they’re bottlenecked,” says Shuham. “The goal is to come in here, retrofit their existing systems, and give them the ability to build additional data centers—or get rid of some of the gas turbines.” Earlier this year, China announced that operations started at the world’s first geothermal plant using supercritical CO2. artigo.texto: Moore signs order setting new Maryland oversight, review standards for data centers MARYLAND (WBFF) — Maryland is tightening oversight of large data center projects as concerns grow about transparency, environmental impacts and rising electricity costs. Gov. Wes Moore on Wednesday signed an executive order setting new guidelines that companies should follow when building data centers in Maryland, including a standardized review process and new state oversight of projects. The Moore administration said the changes are intended to address concerns about transparency, environmental impacts and potential effects on rising electricity costs. The order will apply to data centers that cover 25 megawatts or more, creating a single state standard and review process for projects seeking permits, state incentives or letters of support, according to the order. It also creates the Maryland Data Center Task Force, which will review every covered data center project and maintain the Data Center Dashboard, an online platform that tracks data center development. The task force will include members from the Maryland Energy Administration and state Departments of Commerce, Labor, Environment, Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Planning. “We are establishing clear safeguards to ensure Marylanders do not foot the bill, our people benefit, community voices are heard, and our environment is protected — all while centering transparency and accountability throughout the process,” Moore said in a statement. Moore’s order comes as Baltimore County said it will extend its pause on data center development through the end of 2027, giving county officials more than a year to continue weighing community concerns and potential guardrails on the facilities. artigo.texto: Americans’ views on data centers have turned more negative American attitudes toward data centers have turned noticeably more negative over the course of 2026, according to a new Pew Research Center survey. 54% of U.S. adults now say data centers are mostly bad for the environment, up from 39% in January. Half say they hurt home energy costs (up from 38%), and 49% say they harm quality of life for people living nearby (up from 30%). Only 4% see a mostly positive impact in any of these areas. Views on the economic benefits are more divided. Roughly equal shares, between 21% and 24%, call data centers mostly good or mostly bad for local jobs and tax revenue. But the share seeing a negative effect on jobs rose from 15% to 24%, and on tax revenue from 12% to 21%. Six in ten Americans say they would be uncomfortable with a new data center in their area. That includes 54% of Republicans, 68% of Democrats and 81% of liberal Democrats. Democrats remain more critical overall, but Republican opinion is shifting too: 42% now say data centers harm nearby residents’ quality of life, up from 24% in January. The change is especially notable in rural areas, where most new facilities are planned. Half of rural residents now see data centers as bad for the environment, compared with 32% at the start of the year. The findings come amid spreading local protests against new construction. President Trump remains a strong supporter of data centers. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, however, imposed a statewide moratorium in August, and Democratic governors in Pennsylvania and Illinois have moved toward tighter oversight. Public awareness is also growing. 35% of adults say they have heard a lot about data centers, up from 25% in January, while 12% say they have not heard of them at all. The survey of 10,548 U.S. adults was conducted July 20 to Aug. 9, 2026.

artigo.texto: Rarely do you see complete consensus across local government, public safety agencies, the public, and agricultural leadership. Yet on the proposed 40-acre, 300 megawatt Corby Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), the entire community speaks with one unified voice. The Vacaville City Council, Solano County Board of Supervisors, Dixon Fire Protection District, Vacaville Firefighters Association, Solano County Farm Bureau, Solano Orderly Growth Committee, and thousands of residents all strongly oppose placing this massive 40-acre facility on rural land near homes. Local leaders agree that a dangerous industrial facility of this scale, carrying severe risks of uncontrollable thermal runaway fires, toxic smoke, constant noise, and permanent visual blight, belongs in designated industrial zones like Lambie Industrial Park, where proper safety buffers protect our communities. Yet, Assemblymember Lori Wilson stands alone against her own community. When Keep Vacaville Safe met with her to urge a “no” vote on state legislation (SB 254) that grants energy developers broader authority to override local safety ordinances and local laws, she ignored our warnings and voted “yes” anyway. Combined with her refusal to amend AB 205, the law which gives the state complete authority to permit BESS facilities, she voted to give NextEra the legal leverage to bypass Solano County’s laws. When asked if she would oppose the Corby Project and stand with Solano County, she refused. Why would our state representative ignore local agencies, firefighters, and county and city officials in her own district to vote for state overrides? Public campaign finance records may reveal the answer: Assembly Member Wilson has accepted campaign contributions from NextEra Energy, the parent company behind the Corby project, dating back to 2022, when NextEra first targeted unincorporated Vacaville. Instead of standing shoulder-to-shoulder with local firefighters, county and city leaders, and the families she was elected to represent, Assemblymember Wilson chose to vote for laws that empower an out-of-state energy giant over her own constituents. She took corporate energy money and lined up behind NextEra’s interests rather than ours. When an elected official accepts corporate money and then repeatedly votes to strip away her constituents’ ability to protect their own neighborhoods, public trust is shattered. Vacaville deserves representation that puts community unity and public safety ahead of corporate campaign cash. — Sarah Dunn/President, Keep Vacaville Safe

artigo.texto: Illinois landowners can retain ownership and earn fixed lease income while Lightstar develops standalone battery storage, community solar, and agrivoltaics statewide FULTON COUNTY, Ill., Sept. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Lightstar Renewables, a national leader in community solar and dual-use (agrivoltaic) solar development, today confirmed the continued expansion of its active Illinois portfolio across three service lines: community solar, agrivoltaic solar, and battery energy storage systems (BESS). Lightstar develops these projects on private land throughout Illinois, guiding landowners through an origination-to-operation process that preserves land ownership, delivers fixed long-term lease income, and keeps land in productive use. For landowners, municipalities, and clean energy partners asking who develops community solar and battery energy storage in Illinois, Lightstar's permitted, market-ready project pipeline offers a proven answer. Learn more about Lightstar's Illinois development program at lightstar.com/solutions/illinois. Illinois' Clean Energy Momentum Is Creating Demand for Proven Developers Illinois has emerged as one of the most active clean energy markets in the Midwest, driven by the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act (CEJA) and its target of 100% clean energy by 2050. Supportive programs continue to accelerate deployment: the Illinois Shines Adjustable Block Program opens its 2026–2027 cycle on June 1, 2026, and the Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act (CRGA) expands community solar while permitting co-location of projects up to 10 MW on a single parcel or adjacent properties. In 2026, Illinois also enacted statewide energy storage legislation establishing new storage targets, reinforcing demand for reliable, grid-responsive infrastructure. Lightstar actively monitors these programs and evaluates every Illinois project for eligibility - a track record that has positioned the company as one of the state's most experienced community solar and battery storage developers. US Highway 136: A Community-First Solar Project in Fulton County Lightstar's Illinois portfolio is in part anchored by the US Highway 136 Solar Project in Fulton County, a 2.75 MW AC array that captures the company's community-first approach to development. Developing renewable energy is about more than putting power on the grid, it is about building a better future for the people who live nearby, from generating reliable power to engaging local students. Generating reliable Fulton County solar energy brings major advantages to the area. The facility supplies clean power directly to the local distribution grid, so the energy Lightstar produces here stays here, reducing the community's shared reliance on fossil fuels. Beyond environmental benefits, the project strengthens the local economy: constructing and operating the solar array creates new local jobs, and the facility generates consistent tax revenue for the county that supports essential community services and infrastructure, making Lewistown clean energy a win for everyone. Engaging the Next Generation and Preserving Local History During early site planning, Lightstar's team discovered prehistoric artifacts on the property. The items were carefully cataloged to preserve local history, and the discovery became a chance to connect with local students. A Lightstar team visited VIT Community Unit School District #2 to talk about environmental science and historical preservation: during an elementary school assembly, field expert Amanda brought a hands-on archaeological "dig kit" for show and tell and asked students to imagine what people 100 years from now might learn about them from the items they leave behind. Later that day, Amanda met with junior high and high school students for a Q&A on green career pathways, fielding wide-ranging questions about the renewable energy industry from an engaged audience. Giving Back: Investing in VIT School District's Athletic Fields Lightstar's commitment to Fulton County goes beyond the meter. The company is making a donation to VIT Community Unit School District #2 to help fund renovations to the district's athletic field, and as part of the partnership, Lightstar's logo will be displayed on the field as a proud community sponsor. It's a tangible way for Lightstar to invest in the same community that welcomed its team into classrooms and gymnasiums, turning a single project into a lasting relationship with the students and neighbors nearby. Senior Development Manager Kyle McAdam spearheads the US Highway 136 initiative and works to ensure Lightstar upholds its mission of community stewardship at every step. "We believe that clean energy development must work hand-in-hand with the local community," says McAdam. "By protecting the land, engaging with incredible students right here in Fulton County, and now investing directly in the VIT athletic field, we ensure this project leaves a positive, lasting mark on the region for decades to come." A Simple, Landowner-First Model For Illinois landowners, Lightstar's value proposition is straightforward. Property owners retain full ownership, sign lease terms of 20 or more years, and receive fixed, weather-independent lease income. In Illinois, that means flexible, low-impact development options across community solar and standalone battery energy storage systems (BESS), with end-to-end EPC management so landowners retain ownership, continue compatible land uses where possible, and collect fixed lease income without taking on any operational burden. That model has helped build a national pipeline of more than 1,000 MW across 15 states. Illinois landowners can request a free, no-obligation site assessment at lightstar.com/solutions/illinois to learn whether their property qualifies for community solar, agrivoltaics, or standalone battery storage. artigo.texto: Growth, water contradiction Colorado Springs continues to grow. The Gazette often reports on new companies preparing to move here. That means many new jobs for people who live here and others who move here with the companies. The military presence is strong in the Springs and seems to expand with additional personnel, especially at the present time, for Space Force and Fort Carson. All the above are great for our economy. Recommended Stories But then there is the water situation. The Gazette’s front-page article on the 19th describes the current low-water situation and the concern that it could worsen and require restrictions. Companies will require water for their operations. Employees will require new homes or apartments, and that means additional water use. A big debate is underway about a California company that wants to build a huge AI data center at the west end of Garden of the Gods. The company claims it won’t use as much water as other AI data centers. They estimate they will only use 200,000 gallons of water annually. That number is self‑reported by the developer, not independently verified and could result in much more water being used. Colorado Springs is one of the few, if not the only large cities that doesn’t have a river passing through to supply water. Most of our water comes from the Colorado River and Arkansas River Basins. Both depend on high-elevation snowpack, but the snowpack has trended lower over decades. Snow melts earlier, reducing summer flows and hotter temperatures increase evaporation from reservoirs. That means what we rely on for water is becoming less predictable. The combination of city growth + climate stress + industrial expansion means the water situation could tighten significantly over the next decade. So, we are caught in a situation where growth could contribute to a better economy, but the shortage of water could result in restrictions for water use and water costing us more. Do we want more growth with new businesses and more people and take a chance with our water supply? Can we ever come to an agreement on this issue? Vern Swim Colorado Springs Children belong in the conversation We talk about childcare availability as if it is a yes-or-no question. Is there a spot? Great. Problem solved. Except children do not teleport, and neither do parents. School lets out around 3 p.m. After-school care may get a family to 5:30 or 6. That works beautifully if the parent also stops working at 5 and works somewhere nearby. Plenty of us do neither. Pharmacists, nurses, first responders, retail workers, restaurant employees and other people our community expects to be available evenings and weekends still have to get from work to the child. If my shift ends at 8 p.m., childcare that closes at 6 p.m. is not “available” to me. Frankly, childcare that closes at 8 p.m. is not much better if I still have to drive there. That is the part of the childcare conversation we keep treating like a footnote. Cost matters. The number of slots matters. But usable hours matter, too. So do school breaks, teacher workdays and early-release days. A childcare system can look adequate on paper while leaving working families stitching together the last few hours of every day with relatives, sitters, favors and crossed fingers. Colorado Springs talks constantly about growth, workforce shortages and infrastructure. Childcare belongs in that same conversation. A road that stops three miles before the destination is not a complete road. Neither is childcare that ends before the parent can get there. Danielle Lightsey, RPh Monument Encouraging lifelong readers Recently the Gazette included a quote from Albert Einstein that stuck with me as it relates to education. It reads, “What counts can’t always be counted; what can be counted doesn’t always count”. In elementary school, many priorities compete for the fixed time in a school day. You can’t do it all in six hours. However, in many classrooms, one of the items being omitted is a daily read-aloud time. This is when the teacher reads a well-chosen book to the class that not only entertains but serves as an excellent stepping-off point for all things literary. Discussions, written responses, noticing literary techniques, empathizing with the characters, sharing a class laugh – or cry, all contribute pricelessly to the development of a young reader and to their humanity. Importantly, hearing a powerful, engaging story helps students develop an affection for reading that increases the likelihood they will become lifelong readers. Some experts say that the pressures of acquiring 21st century learning skills do not leave time for something as dated as read-aloud time. I would ask them, for the roughly 25% of students whose parents didn’t read aloud to them as preschoolers and don’t read aloud to them now, when will they ever hear and enjoy a quality story if not in the classroom? Benjamin Fromuth Sr. Colorado Springs Make AI work for its living We wait like the residents of the long-ago little TV town in Andy Griffith’s Mayberry, awaiting something new defined by old ideas. We witness the Fourth Industrial Revolution and decry AI and its emergence through data centers. Just a hundred years ago, “talkies” were awaiting sound in motion pictures; a woman had yet to be the first to cross the Atlantic by plane; Thomas Edison still had six more years left; etc., etc., etc. This Fourth Industrial Revolution followed mechanization, mass production and automation in roughly 100-year leaps starting in 1760. Germany defined the Fourth Industrial Revolution in 2015 as cyber-physical systems. In less than a hundred years, we have come a long way. artigo.texto: At Tuesday’s Second Ward meeting, residents took the opportunity to speak out against a data center’s potential move into West Evanston, though Councilmember Krissie Harris said it’s too early to make any decision on the matter. Tuesday’s meeting followed the RoundTable reporting that an unnamed applicant filed a zoning analysis application with the city for “determination of use for a computer processing center” on Sept. 16. The application appeared on the Sept. 18 city manager’s report and is for a property in the Second Ward at 1265 Hartrey Ave. While the report did not provide further details, Planning Manager Liz Williams confirmed Monday night that the application is for what’s better known as a data center. About five residents attended the meeting in person at the Robert Crown Community Center and 20 joined virtually, mostly to discuss the data center application. According to a memo from Reed Beidler, the property manager for the Hartrey space, the zoning analysis application “asks that the City confirm that the use of a portion of an existing industrial building located at 1265 Hartrey Ave (approximately 20,000 sq. ft.) as a computer processing center is a Permitted Use” of the property under the city’s zoning code. Lark Management, the Evanston property management company that owns the space, last updated a listing for the portion of the property in question in August 2024. Beidler, who property records show is the taxpayer for the space, is listed as a contact for the rental. During Tuesday’s meeting, Harris said she previously met with the property owner about a separate “energy storage plant” in the space but was not aware of the data center possibility and had not yet read the zoning analysis application. “There has been no discussion about the data center,” she said. “I have not seen the proposal yet, and the property owner does want to meet with me about that. I don’t have an opinion yet.” Outside of Robert Crown on Tuesday, resident Michael Courier, a labor union worker, was handing out papers that read “no data centers in Evanston,” and he encouraged residents to speak at the upcoming City Council meeting on Sept. 28. “Data centers disproportionately use more energy and water than other technologies. Data centers also can cause noise pollution and destroy the peacefulness of our neighborhood,” Courier said. “Once the data center is created, few workers are needed to maintain the infrastructure of the building. AI is harming workers, and it is hurting our way of life. Evanston should not be complicit in the technologies that destroy what we hold dear and everything we love about the city.” Although Beidler’s memo identifies the property as 20,000 square feet, the actual size is 19,650 square feet, which one resident pointed out would fall just outside the city’s Healthy Buildings Ordinance. “That feels really icky,” the resident said. “Is this going to get past that ordinance, which is designed to force organizations that are large enough to have an impact on sustainability, on environmental prosperity? It feels like this is a way to cheat that system.” Harris said she plans to follow up with Beidler for a meeting to get clarity on the application. The large property, a former industrial building, also has vacant space from the closures of the Rebuilding Exchange and the WasteShed at 1245 Hartrey Ave. It still houses several other businesses and entities, including the Evanston Township High School Day School at 1233 Hartrey Ave. and Saint Errant Brewing at 2000 Dempster St. Margo Milanowski contributed to reporting

artigo.texto: Over the past few weeks, there have been growing concerns and speculation about the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) to dramatically impact life on Earth as we know it. However, at the same time, a very real but overlooked consequence of the global deployment of AI is actually taking place around the globe. According to a recent report issued by the non-profit environmental group Basel Action Network (BAN), the exponential growth of data centers to support AI will also lead to a “tsunami” of electronic waste (e-waste). The report estimates that e-waste directly connected with AI-supporting data centers will more than triple the annual rate of e-waste generation over the next 25 years. Data centers of all types include warehouse-size collections of computers and data servers that support the global infrastructure, including the growth and deployment of AI-related technologies. These computers and servers typically have a useful life of 2-5 years and will then need to be replaced with new equipment. In addition, the BAN Report says that existing systems may need to be replaced more frequently to support the capacity required for AI applications. Unless data center equipment is specifically designed for repair, reuse, or recycling, BAN projects that e-waste will result in 13 million metric tons annually by the year 2030. Read the Basel Action Network Report, “The Coming AI Waste Wave.”

artigo.texto: What if energy storage could be built directly into the materials that make up everyday products? Our Engineering, Chemistry and Anthropology departments are part of a major new project exploring materials that can combine energy storage and structural performance. Rethinking energy storage The five-year project, called EleComp (Electric Composites), brings together expertise from Durham University, Imperial College London and the University of Bristol. It is backed by a £7m Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) Programme Grant. EleComp aims to develop a new generation of multifunctional materials that challenge conventional ideas about batteries and structures. Researchers will focus on structural power composites, materials that combine mechanical strength with energy storage. Multifunctional materials Most products today use separate batteries that must be housed, protected and connected to the structures around them. Structural power composites offer a different approach. They could allow energy storage to become part of an object's structure rather than a separate component. In future, this could mean vehicle body panels, aircraft components or consumer products can perform both a structural role and store energy. Researchers believe this could lead to lighter, more resource-efficient designs. Tackling scientific challenges Developing materials that are both strong and effective at storing energy presents significant scientific challenges. The EleComp team will investigate how structural electrodes, electrolytes and material interfaces can be designed to balance mechanical performance with electrochemical function. The project will also develop new manufacturing, testing and modelling approaches to support future applications. Researchers will draw inspiration from natural systems and work across disciplines to better understand the performance and long-term potential of these materials. Development and optimisation Dr Natasha Shirshova from our Department of Engineering is coordinating Durham's work on EleComp. Our experts from Departments of Engineering and Chemistry will be leading the development of key materials at the heart of structural batteries, including advanced structural electrolytes and next-generation electrodes that combine strength with storage. Our researchers will also work to optimise how these materials interact and pioneer new testing methods to assess their mechanical and electrochemical performance simultaneously. Alongside this work, Durham is also central to shaping a sustainable roadmap to guide the responsible adoption of this technology across industry and beyond. Colleagues in our Anthropology department will lead an innovative approach to responsible innovation by coordinating collaborations between the different disciplines and stakeholders involved in the project. Potential benefits for society Structural energy storage materials have attracted increasing international attention. In 2025, the World Economic Forum identified structural energy storage materials as one of its leading emerging technologies. The technology could support advances in sectors including transport, aerospace, consumer electronics, healthcare and infrastructure. By combining multiple functions in a single material, researchers hope to reduce material use and improve overall efficiency. The project will also explore wider societal questions, examining how multifunctional materials could influence the design and use of future technologies.

artigo.texto: NEW YORK--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Sep 25, 2026-- NineDot Energy ®, the leading developer of community battery energy storage systems (BESS) in the New York City metro area, joined elected officials, policymakers, and community organizations to celebrate the ribbon-cutting of NineDot’s battery storage site in Hunts Point, The Bronx yesterday afternoon. This clean energy storage system will bring significant benefits to a community which has long suffered environmental injustice and disinvestment. artigo.texto: O potencial de transformar créditos de carbono em ativos financeiros. Além de servir a objetivos ambientais, os créditos de carbono estão sendo cada vez mais reconhecidos como um ativo capaz de se conectar com fluxos de capital internacionais. Báo Tin Tức•23/09/2026 Com o objetivo de estabelecer a Corporação Financeira Internacional do Vietnã (VIFC-DN) em Da Nang , a cidade está se esforçando para criar um ecossistema de financiamento de carbono, desde sistemas de medição, relatórios e avaliação (MRV) até ferramentas financeiras especializadas, abrindo assim mais oportunidades para mobilizar recursos para o crescimento verde. Do potencial de redução de emissões a ativos valiosos No processo de transição para um modelo de crescimento verde, o desafio não é apenas reduzir as emissões de gases de efeito estufa, mas também mensurar, verificar e traduzir os resultados dessa redução em valor econômico real. O Vietnã possui grande potencial para créditos de carbono provenientes da agricultura, silvicultura e energias renováveis; somente a região central pode explorar esse potencial em setores como o de café Robusta, pimenta, pellets de madeira e projetos de energia renovável. No entanto, potencial não se traduz em comercialização. Uma floresta que absorve carbono, uma área de produção agrícola que reduz emissões ou um projeto de energia renovável só podem gerar créditos valiosos se puderem demonstrar o quanto as emissões foram reduzidas e se esse resultado puder ser verificado de forma independente com dados. O Dr. Nguyen Phuong Nam, fundador e CEO da KLINOVA Company, acredita que a conclusão abrangente das regulamentações sobre inventário de gases de efeito estufa, critérios de classificação verde, financiamento verde, Plano de Transição Energética Justa (JETP), sistemas MRV, precificação de carbono e padrões ESG é crucial para conectar o mercado doméstico aos padrões globais. É também aqui que o mercado de carbono deixa de ser uma questão ambiental e passa a ser uma questão financeira. Quando as reduções de emissões são medidas, relatadas e validadas por meio de um sistema suficientemente confiável, esses resultados podem ser creditados, negociados e se tornar um ativo capaz de gerar valor. No plano de desenvolvimento do VIFC-DN, o mercado de carbono está agrupado com finanças verdes, gestão de fundos, serviços financeiros e fintech. Da Nang pretende construir infraestrutura de mercado, um sistema de MRV (Monitoramento, Relato e Verificação) de acordo com padrões internacionais e instrumentos financeiros especializados, conectando assim o valor criado pela redução de emissões com os fluxos de capital internacionais. Não espere a emissão do certificado para procurar um comprador. Se o MRV (Monitoramento, Relato e Verificação) é uma condição para comprovar o valor dos créditos, então a abordagem de mercado determina o potencial de comercialização. Um dos pontos notáveis na orientação de desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono no VIFC-DN é a mudança de mentalidade de "desenvolver o projeto e depois encontrar compradores" para "identificar compradores desde o início". Segundo o Professor Nguyen Xuan Thao, Diretor do Centro de Estudos de Direito Asiático da Faculdade de Direito da Universidade de Washington (EUA), os proprietários de projetos precisam coordenar-se com os compradores desde o início. Identificar as necessidades e os critérios dos compradores desde o princípio ajuda o projeto a selecionar padrões adequados, a desenvolver um sistema de dados e a construir um processo de MRV (Monitoramento, Relato e Verificação) que atenda aos requisitos do mercado internacional. Você também pode gostar Essa abordagem visa evitar situações em que um projeto gera créditos, mas depois tem dificuldades para encontrar um mercado para eles. Para projetos de grande escala, ter um comprador competente envolvido desde o início também ajuda a construir confiança e a criar uma base para a captação de recursos para a implementação. O Dr. Kyle Holland, fundador e CEO da EP Carbon LLC e da Impact Inside, cita o caso da Chestnut Carbon, sua empresa, como um exemplo da potencial conexão entre projetos de carbono e financiamento de capital privado em larga escala. O projeto atraiu a Microsoft como principal compradora e recebeu uma linha de crédito de US$ 210 milhões liderada pelo Morgan Stanley. Essa história ilustra que por trás de um crédito de carbono certificado não existe apenas um projeto de redução de emissões. Existe toda uma cadeia de valor que engloba dados, tecnologia, sistemas de monitoramento, relato e verificação (MRV), organizações de avaliação, investidores, compradores e instituições financeiras. De acordo com a orientação do VIFC-DN, o mercado de carbono não deve ser apenas um local para negociação de créditos, mas também se tornar uma ligação entre projetos verdes no Vietnã e o capital internacional, ao mesmo tempo que forma a infraestrutura para a negociação e a descoberta de preços de carbono. O professor Nguyen Xuan Thao também enfatizou a importância de adotar proativamente mecanismos de cooperação internacional para a troca transfronteiriça de créditos de carbono, conforme o Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris. Isso proporciona uma base para que os projetos verdes do Vietnã se conectem com centros de financiamento de carbono desenvolvidos na região, aumentando assim o valor dos créditos de carbono e as receitas em moeda estrangeira. Diferentemente do mercado doméstico de conformidade com as normas de carbono, o VIFC-DN concentra-se no segmento internacional do mercado voluntário de carbono e em instrumentos financeiros relacionados baseados em crédito. Essa abordagem visa integrar os valores de redução de emissões da agricultura, silvicultura, energias renováveis, etc., em um sistema de negociação transparente, além de abrir canais adicionais para conexão com recursos financeiros internacionais. artigo.texto: Sabah will not rush into carbon market trading 24 SEPTEMBER 2026 KOTA KINABALU: Opportunities in Sabah's carbon market are immense, but the State Government will not allow low unvetted projects to be rushed to market or traded on speculation. "We will protect Sabah's reputation and brand through strong regulatory discipline," said Chief Minister Datuk Seri Panglima Haji Hajiji Haji Noor. He said poorly designed projects, overstated climate claims, undervalued resources, and the exclusion of native communities would ould undermine investor confidence in Sabah's carbon credits. "It is therefore in Sabah's commercial interest to uphold the highest standards of environmental, social, financial, and governance integrity. Buyers will demand full transparency," he said at the Sabah Carbon Market Forum: Unlocking Carbon Market Opportunities for Sabah at the Hilton Hotel here on Thursday. Deputy Chief Minister II/State Finance Minister, Datuk Seri Panglima Masidi Manjun delivered his speech. He said laws like the Sabah Climate Change and Carbon Governance Enactment 2025, legally recognises the State Government's ownership of carbon rights and setting clear rules for carbon-related activities, including project approval and credit trading. "The Sabah Climate Change Action Council (SCCAC) will oversee the State's climate policy, prepare the State carbon budget for ministerial approval and gazettement, and coordinates efforts between State and Federal agencies. "The Sabah Climate Registry and Inventory Centre will provide technical and operational support to the SCCAC. Together, this framework is intended to offer investors a transparent, coordinated regulatory gateway for project approvals and registration of carbon rights," he said. Hajiji said Sabah has Malaysia's first nature-based verified carbon credit initiative through the Kuamut Rainforest Conservation Project, which spans some 83,381 hectares of the state's rich lowland and hill forests. The project, expected to deliver emission reductions of about 800,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide (CO2), has set the benchmark for future initiatives and has since been rated best-in-class by BeZero Carbon, the global carbon credit ratings agency. The Chief Minister said the State Government is also developing a diversified portfolio of carbon assets across key economic sectors, including the Blue Economy, Agriculture, Renewable Energy and Green Technology, as well as Carbon Capture and Storage. Under the Blue Economy sector, Sabah has more than 340,000 hectares of mangroves, the largest continuous mangrove area in Malaysia. "We have strong potential to become a regional leader in the blue economy through marine biotechnology, sustainable aquaculture, and marine ecosystem-based tourism," he said. In the agriculture sector, he said Sabah's oil palm oil industry covers nearly 1.5 million hectares and offers significant opportunities for methane capture and other climate mitigation initiatives using agricultural waste. For the Renewable Energy and Green Technology sector, he said that, guided by the Sabah Energy Roadmap and Master Plan 2040, the State Government will continue expanding solar, hydropower, biomass, and biogas to provide reliable, accessible, and affordable energy. "Sabah aims to increase the share of renewable electricity by 2030 through solar, hydropower, and biomass projects," he said. In the Carbon Capture and Storage sector, Hajiji said Sabah's offshore geological basins, together with our maritime frontier, offer long-term potential for geological carbon storage and position Sabah as a nationally significant industrial storage hub serving the region. The Chief Minister said that with almost 30 per cent of Sabah's landmass designated as Totally Protected Areas (TPAs), this would contribute towards Malaysia's biodiversity commitments and the 2030 global conservation target under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and place the state prominently on the global conservation map. "Sabah is also Malaysia's primary net net carbon sink, , on or carbon-negative state, based on greenhouse gas inventory data. Our extensive forest cover strengthens Malaysia's verall carbon a absorption capacity of roughly 36 per cent. "Through inclusive forest management, created in partnership with local communities, we strive to balance environmental conservation with the socio-economic wellbeing of our people. Sabah's identity and future are deeply rooted in our natural heritage," he said. Under our Sabah Maju Jaya (SMJ) development roadmap, we are moving decisively towards conservation with value, turning the protection of our natural assets into responsible economic opportunities. "The task now is implementation, and that is to develop credible projects, creating market demand, securing financing, and ensuring that conservation delivers lasting value," he said. Hajiji called on financial leaders, including CIMB Bank Berhad, Bursa Malaysia, commercial leaders, and investors, to develop or co-develop practical financing frameworks that can bridge the capital gap for credible carbon projects and meet the 2030 climate targets under the Paris Agreement. "We invite you to partner with us, to invest in Sabah, establish your technical operations here and unlock the true value of our natural capital," he said.

artigo.texto: Residents prepare court petition challenging Statesboro data center rezoning The petition seeks to overturn the rezoning of nearly 27 acres along Burkhalter Road. The zoning change does not constitute final approval for the proposed data center. Above video: Statesboro approves rezoning for data center despite protests A community organization and several property owners have prepared a court petition challenging the Statesboro City Council’s decision to rezone nearly 27 acres along Burkhalter Road for a proposed data center. The “Petition for Review/Appeal and Request for Declaratory Judgment” names Coastal Community United and 11 property owners as petitioners. It identifies the city of Statesboro and 4 AM Development LLC as defendants. The petition follows the council’s August approval of a request to rezone the property from a high-density residential district to an office and business district. Plans call for a two-story data center with about 115,000 square feet on each floor. The petition describes it as a 99-megawatt facility and disputes the developer’s characterization of it as an “edge” data center. The site is surrounded almost entirely by residential properties, according to the city’s Development Services Report. Wetlands have also been identified on the property. The petition alleges the city failed to follow its zoning requirements, relied too heavily on information from the developer and did not obtain independent studies of potential effects on traffic, wildlife, water resources and the electrical grid. Petitioners also cite concerns about noise, traffic, private wells and property values. They allege the rezoning violated their due-process and equal-protection rights and could damage private property without compensation. The allegations have not been proven in court. The petition presents the property owners’ account and does not include responses from the city or the developer. Petitioners are asking a judge to invalidate the rezoning decision, reverse the zoning-map change and return the matter to the City Council for reconsideration. The rezoning does not grant final approval for the project. The proposed data center would still need a special-use permit and would remain subject to the city’s development-review process. WJCL 22 News reached out to the City of Statesboro for a comment. A spokesperson said, "The City of Statesboro confirms it was served with a summons on September 21, requiring a response to the petition within 30 days. The City intends to meet that deadline. Beyond that, we're not able to comment on the details while the matter is pending litigation. The City of Statesboro intends to respond fully through the appropriate legal process."

artigo.texto: Paolla Oliveira, Anitta, famosas veteranas e uma vaga em aberto: conheça as rainhas de bateria do carnaval de 2027 Com o anúncio de Paolla na Imperatriz, a Unidos da Tijuca passa a ser a única escola sem majestade definida para o Grupo Especial Atualizado Faltando cinco meses para o carnaval, 11 das 12 escolas do Grupo Especial já definiram quem ocupará o posto de rainha de bateria em 2027. Na última quarta-feira, Paolla Oliveira foi anunciada como majestade da Imperatriz, cargo que estava vago desde março, quando a cantora Iza anunciou a sua saída. A Grande Rio, deixada pela influenciadora Virgínia Fonseca em agosto, também repôs a vaga, coroando a cantora Anitta no domingo. Gaby Mendes, musa da Mocidade, que ascendeu à rainha no fim do mês passado, foi outra novidade. Agora, no quadro que mescla famosas, crias da comunidade e veteranas, falta apenas a Unidos da Tijuca definir quem sambará à frente dos ritmistas. - Leandro Vieira guardou segredo sobre Paolla Oliveira à frente da bateria da Imperatriz Leopoldinense: 'Animado e de boca calada' - Veja mais: Anitta revela aulas de samba com rainhas de bateria antes de assumir posto na Grande Rio Paolla Oliveira - Imperatriz Paolla Oliveira foi anunciada ontem como a nova soberana dos ritmistas da Imperatriz Leopoldinense. A confirmação é da própria escola. A coroação da atriz já tem até data: 17 de outubro. A artista de 44 anos recebeu o convite da presidente Cátia Drumond para sambar à frente dos ritmistas da Swing da Leopoldina, comandada por Mestre Lolo. A atriz disse que encara o retorno à Sapucaí como mais um desafio. — Estou muito feliz de estar aqui, de coração aberto para começar mais uma história no carnaval. Chego com muito respeito, vontade de estar perto, conhecer, aprender e viver mais uma vez essa experiência rica e coletiva. Tem frio na barriga, claro, mas tem também uma alegria enorme por tudo que está começando — afirmou Paolla. Como é perceptível pela fala da artista, esta não é a sua primeira vez como rainha de bateria. Oliveira foi majestade da Grande Rio por 7 anos, divididos em dois momentos distintos. Em 2009, a atriz estreou no posto e permaneceu para o carnaval seguinte, abandonando a coroa em 2011. O ornamento da escola de Caxias foi retomado por Paolla em 2020 e permaneceu em sua cabeça até 2025. No último período, a atriz viveu uma fase gloriosa da agremiação, marcada pelo único título, conquistado em 2022, com o enredo "Fala Majeté! As sete chaves de Exu", e por vice-campeonatos. Anitta - Grande Rio Agora quem dá o tom do samba para os ritmistas da Grande Rio é a cantora Anitta, coroada na quadra da escola, em Duque de Caxias, no último domingo, em uma cerimônia que misturou referências de seu álbum "Equilibrium II" com elementos do carnaval e símbolos do candomblé. A apresentação também recuperou passagens da trajetória da cantora, criada em Honório Gurgel, na Zona Norte do Rio, e sua relação com a fé. Aos 33 anos, Anitta é consolidada como uma das principais cantoras do Brasil. Cria do subúrbio carioca, ela foi dos paredões de baile funk à projeção internacional no pop e ostenta grandes parcerias com nomes estrangeiros, como Shakira e Snoop Dogg. Para a cantora, o convite da Grande Rio, que defenderá o enredo "Sankofa Tabon, Os retornados da Costa do Ouro e a Estrela Negra da Liberdade" em 2027, ressoa perfeitamente com o momento de sua carreira, o que a motivou a aceitar assumir o posto de rainha de bateria. — Quando você vai falando do enredo, parece que você está falando do meu álbum de tanto link que têm entre ancestralidade e retorno ao passado — disse Anitta sobre o encontro de Equilibrium II com a história que a escola levará para a Avenida em 2027. Viviane Araújo - Salgueiro Antes de Anitta e Paolla estrearem no hall de rainhas, outra famosa já embalava a bateria de uma escola do Grupo Especial: desde 2008, Viviane Araújo é a soberana do Salgueiro. Prestes a completar 19 anos com a coroa e chegar ao 20º carnaval no posto, a atriz de 51 anos é dona do marco de celebridade que esteve mais tempo no trono dos ritmistas. Ao longo de quase duas décadas, Araújo viveu momentos marcantes sambando com a Bateria Furiosa, que já lhe renderam, inclusive, o título de melhor rainha de bateria, oferecido pelo portal EGO em 2016. O tamborim na mão da atriz virou um marco de seu reinado, que não foi interrompido nem durante a gestação de seu primeiro filho: em 2022, a artista foi para a Avenida grávida de 5 meses. Além dos episódios pessoais, Vivi também viu o campeonato do Salgueiro de 2009, com o enredo "Tambor", e o Estandarte de Ouro, prêmio concedido pelos jornais O GLOBO E EXTRA, vencido pela vermelha e branca em 2014. Sabrina Sato - Unidos de Vila Isabel Depois de Viviane Araújo, Sabrina Sato é a celebridade há mais tempo à frente de uma bateria do carnaval carioca. A apresentadora de 45 anos, que se destaca por suas fantasias luxuosas, acumula 14 anos como rainha dos ritmistas da Unidos de Vila Isabel, tempo dividido em duas passagens: de 2011 a 2019 e o retorno em 2022, que perdura até hoje. A sua volta à Swingeira de Noel foi marcada pela aventura de desfilar em São Paulo pela Gaviões da Fiel, que também a tem como majestade, e no Rio, pela Vila, na mesma noite. A empreitada contou com uma grande operação e incentivou o início do reality show Carnaval da Sabrina, em que a artista relata desde sua preparação até os momentos-chaves da sua atuação enquanto majestade. Evelyn Bastos - Mangueira No hall das crias de comunidade, Evelyn Bastos é quem reina há mais tempo. A rainha de 33 anos, que desfila na Mangueira desde a infância, despontou cedo na arte de sambar bonito, de forma que passou a integrar a ala de passista aos 11, idade em que outras meninas ainda costumam estar no setor infantil da escola. A soberana foi, aos poucos, galgando espaço na verde e rosa e começou a se destacar dentro e fora da quadra da escola. artigo.texto: Switzerland-based Energy Vault has acquired a portfolio of more than 2.3GW of US battery energy storage system (BESS) development projects from Colorado’s Goshe Energy Storage. The transaction covers 15 projects and expands the company’s Asset Vault platform, which centres on energy storage and AI infrastructure assets. Discover B2B Marketing That Performs Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms. As part of the acquisition, Energy Vault will add two ready-to-build projects with capacities of 150MW and 200MW. Both are projected to become operational in the first quarter of 2028 and together are expected to generate around $30m in annual run-rate earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) once operational. The company said the acquisition brings forward Asset Vault-specific annual recurring EBITDA timelines and it now expects to reach more than $200m (SFr164.51m) in exit run-rate EBITDA by 2028 under its long-term infrastructure ownership strategy. Asset Vault president Cory Magnuson said: “This portfolio fits squarely within Energy Vault’s strategy of acquiring late-stage, de-risked development projects that can be moved efficiently toward construction and operation. “The team has a track record of originating and advancing high-quality BESS projects, and we are glad to have them join us as we continue to scale our owned-asset portfolio across US markets.” To support the development, construction and operation of its newly acquired portfolio, Energy Vault has secured a credit facility commitment of up to $40m from S2G Investments. This commitment continues a strategic partnership between S2G and Goshe and will fund various stages of project progress. The Goshe team, including development professionals with more than 75 years of combined experience in renewable energy, BESS project management and financial services, will join Energy Vault. Goshe CEO Bailey McCallum said: “Joining Energy Vault allows our team to continue the work we started – developing and delivering the storage projects the grid needs – with the backing of a large, vertically integrated and global platform. “We are pleased that S2G will continue as a financing partner through this transition, and we look forward to seeing this portfolio through to construction and operation as part of Energy Vault’s platform.” Energy Vault’s global portfolio currently includes more than 1.75GW of owned energy and AI compute infrastructure assets that are either operating or under construction. The company’s business model spans the full infrastructure life cycle, from development and construction to ongoing service agreements, aiming to generate stable, recurring revenue. In April 2026, Energy Vault signed a binding agreement to acquire an 850MW portfolio of BESS projects from a domestic energy storage developer in Japan.

artigo.texto: Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s latest restrictions on new data center permits should not be a setback to the Infrakey project planned near Ross, a company official said Wednesday. “I don’t see for our project that we’ll have any issues,” Infrakey executive Sujeeth Draksharam said Wednesday. He said the firm, which is partnering with Lacy-Lakeview on the project, is “ahead of the curve” in anticipating questions from state regulators. Abbott on Monday ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to stop issuing new permits for data centers, strengthening his moratorium on the industry’s development in Texas. The move comes as rapid data center development statewide angers Texas communities ahead of Abbott’s November reelection bid. The Infrakey project, a partnership with the small city of Lacy-Lakeview north of Waco, has stoked grassroots resistance since the proposed 520-acre data campus came to light last fall. Abbott sent the letter to TCEQ Executive Director Kelly Keel, directing the agency to halt all permits to data centers until the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, the state’s nonprofit electric grid operator, and the Texas Water Development Board, which handles state water resource planning, complete an audit of data centers seeking to be built in the state. Those efforts seek information about planned data centers’ electricity use, water use, impact on local communities, ownership information and use of tax breaks. “Simply put, Texans must come first,” Abbott wrote. “Data centers must pay their own way, protect our grid and water and complete the ERCOT and TWDB audits. Until they do, TCEQ will issue no permits sought by data center projects.” Sara Mynarcik, a rural resident of Ross and a leading organizer against the Infrakey project, described the moratorium as an election stunt to distance Abbott from an industry he championed as recently as last year. “If this is something that he’s doing now, why didn’t he do it months ago?” Mynarcik told the Bridge on Tuesday. “The opposition (to data centers) throughout the state is now loud enough and he knows it will affect the ballot.” She also reiterated that Draksharam and other Waco-area partners on the project have well established relationships with the Governor. Abbott appointed Draksharam to a state licensing commission in 2022. TCEQ will need to consider the information collected in the audit when it approves future permit applications, necessitating the pause on approvals, Abbott wrote. Draksharam said Infrakey is prepared to submit the necessary water and energy information to state regulators by the Oct. 12 filing deadline. The new pause continues Abbott’s reversal on the rapid development of data centers in Texas, which he said in November he wants to become an “epicenter of AI development.” In June, Abbott first ordered ERCOT and the agency that regulates it, the Public Utility Commission of Texas, to require data centers fully fund the costs of electric infrastructure needed to serve them and take other measures to reduce electricity costs to residents. On July 17, PUCT Chair Thomas Gleeson responded to Abbott with his own letter outlining efforts the agencies have already taken and calling on the Legislature to grant them more authority to regulate the industry. Abbott then announced his moratorium on new data centers connecting to the state’s electric grid, ordering ERCOT on Aug. 3 to ensure data center developers provide information on tax breaks they will receive; power use and generation; water use and cooling operations; efforts to reduce impacts on local communities; and ownership of the facility. Any projects that fail Abbott’s ordered “comprehensive verification and audit” should be denied connection to the grid, the governor said. Abbott’s latest order appears to address concerns that data center developers who build “behind the meter,” or create their own power generation source so they may bypass electric grid approval, would not be delayed by the ERCOT audit. The ERCOT region also does not encompass the entire state, although the PUC and TWDB jurisdiction does. After as few as 28% of data centers responded to a state-mandated water usage survey, used to determine how much water will be needed in the future, Abbott last Monday directed the TWDB to penalize data centers that do not report their water usage. Abbott instructed the TWDB to partner with the PUC and ERCOT in their audit of the facilities. “Because the information sought by the PUC, ERCOT, and TWDB is necessary to make informed decisions by each of those agencies, no other state agency shall move forward with regulatory approvals related to data centers until this information is acquired,” Abbott wrote in the letter to TCEQ Monday. “This action is consistent with my whole-of-government approach to ensure Texans’ natural resources and way of life are protected.”

artigo.texto: A participação da SOFAR na The smarter E South America marcou uma nova etapa da atuação da fabricante no Brasil, com a apresentação de soluções para diferentes aplicações de armazenamento de energia e o reforço de sua estrutura local de atendimento, logística e pós-venda. Entre os destaques do estande estiveram o PowerMagic 2.0, voltado ao segmento comercial e industrial; o PowerEasy, direcionado a aplicações residenciais e comerciais; e o PowerIn, desenvolvido para projetos comerciais e industriais de menor porte. David Zhong, CEO da companhia esteve no Brasil durante a feira e se reuniu pessoalmente com clientes e parceiros da empresa. Segundo o executivo, a companhia pretende ampliar os investimentos no mercado brasileiro, especialmente nos segmentos de armazenamento de energia. “A SOFAR está neste mercado há cerca de dez anos e hoje nós já estabelecemos um forte serviço local. E este mercado apresenta um grande potencial em armazenamento ESS, C&I e BESS. Eu e a nossa empresa investiremos cada vez mais recursos aqui”, afirmou Zhong. Como parte dessa estratégia, a fabricante inaugurou neste ano um novo centro em Jundiaí (SP), com mais de 2 mil m². A estrutura reúne estoque local de equipamentos e recursos destinados ao atendimento de garantias, à operação da companhia e ao suporte pós-venda. “Recentemente, alugamos um grande armazém, com mais de 2 mil m², para fortalecer nossos serviços e facilitar nossa operação local”, acrescentou o CEO. PowerMagic 2.0 Uma das novidades apresentadas pela SOFAR foi o PowerMagic 2.0, sistema de armazenamento de energia lançado recentemente e incorporado ao portfólio da fabricante no Brasil. Voltada a aplicações comerciais e industriais, a solução possui 125 kW de potência e 261 kWh de capacidade de armazenamento, distribuídos em cinco packs de baterias. Segundo a fabricante, o PowerMagic 2.0 reúne, em um único gabinete, o banco de baterias, um PCS de 125 kW, sistema de refrigeração líquida e os componentes necessários para a conexão à instalação elétrica do cliente. Eduardo Fróes, diretor LATAM da SOFAR, explicou que o sistema pode ser utilizado em diferentes estratégias de gerenciamento de energia, como arbitragem tarifária, peak shaving, regulação de tensão e frequência, além de outras aplicações conectadas à rede. Para projetos que exigem backup ou operação off-grid, a empresa também apresentou um gabinete capaz de integrar diferentes fontes de energia. De acordo com Fróes, o equipamento possui entradas em corrente alternada que permitem conectar, além do sistema fotovoltaico, geradores a diesel, PCHs (Pequenas Centrais Hidrelétricas) e outras fontes de geração. A configuração permite ainda a conexão de até três unidades de BESS em paralelo, ampliando a potência e a capacidade de armazenamento de acordo com a demanda da instalação. Essa arquitetura pode atender diferentes perfis de consumidores, incluindo indústrias e empreendimentos do agronegócio, principalmente em projetos que combinam mais de uma fonte de geração e exigem maior flexibilidade no gerenciamento da energia. De acordo com a SOFAR, o PowerMagic 2.0 está disponível em estoque no Brasil, e as primeiras unidades têm previsão de entrar em operação em projetos no país ainda em setembro. PowerEasy Outro equipamento apresentado durante o evento foi o PowerEasy, solução que integra inversores híbridos e baterias de baixa tensão para aplicações residenciais e comerciais. O sistema é compatível com diferentes padrões de tensão utilizados no Brasil, incluindo 127/220 V, 120/240 V e 220/380 V, característica que amplia sua aplicação em diferentes configurações da rede elétrica. Segundo a SOFAR, o produto oferece capacidade de sobrecarga de até 100%, que pode ser utilizada durante o carregamento das baterias e o atendimento simultâneo de cargas em corrente alternada. A solução também possui corrente de entrada de 20 A, permitindo a conexão com módulos fotovoltaicos de maior potência. Para aplicações comerciais e industriais de menor porte, a fabricante apresentou o PowerIn, que combina geração fotovoltaica e armazenamento de energia em uma única plataforma. De acordo com a empresa, o equipamento suporta sobredimensionamento fotovoltaico de até 200% e capacidade de sobrecarga de 150%. A solução conta ainda com um EMS (Sistema de Gerenciamento de Energia) integrado, responsável pelo controle dos fluxos de energia e pelo gerenciamento das cargas da instalação. O PowerIn também permite a expansão do banco de baterias, possibilitando adequar a capacidade de armazenamento às necessidades de cada projeto. Entre os recursos de segurança estão o grau de proteção IP66 e o AFCI baseado em inteligência artificial, destinado à detecção de falhas por arco elétrico. O sistema também oferece suporte a cargas desequilibradas. Segundo a fabricante, a integração desses recursos busca simplificar a instalação e reduzir incompatibilidades entre equipamentos, principalmente em projetos comerciais e industriais com diferentes configurações elétricas. Monitoramento pela SOFAR Cloud As soluções da fabricante podem ser acompanhadas por meio da SOFAR Cloud, plataforma própria de monitoramento e gerenciamento de energia. O sistema permite acompanhar a geração, o consumo, o armazenamento e o funcionamento dos equipamentos, oferecendo informações para a gestão de instalações residenciais, comerciais e industriais.
