Segundo a fabricante, a iniciativa representa um diferencial importante, pois busca garantir que cada solução seja instalada e entregue de acordo com o projeto e as especificações técnicas definidas pela SOFAR com o objetivo de contribuir para a capacitação e educação do setor, promovendo maior

artigo.texto: The wildfires that have raged across Oregon and Washington this year burned millions of acres. But beyond the immediate destruction, the fires have destroyed something less visible: tens of millions of dollars in California carbon credits, paid for by businesses and consumers under the state’s climate mandates. The fires have scorched tens of thousands of acres enrolled in forest-carbon projects under California’s cap-and-trade program. The system allows companies to meet part of the state’s climate rules by purchasing credits from forest owners who promise to keep carbon locked away in trees for at least 100 years, sometimes in forests hundreds of miles outside of the state. The destruction is the latest evidence that California’s forest-offset program is ineffective at best, counterproductive at worst. Finally, a reason to check your email. Sign up for our free newsletter today. California is home to some of the nation’s strictest climate mandates. Its cap-and-trade program mandates that large emitters obtain allowances for each ton of carbon they emit. They can meet part of that obligation with carbon offsets, including credits generated by forests that purportedly store carbon over long periods. Over the program’s history, California companies have spent billions of dollars on these carbon offsets, the vast majority generated by forest projects. The state’s logic is that a company can continue emitting carbon so long as it pays someone elsewhere to keep enough carbon stored in trees for up to a century. That assumes the forests don’t burn up in the meantime—and this summer, many did. At the Opal Mountain site in central Oregon, more than 85 percent of the 14,000-acre forest-carbon project burned in a wildfire this summer. The project has generated over 500,000 carbon credits, purchased by companies including Southern California Gas, Shell, and Pacific Gas and Electric. Elsewhere, in Washington State, fires this summer burned tens of thousands of acres at the Colville forest-carbon site, an enormous project whose credits have been bought by Chevron and other major firms. Altogether, nearly 80,000 acres of land set aside for California carbon banking have burned in wildfires this year, according to data compiled by the climate-focused nonprofit CarbonPlan. Some of these projects commanded high prices despite significant fire risks. The Opal Mountain project has been marketed as a “premier carbon forestry investment,” with millions of dollars of value tied to its carbon credits. In 2024, California regulators gave the project a “Direct Environmental Benefits in the State” designation, making its credits especially valuable under state rules. California regulations require that at least half the offsets used by a regulated company come from projects deemed to provide direct environmental benefits within the state. Why would protecting trees in Oregon provide a direct environmental benefit to California? The owners of the Opal Mountain site claimed their fire-management activities would reduce the risk of wildfire smoke drifting into California. The approval for its special designation claims that its “forest management plan will reduce the risk of wildfire.” Many of those measures were still being planned or considered, yet California regulators nonetheless approved the designation. Now, less than two years later, a wildfire has burned most of the project—including a fire lookout cited as evidence of its wildfire protection. This isn’t the first time California’s carbon forests have burned. A carbon-offset project on the Warm Springs Reservation in Oregon burned so badly in 2020 that it was retired this year after repeated wildfire losses. The project had generated about $25 million for the tribe, though the surrounding forests had a substantial history of fires. California has tried to account for wildfire risks by establishing a “buffer pool,” to which each project is required to contribute as a kind of insurance policy. When a fire destroys a forest-carbon project, credits from the pool are canceled to cover the loss. But this approach has proven inadequate. A 2022 study found that fires had already consumed at least 95 percent of the credits set aside to cover wildfire losses for a full century. Subsequent research found roughly 10.7 million credits lost to wildfire, far more than the amount reserved for fire risk. Opal Mountain illustrates the problem. State records show that the project contributed roughly 80,000 credits to the buffer pool. Yet CarbonPlan estimates that the recent wildfires could result in the termination of the project, which would wipe out all of its roughly 500,000 credits—more than six times what it contributed to the pool. Such difficulties have long plagued California’s program. A recent analysis by UC Berkeley researchers criticized the state for spending heavily on what they call “highly dubious” offsets from out-of-state projects. The researchers concluded that the program has produced “little-to-no actual climate benefit.” The program may even be deepening the region’s wildfire problem. Western forests need periodic thinning, brush removal, and controlled burns to maintain healthy conditions and reduce extreme fire risks. But forest-carbon projects often get less active management because landowners can make more money if they grow more wood on each acre. The result, as wildfire news and analysis site The Lookout recently reported, is forests that are often “overstocked, prone to insects, drought, and disease, and flammable.” At Warm Springs, much of the burned land had been kept from active management in favor of conservation and carbon revenue. “It burned hot because we weren’t able to get in there and treat it and manage it,” the natural resources manager for the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs told the Bend Bulletin. California shouldn’t need more lessons in wildfire risk. The state has endured some of its most destructive fires in recent years. Y

artigo.texto: Paolla Oliveira é anunciada como a nova rainha de bateria da Imperatriz Leopoldinense Confirmação foi feita pela escola nesta quarta-feira; coroação será no dia 17 de outubro Atualizado A rainha está de volta: Paolla Oliveira foi anunciada, nesta quarta (23), como a nova soberana dos ritmistas da Imperatriz Leopoldinense. A confirmação é da própria escola. A coroação da atriz já tem até data: está marcada para 17 de outubro. Leandro Vieira contou ao GLOBO sobre a chegada da atriz à escola e brincou que os dois são adeptos do "carnaval não monogâmico". Paolla recebeu o convite da presidente Cátia Drumond e vai substituir a cantora Iza, que reinou no desfile deste ano à frente dos ritmistas da Swing da Leopoldina, comandada por Mestre Lolo. A atriz disse que encara o retorno à Sapucaí como mais um desafio. — Estou muito feliz de estar aqui, de coração aberto e para começar mais uma história no carnaval. Chego com muito respeito, vontade de estar perto, conhecer, aprender e viver mais uma vez essa experiência rica e coletiva. Tem frio na barriga, claro, mas tem também uma alegria enorme por tudo que está começando — afirmou a atriz. Com o enredo “A Memória do Rei e o Sumiço de Dona Júlia”, idealizado pelo carnavalesco Leandro Vieira, a Imperatriz Leopoldinense será a quarta escola a desfilar na Marquês de Sapucaí, fechando a segunda-feira de Carnaval, 08 de fevereiro, em busca do 10º título de sua história. — Tenho certeza que ela chega para somar ao nosso time, aos nossos ritmistas e principalmente à comunidade de Ramos e toda Zona da Leopoldina, que está ansiosa para abraçar e reverenciar sua nova majestade. Que ela seja muito bem-vinda e claro, muito feliz conosco — brindou Catia Drumond.

artigo.texto: The Brief - Congressman Derrick Van Orden outlined his position on data centers Thursday, saying he supports them only with strict conditions to protect Wisconsin farmland. - Van Orden says data centers must use closed-loop air-cooled systems, not increase electric rates, and be built on existing military bases. - Rebecca Cooke, Van Orden's opponent, says Van Orden voted for tax breaks for data center developers while cutting health care. MENOMONIE, Wis. (WKBT) -- Congressman Derrick Van Orden held a press conference Thursday at Sand Grains Farm to outline his position on data centers and discuss efforts to protect Wisconsin families, farmers and ratepayers. Van Orden said he supports data centers but only with strict conditions. He said data centers are critically important to national security but must be developed responsibly. "We're going to preserve our farmland," Van Orden said. "One of the issues we're dealing with right now across the globe are data centers. So, data centers are critically important to national security, and we understand that also the Chinese Communist Party understands that. But I have very, very strict provisions that I have in order to build these in the state of Wisconsin." Van Orden outlined four key requirements for data center development in Wisconsin: Local Control: Van Orden says Wisconsin residents must decide what happens in their neighborhoods. Water Usage: Van Orden says data centers must use closed-loop air-cooled systems that use minimal water, comparable to a car wash. Electric Rates: Van Orden says electric rates must not increase. He says companies must sign a rate protection plan, and once they have locally generated power, rates would actually decrease. Location: Van Orden says data centers must be built on existing U.S. military bases. "That's building public-private partnerships on existing United States military bases," Van Orden said. "And every company that would be allowed to build one of these centers, they have to sign the rate protection plan, meaning at a minimum electric rates will not increase." Van Orden also criticized his opponent's past work on data centers. He said Rebecca Cooke worked for organizations that lobbied for data center development on Wisconsin farmland without guardrails. "Rebecca Cook worked for the Third Way and the Wisconsin Technical Board Council. She is responsible for building these data centers right here in Mount Pleasant and in Beaver Dam," Van Orden said. Cooke responded to Van Orden's comments in a statement, saying Van Orden voted to give tax breaks to data center developers. "Only one person in this race voted to give an $83 billion tax break to data center developers while cutting health care for millions of Americans, and that's Derrick Van Orden," Cooke said in her statement. "I'm running to undo those tax breaks for the rich so that working families can build a better life for themselves." Cooke also said she has been advocating for a data center moratorium and accused Van Orden of attempting to rewrite his record late in the campaign. "If Van Orden had held a single town hall in the last four years, he'd know voters are furious about data centers—instead, he's attempting to rewrite his record 40 days before the election," Cooke said. "I have been a strong advocate for a data center moratorium for months." COPYRIGHT 2026 BY NEWS 8 NOW/NEWS 8000. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. artigo.texto: Chinese battery maker CBAK Energy plans to build 12 GWh of annual battery capacity in Nanjing, with new lines capable of producing large cylindrical sodium-ion or lithium-ion cells. The Nasdaq-listed company has signed an investment agreement with the Nanjing Gaochun Economic Development Zone for the project, which will also include research and development as well as battery module and pack integration. CBAK plans to advance the 12 GWh project in the second half of 2027, although construction and production will depend on securing financing, customer demand and project readiness. The company has not disclosed the project’s investment cost. The expansion comes as CBAK tests sodium-ion battery samples with customers for residential and portable energy storage and electric mobility. Its cells are also being evaluated for specialty vehicles, automotive start-stop systems and backup power. Two chemistries share lines A key feature of the planned factory is manufacturing flexibility. CBAK says its production lines will be designed to make either large cylindrical sodium-ion or lithium-ion cells, allowing it to choose the chemistry according to market conditions and customer demand. The company estimates the 12 GWh project could generate RMB4.8 billion to RMB5 billion ($712 million to $741 million) in annual revenue if it operates at full capacity and sells all its output. More from Energy See All That estimate, however, is based on current lithium-ion cell market prices and does not represent contracted sales. Actual revenue will depend on factors including product mix, pricing, manufacturing yields and capacity utilization. The sodium-ion project is separate from another expansion already planned at CBAK’s existing Nanjing plant. The company is targeting an additional 6 GWh of annual production capacity there by the end of 2026. The facility currently has 4.5 GWh of annual capacity for its Model 32140 cylindrical cells. Adding 6 GWh would more than double the site’s capacity to 10.5 GWh annually. Cylindrical capacity ramps higher CBAK is considering installing two production lines for its larger Model 60150 cells as part of the 6 GWh expansion. Strong demand for its existing Model 32140 cells, however, could lead it to install one line for each cell format instead. At full utilization with all output sold, CBAK estimates the additional 6 GWh could generate RMB2.4 billion to RMB2.7 billion ($356 million to $400 million) in annual revenue. “The 6 GWh expansion would more than double annual cell capacity at our existing Nanjing facility and help us meet strong demand for large cylindrical cells,” said Zhiguang Hu, Chief Executive Officer of CBAK Energy. “The 12 GWh investment agreement advances our plans for sodium-ion production. Designing the lines to produce lithium-ion cells as well would give us more options to serve customers as demand develops in both markets.” Combined, the two plans represent 18 GWh of additional annual cell capacity, although they are at different stages and the larger 12 GWh project remains dependent on financing. CBAK currently develops and manufactures both lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries, with operations serving electric vehicles, light electric vehicles, energy storage systems and other high-power applications.

artigo.texto: Volkswagen subsidiary delays opening of $7B St. Thomas, Ont., battery plant to 2029 Conservative MP raises concerns about delay, citing federal subsidies and job promises The Volkswagen subsidiary building an electric vehicle (EV) battery "gigafactory" in St. Thomas, Ont., says the facility is now expected to begin operations in 2029, two years later than originally planned. PowerCo Canada made the announcement in a news release about hiring Mississauga, Ont.-based EllisDon Corporation as the general contractor for construction of the factory. "St. Thomas is now expected to begin operations in 2029 to accommodate next-generation battery technology, while retaining the flexibility to scale over time as market conditions evolve," said a news release. PowerCo declined to make a spokesperson available for an interview with CBC News about the delay. Originally scheduled for a 2027 opening, the $7-billion factory — with a promise of up to $13 billion in subsidies from the federal government — was first announced in 2023. It was estimated it would result in the creation of 3,000 direct jobs and tens of thousands of indirect jobs in the region. - VideoHighway 3 expansion gets underway as St. Thomas prepares for battery plant boom - Construction has started on massive Volkswagen battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont. To prepare for the arrival of the plant, surrounding municipalities and the provincial government have undertaken infrastructure projects to increase sewer and road capacity for the population boom that was expected in 2027. Before the plant was announced, the province allowed St. Thomas to annex land from the neighbouring municipality of Central Elgin to make room for the development. In August 2025, PowerCo Canada announced it had awarded two major construction contracts for the project. Construction began in October 2025, with work starting on the foundations for the facility. St. Thomas Mayor Joe Preston, who has championed the factory as a major driver of economic growth for his city, told CBC News he's unfazed by the two-year delay. "They've picked a great local Canadian general contractor and in doing so, they had to adjust the [opening] date," said Preston. PowerCo has been hiring workers in the St. Thomas area since August 2025. Preston estimates roughly 500 people are currently employed by the company in the surrounding area. He also cited "the number of employees they already have working and living in the city of St. Thomas, the amount of construction that's going on in that site each and every day" as reasons for maintaining confidence in the project. Preston also pointed to Yarmouth Yards, a large industrial park developed by St. Thomas, which is being populated by industries that are complementary to battery production. Provincial officials also welcomed EllisDon's selection as general contractor. In a written statement to CBC News, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade said the contract "represents a major milestone as they work towards the start of production that will create thousands of direct and indirect jobs across the supply chain." The ministry's statement didn't address the two-year delay. "We look forward to continuing to work with PowerCo as they progress on their $7-billion gigafactory in St. Thomas that will position Ontario at the forefront of innovative battery and automotive production for decades to come," it said. Area MP raises concerns Andrew Lawton, the Conservative MP representing Elgin—St. Thomas—London South, called news of the delay disappointing and questioned Volkswagen's commitment to the plant. “I realize that Volkswagen is saying it's just about pace and not about the overall commitment. But ultimately, it is about the commitment because we were expecting this to be moving forward at a speed that we're just not seeing,” Lawton said. Lawton also said he wants to know what the federal government is doing to move things along and ensure Volkswagen remains committed. "We saw $13 billion worth of federal subsidies put forward to this and the promise — the expectation — was 3,000 well-paid local jobs, not to mention the construction jobs. All of this has been thrown into jeopardy right now." EV market shifts affect Ontario auto plans The market conditions cited by PowerCo come as automakers across Ontario have adjusted plans for electric vehicle production amid changes in EV demand. In April 2025, General Motors cited lower-than-expected demand when it announced plans to halt production of the Chevrolet BrightDrop electric delivery van at its CAMI Assembly plant in Ingersoll. Hundreds of workers were laid off. - VideoHundreds of workers laid off at Ingersoll, Ont., assembly plant as GM halts production - Honda more definitively halting $15B EV plant development in Ontario, according to reports Honda also delayed plans for a $15-billion EV plant in Alliston in 2025 before ultimately cancelling the project. The company said it would continue to assess the EV market. At the same time, Canadian EV sales have shown signs of growth. Statistics Canada data released in June showed the number of new EVs purchased by Canadians had increased by more than 20 per cent compared with the same period a year earlier. Canadians bought 8,672 new EVs in January, 12,547 in February and 21,574 in March before sales fell to 17,795 in April.

artigo.texto: CERC Proposes New Congestion Charges for BESS Projects ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: The CERC has proposed new congestion charges and scheduling rules for BESS, while MERC introduced stricter deviation settlement norms and banking frameworks for renewable energy. - Why it matters: These regulatory shifts directly impact the financial viability and operational compliance of energy storage and hybrid renewable projects for developers and EPCs. - Watch: Upcoming final notifications from CERC and MERC regarding grid code amendments and the implementation of capacity-based banking. Background and Context The regulatory landscape for India’s renewable energy sector is undergoing a significant transformation as the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) and various State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) move to stabilize the grid. The CERC has proposed critical amendments to the Indian Electricity Grid Code, specifically targeting the integration of Energy Storage Systems (ESS) and renewable energy assets. These proposals introduce a congestion charge mechanism alongside revised requirements for commissioning, scheduling, and trial runs. Key Details The regulatory updates are widespread. In Maharashtra, the MERC has proposed a capacity-based banking framework for renewable energy systems, regardless of the procurement model. Crucially, the commission is mandating energy storage systems for grid-interactive and behind-the-meter rooftop solar installations exceeding 100 kW. Furthermore, MERC is tightening deviation settlement rules for solar, wind, and hybrid projects, pushing developers toward a stricter schedule-based mechanism that imposes higher financial penalties for generation deviations. On the project front, Lineage Power has secured a ₹4.88 billion (~$48.85 million) order from NTPC GE Power Services to deploy a battery energy storage system at the Barh Super Thermal Power Project, with a completion deadline of December 31, 2026. Additionally, PFC Consulting has invited bids for an interstate transmission system (ISTS) to evacuate 2 GW of renewable energy from the Solapur special economic zone in Maharashtra, with a bid submission deadline of November 25, 2026. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and solar/wind developers, these policy shifts necessitate a higher level of operational precision. The move toward stricter deviation settlement means that forecasting accuracy is no longer just a best practice but a financial necessity. Developers must now account for the mandatory inclusion of BESS in larger rooftop projects and prepare for the operational compliance requirements mandated by the proposed State Grid Code amendments. The focus is clearly shifting from mere capacity addition to grid-responsive, reliable power delivery. What Happens Next As the India renewable energy sector continues to scale, the integration of 2 GW of new capacity in Maharashtra and the deployment of large-scale BESS at NTPC sites will serve as bellwethers for the industry. Stakeholders should monitor the finalization of the CERC congestion charge mechanism and the MERC banking regulations, as these will define the revenue models for future energy storage and hybrid projects across the country.

artigo.texto: There is an intense national conversation underway around the regulation of data center development. A recent Gallup poll found that seven in 10 Americans oppose AI data centers in their local communities, at least 15 states have considered moratoriums, governors across the country (including in Wyoming) have issued executive orders in response to a wave of development proposals, local governments are scrambling to understand the implications of these new projects, and communities are raising legitimate concerns over increasing electricity costs and impacts to water, air and local character. How Wyoming responds in this moment will undoubtedly shape the future of our state. I’ve spent my career leading conservation NGOs in the Mountain West, building coalitions and working on complex issues that intersect conservation, land-use planning and development — and I can tell you that the tone of this conversation is different, and it is heading to a breaking point. Communities of all stripes and colors — blue, red, purple, green — are looking for greater agency, transparency and guardrails to ensure that data center development is done responsibly. What remains to be seen is how and if Wyoming’s leaders will rise to the occasion to define what “responsible” means — on Wyoming’s terms, grounded in what defines us. Fortunately, Wyoming has a precedent for this type of leadership and foresight from which we might draw inspiration. A little over 50 years ago, Wyoming’s leaders came together to do two things that changed the course of development in this state for the better. First, the Wyoming Legislature passed the Industrial Siting Act — a novel regulatory approach that allowed state and local authorities to engage directly in the permitting of large projects and help fund communities to deal with the impacts of these projects. Second, Wyoming had the foresight to create the Permanent Mineral Trust Fund, which takes severance taxes on mineral extraction and invests them to support the state’s finances. That fund now has over $13 billion — it is the largest single fund in Wyoming’s investment portfolio — and plays an essential role in supporting public services and balancing our state budget. These policies came at the right time and at the right scale. Wyoming’s leaders anticipated change, and they guided it, crafting legal mechanisms to empower local communities and invest in the future. Large industrial development took many shapes and forms. We may argue about specific impacts, but we can’t dispute that Wyoming’s leaders had the foresight to make the issue bigger than any one project. Wyoming as a whole benefited as a result. Data centers are a different type of industrial development, and the structures created more than 50 years ago need retooling to ensure Wyoming benefits from this new type of development. Wyoming’s leaders could not have imagined the impacts of data center development on our environment and quality of life in the past. They can now. As Wyoming stares down the barrel of a new digital age, we need vision, leadership and guardrails to guide this development. Communities are demanding more of a say in their future, and today’s boogieman is how future data center developments occur. Fear of what might happen must give way to a vision of what we want, collectively, and how we are going to get there. It’s time we worked together to define what responsible data center development looks like on Wyoming’s terms — now and for future generations. Leaders who fail to give the public modern tools to address modern challenges are merely feeding “Club No.” The Wyoming Outdoor Council is attempting to catalyze this conversation over the next several weeks with a series of community forums across the state, and we hope you’ll be part of the solution. (Editor’s note: the first forum was in Laramie on Sept. 14, and a coverage story was published in the Boomerang’s Sept. 18 editions.) What types of policy guardrails do we want to place around the things money can’t buy — clean air, clean water, dark skies, open lands, peace and quiet, healthy wildlife populations and the quintessential character of so many Wyoming towns? We are eager to help communities advocate for tools to help guide data center development on their terms. We did this some 50 years ago by helping to champion policies like the Industrial Siting Act, and we hope Wyoming leaders and citizens alike will join in doing it again.

artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia A DoGo Power realizou o evento "Formando o Futuro da Energia" - Estratégia e Lançamento de Novos Produtos, lançando globalmente sua estratégia "Orientada a Cenários + Formação de 22 de setembro de 2026 XANGAI, 22 de setembro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A DoGo Power realizou o evento “Formando o Futuro da Energia” – Estratégia e Lançamento de Novos Produtos, lançando globalmente sua estratégia “Orientada a Cenários + Formação de Redes + IA”, juntamente com soluções inteligentes de armazenamento de energia para formação de redes para cenários comerciais e industriais (C&I) de grande e médio porte e em escala de serviços públicos. Robin Zhu, fundador e CEO da DoGo Power, afirmou: “Após uma rápida expansão em escala, o setor de armazenamento de energia entrou em uma fase de desenvolvimento de alta qualidade.” A adaptação de cenários, a formação de redes e a IA tornaram-se elementos essenciais da competitividade. O armazenamento de energia precisa deixar de ser uma “unidade de custo” e se tornar uma “unidade criadora de valor”. A DoGo Power concentra-se no armazenamento de energia em escala de rede para formação de redes elétricas, com o objetivo de ser líder em tecnologia de ponta para o novo tipo de sistema de energia. Buscamos cooperar com parceiros globais para fomentar um novo crescimento industrial através da inovação tecnológica.” A DoGo Power estabeleceu três centros de P&D e dois centros de simulação e testes na China, reunindo 19 grupos de especialistas interdisciplinares liderados por doutores, com mais de 60% da equipe dedicada à P&D. Seus três centros de produção globais oferecem uma capacidade de produção de 10 GWh na primeira fase. Apoiada por uma rede de vendas e serviços que abrange mais de 30 países e regiões, a DoGo evoluiu da exportação de produtos para a operação localizada. Orientação estratégica: Da industrialização da energia renovável à transformação das indústrias tradicionais pelas energias renováveis. A DoGo Power identifica um caminho de evolução em quatro estágios para um novo tipo de sistema de energia: 1-Expansão de P&D, da indústria e das tecnologias, 2-Formação de Grade para Estabilização, 3-IA para Maior Receita e 4-Integração Inteligente Holística. O setor encontra-se atualmente na Fase 2. Com base nisso, a DoGo desenvolve uma solução para a Etapa 3 e implementa negócios globais rumo à Etapa 4 sob dois pilares principais: Integrando EMS, PMS, PCS e BMS, a plataforma 4S constrói estações de armazenamento de energia inteligentes capazes de análise, otimização, tomada de decisões e atualização iterativa. Com o respaldo dessa base técnica, a DoGo fornece soluções em escala de rede adequadas para diversos cenários, requisitos de múltiplas energias e múltiplas escalas temporais em todo o mundo. Soluções de Novos Produtos Baseadas em Cenários Duas soluções emblemáticas de sistemas de armazenamento de energia (ESS) para formação de redes inteligentes foram lançadas para cenários comerciais e industriais (C&I) e de grande escala para concessionárias de serviços públicos. 1.Solução C&I Smart GFM ESS Adotando um design compacto do tipo “1 ESS substitui 8 gabinetes”, esta unidade de 3 metros consolida as funções de seis gabinetes ESS de 260 kWh+, um gabinete combinador, um gabinete on/off-grid e um transformador de isolamento. Isso reduz o CAPEX inicial em 1,2 centavos de dólar por Wh, diminui a ocupação de terras em 35% e encurta a entrega do projeto em 5 a 7 dias. Com suporte para acesso a múltiplas fontes, como painéis fotovoltaicos, geradores a diesel, pontos de recarga, rede elétrica e sistemas de gerenciamento, o sistema permite a comutação perfeita entre conexão e desconexão da rede em ?20ms, atendendo de forma confiável cargas sensíveis e de alta potência e concretizando o conceito de “1 contêiner equivale a 1 microrrede”. A capacidade de dimensionamento flexível suporta a implantação mista de diferentes séries e a compatibilidade com inversores de terceiros para maximizar a utilização dos ativos existentes. 2.Solução de armazenamento de energia GFM inteligente em escala de utilidade pública Desenvolvido para projetos com terrenos complexos e restrições de transporte, o contêiner pesa menos de 22 toneladas, dobrando as rotas de transporte viáveis em comparação com os contêineres convencionais de 20 pés e reduzindo os custos de logística marítima e terrestre. Seu design sem cabos elimina a necessidade de escavações e montagem de cabos no local, com o pré-comissionamento completo do sistema realizado na fábrica. Aproveitando a arquitetura dinâmica de taxa C, os clientes podem começar com uma implementação de duração de 2 horas para controlar o CAPEX e expandir por meio de gabinetes de expansão de data center para ajustar suavemente as taxas C e as durações de backup para corresponder aos modelos de negócios em evolução. Grade-Formando o Núcleo: Arquitetura de Coordenação de 3 Camadas Para equilibrar a estabilidade do sistema e os benefícios econômicos, a DoGo Power adota uma arquitetura de 3 camadas: A arquitetura permite que os sistemas de armazenamento ofereçam suporte à estabilidade e regulação flexível nos lados da geração, da rede e da carga. No que diz respeito à geração, permite uma relação de 4:1 entre energia solar e armazenamento, duplicando a instalação de painéis fotovoltaicos sem necessidade de atualizações no ponto de acoplamento comum (PCC). Do lado da rede elétrica, opera de forma estável em redes fracas (SCR > 1), atenua as flutuações terminais e melhora a confiabilidade do fornecimento de energia em 0,03%. Do lado da carga, realiza a comutação entre sistemas conectados à rede e isolados em menos de 20 ms e fortalece a interação bidirecional entre fonte e carga. artigo.texto: Timâs view On top of power hardware shortages, angry neighbors, and permitting delays, data center developers have a new headache to deal with: skeptical insurers. Wall Street is more than happy to rain cash down on AI infrastructure. But the insurance industry is still struggling to design and price coverage for these massive, super-expensive buildings, Joe Peiser, CEO of risk capital at Aon, told me Wednesday: âInsurance really is a bottleneck.â Climate change impacts are one problem: Data centers consume huge volumes of water, leaving them exposed to drought, and many are being planned in places that are prone to floods, fires, tornadoes, or other disasters. Up to 80% of data center projects globally are exposed to such hazards, a recent study from the risk analytics firm First Street found. Investors and insurers are starting to ask developers more pointed questions about the buildingsâ physical integrity and siting, Peiser said, and asking for better forecasts about future climate exposure. Data centers are also expensive, reaching into the tens of billions of dollars; insurers are starting to get sufficient capital in place to cover that volume of risk, but are struggling to keep up with the requirements of the biggest hyperscalers. The tightness of the power equipment supply chain is another major risk. If a gas turbine breaks, and the queue for replacement parts takes weeks or months, âthat loss to insurers or their policyholder or both is going to be dramatically higher than anyone is currently thinking about,â Peiser said. Usually insurers have a simple way to deal with novel or unknown risks: Just charge more for coverage. In the case of energy infrastructure and oil tankers in the Middle East that were suddenly exposed to missiles and drones this year, for example, insurers adapted quickly rather than walking away. The same story will apply to data centers; theyâre unlikely to become completely uninsurable, even with climate risk. But keeping them covered wonât be cheap. And some critical questions remain unanswered. If power problems, permitting delays, or extreme weather cause a data center to go offline or drag out its launch date, and a Big Tech companyâs AI business suffers as a result, âhow do you quantify that, and how do insurers respond?â Peiser said. âI foresee that being a significant mess.â Notable - AI data center backlash is partly driven by âfear of the unknown,â Nvidiaâs head of sustainability told Semafor at The Next 3 Billion event. He called these fears a âfundamentalâ human response.

artigo.texto: Polo de data centers no futuro da região O Grande ABC pode subir para a nuvem, ao menos na intenção. A ideia veio de Akira Auriani (PSB), prefeito de Rio Grande da Serra, que levou ao Consórcio Intermunicipal a proposta de transformar a região em um novo hub de data centers. O plano ganhou força ontem (22), em São Caetano, diante do ministro do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços, Márcio Elias Rosa. Na teoria, a conta fecha: água e energia são o combustível dessas operações, e Akira garante ter ambas. O desafio é fazer a nuvem descer ao chão. Há um caminho nada glamouroso pela frente: rever Planos Diretores, mapear terrenos e desenhar incentivos fiscais. O próprio prefeito admite que “não é tão simples”. A promessa de empregos e renda é valiosa, mas, até o primeiro servidor ligar, há muita burocracia para processar. Bastidores Compartilhando Que o vereador de São Bernardo José Aurélio Bacelar de Pa ula, presidente do diretório municipal do Podemos, é aliado de primeira hora da presidente nacional da legenda, deputada federal Renata Abreu, que busca a reeleição, não é novidade. O diferencial de Aurélio, porém, parece ir além da lealdade partidária, tanto que o podemista deve acompanhar Renata em agendas de campanha pelo Estado. Na segunda-feira (21), por exemplo, na Associação dos Funcionários Públicos, o fiel escudeiro ficou até o fim do evento ao lado da deputada, enquanto alguns saíram à surdina e deixaram a presidente nacional à procura dos correligionários. A corrida eleitoral do ex-prefeito de São Bernardo Frank Aguiar (Podemos) por vaga no Congresso ganhou reforço estético. Em meio à rotina de campanha, o candidato a deputado federal abriu espaço na agenda para renovar a harmonização facial. Pelo visto, o “Cãozinho dos Teclados” quer garantir o retorno a Brasília com cara de recém-chegado à política. Afinal, para suportar a maratona até a urna sem demonstrar o cansaço na pele, um retoque no visual cai bem. De cá ou de lá? O vereador de São Caetano Bruno Vassari (PSB) tem marcado presença nas agendas de reeleição da deputada estadual Carla Morando (PSD) e da candidatura de Orlando Morando (MDB) à Câmara Federal. No entanto, em evento no município, o parlamentar endossou apoio aos correligionários Caio França (a estadual) e Tabata Amaral (a federal). A movimentação com os aliados de sigla, contudo, foi discreta: não houve sequer um registro fotográfico publicado em seu perfil oficial. Atenção! Os comentários do site são via Facebook. Lembre-se de que o comentário é de inteira responsabilidade do autor e não expressa a opinião do jornal. Comentários que violem a lei, a moral e os bons costumes ou violem direitos de terceiros poderão ser denunciados pelos usuários e sua conta poderá ser banida.

artigo.texto: Washington state is no stranger to data centers, with the first wave of modern facilities going into the small Grant County city of Quincy two decades ago, thanks to state sales tax incentives, affordable land and cheap hydropower electricity. A decade ago, Microsoft’s Columbia Data Center there was considered the largest in the world and consumed up to about 50 megawatts of electricity. But cloud computing and artificial intelligence needs are driving a new boom of “hyperscale” data center projects around the country that plan to use orders of magnitude more power. Take the Piketon, Ohio, project that’s being called the world’s largest AI data center. Planned on a former uranium enrichment site owned by the U.S. Department of Energy, the public-private partnership between the U.S., Japan and OpenAI (the company behind ChatGPT) intends to build a 10-gigawatt data center after finishing environmental cleanup. The facility is slated to use enough electricity to power millions of homes or, as Cincinnati TV station WLWT5 described it, “more power than all of the homes in Ohio.” This year, the environmental nonprofit Columbia Riverkeeper identified more than “100 data center campuses at various stages of development and operation in 12 Washington and Oregon counties bordering the Columbia River.” According to a February report, the organization notes Quincy remains the region’s largest data center hub, with 750 MW of existing capacity, but Microsoft is expanding in East Wenatchee, Google is expanding operations near The Dalles, Oregon, and Amazon plans to add more sites in Eastern Oregon. These massive warehouses — some campuses boast millions of square feet to house servers — also require cooling for the constantly running technology inside, with some using hundreds of millions of gallons of water per year for evaporative cooling. Some use ambient air for cooling in combination with water, while others are looking to conserve water with “closed-loop” cooling systems, which have been likened to car radiators or air conditioning systems. Last year, McKinstry opened a 150,000-square-foot West Plains facility “dedicated to building modular cooling plants and liquid cooling systems for large-scale data center clients,” the company told the Spokane Journal of Business. In an email to the Inlander, McKinstry notes the closed-loop cooling systems can reduce water consumption by up to 99%. Other companies, aware of public concerns, are exploring interesting water solutions. The Delta Gigasite 10 GW data center in Millard County, Utah (also labeled the world’s largest), is proposing to “create” water by recovering condensation from the natural gas it burns to power the campus. However, if science doesn’t prove the process works, “Project Oasis,” which will use a closed-loop cooling system and already has a conditional use permit, will still be built, the Salt-Lake Tribune reports. Against that backdrop, communities across the country have been ringing alarm bells and demanding their local governments regulate the construction and siting of new-era data centers. Major bipartisan concerns include excessive energy and water consumption, the potential to increase electric bills and blackouts, noise pollution, and whether a couple hundred new long-term jobs at these facilities and the increased property tax revenue they contribute is worth it. While concerns over the technology’s impacts on jobs and natural resources are not new, conversations around AI reached a fever pitch in recent weeks. Most notably, on Sept. 8, Jacob Coxon, a researcher for Anthropic, the company behind the AI Claude, publicly posted on social media that he had resigned because AI companies are “acting irresponsibly” as they push their programs toward so-called superintelligence — in other words, to become smarter than humans. “Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources,” Coxon, who also previously worked for OpenAI, wrote on X. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Over the following days, AI leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, called on developers to “slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.” Troubling incidents may have contributed to the impulse to pump the brakes: Multiple times this year, AI “agents” that were supposedly in a “sandboxed” environment (restricted from internet access and isolated from other systems for testing) were able to connect to the internet and hack other companies, as reported by CBS, Wired and other outlets. Similar to other communities, the Inland Northwest is grappling with what to do after learning about multiple data center proposals, including one that could use as much power as all of Avista Utilities’ roughly 418,000 electricity customers combined. Local governments across Eastern Washington and North Idaho are responding by temporarily blocking data center permit applications as they draft new codes and await possible action at the state and federal level. TAKE A PAUSE In March 2025, the Kootenai County Board of Commissioners issued an emergency 182-day moratorium on data center applications after learning some companies were eyeing the area. By October, the board approved new code preventing data centers from building over the Spokane Valley-Rathdrum Prairie Aquifer, the region’s sole source of drinking water. Though the new code effectively bans data centers in unincorporated areas in the north half of Kootenai County, the board also requested staff draft a more permanent ban. However, the three-member commission backed off that request in February, with Kootenai County Commissioners Bruce Mattare and Leslie Duncan noting that some small-scale data centers may be acceptable, as they are used for things like banking and health care. artigo.texto: XIAMEN, China, Sept. 22, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- At its “Powered Day in, Day out” launch event, HiTHIUM unveiled the ∞Power N4.0MWh, a 4 MWh sodium-ion battery energy storage system equipped with its new ∞Cell N785Ah cell. Designed for a 30-year service life, the solution is scheduled to enter full-scale production and delivery in 2027. HiTHIUM said the ∞Cell N785Ah was developed through integrated innovation in materials and manufacturing processes. It uses a polyanionic chemistry based on an NFPP cathode, hard-carbon anode and customized electrolyte, together with ultra-thick electrodes and long-life structural components. Wide-format stacking makes the cell compatible with HiTHIUM’s existing kAh-class lithium-ion manufacturing platform, supporting production scale-up. The cell is designed for 20,000 cycles at 70% state of health and supports storage durations from two to eight hours. At system level, a stacked-cell architecture reduces station footprint by 30%, while PCS rated-power utilization is more than 20% higher than in HiTHIUM’s previous-generation sodium-ion system. HiTHIUM also reports 24-hour comprehensive efficiency above 88%, with operating and standby auxiliary power consumption reduced by 30% and 50%, respectively. The system is designed to align its operating life with a 30-year power-station cycle. “30 years means 10,950 days of validation—a long-term commitment to our customers,” said Dr. Aileen Wang, Director of HiTHIUM’s Battery Research Institute. The product advances support HiTHIUM’s goal of accelerating sodium-ion industrialization. Dr. Nazar Yi, Chief Technology Officer of HiTHIUM, identified affordability and long-term resource availability as the two main requirements for large-scale deployment. HiTHIUM positions the new solution as part of an effort to treat electrochemical storage as long-life energy infrastructure and move levelized storage costs toward RMB 0.1 per kWh. The company views sodium-ion as complementary to lithium-ion rather than a replacement. It will initially target utility-scale storage before expanding into commercial and industrial, residential and broader energy-access applications. HiTHIUM also launched the ∞Edge Pioneer Program to test cells and systems in extreme environments and disclose progress over the next three years. About HiTHIUM Founded in 2019, HiTHIUM specializes in integrated energy storage solutions centered on battery and system technologies. Its capabilities span R&D, manufacturing, delivery, operation and maintenance, with operations across more than 40 countries and regions. HiTHIUM focuses on utility-scale, long-duration and grid-side energy storage. Its strategy combines purpose-built products for different storage durations with expanding global manufacturing, sales and service networks to strengthen localized delivery and lifecycle support. artigo.texto: AUSTRALIA will support the Philippines’ renewable energy development, carbon market, and offshore wind industry through a P2-billion economic development grant over five years. “This is a program that has been developed jointly by the Australian government and the Philippine government to deliver better economic outcomes to boost infrastructure and to improve living standards in communities throughout the Philippines,” Australian Assistant Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade Matt Thistlethwaite told reporters in a briefing on Tuesday. Thistlethwaite said that renewable energy, the establishment of a carbon market, and the development of the offshore wind industry were among the priority areas discussed with Philippine government officials under the Promoting Growth, Resilience, Economic Stability and Sustainability in the Philippines (Progress) program. “We haven’t allocated funding to specific projects yet. We’re very much in the scoping phase,” he said. Thistlethwaite said the Australian government has already allocated the AU$45 million or P2 billion for the program, but individual projects will still have to be identified and approved through a partnership between the two countries. “That will rely on the requests from the Philippine government. This project is very much about providing support for the Philippines government to deliver on their priorities,” he said. Australia has appointed Boston Consulting Group as a partner that will work with Philippine government departments to develop the details of the projects and funding commitments over the five-year period. Thistlethwaite clarified that the grant should not be viewed as a single disbursement for already identified projects. “The individual projects will be determined by the Australian government in partnership with the Filipino government and the government departments,” he said. As projects are approved, Australia and the Philippines will announce them jointly. “At the moment, the funding has been allocated from the Australian Government. It’s now up to us to work together on providing that funding to individual projects,” Thistlethwaite said.

artigo.texto: Alibaba lançou o Zhenwu V900, descrito pela empresa como o chip de IA mais poderoso da China, enquanto prepara forte expansão de sua infraestrutura. O Alibaba Group (NYSE:BABA) apresentou na terça-feira um novo processador de inteligência artificial, descrevendo-o como o chip de IA mais poderoso da China, e delineou planos para expandir a capacidade de seus data centers para mais de 20 gigawatts até 2032. O CEO Eddie Wu apresentou o acelerador Zhenwu V900 na Conferência Apsara anual da Alibaba em Hangzhou, destacando o investimento da empresa em infraestrutura de IA e computação avançada. As ações da Alibaba listadas em Hong Kong fecharam em alta de 2% na terça-feira, enquanto as ações listadas nos EUA subiram mais de 3% nas negociações pré-mercado. O Zhenwu V900 oferece três vezes o desempenho do seu antecessor Segundo a Alibaba, o Zhenwu V900 oferece desempenho três vezes superior ao do processador Zhenwu M890 da geração anterior. Durante seu discurso de abertura, Wu afirmou: “O Zhenwu V900 é o chip de IA mais poderoso da China atualmente, oferecendo três vezes o desempenho de seu antecessor, o Zhenwu M890.” A alegação de desempenho foi feita pela Alibaba e não foi verificada de forma independente no relatório fornecido. Segundo Wu, o novo acelerador pode ser implantado em clusters com até 500.000 unidades para treinar modelos avançados de IA. O processador desempenhará um papel central nos planos da Alibaba de expandir a capacidade de seus data centers para mais de 20 gigawatts até 2032. Alibaba mira em modelos de IA maiores e infraestrutura de computação Wu também descreveu a ambição da Alibaba de treinar um modelo de IA contendo até 10 trilhões de parâmetros. Ele afirmou que a equipe de desenvolvimento do Qwen, da empresa, estava explorando o aprimoramento recursivo, uma abordagem que envolve sistemas de IA contribuindo para melhorias em suas próprias capacidades. A Alibaba investiu dezenas de bilhões de dólares no desenvolvimento de seus modelos Qwen e na construção da infraestrutura computacional necessária para suportá-los. A empresa também destinou recursos substanciais ao desenvolvimento de processadores de IA proprietários, visto que a China busca aumentar a produção nacional de semicondutores e reduzir a dependência de tecnologia estrangeira. Wu descreveu a demanda do cliente impulsionada por IA como “excepcionalmente robusta”, acrescentando que ela estava contribuindo para o crescimento da receita da Alibaba Cloud. Citi prevê potencial para US$ 160 bilhões em receita com nuvem até o ano fiscal de 2033 Analistas do Citi afirmaram que a expansão de infraestrutura proposta pela Alibaba pode impulsionar significativamente o aumento da receita com computação em nuvem nos próximos anos. Em uma nota de pesquisa, eles afirmaram: “Nossa visão preliminar é que a mensagem do CEO da Alibaba, Sr. Wu, de 20 GW de infraestrutura de IA até 2032, ou nossa projeção para o ano fiscal de 2033, poderia se traduzir em US$ 160 bilhões em receitas externas de nuvem até o ano fiscal de 2033, o que poderia representar um aumento de US$ 60 bilhões em relação à nossa estimativa atual de US$ 100 bilhões no ano fiscal de 2031.” Os analistas acrescentaram: “Isso também sugere uma taxa de crescimento anual composta (CAGR) de receita de aproximadamente 40% do ano fiscal de 2026 ao ano fiscal de 2033, o que implica que o ritmo de crescimento acelerado será mantido.” As projeções do Citi indicam que a receita externa com serviços em nuvem poderá atingir US$ 160 bilhões no ano fiscal de 2033, em comparação com a estimativa anterior de US$ 100 bilhões para o ano fiscal de 2031. Esses números representam as estimativas do banco, e não as projeções formais de receita da Alibaba. Os gastos de capital continuam sendo uma consideração fundamental O Alibaba não revisou sua previsão de despesas de capital de 380 bilhões de yuans. No entanto, o Citi afirmou que os comentários anteriores de Wu durante a teleconferência de resultados da empresa sugeriam que o investimento em infraestrutura de IA poderia permanecer elevado nos próximos anos. Os analistas também esperam que a Alibaba financie parte de sua capacidade computacional planejada por meio de parcerias com outros participantes do setor, o que pode envolver despesas operacionais em vez de investimento de capital direto. Os gastos da Alibaba com IA já afetaram a lucratividade. A empresa reportou uma queda de 75% no lucro líquido em seus resultados trimestrais mais recentes, com a compressão das margens ligada ao seu programa de investimentos. No entanto, a receita proveniente de serviços de computação e nuvem com IA aumentou acentuadamente durante o trimestre de junho, refletindo a crescente contribuição desses negócios para as operações do Alibaba. O Alibaba Group também é negociado na B3 por meio da BDR (BOV:BABA34). artigo.texto: Mais de 740.000 hectares de floresta, com potencial para desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono. O Parque Nacional Song Thanh é uma das maiores áreas florestais de uso especial na cidade de Da Nang . Com aproximadamente 76.000 hectares de floresta primária, esta área tem capacidade para absorver e armazenar uma grande quantidade de carbono. De acordo com cálculos preliminares, esta área florestal pode absorver centenas de milhares de toneladas de CO2 anualmente. Se convertermos 1 tonelada de CO2 em um crédito de carbono, a quantidade de carbono absorvida poderia gerar centenas de milhares de créditos de carbono. Segundo os proprietários de florestas de uso especial e proteção, no contexto dos atuais desastres naturais, se a cidade de Da Nang pudesse vender créditos de carbono, isso geraria receita adicional para a restauração florestal, a recuperação da biodiversidade e uma maior adaptação às mudanças climáticas. O Sr. Dinh Van Hong, Diretor do Conselho de Administração do Parque Nacional Song Thanh, em Da Nang, acredita que a venda de créditos de carbono é uma política viável e que essa receita pode contribuir para a melhoria da qualidade de vida das pessoas na zona de amortecimento, além de fortalecer a capacidade de proteção florestal. Da Nang está gradualmente desenvolvendo projetos de carbono florestal. Após a fusão com a província de Quang Nam, a cidade de Da Nang agora possui mais de 740.000 hectares de floresta, incluindo mais de 500.000 hectares de floresta primária. De acordo com os cálculos apresentados na proposta do projeto, a área florestal da cidade tem capacidade para absorver e armazenar carbono. Anteriormente, desde 2021, a província de Quang Nam foi autorizada pelo Primeiro-Ministro a desenvolver um projeto piloto para a venda de créditos de carbono florestal. Até o momento, a cidade de Da Nang aprovou o Projeto para o Desenvolvimento e Gestão de Créditos de Carbono Florestal para o período de 2026 a 2030, com uma visão para 2035. A cidade pretende ter de 1 a 3 projetos de carbono florestal aprovados até 2030, colaborar com pelo menos 2 parceiros nacionais e internacionais, concluir de 1 a 2 dossiês de registro de projetos e assinar pelo menos um contrato de compra de créditos de carbono. A cidade também almeja que pelo menos 70% dos proprietários de florestas, incluindo organizações, famílias e comunidades elegíveis, participem desta iniciativa. A floresta primária no Parque Nacional de Song Thanh tem potencial para gerar créditos de carbono florestal. De acordo com o plano, o Centro Financeiro Internacional de Da Nang colaborará com agências, unidades e organizações internacionais para estudar a viabilidade do desenvolvimento de projetos de carbono florestal vinculados a atividades de gestão, proteção e desenvolvimento florestal em diversas áreas potenciais. O Sr. Duong Duy Khanh, Gerente de Projetos de Restauração Florestal e Desenvolvimento de Meios de Subsistência na cidade de Da Nang, do WWF Vietnam, afirmou que o WWF está apoiando as localidades na finalização de planos de venda de créditos de carbono, visando a participação do Vietnã no mercado global de carbono. Da Nang almeja um mercado de créditos de carbono. Para gerar créditos de carbono negociáveis, os projetos precisam passar por diversas etapas, desde a identificação do potencial e o desenvolvimento do projeto, até a conclusão da documentação e, finalmente, a medição, avaliação e verificação dos resultados da redução de emissões ou do sequestro de carbono. Segundo os líderes do Comitê Popular da cidade de Da Nang, a cidade está implementando créditos de carbono e pretende integrá-los ao mercado global. Os benefícios dessa atividade são identificados como estando ligados aos interesses da nação e das comunidades da zona de amortecimento. Até 2030, Da Nang pretende ter projetos de carbono florestal aprovados, conectando simultaneamente o fornecimento de créditos de carbono florestal da cidade aos mercados de carbono nacionais e internacionais. A cidade identificou o desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono florestal como essencial para o manejo, a proteção e o desenvolvimento florestal, criando recursos adicionais para a restauração florestal, a conservação e a recuperação da biodiversidade e o apoio aos meios de subsistência das comunidades da zona de amortecimento. Com um plano estratégico elaborado até 2030, Da Nang está implementando gradualmente as condições necessárias para estabelecer projetos de carbono florestal e participar do mercado de créditos de carbono. artigo.texto: CATL Starts Trial Production of Battery Cells in Hungary CATL began trial production of battery cells on September 22, 2026, at its Debrecen plant in Hungary, after obtaining all the environmental authorizations required to launch the phase. Chinese battery maker CATL (Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited) began trial production on September 22, 2026, at its newly built battery cell factory in Debrecen, Hungary. The company states it fulfilled all preconditions required to launch this phase, which aims to set up, optimize and validate production equipment and manufacturing processes ahead of the start of series production. CATL says it continues cooperating with the Hungarian government and local authorities to maintain high standards on environmental issues as well as employee health and safety. A site announced in 2022 CATL announced the construction of this second European production site in Debrecen in August 2022, with the stated aim of integrating into the continent's automotive and e-mobility supply chain. This type of investment is part of a broader push to expand energy storage capacity in Europe, illustrated by the emerging market seen in North Macedonia or by the hybrid solar-storage contract signed between Salzgitter Flachstahl and Zelestra in Germany. Construction of the first cell building began in summer 2023, and the site had been equipped, by spring 2026, with the latest production technologies, according to the company. After obtaining the occupancy permit in August 2026, CATL says it gathered all authorizations required under its IPPC permit (Integrated Pollution Prevention and Control, an integrated pollution prevention and reduction permit) before launching, on September 22, trial production on the first two manufacturing lines at the site. Repeated inspections by local authorities Before issuing the occupancy permit, the HajdÃº-Bihar County Government Office carried out regular on-site inspections at CATL's facilities to follow up on issues that had raised concerns among local residents. According to CATL, authority representatives confirmed that the company had resolved all deficiencies identified earlier in the permitting process. The Debrecen site is set to supply European automakers, several of which have already built electric vehicle production capacity in Hungary in recent years. CATL has been manufacturing battery modules there since autumn 2024 and says it has produced 537,000 modules since then. Once all facilities are operational, the Hungarian plant would, according to the company, become its largest manufacturing base outside China, with an announced capacity of 100 GWh. Environmental and health monitoring CATL says it remains committed to working with the government and authorities to protect the health and safety of its employees. Environmental factors, along with employee health and safety, will be monitored throughout the trial production period, with results to be submitted proactively to authorities, according to the company. The group describes the investment as significant not only for Debrecen and its region but also for the Hungarian economy and Europe's e-mobility supply chain. CATL also states it is committed to transparency and says it welcomes authorities to visit its site at any time.

artigo.texto: Oakland is moving closer to hitting pause on new data centers, after a City Council committee approved a proposed 45-day moratorium following testimony from residents on both sides of the issue. While the temporary ban isn't in effect yet, it cleared a key hurdle when the council committee voted in favor of the measure, meaning the city wouldn't accept any new proposals during that period. Watch NBC Bay Area News free wherever you are Environmental concerns drove much of the opposition at the hearing. Among them is a planned project at a 20,000-square-foot downtown building intended to provide computing power for artificial intelligence and robotics. While the developer calls it an "innovation center," members of the public repeatedly referred to it as a "data center." "With the proliferation of Artificial Intelligence there have been a proliferation of data centers that are more resource intensive than the past… consuming significant amounts of electrical power and water," said Oakland City Councilmember Carroll Fife. Councilmember Rowena Brown echoed the need for oversight. "The moratorium is really important because we need to work and identify key regulations we need in our city… so really just to halt and put a pause." Public commenters voiced deep frustration over the wave of development. Local "It doesn’t matter the size of the data center, it's about whether or not we will allow our city to be the playground for the ultra rich," one public commenter said. Another added, "Communities are being asked to sacrifice… this isn’t fair and it’s something we shouldn’t be doing." However, not everyone opposed the projects. A small group of speakers argued that data centers could bring much-needed jobs and new revenue to the city. "What Oakland needs is not more taxes… we need manufacturing… what works… AI," a public commenter argued. The debate mirrors similar conflicts across the Bay Area. Cities like Gilroy and Richmond recently approved their own 45-day moratoriums amid neighbor concerns. The local pushes coincide with state action; Governor Gavin Newsom recently signed seven new data center laws addressing electricity and water use by operators. Brown, who voted in favor of the Oakland committee measure, emphasized that community involvement remains vital. "I would encourage the community to continue to show up and let their voices be heard," she said. The proposed moratorium now heads to the full Oakland City Council, with a final vote scheduled for Oct. 6.

artigo.texto: An Intertek lab in the UK found just 3.4 ppm of lithium in a sample of Donut Lab’s “solid-state” battery, and the Finnish startup is now using that result to argue its cell is neither lithium-ion nor sodium-ion. But the report measured just two elements, on a cell Donut Lab took apart itself. And nine months after CES, there’s still no production vehicle running on the battery. A two-element test The Finnish startup says the goal was to end the debate over what’s inside its cell. “We wanted to put this speculation to rest with an independent test demonstrating that it is neither a lithium-ion nor a sodium battery,” CEO Marko Lehtimäki said in the announcement. That speculation didn’t come out of nowhere. In June, battery researcher Ziroth and more than 20 experts concluded that the cell Donut Lab sent to VTT behaved like a high-nickel lithium-ion cell with a graphite anode, based on its voltage curve and swelling data. Intertek’s report, from its lab in Wilton, UK, is short. Analysts cut about 0.5 g of material from anode, cathode, and current collector pieces, digested it in nitric acid, diluted it to 50 ml, and ran it through an ICP-OES instrument. Results: 3.4 ppm lithium and 632 ppm sodium by weight. A lithium-ion cell carries lithium in the percent range. So if that sample is what Donut Lab says it is, there’s essentially no lithium in it. The lab work itself is fine. The problems start with everything around it. What the report doesn’t show Start with the scope. The job Donut Lab ordered was literally “Quantification of Li and Na by ICP-OES.” Nothing else was measured. The report tells you two things the cell isn’t and zero things about what it is. Potassium, magnesium, zinc, and aluminum were never tested, and Donut Lab still won’t name its chemistry beyond “widely available, affordable and geopolitically secure materials.” Then there’s the sample. According to Intertek, “the samples were delivered in a tear down condition by Donut Lab.” Intertek didn’t open a cell. It matched the pieces to another Intertek report (2608094STO-003) that hasn’t been made public, and the analyzed sample is labeled simply “Pouchcell – Cell 1.” The words “Donut Battery” appear nowhere in the report, and nothing ties this sample to the V1.5 cell that VTT tested for energy density. The press release also says the samples included “the electrolyte situated between” the anode and cathode. Intertek’s report says otherwise, three separate times: only anode, cathode, and current collector parts were analyzed. In a solid-state battery, the electrolyte layer is a pretty important place to look for lithium. And the report went through three versions in five days. The first was issued September 17. A September 21 revision updated the “sample description and origin of samples,” and a September 22 revision made a “wording change requested in experimental.” That’s a lot of editing for a report with a single two-column results table. Finally, Intertek notes that “opinions and interpretations contained herein are outside the scope of UKAS accreditation.” The line that “it is not even possible to build a functional battery with such small amounts of active materials” comes from Donut CTO Ville Piippo, not the lab. It makes the 409 Wh/kg claim harder to believe Near-zero lithium and sodium fits one theory that has followed Donut Lab since CES: a supercapacitor or hybrid capacitor, with carbon electrodes and an electrolyte that doesn’t rely on either element. That would line up with the fast-charging and cycle-life claims. It wouldn’t line up with energy density. Earlier this month, VTT measured 409.3 Wh/kg on a Donut “V1.5” cell, cycled between 2.3 V and 4.25 V. That’s a textbook lithium-ion voltage window, and 409 Wh/kg is a number advanced silicon-anode lithium-ion cells already hit. No rechargeable chemistry without lithium or sodium has come anywhere close to that in a real cell. So either Donut Lab has quietly invented a chemistry that beats every battery lab on the planet, or the cell VTT tested and the pieces Intertek analyzed aren’t the same thing. This report doesn’t tell us which. Electrek’s Take We don’t care much anymore whether Donut Lab’s battery is solid-state and these vague and limited tests that may or may not prove otherwise do very little to Donut Lab’s credibility. Solid-state cells exist. QuantumScape, Factorial, Samsung SDI, and Toyota all have them running in labs and prototype vehicles, and all of them are still working toward mass production. A startup with a promising solid-state prototype is not news in 2026. The only thing that made Donut Lab interesting was the production claim. At CES in January, it said it had the “world’s first solid state battery that is ready for use in OEM vehicle manufacturing,” with Verge motorcycles delivering to customers in Q1 2026. Lehtimäki said it was “already in production.” We’re now at the end of September. There’s no production vehicle on the road with this battery, the Q1 “production” bikes were pre-production units, and Lehtimäki himself admitted that the 409 Wh/kg cell “is not even the cell that’s going to be shipped to customers.” So the claim that set Donut apart turned out to be wrong, and every new report since has been built to answer a different question than the one that matters. artigo.texto: Perhaps even more controversial than artificial intelligence itself is the backbone that powers the technology: Data centers can be loud and polluting, while requiring tremendous amounts of electricity and water resources. These data centers are also a key to future economic growth. AI, like it or not, is here to stay. The question in Massachusetts has become: What approach should the Commonwealth take? Massachusetts is a knowledge economy that already leans heavily on AI. Turning our backs on data centers feels hypocritical. That doesn’t mean, however, that we should roll out the welcome mat with tax credits and let data center builders dictate the shots. Governor Maura Healey has offered up a solid framework to guide any future data center buildout. Her “bring your own clean energy” approach strikes the right note. It says to developers: Yes, you can build here but not on the backs of energy ratepayers. And you can’t burn planet-warming fossil fuels or pass along the costs of connecting your enterprise to the power grid. The governor wants data centers to either build their own clean energy supplies or pay into a ratepayer protection fund. The governor’s stated approach is to try to balance economic growth alongside protections for Massachusetts residents. Healey also signed an executive order this month requiring community approval before state permits are issued to new data centers. Jennifer Granholm, a former secretary of energy under former president Joe Biden, called the governor’s plans a “good blueprint for the rest of the country.” Granholm said Healey “isn’t reflexively saying ‘no’ to data centers, and she isn’t writing them a blank check either. She’s saying: if you want to build here, bring something to the table.” A framework from a governor can offer guidance to state agencies, but it doesn’t carry the weight of law. The Massachusetts Legislature is working on solutions, tucked into two behemoth energy bills making their way through the House and Senate. The House is proposing that data centers “procure” renewable energy to power at least 80 percent of a data center’s needs. The Senate has proposed putting a pause on growth to buy time to study the best path forward. The chamber is also discussing putting limits on tax breaks for data centers. (The governor halted applications for data center tax incentives in June.) As with any new and quickly evolving industry, many questions will need to be sorted out. A key sticking point: What could renewable energy procurement look like? Should data centers be required to physically build solar panels with battery storage, for example? Or, if data centers are relying on renewable power from the grid, how do we ensure this isn’t pushing another customer off of clean energy and onto fossil fuels? Should nuclear energy count as a clean source? Lawmakers and energy regulators should quibble over the details. But Beacon Hill also needs to prioritize getting some set of rules to the governor’s desk before this legislative session adjourns in January. There’s simply too much hand wringing, fear, and confusion in our communities not to establish a legally binding road map. If new guidelines are too onerous, data center developers may say no thank you and move onto the next state. That wouldn’t be the worst thing in the world. “It’s not a big loss,” Erin Baker, a University of Massachusetts Amherst professor who researches mathematical modeling of energy decisions, told the editorial board. “It’s not super clear to me what value we get from data centers in our community. They don’t have a lot of jobs.” In the other scenario, if rules for building data centers are too loose or not established, it would be much harder to go in reverse, warns Democratic state Senator Michael Moore of Millbury, who worries the state could someday be left with gigantic white elephant eyesores. It’s a fair point. The fact is, all technologies become more efficient with time. There’s no reason to expect otherwise with data centers, which should become more efficient and less polluting, and may no longer need vast facilities. If Massachusetts can establish rigorous standards, not outright bans on data centers, other states will undoubtedly follow suit, as Granholm suggested, and a national or regional standard could be set. That sounds much better than the current race to the bottom between states chasing short-term construction jobs. If done right, data centers could even become a way to lower our electricity bills. For example, if data centers were required to pay higher costs for the upkeep of transmission lines, that would help the rest of us. Or imagine a data center powered by solar panels with battery storage sending excess electricity back to the grid. Baker says all this will be tricky to operationalize. But making data centers work for us is worth trying. Editorials represent the views of the Boston Globe Editorial Board. Follow us @GlobeOpinion.

artigo.texto: Ad: “Our Land and Money” Transcript: Chaz Molder: “I’m Chaz Molder. I was born and raised right here in Tennessee, where we’ve produced groundbreaking music, medical innovation, and some really good football. Now, Charlie Hatcher wants to take our land and our money and give it away to AI data centers. Hatcher supported a law giving $70 billion of your tax money to data center developers, driving up electricity costs on all of us. I say, heck no. I approve this message because I’ll always fight for Tennessee.” Analysis: In his latest TV ad, set to begin airing in the Nashville market on Thursday, Chaz Molder is using one of the hottest topics in American politics to attack his opponent Charlie Hatcher. Debates over data centers have exploded in recent months, in both larger cities and more rural areas. Opposition has skyrocketed while crossing political lines, though President Trump and other national Republican figures have continued to support their development for strategic reasons. Molder, the mayor of Columbia and the Democratic nominee in the 5th Congressional District, is elevating the issue in a newly redrawn district particularly attuned to it. Though the district no longer includes part of Nashville, where the data center fight has included a moratorium and efforts to block a high-profile data center proposal near the Nashville Zoo, it has taken on part of Memphis, home to a raging fight over Elon Musk’s data center turbines. More conservative parts of the district, from Maury to Henry counties, have also debated the topic. It does not appear that any data centers have been built in Columbia, where Molder has been mayor for eight years. The ad, part of a seven-figure campaign that launched earlier this month, cites Hatcher’s support for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which included provisions in support of data center constructions. But Hatcher has also spoken more directly about the controversy. “That’s something people are not educated enough on,” Hatcher said in a July interview. “It’s not a yes or no, it’s a case by case. … If we lose the technology/AI war with China, they will own us. You’ve got to have data centers.” He went on to say that concerns about data centers’ use of electric and water resources should be considered before construction. A Hatcher spokesperson added that data centers should bear the financial burden of the infrastructure needed for their development. Hatcher has yet to go on the air, and he entered the general election at a financial disadvantage to Molder. That could be narrowing, however, as Republican donors previously wary of supporting a candidate running against a Trump-endorsed incumbent (Rep. Andy Ogles, whom Hatcher beat in the August primary) can now back him.
