artigo.texto: La Verne lithium battery storage fire forces evacuations near water district facility The Brief - A small explosion and fire broke out in an outdoor lithium battery storage unit at a Metropolitan Water District facility in La Verne. - Hazmat and fire crews responded, prompting mandatory evacuations for nearby shopping centers, neighborhoods, and shelter-in-place orders for two schools. - The fire was largely extinguished by 2:30 p.m. The cause is unknown. LOS ANGELES - Evacuation orders were issued after a fire broke out at an outdoor lithium battery storage unit near a solar panel field at a Metropolitan Water District facility in La Verne Tuesday. What we know The fire was reported around 11:40 a.m. at the facility in the 3200 block of Wheeler Avenue. According to the La Verne Fire Department, a small explosion occurred in the battery unit which stored lithium batteries. Hazmat crews were brought in, and fire crews were mainly spraying the area with water to prevent the flames from spreading. Metropolitan said the water supply was not affected. Nearby neighborhoods evacuated Due to the hazardous nature of lithium batteries, evacuation orders were issued in the areas around the facility. La Verne police said shopping centers along Wheeler north of Foothill Boulevard were evacuated as a precaution. Shelter-in-place orders were issued for Grace Elementary School and Bonita High School. An evacuation center was established at the La Verne Community Center on 3680 D St. By 2:30 p.m., the fire was mainly out. The fire department said one civilian was injured and taken to a hospital. No additional details were released. A short time after that, some evacuation orders were downgraded to warnings, while others were reduced to advisories. An evacuation order remained in place in the immediate vicinity of the facility. The Source Information for this story came from the La Verne Fire Department. A statement was given by the Metropolitan Water District.

artigo.texto: What is repetitive re-trading (RTT) by BESS in the UK, and what is electricity markets operator NESO looking to do about it? What is repetitive re-trading (RTT) A key application of grid-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) is selling energy to the grid. This is typically done when prices are high, after batteries are charged by renewables or from the grid when the price is low. This approach allows companies to gain money from the grid for selling this energy, but there is a specific situation in parts of the UK grid currently where companies ‘sell’ their energy, but that energy doesn’t end up being distributed (for reasons explained further down). The companies can then sell this energy again making money multiple times before it is actually distributed. This scenario is called repetitive re-trading (RTT) and in theory can arise because companies know that there is already too much energy being distributed in a constrained area of the transmission network, but they can still bid to release that energy from their assets. Therefore, companies know that their energy won’t be needed but the bid needs to be paid if accepted, and it has created scenarios where companies are being paid by the government to not sell their energy because of network constraints. While the bidding and energy release process was designed to balance and stabilise the grid, it has turned into what some call a ‘cash cow for private investors’ at the expense of other energy consumers—a point that is argued by the Prospect trade Union. For many years RTT was mainly an issue with long duration assets, such as pumped storage, that could take advantage of high prices and export for long time periods, but the number of batteries now attached to the grid has meant that BESS are causing RTT issues as well. So, why does RTT actually happen? RTT happens when energy storage assets are located behind a constrained area of the transmission system. A discharge energy constraint is a part of the transmission system that caps how fast stored energy can be released from assets into the grid. The most common constraint is a thermal transmission constraint, which manifests when the amount of energy trying to flow through a power line exceeds the physical capacity of the line without causing thermal issues, such as overheating. Asset owners will notify the grid operators that they intend to discharge their assets (due to excess supply or high wholesale prices), which is accompanied by a bid—a price for that energy. This bid is then accepted, and the storage asset can theoretically be discharged. However, when there is a thermal constraint in the network, the National Energy System Operator (NESO) for Great Britain will reduce the output of attached storage assets by turning down the previously accepted bid and accepting a bid in the Balancing Mechanism. This then increases the output of an asset (or assets) elsewhere in the system that are not behind a constraint to replace the lost power. This leads to a curtailment in energy of the assets trying to sell from behind the constraint because the bids to sell the power at the high price are rejected and the energy is supplied from elsewhere that is not behind a constraint. In this scenario, the asset owner has still gained money from their bid, but they still have their stored energy. The money gained is the difference between the bid price and the wholesale market price. Under Transmission Constraint Licence Condition (TCLC) rules, the profit can’t be excessive and be roughly what would have been made if the constraint wasn’t there, plus any additional costs associated with the bid being turned down—but one could argue that it is effectively free money, and it is currently a legitimate way of bidding for energy dispatch. Bids are made in intervals (often half-hourly), but if the constraint still exists, asset owners can continue to bid and get paid without discharging their asset, creating a cycle that enables asset owners to continue to make money of the same stored energy—as NESO has to continue to accept bids and then turn them down when the constraint is still ongoing, a process known as ‘bidding the unit down’. Only when the constraint ends does the RTT cycle finish and the asset finally releases its stored power to the grid as it is no longer prevented from exporting. RTT is a consequence of the existing market design because asset owners are expected to optimise their own storage and discharge schedules based on the national wholesale prices, and when they potential gains are high, owners will schedule to release the energy. Aside from higher balancing costs, RTT can also cause inefficient discharge patterns. RTT is also not a new issue, and there are many areas of the network that are regularly constrained, so some storage asset owners have had significant numbers of bids accepted in constraint periods for years, which is why there is a lot of industry discussion on the topic. The amount of storage connected to the grid, and actions required by NESO to manage constraints, continues to grow. Aside from storage asset growth, there has also been a significant growth in renewable energy systems connected to the grid. Because of this growth, the transmission network around Great Britain has many areas that regularly get congested. This includes north-to-south power flows, export constraints in east England, import constraints in south England, and in north Scotland where there are many wind farms.

artigo.texto: Moore signs order setting new Maryland oversight, review standards for data centers MARYLAND (WBFF) — Maryland is tightening oversight of large data center projects as concerns grow about transparency, environmental impacts and rising electricity costs. Gov. Wes Moore on Wednesday signed an executive order setting new guidelines that companies should follow when building data centers in Maryland, including a standardized review process and new state oversight of projects. The Moore administration said the changes are intended to address concerns about transparency, environmental impacts and potential effects on rising electricity costs. The order will apply to data centers that cover 25 megawatts or more, creating a single state standard and review process for projects seeking permits, state incentives or letters of support, according to the order. It also creates the Maryland Data Center Task Force, which will review every covered data center project and maintain the Data Center Dashboard, an online platform that tracks data center development. The task force will include members from the Maryland Energy Administration and state Departments of Commerce, Labor, Environment, Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Planning. “We are establishing clear safeguards to ensure Marylanders do not foot the bill, our people benefit, community voices are heard, and our environment is protected — all while centering transparency and accountability throughout the process,” Moore said in a statement. Moore’s order comes as Baltimore County said it will extend its pause on data center development through the end of 2027, giving county officials more than a year to continue weighing community concerns and potential guardrails on the facilities. artigo.texto: How data centers shift landscape of rural communities An analysis found 67% of planned data centers are in rural areas CANTON, Miss. (InvestigateTV) — All 50 U.S. states are home to data centers, which power the growth of artificial intelligence. Companies are building large warehouse-like facilities filled with computing technology to expand their capacity. In Madison County, Mississippi, one complex is changing the surrounding area. When Amazon announced it would build two data centers in central Mississippi, state leaders said it marked the largest investment in state history. Just north of Jackson, Amazon Web Services is using dozens of local vendors to help build its $10 billion investment. Five data centers are operational on the site, with seven more under construction. Local businesses see growth Chad Wages owns a local engineering firm. Before AWS announced its plans, he had four employees. He now has 18. “I try to make sure my employees understand the once-in-a-lifetime opportunity,” Wages said. “What we proposed and did for AWS is said, hey, while y’all were figuring out all these technical components, let us handle the earthwork,” Wages said. Dwight Luckett is superintendent of the Canton Public School District. He said AWS funding could help attract teachers and build workforce training programs. “Students now will have the opportunity to get right out of high school, they will be able to go into those programs and start actually working, okay, and earn $50,000, $60,000 or more,” Luckett said. Environmental and utility concerns Data centers can also bring changes to utility rates. The energy required for some plants could be used to power hundreds of thousands of homes. AWS plans to use wastewater to cool its facilities. Data centers still increase carbon dioxide emissions and put pressure on power grids. Abre’ Conner is director of the NAACP’s Center for Environmental and Climate Justice. She said data centers often have negative impacts on already disadvantaged communities. “Companies really need to ask themselves, is what I’m building, would I want that to be next to my home?” Conner said. “You can’t just go to one part of the community and say, see, we invested here and it has nothing to do with air pollution, has nothing to do with water contamination, and then make that seem as though you’re fixing the problem,” Conner said. Temporary job surge The job surge from construction is temporary. Once construction ends, AWS will have roughly 1,000 permanent jobs at the site. There is concern in the data center market generally that supply could outpace demand. Asked whether he worries about being left with employees he doesn’t need once construction ends, Wages said, “It does. It does. You always have to be looking for the future.” Data center growth nationwide As of spring 2026, there were more than 3,000 data centers in operation in the U.S., according to Pew Research. More than 1,500 were in various stages of development. A Pew Research analysis found more than two-thirds, or 67%, of planned data centers are in rural areas, primarily in the Midwest and Southern regions. Among the climate concerns is the water required to cool the processor chips that keep data centers operating. According to a 2025 report from the Environmental and Energy Study Institute, a medium-sized data center can consume up to roughly 110 million gallons of water per year for cooling purposes, equivalent to the water usage of about 1,000 households. Data centers also bring a power struggle. A recent analysis found that between 2019 and 2025, monthly electricity bills among those located near data centers in Virginia rose more than 267%. artigo.texto: HUDSON – The Planning Board is recommending passage of a one-year moratorium on the development of data centers. It’s an effort to give the town time to design a zoning bylaw that would allow the town more discretion over what may get built. The board voted, 5-0, on September 15 in favor of the moratorium, which would last until December 31, 2027. A warrant article will be considered at the November Town Meeting. About 20 residents attended the Planning Board’s public hearing; nobody who spoke disagreed with the proposed moratorium. “I know when we think of data centers we think of the big, scary ones that are being developed in other parts of the country,” said Kristina Johnson, the town’s director of planning and community development. “That’s probably not going to happen in Hudson because of the supply of land and the power capacity.” But Johnson, and others who spoke, cautioned that data centers can take different forms, and some may not encompass many acres of space. Smaller versions called “edge” centers can be just tens of thousands of square feet. One of the first issues addressed was the impact of a moratorium on future development of 75 Reed Road, the former Intel headquarters now owned by National Development. Johnson said Intel filed a “definitive subdivision plan in 2023, which effectively freezes zoning for the parcel.” Accordingly, new zoning restrictions would not apply to that site, and a data center could be sought. National Development’s plans show one building totaling 950,000 square feet, and prepared studies indicate the facility could be a distribution center. Planning Board member Rodney Frias, in response to questions, pointed out that smaller data centers of 30,000 square feet exist, and “you can find plenty of places [for them].” Johnson reiterated the town is not thinking about the “hyperscale” centers. Planning Board chair Robert D’Amelio said some centers are producing their own power on-site, using generators. Marco DiMartino said he supported the temporary moratorium but a data center, if built appropriately, “would be a great thing for 75 Reed Road.” He further said a 1,000,000-square-foot warehouse distribution facility would create “all kinds of major traffic issues,” and added that “it’s a question of making sure we do it right.” DiMartino said the biggest issue from his perspective is noise generated by data centers. The warrant article language specifically says that “during the moratorium period, the Town shall conduct a comprehensive planning process to understand the potential land use, environmental, infrastructure, public safety, and fiscal impacts associated with such facilities, [and] evaluate best practices and regulatory approaches.” Gov. Maura Healey signed an executive order September 8 that pumps the brakes on data centers, requiring large data centers to secure local approval before state permitting could begin. But the order only applies to centers that have a peak electricity demand exceeding 25 megawatts. The November Special Town Meeting is scheduled for Monday, November 16 at 6:30 p.m. at Hudson High School.

Oracle invokes ‘force majeure’ on contested New Mexico data center Oracle sent a “force majeure” notice to a unit of Blue Owl Capital, the developer of a large data center it is building in New Mexico, Bloomberg News reported. Reuters said it could not independently verify the report. Oracle’s shares fell around 3.3% after the news. Rather than exiting as the project’s main tenant, Oracle appears to be using the notice to delay payments if the data center, known as Project Jupiter, fails to come online on schedule in 2028, citing potential delays in securing power for the site. Companies typically invoke force majeure to free themselves from contractual obligations when problems arise beyond their control, a move that can unsettle lenders and investors. Oracle said “Project Jupiter remains on our planned schedule,” and that such notices “are commonplace in developments of this scale” and don’t indicate a delay themselves. Blue Owl, which owns the data center developer Stack Infrastructure, said the notice doesn’t change its financial commitments. Blue Owl earns a 9% yield on its equity during development; once complete, that levered yield is expected to rise to around 11%. Invoking force majeure extends the period Oracle pays the lower, development-stage rent. The 1,400-acre campus, backed by $18 billion in bank loans, is part of Oracle’s broader agreement with OpenAI to provide AI computing capacity. It’s reportedly faced other setbacks too, including a delayed natural gas pipeline and legal challenges over water and air quality permits. Klimado – Navigating climate complexity just got easier. Providers are increasingly using AI to scan patient records for secondary conditions or deploying “ambient scribes” that listen to doctor-patient conversations and automatically draft clinical notes. Visits documented as more medically complex can qualify for higher insurance payments. Between 2024 and 2025, providers billed more often for these secondary conditions, adding $653 million in costs for BCBS insurers compared with 2023. More intensive care overall accounted for $942 million in additional costs over the same period. BCBSA said the shift doesn’t necessarily mean AI is being misused. “If patients are truly sicker, we’d expect to see more treatment,” said Luke Chalker, the association’s senior vice president of product and data science. The hospital industry sees it differently. The American Hospital Association argues insurers want it both ways, treating enrollees as sicker for risk-scoring purposes while pushing back on claims reflecting that same complexity. artigo.texto: A temporary pause on data centers in Oakland has passed a key hurdle. At the City Council’s Life Enrichment Committee meeting Tuesday afternoon, committee members unanimously approved a 45-day moratorium on new data center projects. The full City Council must still vote on the moratorium for it to take effect. Introduced by District 3 Councilmember and Life Enrichment Committee Chair Carroll Fife, the idea is to give the city time to evaluate the impacts of data centers on energy and water consumption, air and noise pollution, land use, and public health. “I’ve always stood for development without displacement,” Fife said. “I still do to this day.” Only one data center project has been proposed for Oakland, and it appears to be a long way from coming to fruition, according to public records. Still, concerns about the tech industry projects, closely linked to the artificial intelligence boom, have grown dramatically in recent months. District 2 Councilmember Charlene Wang had proposed amendments to Fife’s measure, including preparing a report on the Oakland-specific impacts of data centers and prohibiting data center applications from being processed. But Fife pushed back on Wang’s amendments, saying they were redundant and would take too long to process. “It’s short notice. I’ve been working on this for over a month,” said Fife, who also held a town hall meeting last weekend aimed at answering District 3 residents’ questions. Oakland’s deliberations on data centers come as communities nationwide, including in Texas, New York, and the Cherokee Nation, have passed moratoriums and even bans on the construction of these sites. Residents in the Southern California city of Monterey Park overwhelmingly approved a permanent ban on data centers, making it the first city in the nation to do so. Oakley, in East Contra Costa County, has also imposed a data center ban. Fife previously said she had planned to introduce legislation around data centers earlier this year but that the summer recess delayed her plans. In the meantime, Behring Companies, a real estate developer, announced plans to try to build a data center in downtown Oakland inside a building that used to house a Department of Energy supercomputer. That announcement turbo-charged debate around data centers in the city, leading some residents to start organizing against them. Earlier this week, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed into law several bills aimed at preventing data centers from passing on electricity costs to residents and requiring companies to report about water and electricity use. Fife’s proposal drew support from Oakland residents during the public comment portion of the meeting, with dozens urging city officials to use the moratorium as a first step toward stricter regulations or a permanent ban. “Why are we doing a moratorium?” said Toshia Christal, an Oakland teacher, artist, and business owner. “Why are we not just saying no?” Nyah Tisdell, an East Oakland organizer with Communities for a Better Environment, said residents in her community have more immediate needs than data centers. “We’re asking for libraries. We’re asking for parks. We’re asking for clean air and clean water,” she said. Another speaker named Emily echoed Tisdell’s concerns, saying the community needs “money and jobs for education, healthcare, and public transportation.” Other residents raised concerns about the amount of electricity and water data centers can consume, as well as noise, air pollution, and the potential use of fossil fuels to power backup generators. Some also worried that new development could displace Black and brown residents, gentrify their neighborhoods, or worsen public health outcomes. Medina Muñoz, who lives in East Oakland’s Sobrante Park neighborhood, told the committee that she and her daughters struggle with asthma. “We’re tired of living with pollution,” said Muñoz, speaking in Spanish. “Before you approve anything, we need you to study what contaminants would be released.” Not everyone who spoke Tuesday supported the moratorium. Some, like mayoral candidate Mindy Pechenuk, said data centers could bring more jobs, tax revenue, and infrastructure improvements to Oakland. She said the city should focus on regulating the facilities rather than preventing them from being built. Eric Negomir, with the Silicon Valley Leadership Group, urged committee members to engage with the data center industry rather than create more barriers. “Silicon Valley’s leading companies are already deploying real, innovative, and at-scale solutions to drastically reduce water consumption and address other key concerns,” he said. The measure will be considered by the full City Council on Oct. 6. If approved, the moratorium would temporarily prevent the city from approving land-use agreements or entitlements for new data centers while Oakland develops regulations governing these facilities. Data center opponents rally and urge more action An hour before Tuesday’s committee meeting, community members held a demonstration in front of City Hall to support the moratorium and call for a permanent citywide ban. Representatives from Fossil Free California, Food and Water Watch, Local Clean Energy Alliance, and other local groups spoke during the rally. “This is not just an Oakland fight,” said Dohee Kim, an organizer with Local Clean Energy Alliance. “This is a nationwide fight that we are joining, a people-powered movement against AI data centers.” Daryana, an 11th grader at Oakland High School, said she has seen her peers become overly reliant on AI to complete schoolwork, and worries that the expansion of data centers and AI would further stunt young people’s critical thinking skills. “It may seem harmless to use AI for your research, school, and job, but many fail to realize that we are being blinded by a tool that forces marginalized communities to live by data centers,” she said. Background and Context As India accelerates its transition toward a grid dominated by intermittent renewable sources, the demand for robust energy storage solutions has reached a critical inflection point. Ayana Renewable Power, a significant player in the Indian renewable energy landscape, has officially entered the manufacturing arena by seeking a strategic partner for an advanced chemistry cell (ACC) facility. This initiative aligns with the broader national push to localize the battery supply chain and reduce dependence on imported cells for large-scale energy storage projects. Key Details Ayana Renewable Power has invited expressions of interest (EOIs) to select a joint venture partner for setting up an ACC manufacturing facility. The proposed plant is slated to have an initial annual production capacity ranging between 2 GWh and 2.5 GWh. This facility is designed to support the company’s internal requirements for battery energy storage systems (BESS) while potentially serving the broader merchant market. The formal process for selecting a partner is currently underway, with the final date for bid submissions established as October 1, 2026. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and developers, the entry of major IPPs into the manufacturing space indicates a maturing market where supply chain security is becoming a competitive advantage. By securing a domestic source for ACCs, Ayana aims to mitigate risks associated with global price volatility and supply chain disruptions. EPC firms involved in BESS integration should monitor this partnership closely, as it may lead to standardized, cost-effective battery solutions tailored for the Indian climate and grid conditions. Furthermore, this development suggests that large-scale storage projects will increasingly rely on localized manufacturing to meet domestic content requirements and optimize project economics. What Happens Next The immediate focus for the industry will be the October 1, 2026, deadline. Following the selection of a partner, the project will move into the site selection and technology transfer phases. As India continues to scale its renewable energy sector, the integration of domestic battery manufacturing capacity will be a cornerstone of the country’s strategy to manage grid stability and achieve its ambitious 500 GW non-fossil fuel capacity target. Stakeholders should expect further announcements regarding the specific chemistry types—such as LFP or NMC—that will be prioritized for this facility. 📊 Key Data Ayana Renewable Power is seeking a strategic manufacturing partner to bolster its energy storage capabilities through a new ACC facility.

artigo.texto: AURORA, Colo. — Homeowners in Aurora's Windler community and Denver's The Reserve community in the Green Valley Ranch neighborhood say they were kept in the dark about plans for what could become one of Colorado's largest data centers. "I was shocked that we hadn't been informed," said Tara Miller, a homeowner at The Reserve. The project, called Project Trident, would span nearly 900,000 square feet near East 48th Avenue and E-470 in Aurora, according to the city's active development website. A formal development application was submitted to the city in August 2025 and subsequently accepted for review. Since then, city officials told Denver7 the application has been through two formal reviews, with the third submittal currently in progress. The city's response is due back to the applicant at the end of September. Some new homes in the Windler community sit just a stone's throw away from the proposed data center site. "We moved in on August 10th. We have not even made our first house payment yet," said Windler resident Laura Belcher. "You know, we planned on living there for a long time, and now we have to deal with how is that life going to look with a huge data center next to us." ► Watch Adria Iraheta's report in the video below: Residents say they were never given a chance to weigh in on the project. "We're trying to see if we can get [Aurora] City Council to review and have another review, a fourth review of the whole process before they sign the final paperwork to open up the state or get the data center started to be built," said Dan Bergander, a resident of The Reserve. The City of Aurora told Denver7 the Trident proposal is in the AD zone district, an industrial zone district, where data centers are permitted and can be approved administratively — thus, the project does not meet the criteria for a neighborhood meeting. Aurora City Councilmember Amy Wiles says the previous council was able to move the project forward without community input because of these zoning rules. "There doesn't have to be a community hearing. It doesn't go to planning commission. It is essentially administratively approved because it's by right," Aurora City Councilmember Amy Wiles explained. Concerns extend beyond Aurora's borders. Denver City Councilmember Stacie Gilmore, who represents Green Valley Ranch residents, expressed frustration over the lack of communication from Aurora and what this could mean for the regional corridor. "Denver has not heard anything from, you know, Aurora. I've received no correspondence, no meeting invitations," Gilmore said. "What if [the data centers] catch fire? Do we even know that the fire department could put those out, and would it just be Aurora? Would it be Denver? Would it be other municipalities that would need to help?" MSU Denver Real Estate Program Director Jeff Peshut says land-use regulation and zoning traditionally fall under counties and local municipalities rather than the state — and that many existing codes were written before large-scale data centers became common. Legally, he said, there's no requirement for advance notices or hearings in cases like this. "It's a work in progress. The laws are trying to catch up with the technology," Peshut said. Peshut says that's why so many cities and counties are imposing moratoriums on data centers. "We're going to be looking to the to the county and the municipalities, you know, those jurisdictions to address this issue," he said. Back in August, Aurora's City Council voted against a temporary ban on data center construction — instead opting to establish development standards for data centers without the moratorium. Aurora City Council members are set to have a final vote on those regulations on September 28. Wiles, who initially proposed the moratorium, says she hopes the process will include community voices going forward. "I hope that as we move forward with regulations, we can incorporate their input and also make sure we're addressing their concerns," Wiles said. Meanwhile, Gilmore is calling for broader collaboration and action at higher levels of government. "We've got to face what's coming forward and create some laws around it — that the state, we need federal, state laws, and then the city will follow that," Gilmore said. Homeowners say they want a seat at the table. "We really need to have a say in it for what comes into our neighborhood and what we are going to live next to for a very long time," one resident said.

artigo.texto: Optimizing C&I Solar and BESS Strategy for Indian Businesses ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: Businesses are being urged to move beyond fragmented energy decisions toward a layered strategy integrating rooftop solar, BESS, and demand-side management. - Why it matters: With rising HT demand charges (e.g., ₹600 to ₹750/kVA in Maharashtra) and new storage mandates, a structured approach is critical for ROI and grid compliance. - Watch: Future regulatory shifts, such as the 2030–31 mandate requiring 4-hour storage for new solar projects over 100 kW. Background and Context For many commercial and industrial (C&I) entities in India, energy procurement has historically been a reactive process. Decisions regarding rooftop solar installations, open-access contracts, and diesel generator replacements were often made in isolation, leading to inefficiencies. Developing a coherent C&I solar and BESS strategy is now essential to navigate volatile tariff structures and evolving grid regulations. By layering energy assets, businesses can transition from simple cost-cutting to a sophisticated, long-term energy management framework. Key Details The strategy begins with a granular audit of load profiles, accounting for time-of-day and seasonal consumption patterns. In states like Maharashtra, this is particularly vital due to time-of-use (ToU) tariffs and grid support charges for net-metering consumers exceeding 10 kW. Before deploying new assets, businesses must prioritize demand-side management: auditing contracted demand, shifting flexible loads to daytime windows to leverage 15%–30% rebates, and improving power factors to mitigate kVAh billing impacts. Renewable procurement should follow a tiered approach. Rooftop solar is the primary choice to avoid wheeling and cross-subsidy charges. Where roof space is limited, open-access solar—which saw nearly 6 GW of capacity added in H1 2026—serves as the secondary layer. Finally, Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) act as the critical connecting layer. Regulatory mandates are already tightening; in Maharashtra, new projects above 100 kW require storage equivalent to 50% of capacity for two hours, with requirements scaling to four hours by FY 2030–31. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and developers, this shift represents a move toward integrated project delivery. Clients are no longer just seeking solar panels; they require comprehensive energy solutions that include BESS integration and regulatory compliance consulting. Developers must be prepared to advise on ownership models, including capex, operating leases, and storage-as-a-service, to help clients maximize lifetime returns and benefit from accelerated depreciation. What Happens Next As the India renewable energy sector continues to mature, the integration of storage with generation will become the industry standard rather than an optional add-on. EPCs that can demonstrate expertise in load-profile analysis and BESS sizing will capture a larger share of the C&I market. Businesses that act now to align their energy strategy with these emerging regulatory and technical requirements will be best positioned to hedge against rising grid costs and ensure long-term operational sustainability.

artigo.texto: RN aprova regras para licenciamento ambiental de data centers O Conselho Estadual do Meio Ambiente (Conema) aprovou, na segunda-feira (21), uma resolução que estabelece regras para o licenciamento ambiental de data centers no Rio Grande do Norte. A proposta foi apresentada pelo Instituto de Desenvolvimento Sustentável e Meio Ambiente do RN (Idema). A resolução cria critérios para padronizar os procedimentos administrativos, técnicos e ambientais aplicados aos empreendimentos Um dos principais critérios para definir o tipo de licenciamento será a capacidade elétrica instalada. Os empreendimentos serão divididos em cinco categorias: - Micro: até 20 MW; - Pequeno: acima de 20 MW até 50 MW; - Médio: acima de 50 MW até 100 MW; - Grande: acima de 100 MW até 500 MW; - Excepcional: acima de 500 MW. A potência considerada inclui os equipamentos de tecnologia da informação e os sistemas de refrigeração. Consumo de água A modalidade de licenciamento e os estudos ambientais exigidos também vão variar conforme o porte e o sistema de refrigeração utilizado. Nos sistemas fechados, a água usada para resfriar os equipamentos circula em um circuito e é reaproveitada, sem necessidade de reposição constante em grandes volumes. Já os sistemas abertos, que utilizam torres de refrigeração, podem apresentar maior consumo de água. Segundo o diretor-geral do Idema, Werner Farkatt, essa diferença foi um dos pontos considerados na elaboração da resolução, especialmente diante da escassez hídrica no semiárido. “A resolução estabelece um licenciamento mais simplificado para sistemas fechados, enquanto os empreendimentos de grande e excepcional porte e com sistemas abertos estarão sujeitos a estudos ambientais mais complexos”, explicou. Localização também será considerada Independentemente do porte ou do sistema de refrigeração, os data centers serão considerados de significativo impacto ambiental quando estiverem em áreas como unidades de conservação e áreas de preservação permanente. Outra regra determina que dois ou mais data centers do mesmo empreendedor, localizados a até 500 metros de distância um do outro, sejam considerados como um único empreendimento para a avaliação dos impactos ambientais. Caberá ao Idema analisar tecnicamente os processos, realizar vistorias, definir medidas mitigadoras e compensatórias e estabelecer condicionantes específicas. O órgão também poderá solicitar complementações aos estudos apresentados. g1 RN

artigo.texto: Developers are building data centers with or without public support, and writer Elijah Bosslet argues they need to be held accountable. My business ethics class took a survey on our attitude toward AI a couple of weeks ago. As I finished sifting through the initial questions, the room was silent apart from the clicking of touchpads and a few yawns. I assumed the “create your own statement” section at the end would be an afterthought. It wasn’t. Slowly, mouse clicking turned to keyboard clacking. Responses started rolling in, and students began to vote on their peers’ opinions. As the survey went on, one issue came up repeatedly — the environmental impact of AI. When most people talk about AI affecting the environment, they’re talking about the immense water and energy demands that manifest as ugly, huge, invasive buildings known as data centers. It’s not AI itself killing the planet and driving up America’s energy bill. It’s the infrastructure behind it. Nationally, resistance to data center development has become a bipartisan issue. According to a recent study by Absecon Group, there are 717 individual candidate campaigns — on all levels and in both parties — running ads mentioning data centers, with 636 in clear opposition or advocating for restrictions. A University of Massachusetts Amherst poll found that only one in nine Americans support the construction of data centers in their community. While my in-class survey was small — only 36 students — the results followed a rhetorical trend I’ve noticed. It feels like almost every argument against data centers starts and ends with some combination of “AI is taking our jobs” and “AI is killing the planet.” Aligning with my experience, a recent poll by Gallup News found the five most common anti-data center development topics are water and energy use, utility costs, the environment and AI replacing human jobs. Unfortunately, if a state enacts a one-year ban on data center construction, AI development only slows by five to 10 hours. Although it may seem counterintuitive, AI development, as currently regulated, is inevitable with or without more data centers. For those interested in slowing AI to keep their jobs, arguing against data centers is futile. Opposition to the environmental impact of data centers has a stronger argument. There’s no doubt these monstrous temples of tech infrastructure have dire water and energy usage consequences. My concern is the job loss and environmental arguments are too broad and easily swept aside by developers. Sustainability pledges and job creation promises are initiatives developers have had lots of experience with, similar to the fossil fuel industry. When pitching to public officials, developers promise tax revenue, economic stimulus and creation of jobs in exchange for approval. They frame these deals as good for communities, though their negotiation tactics say otherwise. Use of NDAs is a common method. In Janesville,Wis. — a city of about 64,000 people — officials spent a full year in talks with a data center developer under an NDA before residents even knew a deal existed. If the deal was mutually beneficial, there would be no reason to negotiate with such a shady approach. Saline, Mich., provides a wonderful example of how I believe public focus needs to shift. In August 2025, an OpenAI and Oracle development partner, Related Digital, attempted to rezone agricultural land for a data center. Saline Township’s Board of Trustees voted no four to one. Instead of backing down, Related Digital sued the township. Saline is home to just 3,000 residents. They couldn’t afford to fight the lawsuit and were forced to settle for $14 million. Today, there is a 250-acre data center built on a 1,000 acre compound in Saline. Saline didn’t need an NDA to get taken advantage of. When its board tried to offer Related Digital the minimum allowable tax break, they were threatened with a second lawsuit, and the township was forced to cave with a 12-year, 50% tax abatement. The reshaping, both physically and fiscally, of unwilling communities by these giant corporations is frustrating. Constituents are against development, the board votes no, then it’s built anyway. The current system is being taken advantage of. Cities that approve development are banking on the promise they’ll reap significant tax income and create jobs in the future. Data centers underdeliver on both. Tax benefits are completely reliant on the deal the municipality negotiates with these corporations. As seen in Saline, developers cherry-pick easy targets and negotiate huge tax abatements. The number of jobs created is below what is promised by developers. A study conducted by the Brookings Institution suggests that data centers create fewer employment opportunities than what the industry claims. On average, a new data center creates only 20 to 50 permanent jobs. Additionally, these communities are often forced to expand local utilities infrastructure to provide enough electricity and water. If the AI bubble pops before tax abatements expire, this expansion in infrastructure will force taxpayers to fully support infrastructure upgrades for a data center they never wanted to begin with. Communities will be left with no jobs created, no tax benefit and a giant brownfield for the community to clean up or sell. AI is shaping our world. No ban or protest will stop that. What isn’t decided yet is how it happens to these communities, whether a city council gets a fair negotiation or a lawsuit, a public debate or a year of silence under NDA. Saline lost because Related Digital sued instead of argued. Janesville nearly lost before residents even knew there was a fight to have. Inevitable shouldn’t mean unaccountable. If data centers are coming either way, it’s time to start talking about how communities can actually benefit.

artigo.texto: In general, states have responded with a mix of new laws, proposed moratoriums, development restrictions and executive actions. Maryland is now putting its own rules around data center growth, with Gov. Wes Moore signing an executive order Wednesday creating a statewide framework for reviewing large projects. The new policy focuses on five areas: “ratepayer and [power] grid protection, economic benefits for Marylanders, community voice, environmental protections, and transparency and accountability.” So, what does that mean for data centers? The new review applies to facilities with a projected or actual peak demand of 25 megawatts or more, including expansions that add at least that much power. A facility can come under state review when its developer seeks a permit, incentive or other state support. State or local officials can also refer a proposal for review, or a developer can request one. And instead of having different state agencies review projects separately, the order creates a Maryland Data Center Accountability Task Force within the Governor’s Office to coordinate the process. The task force will include representatives from the Maryland Energy Administration and the departments of Commerce, Labor, Environment, Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Planning. At the heart of Maryland’s new strategy is a concern about who pays for the growth. Large data centers can use a lot of electricity and water and require new investments in power generation, transmission, distribution and other public infrastructure. The state says it wants to make sure those costs and risks don’t end up falling on ordinary utility customers or the communities where facilities are built. The governor’s office is also looking to change the state’s tax policy. Moore said he will work with the General Assembly during the upcoming legislative session to repeal Maryland’s Data Center Sales and Use Tax Exemption, which was enacted in 2020. The moves come as the Moore administration criticized what it described as a retreat from environmental and safety protections at the federal level. Moore said “federal inaction” and the rollback of regulations are “raising electricity bills and polluting our air and water.” For developers, that means getting a site and the permits to build will only be part of the equation. The task force will look at whether a facility has a plan to meet its additional energy needs without shifting costs to other utility customers, whether the developer will pay for the infrastructure and services it needs, and whether there is solid evidence behind its projected electricity demand. The economic review also looks at what data centers will bring to Maryland. The state can consider how many jobs a project will create, whether those jobs pay good wages and offer benefits, local hiring, apprenticeship programs and workforce investments. It can also look at whether a project will support Maryland’s technology and research industries and what it will mean for state and local budgets after tax breaks and other public costs are counted. The new rules give communities a bigger role early in the process. Developers will have to share information in plain language and provide a point of contact for residents. The state can look at whether developers have worked with the community on an agreement covering issues such as noise, traffic, air quality, emergency services, jobs and future expansion. Water and environmental impacts are another part of the review. The state will examine whether a project has enough water without harming existing users, water quality or sensitive natural areas. It will consider whether developers can use different cooling systems or other methods to reduce how much water they need. The state will also make more information about data centers available to the public. A new Maryland Data Center Dashboard will be updated at least monthly and serve as a public record of data center development. It will show where facilities are located, who is developing them, their expected power and water use, what state approvals or support they are seeking, the results of the state’s review and any commitments made by developers. The task force will use its review to give each project one of three written determinations: “Aligned,” “Conditionally Aligned” or “Not Aligned.” That designation will shape how the state works with the facility. Those considered “Aligned” or “Conditionally Aligned” can use a coordinated review process involving state agencies, while those deemed “Not Aligned,” and projects later classified as “Non-Performing,” can be excluded from the process and lose access to certain forms of state support. Maryland’s move comes as states across the country grapple with how much electricity, water and infrastructure large data centers can require, while weighing the economic development and technology investment they can bring. On Sept. 18, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger announced a Data Center Accountability Framework alongside an executive order addressing how the state handles data center development including electricity and infrastructure costs, water use, environmental impacts and community involvement. Responses have not been uniform: some states have enacted rules around utility costs, water or tax incentives, while others have relied on executive action or are considering legislation that has yet to become law. But Maryland is now using a statewide review framework to put those questions into one process, with the state’s costs, communities and environmental impacts considered alongside the development itself.

artigo.texto: European Union countries agreed to modify how the bloc’s carbon market operates to keep more CO2 allowances available and reduce the risk of sharp price increases. According to information published by Reuters, member-state ambassadors backed the change during a meeting held on Wednesday. The measure affects the EU Emissions Trading System, known as the ETS by its English initials. The proposal was presented by the European Commission in April and is part of measures put forward in response to rising fuel prices linked to the conflict with Iran. The EU will keep more CO2 allowances Currently, the European carbon market requires major emitters such as power plants and factories to purchase enough allowances to cover their CO2 emissions. These allowances can be traded on the market, and their price changes according to supply and demand. Under the agreement reached by EU countries, surplus allowances would no longer be withdrawn automatically under certain circumstances. Instead, they would remain within the Market Stability Reserve. The aim is to keep those allowances as a supply buffer that can be used when the carbon price posts significant increases. Changes to the Market Stability Reserve The Market Stability Reserve acts as a mechanism to regulate the number of allowances available within the ETS. Under current rules, when the reserve exceeds 400 million CO2 allowances, the surplus can be removed. At the same time, the mechanism provides for the release of 75 million additional allowances when the European carbon price rises to more than double. The agreement backed by the countries introduces a significant change to that framework. According to the draft cited by Reuters, no surplus CO2 allowances would be cancelled until 2030. From 2031, the surplus would begin to be removed when the reserve exceeds 800 million allowances. That threshold would then decrease each year. The ETS and electricity costs in Europe The Emissions Trading System is one of the European Union’s main climate policy tools. Its operation incorporates a cost for CO2 emissions generated by certain industrial and energy activities. However, Reuters notes that the ETS is not the main cause of the rise in energy prices recorded in Europe. The changes respond in part to requests from governments such as Poland and Italy, which seek to limit the contribution of the carbon price to electricity costs. According to the data cited in the report, the ETS accounts on average for about 11% of EU industries’ electricity bills. That impact varies between countries. In economies with power generation more dependent on fossil fuels, such as Poland, the share is higher. In countries with a strong presence of low-emission nuclear energy and renewables, such as Sweden, its weight is lower. The new rules still need to be negotiated The agreement among member states is not yet the final version of the reform. Now, European Union countries will have to negotiate the final rules with the European Parliament before they can enter into force. The discussion will also determine how the Market Stability Reserve will operate going forward and how many CO2 allowances can be kept as a backstop against sharp moves in the carbon price. The amendment therefore adjusts the balance between the availability of emission allowances and the operation of the European carbon market as the EU seeks to contain energy costs. Source: Reuters Photo: Shutterstock

artigo.texto: XIAMEN, China, Sept. 22, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- At its "Powered Day in, Day out" launch event, HiTHIUM unveiled the ∞Power N4.0MWh, a 4 MWh sodium-ion battery energy storage system equipped with its new ∞Cell N785Ah cell. Designed for a 30-year service life, the solution is scheduled to enter full-scale production and delivery in 2027. HiTHIUM said the ∞Cell N785Ah was developed through integrated innovation in materials and manufacturing processes. It uses a polyanionic chemistry based on an NFPP cathode, hard-carbon anode and customized electrolyte, together with ultra-thick electrodes and long-life structural components. Wide-format stacking makes the cell compatible with HiTHIUM's existing kAh-class lithium-ion manufacturing platform, supporting production scale-up. The cell is designed for 20,000 cycles at 70% state of health and supports storage durations from two to eight hours. At system level, a stacked-cell architecture reduces station footprint by 30%, while PCS rated-power utilization is more than 20% higher than in HiTHIUM's previous-generation sodium-ion system. HiTHIUM also reports 24-hour comprehensive efficiency above 88%, with operating and standby auxiliary power consumption reduced by 30% and 50%, respectively. The system is designed to align its operating life with a 30-year power-station cycle. "30 years means 10,950 days of validation—a long-term commitment to our customers," said Dr. Aileen Wang, Director of HiTHIUM's Battery Research Institute. The product advances support HiTHIUM's goal of accelerating sodium-ion industrialization. Dr. Nazar Yi, Chief Technology Officer of HiTHIUM, identified affordability and long-term resource availability as the two main requirements for large-scale deployment. HiTHIUM positions the new solution as part of an effort to treat electrochemical storage as long-life energy infrastructure and move levelized storage costs toward RMB 0.1 per kWh. The company views sodium-ion as complementary to lithium-ion rather than a replacement. It will initially target utility-scale storage before expanding into commercial and industrial, residential and broader energy-access applications. HiTHIUM also launched the ∞Edge Pioneer Program to test cells and systems in extreme environments and disclose progress over the next three years. About HiTHIUM Founded in 2019, HiTHIUM specializes in integrated energy storage solutions centered on battery and system technologies. Its capabilities span R&D, manufacturing, delivery, operation and maintenance, with operations across more than 40 countries and regions.

artigo.texto: Americans living in rural areas are increasingly souring on data centers. In a new poll by the Pew Research Center, which surveyed people in August, half of rural Americans said data centers "are mostly bad for the environment" — a figure substantially higher than in January, when it sat at 32%. 46% of those respondents also said that data centers would drive up home energy costs, up from 32% in January. 45% said they negatively impact the quality of life for those living nearby, while 28% said so in January. While displeasure with data centers increased among Americans across the board, according to Pew, higher levels of antagonism among rural voters are striking because most data centers are built in rural areas. The data center buildout, which proponents say is integral for the US to keep pace with China in the AI race, has been suffering a PR crisis as a bipartisan coalition of lawmakers moves to impose limits on data center construction. Texas Gov. Greg Abbot, who was formerly bullish about building data centers in his state, recently backed away from that optimism. His administration has halted some 1,800 AI data center projects in the state. All across the country, Americans are rallying to fight against AI data centers, which can cost billions to build and span hundreds of acres. Many are concerned about how the sprawling facilities will affect the environment, utility prices, water resources, and noise levels. Some just don't like AI. For AI companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, and others, the issue is existential. Without AI data centers, they can't power the products they sell. Sam Altman has recently suggested that new data centers could be built far from where people lived, such as the desert. Proponents of data centers have said the buildout brings jobs to rural areas. Venture capitalist Gavin Baker recently said that data centers are "probably the best thing that has ever happened to working-class Americans." Tech bros haven't been able to agree on exactly why Americans aren't taking to the data center buildout. Some have postulated that a Chinese-orchestrated psy-op is behind the distrust, while others said tech leaders haven't sold the product well. President Donald Trump, for his part, called the data center buildout "the golden goose," and warned against falling behind China. "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor," Trump said in August in a Truth Social post. In the Pew poll, very few Americans — about 4% — said data centers are "good" for the environment, energy costs, and quality of life. "Americans have grown more negative toward the possible environmental and economic effects of data centers since the beginning of the year," Pew said in a release. "And a majority say they'd be uncomfortable if a new data center started operating in their area."

artigo.texto: BILLINGS — Yellowstone Valley Voices is pushing forward with an amended initiative after a court defeat last month, now seeking both a public vote on data centers and an independent expert review of their potential impacts. The grassroots organization's original effort to collect signatures in Yellowstone County was struck down in court last month. The group says it has not given up and is expanding its initiative to include a push for a third-party expert to objectively examine the water, environmental, and social concerns of bringing data centers into the state. Brian Miller, an attorney representing Yellowstone Valley Voices, said the group wants independent experts with no ties to the data center industry to lead the review. "First step, go and do a study of the problem. And the people that do that study, they have to have no connection to the data center industry. And we want them to have appropriate credentials in hydrology. And, you know, I mean, like for instance, Quantico's talked about establishing a man camp. We need to look at the adverse social impacts. Is that going to bring drugs? How's law enforcement? We need to look at all of these factors before we ever think about this. And so we want people, experts, to look at all of those factors before we ever think about this," Miller said. Miller is also a candidate for the Eastern Congressional District seat, running against current U.S. Rep. Troy Downing. In the coming weeks, MTN will be speaking with Downing and sharing his thoughts on data centers.

The New Mexico project has struggled with permits, including an initial rejection — and subsequent denial of a reconsideration request — for state-land access needed by its natural gas pipeline. Roughly $18 billion of loans tied to the project have also started trading at stressed levels, according to the Financial Times. Blue Owl, though, said the notice doesn’t change its financial commitments to the project. Shares of Oracle have fallen by nearly 60% since their peak roughly a year ago, which suggests investors had already priced in significant concerns around the company’s massive spending. Blue Owl, for its part, has baggage of its own beyond New Mexico. It already pulled out of financing a $10 billion Oracle data center in Michigan last year. artigo.texto: Panasonic Energy Raises Maximum Temperature of Its All-Solid-State Battery from 125°C to 150°C, Creates Smaller Prismatic Cell, and Prepares Samples for October to December 2026, Targeting Sensors and Machinery. Panasonic Energy has advanced its solid-state battery to operate at temperatures up to 150°C, while also creating a new small prismatic design to facilitate installation in industrial equipment and automotive sensors. This new development was revealed by the company’s Chief Technology Officer, Shoichiro Watanabe, during an industry conference in Japan. Until now, the all-solid-state batteries being developed by Panasonic operated with a limit of approximately 125°C. The new design expands this range by 25°C and prepares the technology for environments where high heat reduces the lifespan of conventional batteries. The advancement comes with another significant change: in addition to the coin-shaped cells already tested by the company, Panasonic has developed a small prismatic cell. The rectangular design allows for better fitting within products and systems where internal space needs to be utilized more freely. - Motorola Unveils Signature 27 with 200 MP Camera, Next-Gen Snapdragon, and Diamond Cooling - NASA Captures Earth’s Shifting Views Throughout the Year, Highlighting Continent Positions Due to the Planet’s 23.5° Tilt - Brazilian Rocket Launches from Rio Grande do Norte, Sends Experiments to 92 km Altitude, and Returns Scientific Payload via Parachute - Archaeologists Discover 6,500-Year-Old Beer Production Remnants with Sprouted Grains Used for Malting in Bulgaria Samples Set to Be Released Between October and December 2026 Panasonic plans to begin shipping samples between October and December 2026. This phase will put the battery in the hands of customers and partners for testing under real conditions prior to larger-scale production. The initial focus is on industrial machinery and vehicle sensors, two markets where high temperatures and maintenance challenges make a heat-resistant battery especially valuable. In factories, for example, motors and robots work at a high pace and can raise the internal temperature of sensors and controllers. In vehicles, systems installed near wheels, engines, or components exposed to heat face similar conditions. Panasonic also cites applications related to medical equipment sterilization, where high temperatures are a normal part of the operating process. The commercial goal is to start in niches where thermal resistance provides a clear benefit. Panasonic has been advocating this strategy: launching all-solid-state batteries first in challenging applications for liquid systems, rather than trying to immediately enter massive volume markets like that of electric vehicles. Prismatic Format Aims to Solve a Practical Integration Challenge The new prismatic format addresses a simple engineering limitation. Round or coin-shaped cells may be efficient for certain functions but limit the internal arrangement of compact sensors and equipment. A small rectangular cell can be positioned more flexibly alongside plates, motors, electronic modules, and other components. According to Watanabe, this change could facilitate the final design of the products that will use the battery. The company intends to offer different shapes based on application needs while continuing tests with coin-type cells. All-solid-state technology replaces the liquid electrolyte with a solid material. This type of construction can enhance stability at high temperatures and reduce limitations seen in conventional batteries when operating in very hot environments. Panasonic emphasizes that development relies on precisely controlling the contact between electrodes and the solid electrolyte. In a liquid battery, the electrolyte spreads and adheres to the surface of the electrode. In a solid battery, any loss of contact can hinder ion flow and reduce performance. Mass production is planned for one to two years after sample deliveries If customer testing progresses as expected, Panasonic aims to begin mass production one to two years after the start of sample shipments. This timeframe will be used to assess performance, product integration, and stability under various usage conditions. The company also recently strengthened its research infrastructure in Japan with the Energy Innovation Square in Osaka. This center integrates material development, cell design, prototyping, and analysis, bringing together stages that were previously distributed among different facilities. This concentration of engineering helps to reduce the time between laboratory research and production. Panasonic wants to expedite the transition of new chemistries and cell formats to lines capable of producing samples and, later, commercial volumes. In addition to small solid batteries, Watanabe stated that the company also aims to accelerate the development of cylindrical batteries for humanoid robots. The cylindrical shape can better fit into arms, joints, and curved structures, where available space is limited. The new battery rated for 150°C indicates that the race for solid-state batteries is already advancing in industrial applications. Panasonic is aiming to penetrate markets first where heat, maintenance, and internal space create significant challenges. If the samples confirm performance in sensors, machines, and sterilization environments, the technology could hit the market for industrial applications before making its way into passenger vehicles. artigo.texto: Evelyn Bastos elogia Anitta como rainha de bateria: ‘Existe diferença entre simplesmente ser famosa e compreender o lugar’ A diva pop assumiu o trono da escola de Caxias no último domingo, em uma cerimônia que mesclou números musicais da tour Equilibrium com elementos carnavalescos Atualizado A estreia de Anitta como rainha de bateria da Grande Rio ganhou o aval de quem conhece bem o posto. À frente dos ritmistas da Mangueira, Evelyn Bastos elogiou a postura da cantora durante a coroação na escola de Duque de Caxias e destacou, sobretudo, a forma como a artista reverenciou a história do carnaval, a ancestralidade e a religiosidade afro-brasileira. - Rainha de bateria, Anitta é derrotada na final do samba-enredo da Grande Rio: 'O que ganhar, eu desfilo' - Leandro Vieira guardou segredo sobre Paolla Oliveira à frente da bateria da Imperatriz Leopoldinense: 'Animado e de boca calada' — Anitta chega e se diferencia, mostrando que respeita um pavilhão e a história de uma das maiores manifestações culturais do Brasil — afirmou Evelyn em um vídeo publicado nas redes sociais nesta terça-feira. Anitta foi coroada no último domingo, na quadra da Grande Rio, em uma cerimônia que misturou referências de seu álbum "Equilibrium II" com elementos do carnaval e símbolos do candomblé. A apresentação também recuperou passagens da trajetória da cantora, criada em Honório Gurgel, na Zona Norte do Rio, e sua relação com a fé. Logun Edé, orixá de Anitta, apareceu representado em uma das cenas. Em outro momento, uma criança usou uma fantasia feita de copos plásticos, numa referência a um figurino improvisado pela artista na infância para participar de um concurso escolar que lhe rendeu uma bolsa de estudos. Na encenação, a menina foi entregue a Exu, divindade associada à abertura de caminhos nas religiões de matriz africana. Na sequência, Anitta foi chamada para receber a coroa das mãos de Eloína dos Leopardos, pioneira que se tornou a primeira rainha de bateria travesti do carnaval carioca. A coroação aconteceu ao som de "Você Já Sabe", de "Equilibrium II", antes de a bateria entrar com "Fala Majeté! As Sete Chaves de Exu", samba-enredo com o qual a Grande Rio conquistou seu primeiro título no Grupo Especial, em 2022. Foi então que Anitta deu seus primeiros passos de samba oficialmente como rainha da escola. Após a apresentação, a cantora fez questão de agradecer não apenas aos fãs, mas também à comunidade da Grande Rio. — Estou muito feliz pela presença dos meus fãs, mas quero agradecer também o apoio da comunidade. Como qualquer menina do subúrbio do Rio, eu sempre sonhei em estar nesse lugar. Mas só posso ocupar este posto se a comunidade estiver feliz com a minha presença aqui — disse. Foi justamente essa postura que chamou a atenção de Evelyn. Diretora cultural da Liga Independente das Escolas de Samba do Rio de Janeiro (Liesa), a rainha da Mangueira ressaltou os gestos feitos por Anitta durante a cerimônia e afirmou que ocupar o posto vai além da projeção conquistada fora da Avenida. — Anitta chega falando de ancestralidade, reconhecendo quem veio antes, se ajoelhando e sendo coroada pelas mãos de Eloína dos Leopardos, pedindo licença e trazendo referências da nossa religiosidade. Existe uma diferença entre simplesmente ser famosa e compreender culturalmente o lugar que decidiu representar. E isso só é possível para quem tem repertório cultural e responsabilidade política e social — afirmou Evelyn. A mangueirense também parabenizou a Grande Rio, que completou 38 anos nesta terça-feira, e encerrou a mensagem dando as boas-vindas à nova colega: — Bem-vinda ao reino, Anitta. A recíproca é verdadeira O reconhecimento é recíproco. Depois da coroação, Anitta contou que vem se preparando para o posto e já teve aulas de samba com Mayara Lima, rainha da Paraíso do Tuiuti, e Belinha Delfim, da Unidos do Viradouro. Evelyn está entre as próximas que a cantora pretende procurar. — Também quero marcar com a Evelyn, da Mangueira, com a Gaby, da Mocidade, porque acho que cada uma tem um truque especial que pode trazer para a gente — disse Anitta. artigo.texto: EFFINGHAM COUNTY, Ga. — Environmental activists are suing the Effingham County Industrial Development Authority over what they call unlawful secrecy surrounding OpenAI’s plans for a data center. One Hundred Miles Inc. and five county residents say the authority failed to properly notify the public about a board vote granting OpenAI a 50% tax break, ownership of the land and other details of the deal. "We cannot sacrifice all of our other concerns and well-being at the altar of increasing the tax revenue," said North Coast Advocate Jeff Beauvais. The Effingham County Industrial Development Authority says they will not comment until they are formally served with the lawsuit. One Hundred Miles Inc. says their legal counsel, the Southern Environmental Law Center, sent the notice when it was filed but being formally served takes several days. The Effingham County Industrial Development Authority says they are committed to conducting business legally and supporting the economic interests of Effingham County.

artigo.texto: Forty-five US data-center projects worth approximately $68 billion were blocked or delayed by local opposition between April and June 2026, according to Data Center Watch, a research initiative of AI intelligence company 10a Labs. Those projects represented more than half of the large-scale developments the organization tracked during the quarter, a figure that carries weight for investors and developers monitoring where AI infrastructure spending actually lands. Opposition Has Moved From the Margins to the Map Community resistance to data-center development is no longer confined to isolated disputes; it now spans nearly every US state. Data Center Watch identified 843 opposition groups spread across 49 states. Hawaii is the only state without one on its list. The Q2 figure was lower than Q1 2026, when Data Center Watch counted 75 contested projects valued at roughly $130 billion. That quarter-over-quarter decline does not necessarily establish a retreat, since Q2 projects still accounted for more than half of the large-scale developments the organization tracked during the period. Communities are raising several overlapping concerns: - Grid connections, substations and transmission upgrades required to serve large AI campuses - Water consumption at facilities large enough to place pressure on local supplies, including those using closed-loop cooling systems - Land use, noise and the physical footprint of hyperscale construction - Questions about who bears the cost of utility infrastructure upgrades Legislation and Petitions Are Raising the Stakes State lawmakers and local governments are responding to community pressure with new rules, while online organizing is extending the reach of local opposition. Roughly 30 statehouses introduced or adopted measures addressing data-center siting, electricity use or water consumption during the period. The available reporting combines introduced legislation with enacted measures; those are materially different outcomes, and the underlying state-by-state breakdown was not independently available at publication. Some local governments are moving further, considering moratoriums before developers formally submit permit applications. Online organizing is amplifying local disputes at a scale difficult to achieve through traditional community meetings alone. A petition opposing a proposed Tennessee project reportedly collected more than 500,000 signatures on Change.org during Q2 2026, which would account for more than one-third of all signatures collected on the platform that quarter. That figure has not been independently verified against the original petition page and should be treated as reported rather than confirmed.

artigo.texto: New data center task force will track projects, water use and power demand Maryland Gov. Wes Moore announced he has signed an executive order to codify statewide guardrails for "transparent and accountable data center development" in Maryland. The new order will also establish a Data Center Task Force that will be responsible for reviewing projects for large data centers, maintaining a public dashboard and supporting local governments. The group, composed of members from the Maryland Energy Administration and the departments of Commerce, Labor, Environment, Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Planning. "By signing this executive order, we are establishing clear safeguards to ensure Marylanders do not foot the bill, our people benefit, community voices are heard, and our environment is protected — all while centering transparency and accountability throughout the process," Moore said in a news release. The task force will review proposed large data centers that required more than 25 megawatts. The review process will occur when projects request a state permit, incentive or letter of support. Projects will be considered in terms of five principles, including ratepayer and grid protection, economic benefits for Marylanders, community voice, environmental protections, and transparency and accountability. Following the review process, projects will be qualified as: aligned, conditionally aligned or not aligned. The Governor's Office said Moore will also seek to repeal a 2020 tax exemption that allowed certain data centers to be exempt from paying sales and use tax with the condition the centers would create at least five net new jobs for the duration of the benefit. The 2020 program was intended to incentivize data center investment and job creation in the state. What's the state of data centers in Maryland? According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, lawmakers in 16 states, including Maryland, Virginia, Pennsylvania and Delaware, are considering moratoriums or bans on data centers. Last year, four Republican delegates, including Baltimore's Kathy Szeliga, introduced House Bill 120 to prohibit the construction of data centers in the state. The bill was discussed in a January hearing, but was not taken to a vote. In the Baltimore metro area, multiple counties have passed moratoriums on data centers until 2027. On Tuesday, Baltimore County voted to extend the county's current data center moratorium through December 2027. Last month, the Baltimore City Planning Commission discussed a new bill that lays out proposed new rules and restrictions for data centers in the city. Harford County is the only county in the state to permanently ban data centers. According to the Governor's Office, a new statewide dashboard will show the location of new projects. The website will also disclose the developer, the projected power demand and water use and "every State action the project has requested and its status."

artigo.texto: The flagship sedan will be among BYD’s most luxurious and advanced vehicles to date, with Rolls-Royce-like coach doors, 5-minute Flash Charging, and possibly solid-state batteries. BYD takes on ultra-luxe brands with Yangwang EV sedan Yangwang is BYD’s highest-end brand with ultra-luxury models ranging from electric hypercars to extreme off-road SUVs. BYD also uses Yangwang to showcase its breakthrough technologies. In the past, Yangwang vehicles have debuted with disruptive new tech, including BYD’s quad-motor e4 platform, second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging, and its Disus Intelligent Body Control System. A new Yangwang model was recently spotted testing in China that, according to local reports, will push the brand further into the elite segment. New images of the vehicle surfaced online, revealing a nearly identical design to the Rolls-Royce Phantom. It will even be BYD’s first vehicle with rear-hinged coach doors. Hu Xiaoqing, Yangwang’s general manager, shared a few images of the flagship sedan on Weibo and confirmed that the car’s name has yet to be finalized. Internally, BYD is calling it “HU” for now. The new model is “the culmination of three years of meticulous development by Yangwang, featuring the brand’s signature design language, and is an ultra-luxury executive sedan.” No other details were revealed, but one image shows the vehicle at BYD’s Flash Charging station, suggesting it can support megawatt fast charging. According to local reports and CarNewsChina, Yangwang’s ultra-luxe sedan may be BYD’s first to use solid-state EV batteries. BYD executive vice president Stella Li confirmed in an exclusive interview with Carwow.es earlier this month that the company is “in the leading position” in solid-state battery tech and its commercialization. Li said that BYD will “prove it” with its first vehicle equipped with solid-state batteries set to debut in 2027. BYD’s battery R&D team is “very strong,” Li said, adding that they are studying the battery chemistry as well as the manufacturing and equipment needed for mass production. FinDreams, BYD’s battery business, aims to begin producing sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries in limited batches in 2027, scaling up to mass production by 2030. Will Yangwang’s ultra-luxe sedan be the first to showcase BYD’s solid-state batteries? If it does, it will likely be offered on higher-priced variants, while standard models could still use BYD’s latest Blade LFP batteries. Outside of that, the flagship model is expected to feature BYD’s quad-motor e4 platform, delivering over 1,000 hp combined. BYD has yet to announce prices or any details, but reports estimate the Yangwang sedan will cost over 2 million yuan, or nearly $300,000. The Yangwang U7, the brand’s current luxury electric sedan, starts at just 658,000 yuan ($98,000). FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.
