artigo.texto: Georgia Democratic candidates talk data centers, Flock cameras at Savannah forum Seven Democratic candidates for the Georgia General Assembly gathered in Savannah on Wednesday night to answer voter questions ahead of the midterms. The forum, hosted by Savannah Indivisible and Savannah Black Women Win, focused on issues with both local and statewide implications, including the expansion of data centers in coastal Georgia. State Rep. Anne Allen Westbrook raised concerns about the pace of the industry's growth. "This industry is moving so, so fast. It is moving faster than anybody can keep up with," Westbrook said. "Nobody has made the case of what exactly we get out of this." Supporters of data centers argue that they bring investment, jobs, and local tax revenue. However, the debate over their expansion has drawn bipartisan calls for greater oversight. The candidates also addressed questions about potential new restrictions on Flock cameras and other automated license-plate readers, which have sparked nationwide debates over public safety and privacy. "We have an obligation to make sure that we not only provide our law enforcement resources, but we also protect our rights as well," said MiQuan Green, candidate for Georgia House District 165. Supporters of the technology argue that it helps police locate suspects, stolen vehicles, and missing persons. Critics, however, have raised concerns about who can access the data and how it is shared and stored. No Republican candidates participated in the forum. The Georgia Republican Party was contacted for comment, but no response had been received at time of publication. Four of the Democratic candidates onstage are running unopposed in November, positioning them to serve in the General Assembly next year. Three others will face Republican opponents on Nov. 3.

artigo.texto: Why data centers are choosing Georgia for major expansions Major technology companies are accelerating development in Georgia, transforming thousands of acres of farmland and timber into massive data center campuses. In Columbia County, site work is underway on a future Google data center campus spanning more than 3,300 acres off Interstate 20 in Appling. The sprawling site covers an area roughly equivalent to 77 Mercedes-Benz Stadiums. The Columbia County project is part of a statewide boom. Google data center could generate billions, add jobs, and new households A new study released by the Columbia County Economic Development Authority projects the Google data center campus under construction off Interstate 20 could generate $4 billion over 35 years for the county. About 17 data centers currently operate across Georgia, with 83 projects in various stages of planning and construction. Prospective developments are emerging weekly in rural communities ranging from Statesboro and Metter to an OpenAI development in Effingham County. Why is Georgia attracting data centers? “You look at Effingham County being right along the coast. There’s a lot of infrastructure that’s there,” said Dr. Christopher Kadlec, Georgia Southern University applied cyber education director. “We have power. You think of Plant Vogtle coming up, standing up. As data centers come in, they need infrastructure that’s unique.” Kadlec compared the influx of data centers to historical technology and transportation booms that redefined Georgia communities, including Savannah’s shipping ports, Atlanta’s rail network, and the expansion of the interstate highway system. Deal calls for Google to help pay for Vogtle upgrades Georgia Power struck a deal with Google for the tech giant to help fund upgrades at Plant Vogtle and the state’s other nuclear generating plant. “They missed out and that town economically dried up,” Kadlec said of communities that resisted past infrastructure shifts. “But if we’re in the age of AI, maybe Effingham County is going to be the next Atlanta in the next hundred years from now.” The rapid expansion has also raised local concerns regarding energy consumption, cooling system noise, and heat generation. Kadlec noted that emergency backup power systems present environmental considerations, particularly during severe weather. “And in south Georgia, there will be a disaster,” Kadlec said. “They will have to turn on generators, and those generators will most likely be diesel-powered.” Georgia named No. 1 state for business for 13th straight year Georgia has once again been named the nation’s top state for business by the magazine Area Development. However, Kadlec explained that corporate operating costs naturally drive facilities toward increased energy efficiency over time. He urged municipal leaders and residents to balance economic opportunity with community oversight. “I don’t think the people of Effingham County should discount the idea of something coming in just because they say it’s going to be good, and I don’t think they should keep it out because somebody else says it should be bad,” Kadlec said. artigo.texto: Baltimore County Council unanimously extends data center moratorium until 2027 The Baltimore County Council voted unanimously Tuesday evening to extend the moratorium on building new data centers in the county until December 2027. Several councilmembers said concerns from residents about the environmental and resource impacts of data centers influenced their decision. | BILL TEXT: Read the Baltimore County Council bill extending the moratorium "I went from one end of Baltimore County to the other, and it's clear to me that the citizens have some very legitimate concerns about energy, water, air quality, noise, so they've made it clear to me that they're not interested in data centers," Councilman Julian Jones, D-District 4, said. Jones, who is a candidate for County Executive, said that while he was initially open to the idea of data centers during his campaign, conversations with residents have changed his stance. | GET THE FACTS: More data centers are popping up across the U.S. What are they? "The public has made it clear to me as I continue to campaign around Baltimore County that they're not interested, and therefore I stand with the people," Jones said. In February, the Council voted to impose a moratorium on data centers while the planning board conducted a report on their impacts. Last week, the planning board approved the report and forwarded it to the council. Baltimore County is among several jurisdictions in the Baltimore metro area that have implemented moratoriums on data center construction. "They don't create jobs, they use up enormous amounts of county resources," Councilman Izzy Patoka, D-District 2, said. "Personally, I think we should hit the pause button for a long, long time." Jones reiterated his position, saying, "I do want to see what the state does, I do want to see what other opportunities come about, but to make a long story short, I stand with the people." Governor Wes Moore is expected to sign an executive order on data centers Wednesday to "protect Marylanders."

artigo.texto: Brasil pode atrair data centers com energia excedente, diz CNI Presidente da CNI vê oportunidades para data centers, inteligência artificial e mineração de criptomoedas, mas defende oferta de energia firme e redução da burocracia O presidente da CNI (Confederação Nacional da Indústria), Ricardo Alban, afirmou que o Brasil tem potencial para atrair investimentos em data centers, inteligência artificial e mineração de criptomoedas diante da disponibilidade de energia elétrica no país. Segundo ele, porém, será necessário garantir um fornecimento firme e reduzir entraves burocráticos para aproveitar essas oportunidades. As falas foram ditas durante o CNN Talks Energia: O Brasil diante de um novo mercado, nesta quinta-feira (24), em São Paulo, com especialistas e lideranças do setor. "O mundo inteiro está recusando data centers por problema de energia. Temos energia sobrando, precisamos torná-la firme", afirmou. O presidente da CNI também apontou oportunidades para utilizar a energia excedente em atividades de alto consumo elétrico. Entre os exemplos, citou empresas chinesas que aproveitam a energia sujeita a cortes de geração, conhecidos como curtailment, para atividades de mineração de criptomoedas. Alban ponderou, contudo, que o chamado Custo Brasil e a burocracia podem comprometer a competitividade do país. Segundo ele, esses entraves elevam os custos relativos dos projetos e dificultam a atração de investimentos e a geração de valor. O CNN Talks Energia: O Brasil diante de um novo mercado reúne especialistas e lideranças do setor para debater as principais urgências e apontar caminhos.

artigo.texto: Com a sanção do Governo Federal, o Redata, regime especial de tributação que prevê incentivos fiscais para o setor de data centers, passa a criar condições mais competitivas para a instalação e expansão desses empreendimentos no Brasil. A medida busca reduzir barreiras para investimentos de grande porte, ampliar a atratividade do país para investidores internacionais e acelerar a construção da infraestrutura necessária para sustentar o avanço da economia digital. CONTEÚDO RELACIONADO – Redata pode favorecer data center de IA ligado à estratégia de soberania digital do governo Para Fernando Palamone, CEO da RT-One, desenvolvedora de uma das maiores plataformas de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial da América Latina e responsável pela implantação de parques tecnológicos voltados para IA, o Redata contribui para tornar o setor nacional mais competitivo para novos projetos. “Segundo o relatório aprovado no Senado, o regime pode reduzir em até 30% o investimento inicial de um empreendimento. Na prática, isso pode significar maior capacidade de atração de capital, estímulo à expansão da infraestrutura digital e melhores condições para que empresas que dependem de processamento de alta capacidade escolham o Brasil como base para suas operações”, comenta o CEO. Ao redor da infraestrutura necessária para a construção de data centers podem surgir novos negócios, parcerias com universidades, centros de pesquisa e empresas de tecnologia, destravando um ecossistema econômico formado a partir do Redata. Mas, mesmo com a nova política, Palamone acredita que ainda há desafios para o Brasil no setor. “Haverá energia disponível? Em quanto tempo? A que custo? Haverá conectividade suficiente? O licenciamento será previsível? Existirá mão de obra qualificada? Essas respostas serão determinantes para transformar interesse em investimento efetivo. O Redata deve ser entendido como ponto de partida, e não como ponto de chegada”, pontua Fernando. Outro efeito econômico relevante gerado pelo novo regime é o desenvolvimento de polos de tecnologia e infraestrutura fora dos grandes centros tradicionais, expandindo a economia digital para novas regiões. Perante a crescente demanda por IAs, a RT-One planeja a construção de dois parques tecnológicos de data centers na América Latina, um Minas Gerais e outro no Paraná. “Projetos dessa natureza movimentam fornecedores, demandam profissionais especializados, criam oportunidades de qualificação, aproximam empresas de universidades e centros de pesquisa, e podem contribuir para a atração de novos negócios”, opina Palamone. artigo.texto: The East Hampton School Board provided updates at its meeting this week on evacuation scenarios in the event of an emergency at the battery energy storage system, or BESS, on Cove Hollow Road and on the $128 million trio of bond propositions that voters approved in May, which fund major capital improvements across all three district schools. The board met with Gerry Turza, the East Hampton Village fire and emergency medical services administrator, on Sept. 22 to better understand how to evacuate the district’s three schools in case of an emergency at the BESS facility. Mr. Turza was at the scene of a fire there in 2023 that has since been pinpointed as the source of forever chemicals found in nearby Suffolk County Water Authority wells. “Our singular focus is students’ safety and well-being. If we’re designing an evacuation plan, what is it going to be?” said Adam Fine, the superintendent. “The question really becomes, ‘Do you have enough buses to evacuate all three buildings at the same time?’ And that doesn’t exist right now. Can I get all my kids on my buses? Yes. But it would have to be in stops. Even our neighbors, who have been more than happy to help -Springs, Amagansett, and Montauk -could never get their buses here in time to do that.” The school board’s leadership is going to meet with Village Mayor Jerry Larsen and Town Supervisor Kathee Burke-Gonzalez over the next few weeks, before speaking with the town and village police. “It stops and starts with safety. We need our partners, the town and village, to guide us through how to evacuate our buildings in a timely and safe manner,” said J.P. Foster, the school board president. “It’s really that simple. We’re going to rely on the experts to tell us what they expect of us.” “You’re talking about moving 2,000 people plus staff,” added Christina DeSanti, a school board member. “That doesn’t happen immediately. You also have to find places that are large enough for them to go. You’re talking about a lot of buses all at once and multiple locations because you have to fit them.” Regarding the capital improvement projects, the board said that a new gray turf field has been approved by the New York State Education Department. The athletic director and coaches have reviewed the field markings, which meet Section XI guidelines. “We’re working on the track resurfacing, and the new scoreboard for the big field. Lights are being prepared for submission to the N.Y.S.E.D. Lock systems for the building are being researched. The boiler has also received N.Y.S.E.D. approval,” Mr. Fine said. The district explored adding lanes to expand the track, but there is not enough room. The new track will, however, include a steeplechase water jump. Mr. Fine hopes the work can begin this summer. “Things are moving!” he said. The board also had the opportunity Tuesday to pose with the Hampton Coffee Cup. Todd Gulluscio, the athletic director, brought the trophy to Tuesday’s meeting. It was awarded to the Bonac boys soccer team on Friday night after they defeated Southampton 2-1 to win the tournament sponsored by the local coffee company.

artigo.texto: Share This Article Pulaski County’s top elected official has seven days to decide whether to veto new regulations on data centers approved by the county’s quorum court. The majority-Democrat panel in Arkansas’ most populous county voted 11-4 Tuesday night in favor of the new rules. County Judge Barry Hyde, a Democrat, has seven days to veto it. The measure was written by Wendell Griffen, a former circuit and appeals court judge and current Democratic nominee for county judge, and sponsored by Justice of the Peace Julie Blackwood, a Democrat. According to the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette, Hyde did not say whether he planned to sign the measure and appeared skeptical of it during Tuesday’s meeting. The regulations can also become law without Hyde’s signature if he does not sign or veto them after seven days. The regulations touch on noise, and water and power use, requiring prospective data center projects to submit to the county electrical load analyses, water and wastewater plans, land-use suitability studies and a decommissioning plan, among other requirements. Prospective data center projects are required to demonstrate that the development won’t “materially impair” utilities and other public infrastructure that serve surrounding properties under the new regulations, but do not limit the amount of water or power a project can use. Since the quorum court first considered data center regulations for Arkansas’ most populous county in May, the opposition to the power-hungry computing hubs has grown, with polling showing increasingly broad unpopularity among Americans. That unpopularity has pit pro-data center interests such as the Little Rock Regional Chamber of Commerce against Pulaski County residents opposed to the AVAIO data center project in the unincorporated part of the county. AVAIO is one of six planned data center projects in the state. Two of those projects, in West Memphis and Clarksville, are already under construction. The effort to regulate data centers in Pulaski County has seen fits and starts, even as Little Rock passed its own requirements over the summer. Data center opponents rejoiced in June after a temporary moratorium appeared to pass, only for the county clerk to announce days later that there had been a vote miscount. Debate has also raged over whether to exempt the AVAIO project from the regulations. Blackwood told the Arkansas Times that AVAIO would be required to comply with the new regulations. The fight over data centers has cut across party lines, with elected officials in other states losing their seats amid the backlash. The push to build more and more data centers comes as internet giants like Google, Open AI and Meta seek to capitalize on the rapid growth of artificial intelligence models. While data centers have existed for decades, powering everything from email to social media, the AI models created by tech companies require massive amounts of computing power. artigo.texto: Scott County extends data center moratorium until March Fiscal court gives planning commission until March to finalize rules SCOTT COUNTY, Ky. (WKYT) - The Scott County Fiscal Court voted Thursday to extend a moratorium on data center regulations, giving officials until March to finalize rules. The moratorium was set to expire in December. Staff at the Georgetown-Scott County Planning Commission said they needed more time to prepare. The decision came one week after residents packed a public planning meeting to raise concerns about how data centers could affect their community. Judge-executive explains extension Scott County Judge-Executive Joe Covington said the extension allows officials to gather input and research before presenting options to the planning commission. “That’s what the moratorium is about - to provide time to gather public feedback, to look at research and then put together a path that the planning commission can consider,” Covington said. No outright ban expected County leaders said legal counsel and the Kentucky Resources Council agree that regulating data centers with clear rules would be more effective than an outright ban. Georgetown-Scott County Planning Commission Director Holden Flemming said that if a lawsuit were brought against an ordinance and a court struck it down, the county could be left without protection. “What we don’t want to have happened, and I think this is the worst-case scenario that Mr. Perkins was discussing, is that if an ordinance were to be struck down, there’d be no regulation to fall back on, and that would be the window into which an application is made,” Flemming said. Covington said a total ban carries too much risk. “I’d rather take that route where we have a strong framework of support and state law that backs it then take the route of a total ban that could be challenged then we’d have no backing and no regulation that would protect us from a proposed data center,” Covington said. Covington also said he expects that once the final ordinance is in place, only a limited amount of space in the county would meet the standards required for a data center to operate. The planning commission previously told WKYT the draft places data centers in heavy industrial zones and requires a conditional permit to address impacts on neighbors. Deadline set for March The planning commission and other Scott County leaders now have until March to finalize a solution. Covington said the county’s priorities have not changed. “The number one thing that we want to do is that we protect our community and protect the way of life that we have,” Covington said. The planning commission says it has already begun incorporating community feedback into the draft, including added regulations on water and power usage and stricter noise limits. Copyright 2026 WKYT. artigo.texto: Manifesto conjunto pede aprovação de convênio no Confaz para reduzir a tributação estadual sobre bens e equipamentos destinados à implantação, ampliação e modernização de data centers A Confederação Assespro e outras treze entidades representativas dos setores de tecnologia, telecomunicações, indústria e serviços divulgaram um manifesto conjunto em defesa da aprovação, no Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz), de um convênio para redução do Imposto sobre Circulação de Mercadorias e Serviços (ICMS) incidente sobre bens e equipamentos destinados à implantação, ampliação e modernização de data centers. Intitulado “O Redata é uma realidade, e o Convênio do Confaz é uma necessidade”, o documento destaca que a aprovação do Redata estabeleceu uma base para a atração de investimentos em infraestrutura computacional e sinalizou a intenção do BRASIL de ampliar sua participação na economia de dados, computação em nuvem, inteligência artificial e processamento de alta capacidade. Segundo o manifesto, os data centers exercem papel essencial no funcionamento de serviços digitais, sistemas financeiros, telecomunicações, pesquisa, saúde, educação e governo digital. As entidades também ressaltam que a implantação dessas estruturas movimenta áreas como construção civil, energia, conectividade, equipamentos e serviços especializados, além de contribuir para a formação de profissionais e para o desenvolvimento de polos regionais de inovação. Entidades apontam peso do ICMS nos investimentos O documento argumenta que, embora o Redata tenha reduzido impostos federais, a tributação estadual continua sendo um fator relevante para a competitividade do setor. De acordo com os dados apresentados pelas entidades, o ICMS representa 64% da carga tributária incidente sobre os investimentos de capital (CAPEX) de um data center. Na avaliação apresentada no manifesto, um convênio nacional poderia reduzir diferenças tributárias entre os Estados, ampliar a segurança jurídica e oferecer maior previsibilidade aos investidores, evitando uma competição fiscal descoordenada. As entidades defendem ainda que uma política articulada entre União, Estados e municípios pode favorecer investimentos, geração de renda, inovação, capacidade produtiva e arrecadação de longo prazo. O manifesto também chama atenção para o cenário internacional de expansão dos investimentos em inteligência artificial e infraestrutura digital. Para as organizações signatárias, decisões relacionadas à competitividade tributária ganham relevância diante da disputa global por novos projetos no segmento. Manifesto pede atuação dos Estados e do Distrito Federal Diante desse cenário, as entidades solicitam aos Estados e ao Distrito Federal, reunidos no Confaz, a aprovação de um convênio que permita a redução do ICMS sobre bens e equipamentos utilizados na implantação, ampliação e modernização de data centers. Segundo o documento, a medida daria coerência à estratégia nacional para o setor e ampliaria as condições para o BRASIL disputar investimentos em infraestrutura digital e economia de dados. Além da Confederação Assespro, assinam o manifesto ABEP-TIC, ABES, ABDC, BD30+, Brasscom, CNI, Conexis, dig.ia, Fecomercio SP, Fenainfo, Firjan, Associação NEO e TelComp, reunindo representantes de diferentes segmentos ligados à transformação digital e ao ambiente produtivo nacional. A participação da Confederação Assespro no documento insere a entidade em uma articulação conjunta do setor em torno da infraestrutura digital e das condições tributárias para novos investimentos em data centers no BRASIL.

artigo.texto: Germany Could Connect 150 GW of Solar Via Smart Battery Storage A Fraunhofer IEE study commissioned by BSW-Solar shows smart batteries installed at 1,313 substations could unlock up to 150 GW of additional photovoltaic capacity, with curtailment limited to roughly 1%. Germany's power grid could accommodate significantly more photovoltaic capacity than currently assumed, thanks to battery storage deployed at substations. According to a study commissioned by the Bundesverband Solarwirtschaft (BSW-Solar, Germany's solar industry association) from the Fraunhofer Institute for Energy Economics and Energy System Technology (Fraunhofer IEE), 1,313 rural substations heavily exposed to renewable energy could technically absorb around 150 gigawatts (GW) of additional photovoltaic capacity. That volume exceeds Germany's currently installed solar capacity, estimated at roughly 130 GW. Making better use of existing transformers The method used by the researchers does not rely solely on the rated power of substation transformers, but instead accounts for their actual utilization rate throughout the year. Transformers reach their power limit only at specific times. Large, intelligently controlled batteries can absorb solar production peaks and release the energy later, optimizing the temporal use of available capacity. This principle mirrors dynamics observed elsewhere in the sector, as battery cell manufacturing expands, illustrated by CATL's launch of trial battery cell production in Hungary. The study's central scenario illustrates the potential scale of the effect: a substation could have renewable capacity connected that is twice as high as the simultaneous transmission capacity of its transformer. A properly sized and controlled battery storage system absorbs power peaks and later feeds the electricity back into the grid. Under this scenario, only around 1% of the additional solar output would need to be curtailed on an annual average basis, due to the transformer's power limits. Better use of available grid connection capacity is also seen in other solar markets, as with the 216 MW solar agreement signed between Naver and GurÄ«n Energy. Smart storage control as the decisive factor According to the study's findings, building additional storage capacity alone is not enough. How it operates is decisive: batteries must track actual power flows at the substation and absorb electricity precisely when local feed-in peaks push the transformer to its load limit. This approach helps better balance differences between electricity consumption, wind generation and solar generation. Grid capacity that goes unused for much of the year can thus be made available for connecting additional generation facilities. "The decisive question is not only how much grid we build, but also how intelligently we use every existing megawatt of grid capacity," said Carsten KÃ¶rnig, managing director of BSW-Solar. According to him, controlling batteries in line with solar production peaks would allow targeted relief of grid congestion and enable additional solar output, while generating savings estimated at billions of euros in grid expansion spending. Bundestag urged to amend the grid package BSW-Solar is calling for these findings to be factored into the "grid package" (Netzpaket) currently under discussion in the Bundestag, Germany's federal parliament. The bill, put forward by the federal government, aims to better synchronize the expansion of renewable energy and storage with grid expansion, while also changing the rules for grid connections and congestion management. The association wants existing grid capacity to be used more fully through batteries and more flexible grid operation, rather than seeing large parts of German territory classified as congestion zones for years, with new renewable installations largely blocked by a planned redispatch reserve under the bill. BSW-Solar also identifies levers in the provisions on grid optimization and use set out in Germany's Energy Industry Act (Energiewirtschaftsgesetz, EnWG). According to the association, intelligent grid management combined with storage could complement, and reduce, the scale of grid expansion that will still be required. - Gas45.5 % - Coal15.4 % - Nuclear15.2 % - Solar10.9 % - Wind7.3 % - Hydro4.2 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.3 %

artigo.texto: OSLO, Norway, Sept. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- On 24 September 2026, CATL opened its largest NING SERVICE centre outside Asia in Oslo, extending its battery lifecycle service network in Europe. The 8,000 square metre centre will serve Norway and the wider Nordic region, providing battery services, training local technicians and supporting circular economy efforts across the region. Norway is one of the world's most advanced EV markets. In August, battery electric vehicles made up 98.7% of new passenger car registrations, and electric buses accounted for more than 60% of bus and coach registrations. As this fleet grows and ages, demand for battery diagnostics, repair and life extension is rising. The Norway Centre is built to meet it. Full-lifecycle battery services Circularity and local skills CATL launched the Global Energy Circularity Commitment (GECC) in strategic partnership with the Ellen MacArthur Foundation. In line with its vision, NING SERVICE is building an aftermarket ecosystem that keeps batteries in use for longer and returns their materials into new batteries. "In a circular economy, batteries stay in use at their highest value for as long as possible, and their materials are recovered to make new ones. Inspection, maintenance and repair services are an important part of making that happen at scale," said Miranda Schnitger, Climate Lead at the Ellen MacArthur Foundation. The centre will create skilled green jobs and become NING SERVICE's main training hub in the Nordics. Drawing on a training network across 39 European countries and a team of 14 experienced instructors, it will offer courses certified by CATL and practical training for local technicians. NING SERVICE also plans to work more closely with Norwegian universities and technical institutions to build local expertise. Bringing service closer to customers CATL is expanding its local presence worldwide through local infrastructure and ecosystem partnerships. The Norway Centre will be a key hub in NING SERVICE's European network, bringing high-quality service closer to customers in line with its promise to be "Your Nearby New Energy Service Expert." "CATL brings technology, industry expertise and a trusted brand. Combined with YES-EU's local knowledge and service capabilities, we can build a stronger battery service ecosystem across the Nordics and support the long-term growth of Europe's EV market," said Benedikt G. Gudmundsson, Founder and Chairman of YES-EU Group. "Customers are at the heart of everything we do at NING SERVICE. Working closely with our local partners, we will provide reliable battery lifecycle services that meet the needs of Norway's EV market and support its continued electrification," said Bruce Li, President of Quality Systems, Aftermarket Business Division, CATL. NING SERVICE operates 1,394 service locations across 85 countries and regions. It aims to reach 100 countries and regions by 2027 and 10,000 service locations by 2030.

artigo.texto: Nos últimos dois anos, a ascensão da inteligência artificial promoveu uma guinada histórica no setor de tecnologia: a capacidade computacional deixou de ser um mero detalhe técnico de bastidor para se tornar um recurso estratégico de soberania e crescimento econômico. O movimento se compara aos grandes ciclos de infraestrutura do passado, como a eletrificação na revolução industrial e a construção das redes de transportes e telecomunicações que sustentaram décadas de expansão global. Pela primeira vez, o Brasil se encontra em uma posição privilegiada para liderar essa corrida e se consolidar como um dos principais hubs digitais do planeta. O país já concentra cerca de 200 data centers, o que representa aproximadamente metade de toda a capacidade instalada da América Latina. Com uma demanda por potência que já ultrapassa os 800 MW no setor, dezenas de bilhões de reais em novos investimentos vêm sendo anunciados por hyperscalers, fundos de infraestrutura e investidores institucionais. Por trás dessa atratividade está um trunfo que raros países conseguem oferecer em escala global: a matriz energética. Segundo o Balanço Energético Nacional 2026, elaborado pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), 86,8% da energia elétrica brasileira é proveniente de fontes renováveis – patamar substancialmente superior à média mundial. Em uma era na qual os workloads de inteligência artificial demandam energia em volumes sem precedentes, a disponibilidade de energia limpa tornou-se a moeda decisiva para alocação de capital. Durante muito tempo, os data centers eram vistos basicamente como infraestrutura de suporte, fazendo o hosting de dados nos bastidores. O advento da IA alterou essa lógica. A capacidade computacional passou a ser um recurso estratégico para treinar modelos e sustentar a governança digital. Essa evolução transformou a energia em um diferencial competitivo crucial. Hoje, quando conversamos com fundos de investimento e operadores, a primeira pergunta não é mais onde fica o terreno para investir, mas sim onde existe energia disponível, confiável, renovável e com capacidade de expansão. Regiões como o Nordeste, São Paulo, Minas Gerais e o Sul têm liderado o recebimento desses aportes justamente por responderem a essa equação de infraestrutura elétrica e conectividade. Desafios de execução Apesar do cenário promissor, o avanço do setor impõe desafios complexos. O principal gargalo operacional se deslocou para a qualificação técnica da mão de obra. Os data centers voltados para IA não se parecem com os empreendimentos construídos há uma década: exigem altíssima densidade computacional, sistemas avançados de refrigeração líquida, automação de ponta e níveis elevados de disponibilidade. Embora o Brasil conte com um ecossistema maduro em engenharia e tecnologia, o grande teste será escalar a formação de profissionais especializados para acompanhar o volume e a velocidade dos projetos previstos para os próximos anos. Outro ponto central sob a ótica do investidor estrangeiro é a previsibilidade. Ao comparar o Brasil com outros mercados do portfólio global, como México, Chile, Espanha e Estados Unidos, a qualidade técnica dos ativos brasileiros raramente é colocada em dúvida. As atenções se voltam para a segurança jurídica, o cumprimento de prazos de licenciamento e a estabilidade regulatória para suportar investimentos bilionários de longo prazo. Além do potencial de exportação de capacidade computacional, o Brasil conta com uma demanda interna aquecida. O país ostenta o maior mercado digital da América Latina, ancorado por um setor financeiro sofisticado, e-commerce maduro e um ecossistema vibrante de startups e corporações acelerando a migração para a nuvem e IA. Essa combinação permite aos grandes operadores (hyperscalers) atender tanto ao crescimento do mercado doméstico quanto utilizar o território brasileiro como uma plataforma estratégica para toda América Latina. Em um cenário onde a capacidade computacional global ainda se concentra majoritariamente no Norte Global, o Brasil reúne os elementos necessários para mudar a dinâmica do Sul Global: escala, matriz limpa e a oportunidade real de transitar de mero consumidor de tecnologia para hospedeiro da infraestrutura crítica do futuro. No próximo artigo, mostraremos os principais concorrentes do Brasil e como a China tem olhado para nosso mercado. *Este artigo é uma adaptação da entrevista publicada no The Shift.

artigo.texto: CATL has begun trial production of battery cells at its new factory in Debrecen, Hungary, marking a key step toward supplying European automakers from a local manufacturing base. The Chinese battery maker said on September 22 that the plant had secured the permits and met the regulatory requirements needed to start trial operations. The first two production lines are now being tested as CATL prepares the facility for series production. The company has not provided a date for full-scale manufacturing. First cell lines enter trial operations Trial production will allow CATL to set up, optimize, and validate the equipment and manufacturing processes before series production begins. The company said the Debrecen facility had met all conditions required to begin the trial run. The firm received the plant’s occupancy permit in August 2026. It then obtained the remaining relevant permits and completed the requirements under its Integrated Pollution Prevention and Control (IPPC) permit. Local authorities carried out regular inspections before granting the occupancy permit. The inspections followed up on earlier issues that had caused concerns among local residents. Authorities confirmed that the deficiencies identified during the permitting process had been addressed. Factory targets European automakers CATL announced the Debrecen project in August 2022 as its second European battery plant after its facility in Germany. The company said the project is intended to strengthen its position in Europe’s automotive and electric mobility supply chain. More from Energy See All Construction of the first cell building began in summer 2023, while production equipment installation was completed by spring 2026. The factory reportedly uses flexible production lines designed to meet the requirements of its customers. The facility has already been producing battery modules since autumn 2024. The battery maker said it has produced 537,000 modules at the Hungarian site so far. 100 GWh capacity planned Once all planned facilities are ready, the Debrecen site is expected to become CATL’s largest manufacturing base outside China. The company has put its planned capacity at 100 gigawatt-hours (GWh). The factory is positioned near Hungary’s growing electric vehicle manufacturing sector. CATL said it will supply major European automakers that have established significant EV production capacity in the country. The start of cell trials comes after an earlier target for production. According to reports in September 2025, CATL’s European general manager Matt Shen informed that the company had been aiming to start production in late 2025 or early 2026. CATL steps up European battery production The firm said it will continue working with the Hungarian government and regulatory authorities throughout the trial period. The company will monitor employee health, safety, and environmental indicators and proactively submit the results to regulators. CATL is the world’s largest EV battery maker by installations. Data from South Korean market researcher SNE Research showed that the battery maker recorded 289.6 GWh of global battery installations from January through July 2026, up 26.6 percent from the same period a year earlier. Its global market share increased to 39.9 percent during the period, compared with 38.0 percent a year earlier. The Debrecen plant adds another major manufacturing location as CATL expands its production footprint closer to European vehicle manufacturers.

artigo.texto: Geely challenges BYD with 2.2 MW charging technology Today, Geely Auto officially unveiled its “AI-driven” charging technology, “Geely Smart Charge.” which is powered by Geely’s energy large model, Xingrui PowerMind. The centrepiece of the announcement is the new Geely Smart Charge station, which features a single-gun peak power output of 2,250 kW, setting a new industry record. According to Geely, it has integrated its Xingrui PowerMind energy model to enable three core functions: Extreme Charge, Smart Charge, and Auto Charge. By utilising thermal prediction algorithms, the system can forecast battery temperature changes 30 seconds in advance, dynamically adjusting charging power to keep the battery’s average temperature below 55°C and peak temperatures strictly under 65°C. According to test data from the China Automotive Technology and Research Centre (CATARC), a Lynk & Co 10 model equipped with this technology achieved a peak charging power of 1,093 kW. During a charge from 10% to 97%, the battery maintained temperatures below 55°C for 57% of the total charging time, with a maximum recorded temperature of 64°C. Battery technology Geely also introduced its new generation of Aegis Golden Brick ultra-short blade batteries: - 12C battery: Featured in the Lynk & Co 10 and Zeekr 001, this 395 mm battery achieves a peak charging rate of 12C. Under normal temperatures, it can charge from 10% to 70% in approximately 4 minutes and 30 seconds, and from 10% to 97% in about 8 minutes and 40 seconds. - 6C battery: The 370 mm version, debuting in the new Geely Galaxy E5, offers a peak charging rate of 6C, achieving a 10% to 70% charge in approximately 8 minutes and 25 seconds. Infrastructure and incentive By the end of 2027, the company aims to deploy over 100,000 charging guns nationwide, with more than 50,000 being Geely Smart Charge units, ensuring coverage across all counties in China. To support the rollout, Geely announced a new user incentive policy. First-time owners of new models equipped with Geely Smart Charge technology will receive a charging allowance of 1,000 yuan ( 150 USD) annually for two years (totalling 2,000 yuan / $300), valid for vehicles purchased before January 1, 2028. Additionally, the battery warranty for both new and existing eligible models has been upgraded from 8 years/150,000 km to 8 years/200,000 km. Editor’s comment Geely introduced this technology back in April this year, and we also reported on it at the time. Once charging reaches the megawatt level, the improvement in charging times seems to be very limited, and this charging speed demonstrated is actually slower than CATL’s third-gen Shenxing battery. To compete with BYD, charging speed alone isn’t enough, building charging stations is crucial. After all, BYD will complete construction of 20,000 flash-charging stations this year.

artigo.texto: Milan neighbors oppose proposed battery storage facility City leaders and firefighters raise safety concerns over project scale MILAN, Ill. (KWQC) — Neighbors in rural Milan are opposing a proposed industrial project planned near their homes. City leaders and first responders have raised concerns about the plan. The project would bring a Battery Energy Storage System, known as BESS, to an area currently used to grow crops. Dozens of people who live nearby are getting together over safety concerns the potential facility could bring. Milan Mayor Bruce Stickell said the village is standing with residents concerned about the scale of the project. “We already had one burn up in LaSalle County not far from here. It takes a week — it took a week for that to even get it put out. Our fire chief has said already that they don’t have the equipment to handle this,” Stickell said. Becky Pilger, a volunteer opposing the project, said the proposal includes 200 battery packs. “This particular project, the proposal has 200 different battery packs, which are each pack is about the size of a semi. And if one of those would start burning, it would be very easy to go on to the next set of battery blocks,” Pilger said. Local first responders said they fear a chain reaction they cannot stop. Firefighter Mike Lubers said lithium ion battery fires present specific challenges. “The only way to shut down a lithium ion fire is to completely submerge the battery in water. When you’re looking at a shipping container, 40, 50 feet long... you can’t build a containment system and fill it quick enough with water to have any effect,” Lubers said. The next step for the project is a Rock Island County Zoning Board hearing. The Rock Island County Zoning Board has not yet set a date for that hearing. Until then, the group opposing the project said they will be knocking on doors and handing out yard signs. Copyright 2026 KWQC. All rights reserved.

Suomi NPP is the result of a partnership between NASA, NOAA and the Department of Defense. Héctor Alejandro Arzate Mississippi River Basin Ag & Water Desk Editor’s note: Data centers are increasingly becoming an agricultural issue. According to the American Farm Bureau Federation, “Demand for data centers – large, secure facilities that house computers and servers used to store, process and manage vast amounts of digital data – is accelerating as cloud computing, artificial intelligence and other digital services expand across the United States. According to Data Center Map and analysis by (the federation), it’s estimated there are 4,925 active or under-construction data centers across the United States. The facilities are increasingly sited in rural areas where land availability, energy access and proximity to transmission infrastructure make development feasible.” Wisconsin currently has 53 data centers, according to Data Center Map. Illinois has 242, Iowa has 116 and Minnesota has 81. Numbers of data centers are mapped by Data Center Map. Data Center Map This story is a product of the Mississippi River Basin Ag & Water Desk, an independent reporting network based at the University of Missouri in partnership with Report for America, with major funding from the Walton Family Foundation. Communities work together Mississippi River mayors came together recently to help river communities evaluate data-center proposals, as the facilities continue to rapidly expand across the basin. There are already more than 3,000 active data centers throughout the United States. As the need for artificial intelligence and data storage grows, more cities and counties are being approached by companies interested in building data centers in or near their communities. About three-quarters of the data centers currently planned are in the South or Midwest, according to a report from the Pew Research Center. “We are now dealing with data centers and what that looks like,” said Melisa Logan, mayor of Blytheville, Arkansas. “Construction of data centers in the United States has now reached a record $4.4 billion per month.” Logan is co-chair of the Mississippi River Cities and Towns Initiative, a group of more than 100 river communities that span from Minnesota down to Louisiana. So far more than 75 percent of the initiative’s member cities have already been approached to host some form of artificial-intelligence infrastructure, Logan said. Many have asked the organization for guidance on how to protect community resources, such as water and utility service. At the group’s annual meeting the initiative announced two new resources to help river communities evaluate data-center proposals. The first resource is a data center “wishlist,” which was developed in collaboration with the Sierra Club to help elected officials better understand both the risks and benefits from data-center construction in their areas. Another framework, originally developed by the Future Caucus of the Missouri House of Representatives, aims to help communities evaluate the fiscal return of projects. It factors in public cost protections, resource usage and community benefits. David Goins, the mayor of Alton, Illinois, said it’s important that communities look at possible data centers with “eyes wide open and considerations fully understood.” With 139 data centers already in operation and more than 100 in development, his state houses the most data centers along the Mississippi River. “Communities need to be able to decide for themselves on how to best engage (artificial intelligence) opportunities,” he said. As local communities weigh proposals for data centers, Missouri Rep. Colin Wellenkamp, who also serves as the initiative’s executive director, said he wants elected officials across the Mississippi River Basin to be prepared to engage in those conversations. The purpose of the new resources, he said, is to “help our communities ask the right questions.”

artigo.texto: Evanston’s Environment Board voted Thursday to ask City Council to look into a moratorium on future data centers, as one such facility has been proposed in the 2nd Ward. The last-minute discussion on the matter was prompted by two public comments at the beginning of the meeting, urging the panel to take action in regards to a proposed data center at 1265 Hartrey Ave. The property’s manager, Reed Beidler of Lark Managment, has submitted a zoning analysis application to determine whether a “computer processing center” would be a permitted use for the nearly 20,000 square foot site. Board members mulled potential options, including requesting they review the proposal, however Co-Chair Paula Scholl said they likely would not be able to if it was determined the data center was a permitted use for that location. “We can certainly express concerns, we can talk about what we’re concerned about, but if it’s built by right or operated by right, it is,” said Scholl. The panel agreed that in the meantime, they would send questions to both city staff and the Land Use Commission about the current proposal. Meanwhile, some members of the panel sought a firmer stance in their request to alders, and recommend a moratorium. However, member Jim Cahan, said that was premature, since they didn’t have enough information to take a position. “For us to make a recommendation on a subject that showed up 15 minutes ago, and all of a sudden turn and say that the entire city should have a moratorium on data centers, I think it doesn’t have a basis for doing that,” Cahan said. Concerns and opposition over data centers in Evanston have come up over the past week from residents, including at a 2nd Ward meeting Tuesday. Additionally, Mayor Daniel Biss (who is set to resign in just over three weeks) voice support for a data center moratorium, and opposition against the current data center proposal. “I certainly don’t support that proposal … I haven’t studied the details of it but when I say moratorium I mean moratorium,” Biss said after a congressional candidate forum in Skokie Thursday. Beidler said earlier this week the proposed data center was “not even close” to the massive data center that have faced significant backlash in communities throughout the country. According to the applicant’s proposal, the data center would be contained entirely within the existing building envelope and the existing utility infrastructure would be able to support the new facility.

artigo.texto: Five EU States Push to Ease Carbon Market Rules for Industry Five EU nations are advocating for adjustments to the bloc's carbon market so that European manufacturers gain additional time and leeway to lower emissions without sacrificing competitiveness, based on a document reviewed by Euronews. Austria, Czechia, Hungary, Slovakia and Poland contend that businesses incur massive expenses to decarbonise plants while rivaling producers beyond Europe that do not bear the same carbon levy, Euronews reported. Austrian Industry and Energy Minister Wolfgang Hattmannsdorfer informed journalists on Thursday that an export discount was necessary owing to the challenges firms encounter when conducting business outside the bloc. The request emerged as EU industry ministers convened in Brussels amid discussion over the European Commission's proposed overhaul of the Emissions Trading System, which the Austrian minister said was placed on the Competitiveness Council agenda due to its effect on industry. Within the ETS framework, enterprises in carbon-intensive fields like steel, cement and chemicals are required to purchase allowances for their emissions, so the greater their carbon output, the higher their payment. Hattmannsdorfer urged economic patriotism to retain industries and jobs within Europe, maintaining that preserving European production is vital for regional wealth, welfare and environmental standards. EU ministers have cautioned Brussels that industry requires incentives and adaptability to decarbonise, especially since factories already contend with steep electricity prices. Companies likewise contend that should production grow too costly in Europe, they might relocate elsewhere. Austria's central bank underscored the strains in late 2025, characterising the nation's export industry as under pressure on several fronts. Feeble German industry, US tariffs, elevated wage and energy expenses and intensifying competition from China were all burdening exports. The situation has deteriorated since as the war against Iran has driven up energy expenses, placing additional strain on Austria's and Europe's industrial competitiveness and green transition. The five governments maintain that plants ought to be obligated to undertake significant decarbonisation investments only once fundamental conditions are met, such as affordable electricity, adequate grid capacity, hydrogen supplies and infrastructure for transporting and storing captured CO2. Eliminating protection from carbon costs prior to those conditions being met might produce the reverse outcome to what Brussels intends, the document contends. Instead of putting money into cleaner European production, firms might relocate manufacturing abroad. The document notes that European industry is being requested to make multi-billion-euro investments in electrification, hydrogen, CCS/CCU and new production processes, and that these investments demand affordable electricity, functioning grids, hydrogen along with sufficient input materials availability and CO2 transport and storage infrastructure. Alex Eggert, who leads the steel trade body Eurofer, stated the industry would attain climate-neutrality while manufacturing in Europe. He stated an ETS was required that rewards first movers while aiding the decarbonisation of the entire industry, and that removing carbon leakage protection too rapidly jeopardises the very investments essential to enable the transition. The ETS has assisted in reducing emissions from covered sectors by over 50% since 2005 while producing more than EUR270 billion in revenues, according to European Commission figures. Yet proposals to revise the bloc's carbon market have proven deeply polarising among EU governments, with multiple countries urging Brussels to ease the system's effect on European industry. - 1. artigo.texto: - A majority of Utahns and Americans say it isn’t worth building data centers near residential areas even if competition against China or jobs are at stake. - Experts say the U.S. is racing to “gobble up space” for data centers to maintain its AI lead over China, but Utahns — and Americans broadly — aren’t persuaded that this urgency justifies building near their communities. - The political fight over data centers is intensifying, with 66% of Utahns opposing the Stratos Project in Box Elder County and candidates like Peter Crosby making local control a campaign issue. It’s no secret that Utahns vocally oppose data centers: From Mona’s mega center to Box Elder County’s Stratos project, rural residents rush to community meetings to make their opinions known. Americans across the country feel pretty much the same way, as vulnerable candidates in this year’s midterm elections line up to denounce the continued construction of the centers. But what’s fueling the opposition? In a new Deseret News/Hinckley Institute of Politics poll fielded this month, Americans and Utahns showed most voters are resistant to arguments made by the pro-data center crowd — that they will bring jobs and help the United States maintain its AI edge. When asked to choose between two alternatives — building data centers to compete with China even if some are built near residential communities, or to protect communities from data centers “even if it slows America’s progress in competing with China” — 67% chose the latter. Opposition softened slightly — but only to 59% — when the question was reframed around economic growth. Nationally, a slightly larger percentage supported data centers in both questions, though the majority still opposed. The national poll was fielded among 2,102 registered U.S. voters from Sept. 10 to Sept. 14, and has a margin of error of +/- 2 percentage points. The Utah poll reached 744 registered voters from Sept. 10 to Sept. 15, and has a margin of error of +/- 4 percentage points. Both polls were conducted by Morning Consult. The race to dominate artificial intelligence Aaron Starks, president and CEO of 47G, an aerospace and defense organization, said the four major areas of AI capability are chips, data centers, electricity and talent. “China does energy and electricity very, very well,” he said. “Eighty percent of China is undeveloped. They have a lot of land. This is a top-down authoritarian regime that can build and electrify at their own pace.” The United States, on the other hand, doesn’t have that capability. “But what we do have is we have tremendous data compute capabilities,” Starks added. To catch up, he said the U.S. is trying to “gobble up space” wherever possible to build more data centers — increasingly depending on the Department of Energy to scope out future sites. Zach Boyd, director of the Office of Artificial Intelligence for the State of Utah, agreed that the U.S. does have a “lead” over China — depending on how you measure the race — and the nation should be able to maintain it for some time. Even still, he said: “I think it should be on people’s radar.” Boyd explained Utah’s part: Gov. Spencer Cox has called on the federal government to create more regulatory policy, though the state is considering creating additional legislation itself. “As these agents become more powerful, I think we are going to see definite benefits for society,” Boyd said, “but also the cases where they get out of hand will become more and more serious just because the AI agents are more powerful.” Data centers and AI are not just a consumer or economic development challenge, Starks said, it’s a national priority. “And so it’s not really just about Utah, it’s about our national interests as a whole and whether or not Congress can properly determine and prioritize things, which they can’t,” he said. “They haven’t for many years.” The promise of a better economy In the Deseret News poll, opposition to data center construction eased slightly when the question shifted to economic growth — though a majority of Americans and Utahns still said no. “Things are rough right now for a lot of people,” said Peter Crosby, Democratic nominee for Utah’s 2nd Congressional District. “So, if you tell me that this kind of economic development project is going to bring jobs, then I’m probably going to be more likely to say yes.” Also according to the Deseret News poll, young residents ages 18–34 were more likely to support data centers for job growth (33%) than those ages 35–44 (25%) — which might not come as a surprise, as the Harvard Institute of Politics found nearly half of young Americans say they are personally affected “a lot” by inflation (50%) in a study earlier this year. Another 45% say they are struggling to make ends meet or getting by with little financial security. “Especially right now with the state of the current economy, anything that suggests that it might give somebody a job is probably going to have a slightly more positive response,” Crosby added. The Governor’s Office of Economic Development projected the Creekstone Energy data center in Millard County — which is currently under construction — will produce 106 full-time jobs, averaging $160,000 per job. But not everyone buys those numbers. “Typically, you see a job buildout for about a year or two while the construction actually happens. But that may be a local workforce — it may not,” said Crosby. “But once the center itself is set up, it takes a caretaker crew — you’re looking at 25, 50 folks maybe, because it’s just a warehouse with server banks.” The next steps for Utah politicians Crosby is the Democratic nominee for Utah’s 2nd Congressional District — which includes Box Elder County, where the controversial Stratos Project launched. artigo.texto: The Hajdú-Bihar County Government launched proceedings against the Chinese battery manufacturer CATL on Friday.Continue reading Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL), the world’s largest Chinese battery manufacturer, began test operations on September 22, 2026, at its newly constructed cell manufacturing facility in the eastern Hungarian city of Debrecen. After successfully meeting all regulatory requirements, the first two production lines at the new facility are now up and running. The goal of the test phase is to precisely configure, optimize, validate, and verify the highly complex manufacturing equipment and process chains before regular mass production begins. With the start of cell production, the major project announced in August 2022 has reached its most important milestone to date. The Hungarian factory is the Chinese battery group’s second European site and is designed to integrate directly into the continent’s automotive supply chains. German and European automakers in particular—many of which, for instance, BMW, Mercedes-Benz, and Audi, already have extensive in-house electric vehicle production capacities in Hungary—are expected to benefit from short transport routes and customized deliveries. In addition to cell production, CATL has been manufacturing battery modules in Debrecen since fall 2024. Since then, 537,000 modules have been produced on site. Once all phases of construction are fully completed, the Debrecen plant—with a planned annual capacity of 100 gigawatt-hours (GWh)—will be CATL’s largest production site outside of China. The construction of the plant had been accompanied by intense debate and environmental concerns among the local population. To address these concerns, the permitting process was subject to strict regulatory oversight. Prior to the issuance of the final operating permit in August 2026, the relevant Hajdú-Bihar County government agency conducted regular on-site inspections. Representatives of the regulatory authorities confirmed that the company had rectified all deficiencies and risk points identified in advance as part of the IPPC (Integrated Pollution Prevention and Control) process. Even during the test phase that has now begun, occupational safety, employee health, and environmental parameters are continuously monitored. CATL proactively submits the resulting measurement data to the Hungarian environmental and labor authorities. The company emphasized that it remains committed to maximum transparency and welcomes visits from regulatory agencies at any time. This billion-forint project is considered one of the most significant industrial investments in Hungary’s history. It not only strengthens the regional economy around Debrecen by creating new jobs and expanding local infrastructure, but also solidifies the country’s position as a European heavyweight in the manufacturing of electric vehicles and key components. For the European e-mobility supply chain, the launch in Debrecen represents a decisive step toward supply security and scalability. Via Press Release; Featured photo: Facebook/Joó István

artigo.texto: Gov. JB Pritzker said Thursday he isn’t pursuing a moratorium on new data centers in Illinois, arguing he can’t impose one on his own and that he would rather see lawmakers pass tough regulations on the facilities after the November election. Pritzker’s comments came just a day after Mayor Brandon Johnson proposed a data center moratorium for the city, and after leaders nationwide, including Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul in New York and Republican Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas, have taken a harder line against the facilities this year and in the run-up to the November election. Data centers and their sweeping development across the nation have drawn considerable scrutiny because they require large amounts of water and energy at a time when both are expensive, and they produce noise that adversely affects neighbors. Although tech giants and some unions support data center development, many people oppose it, and conservatives and progressives share that opposition. “We want significant regulation. We want to make sure, again, that we’re protecting the people who live in our state,” Pritzker said after a ribbon-cutting for a manufacturing facility in Monee. “We’re not saying, ‘Absolutely, positively, no,’ everywhere in the state if there are data center locations where they want them.” Pritzker said he wants the Illinois General Assembly to pass the so-called POWER Act in the next legislative session, scheduled for a few weeks after the election. Lawmakers worked on the bill in the spring session but didn’t take it up, which Pritzker said left him “very disappointed.” A separate measure to strengthen local communities’ control over data centers never received a vote in either legislative chamber. But even the Protecting Our Water, Energy, and Ratepayers Act doesn’t include an outright pause on data centers. Instead, the legislation would hold data centers responsible for energy costs and environmental protections. “We want to require them to bring their own power, bring their own water,” Pritzker said. Asked why he wouldn’t order a blanket moratorium on the centers before the election, Pritzker pointed to his June decision to pause tax incentives for data centers. The pause “means for a lot of them, that they’ve got to either slow down or stop,” he said. “I’ve done what is legally allowed by the executive branch, and I think imposing — just saying, ‘I’m imposing a moratorium,’ doesn’t work. You need law in place in order to do things,” Pritzker said. Pritzker is seeking a third term in November and is widely seen as the favorite over Republican nominee Darren Bailey, a former state lawmaker. Bailey has said he would pause all existing data center tax agreements. The governor said the state wants local communities to have a say in where data centers go and wants to keep the facilities from driving up power bills. “That’s all built into the law that’s being crafted now,” he said. Cities, townships and counties can already slow down or block data center projects, he said, “and they should, if they don’t want one.” “There are places that want them,” he added. In addition to the opposition from potential neighbors, data centers — which in some cases are used for artificial intelligence technology — have come under renewed scrutiny, along with the rest of the AI industry, after industry insiders in recent weeks made a series of high-profile, worrying statements and announcements about the technology’s potential for harm. Amid that, the governor announced he would launch an “AI cabinet” to advise state government on artificial intelligence by bringing together experts with leaders from state agencies, but he provided no specifics Thursday about who would be appointed to the cabinet. Earlier this summer, Pritzker signed a first-in-the-nation law requiring third-party audits of large AI developers’ safety practices.

artigo.texto: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore announced he has signed an executive order to codify statewide guardrails for “transparent and accountable data center development” in Maryland. The new order will also establish a Data Center Task Force that will be responsible for reviewing projects for large data centers, maintaining a public dashboard and supporting local governments. The group, composed of members from the Maryland Energy Administration and the departments of Commerce, Labor, Environment, Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Planning. “By signing this executive order, we are establishing clear safeguards to ensure Marylanders do not foot the bill, our people benefit, community voices are heard, and our environment is protected â all while centering transparency and accountability throughout the process,” Moore said in a news release. The task force will review proposed large data centers that required more than 25 megawatts. The review process will occur when projects request a state permit, incentive or letter of support. Projects will be considered in terms of five principles, including ratepayer and grid protection, economic benefits for Marylanders, community voice, environmental protections, and transparency and accountability. Following the review process, projects will be qualified as: aligned, conditionally aligned or not aligned. The Governor’s Office said Moore will also seek to repeal a 2020 tax exemption that allowed certain data centers to be exempt from paying sales and use tax with the condition the centers would create at least five net new jobs for the duration of the benefit. The 2020 program was intended to incentivize data center investment and job creation in the state. What’s the state of data centers in Maryland? According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, lawmakers in 16 states, including Maryland, Virginia, Pennsylvania and Delaware, are considering moratoriums or bans on data centers. Last year, four Republican delegates, including Baltimore’s Kathy Szeliga, introduced House Bill 120 to prohibit the construction of data centers in the state. The bill was discussed in a January hearing, but was not taken to a vote. In the Baltimore metro area, multiple counties have passed moratoriums on data centers until 2027. On Tuesday, Baltimore County voted to extend the county’s current data center moratorium through December 2027. Last month, the Baltimore City Planning Commission discussed a new bill that lays out proposed new rules and restrictions for data centers in the city. Harford County is the only county in the state to permanently ban data centers. According to the Governor’s Office, a new statewide dashboard will show the location of new projects. The website will also disclose the developer, the projected power demand and water use and “every State action the project has requested and its status.”

artigo.texto: The Pima County Supervisors approved a 120-day data center moratorium Tuesday, giving the county time to create new zoning regulations for large-scale data centers. The moratorium passed with a 3-2 vote, with supervisors Steve Christy, of District 4, and Rex Scott, of District 1, opposing the resolution. The Pima County Board of Supervisors voted after spending about an hour in executive session discussing the resolution with county attorneys. Before passing it, supervisors amended the resolution to apply to any development where permits have not yet been submitted, instead of where a permit has not yet been approved. The moratorium would not affect Project Blue but could impact possible projects in Sahuarita. Supervisor Matt Heinz, of District 2, asked the board to direct the health department to keep collecting relevant data of the public health impacts of data centers and create a risk assessment matrix. That request was also approved in the 3-2 vote. Supervisor Andres Cano, of District 5, said the Pima County Health Department has raised serious questions about how data centers might impact the county’s water supply, air quality, heat, noise, energy, and the health of its communities. “In a desert community already confronting drought and rising temperatures, we as a county have a public health responsibility to understand those impacts before we approve any projects that could place significant new demands on our resources and our infrastructure,” Cano said. Supervisor Jennifer Allen, of District 3, agreed with Cano, saying the pause will allow the county health department to continue looking into potential public health impacts of data centers and incorporate those potential impacts into the county’s new zoning laws as they are finalized in the next 120 days. “We need the time to do it right,” Allen said. “We need time so that we are not making land use decisions without understanding the full consequences on public health.” Scott read the limitations section of the public health report attached to the resolution, which says the report is not a formal Health Impact Assessment nor a formal Environmental Impact Assessment.” “Language in this resolution that quotes from the public health review therefore paints with far too broad a brush,” Scott said, adding that he would not support the moratorium based on the advice of legal counsel. The resolution cites the “safety, health and wellbeing” of residents and of the environment as a reason to enact the temporary moratorium. “The Board believes that data centers pose imminent negative public health impacts tied to not only energy demand and reliability, but also air pollution, water use in regions already under water stress, noise, and waste heat dispersion in a region demonstrating annual increases in high-heat temperatures, annually,” according to the resolution. The resolution also acknowledges that Pima County has just been through its sixth hottest summer and is in the middle of a long-term drought, all considerations as the county develops regulations for data centers. The Board of Supervisors is allowed to waive the requirements of the moratorium if a data center developer “shows the projected long-term impact of their project on local communities, air quality, electric and water quality,” the resolution says. But before considering any exceptions, the board is required to give notice to property owners within 1,000 feet of the proposed data center location and is required to hold a public meeting. Within the 120 days, county staff will work with stakeholders and with the health department, make recommendations to the Planning and Zoning Commission in October, and ultimately propose new zoning regulations for data centers to the board for a vote before the moratorium expires. The county started taking measures to strengthen regulations on large-scale data centers a year ago, in response to the backlash of the Project Blue data center land sale. In June 2025, the board of supervisors voted 3-2 to sell unincorporated Pima County land near the fairgrounds southeast of Tucson to Beale Infrastructure, for construction of the Project Blue data center. Since then, the board has created policies that required county staff to take a deeper look at the potential effects of major projects and that created more transparency around non-disclosure agreements. Earlier this month, the board revisited those two policies and voted to expand transparency rules for NDAs and widen the county’s review process for major development projects that use large amounts of water or electricity, updating both year-old policies. While several other cities and counties have rejected individual data center projects and added stricter zoning rules to regulate data centers, Pima County is the second governing body within Arizona to enact a moratorium. In August, the Hualapai Tribal Council passed a resolution “opposing irresponsible hyperscale data centers,” on its tribal land, according to a press release from the tribe. The City of Tucson has also worked to strengthen its policies and regulate large-scale data centers since the Project Blue uproar started more than a year ago. Tucson City Council passed a large water user ordinance last year and updated it on Tuesday with stricter guidelines. Last month, the city approved new regulations on large-scale data centers, making them one of the most regulated land uses in the city. At that August meeting, city council members also directed staff to continue looking into potentially banning large-scale data centers altogether after residents at a public hearing told their elected leaders that anything short of a ban on data centers is unacceptable.

artigo.texto: The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission on Tuesday rejected Commonwealth Edison’s “notice of cancellation” of a transmission security agreement, or TSA, for a 1.8-GW, $20-billion data center PowerHouse Hillwood Holding is developing in Joliet, Illinois. In part, the contract dispute centers on the TSA’s credit support requirements. PowerHouse Hillwood contends it met the agreement’s initial credit requirements via a $1 posting, according to FERC’s decision. The dispute is pending in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, according to the decision. In declining to take jurisdiction over the dispute, FERC said the courts can work it out just as well as the federal agency. “Though we decline to assert primary jurisdiction over the interpretation of ambiguous contract terms involving credit support, our commitment to fair cost allocation, ratepayer protection, and regulatory clarity remains unwavering,” FERC Chairman Laura Swett and Commissioner Lindsay See said in a joint concurrence. FERC’s decision highlights the “criticality” of the potential reforms that the agency proposed in large load interconnection show cause orders it issued in June to regional transmission organizations and independent system operators, the commissioners said. RTOs and ISOs have until mid-November to respond to the show cause orders. Developing “clear and consistent” terms for connecting large loads with the transmission system is crucial, Swett and See said. “It is also more important than ever that RTO/ISOs and their transmission owners may propose pro forma Cost Recovery Agreements,” they said. “And finally, it is more important than ever that any such agreements contain strong, consistent language that both protects customers from improper cost shifting and provides certainty to contracting parties.” FERC Commissioner David Rosner said the dispute shows why the agency in its show cause orders directed RTOs and ISOs to develop pro forma cost‑recovery agreements for large loads. “Requiring security deposits helps ensure both project viability and transparency,” Rosner said. “Cost-recovery agreements matter because they enable efficient and accurate planning, and ensure that project risks stay where they belong: with the developer, not the public.” FERC Commissioner David LaCerte lambasted the $1 letter of credit posted by PowerHouse Hillwood. “The idea that $1 may provide appropriate security to any such agreement strikes me as an embarrassing legal fiction: insulting to the underlying ratepayers, stakeholders, and the grid itself that bear the real risk of this project,” LaCerte said. “Treating that risk as collateralizable for less than the price of a cup of coffee to me trivializes the very obligations that such a guarantee purports to secure.”
