artigo.texto: Terafab may not be impacted by Gov. Abbott’s pause on data centers GRIMES COUNTY, Texas (KBTX) - Gov. Greg Abbott directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality Monday to halt new data center permits while ERCOT, the Public Utility Commission and the Texas Water Development Board audit the industry’s strain on the state’s power grid and water supply. KBTX looked into whether the directive would affect SpaceX’s Terafab project in Grimes County. Here’s what we found: Terafab was originally pitched to the county as a data center. Now, county leaders say it’s classified as a chip manufacturing plant, with a twist. “As far as I know, it does not have any effect on the Terafab project because it is a chip manufacturing operation,” Grimes County Judge Joe Fauth said. “They will have a data center on their site, but it’s only to aid their particular business.” Fauth said he hasn’t heard from the governor’s office and doesn’t believe Terafab’s permits are affected, at least for now. “If it does, then I’m sure he’ll be making contact with Terafab, Terafab will make contact with the court, and we’ll know the status of it at that point in time,” Fauth said. Texas A&M researchers say that distinction matters, but so does the bigger picture. “The number of data centers in the state, and nationally, and globally is growing at a rate that the data center down the road will become a major sector of water and energy in the economy,” said Rabi Mohtar, a Texas A&M professor of biological and agricultural engineering and civil and environmental engineering. Mohtar and colleague Bassel Daher say most data centers don’t publicly disclose how much water or power they use, making Abbott’s audit overdue. “Only 17% of data centers voluntarily disclose their water and energy use,” said Daher, assistant director for sustainable development at the Texas A&M Energy Institute. “Without these public disclosures, it’s hard for us to do this kind of estimation.” Fauth said Terafab can’t use groundwater. Instead, the project will run on recycled surface water from Gibbons Creek Reservoir and its own power supply, separate from the ERCOT grid. Gov. Abbott’s office referred KBTX back to its original press release when asked whether the pause includes Grimes County projects. Neither TCEQ nor SpaceX responded to requests for comment. For now, county leaders say construction is moving forward: permits and the pause are unaffected. TCEQ’s audit report is due back to the governor’s office Oct. 19. Copyright 2026 KBTX. artigo.texto: AI data centers are fueling a growing shortage of skilled construction workers, driving up costs and potentially slowing construction of homes and businesses. In a 2026 survey from the Associated General Contractors of America (AGC) and the National Center for Construction Education and Research (NCCER), 58% of construction firms say data center projects are increasing competition for workers. Another 36% say data centers are making job openings harder to fill, and nearly half say they are feeling pressure to raise wages. Fraser Patterson, founder and CEO of Skillit, a platform that connects skilled tradespeople with contractors, says data centers are competing for many of the same workers needed to build homes, offices and other major projects. "America is suddenly trying to build essentially an enormous amount of infrastructure all at the same time," Patterson said. RELATED STORY | Community debates over data centers boiling over into arrests, reported threats Patterson says five trades account for 54% of the labor demand on his platform. They are the same five trades most needed for data centers: carpenters, electricians, heavy equipment operators, concrete workers, and general labor. Skillit research shows data center jobs pay a premium, with wages about 32% higher than other construction projects. "You're talking about something like $30 an hour becoming maybe $40 an hour on average," Patterson said. Patterson says those higher labor costs could eventually reach consumers through more expensive homes and other building projects. "Those attracting all these electricians and the plumbers and trades, the construction costs are going to rise. It's very hard to pull them away from these lucrative projects," Patterson said. RELATED STORY | Congress moves to shield consumers from AI data center power bills For workers who have those skills, Patterson sees an upside. Beyond higher salaries, he says most data center construction offers safer working environments and workforce development opportunities. "It's a real career-building opportunity as well," Patterson said. Data centers have already faced criticism for consuming massive amounts of electricity and water. California's governor recently signed bills targeting the fast-growing industry. Contractors say data centers aren't the only reason for labor shortages — some also point to immigration enforcement and higher material costs as additional pressures on construction projects.

artigo.texto: Rail Cargo and Transporeon Extend Collaboration Sep 24, 2026 at 12:48 PM Kuehne+Nagel and Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL) have signed a letter of intent to establish a strategic collaboration in the areas of battery logistics, transportation electrification, and emissions reduction initiatives. This partnership aims to drive the energy transition and reduce emissions in the logistics and transportation value chains of both companies. Focus on electrification and battery swapping The collaboration will initially focus on practical initiatives. This includes the electrification of CATL’s transport flows in Europe as well as a pilot project for battery swapping, which is set to launch this year in China for heavy-duty vehicles. Additionally, areas such as battery recycling, after-sales support, and solutions for energy storage and charging infrastructure at logistics sites are part of the cooperation. These activities support both companies‘ efforts to reduce their scope 3 emissions. Akin Li, Executive President of CATL Overseas Business, emphasized the importance of the partnership: “As global leaders in our respective industries, CATL and Kuehne+Nagel share the commitment to accelerate the energy transition and achieve a zero-emission future. Our expanded partnership will not only contribute to the sustainability goals of both parties but also promote a greener future.” Søren Schmidt, Executive Vice President Road Logistics at Kuehne+Nagel, added: “Battery electric vehicles are crucial for the decarbonization of road freight transport. Accelerating the transition requires solutions that are both powerful and operationally feasible. By combining CATL’s battery expertise with our logistics capabilities, we can drive initiatives that help reduce our own emissions as well as those of our customers.” The partnership comes at a time when the demand for electric vehicles and energy storage solutions is rapidly growing. In 2024, the demand for batteries for electric trucks increased by more than 75%, while production capacities for batteries are being further expanded through a growing network of gigafactories worldwide.

artigo.texto: State Chamber CEO: Data centers need to be âregulated properlyâ Randy Zook, CEO of the Arkansas State Chamber of Commerce and the Associated Industries of Arkansas, is on the front lines of economic development in the state. The hot topics of conversation in business recruiting circles these days are data centers and artificial intelligence, AI. Zook sees parallels between the new wave of data center recruiting and the old world of factory chasing. He says the multi-billion dollar data centers can be transformative for communities, on a much bigger scale than a factory location might have been decades ago. In a recent conversation with Talk Business & Politics Editor-in-Chief Roby Brock, Zook addresses some of the myths surrounding the data center debate. Roby Brock: Letâs begin with some of the myths that are out there. For instance, data centers are bad for the community. Tell me why theyâre not bad for a community. Randy Zook: Theyâre not bad for the community, or any community, if theyâre regulated properly with according to all the existing rules and with the existing authorities like the PSC [Public Service Commission], like electric power generation and regulation. All of those things are in place … Itâs a mystery to me how incredibly negative all of this conversation has become on so few facts. Brock: Politically, why do you think that is? Is it just some sort of easy boogeyman? Itâs big dollar. Itâs corporate. Itâs mysterious to some people in some way. Weâve done polling that has showed data centers unpopular with Republicans and Democrats. Zook: Itâs all of the above issues that you mentioned and then some. Letâs be clear. Some people just donât want anything in their lives to change. We donât want railroads, but people who opposed the railroads and others who sought them thrived as a result. Thatâs one of the best analogies Iâve seen is they liken this to the railroads that ushered in the industrial revolution and AI is ushering in the intelligence revolution. It has a wonderful capability thatâs going to help us save lives and reduce disease and cure diseases. Itâs going to be incredible the things and productivity is increasing as a result of its implementation. Brock: Some of the criticism of data centers is the way that land is used, the way that water is used in them? I have seen a lot of projects where those things have been addressed, not enough to shift public opinion at this point, but do you have concerns about land use and water use for data centers?Â Zook: I have very little concern about land use for data centers. Frankly, Iâve got more concern about land use with solar arrays, some of which are part of the equation to power data centers because weâve got to create more power. Weâve got to have more electrons moving for all kinds of purposes.Â Youâve got to generate that electricity one way or another. Some of it eats up a lot of ground. The steel river energy project in Northeast Arkansas, which doesnât get much attention, but when itâs completed it will be the largest solar array in the U.S. â 17,000 acres of solar panels and battery storage. Itâs a big investment. Brock: When you see the controversy thatâs erupted in the last two weeks with Entergy and ratepayers and how thatâs going to be paid for by the data center thatâs coming to town here, there were filings and some information that came out in the press that contradicted that. I donât know if it was complete, but thatâs where the controversy really erupted on that. Would you agree? Zook: I think the biggest eruption was in the failure of a newspaper … they missed 19 years of $83 million a year payments in their calculation. That was just an explosive item. I mean that just blew up the whole conversation. When you go back and do the math properly, you realize they will pay. Theyâre contractually obligated. Google and others, the other data center operators are contractually obligated to pay the full cost of the power they will use. Brock: And thatâs because the state law is set up that way. It passed in the last legislative session, right?Â Zook: The PSC will ensure that in in due time. Brock: Another myth that I think has contributed to the negativity is the aura of secrecy around these projects. Youâve worked at AEDC before and youâve worked in the business landscape for over two decades here. Every economic development project is under some degree of a non-disclosure or secrecy until the project is announced.Â Zook: Businesspeople loathe to be outspoken. They donât want to tip their hand. They donât want to drive up the price of land they might be negotiating for so they try to operate as quietly and below the radar as possible for as long as possible. Ultimately, it all comes out.Â Brock: Does there need to be some change to that? Do you think or are we in this arms race with other states and we just couldnât do it?Â Zook: Well, we would be the first to disarm in that sense. I think weâd be awfully vulnerable and look pretty silly if we disarm and say, âOh gosh, everythingâs going to be on the front page of the paper.â Brock: So how do you restore public trust on that? How could you mitigate that concern? Zook: Iâm not sure you can because theyâre just looking to oppose something. Ultimately, you need to look at the benefits of the projects. You need to look at the incredible increase in in tax revenue to underwrite improved school districts and school teacher pay. The West Memphis [Google] project is going to provide enough money for the West Memphis school system to provide every teacher in the district a $25,000 raise, at least. Thatâs going to be transformative. Thatâs going to change the world in Crittenden County. That and a Buc-eeâs thatâs going to be built in West Memphis.

artigo.texto: Whether to support data center development is a defining issue in this campaign season, and it is a debate that has taken over many Native American tribes. And on this issue, many Native leaders on the ballot—including Deb Haaland running for governor of New Mexico, Sharice Davids running for the House of Representatives from Kansas, Mary Peltola running for the U.S. Senate from Alaska, and Peggy Flanagan in a race for U.S. Senate in Minnesota—are being forced to address the issue head-on. Flanagan won the Democratic-Farmer-Labor primary for the U.S. Senate last month. Her Ojibwe name, Gizhiiwewidamookwe, means Speaks in a Loud and Clear Voice Woman. She has spoken forcefully on data centers, calling AI an “existential threat to us if it gets out of control,” in a July Minnesota Public Radio News debate. This fits a pattern. In her primary against Rep. Angie Craig, Flanagan ran ads attacking Craig’s ties to the crypto industry: “Angie Craig voted to let Trump make billions selling crypto coins. I won’t.” Analysts see AI and data centers as a natural extension of that same anti-corporate-money lane heading into November. Her “existential threat” framing is about AI broadly, tied to job loss, safety, and runaway systems. Davids is a former MMA fighter and lawyer by training; she knows how to throw a punch and how to build a case. On data centers, she’s done neither publicly. But she took a quieter and pragmatic approach in a July KSHB voter guide, stating that “no data center should move forward if it raises electricity costs for families, wastes our limited water resources, or shifts the burden onto Kansas communities.” “Data center decisions are primarily made at the state and local level,” Davids said. It’s also a convenient position: she sits on Transportation, Small Business, and Agriculture committees, not those that would put data centers in her lane anyway. In February, Davids met with the National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers, which proceeded to formally vote against the Section 106 rollback in July, warning it would weaken tribal consultation and expand unilateral agency power. But showing up for a meeting doesn’t carry the same weight as making a public statement. Haaland’s campaign has proposed sun, wind, and geothermal energy generation to offset data center energy consumption alongside requiring high-energy-demand industries to build their own energy infrastructure. But on the state’s biggest data center project, Project Jupiter, she’s said comparatively little. Pressed by a voter in Los Lunas last week, she said: “I don’t have the power to stop Project Jupiter.” Then, last week, her position seemed to have shifted. Haaland’s campaign now says she supports a moratorium on new data center development “until we have strong, reliable guardrails.” This follows Searchlight New Mexico’s report of $87,200 in campaign donations from executives at Oracle and Clayco, the firm actually building Project Jupiter. Santa Fe and Socorro Counties have already passed data center moratoriums. Four Democratic state legislators already proposed one months ago. Haaland’s is a narrower, later, and far more carefully hedged version of the same idea. But the demand for accountability didn’t end there. Over the weekend, a New Mexico climate justice petition started circulating, calling on Haaland to return the $87,200 and commit to no AI data centers, with no carveout for Project Jupiter. Haaland responded fast that she hasn’t discussed returning the money with her team, but “cannot be bowled over” by campaign donations. Realistically, the carveout isn’t nothing: the project is 26% complete according to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure’s own vice president, up from 9% in July, despite the fact that two of its permits have been paused by the New Mexico Supreme Court. Peltola takes a different tack. Asked about data centers at a Fairbanks Labor Day event, she said she takes her “cue from the people of that region,” deferring to local support provided it doesn’t strain the grid for existing ratepayers. It’s a notably different posture from her opponent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, who has pushed to bring data centers onto Alaska’s military installations, and from a $500 million Stak Energy data center proposal already drawing scrutiny in the North Slope. But “the people of that region” is complicated in Alaska. As I’ve reported, a lot of the state’s land—roughly 44 million acres, or 12% of all land in the state—is controlled by Alaska Native corporations, for-profit entities created by a 1971 federal law, whose boards answer to fiduciary duty, not shareholder votes. That structure has already let corporations like the Bering Straits Native Corporation go after federal contracts, ICE included, despite loud shareholder objections boards aren’t obligated to address. In other words, the “local support” Peltola invokes in her interview may not translate into actual votes. This debate also coincides with proposed changes to Section 106, a clause in the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966 that requires federal agencies to assess how development affects historic sites, which are decades in the making. If these changes are enacted, federal land, where Native Nations hold consultation rights under extant law, could theoretically become terrain AI data center developers could claim without a federal review process. More than 700 organizations, including Native Nations, have already signed a letter opposing this change to Section 106—but this isn’t the first time it has been targeted. Near the end of President Donald Trump’s first term, the Secretary of the Interior issued Secretarial Order 3389, exempting major energy and land-management projects from standard Section 106 review. It was a move the Biden administration noticed early on and swiftly reversed. artigo.texto: Fortis Energy and İnelso Energy Systems have agreed to install a 30 MWp solar power plant with a battery in Serbia’s Vojvodina region. The EPC contractor is Enkraft Energy. Fortis Energy, İnelso Energy Systems, and Enkraft Energy are all based in Turkey. Fortis Energy and İnelso Energy Systems have signed a joint investment agreement for a 30 MWp solar power plant combined with a battery energy storage system (BESS) in Vojvodina, Serbia’s northern province, just 33 km from the capital, Belgrade. The EUR 25.5 million project has reached ready-to-build (RTB) status, according to Fortis. The EUR 25.5 million project has reached ready-to-build status With the construction permit expected to be issued within a month, the project is set to advance directly into the construction phase, the company added. The photovoltaic plant is expected to generate more than 40 GWh of electricity annually, equivalent to the consumption of over 11,000 households, while avoiding an estimated 19,000 tonnes of CO2 emissions a year. The project’s offtake structure will combine long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs) with merchant market participation, with the objective of optimizing capture rates while benefiting from the increasing maturity and liquidity of Serbia’s electricity market, Fortis explained. The project supports Fortis Energy’s Green Baseload strategy The integrated BESS is at the core of the project’s design. By enabling energy time-shifting and output firming, the system is designed to transform intermittent solar generation into a more reliable and dispatchable energy asset, the company stressed. This directly supports Fortis Energy’s Green Baseload strategy, which aims to combine renewable generation and storage to provide a more stable and reliable power supply. Enkraft enters Serbia’s market Enkraft Energy will undertake full engineering, procurement, and construciton (EPC) responsibility for the project. The project marks Enkraft’s operational launch as a dedicated EPC platform for solar and energy storage projects across Southeast Europe, Enkraft said. Once the construction permit is issued, mobilization and site works will follow directly, the company added.

artigo.texto: The Pima County Board of Supervisors moved to implement a temporary moratorium on new data centers last night after over an hour of closed-door deliberation and public comment from four individuals supporting the resolution. The resolution places a short-term ban on permits and advancement of any data center projects in Pima County until a zoning code text can be written. A zoning code text is a document outlining rules and standards for how county land can be used in specific projects. The moratorium is set to last 120 days. According to a July memo regarding the zoning code, potential requirements could include closed-loop cooling systems to preserve water, noise reduction measures and design standards. A draft of the new code text is expected by Dec. 15. AZPM reported on the decision to draft the moratorium in early August, which passed after a 3-2 vote with Supervisors Rex Scott and Steve Christy voting against. Last night’s vote was split along the same lines. Scott said his vote was based on legal advice which he could not discuss due to attorney-client privilege. “I will be opposing this resolution for the same reason that I supported the amendments to it, and that is legal counsel the Board has received from the County Attorney’s office,” he said. “My decision to oppose the resolution is based on my review of that counsel from the County Attorney’s office.” Board Chair Jennifer Allen said she supported the measure after listing several potential public health impacts cited in the county’s Data Center Public Health Review. The review was released last month and notes that its purpose is to identify and assess “potential public health concerns across the data center life cycle.” “Why we are putting a moratorium into place is to ensure that our land use policy, our zoning code, actually ensures that we are making good, informed decisions, that we understand proposals’ impacts on those issues that I just described,” said Allen. “Because those are the things that are life and death for our communities.” Scott said the Public Health Review did not reference the impacts of any specific project in Pima County. “The review was clearly not completed to provide justification for this resolution, nor does it provide an evaluation of any specific project,” he said. The moratorium applies to “future development of new data centers where permits have not been submitted for site improvements.” Currently, the city is only considering two data center projects: Project Blue, which has already begun construction; and Project Gravel, a proposed 160-acre data center in Sahuarita. The effect of the moratorium on Project Gravel is unclear, as developers claim the land is already zoned for industrial purposes. The board also voted to consider extending the ban in the coming months while a new zoning code is drafted and the county collects more data on public health effects.

artigo.texto: Audio By Carbonatix Another city in the Denver metro has opted to pause data centers as it weighs the benefits and drawbacks of the highly contested industry. Commerce City’s city council approved a six-month moratorium during a regular business meeting on Monday, Sept. 21. The ordinance ultimately passed, 7-1, with Council Member Rocky Teter being the only “no” vote. While the council did not openly discuss the moratorium during the meeting, the ordinance states that the idea stems from the potential “significant impacts” data centers could have on city infrastructure and resources, like electrical usage, water supply and telecommunications networks. Furthermore, the city’s land development code does not currently include specific regulations or standards for the buildings. The moratorium would give the city time to look into those issues further and craft more rules for any data centers in the future, the proposal says. According to Council Member Charles Dukes, Commerce City currently allows data centers to operate under a conditional use permit, meaning they are allowed in areas that aren’t specifically zoned for them due to the lack of hard definitions in the city’s land development code. “We have had a discussion about data centers for a little bit of time now,” Dukes tells Westword. Dukes says the city is still “open for business,” but the council wants to make all benefits and disadvantages are considered before moving on. “There is a lot of excitement from communities for potential economic benefit. There’s also a lot of fear about what it could be or what it couldn’t be,” he says. “As a council, we just wanted to take a balanced approach.” That fear has been echoing throughout the state since data centers began taking off in the late 2010s. A recent study by Magellan Strategies found that 86% of responding Colorado voters oppose data centers near their neighborhoods while 82% oppose them in their cities or towns, 77% oppose them in their counties and 75% oppose them elsewhere in the state. Data center moratoriums around Colorado Commerce City isn’t the first Colorado municipality or county to do pump the breaks, if only temporarily. The Denver City Council unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on new data center development in May, although data centers under construction were allowed to move forward, including a new data center in north Denver. Shortly after, Jefferson County extended its moratorium on new data centers until next March, while Larimer County extended its moratorium to February. In early June, Boulder County enacted a six-month moratorium on new data centers. A month later, Broomfield passed an 18-month moratorium on new data centers, as well. The City of Aurora opted out of signing a moratorium but is developing new regulations. Earlier this month, the Aurora City Council approved a resolution banning any building, including data centers, from using large-scale evaporative cooling systems. Such cooling systems have been disparaged by anti-data center activists due to their extensive use of water, with around 85% of the water used in evaporative cooling not returning to the system. Similar regulations are on the table for Commerce City, according to Dukes. “What are the noise requirements? What type of cooling systems? What sizes are we talking about? This is an opportunity for us to wrestle with these questions,” he says. Dukes says the influx of local moratoriums and resident pushback is unprecedented for an industry quickly popping its way through the state, but these developments do not just happen overnight. He estimates a new data center would take five to six years to fully develop, and believes that cities should start creating regulations right now. Those in favor of data centers argue that claims around environmental drawbacks and economic boost are often inflated. Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy for the Data Center Coalition, says benefits of data centers include job creation as well as “billions of dollars in economic investment” and “significant local, state and federal tax revenue that helps fund schools, transportation, public safety, tax relief and other local priorities.” Still, most Colorado residents are against data center development wholeheartedly, regulations or not. “The more people learn about data centers, the more they seem to oppose them,” State Sen. Cathy Kipp, a Fort Collins Democrat who sponsored a data center guardrail bill earlier this year, tells Westword. According to DataCenterMap.com, there are 54 data centers in Denver, nine in Aurora and zero in in Commerce City. (That count does not include the already-approved QTS data center facility planned for construction near the I-70 and E-470 interchange in Aurora, which would become the biggest data center in the state, and the CoreSite hyperscale data center being developed in north Denver.)

artigo.texto: AI data centers are fueling a growing shortage of skilled construction workers, driving up costs and potentially slowing construction of homes and businesses. In a 2026 survey from the Associated General Contractors of America (AGC) and the National Center for Construction Education and Research (NCCER), 58% of construction firms say data center projects are increasing competition for workers. Another 36% say data centers are making job openings harder to fill, and nearly half say they are feeling pressure to raise wages. Fraser Patterson, founder and CEO of Skillit, a platform that connects skilled tradespeople with contractors, says data centers are competing for many of the same workers needed to build homes, offices and other major projects. "America is suddenly trying to build essentially an enormous amount of infrastructure all at the same time," Patterson said. RELATED STORY | Community debates over data centers boiling over into arrests, reported threats Patterson says five trades account for 54% of the labor demand on his platform. They are the same five trades most needed for data centers: carpenters, electricians, heavy equipment operators, concrete workers, and general labor. Skillit research shows data center jobs pay a premium, with wages about 32% higher than other construction projects. "You're talking about something like $30 an hour becoming maybe $40 an hour on average," Patterson said. Patterson says those higher labor costs could eventually reach consumers through more expensive homes and other building projects. "Those attracting all these electricians and the plumbers and trades, the construction costs are going to rise. It's very hard to pull them away from these lucrative projects," Patterson said. RELATED STORY | Congress moves to shield consumers from AI data center power bills For workers who have those skills, Patterson sees an upside. Beyond higher salaries, he says most data center construction offers safer working environments and workforce development opportunities. "It's a real career-building opportunity as well," Patterson said. Data centers have already faced criticism for consuming massive amounts of electricity and water. California's governor recently signed bills targeting the fast-growing industry. Contractors say data centers aren't the only reason for labor shortages — some also point to immigration enforcement and higher material costs as additional pressures on construction projects.

artigo.texto: In their third meeting, the Walker County data center study group discussed different zoning districts and whether the county will be able to create an industrial park for future development. Right now, the county has 10 zoning districts according to Walker County’s Zoning and Development site: - A1 – Agricultural - R1 – Residential (single-family only) - R2 – Residential (multi-family and single-family) - R3 – Residential (multi-family, single-family, and manufactured home parks) - RA – Residential/Agricultural - C1 – General Commercial - CN – Neighborhood Commercial - I – Industrial - PUD – Planned Unit Development - CBOD – Chickamauga Battlefield Corridor Overlay District In the previous meeting, the committee learned that the county’s board of commissioners would have to make a formal classification for heavy industrial zoning. It is something that Planning and Zoning Director Jon Pursley explained Thursday evening that it could be an option. It would also give commissioners more opportunity to engage with future developers. "In my opinion, I think you say, ‘Hey, a data center has to go into an industrial park’. If you want to place one, no matter what, on any other parcel, you have to apply for a conditional use variance,” explained Jon Pursley, Walker County’s Planning and Zoning Director. There were discussions that will be continued in future meetings regarding the size of future data development sites and the difference between micro-centers and large-scale centers. There was also an interesting exchange where one appointee asked another, Barney Danks, if he was even a Walker County resident and if he had a personal interest in data centers. Danks responded Thursday evening. "I do not live in Walker County, but I own property in Rossville and in Walker. In terms of data centers, the answer is yes, but I didn't know I had a data center until I saw the definition,” said Barney Danks, an appointee of District 1. Committee Chair Stephanie Watkins did explain that every appointee was chosen by the Walker County Board of Commissioners. There will be another meeting in two weeks at the Walker County Civic Center in Rock Springs. The committee has until December 4, 2026, to come up with guidelines surrounding data center development in the county before they send them to the Planning and Zoning Committee to review and make recommendations. It will then go to the Board of Commissioners to be voted on. That is expected at the beginning of 2027.

artigo.texto: Onondaga County says $500K AI data center study is nearing completion SYRACUSE, N.Y. — The Onondaga County Department of Planning released an update on Wednesday regarding its $500,000 study of A.I. data centers. Department of Planning Director Troy Waffner said the study is nearing completion. The study was launched in June and sought to determine the feasibility of data centers in Onondaga County. Waffner said the county received three proposals. They are being reviewed by the Onondaga County Data Center Investment Task Force, which is studying the infrastructure needs along with potential environmental and health-related impacts of data centers. The task force is made up of the county's Economic Development Department of Planning, the Department of Water & Environmental Protection, the Onondaga County Water Authority and the Department of Health. Executive Ryan McMahon said the task force is the first in New York State to conduct studies on data centers. He said the study will help guide Central New York municipalities with planning for data centers in the future. On July 15, Governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order placing a one-year-long moratorium on the construction of data centers in New York State. The executive order was signed after months of concerns from communities about the negative impacts of data centers. Governor Hochul said the moratorium will allow the state to iron out the kinks before data centers are built. She said she wants to ascertain that they're built the "right way." Data centers can store massive amounts of digital information. That includes websites, banking and personal info, online messages, and more. Yet, they are scrutinized for their massive energy consumption, water usage and noise. The state moratorium followed several moratoriums installed by a few Central New York municipalities. Hochul's order supersedes those that were previously put in place, such as the moratoriums by the Town of Manlius, Town of Clay and the Town of Lysander. The state moratorium did not halt the study of data centers, however. Waffner said the Onondaga County Data Center Investment Task Force study should be complete around Sept. 30.

artigo.texto: RWE to build 400 MW battery to ease grid congestion in Noord-Brabant - RWE has taken final investment decision to build one of the largest battery storage systems in the Netherlands: a 400 MW/1,100 MWh battery at Moerdijk power station - It will be able to supply enough electricity to cover evening peak demand of around 500,000 households - Commissioning planned for second quarter of 2028 - Battery contributes to system integration of OranjeWind offshore project by supporting optimal use of renewable electricity Geertruidenberg, 21 September 2026 The Moerdijk power station site will be home to a flagship large-scale battery system in the Netherlands. RWE has taken the final investment decision to build a 400 megawatts (MW) and 1100 megawatt-hours (MWh) battery storage system at the site. It will consist of 208 containers with lithium-ion batteries and can deliver its full output for almost three hours. Construction is scheduled to start in due course, commissioning is planned for second quarter of 2028. Nikolaus Valerius, CEO of RWE Generation SE: “This battery marks a major milestone for reliable power supply and grid relief in Noord-Brabant. As one of the largest and most powerful battery systems in the Netherlands, it will be capable of covering the evening peak demand of around 500,000 households for almost three hours. At the same time, it can absorb surplus electricity from the grid within seconds. Battery storage plays a crucial role in building a resilient energy system that can accommodate a growing share of renewables.” Mark Lentjes, Regional Director of TenneT Southern Netherlands, said: We are pleased that RWE intends to contribute to a more efficient use of the electricity grid in West Brabant with a large-scale battery that acts as a congestion reliever. ”RWE’s large-scale battery is located close to the 150,000-volt high-voltage substation at Moerdijk-Noord, where it will help to alleviate the regional bottleneck, which in turn has an impact on congestion across the whole of Noord-Brabant.“ Moerdijk battery to relieve grid congestion The new battery system will make best use of the existing infrastructure: It will be connected to the national grid via the existing substation at the RWE power plant in Moerdijk. Through capacity steering agreements with Transmission System Operator TenneT, the battery will be dispatched to relieve congestion in the Noord-Brabant region. Thanks to this development, space is being created on the grid for parties on the waiting list who wish to purchase electricity. TenneT, together with the regional grid operator Enexis, will be investigating what this means in the coming period. The grid operator will take this development, along with other developments in the region, into account when reviewing the congestion management study in December of 2026. The new battery system will also be equipped to provide advanced grid services such as instantaneous reserve (inertia). The Moerdijk site already hosts the first synthetic inertia battery connected to the continental European grid, with a capacity of 7.5 MW/11 MWh. Matching offshore wind with onshore flexibility RWE and TotalEnergies’ 795 MW offshore wind project off the Dutch coast, is designed to combine offshore wind generation with onshore flexibility solutions that help align renewable power production with electricity demand. At Moerdijk, the battery projects play an important role here by storing electricity when wind output is high and feeding it back into the system when needed, helping to balance fluctuations and optimise the use of renewable power. Together with technologies such as electrolysis, e-boilers and smart charging, it supports OranjeWind’s ambition to integrate offshore wind more effectively into the Dutch energy system. Battery storage at RWE As a driver of the energy transition, RWE develops, builds and operates battery storage systems in the US, Europe and Australia. In the Netherlands, RWE currently operates two battery storage systems. In addition to the existing battery at Moerdijk, RWE operates a 35 MW/41 MWh battery at Eemshaven power plant. Globally, RWE currently operates battery storage systems with a total capacity of around 1.7 gigawatts (GW) and 3 GW are under construction. As an integral part of its growth strategy, RWE plans to significantly expand its battery storage capacities worldwide. artigo.texto: As India’s compliance carbon market opens for trading this October, industry, farmers and exporters all start feeling the weight of a new kind of accounting. By Ajay Joshi India is entering the final stretch before the country’s first compliance carbon market begins trading in October, turning carbon emissions into a new financial and business consideration for industry. Nearly 490 large industrial units have already reported their emissions intensity against government-set targets, laying the groundwork for a market in which companies that outperform their targets can earn carbon certificates while those falling short will have to buy them. The scheme is called the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme, and it replaces the older Perform, Achieve and Trade programme, which measured energy savings rather than carbon itself. The change sounds small on paper. In practice it means an aluminium plant or a cement kiln now carries a carbon liability the way it carries a tax liability, something to be planned for, budgeted against, argued over with accountants. Seven sectors are covered so far, aluminium, cement, chlor alkali, pulp and paper, petroleum refining, petrochemicals and textiles. Iron, steel and fertiliser targets are still pending, though officials have floated reductions of two to six percent for those as well. Miss the target and a firm must buy certificates to cover the shortfall, or pay a fine set at twice the average market price of a certificate. That penalty structure is deliberate. It is meant to make buying a certificate cheaper than paying the fine in nearly every case, so companies actually go looking for reductions instead of treating the whole scheme as a line item to absorb. Current estimates put the compliance price somewhere between six hundred and nine hundred rupees a tonne, though nobody will know the real number until trading actually starts and buyers and sellers show up. There is also a trade policy angle to this, and it may turn out to be the more pressing one. From this January, the European Union’s carbon border tax moved out of its reporting phase into the phase where it actually charges money, on steel, aluminium, cement, fertiliser and a few other goods, based on the carbon locked into them during manufacture. Indian steel and aluminium, made with a heavy dependence on coal fired power, carry more embedded carbon than their European counterparts typically do. Exporters can claim a deduction against that European tax if they can show they already paid a carbon price back home. So a scheme that looked, until recently, like a domestic industrial policy question turns out to double as a shield for exporters. Money that might otherwise leave the country as a tariff stays home instead, assuming exporters can actually prove what they paid. Away from the smokestacks, a quieter story is unfolding in the fields. Farmers, most of them working under two hectares, are being pulled into this market too, mainly through agroforestry and through rice and livestock management practices that cut methane. This year’s Union Budget set aside twenty thousand crore rupees for carbon capture and farmer linked carbon projects, and the numbers being floated are striking: a rice wheat farmer switching to a poplar based agroforestry system could see returns rise from a little over three lakh rupees a hectare over seven years to close to nine lakh, once carbon income gets added in. Whether that math survives contact with actual markets is another question. It depends on aggregators, usually Farmer Producer Organisations, doing the unglamorous work of bundling thousands of small plots into something a verifier will accept, and on those aggregators not simply pocketing most of the money themselves. None of this is guaranteed to work as cleanly as the projections suggest. Verifying carbon on a smallholder farm, at scale, across land records that are often incomplete or disputed, costs real money, and it is not obvious who pays for that once the initial funding runs out. The wider voluntary carbon market has already been through one round of trouble, with global transaction volumes dropping by roughly a quarter in 2024 after a string of stories about credits that did not represent real reductions on the ground. Buyers now pay more for projects that can prove their claims, which works in India’s favour since it can produce nature based credits fairly cheaply, but it also raises the bar for what counts as proof. A compliance price that turns out too low will not push any factory to change how it operates. One that turns out too high risks a backlash from industry loud enough to weaken the scheme before it gets a real chance. What India has built, on paper, is unusually deliberate. Rather than opening its carbon exports to anyone willing to pay, it has restricted international sales under the Paris Agreement’s Article 6 to a specific list of thirteen capital heavy activities, green hydrogen, offshore wind, aviation fuel and similar, so that foreign money goes toward financing the hardest and most costly stretch of this change, rather than buying up cheap nature based credits India may need for its own targets later. A bilateral deal with Japan, signed last August, already tests this approach in practice. Whether the logic holds will depend on things well outside Delhi’s control, whether Brussels eventually treats the domestic scheme as an equivalent carbon price, whether enough verifiers can be trained in time to keep pace with 490 companies all reporting at once, whether farmer cooperatives resist the temptation to let easy money change hands without much oversight. The market opens in October. What it becomes after that is still an open question, and will probably stay that way for a few years yet. Ajay Joshi is a Climate & Carbon Markets Professional.

artigo.texto: Mayor Brandon Johnson proposed a data center moratorium ordinance Wednesday aimed at blocking the controversial developments from popping up in Chicago for one year. He described the ordinance, now in aldermen’s hands, as a temporary pause that would give the city time to develop long-term policies regulating concerns around pollution, water use, and electricity costs. The city is “open for business,” Johnson said in a statement, but “not for sale.” “We welcome innovation, investment and the jobs and opportunities that come with it, but growth must be done responsibly and in a way that protects the health, safety and quality of life of Chicago residents,” he wrote in a statement before the measure was introduced in the City Council. “We are taking a thoughtful approach that will allow Chicago to embrace innovation while continuing to make our city safer and more affordable.” Johnson’s moratorium push comes after he signed an executive order early last month directing city departments to intensify scrutiny of new data centers. With his August order, Johnson established a city task force assigned with crafting new regulations. At the time, the mayor also urged aldermen to pass a moratorium, but did not present moratorium legislation. With his new ordinance, Johnson is now trying to take the local mantle of an increasingly pressing political issue as he heads into his re-election campaign, while adding pressure on aldermen. The 12-month ban would give Johnson’s administration time to research and establish new regulations, said Ald. Maria Hadden, 49th, City Council Environmental Committee chair. It’s “a year safeguard,” she said. “Regulation takes time, and we’ve got to work on kind of catching up a little bit,” said Hadden, who is cosponsoring the legislation alongside Alds. Lamont Robinson, 4th, and Leni Manaa-Hoppenworth, 48th, Hadden added that she does not believe data centers should be flatly banned from Chicago, even as popular sentiment mounts nationwide against the increasingly widespread infrastructure key to cloud computing and artificial intelligence. “If we do this right, this moratorium doesn’t even have to last the year, right? Let’s get together, let’s get industry to the table, let’s get organizations to the table, and let’s get our regulatory framework together so that we don’t have to impede progress,” Hadden said. “We’re looking for sustainable data centers. We’re not looking to stop infrastructure. We’re not looking to stop economic growth.” Hadden also sponsored legislation set to face a final vote Wednesday that would spur data centers to report annual water and energy use to the city. The city currently collects such information from large commercial buildings, but not the 39 data centers that already exist in Chicago, she said. Some in the City Council criticized Johnson when he announced his August order, arguing the measure did nothing to immediately address the rise of data centers. Meanwhile, several of Johnson’s top opponents in the race for mayor already staked out their own positions following the mayor’s August call for a moratorium. Illinois Comptroller Susana Mendoza told the Tribune last month she does not support a moratorium. She argued the conversation surrounding data centers must be more truthful. Many already exist in the state, and economic development must be considered as a “whole plan for the city,” said Mendoza, who has championed the potential of artificial intelligence in campaign speeches. “I don’t know if the average person knows that the average data center uses less water than a golf course,” she said. “I don’t think that we should be quick to say, ‘no, no, no,’ to everything without fully studying the issue.” And Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias did not take a clear stance when asked in late August if Chicago should implement a data center moratorium. The data centers that are built “need to be done responsibly,” he said, citing water usage and electricity rates. “If they do it in an environmentally friendly way, if they do it by not using a lot of water, and if they cover theirs and other electric rates, I’d be open to having a conversation,” he said. “But the way it’s being handled right now is not what’s best for Chicago communities.” Johnson’s moratorium push is the start of a conversation on making data centers environmentally friendly, said Jared Policicchio, first deputy commissioner at the city’s Department of Environment, which was eliminated in 2011 by Mayor Rahm Emanuel in a consolidation push and reestablished by Johnson in 2024. The regulations Johnson’s administration is crafting would still require aldermanic approval, Policicchio said. The ordinance is “really just a way to give the mayor and his team time” to craft policy and get it in front of aldermen, he said. “We can’t wait until our work is done with new policy to ensure that folks are protected,” he said. “We know what we have to do. We just need some time to do it.” Policicchio said that technology like data centers is a part of daily life in Chicago. It will continue to be, but the city still needs modernized regulations, and it’s not an “either-or” choice, he added. “I don’t think the mayor sees this as a ban. I think this is a temporary pause,” he said. “It’s truly designed to let us catch up to just a completely changed landscape.”

artigo.texto: VINELAND, N.J. (WPVI) -- New Jersey's largest data center under construction has been fined more than $1 million after state officials determined it violated air pollution laws. Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced the $1.07 million penalty against Data One's Vineland facility, calling it the largest enforcement action against a data center in New Jersey history. The fine stems from a July inspection by the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection that found 62 large natural-gas generators operating at the site without the permits required under the state's Air Pollution Control Act. DEP Commissioner Ed Potosnak said the action is intended to send a message to the industry. "This enforcement action - by far the largest ever taken against a data center in New Jersey and possibly one of the largest such actions in the nation - sends a clear message that these facilities will not be constructed or operated with impunity in this state," Potosnak said. Environmental advocates welcomed the enforcement action but questioned whether the penalty would have a significant impact on the company. Matt Williams of Sustain South Jersey said, "I just know a million dollars, pragmatically, to a billion-dollar company, it's less than a drop in the bucket." In response to the state's announcement, in a statement to Action News, developer Data One said it plans to seek permits for the generators while continuing a transition to a different power source. "As announced in the spring, we are transitioning to low-emission, quiet fuel cells as part of the site's permanent power solution and have the necessary approvals in place for this solution. While we disagree with the temporary generator determination, we will apply for the air permits for the temporary generators and are in communication with the Department of Environmental Protection regarding its findings and the fuel cell transition timeline," a Data One spokesperson said. The generators have been the subject of controversy in recent months. Thermal drone footage captured by nonprofit newsroom Floodlight showed at least 45 of the 62 unpermitted generators operating in August. Residents have also complained about noise from the site, prompting the Cumberland County Health Department to open an investigation earlier this year. "We can all hear it; it's not like you've gotta really listen," said Bennett Palermo-Williford of Millville. In that Floodlight investigation published Aug. 27, former EPA Air Enforcement Chief Bruce Buckheit said the company should immediately stop operating the generators and pay a fine for "their illegal emissions." It remains unclear how long the generators had been operating before regulators discovered them, saying they were not present seven months prior during a December 2025 inspection. Williams said the lack of permits makes it difficult to assess potential impacts. "We don't know because it's unpermitted, so there's really no documentation to track and really see what was going on," he said. According to the DEP, Data One has 45 days to apply for and obtain the required permits or cease any further installation or operation of the equipment.

artigo.texto: - Quincy, Washington is a data center hub because it’s uniquely suited for AI - It includes data centers from Microsoft, Sabey, NTT and others - Ziply has more plans for data center rings, especially on its new Northern Lake long-haul route Bell Canada purchased U.S.-based Ziply Fiber about a year ago for $5.1 billion (CAD $7 billion), and since then it’s been on a mission to expand its fiber footprint. Now, Ziply Fiber has announced the completion of a fiber ring in Quincy, Washington, to connect multiple data centers. The data center business in Quincy is being driven by factors that make it suited for AI, including abundant hydroelectric power, a cool climate and direct access to high-capacity fiber infrastructure. Chris Gellos, general manager of Ziply’s commercial business, told Fierce that the Quincy campus includes data centers owned by the likes of Microsoft, Sabey, NTT, CyrusOne and H5. “It's a desirable location,” said Gellos. “Part of our strategy is being able to provide access and transport to existing data centers. Now that we have the ring, we have them all connected.” If one of these data center owners is transporting traffic from another of its regional data centers, it might not want to pass the traffic through a competing data center. Conversely, Ziply has also connected all the data centers in Quincy to each other, so that traffic can pass from one to the other and not have to go back and forth from the internet backbone if that’s desirable. Gellos said the Quincy ring is similar to a ring it owns Hillsboro, Oregon — another area with a high concentration of data centers. Ziply is laying 874 fiber strands for the Quincy ring. “AI has really changed the game with respect to the amount of bandwidth we see customers now requesting,” said Gellos. The company has tripled its sales of wavelength services over the last year. Not only does Ziply provide two paths to each data center for redundancy, but it also has a policy to never subscribe a fiber span to over 40% of its capacity. That way, if there's ever a fiber cut, it can offloaded traffic from the cut circuit onto the existing circuits without any customer impact. “So that's something that we are super proud of,” said Gellos. That would have been useful in this week’s fiber cut near Newark, New Jersey, that caused massive flight delays on the East Coast. Ziply’s pedigree Ziply came into being in May 2020 when it purchased network assets from Frontier in the states of Washington, Oregon, Idaho and Montana. Now as part of Bell Canada, Ziply has expanded its footprint across other states as well. In April, Ziply announced that its new Northern Link Route had gone live. Northern Link is a 2,100-mile, long-haul transport route connecting sites in Oregon, Washington, Montana and North Dakota with sites in Minnesota, Wisconsin and Illinois. Gellos said, “I think when you look at the cities that you see us stop off at on our Northern Lake route, our intention is to further build into data centers and rings along that route. We are constantly looking at where we can build into data center clusters and serve transport needs.” In addition to its long-haul fiber commercial business, Ziply also has a robust fiber-to-the-home (FTTP) business. Its parent Bell Canada has formed a joint venture with the private equity firm PSP Investments. The JV is called Network FiberCo, and it’s helping Ziply accelerate its last-mile deployments with the aim of eventually reaching 8 million total fiber passings. artigo.texto: (Bloomberg) -- Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. is accelerating its data center expansion in Europe and the Middle East, propelling its 20-gigawatt global infrastructure buildout during China's escalating competition in AI chips and models with the US. Most Read from Bloomberg The Chinese e-commerce leader will set up its first cloud regions in Turkey, Finland and the Netherlands over the next 12 months, Alibaba executive Li Feifei said at the company's flagship Apsara conference in Hangzhou on Wednesday. The company will also expand its data center footprint in Malaysia, Germany, the United Arab Emirates, France and Hong Kong, a move that will boost its ability to provide localized cloud and AI services. Alibaba's growth push means its increasingly going head-to-head with Western competitors such as Amazon.com Group Inc. and Alphabet Inc. in regions beyond Asia. Its global ambition aligns with Chinese President Xi Jinping's vision to share the country's advances with the world, at a time that Trump officials want other countries to prioritize use of US technology offerings and avoid alternatives from China. Alibaba's global cloud network spans from Japan to Southeast Asia and the Middle East. In recent months, it opened new facilities in Brazil and France, aiming to bring generative AI services to local enterprises. "We are committed to working closely with our global ecosystem to make AI more scalable, practical and accessible for businesses," said Li, who serves as chief technology officer and president of international business for Alibaba Cloud Intelligence. Alibaba kickstarted its annual tech summit in Hangzhou earlier this week, demonstrating its full-stack AI capabilities — just days before Xi embarks on his first state visit to the US in over a decade, with AI at the top of his agenda. The company unveiled a new line of AI chips it claims are China's most powerful and built for frontier-model training. It also said it is training new foundation models with 5 trillion to 10 trillion parameters, far larger than existing open-weight models. Underpinning this hardware-and-software push is a plan to build a 20-gigawatt global data center network by 2032 – which Citigroup estimates could drive more than $160 billion in external cloud revenue.

artigo.texto: A possibilidade de instalação de um Data Center em Atibaia, com previsão de conclusão para 2029, coloca a cidade no centro do debate sobre o avanço da inteligência artificial e a sustentabilidade ambiental. Atualmente, o Brasil comporta cerca de 219 data centers, que são grandes infraestruturas físicas responsáveis por armazenar, processar e distribuir dados digitais. Veja mais notícias de Atibaia e região. Em São Paulo, 59 unidades já operam serviços bancários, plataformas de streaming e modelos de Inteligência Artificial (IA) — que representam o principal aumento de demanda para este tipo de empreendimento. De imediato, a chegada de um empreendimento desse porte pode parecer um passo natural rumo ao progresso da década de 2020. No entanto, a iniciativa esbarra em uma preocupação constante da sociedade local: o aumento no consumo de recursos naturais, como água e energia elétrica, e seus impactos diretos na crise climática. Para analisar esse cenário, o Portal Atibaia.com.br convidou Marcelo Laxe, engenheiro químico, produtor rural e liderança na Associação Salve Atibaia. Ele também integra o Coletivo Fora Data Center Atibaia, autor de um abaixo-assinado para permitir a participação popular e lutar por uma regulamentação municipal que impeça a instalação de empreendimentos desse tipo sem avaliação adequada. Onde será construído o novo Data Center em Atibaia? Em 2025, a empresa curitibana DataSpots obteve junto à Operadora Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) cinco licenças para a construção de Data Centers em diferentes pontos do país. O primeiro empreendimento está localizado em Atibaia — no bairro do Tanque, com início das operações planejado para o período entre 2029 e 2030. A firma faz parte do Grupo On, que atua no setor de energia e infraestrutura desde 2018. O conglomerado inclui empresas como Datlaz, SunaEnergy, Enliv.. Entre clientes do grupo, grandes nomes do mercado global, como Ambev, Enel e Shell. Localizado a cerca de 7 km do centro de Atibaia — com acesso pela Rodovia Fernão Dias, o bairro do Tanque é conhecido por sua área rural e por remanescentes importantes da fauna e da flora presentes no bioma da Mata Atlântica e da Serra do Itapetinga. O nome do bairro tem sua origem vinculada à existência de um grande lago — ou tanque — que marcou a região. De acordo com Marcelo Laxe, o que está em risco é justamente o meio ambiente do local. A partir do início das obras, é esperada uma movimentação intensa de caminhões e máquinas, muito ruído, supressão de vegetação, alteração do solo e perturbação da fauna e dos moradores. Já na operação, os principais riscos apontados são o consumo de energia e água, ruído contínuo, geração de calor, resíduos e possíveis impactos sobre o solo e os recursos hídricos. A chegada deste data center a Atibaia está intrinsecamente ligada à autorização da ampliação da Subestação de Energia Fernão Dias, no bairro Boa Vista. A expansão de linhas de transmissão da subestação foi discutida em audiência pública no dia 17 de junho. Laxe e outros moradores de Atibaia perceberam que os avanços dessa ampliação poderiam ter sido feitos para atender a futuros data centers que seriam instalados na região “Não é o tipo de investimento que traz benefícios, pelo contrário, só causa prejuízos ambientais e sociais. A comunidade do Boa Vista já sofre impactos com poluição sonora provocada pela Subestação Fernão Dias, portanto a mobilização foi imediata.”, afirma o ambientalista. Quais são os riscos ambientais para a região? O investimento, com projeto avaliado em R$ 3 bilhões, tem um potencial de carga elétrica instalada de 100 MW. Segundo o Coletivo, essa potência equivale ao consumo de uma cidade de médio porte, podendo gerar instabilidade no abastecimento energético e, consequentemente, afetando a população, setores produtivos e serviços essenciais. Além disso, existem riscos de contaminação do solo e do lençol freático, bem como a possível alteração do microclima local devido à emissão de calor atmosférico pelos sistemas de processamento. O Data Center também representa risco para a biosfera local, sua expansão da infraestrutura elétrica pode provocar supressão de vegetação, impactos sobre a fauna, impermeabilização do solo, consumo elevado de água e energia. O Coletivo lembra que estes sistemas também consomem grandes volumes de água, devido ao seu sistema de resfriamento que absorve água potável. No entanto, existem Data Centers que reduzem o consumo hídrico, mas demandam mais energia. “Para um município que vive às voltas com crises hídricas, como Atibaia, a ameaça de desabastecimento para a população será iminente.”, analisa Laxe. Além disso, a população também poderá ser diretamente afetada com o aumento da poluição sonora na região devido ao funcionamento do empreendimento, realidade já enfrentada pelos moradores do Boa Vista. O Data Center vai gerar empregos na cidade? A promessa do empreendimento é movimentar o mercado de trabalho regional. A estimativa oficial aponta os seguintes dados: - Fase de obras: criação de 150 a 500 postos de trabalho temporários. - Fase de operação: geração de 50 a 200 vagas permanentes. Laxe, no entanto, traz um outro ponto de vista: a maioria destes cargos são temporários e apenas movimentarão a região durante as obras. Será que as vagas permanentes compensam os severos danos ambientais? "Na fase de operação, os data centers são altamente automatizados. Não há inovação ou modernidade, trata-se de um repositório de máquinas que apenas processam dados", afirma a liderança. Há também a preocupação da descaracterização das zonas rurais do município, fato que já acontece no Boa Vista, desde o início das obras da estação elétrica. “Este megaempreendimento mudou completamente a rotina de um bairro caracterizado pela tranquilidade da zona rural. Caminhões esburacam as vias, o lixo se acumula, o barulho é criminoso. A preocupação é que a instalação do data center reproduza ou amplie esses impactos”, relata Laxe. E agora? Futuro de Atibaia e

artigo.texto: Palm Beach County commissioners voted unanimously Thursday to halt new applications for large-scale data centers for up to one year, as the Trump administration pushes to expand the infrastructure needed to support artificial intelligence (AI). The 6-0 vote in Palm Beach County—home to President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate—comes after months of opposition to a proposed expansion of Project Tango, a planned hyperscale AI data center near Arden in western Palm Beach County. The site is about 20 miles west of Trump’s residence and near homes and an elementary school. Several residents addressed the board Thursday, raising concerns about water, higher power bills, environmental impacts and disruptive noise. Thursday’s vote prohibits the county from accepting, processing or approving new applications for data centers in unincorporated Palm Beach County with an anticipated peak electrical load of at least 50 megawatts. It does not undo Project Tango’s earlier approval. In July, commissioners rejected a proposal to dramatically expand the development, but a 2016 approval for two 100,000-square-foot data center buildings remains in place. Newsweek reached out to Project Tango for comment. The moratorium gives the county time to develop new rules governing projects that could place significant demands on local power, water and other infrastructure. Trump has pushed back on similar measures, criticizing New York’s decision in July to impose a one-year moratorium on new large-scale data centers. At the time, Democratic New York Governor Kathy Hochul cited concerns about rising electricity demand, utility costs, environmental impacts and pressure on local communities. Trump called the decision “terrible,” saying data centers are one of the biggest driving forces for jobs in the future. In late August, Trump pushed back on local opposition to data center projects, writing on Truth Social that municipalities rejecting data centers risk becoming “backwards and poor.” “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign,” he wrote. A new Pew Research Center survey found Americans’ views of data centers have shifted more negative since the beginning of the year. More than half of Americans, 54 percent, said data centers are mostly bad for the environment, up from 39 percent in January. Half said they are mostly bad for home energy costs, up from 38 percent, while 49 percent said they are mostly bad for nearby residents' quality of life, up from 30 percent. The survey was conducted from July 20 to August 9 among 10,548 U.S. adults. Palm Beach County joins a growing number of Florida local governments that have moved to restrict or pause large-scale data center development, including Bay, Citrus, Clay, Holmes, Jackson, Leon, Nassau, Pasco and Walton Counties, according to the South Florida Sun Sentinel. County commissioners also directed staff to explore hiring an outside consultant to help review the rules, after rejecting a proposed technical advisory committee. Vice Mayor Marci Woodward said Thursday she feared the advisory committee would “add an extra layer of work.” Mayor Sara Baxter said she supported the idea of hiring a consultant but objected to the potential cost, which she said could range from about $200,000 to $2 million. The higher figure, Baxter said, was “not even a topic of conversation.” No consultant contract or spending was approved Thursday. The moratorium is set to expire September 24, 2027, or earlier if the county completes its development regulations. artigo.texto: When someone asked how many heard about a proposed hyperscale data center nearby, no one raised a hand in a room of about a hundred Green Valley Ranch residents on Tuesday night. The residents of The Reserve, a 55+ community, and surrounding neighborhoods packed a common area during a meeting about Trident Data Center, which is in the final stages of approval by the city of Aurora. Recommended Stories Trident Data Center is the latest project by Vantage Data Centers, which has 30 data centers across 12 countries. The company submitted the application for Trident to the city on Aug. 25, 2025. If built, the data center would be two stories and 1.5 million square feet on 108 acres of land, according to public documents submitted by Vantage through the city’s development portal. The data center would be the largest in the state by square footage if approved. Residents said they feel “totally blindsided” by the proposal. The property where Trident is proposed is in an industrial zone district, where data centers are a permitted use and can be approved administratively as long as no major adjustments are requested, a city spokesperson said. Plans for the new data center, which is proposed to sit at the northwest corner of the intersection of E-470 and East 48th Avenue, have already been through two formal city reviews and a third is underway, the spokesperson also told The Denver Gazette. Comments from the city are due back to Vantage by the end of the month. Until early September, the Aurora residents said they had not heard a word about the plan from the city or Oakwood Homes, the real estate developer for the community. Vantage did not respond to The Denver Gazette’s request for comment. An Oakwood Homes spokesperson declined to say whether the company informed homebuyers of the potential data center, instead saying in a statement that the data center is not its project and it does not own the land. “We’re aware of concerns raised by residents of the Reserve at Green Valley Ranch,” the spokesperson said. “We have encouraged the data center developer to engage with the community and will continue to do so. While this is not our project, we care about our homeowners and will continue to advocate for their concerns to be heard.” The residents’ concerns are familiar — water and energy usage, and noise. Broadly speaking, supporters have argued that data centers bring jobs and investment to local communities as well as new tax revenues. They have also insisted that cultivating and growing data centers in America has positive repercussions for national security. Meanwhile, a political split is emerging in how cities and counties deal with data centers: The Colorado counties that recently approved data center construction are conservative-leaning, while cities calling for or imposing moratoriums lean progressive. Carlene Embree, who is trying to sell her home in Painted Prairie, said a data center feels like a threat to safety and well-being and she worries the development will tank her home’s value. At a recent open house, a potential buyer’s first question and biggest concern was about the house’s proximity to the proposed data center, Embree said. Other residents, especially those who live in age-restricted community The Reserve, worry about health risks, they said Tuesday. Trident would rely on at least 60 diesel backup generators that could emit between 25 and 75 tons per year of fine particulate matter, noxious fumes and more than 800 tons per year of nitrogen oxides, according to documents created by Green Valley Ranch residents. Such emissions can cause respiratory and cardiovascular risks, they said. Residents also said they worry about noise, adding that hyperscale data centers emit low-frequency noise that will likely impact the surrounding area. Residents Tuesday pointed to Loudoun County, Virginia, which has become known as “data center alley” for having the world’s largest concentration of data centers, according to the county’s website. Local news publications in the county, such as 7News, have reported on the impacts of those data centers, which included neighbor complaints about a constant hum at all hours and fumes that irritate people’s throats and lungs. The residents also worry about electrical demand on the Xcel Energy Denver Metro Division grid they share with Denver International Airport, they said. DIA now uses about 45 megawatts of energy and, as the airport grows, it is anticipated to need 400 megawatts by 2045. If Trident is approved, it would use about 500 megawatts of power, according to area residents Tuesday. Residents also worry about water use as the city of Aurora and much of the state face drought conditions and restrictions. Vantage documents stated that the data center will initially need 800,000 gallons of water for 10 chiller units but will then use closed-loop cooling systems. Water consumption by data centers has often been criticized, but many companies — Microsoft, for example — are moving toward “zero-water” cooling techniques that use closed-loop systems and engineered fluids, reducing reliance on local resources. Some experts have said access to energy is the real problem — water matters, but much less at scale. Colorado Energy Office Director Will Toor earlier noted data modeling on center energy and water use across the West conducted by Western Resource Advocates, a nonprofit environmental law and policy outfit. “If you look at their numbers, they project that, by 10 years from now, there might be about 6,000 acre-feet of water used for data center cooling in Colorado,” Toor had said. “Right now, we use about 6 million acre-feet a year for consumptive use.” “(Water) is not a really big issue or constraint on data center development in a way that I think getting the energy policy right is,” the energy official said. artigo.texto: Órgão destaca consulta prévia, direito de recusa e proteção de territórios indígenas O MPF reforçou sua atuação na proteção de povos e comunidades tradicionais diante do avanço do mercado de carbono no Brasil. A posição foi apresentada pelo procurador da República Felipe Moura Palha durante seminário realizado pelo Conselho Nacional do Ministério Público (CNMP), em Brasília. Segundo o representante do MPF, a missão da instituição é garantir direitos humanos, proteção dos territórios, autonomia e autodeterminação das comunidades. A Lei nº 15.042/2024, que criou o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões, prevê a participação da Câmara de Populações Indígenas e Comunidades Tradicionais do órgão. O MPF também defende que projetos de carbono respeitem a consulta prévia, livre e conduzida pelo poder público. As comunidades devem ter o direito de recusar projetos, enquanto territórios com presença de povos indígenas isolados não podem ser incluídos nessas iniciativas, conforme as diretrizes apresentadas no evento. A instituição afirma que sua atuação no tema reúne quase 20 anos de experiência, com os primeiros casos analisados ainda em 2007. O MPF mantém um roteiro nacional de atuação sobre créditos de carbono e destaca a necessidade de avaliar os impactos dos projetos sobre direitos fundamentais e a efetividade climática dos mecanismos adotados.
