artigo.texto: In 2019, textile factory Swastik Poly Prints joined the emissions trading scheme (ETS) of Surat, a city in the Indian state of Gujarat. Since then, the company has reduced its particulate matter emissions by at least 30 per cent, claims its owner Binay Agrawal. The ETS is a cap-and-trade system which seeks to curb air pollution by allowing companies to buy and sell permits for particulate matter emissions. Participating companies have access to an online dashboard which helps them track emissions. In Surat, factories like Swastik Poly Prints emitted 20-30 per cent less particulate pollution than those operating under conventional regulations, notes Emissions Market Accelerator (EMA), which brought the cap-and-trade system to Gujarat. Agrawal says continuous emissions data via the ETS helped inform the company’s decisions on how to improve combustion efficiency, such as fine-tuning and upgrading its auto-firing systems, pollution-control equipment and filtration devices. Now, the company is “well within the limit” of its ETS cap, he notes. Gujarat’s emissions trading scheme was a finalist for the 2025 Earthshot Prize hosted in Rio de Janeiro, where it piqued the interest of local officials. Now, the Brazilian city is exploring whether a similar market-based approach could help it tackle industrial pollution. If implemented, this market would be the first of its kind in South America. A memorandum of understanding between EMA and the city of Rio, which would lay the foundations for the partnership, is now in legal review, says Kaushik Deb, executive director of EPIC India. In June 2026, Rio de Janeiro announced a partnership with EMA. The accelerator is a partnership between the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago (EPIC) and the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab, a global research centre. “ The aim is to reduce the total volume of emissions and enable this reduction to take place more efficiently – at a lower cost and in a manner better suited to each business’s specific profile. Osmar Lima, secretary for economic development, Rio According to Osmar Lima, Rio’s secretary for economic development, “some variables” are currently under assessment until June. These include “the pollutants that may be regulated, the facilities potentially covered, the emissions cap, the initial number of permits, the governance model, the trading platform and the monitoring, reporting and verification mechanisms”, Lima says. Dialogue Earth spoke to researchers involved in the Gujarat experiment, the technical team working with Rio de Janeiro, and independent experts to examine what the model can deliver. Gujarat’s results offer a promising proof of concept, with some high polluters showing lowered emissions. But questions remain over the transparency of emissions data, the capacity of regulators to run such markets and whether reductions in factory-level emissions translate into cleaner air for nearby communities, experts say. Answers to those questions are important for Rio, which is still assessing whether a pollution-control model developed in an industrial hub in western India can work in its unique regulatory, industrial and environmental context. “The idea at the outset is not just to set up an emissions trading scheme. We want to try and understand what the situation in Rio is,” Deb tells Dialogue Earth. Some lessons from Gujarat, including how to set an emissions cap and measure the total industrial emissions, may be transferable. But regulation, local laws and institutional capacity could prove harder to replicate, he notes. The Surat model Emissions trading is not a new concept. Over the years, markets for pollution control have cropped up in the United States and across Europe to reduce pollutants such as sulphur dioxide and greenhouse gases. But Surat’s was the world’s first emissions trading scheme specifically targeting particulate matter, and in a polluted textile manufacturing hub. The pilot in Surat covered 342 industrial units over seven months. A randomised selection of 168 participated in the scheme while 174 remained under conventional regulation. Participating plants reduced their particulate matter emissions by about 24 per cent compared with the control group. The latter failed to comply with pollution rules roughly a third of the time, while non-compliance fell to about 1 per cent among participants. The market does not, however, replace regulation. It is a compliance market: regulators determine which industries participate, which pollutants are covered and how the cap is set. “Let’s say, in Gujarat, the initial cap was 280 [tonnes of particulate emission] and was reduced to 170 [tonnes] over two years,” says Dheeraj Alshetty, deputy director of EPIC India. The idea was to tighten the ceiling gradually rather than impose an immediate reduction that could result in major costs and resistance from industry, he adds. At Swastik Poly Prints, the financial gain from selling surplus permits was one factor behind investment in cleaner technology, says Agrawal. But the bigger benefit was improved fuel efficiency. Better combustion reduced fuel consumption and costs, while also keeping the company comfortably within its emissions limit, he notes. The hope is that these financial and reputational incentives encourage companies to invest in cleaner technology and more efficient production, Alshetty says. Before the ETS was set up in parts of Gujarat, like other Indian states it relied on traditional “command-and-control” regulation. Under that system, regulators set emissions standards for industrial plants. “Compliance was expected and only non-compliance was penalised,” says Tejas Patel, deputy environmental engineer at the Gujarat Pollution Control Board. Plants that performed better had little financial incentive to reduce emissions further. artigo.texto: California voters oppose new data centers, poll finds A majority of California voters oppose building new data centers in the state, and even more say they oppose putting one in their own community, according to a new poll by POLITICO and its partners. The findings come as data centers have become a flashpoint in the war over AI — no more so than in California, the hub of the global tech industry. Just over half of registered voters in the state — 51% — say they oppose building new data centers that power the technology, while about a quarter support the idea, the UC Berkeley Citrin Center for Public Opinion Research-POLITICO poll found. Opposition grows stronger against data centers if one were to be sited in a voters' own community, with 61% opposed. "It's clear that people have a desire for local control," said Jack Citrin, a UC Berkeley political science professor and co-director of the poll. Those attitudes reflect a broader rush of anxiety about AI both at the state and global level. And the data center findings suggest a deepening opposition not just to increasingly capable AI systems and the threats they represent, but to the server farms that underpin the technology. The results land as politicians across the country and political spectrum begin to embrace curbs on their development. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, have been among them, while California Gov. Gavin Newsom has become more amenable to state oversight of AI factories this year. The issue ranks near the bottom on the list of priorities for California voters overall. Only 3% of voters overall said data centers and AI were the most important issues facing the state, according to the poll. And public opinion on data centers in California still breaks down starkly over party lines. A plurality of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents polled — 45% — said they supported new data centers going up in California, compared to only about an eighth of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents surveyed. Support shrank at the prospect of a data center being sited in their local community. The not-in-my-backyard sentiment revealed in the polls is playing out in communities around the state, including San Francisco, Monterey Park, and Fresno, that have adopted or are considering bans on new data centers. The moves to block their expansion have accelerated despite warnings from the industry and tech advocates that they are critical for powering the state's tech sector, which underpins much of the economy. Those local initiatives may be just the start. The poll found voters across party lines favored local rather than state control when it comes to government oversight of data centers. About 40% of voters said either the local government, or a mix of state and local officials, should have more authority over whether a large data center is built in a community. Only about one in 10 voters said California's state government should have more power over the issue, a number which fluctuated only slightly when partisan leanings were factored in. Much of the debate over data centers has centered on issues like noise and utility rates and the centers' demand for power and water. Industry boosters have argued the facilities create jobs and power economic activity, including in more rural areas where space is at less of a premium. The economic argument is resonating with rightward-leaning voters in California, the poll showed. Just more than half of Republican and Republican-leaning independents surveyed said they thought data centers were mostly good for local jobs, a sentiment only a fifth of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents agreed with. Some studies show that data centers do increase local employment, although they do not always spin off as many jobs as promised, and the staying power of those roles is disputed. Opposition to data centers also registered in a concurrent survey of POLITICO's audience of key political and policy influencers in the state, including political staffers, lobbyists, policy advisers and others deeply versed in California's political landscape, with 45 percent opposed to building new facilities in the state. As with voters, opposition grew even larger to the idea of a data center in their own community, with 60 percent of influencers opposed. These data come from parallel surveys of California voters and policy influencers, fielded by TrueDot, the AI-accelerated research platform, in collaboration with the Citrin Center at UC Berkeley and POLITICO. Interviews for the voter survey were conducted online in English and Spanish from Sept. 8-14, among a sample of 2,418 registered voters, including 1,983 likely voters, selected at random through Political Data Inc. and Verasight, with supplemental online panel recruitment. Voter results were weighted to California registered-voter benchmarks for age, educational attainment, race and ethnicity, gender, and geography, with additional calibration to 2024 presidential vote by region. From Sept. 11-16, a parallel study was conducted in partnership with POLITICO among its audience of key political and policy influencers in California. The audience was defined based on job title and organizational affiliation and included state and local government employees, political staffers, lobbyists, policy advisers, consultants, business decision-makers and subject matter experts. The margin of error is plus or minus 2.7% for the registered voter survey, plus or minus 3% for likely voters and plus or minus 4.5% for the influencers.

artigo.texto: Applied Digital confirms $3.2 billion data center campus in Brookwood BROOKWOOD, Ala. (WBRC) - Applied Digital has confirmed its Delta Forge 2 AI Factory campus will be built in Brookwood, following weeks of environmental and transparency concerns about the site. The company, which designs, builds and operates hyperscale data centers, had been linked to the Brookwood site since July 20, when Alabama’s Department of Environmental Management approved a permit application indicating Applied Digital was planning to build a 2-million-square-foot data center in the city. At the time, the company said no decision had been made. On Sept. 2, Brookwood Mayor Joe Barger confirmed for the first time that a proposed development in the city was an AI data center. Barger made the confirmation during a city council meeting held at the G.G. Hardin Center. Barger said at the time there was no signed project yet. On Thursday, Applied Digital said Delta Forge 2 will span about 1.26 million square feet across 160 acres of a nearly 1,300-acre site in Brookwood. According to a release from Applied Digital, the campus represents an investment of more than $3.2 billion from the company and its tenant. Construction employment is expected to peak at more than 1,000 workers, and the completed campus is expected to support more than 100 full-time employees onsite. Applied Digital said it is committing $270 million in community benefits payments to the Tuscaloosa County Economic Development Authority over 20 years, in addition to its educational tax contributions. “This annual revenue stream will directly support local entities whose taxes are being abated, including the cities of Brookwood, Tuscaloosa and Northport, Tuscaloosa County, the Tuscaloosa County Road Improvement Commission, and DCH Health System,” Applied Digital wrote. “Each entity will receive a share proportional to its current local tax distribution.” The Tuscaloosa County Economic Development Authority signed off on the project Thursday. Probate Judge Rob Robertson, who is also Chairman of the Tuscaloosa County Commission, calls it a major investment. “It’s going to create some significant new revenue for our schools. I’m happy for the city of Brookwood,” Robertson said. Robertson told WBRC he understands why people have questions, but expects more chances for the public to weigh in and learn about the project. “I think that anything like this that’s new, and there are a lot of very legitimate questions, but there’s a lot in this project that I think the city of Brookwood will work hard to answer and the company that will be building. I think they ahve some town halls planned,” Robertson said. The project is expected to generate about $131.5 million in education taxes over the same period, along with ongoing sales, use and lodging tax revenue associated with the development and operations, according to Applied Digital. “For our community, this project is about creating opportunities for local families, strengthening our schools and positioning Brookwood for the future,” Barger said in a quote included in Applied Digital’s announcement. “We anticipate that Applied Digital will be a good neighbor and a long-term community partner, and expect this $3.2 billion investment to benefit Brookwood residents for generations to come.” Find more on this data center project and others in the area by clicking or tapping here. artigo.texto: Washington’s carbon market nears linkage with Quebec and California OLYMPIA – Washington hit another milestone in a yearslong project to link the state’s carbon market with California and Quebec, which supporters say will bring greater stability to the program. During the Climate Alliance conference in New York City, Gov. Bob Ferguson announced the state had reached agreement with California on the regulatory changes needed to link the state’s carbon market with California and Quebec. While Ferguson initially planned to attend the conference in person, travel issues scuttled the trip. California Gov. Gavin Newsom also announced Wednesday he had authorized the state to proceed with linking the markets, which is expected to be completed next year. The Climate Alliance is comprised of 24 governors from across the country. It was founded during the first Trump administration to pursue climate policy. “States and subnational governments are stepping up and leading at a time when the federal government is trying to dismantle U.S. climate policy,” Ferguson said in a statement. “Linkage isn’t just good climate policy – it’s smart economics. Linking will unlock greater emissions reductions, lower the cost of clean technologies, and create good‑paying jobs in high‑growth industries. We’re excited to be moving forward.” Washington first launched its carbon market in 2023 under former Gov. Jay Inslee. Under the program, major polluters can purchase credits for each metric ton of greenhouse gases they emit through quarterly auctions. The number of available credits will decrease overtime as the state works toward a goal of net-zero carbon emissions by 2050. The state has raised more than $5 billion through the sale of credits since the market launched in 2023, according to the state Department of Ecology. By law, revenue from the program funds climate and air quality projects around the state. The market was established in 2021 through the Climate Commitment Act. During the most recent auction, which was conducted in early September, the cost of a credit was set at $32 and raised $116 million. Credits during the most recent auction in Quebec and California sold at $32.48 per metric ton. Under the agreement, carbon credits would be the same price across all three jurisdictions, and companies would be able to trade their credits from one jurisdiction to another. Supporters of the program say that by linking the markets, the three jurisdictions will create a larger and more stable market, giving large companies greater ability to plan for long‑term, capital‑intensive projects. “We will have a stable and larger market that connects those three jurisdictions,” Newsom said as he announced the agreement during a panel discussion. “And that ain’t so bad in a world of Donald Trump.” Todd Myers, vice president for research at Washington Policy Center, said in an interview that linking the markets was a “good decision.” Myers said that prior to the most recent carbon auction, California and Quebec’s carbon credits have been “consistently half” the price of Washington’s price. “So what that means, essentially, is they are assuming a big chunk of risk that we are currently for,” Myers said. “And so that’s great. That’s California subsidizing Washington. I don’t know why California wants to do that, I know why it’s good for us.” Myers said the bigger market will also create more stability. “So if we have a really bad snow pack year, and our electricity-related emissions go up, we can deal with it,” Myers said. “As opposed to we’re sort of on our own. So that’s good.” Prior to formal linkage of the markets, the California Air Resources Board must complete its formal regulatory process.

artigo.texto: General election voters in Butte-Silver Bow County may now consider a proposed ballot initiative that would require citizen approval of data center development, after the Montana Supreme Court on Tuesday overturned a lower court ruling that prevented the initiative from appearing on the November ballot. In a Wednesday court filing responding to the decision, the county said it intends to comply, but is unsure of how to follow the ruling and remain in compliance with the Montana Election Code, since ballots have already been printed — and some have already been sent and returned — without the initiative. The county asks the court for direction, and proposes options including modifying existing ballots or issuing supplemental ballots containing the initiative. The ruling is the latest development in a dispute over a law passed by the 2025 Legislature. The Butte initiative, organized by 406 People First and Denise Kelly, would require a special election in which two-thirds of all registered voters approve a data center project before the county can authorize its construction or expansion. Initiative organizers sued Butte-Silver Bow County in August after election officials notified them that the deadline they had originally been given to submit petition signatures was incorrect. RELATED Court rejects Butte data center ballot initiative A district court judge has rejected a Butte organizer’s request to put a data center initiative on the November ballot after confusion about the signature-gathering deadline tanked the initiative. John Meyer, the lawyer representing the plaintiffs, said they have appealed the decision. According to court documents, the county initially told organizers they had until Aug. 14 to submit 3,652 valid signatures. Election Administrator Cynthia Sherman informed organizers July 31 they had met the requirement. But on Aug. 10, the county notified organizers that Senate Bill 11, enacted in 2025, required that signatures be submitted by July 13. The law requires petition signatures to be submitted four weeks before the ballot certification deadline, which is 85 days before the election. The same law affected a similar initiative in Yellowstone County, where organizers had been told they could submit signatures until Aug. 12. Yellowstone County Attorney Scott Twito told MTFP in August that data center developer Quantica Infrastructure, whose Broadview data center recently began construction, brought the earlier statutory deadline to his attention on July 30. The county subsequently informed organizers that their signature deadline had already passed. In Butte, a district court judge rejected the organizers’ request for relief on Aug. 28, concluding that the statutory deadline applied despite the county’s incorrect instructions. Organizers appealed to the Montana Supreme Court. In its Tuesday ruling, the Supreme Court temporarily prohibited the county from rejecting the initiative on the basis of the missed deadline. The order notes that Butte-Silver Bow County did not oppose the organizers’ request for the injunction. The justices concluded that excluding the initiative from the November ballot while the organizers’ appeal proceeds could irreparably harm voters’ constitutional rights. The court also acknowledged that the initiative might ultimately be invalidated, even if voters approve it, should the justices later determine it was improperly placed on the ballot. Evan Barrett, a member of 406 People First who helped prepare the petition, acknowledged that possibility, but said allowing the election to proceed with the initiative on the ballot would preserve voters’ opportunity to consider the measure. “If the merits of our case are not good enough and the court says, ‘this election doesn’t count,’ that’s possible,” Barrett said. “But it’s impossible to make the choice without the election.” The injunction will remain in effect until the Supreme Court resolves the appeal. In response to Butte-Silver Bow’s Wednesday filing, the Supreme Court gave initiative organizers until noon on Thursday to respond to the county’s proposed options. The court has said the justices will issue a ruling as expeditiously as possible. artigo.texto: Republican Tom Tiffany and Democrat David Crowley are staking out positions on artificial intelligence as the technology reshapes government, the economy, and the state's energy landscape. Artificial intelligence is driving demand for hyperscale AI data centers — including one in Port Washington — and has become a major flashpoint in the Wisconsin governor's race. TMJ4 News reporter Charles Brenson has more on how each candidate is tackling the issue in Wisconsin: Republicans have criticized Crowley for suggesting Wisconsin could become a "global hub" for data centers, even as his campaign ads call for accountability from the industry. "Hold data centers accountable and make them pay," a Crowley campaign commercial said. Democrats have criticized Tiffany for voting on a House bill to fast-track data centers, but the SPEED Act stalled in the Senate. He also supported a proposed 10-year moratorium that would have blocked state efforts to restrict AI data centers. The Senate later removed that provision. Tiffany's campaign ads push back on the industry as well. "Stop Wall Street from buying our homes — big data from bulldozing our farms," a Tiffany campaign commercial said. The next governor will have to navigate Wisconsin through the fast-changing world of artificial intelligence and determine how it can be used across state government. State agencies are currently allowed to use AI to "leverage their capabilities in gaining unique insights, problem solving, and enhancing productivity," according to the state's website. Employees are asked to be "vigilant in using generative AI tools" and are "prohibited from sharing Non-Public Information with any generative AI platform that has not been authorized." The state also directs employees to "exercise critical judgment and verify the completeness and accuracy of all information from any AI platform." Tiffany said he sees a need for privacy protections and a measured approach to the technology's expansion. "Certainly have concerns. There needs to be guardrails. I think we need to make sure we protect people's privacy. We need to make sure people's data is not being sent to, especially adversaries, including communist China, who's always trying to harvest our data," Tiffany said. "So I think there needs to be some guardrails around this that we need to take a, a bit of a go slow approach." He said the technology carries both promise and risk. "I think it's like any technology. There are benefits to it, but there's also risks, and that's what we need to do is that assessment," Tiffany said. Crowley said AI should serve as a tool for workers, not a replacement for human decision-making. "I think that artificial intelligence, it can be used as a tool, but it should not replace human judgment. It shouldn't be the end all, be all. And I believe that we need to have strict guardrails here in the state of Wisconsin," Crowley said. Crowley said protecting jobs and personal data would guide his approach to deploying AI in state government. "Well, one, I don't think artificial intelligence should be replacing our jobs. I wanted to increase and enhance our efficiencies and be able to assist all of our workers within a state government," Crowley said. "But again, we have to make sure those protections are there, making sure there aren't any personal identifiers out there, that the privacy, the accountability, but also the public knows exactly how we're utilize." artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Amazon fecha acordo de US$ 2,4 bi para garantir energia a data centers Publicado 23/09/2026 • 20:00 | Atualizado há 14 horas KEY POINTS Foto: AFP A expansão dos data centers aumenta a necessidade de fontes de energia capazes de manter as operações mesmo diante de quedas. Para reforçar essa estrutura, a Amazon fechou um acordo de US$ 2,4 bilhões (R$ 12,2 bilhões) para comprar geradores de reserva. O contrato prevê as primeiras entregas para 2027 e 2028 e amplia a relação entre duas empresas em um momento de forte crescimento da infraestrutura voltada à inteligência artificial. Leia também: Trump divulga 1.156 transações e movimenta até US$ 270 milhões em investimentos, incluindo Amazon e Microsoft O acordo entre Amazon e Generac envolve geradores destinados aos data centers da empresa americana. Esses equipamentos ajudam a manter o fornecimento de eletricidade em situações de interrupção e garantem maior segurança durante as operações. A Generac informou o contrato em documento enviado à Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), órgão regulador do mercado financeiro dos Estados Unidos. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC Além do contrato de fornecimento, a Generac concedeu à Amazon uma garantia que permite à companhia comprar mais de 1,6 milhão de ações da fabricante por US$ 200 cada (R$ 1 mil). Desse total, cerca de 308 mil ações já podem ser adquiridas pela gigante americana. A liberação das demais parcelas dependerá dos pagamentos que a Amazon fizer pela compra dos geradores ao longo do contrato. Leia também: Amazon barra Muse, agente de IA da Meta, após tentativas de compras automáticas O acordo entre as empresas também explica como a inteligência artificial amplia a necessidade de infraestrutura energética. Data centers precisam de grandes volumes de eletricidade para manter servidores e sistemas em funcionamento. artigo.texto: Publicidade A Oracle emitiu uma notificação de “força maior” a uma unidade da Blue Owl, desenvolvedora de um grande data center no estado norte-americano do Novo México, citando possíveis atrasos no fornecimento de energia para o projeto, informou uma fonte a par do assunto à Reuters nesta quinta-feira. As ações da Oracle caíam 3,3%. A fonte afirmou que garantir o fornecimento de energia para o local é de responsabilidade da Oracle, conforme previsto no contrato. A Oracle não pode rescindir o contrato de locação sob nenhuma circunstância, disse a fonte, acrescentando que a gestora de ativos alternativos Blue Owl possui cerca de US$ 3 bilhões em capital próprio no projeto, sendo a Oracle responsável pelo pagamento dos custos da dívida. As empresas costumam invocar força maior para se isentar de obrigações contratuais quando surgem problemas fora de seu controle, uma medida que pode gerar preocupações entre credores e investidores. Em vez de sair como locatária principal, a Oracle está tentando adiar os pagamentos caso o data center, chamado de Projeto Júpiter, sofra atrasos e não entre em operação em 2028, conforme planejado, de acordo com uma reportagem da Bloomberg. Treasuries disparam outra vez: como isso afeta o Brasil e o que fazer agora? Taxa dos títulos de 10 anos dos EUA fecha a 5,11% e eleva o retorno mínimo exigido de todos os investimentos; especialistas divergem sobre prazo, e há quem veja oportunidade para quem tem dinheiro parado Stuhlberger: Flávio é “fraco” e não tem plano, mas bolsa pode subir 30% com vitória Gestor vê maior impacto da eleição em ações e espera euforia de curto prazo, mas dificuldades para aprovação de reformas mesmo para a oposição A Oracle não respondeu imediatamente a um pedido de comentário da Reuters. “O Projeto Júpiter continua dentro do cronograma planejado”, afirmou a empresa no início do dia. Continua depois da publicidade A Blue Owl, proprietária da Stack Infrastructure, desenvolvedora da central de processamento de dados, afirmou que a notificação não altera os compromissos financeiros com esse projeto plurianual. Durante a fase de desenvolvimento, a Blue Owl obtém um rendimento de 9% sobre seu capital próprio, disse a fonte, acrescentando que, após a conclusão do projeto, o rendimento alavancado deverá ficar em torno de 11%. Ao invocar força maior, a Oracle prorroga o período durante o qual paga à Blue Owl o aluguel mais baixo da fase de desenvolvimento. A Blue Owl ainda receberá o aluguel mais alto pelo prazo originalmente planejado, mas o início desse pagamento será adiado, segundo a fonte. Continua depois da publicidade O campus do Projeto Júpiter, com cerca de 570 hectares e que garantiu US$ 18 bilhões em empréstimos de um consórcio de bancos, segundo reportagens da mídia, faz parte de um acordo mais amplo da Oracle com a OpenAI para fornecer capacidade de computação em IA. O campus do data center enfrenta vários contratempos de infraestrutura, incluindo atrasos na construção de um gasoduto e contestação judicial em relação a licenças relacionadas à água e à qualidade do ar. O projeto faz parte do Stargate, uma iniciativa para construir infraestrutura de IA nos EUA sob um compromisso de investimento de US$ 500 bilhões envolvendo OpenAI, SoftBank Group e parceiros, incluindo a Oracle. Continua depois da publicidade A construção dessa infraestrutura de IA em grande escala tem enfrentado desafios crescentes, à medida que os desenvolvedores correm para garantir energia e outros recursos, ao mesmo tempo em que gerenciam os enormes custos da implantação de capacidade computacional para parceiros como a OpenAI. A crescente oposição do público norte-americano transformou os data centers em um ponto nevrálgico político, com comunidades próximas aos projetos de centrais de processamento de dados manifestando preocupações quanto ao impacto sobre o abastecimento local de energia, água e outros recursos naturais. A corretora William Blair afirmou que, embora essa notícia intensifique as preocupações com atrasos regulatórios e relacionados ao fornecimento de energia que afetam as implantações de IA, ela espera um impacto mínimo no curto prazo para a Oracle. Continua depois da publicidade “Na prática, o ano fiscal de 2027 não deve ser afetado, já que o Jupiter não gera receita neste ano.”

artigo.texto: O que falta para o Google construir um novo data center no Brasil? Por Marcelo Fischer • Editado por Jones Oliveira | O Google anunciou nesta quinta-feira (24) que vai dobrar a infraestrutura técnica que tem no Brasil até 2030. Mas, mesmo com o boom da inteligência artificial (IA) e com a aprovação do Redata — regime criado para estimular novos data centers no país —, a big tech ainda não confirma a construção de uma nova instalação desse porte em território nacional. Em coletiva de imprensa durante o Google Cloud Summit Brasil, o Canaltech questionou Eduardo López, presidente do Google Cloud para a América Latina, sobre o que ainda falta para que a companhia construa um novo grande data center no Brasil. A primeira reação do executivo veio em tom de brincadeira: “Eu perguntaria para você: por que você acha que o que nós temos hoje não é grande?”. Na sequência, López explicou que o principal fator considerado pelo Google na hora de definir novos investimentos é a demanda. “Todo o nosso desenho de investimento tem a ver com a demanda”, afirmou. Segundo ele, a decisão de dobrar a capacidade no país representa uma aposta no crescimento do uso das plataformas do Google Cloud e das ferramentas de IA pelas empresas brasileiras. Cenário parece favorável (até demais) A pergunta surge em um momento particularmente favorável para investimentos em infraestrutura digital no Brasil. Em 15 de setembro, o Governo Federal sancionou o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata). A legislação reduz a carga tributária sobre equipamentos destinados à implantação, modernização e ampliação de centros de dados, mas exige uma série de contrapartidas das empresas beneficiadas. Uma delas está alinhada com o discurso de soberania digital adotado pelo Google nesta quinta-feira. Empresas que aderirem ao programa terão de destinar ao mercado brasileiro ao menos 10% da capacidade de processamento, armazenamento e tratamento de dados instalada com os incentivos do Redata. Hoje, segundo o Governo, cerca de 60% das cargas digitais brasileiras são processadas fora do país. O regime também estabelece exigências ambientais. Os data centers beneficiados precisam atender toda a demanda contratada de eletricidade com energia proveniente de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão, além de cumprir critérios de eficiência hídrica. López avaliou que a nova política pode ajudar o setor: “Eu acho que o Redata ajuda bastante no que é custo operacional das infraestruturas, especialmente quando compramos componentes”. A exigência energética também encontra um Google que vem ampliando projetos ligados à descarbonização no país. A empresa anunciou recentemente sua maior compra de remoção de carbono até hoje, ligada a um projeto da Terradot que atua, entre outras áreas, em fazendas de arroz no Rio Grande do Sul. A iniciativa pretende eliminar o equivalente a 1 milhão de toneladas de CO2 no curto prazo até 2030 e remover permanentemente outro 1 milhão de toneladas até 2040. O projeto não envolve a construção de data centers, mas se encaixa em uma das questões centrais para a expansão desse tipo de infraestrutura: como aumentar a capacidade computacional exigida pela IA sem ampliar na mesma proporção as emissões de carbono. Google vai dobrar infraestrutura no Brasil O anúncio desta quinta-feira adiciona outro elemento a esse cenário. O Google pretende dobrar sua infraestrutura técnica no Brasil até 2030, ampliando a capacidade local de processamento, armazenamento e computação de IA de alto desempenho. A empresa também anunciou que, a partir de 15 de outubro, o Gemini Enterprise terá processamento local de dados do Gemini 3.5 Flash. Além disso, máquinas virtuais G4 equipadas com GPUs Nvidia RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell já estão disponíveis na região de nuvem de São Paulo. A localização é especialmente relevante para empresas que precisam manter dados e processamento dentro do território brasileiro por questões regulatórias, de segurança ou soberania. Ainda assim, dobrar infraestrutura não significa necessariamente construir um novo campus de data center. Data center é só uma parte da equação Na resposta ao Canaltech, López também destacou que aumentar a capacidade computacional dentro do Brasil é apenas uma parte da estratégia de infraestrutura do Google. “Quando você fala de latência, quando você fala de soluções, são duas variáveis muito importantes: as infraestruturas — o data center — e a conectividade”, explicou. O executivo citou os cabos submarinos como outro componente essencial. Eles ligam a infraestrutura brasileira à rede global do Google e ajudam a reduzir o tempo necessário para que informações circulem entre diferentes regiões. A empresa já investiu em cabos como Firmina, Tannat, Curie e Humboldt na América Latina, ao mesmo tempo em que ampliou regiões de nuvem e data centers no continente. “Nós trabalhamos as duas coisas sempre: a conectividade, com os cabos submarinos que chegam ao Brasil, e nossa infraestrutura no Brasil para dar capacidade de processamento e soberania de dados aqui”, afirmou López. Por enquanto, portanto, o Google não coloca um novo data center brasileiro no calendário. Veja mais no Canaltech: O que é data center?

artigo.texto: EU Council Raises Cap on Carbon Allowances Held in Reserve to 800 Million The Council of the European Union has set its negotiating position on the invalidation of carbon allowances held in the market stability reserve, ahead of talks with the European Parliament. The Council of the European Union set out, on September 23, 2026, its negotiating position on a targeted amendment to the market stability reserve (MSR), a mechanism within the emissions trading system (ETS) that covers electricity production and industry, among other sectors. The mandate, adopted at the level of member states' ambassadors, must now be negotiated with the European Parliament, which has not yet set its own position. The new rules have therefore not entered into force. A mechanism for regulating the allowance surplus The reserve withdraws allowances from volumes offered at auction when the total number of allowances in circulation (TNAC), a measure of the market surplus, exceeds a certain threshold. Conversely, it can release allowances back to auction when the surplus becomes low. This mechanism follows predefined thresholds, distinct from the invalidation mechanism. Holding more allowances in the reserve therefore does not mean putting them immediately on the market: any future release depends on the reserve's own trigger rules. Under the currently applicable rules, allowances held in the reserve above a cap of 400 million are permanently invalidated. The European Commission had proposed ending this invalidation with no end date. The Council instead opted for a temporary suspension of invalidation until December 31, 2030, followed, from January 1, 2031, by invalidation of allowances held above a raised cap of 800 million, according to the Coreper mandate. This divergence between the institutional positions is expected to shape the further negotiations with the European Parliament. Pace of cap reduction referred to the broader ETS review The Council's mandate refers any eventual annual reduction of the future 800 million cap to the broader review of the emissions trading system, currently in preparation. The pace of this reduction does not appear in the targeted amendment examined by member states' ambassadors. This element therefore remains a separate matter for negotiation, rather than an already settled rule. The Council states its objective of preserving a reserve capable of absorbing future tensions on allowance supply, while maintaining the price signal meant to guide decarbonization investments. Darragh O'Brien, Ireland's Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment, commented on the agreement on behalf of the Council presidency of the European Union. However, the scale of any effect on the carbon price or on electricity bills cannot be inferred from the volume of allowances held alone: it will also depend on the surplus actually in circulation and on other market rules. Recent data, but no price forecast Data published by the European Commission show that the reserve continues to withdraw allowances from auction volumes. These figures illustrate the recent trajectory of the allowance surplus but do not constitute a price forecast for the period following any eventual adoption of the reform. The exceptional release of allowances during a sharp rise in the carbon price, moreover, is governed by a provision separate from the ordinary rule based on the surplus level. This distinction between the two mechanisms matters when assessing how quickly allowances currently held in the reserve could, if applicable, be returned to the market.

artigo.texto: During the Battery & Energy Storage Tech Expo in Barcelona, Spain, Energy-Storage.news spoke with Ken Davies, chief commercial officer at Digital Product Passport (DPP) provider DigiProd Pass and conference program director of the event, about the upcoming implementation of the EU Battery Passport. Starting on 18 February 2027, any battery exceeding 2kWh will be required to have a digital product passport. These passports function as a URL accessed via a scannable QR code and will contain approximately 75 data points, including static manufacturing data such as raw materials and processes, as well as dynamic life-cycle data such as repairs, sales, recycling history and performance metrics from the battery management system. “Battery actually represents the very start of a complete revolution in data and circularity in all products,” explains Davies. He adds that the reason that these passports exist is twofold: the primary one is for recyclers and other companies involved at the end-of-life cycle of the batteries to know the specific information about each individual battery that can be easily accessed through a QR code that sends to a website with all the details of the battery throughout its lifetime. Davies says that the second reason is that it gives authorities a clearer vision and view of where everything has been made, how it was made, and whether the product is legitimate or counterfeit. How to prepare ahead of February 2027 With only a few months until implementation, Davies mentions that major manufacturers and big organisations are well advanced in implementing this new EU requirement. However, the pressure point will be towards mid-scale companies that “perhaps haven’t got major resources in terms of sustainability and circularity and regulatory compliance,” explains Davies, adding that “we’re getting lots of inquiries about these things now.” “But you’d be surprised. We’re getting major EV companies asking us about it now, as well as mid-scale companies. “The moral is there’s no need to panic. It is probably something that organisations need to have in place within maybe two months. In that regard, they’ve got a system and are trying to apply it. Because what you don’t really want to do is have a system going live on 17 February, ideally you want a situation whereby you’ve got things probably by the end of the year,” explains Davies. Ahead of that deadline, Davies highlights three key priorities for compliance: data, how to transfer that data (including which format), and, lastly, their operations and when they want to apply the data. “Because maybe we don’t want to apply a battery right at the start of the process. Probably just before we say that is a product that we’re happy with, and we’re about to either put it into stock or we’re going to sell it to a client.” For the data and how a company will facilitate the transfer of the battery’s data from their system into the data that will be acquired on the battery passport, Davies mentions that any battery passport provider can provide the information needed for that step, including the format that is needed, which he mentions is called a schema. Furthermore, considering that these passports will work throughout the entire lifetime of a battery, it could happen that the original manufacturer has ceased to exist. Davies explains this will not be an issue, given that information will also be held on an EU register separate from the battery passport itself, while a third party will also hold all the information in case the original battery manufacturer goes out of business. “There’ll never be a situation whereby the information on that battery won’t be accessible either from the original manufacturer, from the third party in the case of the disappearance of the manufacturer, or from the EU registrar.” An evolving passport Moreover, the implementation of that new EU Battery Passport in February 2027 should not be viewed as a one-off, but rather an evolving mechanism that will add new elements in the coming months. “What’s been announced by the regulators is a fairly simple system in order to get it operational. It will develop. So, what will happen is there’ll be more and more information required on that DPP on the battery passport, so don’t necessarily think. In fact, you can be sure. Don’t think that once we’re compliant on February 18th, that’s it to forget about,” says Davies. He mentions how, in the coming months after February 2027, there will be more information required to be added into the product’s passport, such as the carbon footprint information, which is not necessary now, but “it almost certainly will be within a matter of months.” “It’s very much the first step. We are right at the cutting edge of a big revolution. This is the first one, so there’s no doubt it will evolve from there,” concludes Davies.

artigo.texto: Generac is ramping up its production for data centers and it could soon outpace company sales in residential power generators. The Waukesha-based power company is preparing to deliver to Amazon worth roughly $2.4 billion worth of backup generators for its data centers in 2027 and 2028. The company is accelerating production capacity at its Oshkosh and Sussex facilities, but some of the orders will be fulfilled internationally a company spokesperson said. The spokesperson added the company's commercial and industrial segment growth, which includes work with data centers, has caused the Generac to add more than 100 manufacturing jobs in Sussex. The deal Generac made with Amazon is worth up to $8 billion, according to a filing from the company on Sept. 16. As part of the deal Amazon received 307,954 shares of Generac stock making the company a minority common shareholder. Amazon has the option to acquire 1,693,745 shares of stock by September 16, 2033. If Amazon does take full advantage of the stock opportunity and acquires all the shares, the company would represent a 2.57% of common shares. One interesting part of this situation is there is no exclusivity. Generac can work with other hyperscale data center companies along with non-hyperscale companies. Generac is near the tail end of its third quarter and will likely announce its results in October or early November. In May, the company said it had a "non-binding 'notice to proceed' with a hyperscale customer" for up to $600 million which the company said is not related to the Amazon agreement. In July, Generac said net sales had increased 11% in the second quarter to $1.17 billion compared to last year at $1.06 billion. The commercial and industrial segment sales increased 29% to $556 million compared to $431 million at this point in 2025. Generac is well known for its residential home generators, a business line that is very dependent on weather and power outages. In the second quarter, Generac reported residential sales were down 2% to $617 million. The company reported a profit of $43 million in the quarter. Residential sales have been declining, data centers become a key focus In October 2025, Aaron Jagdfeld, president and CEO of Generac said of the summer weather season: "It was a crappy season, I mean, let's be honest. The weather was really nice everywhere," Jagdfeld said at the time. "We plan the business around normal baseline outage, and we got nowhere near normal." At this time last year, sales of residential products decreased 13% to $627 million as compared to $723 million in 2024.

artigo.texto: Nova York concede 950MW no primeiro leilão de armazenamento de energia em larga escala O primeiro processo competitivo de Nova York para armazenamento de energia em escala de concessionária resultou em 950MW de propostas selecionadas, conforme definido pela New York State Energy Research and Development Agency (NYSERDA). Por meio da primeira de três solicitações anuais de propostas (RfPs) previstas até 2027 — cada uma com o objetivo de um gigawatt em ativos de armazenamento em larga escala conectados à rede —,a NYSERDA selecionou oito projetos. As propostas vencedoras foram divulgadas em 23 de setembro, junto com os resultados da solicitação de energia renovável terrestre de 2025 da NYSERDA, que concedeu contratos a 13 projetos, totalizando 719MW de capacidade de geração. Na terminologia estadual, Em Larga Escala designa recursos de armazenamento de grande porte na frente do medidor (FTM) com potência superior a 5MW, enquanto as categorias atrás do medidor (BTM) são atendidas por iniciativas de apoio distintas nos segmentos Residencial e Varejo (comercial e industrial). As inscrições para a RfP de Armazenamento de Energia em Larga Escala foram aceitas a partir de julho de 2025, representando o marco mais recente do longo esforço do Estado de Nova York para ampliar a implantação de armazenamento de grande porte, principalmente novas instalações de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS). A New York Public Service Commission (PSC) havia determinado que a NYSERDA criasse o programa no âmbito do Roteiro de Armazenamento de Energia 2.0 do estado. O roteiro de 2024 traçou o caminho de Nova York rumo à sua ambiciosa meta de política de armazenamento de 6GW até 2030, sucedendo o Roteiro 1.0, de 2018, que introduziu mecanismos de apoio bem-sucedidos nas implantações Residenciais e de Varejo, mas com resultados menores no segmento de Larga Escala. Diversos fatores foram identificados para a adoção lenta do BESS em escala de concessionária em Nova York, com destaque para o desenho do mercado atacadista do operador da rede NYISO, que impede as receitas de mercado disponíveis em mercados de eletricidade mais voláteis, como o ERCOT, no Texas, por exemplo. Observadores do setor haviam notado que isso efetivamente criava um problema de receita ausente para os desenvolvedores em Nova York. O novo programa se baseia em um instrumento contratual conhecido como Crédito de Armazenamento Indexado, por meio do qual a NYSERDA estabelece um preço de exercício garantido para a injeção de energia armazenada nos mercados da NYISO. Caso um projeto gere mais do que o preço de exercício, os participantes devolvem o excedente; caso as receitas caiam abaixo do preço de exercício, a NYSERDA fornece um complemento. Essa abordagem visa oferecer previsibilidade de receita a desenvolvedores e investidores, sem onerar financeiramente os contribuintes de Nova York. Os desembolsos começam após os projetos entrarem em operação comercial. A expectativa é que os projetos estejam operacionais até o fim de 2030. Um elemento das solicitações provavelmente sob observação atenta em todo o mundo é a abordagem de Nova York para lidar com preocupações de segurança contra incêndio no armazenamento em baterias. Em 2023, a governadora Kathy Hochul criou o New York State Inter-Agency Fire Safety Working Group em resposta a preocupações de moradores e comunidades, e modificações no Código de Incêndio de Nova York foram implementadas um ano depois, seguindo as recomendações do grupo. Esses códigos atualizados foram incorporados à solicitação de Armazenamento de Energia em Larga Escala. A NYSERDA não vinculou nomes de desenvolvedores ao anúncio do portfólio contratado, portanto parte dos detalhes a seguir decorre de apuração do Energy-Storage.news. Parece que os desenvolvedores Flatiron, Key Capture Energy e Grid Connected Infrastructure (GCI) garantiram contratos para dois projetos de BESS cada um, enquanto Savion e Zenobe obtiveram um projeto cada. William Acker, diretor executivo da associação comercial e aceleradora de tecnologia NY-BEST, comentou que Nova York acabara de dar um passo significativo rumo à rede acessível e confiável de que o estado precisa. Ele afirmou que a NY-BEST parabenizou a governadora Hochul e a NYSERDA por esse marco crucial na primeira aquisição de armazenamento de energia em larga escala do estado, observando que esses projetos reforçariam a rede, reduziriam custos e ajudariam a atender à crescente demanda de eletricidade de Nova York. artigo.texto: BYD Teases Shark Pickup China Launch After Selling 29,997 Units Overseas In this article (9) BYD began promoting the domestic launch of its Shark plug-in hybrid pickup truck on September 24, after selling 29,997 units across international markets in the first eight months of 2026. The carmaker released official promotional images across its social media channels under the slogan “The overseas champion returns,” assigning the model to its specialized Fang Cheng Bao sub-brand. The campaign follows two years of sales abroad, reversing the standard practice among Chinese vehicle manufacturers of establishing domestic volume before attempting foreign distribution. Export track record and platform specifications Overseas deliveries of the Shark reached 4,300 units in August alone. BYD first introduced the pickup in Mexico in May 2024, followed by rollouts in Australia, Brazil, Cambodia and Pakistan. Built on the company’s off-road dual-mode platform, the truck pairs a 1.5-litre turbocharged petrol engine with two electric motors. Regulatory filings published by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology in July show peak motor outputs of 170 kW at the front axle and 150 kW at the rear. Retail buyers in China have historically treated pickups as commercial workhorses rather than lifestyle vehicles, constrained by municipal traffic bans that restrict light trucks from entering major downtown cores. Those regulatory limits keep the overall category small relative to passenger cars. Electrified pickup sales climbed 18 per cent year on year to 62,000 units through August. artigo.texto: New Hanover County leaders question data center rules amid AI boom WILMINGTON, N.C. (WECT) - New Hanover County leaders are reconsidering how local development rules handle massive data centers as growing demand for artificial intelligence and cloud computing puts pressure on land and power grids across North Carolina. County commissioners held an informational work session to review whether existing ordinances can adequately manage large-scale or “hyperscale” computing campuses. While the board took no formal vote and did not enact a moratorium, members clearly signaled they want more direct oversight before any major projects move forward. County staff told commissioners that county rules have defined data centers as an industrial use since 2020. Under current regulations, facilities are permitted by right in four zoning districts: commercial service, airport commerce, light industrial and heavy industrial. That broad definition allows projects to receive staff-level administrative approval without public hearings or commissioner review, applying whether a site houses an existing business’s small server room or a sprawling computing campus. Commissioners repeatedly questioned whether New Hanover County, one of the state’s smallest and most densely populated counties, can handle the resource-heavy footprint of large facilities, citing power grid demands, water use for cooling and equipment noise. Several board members voiced concern over the lack of elected oversight under the current by-right setup. “I would hate for our hands to be bound and unable to take any sort of action that is appropriate for our community and have to say, ‘Sorry, we don’t have any authority here. This is entirely a staff-driven process,’” Commissioner Dane Scalise said during the discussion. “I’d like to explore what returning some of a decision like this back to the elected body might look like.” Staff noted that while vacant industrial parcels are limited, a developer could assemble acreage by purchasing and demolishing existing structures. The board also pointed to neighboring jurisdictions that have moved to pause or restrict facilities while reevaluating their policies. “Let’s assume that we do have one piece [of land], and if there’s an application that’s put on the table and we’re not prepared for it, that’s a problem,” Commissioner LeAnn Pierce noted. “I think I hear the commissioners saying they would like to have some say-so in a possible application. Maybe we never get one, but we should plan for that scenario.” Commissioners emphasized the need to balance community protections with local employers’ operational needs, cautioning against drafting rules so rigid that established manufacturers face hurdles expanding internal IT infrastructure. Staff cautioned that the county cannot simply enact a blanket ban on large data centers. While a special-use permit process offers conditional paths to approval, commissioners discussed conditional rezoning as another tool to ensure public input and give the board greater discretion. County planning staff will study policy alternatives, including updating zoning districts, ending by-right approvals for commercial-scale facilities, and drafting performance standards for noise and natural resource protections before returning to commissioners for formal action. artigo.texto: New data center development in Pima County is paused for 120 days after a narrow Board of Supervisors vote Tuesday. The moratorium passed in a 3-2 vote, with Supervisors Rex Scott and Steve Christy voting against the pause. The county resolution states data centers produce “imminent negative public health impacts,” and argues the four-month pause is needed to iron out sections of the county’s zoning codes to encourage more sustainable development. The moratorium only applies to companies or developers who have not yet submitted permit applications for site improvements like grading, paving, flood control, or construction. Supervisor Matt Heinz moved to change the moratorium cutoff from when the permit is issued to when a developer applies for one. Projects with applications already pending are exempt from the pause. The language change came after the board met in executive session for over an hour with Pima County Attorney Laura Conover for legal counsel. People are also reading… The land for the proposed Project Gravel, an eight-building data center that could encompass 160 acres near Sahuarita, has been under review by contractors since Aug. 2025, according to traffic studies, hydrologic data sheets, watershed maps, cultural resource inventories, and other assessments the Star received through a public records request. Reed Spurling, a member of the No Desert Data Center Coalition, said the moratorium was a step in the right direction shortly after Tuesday night’s vote. “I’m really happy that they passed this temporary moratorium on data centers…we want to see this strengthened into a ban ultimately, so that this is not a temporary prohibition, but a permanent prohibition,” they said. Besides the moratorium, the county has been working on making permanent code changes that would impose stricter development standards for data center developers. They are currently accepting public feedback on the proposed changes. Last month, the Pima County health department also released its Data Center Public Health Review, a report of existing knowledge of how data centers can impact public health from pollution, excess heat, dust, and noise, among others. Board Chair Jen Allen said the moratorium, the Health Department’s report and the code amendment process were “three legs of a stool.” “We need time, so that we are not making land use decisions without understanding the full consequences on public health. And public health is one of those statutorily defined roles of Pima County,” she said. The moratorium language reads that Pima County has existing vulnerabilities in respiratory and cardiovascular health compared to the rest of the state, and a proximity to data centers has the potential to exacerbate these conditions, which is a broad summary of the Data Center Public Health Review. Scott said he voted against the moratorium for legal reasons. “I cannot comment publicly on the content of said counsel because it came to us in an attorney-client privilege communication,” he said. Scott also said the portion of the moratorium that relied on the Data Center Public Health Review “paints with far too broad a brush.” “The review was clearly not completed to provide justification for this resolution, nor does it provide an evaluation of any specific project. Although I appreciate the completion of the review and see its utility moving forward, it is merely a framework that will only be effective or useful if it is employed in conjunction with criteria specific to any development proposal that may come before us,” he said. Scott highlighted the limitations of the review, mainly the lack of localized scientific studies on health impacts in communities near data centers. These largely do not exist yet, Pima County Health Department Director Dr. Theresa Cullen previously told the Star, because the technology is so new. Most studies have been targeted towards the environmental impacts of data centers instead of health, the review reads. Allen then told Scott she agreed the public health review was a framework, but pushed back on his claim that the framework could only be helpful with a specific proposal. “The moratorium is a means to ensure…our code text amendment, our zoning, is as strong as possible ... and indeed takes to heart the issues that were outlined by the health department,” she said. Supervisor Andrés Cano said the county has a public health responsibility to understand the health department’s findings in his vote for the moratorium. “I support our county setting clear standards so that if and when these projects come to Pima County, these standards will protect our natural resources, our neighborhoods, and the people who already live here, and that is what this temporary pause allows us to do,” he said. In two last-minute amendments, the board also added the ability to bring back the moratorium discussion before the end of 120 days for possible extension, and directed the Health Department to continue to collect data on data center public health impacts and create a risk assessment.

artigo.texto: Google data center could generate billions, add jobs, and new households EVANS, Ga. (WRDW/WAGT) - A new study released by the Columbia County Economic Development Authority projects the Google data center campus under construction off Interstate 20 could generate $4 billion over 35 years for the county. The study says money spent on items such as property taxes and spending by people moving to the area for the data center could total $4 billion over 35 years. Deal calls for Google to help pay for Vogtle upgrades Georgia Power struck a deal with Google for the tech giant to help fund upgrades at Plant Vogtle and the state’s other nuclear generating plant. The study also projects the project could create 1,600 new jobs, 472 new local households and 307 new students in the Columbia County School System. The Development Authority said the job and household figures are based on research of other, similar facilities. The data center campus covers 3,358 acres of land off I-20’s exit in Appling. Construction is underway, with full completion still years away. The land currently generates $22,000 a year in taxes for the county and schools. The county’s projected tax revenue from the site is $12 billion. The study was produced by a third party and released by the Development Authority on the County’s data center project website (https://roadtorelief-columbiagagis.hub.arcgis.com). Google has signed a $280 million deal with Columbia County. The money will be paid to the county over seven years and will fund homestead property tax relief for people living in Columbia County before construction finishes. The tax break would start in the first year if voters approve it this November. If approved, homeowners would receive an $18,000 credit for each home. The county is lobbying Georgia lawmakers to amend a cap that would allow a full property tax credit in the future. Copyright 2026 WRDW/WAGT. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: ‘Overwhelmed with misinformation’: What data centers mean for the environment LANSING, Mich. (News 10) - Michigan State University’s Institute for Public Policy and Social Research held a conversation Tuesday to discuss common misconceptions about data centers, including their impact on the state’s electrical grid. Dr. Erik Nordman, director of the Institute of Public Utilities at Michigan State University, said a more reliable electricity system benefits everyone. “If the electricity system is more reliable, we’re all going to benefit from that,” Nordman said. Many people have voiced concerns about water usage, but experts at MSU said developers hear those concerns. “Most data centers that are being built today are trying to conserve water because they see the controversies happening around water and they want to be responsible developers,” said Jean Hardy, associate director of the Quello Center at Michigan State University. However, Hardy said not every facility is being developed that way. “For example, the Google data center being proposed in Van Buren Township is supposed to use, I believe, upwards of two million gallons of water a day,” Hardy said. Across the street from the conversation, at the Capitol, environmental groups held their own conference urging for more transparency and seats at the table. “[We’re hearing] Sam Altman, Elon Musk are saying ‘we need to slow down AI ’; we’re seeing [the Michigan Economic Development Corporation] saying that they’re not going to provide any transparency for these tax breaks. Every week it seems like new information comes out on the dangers of AI technology,” said Marta Johnson, Legislative and Political Organizer at the Sierra Club Michigan. Environmental groups, including the Sierra Club of Michigan and Clean Water Action, said regulation is increasingly needed but isn’t happening. That’s why they say more seats are needed at the table. “Because we listen to the communities that are a part of our network...We’ve been hearing from them for a year and a half now. They’re just really concerned; they’re overwhelmed with misinformation. They don’t know what information to trust,” Amanda Robert, Network Director for Michigan Climate Action Network. They also said they are skeptical of claims that some data center developers are responsible. “If responsible data center owners exist, they shouldn’t be worried about real strong protections that are codified into law, enforceable, hold people accountable, because if they’re already doing that, what’s the problem with having those protections in place?” said Nichole Keway Biber, a Water Justice Manager with Clean Water Action. A instalação contará com 600 MW de potência e capacidade de 2,4 GWh, prometendo otimizar o sistema elétrico do país ao armazenar energia durante os picos de produção renovável e distribuí-la conforme a procura, refere a energética em comunicado. A BYD Energy Storage fornecerá as baterias, compondo um sistema de 210 contentores de baterias e 105 de transformadores. O objetivo é "colocar Siedlce em operação até ao final de 2027”, afirma Weronika Nowak, CEO da Greenvolt Power, também citada no mesmo comunicado. Além de Siedlce, a empresa já opera um projeto em Turośń Kościelna e prepara-se para lançar outro em Ełk, ambos com capacidades de 200 MW/800 MWh. Juntas, estas iniciativas representarão um total de 1 GW de potência e 4 GWh de armazenamento, reforçando a presença da Greenvolt no setor energético polaco.

artigo.texto: The US installed 5.4 GW/18.9 GWh of battery energy storage systems in the second quarter of 2026, setting a new quarterly record in terms of energy capacity. According to the latest US Energy Storage Monitor, released by the American Clean Power Association (ACP) and Wood Mackenzie, GWh deployments increased 17% year-on-year, despite a 7% decline in newly installed power capacity, measured in GW, compared with the same quarter of 2025. The divergence between the two figures largely reflects the deployment of battery systems capable of storing energy for longer periods. The national average duration of newly installed battery storage systems increased from 2.8 hours in Q2 2025 to 3.5 hours a year later, driven by growing resource adequacy needs. Utility-scale storage accounts for 17.6 GWh The utility-scale segment continued to account for the vast majority of new capacity, with 4.7 GW/17.6 GWh deployed during the second quarter. In power terms, utility-scale installations declined 8% year-on-year as some key markets became increasingly saturated. However, deployments during the first half of 2026 were 5% higher than in the same period of 2025. Average project duration continued to increase during the quarter, partly driven by a long-duration storage project in California designed to support state targets and utility-contracted storage assets deployed in Texas. “Battery storage is one of the most important tools we have to meet growing electricity demand,” said John Hensley, Senior Vice President of Markets and Policy Analysis at American Clean Power. Hensley highlighted storage’s ability to be deployed quickly, strengthen grid reliability and enable the power system to make better use of both existing and new generation. Residential storage installs 676 MW The residential segment recorded its fourth-largest quarter on record, with 676 MW installed. This represented a 15% decline from the previous quarter but a 3% increase year-on-year. California, Texas, Puerto Rico, Arizona and Illinois collectively accounted for 88% of residential storage capacity installed in Q2, although all five markets recorded quarter-on-quarter declines. Puerto Rico posted the largest decline in absolute terms, falling from 129 MW in Q1 to 73 MW in Q2. Meanwhile, the national residential solar-plus-storage attachment rate reached 46%, up from 41% in the second quarter of 2025. Despite these figures, ACP and Wood Mackenzie expect the US residential storage market to contract by 4% in 2026, amid the elimination of tax credits, consumer hesitancy and a challenging transition toward third-party ownership models. Commercial and industrial segment installs 48 MW The community, commercial and industrial (CCI) segment deployed 48 MW during the quarter, returning to historical deployment levels following California’s record first quarter, which was driven by the deadline to qualify under the state’s Net Energy Metering 2.0 framework. Overall, the segment declined 2% year-on-year, although above-average growth in Hawaii, New Mexico and Texas helped offset some of the contraction. US storage capacity could reach 207 GW/715 GWh by 2031 The outlook points to strong expansion over the next five years. ACP and Wood Mackenzie expect annual US energy storage installations to grow by more than 50% in MW terms over that period. Under the forecast, cumulative installed storage capacity in the country would reach 207 GW/715 GWh by 2031. One of the main drivers will be rapidly increasing electricity demand from data centers. Wood Mackenzie expects utility-scale storage to grow at an average annual rate of 8% over the next five years. “Data center buildout strengthens the US storage outlook across all sectors,” said Allison Feeney, research analyst at Wood Mackenzie. According to Feeney, as hyperscalers face increasing grid-connection bottlenecks, utility-scale storage can provide faster access to the power capacity required by data centers. The CCI segment is projected to grow 27% between 2026 and 2031, supported by deployment expanding beyond California into emerging markets such as Maryland and Texas. The residential market is also expected to rebound from 2027 and grow at an average annual rate of 9% through 2031. Utility-scale battery system prices fall 2% The report also points to declining costs. Utility-scale battery system prices fell 2% year-on-year to $916/kW in the second quarter of 2026. At the same time, the share of hybrid utility-scale installations declined to 33%, down from 45% in Q2 2025, mainly due to a contraction in the California market. Supply chain dynamics remain a key source of uncertainty. Potential trade restrictions could create near-term bottlenecks and lead to some stagnation in the utility-scale segment during 2026 and 2027. Wood Mackenzie nevertheless expects growth to resume in 2028 and average 11% annually through 2031, supported by the expansion of domestic battery cell manufacturing. Against this backdrop, slowing electric vehicle demand is providing an unexpected boost to stationary storage. Allison Weis, Global Head of Energy Storage at Wood Mackenzie, said manufacturers are repurposing idle EV cell production capacity, helping accelerate the development of the domestic storage supply chain.

artigo.texto: Revera Energy Reaches Financial Close on 400 MW Hunterston Battery Storage Backed by Carlyle, Revera Energy has closed financing on its second UK battery storage project of 2026, targeting commercial operations in the third quarter of 2028. Revera Energy, a global independent energy platform backed by investment firm Carlyle, has announced the completion of project financing for its second UK battery storage site of 2026. The Hunterston Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), with a capacity of 400 megawatts (MW) and 800 megawatt-hours (MWh), is located in North Ayrshire, Scotland, approximately 50 kilometers southwest of Glasgow. Alongside the financial close, Revera Energy issued a notice to proceed (NTP) authorizing immediate commencement of construction, with commercial operations expected in the third quarter of 2028. This step follows the final investment decision announced in June 2026. A Project Positioned at a Grid Bottleneck The Hunterston site is described by the company as located north of the B6 boundary, one of the most persistent congestion points on the UK power grid. According to Revera Energy, the project is intended to contribute to grid resilience and help unlock the transmission bottleneck separating Scottish wind generation from electricity demand in England, as part of the UK government's Clean Power 2030 Action Plan. This grid connectivity challenge echoes issues seen elsewhere in Europe, where Germany is relying on smart storage to absorb more solar capacity. Revera Energy states it continues to pursue its strategy as a BESS developer, owner and operator in the UK. Top-Tier Financial and Industrial Partners Non-recourse senior debt financing for the project is being provided by Santander, Barclays, Commonwealth Bank of Australia and NatWest, according to the company's statement. Sungrow will supply the battery system along with a long-term service agreement, while OCU Group has been engaged as the Balance of Plant contractor, covering auxiliary site equipment, and as operations and maintenance provider. Danske Commodities and bp will provide trading and optimization services for the project, with bp establishing a long-term tolling structure and Danske Commodities a long-term floor structure. Revera Energy will retain oversight of construction and long-term asset management. Company Carlyle: company profile CG "We are delighted to complete the financing for Hunterston BESS, a key milestone that enables the construction of this critical project," said Ron Kiecana, Acting Head of Revera UK, as quoted in the statement. Sam Lewis, Senior Project Manager on Hunterston BESS, in turn highlighted the team's ability to identify quality projects, secure top-tier supply chain relationships and unlock financing within what the company described as an impressively short period. An Expanding Portfolio in the UK and Australia Hunterston BESS is Revera Energy's second UK transmission-connected battery storage project to reach financial close in 2026. The Windyhill BESS (200 MW / 400 MWh) is progressing through construction, with commercial operations targeted for the fourth quarter of 2027. The company also holds up to 400 MW / 1,600 MWh of additional capacity with approved planning consents, land rights, grid access through the NESO Gate 2 process run by grid operator National Energy System Operator, and 15-year capacity market contracts, with construction proposed to begin in the coming months. This combination of renewable generation and storage is also found in other European projects, such as the 98 MW wind-storage energy park developed by PNE and ENERCON in Germany. With up to 1 gigawatt (GW) / 2.8 gigawatt-hours (GWh) targeted, Revera Energy's UK BESS portfolio would become, according to the company, one of the largest such platforms in Europe. In Australia, Revera Energy's battery storage portfolio continues its progress. Stage 1 of the Bungama BESS (150 MW / 300 MWh) began commercial operations in the second quarter of 2026. The company is now accelerating its 1,000 MW battery storage portfolio in Australia, with Stage 1 of the Robertstown BESS project expected to reach financial close in the fourth quarter of 2026. The battery storage sector continues to attract significant financing globally, as illustrated by the 1.4 billion dollar amount secured by Jupiter Power for ten storage projects. - Gas45.5 % - Coal15.4 % - Nuclear15.2 % - Solar10.9 % - Wind7.3 % - Hydro4.2 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.3 %
