artigo.texto: Marisa Wanzeller, Lais Carregosa e Geraldo Campos Jr., da Agência iNFRA O diretor-geral da ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica), Sandoval Feitosa, propôs uma regra de transição na Pnast (Política Nacional de Acesso ao Sistema de Transmissão) para atender cargas como data centers. A proposta teria alcance até 2029 e beneficiaria os centros de processamento de dados que têm implementação por etapas, o que levaria ao aumento do consumo de energia nos próximos anos. Conforme voto-vista apresentado nesta quinta-feira (24), o ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico) deverá priorizar, no acesso ao sistema de transmissão de energia, os empreendimentos que já tinham parecer positivo de viabilidade técnica emitido antes das novas regras, que começaram a valer em dezembro de 2025. Sandoval argumenta que o decreto que criou a Pnast, ao ter vigência imediata, impediu a “adoção de providências prévias” por consumidores como data centers, que têm previsão de acesso escalonada à carga. Ou seja, aqueles que já tinham acesso ao sistema e estavam aumentando o seu montante de uso de energia ano a ano teriam sido prejudicados pela criação da política, que substituiu a análise dos pedidos de forma cronológica pelas Temporadas de Acesso. O processo era relatado pelo ex-diretor Fernando Mosna, que apresentou voto em julho deste ano, quando Sandoval pediu vista. O assunto está na pauta do circuito deliberativo da ANEEL, marcado para terça-feira (29). Se aprovado, será iniciada consulta pública de 45 dias.

artigo.texto: Geraldo Campos Jr., da Agência iNFRA Um estudo da Volt Robotics apontou que as usinas hidrelétricas tendem a ser mais beneficiadas pela contratação de baterias no sistema elétrico do que as fontes eólica e solar. O trabalho, apresentado nesta terça-feira (22) durante o evento Encontro Técnico Armazenamento 2030, indicou que 88% da energia a ser usada para carregar as baterias viria de plantas renováveis, sendo a maioria por meio da redução do vertimento turbinável das hídricas. Segundo números apresentados pelo CEO da Volt, Donato Filho, a redução do vertimento turbinável por causa das baterias traria ganhos de 66% para as hidrelétricas, que ainda teriam um incremento da geração da ordem de 18%. Isso reduziria também o risco hidrológico, o que tem efeito sobre os consumidores. Já o efeito projetado das baterias sobre a redução do curtailment de eólicas e solares seria de 16%. Considerando os cortes entre 2024 e 2026, até o primeiro semestre, o ganho com a entrada das baterias seria de R$ 2,7 bilhões para hídricas e renováveis. Durante o evento, realizado em Brasília pela Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia), Donato Filho explicou que o benefício maior das hídricas se deve ao fato de que a parcela que sofre com o vertimento turbinável é bem maior que a dos cortes de eólica e solar. No entanto, tudo dependerá da ordem de cortes a ser definida pela ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) na CP (Consulta Pública) 45/2019. “Com as baterias sendo carregadas, de manhã vai aumentar a carga. Então vai ter que ter uma decisão sobre quem vai ser cortado menos. Que é a regra para alocar o corte que está em discussão na CP 45”, disse Donato, que continuou: “No estudo, a gente aplicou uma regra proporcional à potência que está sendo disponibilizada pelas fontes, e, como as hídricas são bem maiores, elas acabam sendo mais usadas para alimentar as baterias”. Além disso, o armazenamento poderá reduzir em cerca de R$ 630 milhões por ano o montante de encargos hoje repassados aos consumidores, conforme o estudo. Isso porque os sistemas ajudariam a baixar alguns dos encargos existentes hoje, sobretudo pelo menor uso de térmicas, menor restrição da geração e redução do deslocamento hídrico. Ainda segundo o estudo, a receita fixa das baterias deve ficar de 38% a 64% menor que a média do LRCAP (Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência) que contratou térmicas, realizado em março. Custeio O estudo abordou ainda o encargo de remuneração das baterias, cujo modelo de pagamento – que conforme a lei, será rateado entre os geradores – está em discussão na ANEEL. De acordo com a Volt, parte do custo pode ser repassada integralmente ao consumidor por causa de uma cláusula existente em contratos de geração do ambiente regulado que prevê que novos tributos e encargos criados após o leilão serão repassados para a tarifa. Donato explicou, no entanto, que parte expressiva da capacidade instalada das fontes com vendas no ambiente regulado tem esse modelo de contrato e, por isso, não pagariam o encargo – repassando ao consumidor integralmente. Pelo estudo, 100% das térmicas do ambiente regulado têm em seus contratos essa cláusula. Nas usinas a biomassa, isso se aplica a 80%. Para eólica, o modelo existe em 60% do parque, e, na solar centralizada, 30%.

artigo.texto: Os planos de governo de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), Ronaldo Caiado (PSD), Romeu Zema (Novo) e Renan Santos (Missão) defendem, cada um a seu modo, incentivos à instalação ou expansão de data centers no Brasil. Em uma eleição marcada pela polarização, há uma espécie de consenso, ainda que limitado, sobre o tema entre os principais candidatos. As propostas, porém, diferem quanto ao papel do Estado, à atração de empresas estrangeiras e às exigências ambientais. O que cada plano propõe? Lula associa data centers à soberania digital, com infraestrutura computacional nacional, serviços de nuvem e supercomputadores desenvolvidos no país. Em agosto, ele anunciou em Macaíba (RN) um supercomputador de IA orçado em R$ 1 bilhão. Flávio Bolsonaro propõe transformar o país em um hub global de data centers sustentáveis, aproveitando a matriz energética renovável. Romeu Zema defende usar a energia limpa e competitiva do Brasil para atrair indústrias intensivas em energia, IA e data centers. Zema também promete evitar regulamentação precoce e ampla da inteligência artificial, aplicando regras pontuais só onde houver dano comprovado. Caiado inclui incentivo a data centers no programa, com menos detalhamento público que os outros dois. O que falta nos planos, segundo especialistas? Especialistas ouvidos pela BBC News Brasil afirmam que a expansão de data centers pode ajudar o país a desenvolver capacidade tecnológica, mas não produz automaticamente a chamada soberania digital. Para eles, os planos ainda não explicam um ponto central. Os especialistas dizem que os candidatos ainda precisam esclarecer que tipo de data center pretendem atrair, quais benefícios ficam no Brasil e quem paga os custos de energia, água e infraestrutura. Nenhum plano detalha esses pontos. O consenso sobre atrair data centers não significa consenso sobre quem banca a conta de energia e água que essas instalações consomem. Só três dos cinco planos trazem proposta específica de regulamentação da inteligência artificial: os de Lula, Caiado e Zema, cada um com um modelo distinto. Flávio Bolsonaro e Renan Santos preveem o uso da tecnologia, mas não estabelecem regras específicas para o setor.

artigo.texto: CATL has officially begun trial production at its newly built battery cell factory in Debrecen, Hungary, marking a major milestone for the company’s European manufacturing expansion. The trial run started on September 22, 2026, after CATL completed all the required conditions and obtained the necessary permits to begin operations. The initial trial production covers the first two cell manufacturing lines at the facility. The purpose of the trial phase is to set up, optimize and validate the factory’s production equipment and manufacturing processes before series production begins. CATL said it will continue working closely with the Hungarian government and local authorities throughout the trial period, with particular attention to environmental protection, employee health and workplace safety. CATL announced plans for its second European battery plant in Debrecen in August 2022. The facility was designed to strengthen the company’s position in Europe’s automotive and electric mobility supply chain while allowing it to better serve major European automakers. Construction of the first cell manufacturing building began in summer 2023. By spring 2026, the building had been equipped with what CATL describes as advanced manufacturing technology. The company received the facility’s occupancy permit in August 2026 and subsequently completed the remaining requirements associated with its Integrated Pollution Prevention and Control (IPPC) permit. Those steps cleared the way for trial operations to begin on September 22. Before the occupancy permit was issued, the Hajdú-Bihar County Government Office carried out regular inspections at CATL’s facilities. The inspections followed earlier concerns raised during the permitting process. According to the authorities, CATL had addressed the deficiencies previously identified. Once fully operational, the Debrecen facility is expected to become CATL’s largest manufacturing site outside China, with planned annual battery cell production capacity of 100 GWh. The factory is strategically located within Hungary’s growing automotive manufacturing network. Several major automakers have established significant electric vehicle production capacity in the country, creating increasing demand for locally produced batteries. CATL says the Debrecen plant uses flexible production lines designed to accommodate the requirements of its automotive customers. The company has already been producing battery modules at the Debrecen site since autumn 2024. CATL says the facility has produced approximately 537,000 battery modules to date. The transition to cell production represents the next major stage in the development of the Hungarian factory and could further integrate CATL into Europe’s rapidly expanding EV battery supply chain. CATL says environmental protection, employee health and workplace safety will remain key priorities during the trial production phase. The company plans to closely monitor health, safety and environmental factors throughout the initial operations and proactively submit the results to the relevant authorities. CATL also said it remains committed to transparency and welcomes inspections by government and regulatory authorities at the Debrecen site. The start of trial production represents an important step toward full-scale battery cell manufacturing in Hungary. For CATL, the Debrecen facility is intended to strengthen its European production footprint, while for Hungary it further expands the country’s role in the continent’s electric vehicle and battery manufacturing ecosystem. [source: CATL]

artigo.texto: Congress did not vote up-or-down on giving data center operators a $68 billion tax break, despite that claim in an ad targeting U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany. Tiffany, a northern Wisconsin Republican, is running for governor in the Nov. 3 election. The ad from a Democratic Governors Association-backed group cites Tiffany’s 2025 vote for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. A yes vote on the nearly 900-page federal budget package, filled with hundreds of tax breaks and spending cuts, was not necessarily a yes vote for any single provision. A left-leaning think tank said four tech companies — Microsoft, Meta, Alphabet and Amazon — avoided $68 billion in 2025 taxes from the depreciation and three other tax breaks in the bill. artigo.texto: AI data centers are fueling a growing shortage of skilled construction workers, driving up costs and potentially slowing construction of homes and businesses. In a 2026 survey from the Associated General Contractors of America (AGC) and the National Center for Construction Education and Research (NCCER), 58% of construction firms say data center projects are increasing competition for workers. Another 36% say data centers are making job openings harder to fill, and nearly half say they are feeling pressure to raise wages. Fraser Patterson, founder and CEO of Skillit, a platform that connects skilled tradespeople with contractors, says data centers are competing for many of the same workers needed to build homes, offices and other major projects. "America is suddenly trying to build essentially an enormous amount of infrastructure all at the same time," Patterson said. RELATED STORY | Community debates over data centers boiling over into arrests, reported threats Patterson says five trades account for 54% of the labor demand on his platform. They are the same five trades most needed for data centers: carpenters, electricians, heavy equipment operators, concrete workers, and general labor. Skillit research shows data center jobs pay a premium, with wages about 32% higher than other construction projects. "You're talking about something like $30 an hour becoming maybe $40 an hour on average," Patterson said. Patterson says those higher labor costs could eventually reach consumers through more expensive homes and other building projects. "Those attracting all these electricians and the plumbers and trades, the construction costs are going to rise. It's very hard to pull them away from these lucrative projects," Patterson said. RELATED STORY | Congress moves to shield consumers from AI data center power bills For workers who have those skills, Patterson sees an upside. Beyond higher salaries, he says most data center construction offers safer working environments and workforce development opportunities. "It's a real career-building opportunity as well," Patterson said. Data centers have already faced criticism for consuming massive amounts of electricity and water. California's governor recently signed bills targeting the fast-growing industry. Contractors say data centers aren't the only reason for labor shortages — some also point to immigration enforcement and higher material costs as additional pressures on construction projects.

artigo.texto: OPINION: How I learned to stop worrying and love data centers If we're not careful, an actual policy discussion might break out amid the political absurdity saturating our news feeds. Considering the crazed, unhinged and outrageous state of modern politics, the fact that data centers — and the nuanced public policy surrounding them — have somehow taken center stage in Nevada's gubernatorial race is actually quite refreshing. To be sure, not all the rhetoric surrounding this issue is as well thought out as it should be. For example, there seems to be a growing contingent of voters (and lawmakers) who seemingly want every planned data center project to be permanently banned from now until the end of time throughout the known universe and beyond. Others simply don't want them anywhere near their homes. However, such NIMBY prohibitionist attitudes probably aren't practical in the long run — at least not if we want to carry on happily in our wondrous age of technological advancement. The truth is that data centers are like any other major infrastructure project. From giant dams built to contain seasonal floods to power lines that keep electricity flowing to our homes, they're merely a component of what it takes to keep our civilized society moving forward. Far from merely being a way to power AI slop, these centers power the technological world most of us take for granted. Uploading a picture to your Google Drive? Listening to a song on Spotify? Maybe OneDrive just backed up that project you're completing for a client. All these things depend on data centers to perform the marvel of modern cloud computing — which means virtually everything we do online or on most of our smartphones requires some warehouse to be built somewhere full of RAM to keep our digital era functioning well. The question isn't whether we should build them, because at the end of the day we have to. Instead, the questions should be where do we build them and what guardrails should be erected to make sure they are not a net drain on a local community's resources. And the answer to these questions largely depends on the details of any specific project. As The Nevada Independent recently explained, not all data centers are created equal. Some use massive amounts of water to feed their evaporative cooling systems — cooling systems that the Southern Nevada Water Authority has recently banned. More efficient closed-loop systems are better, but they do still consume scarce water in the same way other large-scale projects for various industries might. Similarly, the power requirements vary greatly by center and local utilities are already trying to devise ways to protect average ratepayers from the effects of increased power requirements on the grid. In other words, data centers — just like any other infrastructure project — come with certain trade-offs and benefits for local communities. And while it's easy to only look at one side of the ledger and jump on some populist bandwagon, most legitimate concerns about these projects don't represent insurmountable challenges for the tech industry, lawmakers or local community leaders. And in some cases, more pragmatic approaches to the issue are already taking place. As the Brookings Institution noted in a recent white paper on the topic, for example, Microsoft has penned some deals that directly invest in the local community, even beyond the usual promise of a few thousand construction jobs. And virtually all the big industry players — including Meta, Microsoft and Google — are already actively working to make their water usage efficient enough to substantially contribute to a local region's long-term water sustainability goals. That's not to say that every proposed center should be automatically greenlit by regulators. But it does illustrate that sound public policy and public discussion can mitigate many of the concerns associated with such construction. And the fact that Nevada's gubernatorial race is on the verge of steering into such policy discussions is good news for our era of nonstop performative politics. Even better is the fact that some good-government reforms are already taking place as a result. Just last week, for example, Gov. Joe Lombardo (R) signed an executive order limiting the sort of tax incentives data centers can enjoy. Similarly, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford has reversed his previous support for data center tax breaks, promising to place a moratorium on such incentives if elected governor. Cynics would argue that both candidates are merely placating the public's apparent distrust of the industry — but so what? Restricting or eliminating corporate handouts for any politically connected industry should be seen as a step in the right direction, regardless of whether it was merely in response to public backlash. Indeed, of all the concerns regarding data centers, the issue of economically distortive corporate welfare being handed out to massively profitable companies is probably the lowest-hanging fruit for policymakers to pick right now. One doesn't even have to feel particularly animated about the infrastructure needed to keep our Google Drive functioning properly to get on board with a little less political cronyism. Importantly, this is the real reason a lawmaker's past support for such subsidies should be considered problematic — not merely because their stance on the issue has conveniently evolved with public opinion, but because their past support demonstrates a belief that government's job is to use our tax dollars to manipulate the economy for the benefit of those who have the best lobbyists. Unfortunately, in Nevada, that tends to be the default position for a great many lawmakers, regardless of political party. Governors, legislators and policymakers in our state routinely use the term "economic development" as a catchall excuse to redistribute wealth to politically connected corporations — whether those corporations be sports teams, Hol

A apreensão de moradores de Barão Geraldo, Alphaville e Jardim Miriam diante do projeto para a Fazenda Pau D’Alho reflete uma reação que ganha força no cenário internacional. Nos Estados Unidos, a oposição sistêmica e popular à instalação desses complexos cresce aceleradamente, movida pelo consumo vertiginoso de recursos naturais e do meio ambiente, e pela perturbação do sossego, consolidando um cenário em que ninguém quer ter um mega data center por perto. É sob esse clima de dúvidas e pressão popular que a Comissão Permanente de Meio Ambiente da Câmara Municipal de Campinas realiza, nesta quinta-feira, às 14h, uma reunião pública para debater os potenciais impactos ambientais e urbanísticos do empreendimento. O encontro, promovido pelo vereador Vagner Romão, reunirá a comunidade e autoridades para discutir os riscos microclimáticos e a demanda de recursos da estrutura. A reunião contará com a participação da secretária municipal de Urbanismo, Carolina Baracat Lazinho, e do professor Paulo José da Silva e Silva, do Departamento de Matemática Aplicada da Unicamp, que comanda a infraestrutura de processamento de dados da universidade. O debate é aberto a toda a população interessada. Alertas do Comdema e a Mata de Santa Genebra O debate na Câmara ocorre simultaneamente à pressão exercida pelo Conselho Municipal de Meio Ambiente (Comdema). Em documento publicado no Diário Oficial, o órgão requereu um parecer técnico-científico à Fundação José Pedro de Oliveira (FJPO) para avaliar os impactos do empreendimento na Zona de Amortecimento da ARIE Mata de Santa Genebra. O Comdema elencou quatro vetores de impacto críticos para a Unidade de Conservação: 1. Alteração do microclima florestal por rejeição térmica contínua; 2. Poluição sonora contínua e de baixa frequência emitida por geradores e sistemas de resfriamento; 3. Ruptura de corredores ecológicos entre a mata, a Unicamp e a Bacia do Rio Atibaia; 4. Poluição luminosa e eletromagnética na área de amortecimento. O conselho também questionou a emissão de licenças sem deliberação prévia do seu plenário e o licenciamento isolado da subestação de energia. Prefeitura nega irregularidades e destaca caráter público da subestação Procurada pela reportagem, a Prefeitura de Campinas informou que as licenças e alvarás expedidos até o momento destinam-se exclusivamente à implantação de uma subestação de energia elétrica, tendo avaliado a compatibilidade da infraestrutura viária e urbanística local. Segundo a Administração Municipal, a subestação não será de uso restrito do data center: ela atenderá também a rede elétrica de Campinas e será instalada em uma área pública que será doada ao município. A Prefeitura ressaltou que a licença atual impõe regras estritas para drenagem, terraplenagem e gestão de resíduos, garantindo que não haverá supressão de árvores nem intervenções em Áreas de Preservação Permanente (APP) sem autorização ambiental prévia. As etapas relativas à ocupação do data center em si seguem em análise multidisciplinar. Sobre o questionamento do Comdema quanto à aprovação prévia, o Executivo declarou que, segundo o Decreto Municipal nº 18.705/2015, a emissão de licenças ambientais é de competência legal da Prefeitura. A legislação prevê a participação do conselho, mas não estabelece que sua manifestação seja obrigatória antes da emissão de todas as licenças. O processo foi encaminhado ao Comdema em 18 de agosto de 2026. A Prefeitura confirmou que a equipe técnica da Fundação José Pedro de Oliveira (FJPO) já está elaborando o parecer sobre a Mata de Santa Genebra solicitado pelo COMDEMA e que aguarda a definição de data para participar da Sessão Técnica Multissetorial convocada pelo conselho.

artigo.texto: Bulgaria Leads Europe in Battery Storage as Drought Drives Export Demand Bulgaria has emerged as a regional leader in battery storage, a development that unfolded as an unprecedented drought squeezed the power industry across Eastern Europe. Close to 100 battery energy storage system facilities are currently in service nationwide, the bulk of which have been commissioned within the last two years. Storage projects repurpose industrial and power sites These sizable installations occupy disused industrial land and former airfields, while others have been folded into operating power stations, coal-fired ones among them. Stavros Papathanassiou, a professor at the National Technical University of Athens, characterized the magnitude and pace of Bulgaria's storage rollout as unmatched anywhere in Europe. Analysts credit light administrative requirements, a market open to clean energy and EU financing as factors behind the nation's front-running position in the region. The batteries soak up excess solar output and return it to the grid at times of higher demand. Drought drives up export demand This came in handy when unusually low water levels on the River Danube curtailed generation at nuclear and hydroelectric facilities across Eastern Europe, increasing the need for imported electricity. During July and August, Bulgaria, among the EU's least wealthy members, posted net electricity exports of roughly 830 gigawatt-hours per month, over double the May and June average. In July by itself, Romania took in close to half of Bulgaria's outbound electricity transfers, worth an estimated EUR74 million. Former coal plant finds new purpose At Maritsa East 3, formerly Bulgaria's second-biggest coal-fired power station, the move away from the fuel is plain to see. Constructed during the communist era with four generating units, the site cut back coal operations sharply in 2024, adapting its existing grid infrastructure for a battery installation. Vassil Shtonov, who leads Bulgaria operations for the UK-based power company ContourGlobal, explained that the substantial grid connection could be put to use, prompting the decision to retire one coal unit and hook up batteries instead. Shtonov remarked that coal has given way to batteries, calling it a case of the right place at the right time, while cautioning that Bulgaria ought to keep a minimum coal-fired reserve for harsh winters or interruptions to gas supplies. A model for the region Although Bulgaria represented roughly 9% of European battery-storage additions and about 2% of solar additions in 2025, Lennart Herrmann of the Munich-based research and consulting firm FfE said the country can act as a positive model for other European nations. Herrmann noted that properly designed incentives can pave the way for a rapid energy transition. Bulgaria's energy ministry reported that the country possessed approximately 5.7 gigawatts of operational battery-storage power capacity as of this month. In power terms, that amounts to almost a quarter of Bulgaria's total installed generation capacity and exceeds neighbouring Romania's operational battery capacity by more than fivefold. Bulgarian businesses have additionally secured contracts for close to 14 gigawatt-hours of large-scale storage, with some of that capacity already connected. The ministry stated that the goal is for storage systems to secure a lasting place in the market, adding that this needs to proceed alongside other investments, including in transmission and distribution grids. Nikola Gazdov, who heads Bulgaria's Association for Production, Storage and Trading of Electricity, traced the battery surge to a mix of circumstances rather than deliberate planning, noting that it all came about almost accidentally. Solar and wind capacity has grown quickly throughout the region, yet Bulgaria's renewable expansion has leaned heavily toward solar, generating mounting daytime surpluses. Gazdov added that in Bulgaria, major battery projects can become operational in only nine to 18 months, far quicker than many solar or wind developments. Constraints persist Battery storage technology nonetheless has its constraints. For one, cross-border grid connections with neighbouring countries can carry only a limited amount of current. For another, today's batteries can hold power only for fairly brief stretches, usually one to six hours and occasionally as many as eight, according to Herrmann of FfE. So although they can shore up the grid during a short-lived supply dip, they are no substitute for a nuclear reactor forced offline by drought. And their very success may eventually erode their profitability, since as more BESS operators purchase electricity at low prices and resell it during peak periods, the spread between the two price windows will shrink. - 1. artigo.texto: Lower Chichester Township commissioners assured residents Monday night that their voices will be heard as concern about a possible data center ripples through the community. At the monthly board meeting, officials spoke to residents about a proposed 443,000-square-foot project along Ridge Road, mostly in Trainer but with a potion in Lower Chichester. The property being marketed by Link Logistics is in the area of the Congoleum facility. On Sept. 12, Leonard B. Altieri, the attorney for the property, posted a legal notice in the Daily Times stating the developer had been given a favorable preliminary opinion for a data center in the Trainer portion of the development. Lower Chichester has issued a zoning decision that a data center is not a permitted use in the township Limited Industrial District because the township does not yet have enough information about the project. A July letter from the township zoning officer to Altieri reads that a preliminary opinion on the project at 4401 Ridge Road could not be given because “data center” is not a permitted use in the Limited Industrial District. Developers of the proposed facility are promising to engage with the community as the company explores options. Trainer officials have not publicly discussed any plans. On Friday, borough Zoning Officer Charles Remaley said “no comment” when asked about the proposed facility. The developer, Link Logistics, has not applied for a building permit in either municipality but was happy with Trainer’s preliminary opinion. “We are pleased to have received a favorable Preliminary Opinion from Trainer Borough,” a spokesperson for Link Logistics wrote Monday afternoon. “This is not a building permit; any project, should we decide to pursue, will require an application and Borough approvals.” “We regularly evaluate opportunities to enhance the property in ways that support the region’s industrial and economic growth. We appreciate the feedback we are hearing from the community, and if plans for the property move forward, transparent community engagement will be an essential part of the planning process, including engaging residents and stakeholders throughout the Borough’s full review process.” At Monday night’s meeting, residents complained of a lack of information from Trainer, with Lower Chichester officials advising them to go to that municipality to ask for the zoning report. Officials said that typically after a public announcement of a decision there is a 30-day period to appeal the decision. “We don’t have any more information than they do,” said Francis J. Catania, township solicitor. “We have no separate line of communication with Trainer borough, no plan, no conversation, no document, nothing. We don’t know, even though the property is partially in Lower Chichester Township,” he said. “Believe me we are going to be involved if this goes forward. Part of it is in Lower Chichester Township, maybe only 10 percent … and the residents who are most affected by this are all from Lower Chichester. We’ll make sure their voices are heard.” Residents also had questions about the state’s part in data centers, with Amazon investment in two data centers, one in Salem Township in northeastern Pennsylvania, and the other in Falls Township, Bucks County, along with Gov. Josh Shapiro’s executive order setting out tougher statewide requirements for data center development, called the GRID regulations. Activists are planning a public meeting to discuss the possible data center. On Wednesday night, Chester Residents Concerned for Quality Living (CRCQL), an environmental activist group, will hold a public meeting from 6 to 9 p.m. at 1405 Meetinghouse Road in Boothwyn to discuss the project and potential impacts to the community, and what residents can do. Physicians for Social Responsibility, Pennsylvania will also be speaking at the public meeting. Shapiro’s Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development, GRID, standards set out these conditions: • Requiring developers to bear the cost of all new energy infrastructure that would not have been needed “but for” the data center project. • Commitment to sourcing nearly one-third of power consumption from — or at least making equivalent investments in — “clean” energy by 2035. • New transparency standards that require identification of a project’s end user, plus key information about energy and water usage and overall project scale, plus “engagement with local residents and leaders… early enough in the process to allow meaningful public input on major design decisions.” • Community Benefit Agreements for data center host communities that go above and beyond tax revenues • Commitments to meeting certain job creation and salary benchmarks.

artigo.texto: Sustainable investment manager Mirova has committed €65m to launch its Nordic Storage Platform (NSP) alongside developer Ingrid Capacity, targeting utility-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) across the Nordic region. The Natixis Investment Managers affiliate is investing in a two-project portfolio in Finland and Sweden totaling 145MW of power capacity and 290MWh of storage capacity. Under the partnership, Ingrid Capacity will manage development, construction, technical operations and commerclial optimisation across the platform. Antoine Blayau, investment director at Mirova, said: “Battery storage is becoming a critical component of Europe’s energy infrastructure, enhancing grid flexibility, supporting renewable integration and strengthening security of supply. “This initial portfolio is underpinned by attractive market fundamentals and a resilient risk-return profile, including an offtake agreement for the Pedersöre project. We look forward to scaling the platform and supporting the development of more resilient energy systems across the Nordic region.” Axel Holmberg, CEO of Ingrid Capacity, said: “We are pleased to be Mirova’s first BESS partner in the Nordics. Strong partnerships are essential when creating value for the long term and our two institutions share the same sense of responsibility in doing so. “Both companies understand the critical role for BESS in building a better grid and European resilience. Our mission is to build Europe’s leading integrated flexibility platform. Trusted partners like French Mirova are key to that growth journey.” To read the latest IPE Real Assets magazine click here.

artigo.texto: A experiência da China com redes inteligentes, armazenamento de energia, veículos elétricos e data centers reforçou a visão positiva do Safra sobre a CPFL (CPFE3), segundo relatório divulgado pelo banco após uma viagem de analistas a Pequim e a diferentes instalações do setor elétrico chinês. Para o Safra, a expertise de longo prazo da State Grid Corporation of China (SGCC), controladora da CPFL, pode ajudar a companhia brasileira a direcionar investimentos e alocar capital diante das novas demandas do mercado de energia. O banco destaca que a SGCC considera o Brasil um mercado estratégico e vê a CPFL como uma de suas principais subsidiárias e um ativo de destaque entre seus investimentos internacionais. A percepção foi reforçada por executivos da State Grid International Development (SGID), braço responsável pelos investimentos da estatal fora da China. Segundo o relatório, 64% dos investimentos da SGID estão na América do Sul. A estratégia da controladora chinesa também pode abrir espaço para novos investimentos da CPFL em infraestrutura de distribuição. De acordo com o Safra, a SGID continua interessada em direcionar capital para o segmento e avalia oportunidades relacionadas a leilões, especialmente projetos de sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias (BESS), além de potenciais aquisições, como ativos da Enel SP, e alternativas de financiamento subsidiado. O Safra mantém recomendação neutra para CPFE3 e preço-alvo de R$ 58,70, ante cotação de R$ 45,23 considerada no relatório. O preço-alvo implica potencial de valorização de aproximadamente 30% em relação àquele nível. Para 2026, o banco projeta múltiplo EV/Ebitda de 6,4 vezes, relação preço/lucro de 10,6 vezes e dividend yield de 7,5% para a CPFL. A ação acumulava queda de 16% no ano até a data de referência do relatório, enquanto o desempenho em 12 meses era positivo em 17%. China antecipa tendências Um dos principais aprendizados da viagem, segundo o Safra, foi a escala alcançada pela China na implantação de redes inteligentes. A SGCC iniciou o processo em 2009 e chegou a uma cobertura próxima da universalização em 2024. Na província de Jiangsu, o sistema já havia sido concluído em 2014. Os medidores inteligentes utilizados pela companhia chinesa enviam informações a cada 15 minutos e permitem o uso de cerca de 90 tipos de dados. Entre as aplicações estão a identificação das áreas afetadas por interrupções no fornecimento, a otimização de preços, a detecção de falhas e o gerenciamento remoto de recursos por meio de usinas virtuais, conhecidas como VPPs. Para o Safra, essa experiência pode servir como referência para a evolução das redes elétricas brasileiras, especialmente à medida que aumenta a necessidade de administrar uma matriz mais complexa e com maior participação de fontes intermitentes. Outro destaque foi o armazenamento de energia. Os analistas visitaram a usina hidrelétrica reversível de Tianhuangping, com capacidade de 1,8 GW, que utiliza a diferença de preços entre os períodos de maior e menor demanda para armazenar energia e posteriormente devolvê-la ao sistema. O banco também chamou atenção para o avanço das baterias de brometo de zinco desenvolvidas na China. A tecnologia apresenta, segundo o relatório, maior segurança e vida útil, chegando a cerca de 13 mil ciclos, embora tenha custo superior ao das baterias de íons de lítio. Data centers: nova fronteira de demanda O crescimento dos data centers também apareceu como uma das principais tendências observadas pelos analistas. O Safra visitou o Yangzhou Big Data Industrial Park, que reúne cerca de 1 GW de capacidade distribuída em seis centros de dados. Aproximadamente 90% da estrutura está relacionada a armazenamento e 10% à inteligência artificial. O banco afirma que investimentos regionais nesse segmento podem chegar a 100 bilhões de yuans nos próximos cinco anos. Para o mercado brasileiro, a tendência é especialmente relevante diante do aumento da demanda de energia associada à expansão dos data centers no país. Na avaliação do Safra, esse movimento pode representar uma nova frente de crescimento para as empresas de infraestrutura elétrica, ao mesmo tempo em que aumenta a necessidade de investimentos em redes, capacidade de geração e soluções para gerenciamento da demanda. artigo.texto: The News Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, wants the Senate to stay in session until the body votes on his endangered colleagueâs signature bill. Moreno told Semafor he believes the Senate should stay in until thereâs a roll call vote on the Ratepayer Protection Act, data center-focused energy legislation from Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio. Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., blocked the bill last week. âAbsolutely, 100%, they all hide behind Martin now, like itâs one Democrat. We need to put them on the record,â Moreno said. Republican senators have discussed the idea but made no final decision. âI have heard a lot of support from my colleagues about getting it done,â Husted told Semafor. âI hope we give [Democrats] another chance to get it right.â The Senate is scheduled to be in next week, but may cut the session short so lawmakers can hit the campaign trail. Know More Itâs crunch time for the Senate schedule, and some Republicans would prefer the Senate break for the midterms and allow Republicans locked in difficult reelection battles to campaign. But for Husted, getting his bill done might be just as valuable as a week of campaigning. Rising public opposition to data centers, driven in part by their costs, has put pressure on lawmakers in Washington to come up with a solution. âVoters overwhelmingly support the idea of data centers paying their own way, so that they donât run the risk of having to pay higher electricity prices as a result,â Husted said. âIt could be the law of the land, and it could prove to Americans that we heard them, that we did something about it.â Heinrich blocked Hustedâs bill and instead offered his own GRID Savings Act, which would require data centers to pay for power grid connections rather than making it voluntary. Other Democrats have criticized Hustedâs bill as lacking teeth: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the measure, which passed the House overwhelmingly, a âfraud.â Senate Majority Leader John Thune acknowledged a âsignificant level of interestâ in passing the bill. As he left the Capitol on Wednesday evening, his guidance for the Senate schedule was simply: âDonât make any plans yet.â

artigo.texto: OPINION: How I learned to stop worrying and love data centers If we're not careful, an actual policy discussion might break out amid the political absurdity saturating our news feeds. Considering the crazed, unhinged and outrageous state of modern politics, the fact that data centers — and the nuanced public policy surrounding them — have somehow taken center stage in Nevada's gubernatorial race is actually quite refreshing. To be sure, not all the rhetoric surrounding this issue is as well thought out as it should be. For example, there seems to be a growing contingent of voters (and lawmakers) who seemingly want every planned data center project to be permanently banned from now until the end of time throughout the known universe and beyond. Others simply don't want them anywhere near their homes. However, such NIMBY prohibitionist attitudes probably aren't practical in the long run — at least not if we want to carry on happily in our wondrous age of technological advancement. The truth is that data centers are like any other major infrastructure project. From giant dams built to contain seasonal floods to power lines that keep electricity flowing to our homes, they're merely a component of what it takes to keep our civilized society moving forward. Far from merely being a way to power AI slop, these centers power the technological world most of us take for granted. Uploading a picture to your Google Drive? Listening to a song on Spotify? Maybe OneDrive just backed up that project you're completing for a client. All these things depend on data centers to perform the marvel of modern cloud computing — which means virtually everything we do online or on most of our smartphones requires some warehouse to be built somewhere full of RAM to keep our digital era functioning well. The question isn't whether we should build them, because at the end of the day we have to. Instead, the questions should be where do we build them and what guardrails should be erected to make sure they are not a net drain on a local community's resources. And the answer to these questions largely depends on the details of any specific project. As The Nevada Independent recently explained, not all data centers are created equal. Some use massive amounts of water to feed their evaporative cooling systems — cooling systems that the Southern Nevada Water Authority has recently banned. More efficient closed-loop systems are better, but they do still consume scarce water in the same way other large-scale projects for various industries might. Similarly, the power requirements vary greatly by center and local utilities are already trying to devise ways to protect average ratepayers from the effects of increased power requirements on the grid. In other words, data centers — just like any other infrastructure project — come with certain trade-offs and benefits for local communities. And while it's easy to only look at one side of the ledger and jump on some populist bandwagon, most legitimate concerns about these projects don't represent insurmountable challenges for the tech industry, lawmakers or local community leaders. And in some cases, more pragmatic approaches to the issue are already taking place. As the Brookings Institution noted in a recent white paper on the topic, for example, Microsoft has penned some deals that directly invest in the local community, even beyond the usual promise of a few thousand construction jobs. And virtually all the big industry players — including Meta, Microsoft and Google — are already actively working to make their water usage efficient enough to substantially contribute to a local region's long-term water sustainability goals. That's not to say that every proposed center should be automatically greenlit by regulators. But it does illustrate that sound public policy and public discussion can mitigate many of the concerns associated with such construction. And the fact that Nevada's gubernatorial race is on the verge of steering into such policy discussions is good news for our era of nonstop performative politics. Even better is the fact that some good-government reforms are already taking place as a result. Just last week, for example, Gov. Joe Lombardo (R) signed an executive order limiting the sort of tax incentives data centers can enjoy. Similarly, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford has reversed his previous support for data center tax breaks, promising to place a moratorium on such incentives if elected governor. Cynics would argue that both candidates are merely placating the public's apparent distrust of the industry — but so what? Restricting or eliminating corporate handouts for any politically connected industry should be seen as a step in the right direction, regardless of whether it was merely in response to public backlash. Indeed, of all the concerns regarding data centers, the issue of economically distortive corporate welfare being handed out to massively profitable companies is probably the lowest-hanging fruit for policymakers to pick right now. One doesn't even have to feel particularly animated about the infrastructure needed to keep our Google Drive functioning properly to get on board with a little less political cronyism. Importantly, this is the real reason a lawmaker's past support for such subsidies should be considered problematic — not merely because their stance on the issue has conveniently evolved with public opinion, but because their past support demonstrates a belief that government's job is to use our tax dollars to manipulate the economy for the benefit of those who have the best lobbyists. Unfortunately, in Nevada, that tends to be the default position for a great many lawmakers, regardless of political party. Governors, legislators and policymakers in our state routinely use the term "economic development" as a catchall excuse to redistribute wealth to politically connected corporations — whether those corporations be sports teams, Hol

artigo.texto: Sep 24, 2026 AEG Launches AC-Coupled Solarcube Pro Residential Battery Storage System AEG has unveiled an AC-coupled, low-voltage storage system aimed at residential use, as reported by pv magazine. Dutch firms BM Energy and Apex Power Supplies developed the system, concentrating on the needs of the Dutch home market. BM Energy serves as an importer, distributor and wholesaler of renewable-energy goods for residential and commercial sectors. Apex Power Supplies, located in Poeldijk, distributes residential batteries and energy storage systems to installers and energy professionals. Govert Zaalberg, BM Energy's chief operating officer, told the publication that the Solarcube Pro extends the existing AEG Solarcube lineup. Technical Specifications Per the product datasheet, the Solarcube Pro offers 6.0 kWh of nominal battery capacity and 6.028 kWh of nominal battery energy, relying on lithium iron phosphate cells. The 6 kWh setup pairs a 3 kWh base unit with a 3 kWh battery power module. AEG markets the product as a plug-and-play system built for integration into residential properties. Charging and discharging can reach up to 3 kW. Standard on-grid AC output is rated at 800 W, with a 1,500 W premium setting available. The manufacturer cautions that enabling the premium function depends on local regulations and must only be done by authorized personnel. The system runs at a 90% depth of discharge, a figure the datasheet says comes from testing at 25 C. The 6 kWh version measures 575.5 mm by 460 mm by 281 mm and weighs 54 kg. It features an IP66 enclosure and operates between -20 C and 55 C. Communication options include Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and CAN. Features and Standards AEG says the storage system enables dynamic electricity pricing and self-consumption, plus AI-optimized power consumption and virtual power plant applications. The company adds that the product delivers backup power functionality. The new product comes with a 10-year technical warranty and a stated 15-year service life. The datasheet lists cumulative discharged energy of 18.3 MWh per battery across 10 years, based on 70% end-of-life capacity. artigo.texto: Cameroon’s Electricity Sector Regulatory Authority (ARSEL) has started reviewing two proposed solar power projects with a combined capacity of 294 MW, as the country looks to expand renewable energy generation in the Centre and Adamawa regions. The regulatory review is focused on assessing the technical, legal and financial aspects of the projects before they advance to the next stages of development. The larger project is a 250 MW solar photovoltaic facility planned in Ntui in Cameroon’s Centre region. The project is being developed with the involvement of international and local engineering companies and is expected to supply renewable electricity to the national grid. The proposed plant is intended to strengthen power availability while increasing the contribution of solar energy to Cameroon’s electricity mix. The development of the Ntui solar project is also expected to support diversification of electricity generation. Cameroon has traditionally relied significantly on hydropower, making additional solar capacity an option for reducing dependence on a single major renewable generation source. The project could also contribute to improving electricity availability for businesses and households in areas facing supply constraints. The second project under review is a 44 MW solar power facility proposed in Banyo, in the Adamawa region. Unlike the larger Ntui project, the Banyo development is planned with a battery energy storage system. The combination of solar generation and battery storage is intended to improve the reliability and flexibility of electricity supply. The battery system would allow electricity produced during periods of strong solar irradiation to be stored and supplied later when solar generation declines or demand increases. Such an arrangement can help address the variable nature of solar generation and provide additional support to local electricity networks. ARSEL’s ongoing review will provide regulatory guidance for both projects and help ensure that the proposed developments comply with Cameroon’s electricity-sector requirements. The review covers key aspects that need to be addressed before the projects can proceed toward implementation. Both projects remain at the preliminary development stage, and no official power purchase agreements have been finalized so far. Their progress will therefore depend on the completion of regulatory assessments, project development activities and other commercial requirements. Together, the proposed 294 MW of solar capacity represents a significant planned addition to Cameroon’s renewable energy pipeline. The projects are expected to support the country’s efforts to increase clean electricity generation, improve regional power availability and strengthen the role of renewable energy in meeting future electricity demand. artigo.texto: Brasil concentra 71% da capacidade de data centers em construção na América Latina O crescimento da inteligência artificial, da computação em nuvem, do comércio eletrônico e dos serviços digitais está acelerando a implantação de data centers no Brasil. Segundo o Latin America Data Center Report , publicado pela JLL, o país concentra 71% da capacidade de data centers atualmente em construção na América Latina e aproximadamente 48% da capacidade instalada em operação na região. Os números consolidam o Brasil como o principal mercado latino-americano de infraestrutura digital e ampliam a demanda por projetos de engenharia capazes de garantir disponibilidade, segurança, eficiência energética e funcionamento ininterrupto. A expansão está diretamente relacionada à transformação dos hábitos de consumidores, empresas e governos. A migração de sistemas corporativos para a nuvem, o avanço dos bancos digitais, do streaming, da saúde conectada, do trabalho remoto e das aplicações de inteligência artificial aumentaram significativamente o volume de informações que precisam ser armazenadas, processadas e transmitidas. Mais do que edifícios destinados a abrigar servidores, os data centers são estruturas de missão crítica. Uma interrupção pode comprometer serviços financeiros, plataformas digitais, operações industriais, sistemas públicos e atividades essenciais de grandes organizações. Energia renovável fortalece a competitividade brasileira A disponibilidade de fontes renováveis representa uma das principais vantagens competitivas do Brasil. A participação das fontes hidrelétrica, eólica e solar na matriz elétrica favorece a implantação de empreendimentos alinhados às metas globais de redução das emissões de carbono. Além da origem da energia, os novos projetos vêm incorporando soluções de eficiência ambiental, sistemas avançados de refrigeração, redução do consumo de água e busca por certificações internacionais, como LEED e normas ISO. Ao mesmo tempo, o crescimento do setor exige grandes volumes de energia com qualidade, estabilidade e redundância, além de conectividade, segurança física, climatização de alta precisão, automação e equipes especializadas para assegurar o funcionamento contínuo das instalações. “Um data center precisa ser concebido como um ecossistema integrado. Sistemas elétricos, climatização, automação, conectividade, segurança e prevenção de incêndios devem funcionar de maneira coordenada, com alta disponibilidade e redundância. É essa visão completa que permite reduzir riscos e garantir a continuidade das operações”, afirma Marco Alberto Silva, cofundador e CEO do Grupo Engemon. Engenharia integrada reduz riscos, custos e prazos Com experiência no desenvolvimento de infraestruturas críticas, a Engemon atua nesse mercado por meio de soluções que podem envolver planejamento, engenharia, construção, implantação tecnológica, operação e manutenção. A empresa desenvolve projetos personalizados de acordo com as características técnicas, operacionais e estratégicas de cada cliente. Esse modelo permite acompanhar o empreendimento desde sua concepção até o monitoramento da operação, com foco na redução de riscos, no cumprimento dos prazos e na eficiência dos investimentos. A atuação integrada também favorece a compatibilização entre os sistemas elétricos, mecânicos, de automação, refrigeração, telecomunicações, segurança e prevenção de incêndios. Em uma instalação que precisa funcionar 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana, essa coordenação é determinante para a confiabilidade do empreendimento. “Na Engemon, trabalhamos para que cada solução seja dimensionada de acordo com a realidade e as necessidades do cliente. A integração entre engenharia, construção, tecnologia, operação e manutenção permite antecipar interferências, acelerar a implantação e entregar uma infraestrutura mais segura, eficiente e preparada para futuras expansões”, acrescenta Silva. Os projetos podem, portanto, ir além da engenharia e da construção dos espaços físicos. A Engemon também integra serviços de operação e manutenção, assegurando monitoramento, controle e funcionamento contínuo das instalações. Esse modelo reduz a fragmentação entre diferentes fornecedores, amplia a previsibilidade do empreendimento e contribui para diminuir riscos em projetos caracterizados por alta complexidade técnica, grandes investimentos e margens reduzidas para falhas. Brasil ainda busca maior protagonismo global Apesar da liderança latino-americana, o Brasil ainda enfrenta o desafio de se aproximar dos maiores mercados globais de data centers. Para ampliar sua competitividade, o país precisará expandir a infraestrutura energética, fortalecer a conectividade, estimular a formação de profissionais especializados e oferecer maior previsibilidade regulatória e tributária aos investimentos de longo prazo. A expectativa é de que a demanda continue crescendo com a popularização da inteligência artificial generativa, a digitalização dos processos industriais e a necessidade de processamento de dados cada vez mais próximo dos usuários. O relatório da JLL mostra ainda que os mercados de colocation e hyperscale mantiveram crescimento sustentável na América Latina em 2025, enquanto o inventário de colocation da região avançou 20% em um ano. Nesse ambiente, empresas capazes de integrar engenharia, tecnologia, sustentabilidade, operação e manutenção terão papel estratégico na transformação do potencial brasileiro em infraestrutura efetivamente instalada. A liderança regional já foi conquistada. O próximo desafio será transformar as vantagens energéticas, técnicas e territoriais do Brasil em condições para que o país avance também entre os principais pólos globais da economia digital.

artigo.texto: Governor Wes Moore is putting new statewide rules in place for large data centers in Maryland while also pushing to end the industry's tax break. But counties across Maryland have already taken action, with some banning data centers and others pausing development or imposing new restrictions. So, where does your county stand? Anne Arundel County Current stance: Proposed moratorium - The County Council is considering a roughly 15-month pause on new data centers, replacing an earlier proposal for a ban. - Existing projects and certain future phases would be allowed to continue. - The amended bill returns to the council October 5 Baltimore City Current stance: Moratorium - A one-year moratorium on large data centers took effect in July. - It applies to facilities capable of using 10 megawatts or more of electricity. - The city is using the pause as it considers how to regulate data centers long-term Baltimore County Current stance: Moratorium - The County Council extended its pause on new data center development through December 31, 2027. - The extension passed unanimously on September 22. - The county is reviewing a Planning Board study on the potential impacts and regulation of data centers Carroll County Current stance: Moratorium - The Board of Commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on new data center applications on February 19, 2026. - The county is using the pause to study potential impacts and how to regulate data centers. Cecil County Current Stance: No specific regulations - Cecil County has not yet introduced any specific legislation regarding data centers. Frederick County Current stance: Moratorium on new applications - The county has paused new data center applications until July 1, 2027. - Existing projects and certain previously approved projects are exempt from the pause. - Data center development is limited to a roughly 2,600-acre designated overlay zone. Harford County: Current stance: Ban - Harford County banned data centers in June, becoming the first county in Maryland to do so. - The County Council unanimously approved the legislation, and County Executive Bob Cassilly signed it into law on June 10 Howard County Current stance: Moratorium - The County Council approved a temporary moratorium on new data center development in June. - The moratorium took effect August 4, while a task force studies impacts and recommends future regulations. - The pause runs through November 2, 2027. Now, the debate is also playing out at the state level, where Gov. Wes Moore is putting new guardrails in place for large data centers and pushing to end the industry's tax break. artigo.texto: Stephen Sanders expresses confidence in Lubbock data center resolution LUBBOCK, Texas (KCBD) - It takes a village to make a change in government. Just ask Stephen Sanders, who put together the ‘Save Lubbock’ group in May following the conversation about data centers at Texas Tech in May. After months of discussion, he was able to meet with city council and put pen to paper. “We sat down, we went line-by-line,” Sanders said. “Christy Martinez-Garcia, Gordon Harris, the city’s attorney, we were all there at the table in Mark (McBrayer’s) office at Citizen’s Tower going through the information. Making sure it was legal and everyone was happy with the final product.” After Tuesday’s council call for a temporary pause on large-scale data center approval in Lubbock, Sanders says things are heading in the right direction. “I feel really comfortable and really confident in our P&Z committee and the city council when it comes to putting these guardrails in place, and they’ve been real clear about that,” Sanders said. Not every council member agreed with the resolution, with Tim Collins and Tim Green voting against it. Green says there’s misinformation when it comes to data centers, suggesting residents are being misled on what they are. “A lot of the misinformation is that all data centers use a lot of water, they don’t,” Green said. “The data centers didn’t do themselves any favors in the past, they did use a lot of water. Nowadays, they have new technologies. They want to be good stewards of the environment.” Collins agreed with Green on one thing. He believes water usage is also not as great as has been reported but says being good stewards of city resources is job one as a member of city government. His decision to vote against the resolution had more to do with timing “My hope would have been, and what I tried to express Tuesday, is not to say no to a moratorium, but let’s hold this in our pockets until such a time it becomes necessary to understand what new governance we may have coming from Austin, and I expect there will be some,” Collins said. “Let us understand that and then we can come in and say pause.” While one chapter of the Lubbock data center conversation is finished, the book is still being written, and whatever side you’re on, work is underway to minimize the impact they may have on the city long-term. “It’s going to be hard for data centers to come into Lubbock,” Sanders said. “You’re going to have to jump through some hoops, you’re going to have to do it our way and we’re going to regulate you or you’re not going to be doing business in our city. But we are open to business.” Copyright 2026 KCBD. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Judge Dismisses Challenge To Port Washington Data Center Subsidy Ruling backs $15 billion campus incentives, but opponents vow to keep fighting the district. An Ozaukee County judge has dismissed a lawsuit challenging local development incentives supporting a $15 billion data center campus under construction in Port Washington. Earlier this year, Great Lakes Neighbors United — a community group opposed to the Port Washington data center — sued the city, challenging its creation of a tax incremental district to fund around $175 million in infrastructure improvements for the project. Tax increment districts, or TIDs, are a geographic area within a municipality that’s being targeted for development, where local governments divert increased property tax revenue generated from the district’s growth to finance development infrastructure or incentives. Port Washington created TID No. 5 to support the data center campus being developed by Vantage Data Centers, OpenAI and Oracle. The city’s development agreement is with Vantage. The suit against the city said the TID would lead to the city issuing more than $458 million in property tax reimbursement and interest payments to the developer over 18 years. The suit argued the project didn’t need the “public subsidy.” But Ozaukee County Circuit Court Judge Adam Gerol dismissed Great Lakes Neighbors’ lawsuit at an oral ruling last week, according to the county’s clerk of courts. A proposed order would dismiss the case “with prejudice,” meaning Great Lakes Neighbors would not be able to refile the same claim. The order still needs to be signed by the court. In a statement, Great Lakes Neighbors said the dismissal did not resolve their concerns about the district. “The court’s ruling does not close the question itself,” Great Lakes Neighbors United founder Christine Le Jeune said in a statement. “Residents still deserve a full and transparent accounting of how TID No. 5 was created and administered, and we will continue to pursue it in every way available to us.” In court filings, the city had argued Great Lakes Neighbors incorrectly claimed Port Washington would not receive property tax benefits from the project and omitted “crucial deal points.” In a statement, the city of Port Washington said the court’s decision affirmed the city’s process for approving the TID. The city said Vantage Data Centers is covering the $175 million in infrastructure costs upfront and would later be reimbursed through the TID. “There is no money from taxpayers other than Vantage involved in the TID,” the city stated. “Once the TID closes, the City anticipates receiving the increased property tax revenue and increment made possible by the improvements that comprise this project.” The controversy around the data center and TID No. 5 also spurred a ballot initiative. Roughly two-thirds of Port Washington voters approved a referendum giving them more say over future development incentives. The ordinance passed by voters would require future tax incremental districts with project costs or a base value of at least $10 million receive approval from voters before they can move forward. Earlier this year, business groups sued the city of Port Washington, challenging the legality of the ordinance. They argue the ordinance would harm employers and slow economic development. The city’s legal filing responding to their lawsuit said the city also has “concerns related to the legality of the proposed ordinance.” Great Lakes Neighbors United has joined that case to argue in favor of the ordinance. An oral ruling in that case is scheduled for Oct. 19. Brigitte Pyzyk, a researcher for Great Lakes Neighbors, said they’re hoping the judge sides with voters. “We would hope that the court would acknowledge that a vast majority of the citizens in Port Washington have voted on direct legislation, and they want a say on future TIDs,” she said. Beyond those court cases, Great Lakes Neighbors said in a statement that the organization “will pursue further action through additional avenues.” That could include filing complaints with the state Department of Revenue and trying to build support among state lawmakers to approve an audit related to TID No. 5, Pyzyk said. She said those complaints would likely center around whether the TID follows rules set by the state. She also said the community group was still working to determine next steps and ways forward. Judge dismisses lawsuit challenging Port Washington data center TID was originally published by Wisconsin Public Radio. artigo.texto: O que dizem os três departamentos — Florestal, Marinho e Ilhas, e Mudanças Climáticas — sobre o carbono azul? (CLO) Representantes do Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas, do Departamento de Silvicultura e Proteção Florestal e do Departamento de Mares e Ilhas do Vietnã concordaram que um roteiro para o carbono verde precisa partir de uma base legal, dados e potencial real, além de resolver o problema dos recursos para evitar que permaneça apenas na fase de planejamento. Công Luận•23/09/2026 No dia 23 de setembro, em Hanói, o Ministério da Agricultura e do Meio Ambiente, em colaboração com o Programa das Nações Unidas para o Desenvolvimento (PNUD) no Vietnã, organizou a segunda reunião do Grupo de Trabalho sobre a Implementação da Parceria de Ação para o Carbono Azul (NBCAP) no Vietnã. A reunião teve como foco a discussão de seis grupos de ação prioritários no Projeto de Roteiro Nacional de Ação para o Carbono Azul para o período de 2026 a 2030, incluindo políticas e governança; conservação e restauração de ecossistemas; financiamento e investimento; ciência , dados e sistemas de medição, relatórios e verificação (MRV); setor privado e meios de subsistência sustentáveis; capacitação e comunicação. Precisamos de um roteiro concreto, não apenas de algo no papel. Segundo o Dr. Luong Quang Huy, chefe do Departamento de Redução de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa e Proteção da Camada de Ozônio da Agência de Mudanças Climáticas (Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente), em termos de políticas públicas, o Vietnã está estudando emendas à Lei do Mar e das Ilhas e à Lei de Proteção Ambiental. Até o momento, as duas versões básicas das leis foram concluídas e os conteúdos relacionados ao carbono azul já foram abordados. Segundo o Sr. Huy, esta é uma base jurídica importante para a implementação de atividades no próximo período. O desafio é desenvolver um roteiro específico, definindo claramente quem faz o quê em cada etapa, qual conteúdo precisa ser implementado e como incorporar essas tarefas ao programa de ação nacional. Entretanto, representantes do Departamento de Silvicultura e Proteção Florestal argumentaram que, se quisermos abordar o carbono azul como uma nova fonte de receita proveniente de créditos de carbono, devemos primeiro abordá-lo sob uma perspectiva de gestão. Como a gestão estatal se relaciona com a gestão de créditos de carbono? Segundo representantes do Departamento de Silvicultura e Proteção Florestal, o sistema jurídico e os decretos relacionados à gestão de créditos de carbono já possuem regulamentações fundamentais. Portanto, o roteiro para o carbono azul precisa ser baseado na estrutura legal atual e na orientação de desenvolvimento de mercado do sistema de carbono, visto que o carbono azul representa apenas uma pequena parte do sistema de carbono como um todo. "Se a política de gestão do desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono priorizar o uso de créditos de carbono no mercado interno, então, atualmente, os créditos de carbono azul não serão capazes de competir com outros tipos de créditos", afirmou um representante do Departamento de Silvicultura e Proteção Florestal. De acordo com essa análise, mesmo os créditos de carbono do setor florestal podem ter dificuldades para competir no mercado interno devido à oferta de créditos de muitos outros setores. Portanto, se o objetivo do carbono azul é principalmente gerar benefícios econômicos no mercado interno, considera-se que esse objetivo é difícil de alcançar. De onde virá o dinheiro para isso? Você também pode gostar Segundo um representante do Departamento de Mares e Ilhas do Vietnã, a principal preocupação é a legalidade da implementação do roteiro. O representante afirmou que ainda não está claro qual será a forma de aprovação do roteiro e expressou o desejo de que a minuta seja enviada às unidades relevantes do Ministério para receber pareceres e aprimoramentos oficiais antes de ser submetida às autoridades competentes para apreciação. "O que mais espero é a base legal para a implementação deste roteiro", disse um representante do Departamento de Mares e Ilhas do Vietnã. Além disso, representantes dessa agência afirmaram que, embora a minuta do roteiro tenha abordado documentos legais existentes e proposto muitas atividades, ainda são necessários esclarecimentos sobre os métodos de implementação e o apoio específico necessário para traduzir esses conteúdos em ações concretas. Segundo representantes do Departamento de Mares e Ilhas do Vietnã, entre os ecossistemas de carbono azul, os manguezais são uma área relativamente acessível, e o Vietnã tem investido muitos anos em pesquisa e implementação de projetos nesse campo. Entretanto, ecossistemas de acesso mais difícil, como os leitos de ervas marinhas, ainda requerem dados adicionais, metodologias e estratégias de implementação específicas. Em particular, os recursos financeiros são considerados um dos principais desafios para a implementação do roteiro. "De onde virá o dinheiro para isso?", perguntou um representante do Departamento de Mares e Ilhas do Vietnã, acrescentando que, sem um orçamento, seria muito difícil atingir as metas estabelecidas. Segundo esse representante, embora a tendência atual enfatize que o financiamento de atividades climáticas exige a participação do Estado, a alocação e a aprovação de recursos financeiros específicos continuam sendo uma questão que precisa ser abordada. Além dos recursos internos, representantes do Departamento de Mares e Ilhas do Vietnã propuseram que os parceiros internacionais assumam compromissos mais específicos em relação ao financiamento, à organização da implementação e à escala do apoio. "Não podemos continuar a confiar apenas na teoria", enfatizou um representante do Departamento de Mares e Ilhas do Vietname, acrescentando que é necessário identificar claramente quais organizações internacionais participarão, qual será o seu compromisso e quais os métodos de apoio que irão fornecer. artigo.texto: Mato Grosso ganhará, em setembro, um encontro técnico dedicado a uma das principais fronteiras do setor elétrico: o armazenamento de energia. A Associação Brasileira de Engenheiros Eletricistas, Seção Mato Grosso (ABEE-MT), realizará o Fórum Mato-Grossense de Engenharia Elétrica e Energias Sustentáveis (FMEES 2026), com programação em Cuiabá e Rondonópolis. O encontro será realizado no dia 28 de setembro, no Casarão 154, em Cuiabá, e no dia 30 de setembro, em Rondonópolis. O evento conta com apoio institucional do Conselho Regional de Engenharia e Agronomia de Mato Grosso (Crea-MT) e da Mútua, Caixa de Assistência dos Profissionais do CREA, que também está entre os patrocinadores. O tema central desta edição será o BESS, sigla em inglês para Battery Energy Storage Systems, ou sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias. A tecnologia permite armazenar a energia produzida nos horários de maior geração solar para utilização posterior, especialmente nos períodos de maior demanda, menor produção ou tarifas mais elevadas. As soluções de armazenamento vêm ganhando espaço em projetos de geração distribuída e em aplicações voltadas ao agronegócio, à indústria e ao comércio. Além de ampliar o aproveitamento da energia produzida, os sistemas podem contribuir para a segurança energética, a estabilidade das instalações e a redução de custos. Para o presidente da ABEE-MT, Robson Vaz, o fórum nasce da necessidade de preparar os profissionais e as empresas do estado para uma nova etapa do mercado energético. “Mato Grosso avançou de forma significativa na geração solar e agora precisa aprofundar o debate sobre como armazenar e utilizar essa energia com eficiência, segurança e viabilidade econômica. O FMEES foi criado para aproximar profissionais, fabricantes e instituições, compartilhar conhecimento técnico e preparar o setor para as oportunidades que os sistemas de armazenamento já estão trazendo ao país”, afirma Robson Vaz. Apresentações: Em Cuiabá, a programação será realizada das 17h30 às 23h, em formato concentrado, para facilitar a participação dos profissionais que trabalham durante o dia. Após o credenciamento e a abertura institucional da ABEE-MT, do CREA-MT e da Mútua-MT, o público acompanhará apresentações de seis empresas do setor: WEG, DCCO, Condutive, Sungrow, BelEnergy e e4uatro, responsável pela palestra de encerramento. As apresentações abordarão tecnologias e soluções para o novo mercado de energia, além de dimensionamento, aplicações práticas e viabilidade financeira dos sistemas de armazenamento. O encontro presencial também integra a proposta do evento. A programação reserva 45 minutos para um jantar de relacionamento entre participantes, palestrantes e patrocinadores. As atividades terminam com uma confraternização aberta até as 23h. Público e inscrições O FMEES 2026 é voltado a engenheiros eletricistas, projetistas, integradores, empresas de engenharia, suprimentos e construção, conhecidas como EPCs, fabricantes, distribuidoras, consultores, docentes e estudantes ligados ao setor elétrico. Os participantes receberão certificado. As inscrições podem ser feitas pelo site forumbess.abeemt.org.br. As vagas são limitadas e parte da experiência será subsidiada pela ABEE-MT. Crianças a partir de 7 anos também precisam de inscrição própria. Além da Mútua, o evento conta com o patrocínio de CCR, Sonare Engenharia, Caberlin Engenharia, RUAH Engenharia, GD PRO, Solvaz Engenharia e Consultoria, MIESE Energia Solar e Standart Engenharia Elétrica.
