artigo.texto: Launching in California, Arizona, Texas, and Florida, with additional state launches planned by the end of 2026 HOUSTON & LOS ANGELES--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Sep. 24, 2026-- Otovo ASA (Euronext Oslo Børs: OTOVO; "Otovo"), a leading provider of behind-the-meter energy services for homes and businesses, today announced a service partnership with InCharge Energy ("InCharge"), a trusted national provider of EV charging installation and maintenance services. By combining their service offerings, which together span more than 100,000 energy assets, Otovo and InCharge can provide commercial customers with a single service relationship covering solar, battery storage, and EV charging equipment across key U.S. markets. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260924902720/en/ InCharge Energy operates more than 40,000 EV chargers across the U.S. Together, Otovo and InCharge will offer each other's preventive maintenance plans, with each company dispatching its own technicians, expanding the footprint and capabilities of each service provider. Otovo will bring its Endurance™ AI platform to the shared work, so a job originating with either company is logged, dispatched and closed against one record of the site. Each company continues to sell and perform under its own brand. "We built this partnership around a simple idea: a customer shouldn't need multiple vendors just because their energy assets came from different systems," said William J. (John) Berger, Chief Executive Officer of Otovo. "By joining forces on commercial energy service, we can seamlessly integrate work orders through Endurance™, giving customers one call and one relationship instead of separate vendors and contracts for every system on site." “Technology alone doesn’t keep critical energy infrastructure operating – it takes highly-skilled people in the field,” said Rich Mohr, Chief Executive Officer of InCharge Energy. “Otovo and InCharge have both made significant investments in technical talent and electrical field service capabilities, and we will continue to invest as these systems become more critical to our customers’ operations. By utilizing InControl™ and Endurance™ together, we can bring better asset intelligence to our field teams and enable a more proactive approach to how EV charging, solar, battery storage and supporting electrical infrastructure are managed and maintained.” The partnership draws on established scale on both sides. Otovo currently services more than 60,000 customers, and InCharge’s InControl software platform connects and supports more than 40,000 EV charging assets across more than 1,060 completed infrastructure projects. In 2025, InCharge’s team completed more than 24,000 support cases, resolving approximately 80% of charger issues remotely, with the InControl platform maintaining 99.99% uptime. InCharge’s broader network spans every U.S. state and Canadian province, supported by regional sales and service offices in Los Angeles, CA, Richmond, VA, and Fort Worth, TX, and includes more than 100 field service staff. That scale underpins the companies’ plans to expand this partnership into new markets. Work orders will pass directly between Otovo and InCharge, with Endurance™, Otovo’s industry-leading AI platform, handling intake, dispatch and scheduling on the Otovo side. Each company will act as a reseller of the other's preventive maintenance plans in the launch geographies, holding its own customer relationship. Pricing on the reciprocal plans is matched between the companies. The partnership addresses a structural gap for commercial sites carrying multiple energy assets. A property with rooftop solar, battery storage, EV chargers and a backup generator typically holds a separate contract, a separate response commitment and a separate point of contact for each one. About InCharge Energy InCharge Energy is a full lifecycle energy infrastructure partner, delivering EV charging, electrical and lighting, and distributed energy solutions. InCharge supports customers from initial concept and construction through long-term ongoing operations and maintenance. By providing one accountable partner across the energy lifecycle, InCharge Energy helps organizations operate more reliably, scale with confidence, and reduce total cost of ownership through best-in-class service and maintenance. More information is available at www.inchargeus.com. About Otovo Otovo is an AI-Native behind-the-meter energy services company serving homes and businesses across 15 European markets, Israel and the United States. Otovo combines equipment monitoring, rapid repairs, dependable power supply and grid participation in one service. Endurance™, Otovo’s AI platform, monitors installed equipment, optimizes service from problem detection to resolution and coordinates repairs around the clock. “Your Power, Backed by Ours™.” Otovo is listed on Euronext Oslo Børs under the ticker OTOVO. Visit us at www.otovo.com. View source version on businesswire.com: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260924902720/en/ Matt Dallas 917-363-1333 [email protected] Source: Otovo ASA

artigo.texto: - Attack ads suggests GOP governor candidate John James voted for data center tax breaks, is funded by data center developers - Dems point to James’ vote for Big Beautiful Bill, which had broad tax breaks that were not specific to data centers but benefited them - Donors with ties to data center industry have donated to various James campaigns, including gubernatorial run As data centers continue to stir controversy across Michigan, related attacks are emerging in the governor’s race between Democrat Jocelyn Benson and Republican John James. New online ads from Making Michigan’s Future, a group supporting Benson’s campaign, claims James voted for $70 billion in tax breaks for data centers as a member of the US House and has received more than $100,000 in campaign donations from data center developers. Related fact checks: - Jocelyn Benson’s family ties to Saline data center - Democrats claim John James used Congress to enrich himself - Republicans tie Jocelyn Benson to SPLC criminal case The donations claim is largely true, although some of those contributions to James were for his past campaigns for other offices. The claim that James voted for a $70 billion tax break for data centers is less straightforward. The ads are among several that Bridge Michigan is fact-checking in the gubernatorial race, including claims about Benson’s family ties to a data center project. The general election winner will succeed Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, who is term-limited. Data center tax breaks One recent online ad from Making Michigan’s Future, which is backed by the Democratic Governors Association, claims that James “voted to give data centers a $70 billion tax break.” The ad cites an analysis from the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP), a left-leaning think tank, that said large tech companies like Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Tesla received a collective $50.8 billion in tax breaks in 2025, “likely from” President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. A second analysis from the think tank, published on Sept. 17, claims that Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle received a total of $69.78 billion in tax breaks in 2025, although it isn’t clear how much was directly related to data centers. In Congress, James voted for the “big, beautiful” law, which included provisions that increased tax write-offs for corporations making infrastructure and equipment investments. While companies building data centers are eligible for those tax breaks, they aren’t exclusive to data centers, according to a separate analysis from the nonpartisan Tax Foundation. On Sept. 16, House Democrats introduced a bill that would bar data centers from claiming those tax breaks. James voted for a law that “handed massive tax breaks to the Big Tech companies building data centers,” Sam Newton, a spokesperson for Making Michigan’s Future, said in a statement to Bridge Michigan. He cited ITEP and a Tax Notes analysis saying the write-off provisions could be “especially important” to data center developers. “James can try to run from his record, but all Michiganders need to do is follow the money to see whose side he’s on,” Newton said. In addition to the final bill, James voted for an earlier House version of the “big, beautiful bill” that included a section called the “Artificial Intelligence and Information Technology Modernization Initiative,” which would have barred state and local jurisdictions from creating laws to regulate data centers. James has since changed his position on local regulations, saying he supports a moratorium on new data centers until additional regulations are established. “The standards of my moratorium have been clear: no new data centers until we protect our people. We must re-establish local control, ensure no utility rate increases for residents, protect our water, air, land and noise from pollution while prioritizing brownfields and preserving farmland,” James told Bridge in a statement. James did not answer a question about providing tax breaks to data centers. Benson’s campaign did not respond to requests for comment. She too has proposed a moratorium on new data centers. Data center-linked donations Making Michigan’s Future is running a second ad on Facebook and Instagram that highlights political contributions from data center developers to James. In a video, a narrator claims that “John James won’t stand up to data center corporations while he’s cashing their checks.” Text that appears in the video includes “James took over $100k from data center developers” and “John James won’t stand up for US.” In July, Bridge Michigan found that James had received more than $100,000 in political contributions from donors with data center ties, although that figure is an accumulation from multiple election cycles dating back to 2018. Many of those contributions came from members of the Rakolta family, who founded and run Walbridge, a Detroit-based construction company contracted to build the hyperscale data center facility in Saline. Michael Haller, Walbridge’s CEO, has also previously donated to James’ campaigns. In January, Walbridge chair John Rakolta Jr. and his wife Terry Rakolta each donated $8,325 to James’ gubernatorial campaign, according to Michigan campaign finance records. $8,325 is the maximum allowed by an individual to a gubernatorial campaign in Michigan. Rakolta is a longtime GOP booster and has also been a supporter of President Donald Trump, who he shared a stage with in 2024 during a Trump campaign stop in Detroit. Bottom line John James has received campaign donations from individuals with ties to data center developers in Michigan. While James didn’t vote specifically to give data centers a $70 billion tax break, he did vote for the “big, beautiful bill,” which broadened corporate tax breaks that data center developers have benefitted from.

artigo.texto: Publicidade SÃO FRANCISCO (EUA) — Em um laboratório de São Francisco no mês passado, uma equipe de técnicos usando trajes de proteção e redes para cabelo examinava, ajustava e inspecionava um satélite do tamanho de uma geladeira encomendado pelo Google. Primeiro, os especialistas analisaram os painéis solares do equipamento, que serão abertos no espaço e ficarão voltados para o Sol. Em seguida, o satélite foi colocado sobre uma plataforma e submetido a um intenso teste de vibração para verificar se os chips internos seriam danificados ou se a estrutura se desmontaria durante a viagem ao espaço. Os técnicos pintaram cuidadosamente uma pequena linha sobre cada parafuso para identificar qualquer afrouxamento durante o teste. O satélite passou no exame: os parafusos permaneceram no lugar e os chips seguiram intactos. James Manyika, vice-presidente sênior de pesquisa do Google, classificou os resultados como “excelentes”, mas afirmou que ainda se pergunta o que acontecerá quando o equipamento chegar ao espaço. Continua depois da publicidade O trabalho faz parte de uma iniciativa ambiciosa do Google chamada Projeto Suncatcher, cujo objetivo é instalar data centers de inteligência artificial em órbita e utilizar a energia solar para alimentá-los. Em 1º de outubro, o satélite desenvolvido no laboratório de São Francisco, batizado de MVP, deverá dar o primeiro passo nessa direção por parte de uma grande empresa de tecnologia. Ele será acoplado a um foguete Falcon 9, da SpaceX, na Base da Força Espacial de Vandenberg, próxima a Santa Barbara, na Califórnia, e lançado em órbita. O Google concedeu ao The New York Times o primeiro acesso aos bastidores do projeto, que até um ano atrás parecia uma ideia saída da ficção científica. Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Sam Altman e outros executivos já manifestaram apoio à ideia de data centers orbitais, mas o conceito enfrenta desafios significativos, incluindo a exposição à radiação espacial e os altos custos de levar equipamentos além da atmosfera terrestre. Ainda assim, diante da crescente oposição à construção de data centers em terra e das limitações físicas desses projetos, a possibilidade de transferir parte da infraestrutura computacional para o espaço tornou-se mais atraente. Continua depois da publicidade Convém esclarecer: o Google não está enviando um data center completo para o espaço, mas apenas um protótipo experimental. O MVP abriga quatro chips especializados conhecidos como TPUs (Tensor Processing Units), com capacidade de processamento equivalente à de um único servidor de data center. Seus painéis solares fornecerão apenas cerca de 1 quilowatt de energia, aproximadamente o necessário para alimentar um secador de cabelo. Mesmo assim, isso será suficiente para que a empresa teste seu hardware nas condições extremas do espaço. O satélite responderá a consultas simples de IA e operará por um ano, embora deva permanecer orbitando a Terra por até seis anos. Ao final, espera-se que seja atraído pela gravidade terrestre e se desintegre ao reentrar na atmosfera. Manyika afirmou que as expectativas do Google para o projeto são moderadas. Continua depois da publicidade “Para ser totalmente sincero, não esperamos ter nada realmente operacional nos próximos anos”, disse. Ele comparou a iniciativa aos primeiros esforços da companhia para desenvolver carros autônomos. “Lembram quanto tempo o Google pesquisou antes que algo aparecesse? Acho que isso vai se parecer com aquilo.” Expandir de um único satélite para uma vasta rede funcionando como um gigantesco data center exigirá muitos anos e investimentos expressivos, afirma Brandon Lucia, professor de engenharia elétrica e computação da Universidade Carnegie Mellon. “Se você fizer isso em larga escala, surgem problemas adicionais de engenharia”, disse. “Estamos entrando em território desconhecido.” Continua depois da publicidade O Projeto Suncatcher nasceu da ideia de Blaise Agüera y Arcas, vice-presidente do Google e pesquisador de IA que lidera uma equipe focada em estudos sobre inteligência. Há cerca de três anos, ele participou de um encontro entre empreendedores e pesquisadores de inteligência artificial em que o principal tema era o crescente consumo de energia dos sistemas de IA. Ao sair do evento, concluiu que os data centers precisavam migrar para o espaço para aproveitar a energia solar. “Isso está na minha cabeça desde a infância”, afirmou. “A ficção científica tem uma longa tradição de imaginar estrelas sendo usadas para computação.” Pouco depois, Agüera y Arcas apresentou a ideia a Manyika, que inicialmente acreditava que ela não funcionaria. Ainda assim, autorizou uma série de testes para avaliar se os chips de IA poderiam ser resfriados no espaço e resistir à radiação. Em fevereiro de 2025, o Google começou a levar seus chips ao Crocker Nuclear Laboratory, em Davis, na Califórnia. Lá, um enorme acelerador de partículas conhecido como ciclotron, equipado com ímãs utilizados em projetos da época do Projeto Manhattan, bombardeou os componentes com uma dose de radiação equivalente a cinco anos de exposição no espaço. A radiação pode provocar os chamados “bit flips”, falhas que alteram o código binário de um circuito, transformando um zero em um ou vice-versa. Esses erros podem causar grandes problemas em sistemas de computação. Mas os resultados foram encorajadores: o Google descobriu que, na maioria das vezes, bastava reiniciar os chips para corrigir as falhas. Em maio de 2025, Agüera y Arcas participou de uma reunião organizada por Manyika para apresentar o projeto a Sundar Pichai, CEO do Google. Para sua surpresa, outro participante estava presente: Sergey Brin, cofundador da companhia. Os dois executivos aprovaram rapidamente a iniciativa. “Ok, então essa é uma boa ideia”, teria dito Brin, segundo Agüera y Arcas. “Vamos discutir como fazer isso.” Com o aval da liderança, o Projeto Suncatcher acelerou. artigo.texto: Paxton to investigate hundreds of Texas data centers over water use reporting Lubbock included in list of counties to be investigated AUSTIN, Texas (KCBD) - Attorney General Ken Paxton will be investigating Texas data center developments that have not yet responded to the required water use survey, including data centers in Lubbock, Randall and Ector County. Paxton has ordered the Office of the Attorney General to ensure all data center developments in Texas provide up-to-date and accurate information regarding water usage. State law requires water use surveys Under Texas law, the Texas Water Development Board is required to conduct surveys of entities that use ground water and surface water for municipal, industrial, power generation or mining purposes. Paxton is demanding that all data centers in Texas meet this requirement by submitting a survey response in full compliance with the law. The Office of the Attorney General has launched an ongoing investigation into all data center developments in Texas. Attorney general’s statement “My office is currently investigating hundreds of data center developments to ensure that they are transparent about their water usage and fully compliant with the law,” Paxton said. “It is our responsibility to steward our state’s land well, and we cannot do that if companies are blatantly disregarding their legal obligations to Texas and to our citizens. We cannot sacrifice our resources, water, or energy supply, and I will continue to fight for our communities across this state.” Counties under investigation Data centers are under initial investigation in counties across Texas, including Harris, Montgomery, Travis, Dallas, Tarrant, Smith, Bexar, Tom Green, Potter, Randall, Lubbock, Midland, Ector, Wichita, Victoria, Brazos, Nueces and El Paso. artigo.texto: Maryland Governor Wes Moore is putting new rules in place for large data centers across the state. Moore signed an executive order Wednesday creating a state task force to review proposed data centers that use at least 25 megawatts of power when they seek state permits, incentives or other support. Projects will be evaluated on five areas, including protecting electricity ratepayers and the power grid, economic benefits, community input, environmental protections, and transparency. The task force will issue a public determination on each project, and a new online dashboard will track proposed data centers, including their expected electricity and water use. Moore also says he’ll work with lawmakers next year to repeal Maryland’s data center sales and use tax exemption. Local governments will still have the final say on whether projects are approved. artigo.texto: 24 de set, 2026 Enquanto diversos grupos do setor elétrico se preparam para um leilão de projetos de armazenamento de energia com baterias agendado pelo Governo para dezembro, a Copel decidiu colocar suas fichas numa aposta diferente: as chamadas hidrelétricas reversíveis. Essas usinas, com dois reservatórios, podem guardar água para produzir nos momentos mais necessários para o sistema, funcionando na prática como uma bateria – porém com capacidade para entregar energia por períodos muito mais longos. “No mundo hoje já existem 190 GW de potência de usinas reversíveis contra 120 GW de BESS, ou baterias,” o CEO Daniel Slaviero disse nesta entrevista gravada durante o J. Safra Investment Conference 2026. Segundo ele, a companhia trabalha hoje em projetos que somam 4 GW em capacidade e devem ser apresentados até o final do ano numa chamada pública aberta pela estatal Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) em busca de empreendimentos com a tecnologia. “Meu sentimento é que a Copel vai estar na vanguarda nesse assunto,” disse Slaviero. Ele defendeu que o Governo permita que as usinas reversíveis possam disputar os próximos leilões de capacidade, argumentando que elas podem entregar energia à rede por vinte horas, contra quatro horas das baterias. “Além disso, as reversíveis reforçam uma característica natural do País, que é a força e contribuição das hidrelétricas para o sistema elétrico,” disse Slaviero. A China é hoje a líder em hidrelétricas reversíveis no mundo. Em paralelo, a Copel também está pronta para disputar o próximo leilão de capacidade com ao menos um projeto, de 1 GW, para ampliação de sua usina Salto Caxias, disse o CEO. No leilão deste ano, a companhia foi uma das principais vencedoras, conseguindo contratos para expansão das hidrelétricas de Foz do Areia e Segredo com 2 GW adicionais – um investimento de R$ 5 bilhões. Para o CEO da Copel, o setor elétrico e seus leilões são um modelo de sucesso, mas o próximo Governo precisará fazer ajustes na regulamentação, seja quem for o vencedor das eleições. Entre os problemas mais graves a serem enfrentados estão o peso dos subsídios e encargos nas tarifas de energia e distorções nos sinais de preço da energia, além do crescimento desordenado da geração distribuída (as placas solares em telhados), disse Slaviero. “Chegou num ponto de inflexão, e temos uma janela, na nossa visão, que são os próximos dois anos, para pensar e preparar os próximos dez, quinze anos.”

artigo.texto: - The biodiversity credit market should stop trying to copy the carbon market’s method of reducing everything to one tradable unit, a new op-ed argues. - Instead, these credits should be measured by how continuously and independently a claim can be verified, since their benefit cannot be expressed as simply as carbon credits can. - “A hectare of mangrove forest is not interchangeable with a hectare of grassland: pretending otherwise is closer to a category error than a measurement gap, and I suspect it is the real reason estimates of this market vary by a factor of 80,” the author writes. - This article is a commentary. The views expressed are those of the author, not necessarily of Mongabay. Here is the argument I want to make plainly, before anything else: the biodiversity credit market should stop trying to copy carbon’s trick of reducing everything to one tradable unit, and should instead measure its own success by how continuously and independently a claim can be verified. Chasing a single elegant number, the way carbon markets did with metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e), is not what this field should be racing toward. It may, in fact, be the wrong goal altogether. The clearest evidence for this sits in plain view, in numbers that most people read as an embarrassment rather than as information. Every few months, a new market research report tells us exactly how large the global biodiversity credit market is. The trouble is, no two reports agree. One puts the 2025 market at roughly $90 million. Another, published around the same time, puts it at $7.1 billion. A third lands somewhere near $5.7 billion. These are not small rounding-off differences. They are the same year, the same broad market, and estimates that differ by a factor of nearly 80. Most commentary treats this gap as a sign that the data are still catching up with a young market, but I read it differently. The disagreement is not a data problem waiting for better satellites to fix. It is telling us something true about biodiversity that the carbon market never had to reckon with. Carbon succeeded, commercially speaking, because it found one clean unit. The tCO2e behaves the same whether it was avoided in Assam or Amazonas. That fungibility is precisely what let carbon markets scale into the billions, and it is why so many people now assume biodiversity simply needs its own version of the same trick: one tidy number that a hectare of restored mangrove and a hectare of protected grassland can both be reduced to. But a hectare of mangrove forest is not interchangeable with a hectare of grassland: pretending otherwise is closer to a category error than a measurement gap, and I suspect it is the real reason estimates of this market vary by a factor of 80, depending on who is counting. Different analysts are not simply using different data. They are quietly making different assumptions about what should even count as a biodiversity credit in the first place, because there is no shared definition anchoring the count the way tCO2e anchors carbon. This has a name in the policy world now. Researchers evaluating biodiversity credit suppliers against integrity criteria set by bodies such as the International Advisory Panel on Biodiversity Credits have found that achieving both “commensurability” — the ability to compare things by a common standard, like one credit against another — and genuine ecological meaning in a single metric is a real and possibly unresolved tension, not a matter of trying harder. Some in the field are now openly discussing a more plural approach of considering several honest metrics together, rather than one number pretending to hold everything a landscape means. This lends real weight to the argument I opened with. There is a second, harder reason to resist chasing carbon’s model, and it comes directly from carbon’s own recent history. In January 2023, a nine-month investigation by The Guardian, Die Zeit, and the nonprofit Source Material found that more than 90% of the rainforest offset credits certified by Verra, the world’s largest carbon credit certifier — credits used by companies including Disney, Shell and Gucci — were likely worthless, and the promised climate benefits may not have actually been delivered. A separate, and to my mind even more revealing, episode followed. In October 2024, U.S. authorities filed criminal charges, including for wire fraud and securities fraud, against Ken Newcombe, a former chief executive of the carbon project developer C-Quest Capital, over the alleged over-issuance of more than 5 million carbon credits. Newcombe denies the charges, and the matter remains before the courts, so that much should be said plainly. What is not in dispute is this: Newcombe sat on Verra’s board from 2007 until December 2023, and Verra had adopted a crediting methodology that he himself helped write. The regulator and the regulated were, for a period, quite literally at the same table. I raise this not to single out one certifier for blame, but because it points at something structural, and it is exactly the trap the biodiversity market risks walking into. A market built around chasing one simple, tradable number creates a strong incentive to keep that number moving, and whoever controls how the number gets calculated ends up holding real power over whether it can be trusted. Carbon learned this the expensive way, after the credits had already been sold, retired, and used to back real corporate climate claims. Biodiversity credit markets are still young enough to learn this lesson in advance rather than after the fact. That is the actual opportunity sitting inside all this market size confusion: rather than a data gap to be closed as quickly as possible, it’s a genuine invitation to design differently from the outset. artigo.texto: EUROFER alerta que revisão do EU ETS pode dobrar custos de carbono do aço até 2031 O setor siderúrgico europeu pode ver seus gastos anuais com cotas de carbono subirem de EUR3,4 bilhões em 2026 para EUR8,2 bilhões em 2031 sob uma revisão proposta do Regime de Comércio de Emissões da UE, segundo a Associação Europeia do Aço, conhecida como EUROFER. As estimativas da associação indicam que os custos de carbono da produção convencional de aço em altos-fornos praticamente dobrariam, chegando a EUR100 por tonelada até 2030 e superando EUR200 por tonelada a partir de 2031, patamar que a EUROFER considera tornaria a indústria economicamente inviável. A EUROFER pede uma transição justa e pragmática para o Mecanismo de Ajuste de Carbono na Fronteira. Atualmente, os produtores europeus recebem parte de suas cotas de emissão sem custo, como proteção contra concorrentes sediados em países com regras ambientais menos rigorosas. A introdução do mecanismo envolveria a eliminação dessas cotas gratuitas, e a EUROFER busca uma eliminação mais gradual ao longo dos próximos cinco anos, para que a precificação de carbono reflita as condições reais de investimento. As exportações representam uma preocupação específica, já que os fabricantes estrangeiros pagam a taxa de carbono da UE apenas sobre os bens vendidos no mercado europeu, enquanto as empresas da UE arcam com esses custos em toda a sua produção, enfraquecendo sua posição nos mercados globais. O diretor-geral da EUROFER, Axel Eggert, indicou que a indústria siderúrgica europeia tem como meta a neutralidade climática até 2050 e já assumiu decisões de investimento em projetos capazes de produzir cerca de 35 milhões de toneladas de aço de baixo carbono. No entanto, devido ao agravamento das condições econômicas, projetos que cobririam 10 milhões de toneladas adicionais foram suspensos. Para que a transição tenha êxito, a indústria precisa, além da precificação de carbono, de energia verde acessível, salvaguardas contra a concorrência desleal, acesso a sucata e apoio ao investimento, nenhum dos quais está atualmente disponível em todas as partes da Europa. A EUROFER pede que o princípio da solidariedade entre os Estados-membros da UE seja mantido durante a revisão do ETS. Conforme noticiado pelo GMK Center, os Estados-membros da UE chegaram a um acordo em meados de setembro sobre uma decisão de conceder cotas gratuitas adicionais de emissão de carbono a empresas de indústria pesada, medida destinada a apoiar sua competitividade econômica. Segundo o Conselho da UE, sob a proposta da Comissão Europeia, 121 milhões de cotas gratuitas adicionais de CO2 seriam alocadas a setores industriais entre 2026 e 2030, calculadas com base em dados de consumo de combustível e produção de calor, permitindo às empresas economizar cerca de EUR8,25 bilhões, ou USD9,52 bilhões, em custos de carbono. artigo.texto: O crescimento da Inteligência Artificial, da Computação em Nuvem, do comércio eletrônico e dos serviços digitais está acelerando a implantação de Data Centers no Brasil. Segundo o Latin America Data Center Report , publicado pela JLL, o País concentra 71% da capacidade de Data Centers atualmente em construção na América Latina e aproximadamente 48% da capacidade instalada em operação na região. Os números consolidam o Brasil como o principal mercado latino-americano de infraestrutura digital e ampliam a demanda por projetos de engenharia capazes de garantir disponibilidade, Segurança, eficiência energética e funcionamento ininterrupto. A expansão está diretamente relacionada à transformação dos hábitos de consumidores, empresas e governos. A migração de sistemas corporativos para a Nuvem, o avanço dos bancos digitais, do streaming, da saúde conectada, do trabalho remoto e das aplicações de Inteligência Artificial aumentaram significativamente o volume de informações que precisam ser armazenadas, processadas e transmitidas. Mais do que edifícios destinados a abrigar servidores, os Data Centers são estruturas de missão crítica. Uma interrupção pode comprometer serviços financeiros, plataformas digitais, operações industriais, sistemas públicos e atividades essenciais de grandes organizações. Energia renovável fortalece a competitividade brasileira A disponibilidade de fontes renováveis representa uma das principais vantagens competitivas do Brasil. A participação das fontes hidrelétrica, eólica e solar na matriz elétrica favorece a implantação de empreendimentos alinhados às metas globais de redução das emissões de carbono. Além da origem da energia, os novos projetos vêm incorporando soluções de eficiência ambiental, sistemas avançados de refrigeração, redução do consumo de água e busca por certificações internacionais, como LEED e normas ISO. Ao mesmo tempo, o crescimento do setor exige grandes volumes de energia com qualidade, estabilidade e redundância, além de Conectividade, Segurança física, climatização de alta precisão, Automação e equipes especializadas para assegurar o funcionamento contínuo das instalações. “Um Data Center precisa ser concebido como um ecossistema integrado. Sistemas elétricos, climatização, automação, conectividade, segurança e prevenção de incêndios devem funcionar de maneira coordenada, com alta disponibilidade e redundância. É essa visão completa que permite reduzir riscos e garantir a continuidade das operações”, afirma Marco Alberto Silva, cofundador e CEO do Grupo Engemon. Engenharia integrada reduz riscos, custos e prazos Com experiência no desenvolvimento de infraestruturas críticas, a Engemon atua nesse mercado por meio de soluções que podem envolver planejamento, engenharia, construção, implementação tecnológica, operação e manutenção. A empresa desenvolve projetos personalizados de acordo com as características técnicas, operacionais e estratégicas de cada cliente. Esse modelo permite acompanhar o empreendimento desde sua concepção até o monitoramento da operação, com foco na redução de riscos, no cumprimento dos prazos e na eficiência dos investimentos. A atuação integrada também favorece a compatibilização entre os sistemas elétricos, mecânicos, de Automação, refrigeração, telecomunicações, segurança e prevenção de incêndios. Em uma instalação que precisa funcionar 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana, essa coordenação é determinante para a confiabilidade do empreendimento. “Na Engemon, trabalhamos para que cada solução seja dimensionada de acordo com a realidade e as necessidades do cliente. A integração entre engenharia, construção, tecnologia, operação e manutenção permite antecipar interferências, acelerar a implantação e entregar uma infraestrutura mais segura, eficiente e preparada para futuras expansões”, acrescenta Silva. Os projetos podem, portanto, ir além da engenharia e da construção dos espaços físicos. A Engemon também integra serviços de operação e manutenção, assegurando monitoramento, controle e funcionamento contínuo das instalações. Esse modelo reduz a fragmentação entre diferentes fornecedores, amplia a previsibilidade do empreendimento e contribui para diminuir riscos em projetos caracterizados por alta complexidade técnica, grandes investimentos e margens reduzidas para falhas. Brasil ainda busca maior protagonismo global Apesar da liderança latino-americana, o Brasil ainda enfrenta o desafio de se aproximar dos maiores mercados globais de data centers. Para ampliar sua competitividade, o País precisará expandir a infraestrutura energética, fortalecer a Conectividade, estimular a formação de profissionais especializados e oferecer maior previsibilidade regulatória e tributária aos investimentos de longo prazo. A expectativa é de que a demanda continue crescendo com a popularização da Inteligência Artificial Generativa, a digitalização dos processos industriais e a necessidade de processamento de Dados cada vez mais próximo dos usuários. O relatório da JLL mostra ainda que os mercados de colocation e hyperscale mantiveram crescimento sustentável na América Latina em 2025, enquanto o inventário de colocation da região avançou 20% em um ano. Nesse ambiente, empresas capazes de integrar engenharia, tecnologia, sustentabilidade, operação e manutenção terão papel estratégico na transformação do potencial brasileiro em infraestrutura efetivamente instalada. A liderança regional já foi conquistada. O próximo desafio será transformar as vantagens energéticas, técnicas e territoriais do Brasil em condições para que o País avance também entre os principais polos globais da economia digital.

artigo.texto: The nationwide backlash against the AI buildout promises to play a decisive role in a handful of Senate races this year, and could in turn determine who will control Congress for the second half of Donald Trump’s presidency. Evidence is mixed when it comes to which party voters trust on the issue, though Democrats seem to be maintaining a slight advantage. Recent NBC News polling found that they held a 12-point lead when it came to “dealing with data centers”—32 percent to 20 percent—though 19 percent said both parties were “about the same” and a quarter responded that neither could be trusted. Republicans, however, had a two-point edge on the more general matter of artificial intelligence in a New York Times/Siena poll published last week—within its margin of error. But among voters, opposition to their construction has emerged as one of the only positions drawing bipartisan support this cycle. In June, 64 percent of respondents told a Reuters/Ipsos survey that they disagreed with constructing data centers at scale and pace, and the latest NBC News poll found that the same share of registered voters would be less likely to support a candidate who backs building these facilities in their community. The sleeper issue has become a potentially election-deciding matter, formerly pro-development politicians are now vocal skeptics of an unchecked development push, and campaigns for the House and Senate increasingly read like competitions for who can appear more anti-AI, with Republican strategists telling Newsweek candidates are now “fleeing” from their initial stances on the buildings given alarming levels of local opposition. “Frankly, any incumbent, Republican or Democrat, should be concerned about being tagged as pro-data center,” political strategist Pete Seat told Newsweek. “The loudest voices are being heard, and policy is being made with those voices leading the charge," he said, adding that this trend he says will continue “until the pro-development side can marshal a grassroots army of its own.” Where Data Centers Could Decide Senate Races Jaymie Scotto Cutaia, founder and CEO of the data center PR firm JSA, told Newsweek that voter concerns about grid capacity, water usage and local community impacts were “resonating with voters across party lines," which in turn "creates an incentive for candidates to adopt increasingly aggressive positions, particularly in closely contested races.” And veteran GOP strategist John Thomas said that, while not nationally a priority on the same level as immigration and the economy, data centers’ political implications appeared to correlate with the presence and scale of a local buildout. Given this, Newsweek charted the tight Senate races that are taking place in states with significant numbers of planned data centers. According to the nonpartisan Cook Political Report’s latest update, seven races are currently considered “toss ups,” with two that “lean Democrat” meaning a total of nine could be considered close. Of these, the power-infrastructure tracking website Cleanview.co shows that eight have at least one planned data center—i.e., formally proposed or documented in records but not yet operational. This includes closely watched contests like Maine, where the incumbent Republican Susan Collins is taking on the Democrat Troy Jackson, and where three data center projects are currently planned. Alongside Virginia, Texas is leading the data center development push—with over 300 data centers in the works, per Cleanview. And this has now shown signs of becoming a key attack line in the contest between Democratic State Representative James Talarico and his Republican rival, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. "Ken Paxton has taken nearly half a million linked to the data center industry,” Talarico said in a recent CBS News interview, in which he called Paxton “bought and paid for” by the industry and bragged that he himself receives no center-linked campaign donations. And in Ohio, where 155 data centers are currently planned, Senate candidate Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, recently began running ads which hail the incumbent Senator Jon Husted as the “face of data centers” Republicans ‘Fleeing’ From Data Centers Ahead of Midterms A memo first published by Axios last month revealed that Republican leadership were concerned that data centers—and the party’s apparent proximity to the industry—were becoming a burden for GOP candidates in the midterms. The memo made specific mention of the Ohio race and Brown’s AI-focused strategy. “If [Husted] loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice—and they will not go near the next one,” the National Republican Senatorial Committee wrote. “This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle.” Experts share this sentiment, though they have expressed doubt that either party had yet secured an advantage in painting themselves as less pro-data center. “I don't think it's a partisan issue,” Douglas Heye, a senior adviser to the Iowa Republican Party, told Newsweek. He pointed to the fact that the Republican governor of Texas, Greg Abbott, has been among the most notable buildout skeptics both rhetorically and legislatively in 2026. However, Republican political consultant Mike Madrid said that examples like Texas show that Republicans are “fleeing from early support of data centers”—a pivot perhaps delayed by Trump’s overt backing of a rapid and nationwide development push. And the party itself has now tried to cast Democrats as, if not more pro-data center, at least less committed to protecting voters from the cost of these facilities. “Republicans are building the AI infrastructure America needs while ensuring companies are paying their own way, shielding families from higher utility bills, and safeguarding local water and natural resources,” Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the Republican National Committee, told Newsweek. artigo.texto: HSI breaks 25,000: Time to buy Hong Kong stocks? BYD is in “the leading position,” according to executive vice president Stella Li, with plans to introduce its first EV equipped with solid-state batteries in 2027. When will BYD launch an EV with solid-state batteries? We’ve been hearing it for over a decade now. Solid-state batteries, the “holy grail” of battery tech, are just around the corner. By now, it’s become something of a joke: Toyota or another automaker claims another “breakthrough” promising ultra-long range and fast-charging capabilities. According to the world’s leading EV manufacturer, solid-state batteries are advancing and will be used to power vehicles on the road as soon as 2027. In an exclusive interview with Carwow.es (you can watch the video below) about the company’s expansion into Spain and the launch of its luxury Denza brand in Europe, BYD executive vice president Stella Li offered a behind-the-scenes look at what’s to come. Denza Z9 GT (Source: Denza) The Denza Z9 GT, the brand’s first vehicle to launch in Europe with its 5-minute “Flash Charging” technology, is now on sale. BYD’s latest Blade Batteries 2.0 and Flash Charging tech enable vehicles to recharge from 10% to 70% in just 5 minutes. A full recharge, from 20% to 97%, takes only 9 minutes. BYD is offering Denza buyers 6 months of free charging to build awareness as it expands into higher-end segments. While the new battery tech is already drawing buyers in, BYD is not wasting time advancing several types of next-gen EV batteries, including solid-state. “You can name any battery technology, and I will guarantee you will find it in one corner of BYD R&D that we are studying, Li said. Regarding solid-state batteries, “BYD is in the leading position,” Li added, in both commercialization and technology. According to Li, BYD will “prove that” with its first model equipped with the new battery tech due out in 2027. It will be BYD’s first EV to use solid-state batteries. The battery R&D team is “very strong,” Li said, adding that they are studying not only the battery chemistry but also the manufacturing and equipment needed to mass-produce it. Li didn’t offer specific details, but during a conference in Apr, BYD Group’s chief scientist, Lian Yubo, said all-solid-state EV batteries have reached “a critical stage,” warning there are still a few hurdles to clear before they move to commercialization. BYD’s battery business, FinDreams, aims to begin producing sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries in limited batches in 2027, ramping up to mass production by 2030. Sun Huajun, CTO of Shenzhen BYD Lithium Battery Co., said last year that sulfide electrolytes last longer and are more stable than traditional liquid lithium-ion batteries, meaning they are safer, charge faster, and offer a longer driving range. The first vehicles to launch with solid-state EV batteries will likely be from BYD’s premium brands like Denza, Yangwang, and Feng Chang Bao, before it trickles down to higher-volume models. Electrek’s Take While BYD plans to introduce its first solid-state battery-powered EV next year, several automakers and other companies have revealed similar timelines. China’s Geely, Changan Auto, and CATL are targeting 2027, while Toyota, Stellantis, and Mercedes-Benz are also aiming to launch solid-state batteries next year. Although the new battery tech will begin rolling out as soon as 2027, commercialization is still not expected until closer to 2029 or 2030. Meanwhile, a few are already testing it out in the real world. Last fall, Mercedes-Benz drove a modified EQS over 745 miles (1,200 km) using solid-state battery cells from Factorial Energy. artigo.texto: TVA raises rates for data centers, adding upfront fee for new and existing facilities HUNTSVILLE, Ala. (WAFF) - The Tennessee Valley Authority is raising rates on all new and existing data centers, officials announced Thursday night. TVA officials, along with Huntsville Utilities leaders, presented the rate change to the Huntsville City Council to have it officially amended on the city’s books. TVA received approval to change its wholesale rate structure by October 1, applying only to data center customers. Rates are going up 10% to accommodate the cost to the system of supplying data centers. Data center customers will also have to pay an upfront fee. Officials say the rate hike applies solely to current or potential data centers. “This rate change protects residential and existing impacts of the changing energy landscape... and that rates remain affordable,” TVA Customer Relations spokesperson Robbie Jones said. There was no talk of construction of a new data center in the area. Meta’s facility in the North Huntsville Industrial Park was brought up during the discussion. It receives power directly from TVA, but Huntsville Utilities supplies its water. Meta representatives will address the public at the December 3 city council meeting. artigo.texto: A $6.8 billion battery plant is rising in Kenitra, Morocco, only 15 kilometers from Spain. With Chinese giant Gotion High-Tech behind it, this project could shake up the electric vehicle race in southern Europe. Morocco has put Spain’s electric car industry on notice. The country signed a $6.8 billion deal with China’s Gotion High-Tech to build Africa’s first battery gigafactory in Kenitra, just north of Rabat. This plant is set up to supply batteries to both Moroccan and southern European carmakers, putting Spanish battery projects in Valencia, Zaragoza, and Extremadura under real pressure. Gotion High-Tech, working through its local branch Gotion Power Morocco, is building the factory inside Kenitra’s Atlantic Free Zone. The location is no accident. Stellantis and Renault already assemble up to 700,000 vehicles a year in this corridor. The gigafactory will start with a capacity of 10 GWh a year. That’s enough for more than 100,000 electric cars or for storing extra energy from big solar parks. The plan is to ramp up to 100 GWh, which would put Kenitra in the same league as the biggest battery plants in Europe and Asia. The Kenitra plant will use LFP (lithium iron phosphate) battery technology. This chemistry builds the cathode right into the cell, which cuts costs and makes the batteries safer in terms of heat. LFP batteries don’t pack quite as much energy as NMC (nickel-manganese-cobalt) types, but for mass-market electric cars and stationary storage—the main targets for Kenitra—they are the most cost-effective choice right now. China’s play is simple: move battery production closer to Europe, cut shipping costs, and beat rivals by supplying car factories from just across the Strait of Gibraltar. Kenitra is only 15 kilometers from Algeciras, Spain’s southernmost port. That makes it a direct competitor to Spanish battery projects that are still in the planning stage. Morocco is aiming higher than its old mainstays like fishing and farming. The country is expanding the port of Nador to compete with Algeciras and Alicante. It’s building up an industrial network: parts suppliers, direct shipping routes to the Mediterranean and Atlantic, EU trade deals, and labor costs much lower than Europe’s. Stellantis, for example, plans to more than double its Kenitra output to 535,000 vehicles a year by 2025, focusing on small electric cars like the Citroën Ami, Opel Rocks-e, and Fiat Topolino. Khalid Qalam, who leads Gotion Power Morocco, says batteries from Kenitra will mainly go to Morocco’s car plants and to southern Europe through existing supply chains. That includes Spain. The project has a €100 million loan from the African Development Bank, with another €141 million expected from partner institutions. Spain’s own gigafactory plans are still at the early stage. PowerCo, Volkswagen’s battery arm, is building a plant in Sagunto (Valencia) with an initial 40 GWh capacity, expandable to 60 GWh, but production won’t start before 2026. Stellantis and CATL have started work in Figueruelas (Zaragoza) on a 50 GWh plant, with test cells due at the end of that year. Envision AESC is preparing a 30 GWh plant in Navalmoral de la Mata (Extremadura), aiming for the second half of 2027. Even Gotion has a project in Valladolid—€940 million for a plant with recycling and cathode integration—but construction hasn’t begun yet. This puts Gotion on both sides of the Strait, with projects in Morocco and Spain. The real race is inside the company: which plant opens first, which lands the best supply deals, and which supply chain takes the lead. Spain is not about to lose its car industry overnight. It’s still a major player in Europe. But the bigger risk is structural. If Kenitra starts locking in low-cost electric models, battery contracts, and the most profitable parts of the value chain before Spanish plants are up and running, Spain’s long experience and strong supplier networks may not be enough to keep production at home. Spain’s strengths—deep production know-how, full access to the EU single market, a strong supplier base, and technical talent—are real. But they need defending. That means faster permits, cheaper energy, targeted training, and bringing in electric models that make it worth keeping factories in Spain. As the industry shifts to electric, whoever controls the battery supply will decide which factories survive. Africa’s first battery gigafactory now has a clear address: Kenitra, Morocco. For context, Spain’s electric car sector has seen bold moves before, as reported earlier with the Liux BIG’s pre-launch reservations. But Morocco’s project, with Chinese money and multilateral backing, is moving faster and on a bigger scale. It marks a new phase in the race for electric mobility in the region.

artigo.texto: Massive new data centers are the physical foundation for tech companies’ hopes and dreams for AI. But the rush to expand warehouses full of energy-hungry servers has also kicked up fights across the world over their impact on power grids, utility bills, nearby communities, and the environment. From audacious plans to launch data centers into space to the latest legal battles over pollution, The Verge has the biggest news and reporting surrounding data centers. - Google is sending an AI satellite into space next weekGoogle is getting ready to launch a satellite with its AI processors to test how well they perform in space, as reported earlier by The New York Times. The move is part of Google’s Project Suncatcher, the company’s experimental initiative that could eventually put AI data centers into orbit. The satellite, equipped with Google’s Tensor Processing Units, will launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on October 1st, allowing it to harness the power of the sun in low Earth orbit. As noted by Google, the goal of the mission is to measure how well its TPUs “handle the physical stress of spaceflight and the radiation and thermal extremes of space.” Read Article > - Data centers are black boxes, but California wants to change thatCalifornia Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a slate of bills on Monday that could finally give communities better data — and more say — on how data centers impact their electricity bills and water supply. As data centers invade a growing number of communities across the US, they’ve triggered protests over how the infrastructure underpinning AI might stress power grids and local water systems. That’s fueled partly by concerns about how difficult it is to see just how much electricity or water they’re actually gobbling up. California’s new disclosure rules won’t offer a full picture, but starting next year, data center operators will have to start sharing some of these details. The transparency will help scientists and the public see whether data centers are raising bills, draining dwindling resources, and making good on sustainability commitments. Read Article > - Americans sour even more on data centers.A new report from the Pew Research Center adds more data points to the thing everyone seems to know by now: data centers are pretty unpopular. Negative marks are up in every category Pew surveyed, with only 4% of respondents thinking that data centers “have a mostly good impact” across the board. Remarkably, in just 7 months, people who say they’ve heard “nothing at all” about data centers dropped from 25% to 12%. Makes sense: they’re big, noisy, and increasingly have nowhere to hide. Americans’ views of data centers have turned more negative[Pew Research Center] - California tightens rules on AI data center energy and water useCalifornia Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed seven bills designed to prevent AI data centers from passing utility costs onto residents, as reported earlier by the Los Angeles Times. The package of laws requires the California Public Utilities Commission to introduce a new rate classification for data centers while forcing them to pay for upgrades to local power grids and water systems. Other bills included in the package will require proposed data centers to disclose their estimated water use to local governments, along with information about energy efficiency and drought planning. They must also meet certain energy, water, and fuel consumption requirements before qualifying for a streamlined approval process. Last week, Newsom signed an executive order to speed up the creation of an AI “kill switch.” Read Article > - Virginia governor creates an AI task force and moves to restrain data centersVirginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger ordered the state government to take steps that could empower local communities to have a larger say in data center development and slow down approvals in a state that is already home to the data center capital of the world. Executive Order 22 bans executive branch officials from signing nondisclosure agreements for data center projects, requires expedited noise regulations, and requires a review of backup-generation operations used by data centers, among other requirements. The order also establishes an AI task force responsible for evaluating how the state government can address risks to Virginians like workforce displacement and data privacy issues, and determining how existing law can be applied to AI harms. Read Article > - The AI data center e-waste problem is huge — and getting biggerE-waste from the AI boom has been vastly underestimated, a new report warns. By 2050, it could become enough trash to fill 23 million shipping containers — roughly enough 40-foot containers to circle the world six times if lined up in a row. It’s a significantly higher estimate of AI’s e-waste than previous studies have found because the authors of the new report factor in all the infrastructure needed to support servers in data centers. The broader scope provides a clearer picture of junk AI leaves behind, according to the nonprofit Basel Action Network (BAN), which published the paper today. What are you reading / watching / playing / interested in this week? Tell me so I can tell everyone! artigo.texto: 'Let Data Reign': Trump goes all in on controversial data centers Trump argued that data centers will make communities "successful and rich." President Donald Trump on Monday stressed his strong support for controversial data centers, a key issue ahead of midterm elections, with the president urging communities to "let Data Reign." "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign," Trump wrote in a social media post on Monday morning. The president has long emphasized the importance of artificial intelligence advancement, repeatedly expressing his desire for the U.S. to beat China in the global AI race. "If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame. China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement. Actually, they can’t believe it is happening!" Trump wrote. Data centers provide the computing power necessary to process large amounts of data, such as the kind needed to run AI systems. They typically house thousands of computer servers and require tremendous amounts of land, water for cooling, and energy, potentially straining local power grids, while employing few workers long-term, relative to their size. The issue of data centers has been a hot topic ahead of the midterm elections, with AI companies spending millions on congressional races and primaries for and against candidates on the issue of artificial intelligence regulation. Asked on Monday about Trump's post and how it might land ahead of the midterms, Vice President JD Vance said the president's message was focused on the economics around data centers. "What the president said about data centers is they're an important part of the AI economy. But when people build them, they have to build the power plants along with the data centers,” Vance said. Vance acknowledged the backlash surrounding data centers, expressing his belief that the concern stems from higher utility and electricity bills. But he argued that this wouldn't be a problem if companies take advantage of deregulation efforts. "I think probably 99% of the backlash to data centers has come in areas where building a data center means higher utility and higher electricity for the people on the ground," Vance said. "So I think what these companies have to do is take advantage of some of the federal deregulatory efforts that we've undertaken. If you build a data center, you should be putting power back into the grid, not taking it out. And if that is happening, I don't think the data centers are that controversial," Vance said. Earlier this month, the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the Senate GOP's campaign committee, wrote a memo to AI companies operating in Ohio and warned that backlash to data centers could hurt incumbent Republican Sen. John Husted’s chances at reelection. Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott also recently paused new data center projects to ensure compliance -- something that Trump had criticized as a "mistake." "I saw Texas the other day sort of is against data centers. I think it's a mistake. And I’m not taking positions, I just think it’s a mistake, because there are other communities that want it. When a community wants it, it means a lot of money is going to come into that community," Trump had said during a Punchbowl interview earlier this month. In the Punchbowl interview, the president expressed his belief that data centers are "tremendously important for the economics" and said they could be "bigger than oil."

artigo.texto: NYS announces awards for 8 battery storage plants statewide, 2 in Brookhaven New York State on Wednesday announced awards for eight new battery-energy storage plants, including two in Brookhaven Town, where opposition has been coalescing for more than a year. The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority announced the awards as part of Gov. Kathy Hochul’s plan to install about 6,000 megawatts of battery-energy storage around the state by 2030. All of the projects awarded this week propose using lithium-ion batteries and all are slated to be in operation by 2030, adhering to stricter new fire-code safety standards. NYSERDA also plans to announce more award winners by year's end. The awards come just over a week after the state announced the results of toxic plume investigation in East Hampton that confirmed it was the result of a fire-suppression system used at a much smaller battery plant following a 30-hour thermal-runaway fire in 2023. NYSERDA, in announcing the awards, said the latest projects "will provide public health benefits from reduced exposure to harmful pollutants" among other benefits. NYSERDA chief executive Doreen Harris and other officials were not available for interviews, a spokeswoman said. WHAT NEWSDAY FOUND - New York State on Wednesday announced awards for eight new battery-energy storage plants, including two in Brookhaven Town. - All of the projects awarded this week propose using lithium-ion batteries and all are slated to be in operation by 2030, adhering to stricter new fire-code safety standards. - The two Brookhaven projects, one on Morris Avenue in Holtsville and the other at 62 Weeks Ave. in Manorville, already have many of their needed permits, Newsday has reported. The two Brookhaven projects, one on Morris Avenue in Holtsville and the other at 62 Weeks Ave. in Manorville, already have many of their needed permits, Newsday has reported. But the Town of Brookhaven in recent months has indicated a hesitancy to move forward with issuing final construction permits for plants given what Brookhaven Supervisor Dan Panico has said was a lack of support for batteries from Hochul's administration. Brookhaven is one of the few Long Island towns that does not have a moratorium on batteries, and Islip Town last week approved a ban on so-called Tier 3 battery plants that would prevent the largest plants from being built, including a proposed 79-megawatt plant by Key Capture Energy, which is building the Manorville plant. Panico wasn’t available for comment. Fran Lunati, a Holbrook resident, said she and other opponents of the Holtsville battery plant which is less than a mile from their homes, will continue to fight it. "Gov. [Kathy] Hochul shouldn’t have the ability to decide what’s happening in our town," Lunati said, vowing to "continue to fight with the people in my community for our drinking water and clean air." Opponents have been fighting the plant since the state Public Service Commission issued a needed certificate for the facility in 2023. The project is the subject of a lawsuit by developer, Savion Energy, which sued Suffolk County after Suffolk declined to grant a needed variance, citing the storage of over-the-limit toxic liquids at the site. Savion won the case in state Supreme Court, but Suffolk has filed an appeal with the state Appellate Division. Savion spokeswoman Johnna Guinty declined comment. William J. Miller, an energy expert at ClearView Consultants who has advised developers of the Holtsville project, said its location makes it ideal for the LIPA grid given a related interconnection point for Sunrise Wind, which is expected to provide power for the 110-megawatts of batteries. "Not all battery storage projects are created equal," he said, but Holtsville "has exceptionally high location value and is connected directly to the same interconnection point as Sunrise Wind." The Manorville storage project is even larger, at 150 megawatts on three parcels of just over 9 acres south of the Long Island Expressway. Chris Linsmayer, a spokesman for Key Capture Energy, said KCE officials weren’t available to discuss the project. In a statement via email, he wrote the project will "help Long Island meet growing energy demand, support grid reliability for the region, and help households and businesses save on energy costs." He declined to say what the project would cost or specifically how it would reduce customer bills. "KCE has met with and will continue to meet with local fire departments and officials," Linsmayer wrote in the email, noting the project is to be located more than 1.5 miles from the Eastport-South Manor Junior-Senior High School. "A comprehensive emergency response plan will be finalized in partnership with the fire department before the facility begins operating, a requirement of the updated New York fire code." artigo.texto: The batteries were delivered by semi-truck and carefully lifted into place by crane in late August. Roughly the size of a 40-foot shipping container, they are the first of 54 units that will make up the 40-megawatt (MW), 160-megawatt-hour (MWh) battery energy storage system, one of the largest in Hawaii. Approved by the Public Utilities Commission in 2023, the project is the first battery storage project to be developed by Hawaiian Electric and part of the company’s plans to reduce carbon emissions and to use renewable resources to generate 100% of electricity by 2045. Currently, about 41% of Maui County’s electricity comes from renewables, including more than 18,000 customer solar systems. The system will also incorporate grid-forming technology, which can help maintain grid stability as the island uses more variable energy resources, including wind and solar. As Maui continues its transition to clean energy, battery storage is becoming increasingly important. Once in service, the system will store excess energy and deliver it back to the grid when it is needed most. The battery doesn’t generate electricity but stores it, shifting energy from resources such as solar and wind, which are often abundant during daylight hours, to better align with customer demand at night. "This project has been years in the making, and seeing the batteries arrive on site brings us one step closer to providing Maui with a more renewable electric grid," said Shelley Takasato, manager of Generation Project Development for Hawaiian Electric. The remaining battery units will arrive in phases over the coming months as construction continues. The project is expected to enter service in 2027. The arrival of the first battery units marks an important step toward a more renewable energy future for Maui.

artigo.texto: “A fraction of proposed data centers will get built. Utilities are wising up.” That was the headline on a May 2025 Utility Dive article that explored the conundrum speculative data center requests pose for U.S. electric utilities. More than a year later, it’s unclear how much has changed. Community opposition has emerged as a major barrier to data center development, with other challenges including construction labor shortages, long lead times for critical electrical equipment, limited power availability in key markets and uncertainty around consumer demand for artificial intelligence tools. More than $170 billion in AI data center capacity has been “blocked, withdrawn, or stalled” by community opposition since January 2024, the energy advisory company Relae, formerly Carbon Direct, said in June. That’s a sizable chunk of the roughly $581 billion Goldman Sachs expects the big tech companies known as hyperscalers to spend in the U.S. on AI infrastructure, including data center construction, this year. Yet market analysts see no sign that the AI-driven construction boom will disappear anytime soon, despite challenges. Goldman Sachs said in May it sees U.S. data center power demand more than doubling from its 2025 levels to reach 66 GW in 2027. Only about half of data center capacity scheduled for the next one to two years is expected to come online on time amid delays and cancellations, it said. The Electric Power Research Institute, a research nonprofit, said in February that data centers will represent 9% to 17% of U.S. electricity demand in 2030 and up to 20% by 2035. Questions persist around the scale, timing and location of new data center load. If anything, the uncertainty is growing amid public backlash to data centers that is fueling state-led efforts to impose stricter rules on data center development, up to and including moratoriums on new facilities in some places. Firmer answers would benefit not only the utility planners and regulators ensuring that the electric grid is neither over- nor under-built, but also the millions of other customers who could bear the consequences of a disorderly buildout, industry experts say. Texas hits the brakes on large loads as states assert control Many utilities and their regulators have turned to large-load tariffs to try and weed out speculative load by requiring minimum contract durations, minimum billing demand and collateral requirements, upfront payments for impact studies, exit fees and specific ramp schedules. Some states have also introduced incentives for developers that bring their own capacity, agree to be flexible in their energy use or commit to state clean energy or economic development goals. The question of just how much data center capacity is going to come online, and when, is particularly urgent in Texas, which has paused new data center interconnections pending an audit of its 474-GW queue. That’s more than five times the Texas grid’s recent all-time peak demand record of a little over 90 GW set this summer. Few experts expect all that load to materialize. Pablo Vegas, president and CEO of the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, is among the skeptics. “We believe this forecast to be higher than expected future load growth,” Vegas said in an April statement, citing uncertainty around protocols for identifying, verifying and incorporating large load demand into long-range planning. Vegas said ERCOT would work with the Public Utilities Commission of Texas to adjust its forecasting methodology. Thomas Gleeson, the PUCT’s chairman, was more blunt in an appearance on the Energy Capital podcast in June. “The projections are extremely high, and what we know is that a lot of that load will not actually come here. A lot of it is speculative,” Gleeson said in comments made before the interconnection pause. The sheer number of large-load interconnection requests compounds the state’s challenge. Texas’s load growth — not only from large computing and industrial loads, but also garden-variety residential and commercial demand — is leading to congestion in load pockets that previously had capacity to spare, Gleeson said. That creates unwelcome uncertainty for large-load customers eager to put steel in the ground. “That has been the problem we have been trying to solve for the past eight or so months — that when [a customer has] an interconnection agreement and they are ready to move forward, they know that the capacity will be there to serve them so they can make proper business decisions,” Gleeson said. Texas has developed “gating” conditions to discourage speculative interconnection requests, balance load and capacity and “make sure that no one is harmed by these large loads,” Gleeson said. Last summer, Gov. Greg Abbott, R, signed Senate Bill 6, a sweeping measure requiring prospective large-load customers to demonstrate site control, substantially cover necessary grid upgrades, disclose duplicative interconnection requests elsewhere in Texas and accept curtailment during firm load shed events, among other provisions. On June 18, the PUCT adopted a cluster study framework for prospective loads larger than 75 MW that officials said would streamline a “lengthy and repetitive” sequential study process as ERCOT stakeholders work to develop a comprehensive transmission planning framework later this year. ERCOT said at the time that it expected to publish a final transmission plan for the first study cluster, known as “Batch Zero,” in late 2027. Gleeson said on the podcast that the cluster study and transmission planning frameworks will mitigate uncertainty for large loads, grid operators and generation owners across Texas. Together, they assure loads that “once they interconnect, they will get the electricity they need to fully energize,” and they assure other stakeholders that “all the loads coming here are real and will stay,” he said. artigo.texto: As large-scale data center proposals pop up around the St. Louis region, one of the biggest concerns among residents is noise pollution. Across the country, people living near the largest data centers have complained about the sounds they emit, even taking their arguments to the courts with multiple lawsuits. Here’s the sound of the Space X Colossus 1 facility in Memphis, recorded by Richard Banks at WBHM in Birmingham, Alabama, for a series on data centers. To understand how data center noise is different from other sounds, St. Louis Public Radio’s Kate Grumke sat down with St. Louis University professor Kasey Fowler-Finn, who studies sound and especially low-frequency noise. Here are three takeaways from their conversation. 1. Data center noise can stand out from other city noise Data center noise is fundamentally different from other noises humans produce in cities, Fowler-Finn explained. “A lot of the sound that is produced by traffic, by normal industrial installations is going to be mid- to high frequency, and it's also going to be spread out over a bunch of different frequencies,” she said. “So that's going to sound kind of broadband, like maybe hissing, there may be clunks in there, but it's going to be more spread out across multiple frequencies.” Noise from large data centers, on the other hand, is concentrated in low frequencies, Fowler-Finn said. That makes it sound like a hum that stands out. Fowler-Finn compares regular city noise to the rumble of a train passing by and data center noise to a child’s scream. “You can still hear that scream above the train because all of the sound is concentrated into a single frequency,” Fowler-Finn said. “And that's why these data center hums tend to be so piercing and so evident is because they're concentrated in single frequencies and they really stand out from background noise no matter how loud or what frequency that background noise is in.” Fowler-Finn also said the low frequency noise is harder to dampen with structures or plants. That means it can travel farther. “For traffic sound, you may not be able to hear it past, like, 300 feet,” Fowler-Finn said. “But a low-frequency hum from a data center might travel 800 feet or further. We know that the greatest area of impact from these large data centers is 3,000 feet, which is about half a mile.” 2. Sound pollution can impact health Excessive noise can hurt human health, according to the World Health Organization and multiple studies. “There's a pretty big body of literature on how noise pollution impacts human health, and this applies to both low frequencies and high frequencies,” Fowler-Finn said. Noise is a form of environmental pollution, Fowler-Finn said, and like other pollutants it can negatively affect both humans and other living beings. Negative health impacts can include sleep disruption, hypertension and hearing and cognitive impairment, the WHO reports. And the sound from data centers can have far-reaching impacts on human health, Fowler-Finn said. “They increase cortisol. They increase cardiovascular risk. They decrease cognitive functioning, especially in children. In a hospital setting, they can delay healing and recovery,” she said. Fowler-Finn is especially concerned about those health impacts in the area around a proposed project in Midtown, known as the Armory Data Center, and she has brought those concerns to public hearings. She points to St. Louis University dorms and the new Children’s Hospital wing that are within a half-mile of the site. “I suspect that anyone within that radius is going to be having a much harder time sleeping, concentrating, their health is going to be impacted by a data center in that site,” Fowler-Finn said. The developer behind the Armory project said they are taking the question of low-frequency sound seriously and contend that sound is not only a problem with data centers. “What's different about the Armory Innovation District is that our permit imposes tougher restrictions on this site, beyond the city's general noise rules which regulate other commercial uses,” said David Daneshforooz, CEO and co-founder of TerraWatt, the company developing the project. 3. Fowler-Finn wants cities to do more to regulate data center sound St. Louis recently passed new regulations for data centers that include multiple measures targeting noise pollution. They require annual third-party reports on noise emissions, acoustically treated enclosures around noisy equipment and 600-feet setbacks for major data centers from schools, residential facilities or parks. But Fowler-Finn said the setbacks are “woefully insufficient” because the most severe impacts fall within 3,000 feet. She said other measures in the new policy should be tightened to better monitor low-frequency sound. The new policies also don’t apply to the Midtown data center project because it was approved before they were in place. The data center is instead regulated by its conditional use permit, which has different policies on sound. “Once in operation, independent monitoring will measure the sound produced, including low-frequency, identify any issues so that we can address them,” Daneshforooz said in the statement. “These are enforceable requirements of the project’s approval, not voluntary promises. Our responsibility is to meet those requirements and be a good neighbor.” For any city considering allowing a large data center to build in its midst, Fowler-Finn has written a policy framework on sound regulations. She also wants data center companies to do more on their end. “If developers have multiple billions of dollars to produce these installations, instead of fighting to put these in where people live and work, they should be working on technology that makes these friendlier to the environment,” Fowler-Finn said.
