artigo.texto: ADM is entering the voluntary carbon removal market, with a project supported by its Columbus, Nebraska facility, which can capture more than 800,000 tons of CO2 per year, the company shared in a press release. The commodity company is working with Puro.earth to certify and issue carbon dioxide removal credits for its corn processing facility in Columbus, using global crediting company’s Geologically Stored Carbon methodology. These initial carbon credits will be available by the end of the year, and ADM will issue certifications for a 15-year crediting period, the company stated. This announcement is built on ADM’s previous partnership with energy infrastructure company Tallgrass in 2025, which captures biogenic CO2 from ethanol fermentation and stores it at Tallgrass’ Eastern Wyoming Sequestration Hub. This hub houses underground carbon capture and sequestration wells that are regulated through the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality Class VI permit. “Certifying carbon removal at this scale demands real rigor, and we believe ADM has approached every stage – from measurement and data collection through to third-party audit – with the discipline and transparency that an investment-grade market requires. The audit process has run exceptionally smoothly, which is testament to the team ADM has built around this asset, and the hard work of the Puro.earth team coordinating with them. That partnership is what turns one of the world’s largest bioethanol carbon capture facilities into verified, investable carbon removal, and it sets a replicable benchmark for this sector worldwide,” Jan-Willem Bode, president of Puro.earth, said in the press release. ADM’s decarbonization efforts pay off This announcement comes less than a week since ADM released its 2025 regen ag report, with the company reporting that it has cut nearly a million metric tons of CO2 emissions through sustainable farming practices. “Our growth strategy is predicated on smart investments that build on our world-class footprint, and carbon capture is a great example of that. More broadly, we view agriculture as a powerful engine to lower carbon, and our capabilities uniquely position us to help deliver for stakeholders across value chains,” Kris Lutt, VP of innovation and growth at ADM. He added, “ADM has more than a decade of experience supporting carbon capture and geologic storage, including operating Class VI wells at our Decatur, Illinois, facility. That experience, together with Tallgrass’ CO2 transportation and sequestration system and the capabilities of other project participants, positions us to connect agricultural production with growing carbon removal markets at scale.”

artigo.texto: Data centre buildout is uplifting the US battery energy storage system (BESS) outlook across all market segments, according to market research firm Wood Mackenzie. Wood Mackenzie released its Q3 2026 US Energy Storage Monitor report on 23 September, which predicted US energy storage installations will grow over 50% in megawatt terms over the next five years, as low costs propel storage into new regions and use cases. According to the report, the US BESS market installed a record 5.4GW/18.9GWh in Q2 2026, even as installed power fell 7% year-over-year. Extended-duration utility-scale and residential BESS fuelled MWh expansion even as MW installations weakened. Utility-scale projects reached 4.7GW/17.6GWh in Q2, representing an 8% year-over-year decline in MW capacity as major markets approach saturation. artigo.texto: DALLAS — Data centers, artificial intelligence and the power needed to run it all were at the center of conversations at Data Center World Power 2026 in North Texas. The event brought together people working on the technology and infrastructure behind the digital economy. “Data centers are here. They're being used for literally everything,” said Bill Kleyman of Data Center World. Kleyman said one of the biggest challenges facing the industry is having enough electricity to keep up with demand. “The challenge in our environment is that we certainly don't have enough power,” Kleyman said. Artificial intelligence is driving demand for new data centers, and those facilities can require enormous amounts of electricity. “This has never been seen in this country before," said Scott Byer of Mesa Power Solutions. "This amount of load growth that is just, in some ways, it's unfathomable how we're going to build this much so fast." In Texas, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) projects peak electricity demand could reach nearly 368,000 megawatts by 2032. That means the conversations at the event weren't just about building more data centers. They were about finding new ways to power them. Some companies are looking to generate electricity directly at the data center. “The power core is a half megawatt engine we package ourselves that we then train into a 3 megawatt train,” said Byer. Others are looking to batteries and microgrids to help manage demand. “The batteries are smoothing the problem so that there is no increased burden for the overall grid for the consumers,” said Pasi Taimela of Flex Gen. The goal is to meet growing demand while helping limit additional pressure on the electric grid. “Now within our grid, we are seeing ways that we can use all these kinds of systems to bolster it, make them more secure, you know, reduce brownouts and reduce outages,” Kleyman said. Kleyman said the technology showcased at the event isn't just about what happens inside a data center. “They impact how we communicate, how we do things every single day,” Kleyman said. “This technology, it's our lifeblood. It's literally a part of a digital economy." As demand for electricity grows, so does the focus on how Texas will generate and deliver enough power to support the next generation of data centers while maintaining reliability for other electricity users. The challenge lies in expanding the power system quickly enough to support a growing digital economy.

artigo.texto: The Montana Supreme Court on Thursday vacated its own injunction, which temporarily allowed a proposed data center initiative to appear on the November ballot in Butte-Silver Bow County, less than 48 hours after issuing it. In its five-page order, the court said it stands by its earlier reasoning: that allowing voters to consider the initiative, even if it were later invalidated, is preferable to denying them the opportunity to vote on a measure that might ultimately be found eligible for the ballot. RELATED Supreme Court puts Butte’s data center initiative back on the ballot General election voters in Butte-Silver Bow County may now consider a proposed ballot initiative that would require citizen approval of data center development, after the Montana Supreme Court overturned a lower court ruling that prevented the initiative from appearing on the November ballot. In a court filing responding to the decision, the county said it… Still, the justices said Thursday, they would not have granted initiative organizers’ request for an injunction had they known that the county’s ballots have already been printed and mailed, with some having already been returned by voters. The justices said Montana election law does not provide a process for adding an initiative after ballots have been prepared, or for issuing supplemental ballots to voters who have already cast their ballots. “The situation the parties and this Court find themselves in was entirely avoidable,” the court wrote. The justices said court filings by the initiative organizers implied that ballots had not yet been printed and mailed. The court also noted that the county, having taken no position on the organizers’ request for an injunction, also failed to inform the justices that ballots had already been printed and mailed. “Surely it could have taken this opportunity to advise the Court about what Proponents had neglected to mention in their emergency motion,” the justices wrote of the county’s failure to disclose that ballots have already been printed and mailed. In vacating the injunction, the court rejected the organizers’ proposal to issue separate ballots containing only the initiative, saying organizers had not explained how that process would comply with Montana election law. The decision reverses Tuesday’s temporary order, which prohibited the county from rejecting the initiative over organizers’ failure to meet a signature-submission deadline due to incorrect information initially provided by election officials. The organizers’ appeal of a district court decision rejecting their request to place the initiative on the ballot remains pending. artigo.texto: Derrick Van Orden holds press conference discussing his view on data centers MENOMONIE, Wis. (WEAU) - The data center debate is hitting Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District race. Republican Incumbent, Derrick Van Orden, held a press conference in Menomonie on Thursday looking to clear his record. This comes as political ads are running that criticize Van Orden for taking campaign contributions from people and organizations tied to the data center industry. The ad also criticizes the congressman for voting for the One Big Beautiful Bill act, which included tax breaks that data center developers have used over the past year. Van Orden says his opponent, Democratic Candidate Rebecca Cooke, has worked with the Wisconsin Technology Council and the think tank Third Way. artigo.texto: Data centers have become a contentious issue across the country. Owing in large part to the increased use of artificial intelligence, more and more data centers are being constructed in the U.S. This has come with significant costs. Data centers gobble up a tremendous amount of energy, most of which still comes from fossil fuels. This has also increased energy prices for consumers. Data centers use up to millions of gallons of water a day, threatening the availability and affordability of local supplies. In light of these concerns, Shinsuke Tanaka, assistant professor of agricultural and resource economics in the College of Agriculture, Health and Natural Resources (CAHNR), an expert on health and environmental economics, weighs in on how these issues are impacting human and environmental health. Connecticut began offering tax incentives for developers to build data centers in the state starting in 2021. Since then, local opposition to data center projects has grown. Groton, West Haven, and Morris have instituted moratoriums on data center construction in their communities. Many others are weighing implementing their own bans. “This is really not just a local issue,” Tanaka says. One of the largest issues when it comes to data centers and health, Tanaka says, is that data centers are contributing to increased air pollution. “The biggest issue is that data centers use a lot of energy,” Tanaka says. “Currently, fossil fuels are still used as a major energy source, and they emit pollution as electricity is generated.” Tanaka has previously demonstrated that downwind pollution from power plants led to higher COVID-19 mortality rates. According to the World Health Organization, air pollution has also been linked to a host of other health conditions. Because energy is generated regionally, the impact of data centers extends beyond the area immediately surrounding a center. “Air pollution has a huge impact on human health,” Tanaka says. “There are a lot of studies on this topic. The data centers are just increasing and expanding and the trajectory is skyrocketing, and the concern about air pollution is not just local, but it’s regional.” On a local level, data centers are equipped with diesel generators for backup power, creating air pollution there as well. Because the data center boom is so new, there has not yet been a comprehensive study analyzing how much more electricity and hence pollution is being generated to power them. But a Cornell University study projects data centers will put an additional 24 to 44 million metric tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere by 2030. While the exact numbers may be unclear, researchers already know a lot about the health impacts of air pollution. “The concerns that come from increased energy consumption and increased pollution in terms of how that affects local health and the environment – it is known,” Tanaka says. “We can extrapolate evidence from different contexts to data centers.” Another consideration is that data centers are built where land is cheap. This means that these areas are generally already under-resourced communities, and often communities of color. This can exacerbate existing health disparities. “They’re the ones that are affected by the existence of data centers,” Tanaka says. Data centers also produce 24/7 noise pollution which, based on studies looking at noise pollution from wind turbines and airports, has been linked to increased rates of depression and suicide. Noise pollution also leads to lower home values. Further, data centers’ water usage has become an even more serious concern as many regions face hotter, drier climates. This could also lead to higher water utility prices for consumers. “They’re consuming a lot of water,” Tanaka says. “Especially now, we’ve seen a lot of hot air and a lack of rain, and this year a lot of regions faced drought. So, that has been another concern.” There are ways that data centers can be run more sustainably, Tanaka explains. For example, there is a push to require data centers to use battery storage for backup power instead of diesel generators, which can use energy more efficiently and do not directly produce air pollution. Data centers can also draw more of their electricity from renewable forms of energy. “I think we can achieve both economic prosperity along with environmental sustainability and protection,” says Tanaka. “The key isn’t just prohibiting data centers. So, we need to think about how to generate electricity.” Anna Zarra Aldrich is with UConn Today. This story is shared in cooperation with UConn Today.

artigo.texto: Gov. Greg Abbott discusses property taxes, data centers during Sherman visit SHERMAN, Texas (KXII) - Texas Gov. Greg Abbott visited MG’s in Sherman Thursday to discuss two key priorities ahead of the November election: data centers and affordability. Sherman Mayor Shawn Teamann said residents have raised concerns about several issues. “It’s cost of living, it’s gas, it’s insurance, it’s housing, it’s taxation, it’s efficiency,” Teamann said. Abbott said he wants to give residents the power to decide whether a data center can come to their community. “Those local residents will be working with their city officials, with their county officials to make sure that what may be wanted in Grayson County may be different than what’s wanted in some other county,” Abbott said. Property tax cuts Another focus of Abbott’s visit was cutting property taxes. Cities within Grayson County have sales tax, but the county itself relies purely on property taxes. Abbott was asked what safeguards would be put in place for counties if property taxes were cut. “One thing that we must pass this next session is a reduction in those unfunded mandates onto our cities and small towns, and that will go a long way toward them saving money. Second, the way that the spending limit works for the state of Texas, it adjusts for inflation plus population growth,” Abbott said. District 62 State Rep. Shelley Luther said lawmakers are preparing to partner with the governor to deliver on those priorities. “We are going to tackle these things. And I’m serious when I say the Republican Party has never been more united than it is right now,” Luther said. Democratic response Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa has called on Abbott to debate ahead of the November election. “Let me tell you what I’m doing. I’m doing the most important thing a candidate could do. And that is I’m going to community after community,” Abbott said. In response to Thursday’s visit, Texas Democratic Party spokesman Jacob Long issued the following statement. Copyright 2026 KXII. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Craig Thompson is co-founder of Austin, Texas-based specialty executive recruitment firm Allegiance Search, which focuses on digital infrastructure, energy and advanced manufacturing teams. Opinions are the author’s own. Power has been the defining barrier to the data center industry growth for years. But in August, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott gave the industry a very public reminder that access to power is not the only thing developers need to worry about. Abbott temporarily halted approvals for new data center projects within Texas’ grid interconnection process and ordered an audit of pending developments amid concerns over grid reliability and the extraordinary volume of proposed new electricity demand. It was reported that around 90% of the 474 GW of proposed new load requests in the state were linked to data centers. For anyone working in digital infrastructure, let alone Texas developments, this is a bit of a jaw-dropper. Texas is one of the most pro-development states in the country and expected to become one of the most important data center markets in the world. Yet the state is now effectively saying that expansion has to happen on terms that protect the existing grid and the communities already relying on it. I think that points to the next major development challenge for this industry. On top of powered land and capital, developers need public support. The residents pushing back have a point It’s easy for us to characterize community opposition as people failing to understand the economic opportunity data centers create. I think that would be a mistake. Let’s look at the development through the eyes of someone living in one of the smaller communities where these projects are often being built. They are not thinking about artificial intelligence compute demand or the long-term value of hyperscale infrastructure. They are thinking about what has changed outside their front door: construction traffic, noise pollution, open land suddenly becoming a construction site and, of course, energy costs. If residents believe a huge new user of electricity is contributing to higher costs or putting additional strain on the infrastructure they already depend on, telling them the project will ultimately be good for the local economy is not going to win them over. Abbott’s intervention is important precisely because those concerns have moved beyond local protest and into state-level infrastructure policy. Texas is now scrutinizing whether proposed data center demand is realistic and whether the grid can support it without placing an unreasonable burden on existing customers. That is a significant change in the conversation. The benefits are real, but they arrive later There is obviously the other side to this — and for the record, the side I believe really matters. Data centers bring substantial economic benefits to the communities where they are developed. The construction phase creates thousands of jobs. Once operational, the projects provide permanent employment and can generate significant local tax revenue. Over time, that money contributes to roads, public services and wider infrastructure improvements. The problem is that the costs and benefits arrive on completely different timelines. The disruption begins as soon as construction starts. The larger economic benefits might take years to materialize. That gap is where developers risk losing people. If your commute gets worse this month, your electricity costs increase and the landscape around your town changes dramatically, it is understandable that the promise of better infrastructure five or 10 years from now does not immediately feel like much of a win. Community relations as a development function This hurdle has given rise to community relations as a genuine leadership function. At scale, more developers are hiring senior people specifically to manage the relationship between projects and the communities around them. The title varies. In some businesses it sits under community relations, while elsewhere it falls closer to external affairs. The purpose is the same. These people are the link between the developer and the community. Their job is to explain what is being built, why it is being built and what the long-term benefits could be. Just as importantly, they need to understand local concerns early and make sure those concerns reach the people making decisions inside the business. That is why I think the role is moving well beyond traditional public relations. When projects create visible disruption before the benefits arrive, somebody has to own that communication. Developers need people who can engage credibly with local leaders and residents while also giving the internal team a much clearer understanding of how the project is being received — before the cardboard signs come out. As data center projects become more politically and publicly visible, community relations is moving closer to the core of how those projects are developed, and I expect that to continue. Over the next few years, I think we will see community relations professionals become a much bigger board-level priority, particularly for those building at scale across multiple markets. The companies that recognize that early will be better prepared for the next phase of data center growth.

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Monday signed seven bills aimed at giving communities more information about proposed data centers’ energy, water, workforce and land use to help weigh their economic costs and benefits. - The new laws require data centers “pay their fair share of grid update costs,” disclose water use to local governments and give up eligibility for blanket environmental exemptions, according to the governor’s office. - They come on the heels of Los Angeles County’s planning director ordering a temporary ban on development of large-scale AI data centers in unincorporated areas of California’s most populous county, according to multiple news reports. Dive Insight: California is home to 296 data centers, the third highest number in the U.S., according to Data Center Map. “Communities are left to deal with the consequences — higher electricity demand, grid constraints, water use, and pollution,” Newsom said in a statement. “With these laws, we are ensuring that Californians remain in the driver’s seat — and that those profiting from data centers aren’t doing so at our expense.” The bills Newsom signed Monday include: SB 1168: Directs the California Public Utilities Commission to examine data centers’ energy use and ensure they pay for transmission and distribution upgrades and load increases. “Californians’ utility bills are already among the highest in the nation, and the rapid growth of data centers is threatening to send rates through the roof,” state Sen. Jerry McNerney, the bill’s sponsor, said in a statement. SB 886 and SB 887: Require data centers to pay all infrastructure upgrade and generation costs, bear a larger share of wildfire mitigation and liability costs, and undergo environmental review. The bills will also ensure local communities have a say in data center projects, according to a news release from state Sen. Steve Padilla, the bills’ sponsor. “These are some of the nation’s strongest data center ratepayer protections — stopping Big Tech from sticking California families with the bill for their data centers,” Padilla said in a statement. AB 1577: Requires monthly reporting of data centers’ energy consumption and efficiency metrics to the California Energy Commission and estimated energy usage to local agencies as part of permitting. AB 2383: Incentivizes data centers to use onsite clean energy resources to help California “responsibly plan for the future of our electrical grid while keeping electricity costs down for consumers,” the bill’s sponsor, Assemblyman Rick Chavez Zbur, said in a statement. AB 2469 and AB 2619: Strengthen oversight of data center water use by requiring potential data center developers to complete a water supply assessment and develop a water scarcity plan during permitting and establishing a statewide water reporting requirement to obtain and renew business licenses. “Every drop counts,” Assemblymember Diane Papan, chair of the Assembly Water Committee and sponsor of the bills, said in a statement. “We cannot manage what we do not measure.”

artigo.texto: CHESTERFIELD COUNTY, Va. — Chesterfield County residents are speaking out about how the county should spend revenue expected from three approved Google data center campuses, as the Board of Supervisors prepares to vote on a proposal that would use that money to lower the car tax. The local NAACP chapter hosted a roundtable Tuesday night, bringing together neighbors, faith leaders and civic organizers from communities closest to the three sites where Google is already approved to build data center campuses. Representatives from Google were invited but backed out, according to the NAACP. "So what I want them to do is go back to the drawing board and actually see like this is not about capitalism, this is not about your stakeholders. This is about the people and we will hold the fort for the people," one attendee said. "I believe that once the community speaks up, that's when change happens. And if we can get consistent community engagement and education, then the community is going to do what needs to be done," another attendee said. Chesterfield officials say they are not accepting any new data center proposals, but the three Google campuses, that include a total of nine buildings, are already approved and set to open in about a decade. The three projects are: - Project Peanut at 2100 Bermuda Hundred Road - Project Loch at 750 Watkins Center Parkway - Project Skye at 4201 Moseley Road Once finished, Google will be the largest commercial taxpayer in the county. Google is projecting revenue of $300 to $500 million per building. County leaders say that level of revenue would reduce the $3.25 car tax rate to about $1.79. The allocation of data center-derived tax revenue is on the Board of Supervisors' agenda today. During August's board meeting, supervisors tabled the car tax vote and spent the month meeting with residents in their respective districts to hear their thoughts on where they want the money directed. "I'm just simply saying that I just think that there's a lot of better ways that would cover things that we should be paying for or making available as resources in the county, and is reducing a personal property tax the best way to do that?" board member Jessica Schneider said during August's board meeting. The Board of Supervisors meeting starts at 6 p.m. in the Public Meeting Room at 10001 Iron Bridge Road. The board will also celebrate 21 residents who are 100 years of age or older during the meeting, in conjunction with National Centenarian's Day, observed annually on Sept. 22. CBS 6 is committed to sharing community voices on this important topic. artigo.texto: BYD is preparing to launch a new electric saloon capable of travelling more than 700km on a single charge. The new Seal 07 EV will offer up to 718km – around 446 miles – of range under Europe's WLTP testing standard, according to information published by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. The flagship version combines an 88.682kWh Blade 2.0 lithium iron phosphate battery with a 300kW electric motor producing around 408hp. It will also have a top speed of 240km/h – approximately 149mph. A cheaper version will use a smaller 76.744kWh battery and 245kW motor producing around 329hp. That model has a claimed 775km range under China's CLTC testing cycle, equivalent to a reported 636km – around 395 miles – using WLTP. BYD's new battery technology also promises dramatically shorter charging stops. The smaller battery is claimed to be capable of charging from 10% to 97% in just nine minutes when connected to suitable high-powered charging infrastructure. At 5,080mm long and 1,960mm wide, the new Seal 07 is a sizeable four-door model and has a 2,960mm wheelbase. It will sit below the flagship Seal 08 in BYD's Ocean range and is set to replace the current Seal 07, which only entered the Chinese market in March. Buyers in China will also be offered a plug-in hybrid Seal 07. That version combines a 1.5-litre turbocharged petrol engine with a 160kW electric motor and 38.029kWh battery. It is claimed to offer 245km of electric-only driving and fuel consumption of 4.25 litres per 100km when the battery is depleted. The rapid replacement comes after relatively modest sales for the existing model, with 1,005 electric and plug-in hybrid Seal 07s reportedly delivered during August. A launch date and pricing for the new generation have yet to be detailed in the supplied information.

artigo.texto: Alyssa Theriot of Catahoula, who recently started her junior year and clinical coursework as a nursing major at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette’s College of Nursing and Health Sciences was an inaugural recipient of the Dolores Bess Scholars award, established through a significant bequest from the estate of Dolores Bess, a 25-year faculty member and devoted advocate for nursing education, who passed away at 91 in 2024. Bess and her husband, William, established the Dolores C. Bess Endowed Scholarship in Nursing in 2012 to support upper-level nursing students through the rigorous demands of clinical coursework. After she passed away, her estate substantially increased the endowment, enabling the College to award larger financial support to a select group of students during their final four semesters; a period when clinical rotations leave little time for part-time work. “Mrs. Bess’s dream was to leave behind a legacy that would make the biggest possible impact on students,” said Dr. Lisa Broussard, dean of the College of Nursing & Health Sciences. “Her scholarship had already benefited 116 recipients since 2012, so when we received her final gift, I knew that increasing the award amount to create even deeper impact would be exactly what she would have wanted.” Theriot, who realized nursing was her calling after witnessing the kindness and empathy of a hospice nurse who cared for her grandmother in her final days of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), said becoming a Dolores Bess Scholar is both a financial lifeline and a confidence booster. “I’m super grateful because my parents sacrificed a lot to get me to this point. Being chosen out of so many applicants has given me the confidence to know I belong here,” she said. Maria Moya of Lafayette was also a recipient of the award. Both women said they are inspired by the kindness and empathy of those who choose to enter the nursing profession. Theriot said, “my grandmother’s hospice nurse cared for her through her hardest days, taking time to be present with her, talk to her and hold her hand. It was then that I learned how important the role of being a caregiver is in supporting someone as they transition to death.” “My grandmother did not speak English, and watching the nurses figure out ways to communicate with and care for her with the utmost compassion was soul touching,” said Moya. “Being bilingual myself, I recognized I could be the person to offer reassurance and comfort to patients who might feel alone or scared due to a language barrier.” To learn more about the College of Nursing & Health Sciences or other University initiatives, contact the University of Louisiana at Lafayette Foundation at (337) 482-0700, email [email protected], or visit give.louisiana.edu.

artigo.texto: The flagship sedan will be among BYD’s most luxurious and advanced vehicles to date, with Rolls-Royce-like coach doors, 5-minute Flash Charging, and possibly solid-state batteries. BYD takes on ultra-luxe brands with Yangwang EV sedan Yangwang is BYD’s highest-end brand with ultra-luxury models ranging from electric hypercars to extreme off-road SUVs. BYD also uses Yangwang to showcase its breakthrough technologies. In the past, Yangwang vehicles have debuted with disruptive new tech, including BYD’s quad-motor e4 platform, second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging, and its Disus Intelligent Body Control System. A new Yangwang model was recently spotted testing in China that, according to local reports, will push the brand further into the elite segment. New images of the vehicle surfaced online, revealing a nearly identical design to the Rolls-Royce Phantom. It will even be BYD’s first vehicle with rear-hinged coach doors. Hu Xiaoqing, Yangwang’s general manager, shared a few images of the flagship sedan on Weibo and confirmed that the car’s name has yet to be finalized. Internally, BYD is calling it “HU” for now. The new model is “the culmination of three years of meticulous development by Yangwang, featuring the brand’s signature design language, and is an ultra-luxury executive sedan.” No other details were revealed, but one image shows the vehicle at BYD’s Flash Charging station, suggesting it can support megawatt fast charging. According to local reports and CarNewsChina, Yangwang’s ultra-luxe sedan may be BYD’s first to use solid-state EV batteries. BYD executive vice president Stella Li confirmed in an exclusive interview with Carwow.es earlier this month that the company is “in the leading position” in solid-state battery tech and its commercialization. Li said that BYD will “prove it” with its first vehicle equipped with solid-state batteries set to debut in 2027. BYD’s battery R&D team is “very strong,” Li said, adding that they are studying the battery chemistry as well as the manufacturing and equipment needed for mass production. FinDreams, BYD’s battery business, aims to begin producing sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries in limited batches in 2027, scaling up to mass production by 2030. Will Yangwang’s ultra-luxe sedan be the first to showcase BYD’s solid-state batteries? If it does, it will likely be offered on higher-priced variants, while standard models could still use BYD’s latest Blade LFP batteries. Outside of that, the flagship model is expected to feature BYD’s quad-motor e4 platform, delivering over 1,000 hp combined. BYD has yet to announce prices or any details, but reports estimate the Yangwang sedan will cost over 2 million yuan, or nearly $300,000. The Yangwang U7, the brand’s current luxury electric sedan, starts at just 658,000 yuan ($98,000). FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.

artigo.texto: O sistema de armazenamento de energia (ESS) da DoGo Power, que forma redes inteligentes, foi lançado e está pronto para encomendas globais. AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 22 de setembro de 2026 XANGAI, 22 de setembro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A DoGo Power realizou o evento “Formando o Futuro da Energia” – Estratégia e Lançamento de Novos Produtos, lançando globalmente sua estratégia “Orientada a Cenários + Formação de Redes + IA”, juntamente com soluções inteligentes de armazenamento de energia para formação de redes para cenários comerciais e industriais (C&I) de grande e médio porte e em escala de serviços públicos. Robin Zhu, fundador e CEO da DoGo Power, afirmou: “Após uma rápida expansão em escala, o setor de armazenamento de energia entrou em uma fase de desenvolvimento de alta qualidade.” A adaptação de cenários, a formação de redes e a IA tornaram-se elementos essenciais da competitividade. O armazenamento de energia precisa deixar de ser uma “unidade de custo” e se tornar uma “unidade criadora de valor”. A DoGo Power concentra-se no armazenamento de energia em escala de rede para formação de redes elétricas, com o objetivo de ser líder em tecnologia de ponta para o novo tipo de sistema de energia. Buscamos cooperar com parceiros globais para fomentar um novo crescimento industrial através da inovação tecnológica.” A DoGo Power estabeleceu três centros de P&D e dois centros de simulação e testes na China, reunindo 19 grupos de especialistas interdisciplinares liderados por doutores, com mais de 60% da equipe dedicada à P&D. Seus três centros de produção globais oferecem uma capacidade de produção de 10 GWh na primeira fase. Apoiada por uma rede de vendas e serviços que abrange mais de 30 países e regiões, a DoGo evoluiu da exportação de produtos para a operação localizada. Orientação estratégica: Da industrialização da energia renovável à transformação das indústrias tradicionais pelas energias renováveis. A DoGo Power identifica um caminho de evolução em quatro estágios para um novo tipo de sistema de energia: 1-Expansão de P&D, da indústria e das tecnologias, 2-Formação de Grade para Estabilização, 3-IA para Maior Receita e 4-Integração Inteligente Holística. O setor encontra-se atualmente na Fase 2. Com base nisso, a DoGo desenvolve uma solução para a Etapa 3 e implementa negócios globais rumo à Etapa 4 sob dois pilares principais: - Definição de soluções baseada em cenários reais de clientes, desafios práticos e valor comercial mensurável. - A plataforma tecnológica 4S, desenvolvida internamente, impulsionada duplamente pela formação de redes e pela IA, possibilita um sistema de energia definido por algoritmo. Integrando EMS, PMS, PCS e BMS, a plataforma 4S constrói estações de armazenamento de energia inteligentes capazes de análise, otimização, tomada de decisões e atualização iterativa. Com o respaldo dessa base técnica, a DoGo fornece soluções em escala de rede adequadas para diversos cenários, requisitos de múltiplas energias e múltiplas escalas temporais em todo o mundo. Soluções de Novos Produtos Baseadas em Cenários Duas soluções emblemáticas de sistemas de armazenamento de energia (ESS) para formação de redes inteligentes foram lançadas para cenários comerciais e industriais (C&I) e de grande escala para concessionárias de serviços públicos. 1.Solução C&I Smart GFM ESS Adotando um design compacto do tipo “1 ESS substitui 8 gabinetes”, esta unidade de 3 metros consolida as funções de seis gabinetes ESS de 260 kWh+, um gabinete combinador, um gabinete on/off-grid e um transformador de isolamento. Isso reduz o CAPEX inicial em 1,2 centavos de dólar por Wh, diminui a ocupação de terras em 35% e encurta a entrega do projeto em 5 a 7 dias. Com suporte para acesso a múltiplas fontes, como painéis fotovoltaicos, geradores a diesel, pontos de recarga, rede elétrica e sistemas de gerenciamento, o sistema permite a comutação perfeita entre conexão e desconexão da rede em ?20ms, atendendo de forma confiável cargas sensíveis e de alta potência e concretizando o conceito de “1 contêiner equivale a 1 microrrede”. A capacidade de dimensionamento flexível suporta a implantação mista de diferentes séries e a compatibilidade com inversores de terceiros para maximizar a utilização dos ativos existentes. 2.Solução de armazenamento de energia GFM inteligente em escala de utilidade pública Desenvolvido para projetos com terrenos complexos e restrições de transporte, o contêiner pesa menos de 22 toneladas, dobrando as rotas de transporte viáveis em comparação com os contêineres convencionais de 20 pés e reduzindo os custos de logística marítima e terrestre. Seu design sem cabos elimina a necessidade de escavações e montagem de cabos no local, com o pré-comissionamento completo do sistema realizado na fábrica. Aproveitando a arquitetura dinâmica de taxa C, os clientes podem começar com uma implementação de duração de 2 horas para controlar o CAPEX e expandir por meio de gabinetes de expansão de data center para ajustar suavemente as taxas C e as durações de backup para corresponder aos modelos de negócios em evolução. Grade-Formando o Núcleo: Arquitetura de Coordenação de 3 Camadas Para equilibrar a estabilidade do sistema e os benefícios econômicos, a DoGo Power adota uma arquitetura de 3 camadas: - Camada de controle formadora de grade estável inferior: Atende às demandas de estabilidade em nível de milissegundos, incluindo a resposta inercial. - Camada intermediária de controle de coordenação eficiente: Executa funções de nível de centenas de milissegundos, como regulação secundária de frequência e tensão e partida a frio rápida. - Camada superior de despacho de otimização inteligente: Oferece previsão e otimização globais para maximizar os retornos econômicos em condições de operação estáveis. artigo.texto: LA VERNE, Calif. (KABC) -- A fire erupted at a battery storage unit at a Metropolitan Water District facility in La Verne on Tuesday, prompting nearby schools to evacuate. The lithium battery fire was reported around 11:40 a.m. near a solar panel field on the northeast side of the facility in the 3200 block of Wheeler Avenue. Crews from the La Verne Fire Department and Los Angeles County Fire Department responded. One employee suffered minor injuries and was taken to a local hospital, according to La Verne Fire Department Battalion Chief Mark Savage. Shortly after 3 p.m., the L.A. County Fire Department said the fire had been knocked down. AIR7 video shows firefighters dousing the flames with water. La Verne fire crews were still monitoring the scene and mopping up, noting that there was still a risk, with more lithium batteries at the site. By Tuesday evening, no flare-ups had been reported, and crews were using a drone to monitor the batteries. Firefighters estimate there are fewer than 20 lithium batteries in the storage facility. "These things do not like any kind of additional heat, and the understanding is, there is something going on with that bank now that it is reacting to the previous heat that it was exposed to," said Batt. Chief Mark Savage. "So we are monitoring closely. We have reinitiated cooling measures for that battery bank now. But it's one of those things that, once it gets started, it's extremely difficult to stop, if not impossible to stop." The fire prompted evacuation orders and warnings near Bonita Avenue and Wheeler Avenue and a shelter-in-place for the surrounding residential neighborhood. Click here to see if you are in an impacted area. Some evacuation orders were later downgraded to warnings. By early Tuesday evening, firefighters said the orders were only impacting the approximately 185 properties closest to the facility. La Verne police said shopping centers along Wheeler Avenue north of Foothill Boulevard were evacuated as a precaution. Grace Miller Elementary School, located just east of the facility, was under a shelter-in-place order, and Holly Oak Street south of the campus was closed to traffic. Savage said students appeared to be released from the school while firefighters battled the blaze. Parents told Eyewitness News that Ramona Middle School and Bonita High School were also affected. Holy Name of Mary School, Damien High School and the University of La Verne were evacuated. The university said all classes were canceled until further notice. Eyewitness News spoke to Ramona Middle School parents who arrived to pick up their kids. By the time most parents arrived, it was already the school's normal pick-up time. "They're blocking off Wheeler, so it makes it a little hectic but scary at the same time, so we're just here getting the kids out of safety," said parent Irene Flores. "We got it on our phones, the emergency message to evacuate our facility. So might as well come get the kids, make sure they're safe," said parent Jason Wagner. "In La Verne, we've never seen these kind of things." The Metropolitan Water District said its water supply was not affected by the fire. The cause of the fire is still under investigation. Savage said nothing like this has happened there before, but it's raising concerns for neighbors who had no clue that the water treatment plant housed massive battery banks with the potential to catch fire. If you're wondering if you live near a facility that houses potentially dangerous or hazardous items, you can find out. Back in May, 7 On Your Side did an investigation and we shared the Environmental Protection Agency's interactive map, where you can learn about the enforcement and compliance history of facilities near you. City News Service contributed to this report.

artigo.texto: Philippines to strengthen carbon market readiness, Article 6 implementation Manila, Philippines As the Philippines advances its carbon market development and strengthens its climate policy framework, national government agencies, private sector, civil society organizations, and international organizations convened for a country workshop on carbon pricing in Mandaluyong City on 18 September 2026. The workshop discusses the Philippines’ institutional and regulatory readiness for carbon market development. It also probed into how the country can better situate itself within the evolving carbon market landscape in Asia and the Pacific, particularly under Article 6 implementation. “We are encouraged by the Philippines’ commitment to climate action through updating of the Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), which will be a fantastic roadmap for all of us. Today’s discussions are an important contribution to [equipping us with] more tools to help move faster in the right direction, towards a low-carbon economy. This is not just a climate agenda, but also an economic agenda, a social agenda, a fiscal agenda,” said Arnaud Peral, United Nations Resident Coordinator in the Philippines. In February 2026, the Philippines adopted the Roadmap to Readiness in the Voluntary Forest Carbon Market to strategically position the country as a high-integrity investment destination for forest carbon. This was followed by the signing of the Philippines and Singapore’s first bilateral implementation of Article 6 during the ASEAN Climate Week in Manila in April 2026, opening pathways for international carbon finance and emissions reduction projects. Despite these developments, the Philippines remains at the early stages of its carbon markets journey. “Carbon prices, sectoral coverage, exemptions, and revenue use differ widely. For the Philippines, the first question is not how to build a carbon market. It is what policy problem a carbon price is expected to solve, and whether carbon pricing is the appropriate instrument designed around national development priorities and our NDC," said Secretary Robert E.A. Borje, Vice Chairperson and Executive Director of the Climate Change Commission (CCC), in his opening remarks. Secretary Borje further emphasized that carbon pricing is one instrument within a wider policy package, and is not a replacement to climate finance, technology development and transfer, and capacity building. The effectiveness of carbon markets in the Philippines will also depend on the country’s existing policies, infrastructure, institutions, and investment environment. “The relevant test is not whether a carbon market can generate trade. It is whether the chosen instrument can reduce emissions cost-effectively, distribute burdens fairly, and support Philippine development and implementation of our NDC.” “With a climate crisis that is threatening to render us extinct, reimagining and reinventing the way we live and do business are a moral and a categorical imperative. Indeed, we do not have a moment to lose—we have to be part of the solution,” said Hon. Rep. Anna Victoria Veloso-Tuazon, Chair of the Committee on Climate Change of the House of Representatives, as she highlighted developments in Philippine climate policies such as the Low Carbon Economy Investment Bill and Climate Accountability Bill. The workshop is organized by the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP), together with the Institute for Climate and Sustainable Cities (ICSC), the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI), the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), and the Asia Society for Social Improvement and Sustainable Transformation (ASSIST). Its findings will feed into a policy paper jointly being developed by UN ESCAP, GGGI, IEEFA and the Southeast Asia Energy Transition Partnership (ETP) to be launched at COP31 in Turkiye. It is a joint publication on forward-looking recommendations and policy signals on carbon pricing in the region, informed by country snapshots of China, Thailand, the Philippines, Republic of Korea, Japan, Indonesia, and Vietnam. About the Organizers The Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP) is the most inclusive intergovernmental platform in the Asia-Pacific region. The Commission promotes cooperation among members in pursuit of solutions to sustainable development challenges. ESCAP is one of the five regional commissions of the United Nations. The Institute for Climate and Sustainable Cities is a Philippine-based non-governmental organization that advances climate, energy, and low-carbon solutions to enable fair and climate-resilient development at the national and international levels. The Global Green Growth Institute is a treaty-based international, inter-governmental organization dedicated to supporting and promoting strong, inclusive and sustainable economic growth in developing countries and emerging economies. The Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis provides independent, evidence-based financial analysis of global energy markets, investment trends, and policies. IEEFA’s work helps investors, policymakers, regulators, communities and the media better understand risks, opportunities and market dynamics shaping the energy transition. The Asia Society for Social Improvement and Sustainable Transformation is an international capacity building NGO that aims to achieve and witness meaningful changes to and for our planet and the people. It works towards the development and protection of the economic, social and environmental conditions.

artigo.texto: Otovo and InCharge Energy Partner to Offer Solar, Battery Storage and EV Charging Services Across U.S. Press Release Date 09-24-2026 Launching in California, Arizona, Texas, and Florida, with additional state launches planned by the end of 2026 HOUSTON & LOS ANGELES--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Otovo ASA (Euronext Oslo Børs: OTOVO; "Otovo"), a leading provider of behind-the-meter energy services for homes and businesses, today announced a service partnership with InCharge Energy ("InCharge"), a trusted national provider of EV charging installation and maintenance services. By combining their service offerings, which together span more than 100,000 energy assets, Otovo and InCharge can provide commercial customers with a single service relationship covering solar, battery storage, and EV charging equipment across key U.S. markets. Together, Otovo and InCharge will offer each other's preventive maintenance plans, with each company dispatching its own technicians, expanding the footprint and capabilities of each service provider. Otovo will bring its Endurance™ AI platform to the shared work, so a job originating with either company is logged, dispatched and closed against one record of the site. Each company continues to sell and perform under its own brand. "We built this partnership around a simple idea: a customer shouldn't need multiple vendors just because their energy assets came from different systems," said William J. (John) Berger, Chief Executive Officer of Otovo. "By joining forces on commercial energy service, we can seamlessly integrate work orders through Endurance™, giving customers one call and one relationship instead of separate vendors and contracts for every system on site." “Technology alone doesn’t keep critical energy infrastructure operating – it takes highly-skilled people in the field,” said Rich Mohr, Chief Executive Officer of InCharge Energy. “Otovo and InCharge have both made significant investments in technical talent and electrical field service capabilities, and we will continue to invest as these systems become more critical to our customers’ operations. By utilizing InControl™ and Endurance™ together, we can bring better asset intelligence to our field teams and enable a more proactive approach to how EV charging, solar, battery storage and supporting electrical infrastructure are managed and maintained.” The partnership draws on established scale on both sides. Otovo currently services more than 60,000 customers, and InCharge’s InControl software platform connects and supports more than 40,000 EV charging assets across more than 1,060 completed infrastructure projects. In 2025, InCharge’s team completed more than 24,000 support cases, resolving approximately 80% of charger issues remotely, with the InControl platform maintaining 99.99% uptime. InCharge’s broader network spans every U.S. state and Canadian province, supported by regional sales and service offices in Los Angeles, CA, Richmond, VA, and Fort Worth, TX, and includes more than 100 field service staff. That scale underpins the companies’ plans to expand this partnership into new markets. Work orders will pass directly between Otovo and InCharge, with Endurance™, Otovo’s industry-leading AI platform, handling intake, dispatch and scheduling on the Otovo side. Each company will act as a reseller of the other's preventive maintenance plans in the launch geographies, holding its own customer relationship. Pricing on the reciprocal plans is matched between the companies. The partnership addresses a structural gap for commercial sites carrying multiple energy assets. A property with rooftop solar, battery storage, EV chargers and a backup generator typically holds a separate contract, a separate response commitment and a separate point of contact for each one. About InCharge Energy InCharge Energy is a full lifecycle energy infrastructure partner, delivering EV charging, electrical and lighting, and distributed energy solutions. InCharge supports customers from initial concept and construction through long-term ongoing operations and maintenance. By providing one accountable partner across the energy lifecycle, InCharge Energy helps organizations operate more reliably, scale with confidence, and reduce total cost of ownership through best-in-class service and maintenance. More information is available at www.inchargeus.com. About Otovo Otovo is an AI-Native behind-the-meter energy services company serving homes and businesses across 15 European markets, Israel and the United States. Otovo combines equipment monitoring, rapid repairs, dependable power supply and grid participation in one service. Endurance™, Otovo’s AI platform, monitors installed equipment, optimizes service from problem detection to resolution and coordinates repairs around the clock. “Your Power, Backed by Ours™.” Otovo is listed on Euronext Oslo Børs under the ticker OTOVO. Visit us at www.otovo.com. Contacts Matt Dallas 917-363-1333 matt.dallas@icrinc.com

artigo.texto: Clear answers remain elusive regarding the fire suppression systems currently installed at the Cove Hollow battery energy storage system — or BESS — in East Hampton During an appearance before the East Hampton Town Board last week, representatives from the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) deferred questions on the fire suppression mechanisms to the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA). “NYSERDA is currently reviewing information about fire suppression systems used across New York’s battery storage portfolio, obtained by the Inter-agency Fire Safety Working Group (FSWG) during inspections conducted in 2024/25, and will be considering changes to our program rules going forward to address concerns raised by the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation’s report,” the authority said in a statement. “For information about this specific project please contact NextEra.” NextEra Energy did not return multiple requests for information sent to its press office regarding the facility’s fire suppression mechanics. Calls for a shutdown of the BESS facility have swelled since contaminated water was detected in two Suffolk County Water Authority wells about a quarter-mile south of the plant. Suffolk County Executive Ed Romaine was among the first to advocate for closure, with East Hampton Village Mayor Jerry Larsen soon following suit. East Hampton Town officials have not yet joined those calls. Asked about the town’s stance on a shutdown following the DEC’s presentation at the Town Board meeting, town spokesman Patrick Derenze said only that officials are assessing their options. The BESS plant was previously equipped with a gaseous fire suppression system called NOVEC 1230. During a May 2023 fire, the chemical reportedly mixed with water, broke down into a so-called “forever chemical” called PFPrA, and seeped into the groundwater. Testing samples collected by the State DEC showed contaminant levels as high as 10,000 parts per billion, dwarfing the referential 3 parts per billion site specific screening value previously set by the state. The lack of concrete information on the facility’s current fire suppression setup remains a major concern for nearby residents and the East Hampton Village fire administrator — one of the few officials on scene during the May 2023 fire linked to the contamination.

artigo.texto: By — Matt Loffman Matt Loffman Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/voters-dont-like-data-centers-they-really-dont-like-them-close-to-home Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Voters don't like data centers. They really don't like them close to home Politics Sep 23, 2026 5:00 AM EDT Voters share an opposition to data centers that scrambles usual party lines, according to the latest poll from PBS News, NPR and Marist. Public opposition especially hardens when people are asked about construction in their own communities. Fifty-eight percent of U.S. voters say the construction of new data centers by companies like Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI will mostly have a negative effect on the country. And 65% of voters oppose construction in their communities, including 43% who are strongly opposed. A quarter of voters say they support data center construction. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The opposition barely follows party or geography. It runs above 60% in big cities, suburbs, small towns and rural areas alike. More than 80% of Democrats oppose local construction. Republicans overall are close to evenly split, with 46% in favor and 44% opposed. The president's core supporters are an exception. More than half of self-identified MAGA supporters are in favor of data centers in their own communities, the only group that favors construction. MORE: Why communities are revolting against data centers The intense opposition to data centers has had far-reaching effects this year. At least 75 data center projects worth roughly $130 billion were blocked or delayed in the first three months of 2026, according to Data Center Watch, a research project tracking opposition efforts. The National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in an August memo obtained by Axios that data centers had become a "sleeper issue" for the entire cycle. And candidates in both parties have featured ads on the issue. WATCH: How data centers became a major issue in the midterms What to do about data centers is another issue entirely as lawmakers scramble for solutions. Last week, the House overwhelmingly passed bipartisan legislation that would require state energy regulators to consider requiring data centers to pay for electrical upgrades in their communities. Trump, however, remains on the side of data centers. Communities that oppose construction will be "backwards and poor," he wrote on social media last month. "China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement." The split leaves Republicans in districts with angry constituents choosing between them and him. "I understand the balancing act that Donald Trump is doing," despite public concern and rising energy costs, Republican strategist Melik Abdul said. "From Donald Trump's perspective, it should just be a wild, wild west because he doesn't want the regulations." Trump, Abdul argued, is worried that more government oversight would lead to a competitive advantage for China, which has fewer regulations. WATCH: Sen. Mark Warner says U.S. can strengthen AI safety without losing race to China Democratic strategist Joel Payne said the president is trying to pull his party along with him. "He is essentially trying to make it a litmus test for Republicans," he said. "I don't believe that has been met with the success that he intends for it to." The president is "out there on his own on this one," said Lee Miringoff, director of the Marist Institute for Public Opinion. He added that the anxiety increasingly runs through a broader fear of artificial intelligence. Neither party, Payne argued, can afford non-answers on this issue. "From a political standpoint, there is no nuance. The public has no nuance within how they think about AI and data centers." They're less sure about the mail PBS News, NPR and Marist Poll conducted a survey from Sept. 14 to 15, 2026, that polled 1,280 registered voters by phone, text and online with a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points. artigo.texto: Secretary Of State On Data Centers At the recent Paden City Labor Day Parade, our Secretary of State, Kris Warner participated in the day’s events. Upon the conclusion of the parade I caught up with him to ask a couple important questions state citizens are now asking. First, his thoughts on the state and incoming data centers. He began by stating that two years ago, the footprint of incoming data centers was much different than it is today. He pointed out that in the beginning centers were using local water supplied from creeks, and rivers to cool the heat generated by the massive electronics within the centers. Mr. Warner now indicated that newer centers are using closed loop cooling systems. Thus, reducing environmental impact on our valuable natural resource, water. Generators that are necessary for data centers create noise pollution for those living near the centers. Warner explained new generator stations now are being designed with barriers to deflect sound up and away. When he was asked about increased electrical costs to state residences. Warner said, “power companies must increase generation capacity and transmission lines to accommodate the center.” What he failed to say was the cost is passed onto customers of the utility companies. Companies go before the PSC requesting increases to offset cost. Most often the increase is granted. Lawsuits delay and sometimes prevent increases, but in the end, they generally are applied to your monthly bill. Mr. Warner explained it’s an issue that will be brought before the legislature during the next session. At the present time, it should be up to the county as to how cost is disseminated. But, Mr. Warner did say, one of the issues he has is the loss of control at the local levels, which was taken away by Charleston. That means in the business offices of companies and state offices, the details of costs are worked out away from the people who should be deciding how cost should be applied. In the state of Georgia it is mandated that any cost associated with a data center coming into an area is paid by the company, not local citizens. Charleston has taken away local governments ability to protect local businesses and homeowners from runaway electrical costs. Mr. Warner did however say, “At the present time, when a data center comes into a county in West Virginia, it will pay one hundred million dollars in taxes. Half goes to the county, and one million goes to every county in the state.” That is how it is today, according to Mr. Warner. Data centers have rapidly come to the forefront in the last few years due to their massive growth to respond to the AI boom. At present time there are several major projects that have been announced. Berkeley County, a $4 Billion dollar investment. It will take 1,000 construction workers to complete the project. Once it is up and running it could provide 125 permanent jobs. Putnam County an estimated $7 Billion dollar project. It is estimated to pay $8.5 million in taxes each year. Mason County, First Phase of the project estimated at $69 Billion, providing 4,300 construction jobs and 645 permanent jobs. Mason County, $12 Billion investment being built with a closed loop cooling system. Anthropic, plans to lease one-third of the Monarch Campus with a $45 Billion deal. Near Point Pleasant’s data center there are three large buildings housing the electronics. In order to guarantee a continuous power supply, the center will have on-site 1,000 natural gas and diesel engines that will support the generators. The future of our country is inching ever closer to being operated and controlled by thousands of data centers. Each center, once started, can never lose electricity. The loss would be catastrophic in the amount of data lost. Therefore, thousands of locations have standby generators. Those same data centers will be in control of the power grid. In an emergency when only so much power is available during a heat wave, will it choose your home or the data center? Keep a hospital operating, or the data center? Those companies operating AI centers, recently sounded the alarm on their own systems. Some even predicted humans will soon lose control of this emerging technology to our demise. Some refer to our heading into a Terminator future. I think that’s a little over the top, but not impossible. Mr. Warner in his words made it clear, he is only allowed to do his job by using the direction and policies of the legislature. He points out that on local levels we have no control. On the state level, even he has to do what he is directed to do. Data centers and their financial backers are about Billions upon Billions, and heading for the trillion-dollar number. Fearing AI is important, especially when people with trillions of dollars invested can buy whatever they want. But money cannot stop what may be coming, only people with good sense to evaluate how fast we move toward the AI age, can prevent a future that even the terminator could not imagine looking Through the Lens.

artigo.texto: Projetos de data centers em São Paulo saltam de 375 MW para mais de 2 GW Corrida por infraestrutura para nuvem e inteligência artificial multiplica por mais de cinco a capacidade planejada no eixo São Paulo-Campinas A corrida por data centers ganhou uma nova dimensão em São Paulo. A capacidade de projetos planejados no eixo entre a capital e Campinas saltou de 375 megawatts no primeiro semestre de 2025 para 2.066 megawatts no mesmo período deste ano, segundo dados da Cushman & Wakefield. É um crescimento de 451% em apenas doze meses. O avanço do pipeline é ainda mais acelerado do que o da infraestrutura que já entrou em operação. A capacidade efetivamente instalada passou de 346 MW para 661 MW no mesmo intervalo, alta de 91%. São Paulo já é o maior mercado de data centers da América Latina e aparece entre os polos das Américas que mais cresceram no período. A explosão dos projetos reflete principalmente a demanda por computação em nuvem e inteligência artificial. No primeiro semestre deste ano, a região absorveu mais 38 MW de capacidade, enquanto a vacância dos data centers de colocation caiu para apenas 4,1%. Um ano antes, esse indicador estava em 13,3%. Há uma peculiaridade nos números: apesar da multiplicação dos projetos futuros, a capacidade atualmente em construção ficou praticamente estável na comparação anual — 250 MW agora, ante 254 MW no primeiro semestre de 2025. Isso mostra que transformar os anúncios em data centers efetivamente ligados à rede será a próxima fronteira da expansão. Energia, conexão à rede de transmissão, disponibilidade de terrenos e licenciamento estão entre os gargalos que podem definir quais desses mais de 2 GW planejados efetivamente sairão do papel. O cenário ganha um incentivo adicional com o Redata, regime aprovado neste mês para reduzir a carga tributária sobre equipamentos destinados à instalação e expansão dos data centers. Mesmo antes do incentivo, porém, os números já mostram a mudança de escala do mercado. Em um ano, São Paulo deixou de ter algumas centenas de megawatts no horizonte para acumular projetos equivalentes a mais de três vezes toda a capacidade atualmente em operação.

artigo.texto: Americans have grown more negative toward the possible environmental and economic effects of data centers since the beginning of the year. And a majority say they’d be uncomfortable if a new data center started operating in their area, according to a new Pew Research Center survey. The survey comes as protests against new data center construction have spread, and as some state and local politicians have spoken out against data centers. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has been a vocal supporter of data centers. More than half of Americans (54%) now say data centers are mostly bad for the environment, up from 39% in January. Half say they are mostly bad for home energy costs, up from 38%. And 49% say they are mostly bad for people’s quality of life nearby, up from 30%. The new survey was conducted from July 20 to Aug. 9 among 10,548 U.S. adults. Just 4% of Americans think data centers have a mostly good impact in each of these areas. Views on how data centers impact local tax revenue and jobs are mixed. Similar shares (between 21% and 24%) say data centers are mostly good and mostly bad for these things. Since January, there have been increases of 9 percentage points in the shares of Americans who say data centers are mostly bad for local jobs (from 15% to 24%) and local tax revenue (from 12% to 21%). Many Americans are still unsure or unfamiliar with data centers altogether. Shares ranging from 18% to 32% say they are not sure how data centers impact the five things we asked about. And overall, 12% say they haven’t heard of data centers. Jump to the following sections for more: - Views of data centers have become more negative across groups - Changing partisan views on data centers’ impact on local jobs and tax revenue - A majority of Americans would be uncomfortable with a new local data center - Awareness of data centers continues to grow Views of data centers have become more negative across groups Americans in a variety of demographic and partisan subgroups have become more negative in their views of data centers. Men and women alike, as well as adults across age groups and education levels, have become more likely since January to say data centers have a mostly bad impact on the things we asked about. For example, rural Americans have become more likely to say data centers are mostly bad for the environment (from 32% in January to 50% in August), home energy costs (32% to 46%) and the quality of people living nearby (28% to 45%). Most data centers currently being planned or under development will be in rural areas. Americans in urban and suburban areas have also become more likely to say data centers areas are mostly bad for these things. As was the case earlier this year, Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents are more likely than Republicans and Republican leaners to view the impacts of data centers negatively. Still, Republicans’ views have also turned more negative: In the new survey, for example, 42% say the facilities are mostly bad for the quality of life of people nearby, up from 24% in January. Republican elected officials have staked out varying positions on data centers. While Trump has consistently supported their construction in his second term, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott previously supported expansion but issued a statewide moratorium on new data centers in August. Some Democrats, such as Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, have also recently shifted their positions to support additional rules and oversight on data center construction and operation. Changing partisan views about impact on local jobs and tax revenue Among Democrats and Republicans alike, views on the effects of data centers on local jobs and tax revenue are somewhat more negative than they were at the start of the year. But many people in both partisan groups either say that they’re not sure or that the effects are neither good nor bad. More Democrats now say the effects of data centers in these two areas are mostly bad than mostly good. Liberal Democrats have primarily driven this shift: For example, 34% of liberals now say data centers are mostly bad for local tax revenue, up from 19% in January. More Republicans continue to say the effects of data centers on local jobs and tax revenue are mostly good than mostly bad. Still, Republicans are now 7 percentage points more likely than in January to say the effects in both areas are mostly bad. A majority of Americans would be uncomfortable with a new local data center The new survey also finds that 60% of Americans say they would be not too or at all comfortable with a new data center operating in their area. Much smaller shares say they would be somewhat comfortable (19%) or extremely or very comfortable (7%) with this. Just over half of Republicans (54%) and about two-thirds of Democrats (68%) say they’d be not too or not at all comfortable with a new local data center. Liberal Democrats stand out, with 81% saying they’d be uncomfortable. Majorities of urban, suburban and rural Americans say they would be not too or not at all comfortable with a new data center in their area. Awareness of data centers continues to grow Americans are more aware of data centers than they were earlier in the year. The share of Americans who say they have heard or read a lot about them has increased from 25% in January to 35% today. About nine-in-ten adults (88%) have now heard at least a little about data centers. As was the case in January, awareness of data centers is higher among men than women, and higher among people with at least a bachelor’s degree than those with less education. artigo.texto: CATL announces a battery for electric trucks that offers a range of up to 1000 kilometers CATL presents Tectrans II: a battery for electric trucks with up to 1.000 km of range and recharging to 80 percent in 25 minutes. CATL unveiled its new Tectrans II battery solution at the IAA Transportation trade fair in Hanover . Designed primarily for heavy-duty electric transport, it can also be used in medium-duty trucks and buses. The system is available in various housing formats and can be mounted on the vehicle floor or roof. The company emphasized that its main focus is long-haul transport, where range, charging times, and operating costs are key advantages. In its maximum configuration, CATL claims the system can travel up to 1.000 kilometers , although the homologation cycle has not yet been specified. With megawatt-level charging, the battery would reach 80 percent in about 25 minutes . The packs are designed to be combined with both central transmissions and electric axles and, in theory, could also be installed as a swappable battery. This latter option aligns with CATL's experience in the battery swapping business in China and with plans to bring this model to Europe in partnership with Octopus Energy. A key feature is the standardization of modules, electrical interfaces, and communication protocols. This will allow manufacturers to incorporate future generations of batteries without having to fundamentally redesign their vehicle platforms—a crucial point in a rapidly evolving technological landscape. Higher payload for the same range The energy density of this new battery is 170 Wh/kg, which CATL claims is 13 percent above the industry average . With the same capacity as a conventional battery, this would translate to approximately 600 kg of extra payload . The manufacturer claims a lifespan of 12 years or 1,5 million kilometers while maintaining 70% of its capacity. Technical innovations include a more robust corrosion protection system and a more stable base plate. CATL has not disclosed the cell chemistry, although it is reasonable to assume the system could be based on either LFP or NMC, two technologies the Chinese company has mastered. At the same trade fair, CATL signed a letter of intent with the DHL Group to promote green freight corridors in Europe . The agreement expands upon the understanding reached in September 2024 and includes energy storage systems and management platforms for DHL's logistics parks, as well as battery swapping stations, ultra-fast charging, and pilot projects with electric vehicles.
