artigo.texto: Estimated read time: 2-3 minutes - Eagle Mountain's rezoning for a potential data center faced minimal opposition. - Only two residents commented during the Planning Commission meeting on the proposal. - The commission unanimously recommended approval; City Council will consider it next month. EAGLE MOUNTAIN — While proposed data centers have sparked heated debates in communities across Utah and the country, a public hearing in Eagle Mountain drew little public interest Tuesday night. Only two residents offered public comment during a planning commission meeting on a rezoning request that could eventually make way for another data center near existing facilities already operating in the city. South of Eagle Mountain, surrounded by open land, two major data center projects already dominate the area. Meta has operated its Eagle Mountain data center for about five years and employs roughly 1,200 people. Another facility, QTS Data Centers, is expected to be completed in the coming months and is projected to bring about 2,000 jobs to the area. City leaders said residents have become familiar with how data centers operate and the economic benefits they can provide. "What's happening here is very new, different technology than what's happening across the U.S.," said Eagle Mountain Economic Development Director Abby Ivory. "This is going in an area that really can't be used or developed for anything else." She believes the city's approach to educating residents and working closely with data center operators has helped build public trust. The discussion centered on a request from property owner Reagan Peck, who owns 41 acres adjacent to the Meta and QTS sites. Related: Peck told the commission the request is simply to change the property's zoning and does not guarantee a data center will be built there. "It doesn't mean it's going to be a data center," Peck said. "We don't have a buyer right now; we don't have a builder. We want to make sure we have this development agreement, this zoning in place so that if we were to advertise it, we could control how we did it." However, the zoning change would allow the property to be marketed for that use in the future if the owner chooses to sell. When the public comment period opened, only two residents addressed the commission. One urged city leaders to move cautiously. "If there is no need, don't do it," said Elbamara Perez. "We really need to figure out what's going on in the city we are living in." Another resident encouraged commissioners to carefully consider the long-term impact of the decision. "Consider carefully what you are opening up and what your making possible when you do this," said Teresa Edwards. Despite those concerns, the planning commission unanimously voted to recommend approval of the zoning change and forward it to the City Council for final consideration. The rezoning proposal is expected to go before the Eagle Mountain City Council next month, where members of the public will have another opportunity to comment.

artigo.texto: Data center gold rush is here, MA towns unprepared Massachusetts is at a critical crossroads. As state leaders double down on transforming the Bay State into a global hub for artificial intelligence, a quieter, infrastructure-heavy reality is unfolding on the ground: the rapid push to construct massive AI data centers across local communities. While state tech advocates champion these multi-million-dollar developments for their tax revenues and economic prestige, residents and local boards are left asking a fundamental question: Are our towns ready for the sheer physical cost of powering the digital future? Generative AI isn’t just floating in the cloud; it runs on physical infrastructure, in enormous facilities packed with thousands of high-powered server racks. A single high-capacity data center can consume as much electricity as a small city, demanding tens to hundreds of megawatts of continuous power. In a state already grappling with some of the highest residential electricity rates in the nation and an aging grid infrastructure, adding massive commercial loads risks driving up costs for everyday utility ratepayers. Then there is the issue of natural resources. Cooling advanced server arrays requires staggering amounts of water or massive industrial HVAC units operating 24/7. Neighborhoods near proposed sites are rightly concerned about ambient industrial noise pollution, strain on municipal water systems, and local air quality risks from diesel backup generators. In response to growing municipal pushback, Governor Maura Healey recently issued an executive order setting environmental and public health guardrails for data center developments over 25 megawatts, requiring community benefit agreements. While this is a welcome first step, it places the burden of defense back on municipal shoulders. Our local Planning Boards and Select Boards were built to evaluate single-family subdivisions, strip malls, and light industrial parks — not regional energy juggernauts disguised as commercial real estate. Without strong local bylaws, transparent public hearings, and firm municipal oversight, local communities risk signing away precious resources for short-term tax incentives. Progress and technological innovation are necessary, but they should not come at the expense of local grid stability, environmental health, and quality of life. Before your town board votes to approve the next “clean tech” facility in your backyard, insist that local leaders demand comprehensive environmental impacts, strict water-use caps, and enforceable noise mitigation. The digital future is coming to Massachusetts — let’s ensure our towns dictate the terms, rather than pay the price. George Ferdinand Tewksbury, MA Pause on data centers ‘reasonable’ If data centers were truly “improving” neighborhoods, as data center owner Markley Lowell contends, they would be popping up in the rich communities of their investors and owners. They are not. That should tell you a lot about who really benefits from these data centers and who is paying the price. The trouble with data centers is that they use public resources (water, air, etc.) to make a lot of money for private investors. Meanwhile the pollution they create and the energy they use is a burden on us, the public, and especially the public that happens to live near them, as in Lowell. A pause on this sudden boom seems reasonable, and New York State has wisely chosen that course. In the meantime communities can weigh the real costs of these centers. If they are such incredible job-creating investments, then they can be created using renewable, non-polluting energy in locations that do not endanger water supplies or sensitive environments. Mary Memmott Framingham, MA Democratic candidates should debate It is unacceptable that democratic candidates refuse to debate their republican opponents. What are they hiding? Insist that all candidates speak to the issues we face as a state. The people of Massachusetts deserve to make informed voting decisions. I want to see the following debates: Minogue vs. Healey, Deaton vs. Markey, Jones vs. Koh Paul DiTucci Topsfield, MA Enforce the rules on the Bruce Freeman Rail Tail The Bruce Freeman Rail Trail was built for walkers, runners, cyclists, and families — not motorized and gas-powered vehicles. Yet these vehicles are increasingly using the trail in Lowell, Chelmsford, and Westford. They are fast, noisy, and dangerous to people using the trail as intended. The rules already prohibit them. The problem is not the rules. The problem is enforcement. Lowell, Chelmsford and Westford need to enforce the existing prohibition. Increase patrols. Stop the violations. Ticket violators. Don’t wait until someone gets seriously hurt. Enforce the rules now. Brad MacGowan Chelmsford, MA Ballot Question 7 November 3rd’s Ballot Question 7 is not a housing slogan. It is a statewide rewrite of who controls a suburban lot. A “yes” vote would require cities and towns to allow a single-family house on a residentially zoned parcel of at least 5,000 square feet, with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer. Height, setbacks, parking, and short-term rentals could still be regulated. A “no” vote leaves today’s local lot-size rules in place. Supporters are right that oversized lots make land expensive and push McMansions. Independent Tufts analysis projects a real but modest gain—about 350 to 1,200 extra homes a year, concentrated in sewered suburbs. That would not end the shortage. Opponents at the Massachusetts Municipal Association are also right. Lot size is how many towns manage schools, pipes, and neighborhood form. The measure does not cap house size or price, so “starter home” is a hope, not a requirement. The choice is modest new supply versus less local control. Decide based on what would happen on your own street, not on the campaign brochure. Ronald Beaty West Barnstable, MA Recognizing direct support professionals Direct support profess

artigo.texto: In this week’s installment of Ask The Mayor, Terre Haute Mayor Brandon Sakbun addresses this issue and more at city hall. Listen to the full conversation with Indiana Newsdesk anchor Joe Hren by clicking on the play button above or read some of the questions and answers below. A portion of this segment airs 6:45 and 8:45 a.m. Wednesday on WFIU. Here are some highlights. This conversation has been edited for clarity and conciseness. Hren: Let's start with crafting next year's budget. This year's budget was $135 million. Next year's budget is $142 million. So where is that $7 million coming from? How's it coming together? Sakbun: About three of that seven million is just our net assessed value growth. So, the city was growing, and we grew enough to have $3 million more than last year. The other four is coming from our cash reserves because we have several quality of life and infrastructure projects that we'd like to finish. We've been very diligent, very responsible, and there's $14 to $15 million left in that bucket. We continue to grow the reserves there, so I communicated to the council that I'd like to take some of those reserves, and really improve the Booker T. Washington Community Center. We're going to pave more. We're paving $4.1 million dollars' worth of streets alone next year, and we're going to show that infrastructure is not just a buzzword; it's something that we've needed to do. Hren: Are you seeing loss of federal funding that's affecting your budget? Sakbun: There's been immense challenges because of loss of federal funding. A great example is Susie's Place right across the street that lost $150,000 and a lot of those organizations have nowhere to go, nowhere to turn, other than the city, county, and then the business community. There's been some tough conversations about, hey, you know, we're going to have to trim this or trim that or completely cancel much-needed programs. I think what's more frustrating is we're having this conversation about federal cuts we're seeing locally. Meanwhile, the nation continues to go trillions and trillions of trillions of dollars into debt. I'm frustrated because big businesses keep getting handouts, and I've not seen these economics trickle down to the average citizen. Prices are up, wage growth isn't what it used to be, war continues to ravage across the Middle East, and some of those challenges are affecting us here in the Hoosier state. Hren: Let's talk about data centers a bit because you wrote about needing checks and balances. Columbus City Council added an ordinance that would require any proposal to go through a government branch, which in turn requires public input. Is Terre Haute doing anything regarding data centers? Sakbun: So we have not been approached by any data center organizations. I've not been approached by any group that wants to sign an NDA, and I do like some of the stuff that Columbus, Indiana, is doing when it comes to ensuring there's public input. If you look at the city of Terre Haute, we don't have the right land around certain utilities for one within city limits. I've always said that if you want to have a conversation about data centers, there's a few things that you got to be very clear on: no tax breaks, absolutely none. They cannot increase our utilities. They need to guarantee and have legal ramification if utility bills go up because of a data center. They need to guarantee that they're not going to take our water. They need to be prepared to financially support the priorities of that community. Hren: Are those protections in place? Sakbun: I think we have a team on standby in the event that we need to. We have a couple of different strong municipal attorneys that we would call on. And honestly, the beauty of having a university is there's a lot of folks with a PhD you can call if you need it. Hren: I know there have been some people upset in Bloomington wondering, "Why are you doing these big road construction projects in the fall when school's back in session? There are football games, fall festivals, everything going on." Does the same thing happen here? Sakbun: When you realize that the cost of paving a square mile of interstate has increased by 5 times in 10 years, you have to ask yourself as a community: Are you willing to pave streets from March to end of October, or just April to July, because when you start moving things to another construction season, prices aren't going down. And there's a harsh reality if you keep saying, "Well, we can only tolerate construction during these weeks or those months," and then it starts raining and things get delayed. If you kick that can down the road and that price goes up, your residents truly suffer even more long term. There's never a great time to cut into a street. There's never a great time to pave a street. It will always affect at least one resident, and it's a hard conversation of hey, your business is going to be affected for a couple of weeks, but then when it's all done, more often than not, people enjoy the success of what we did. Hren: I know both of our other mayors indicated they do plan to run again next year. Have you made any announcement to run again for reelection? Sakbun: I do plan to make a more formal announcement in November. But since you asked me, and you're the first news outlet to ask me, and I like you and I love the organization you work for, I'll come out and be very direct. I do plan on running again in 2027 and look forward to winning the mayor's office again.

artigo.texto: EnerVenue has secured its first multi-megawatt-hour commercial order for the deployment of its Energy Prism battery storage systems at an oilfield in northern China. The project will comprise 26 containerized Energy Prism units with a combined storage capacity of 11 MWh. The systems will store electricity generated by an onsite solar array and supply power to the oilfield operation. The order was placed by a major Chinese oil and gas producer for one of its existing production sites. The first three Energy Prism units are scheduled for shipment in December 2026, with the remaining 23 units expected to follow in March 2027. The project will use EnerVenue’s fourth-generation Aqueous Metal Cell (AMC) technology. The company said the water-based, non-flammable electrolyte and absence of lithium are designed to address stringent fire-safety requirements at industrial sites. EnerVenue stated that its Aqueous Metal Cell has passed UL 9540A testing, a standard used to evaluate thermal runaway and fire propagation in battery energy storage systems. The company said the technology does not exhibit the same progression of events associated with thermal runaway in conventional battery chemistries. The Energy Prism systems will integrate onsite solar generation with battery storage, enabling daytime solar output to be shifted to periods when the oilfield requires electricity. The systems will be supplied as complete containerized units designed to connect with the site’s power conversion equipment. The deployment follows EnerVenue’s first Aqueous Metal Cell installation, a 150 kWh system integrating renewable generation with electric bus charging at Jintan in Changzhou, China, which has been operating since November 2025. EnerVenue Expands Manufacturing Capacity in China The cells for the northern China project will be manufactured at EnerVenue’s new high-volume production facility in Changzhou, Jiangsu. The facility, scheduled to open on September 24, 2026, will initially have an annual production capacity of 250 MWh of Aqueous Metal Cells. EnerVenue plans to scale production to 1 GWh in 2027 and subsequently expand to multi-gigawatt-hour capacity by 2028. The company said the Changzhou facility is its first plant designed for large-scale production of its Aqueous Metal Cell technology. EnerVenue is also set to introduce its Energy Core, Energy Cube, Energy Rack and Energy Prism product platforms at the facility. The products range from 30 kWh distributed systems to utility-scale and heavy-industrial storage systems, all based on the company’s Aqueous Metal Cell chemistry. The Aqueous Metal Cell uses nickel-hydrogen chemistry with a water-based electrolyte. EnerVenue said the technology is designed for up to 30,000 charge cycles, equivalent to operating for up to 30 years at three cycles per day. The company also said the systems are designed without scheduled augmentation over their operating life and do not require active cooling. Depending on local regulations, fire suppression systems may also not be required. EnerVenue currently has customer projects across China, Australia, the United States, the European Union, Saudi Arabia and Canada. Its customers include Radiance Energy, PowerSecure and Horizon Power. The Changzhou manufacturing facility is being funded through EnerVenue’s $300 million Series B extension announced in March 2026. The company said it has raised more than $700 million to date. Discover more from SolarQuarter Subscribe to get the latest posts sent to your email.

artigo.texto: CATL Begins Trial Production at Debrecen Battery Cell Plant on 22 September 2026 CATL has started trial production at its newly constructed battery cell factory in Debrecen, Hungary, effective 22 September 2026, according to a company press release. The company stated that all preconditions needed to begin the trial run had been satisfied before operations commenced. The trial phase is intended to set up, optimise and validate production equipment and manufacturing processes before series production begins. The company said its Debrecen operation continues to work closely with the government and authorities to maintain high environmental standards and protect employee health and safety. CATL announced the Debrecen plant, its second European battery facility, in August 2022, with the goal of joining the European automotive and e-mobility supply chain and serving leading European automakers. Construction of the first cell building began in summer 2023, and by spring 2026 the building had been fitted with advanced technology. After receiving the occupancy permit in August 2026, the company secured all relevant permits and completed the preconditions tied to its IPPC permit, allowing trial operations to start on 22 September on the first two production lines of the cell manufacturing facility. Before the occupancy permit was issued, the Hajdú-Bihar County Government Office conducted regular on-site inspections at CATL facilities to follow up on earlier issues that had raised serious concerns among local residents. Authority representatives confirmed that the company had resolved all deficiencies identified during the permitting process. CATL described the Debrecen site as a strategic manufacturing hub that will supply well-known European automakers, which have already built substantial electric vehicle production capacity in Hungary in recent years. The company said it installed advanced, flexible production lines in Debrecen to meet client needs. CATL has been manufacturing battery modules in Debrecen since autumn 2024 and has produced 537,000 modules since then. Once all facilities are complete, the Hungarian plant will be CATL's largest manufacturing base outside China, with a capacity of 100 GWH. Beyond obtaining permits and completing preconditions for trial operations, CATL Debrecen said it remains committed to working closely with the government and authorities, prioritising employee health and safety. Employee health, safety and environmental factors will be thoroughly monitored during trial operation, with results submitted proactively to the authority. The company said its investment is important not only for Debrecen and its region but also for the Hungarian economy and the European e-mobility supply chain. CATL stated it is committed to transparency and welcomes authorities to visit its site at any time. - 1. artigo.texto: Fundo Imobiliário de data centers da AZ Quest capta R$ 482 milhões O fundo imobiliário de data centers da AZ Quest captou R$ 482 milhões na primeira emissão de cotas e reuniu mais de 7 mil investidores, segundo informações da gestora divulgadas em entrevista ao Estadão. O valor corresponde ao teto da oferta. O AZ Quest Panorama Data Centers FII teve o registro concedido pela CVM em 3 de julho de 2026, pelo rito automático. A oferta previa a emissão de 4,82 milhões de cotas a R$ 100 cada, com captação mínima condicionada a R$ 291 milhões. Quer conferir notícias de finanças em tempo real, direto do seu WhatsApp, de maneira gratuita? Clique e confira a nova comunidade de notícias da Status Invest. Pela classificação ANBIMA, o fundo é de tijolo, com gestão ativa e subclassificação de renda. A administração é do Banco Daycoval e a gestão, da AZ Quest Panorama. Quatro ativos da Scala, com projeção de retorno equivalente a IPCA + 9,5% Os recursos foram destinados à compra de quatro imóveis da Scala Data Centers: o data center de Fortaleza (CE) e sua subestação elétrica, além de duas subestações em Tamboré (SP) e Jundiaí (SP). O ativo cearense e sua subestação respondem por cerca de 60% do valor econômico da operação, de acordo com o estudo de viabilidade da oferta. O empreendimento fica na Praia do Futuro, região por onde chega a maior parte dos cabos de fibra óptica internacionais que conectam o país. A estrutura é de sale and leaseback: a Scala vendeu os imóveis, recebeu os recursos e segue como locatária, com contrato de dez anos. O fundo tem prazo de duração equivalente, prorrogável por mais 18 meses, e o contrato prevê três janelas de recompra pela Scala — no 36º mês, com prêmio de 9% sobre o cap rate de entrada; no 72º, com 5%; e no 120º, sem prêmio. Os documentos da oferta projetam rentabilidade líquida equivalente a IPCA + 9,5% ao ano no cenário de captação máxima, já considerando a recompra ao fim do contrato. Trata-se de projeção do estudo de viabilidade, sem garantia de retorno. O fundo imobiliário aproveita o crescimento do setor A operação ocorre em um ciclo de expansão da infraestrutura digital no Brasil. A Associação Brasileira de Data Centers (ABDC) estima investimentos de R$ 500 bilhões no país até 2030, com a capacidade instalada saindo de 730 MW para 3,2 GW. Fundada em 2020, a Scala opera 13 unidades no Brasil, com cerca de 200 MW instalados, e é controlada pela DigitalBridge. A companhia atende grandes empresas de tecnologia e já era conhecida da gestora: em maio de 2024, o AZIN11 alocou R$ 50 milhões em debêntures da SDC Participações, holding do grupo. A AZ Quest tem R$ 36,7 bilhões sob gestão, dos quais R$ 1,1 bilhão em estratégias imobiliárias. Com a conclusão da oferta, o FII de data centers passa a integrar a prateleira de ativos alternativos que a casa vem ampliando desde 2022.

artigo.texto: Baltimore County leaders have spent months wrestling with how to regulate data centers amid a furious backlash against the tech facilities. The latest step was to give themselves more time. The County Council unanimously passed a bill Tuesday night extending the county’s moratorium on data centers through the end of 2027. The county had already paused data center development until around Jan. 1. Now the freeze will continue for at least another year. “Before we open more of this up to Baltimore County and development, I think that it’s crucial we get it right,” Republican council member Nino Mangione said at the meeting. Here are five things to know about the county’s approach to data centers: A new council can weigh in The council will soon undergo wholesale changes, with at least six new members set to take office after the Nov. 3 election. The extended moratorium will give them a chance to weigh in on a contentious issue that has drawn intense public scrutiny. Read More Views on the issue don’t divide neatly along party lines. Both Republican and Democratic candidates have publicly supported continuing the pause, while others have called for bans. Shawn McIntosh, a Democrat running against Mangione to represent North County’s District 5, said she favors a ban because it puts the onus on the industry, rather than local governments, to address concerns about data centers. “If data center companies want to operate in Baltimore County, they should have to develop better technology and demonstrate that these facilities can be built without consuming disproportionate amounts of electricity, water and land,” McIntosh said at a hearing last week. “If they do, we can reconsider.” Where the county executive candidates stand The two candidates running for Baltimore County’s top office said in interviews that they support the moratorium extension rather than a ban. Council member Julian Jones, a Woodstock Democrat, co-sponsored the moratorium bill, citing widespread public opposition to data centers. He said a ban could tie the hands of future administrations. “I’ve heard from citizens from all different parts of the county, and what I heard loud and clear is that they overwhelmingly do not support data centers,” Jones said. “So I support the moratorium, and I don’t support any data centers.” Republican Pat Dyer said a longer moratorium gives the county time to consider regulations and environmental protections. “I am not opposed to data centers, per se, because I think they can provide tremendous potential for our area,” Dyer said. “However, the control has to reside within neighborhoods and the communities.” A new report lays out guardrails The county planning board approved a data center study last week that recommends stricter oversight of the tech facilities and provides lawmakers a roadmap for regulating them. The report recommends prohibiting data centers on agricultural land, within 750 feet of homes, and in areas outside the Urban-Rural Demarcation Line. In communities the state classifies as overburdened or underserved, proposals would require case-by-case review by an administrative law judge. The report also suggests requiring developers to minimize water use, making data centers ineligible for financial incentives, and prohibiting by-right approvals of the tech facilities. The work group that drafted the report stopped short of recommending a ban, saying it did not have the authority to do so. Instead, it sought to balance data centers’ economic benefits with concerns about water use, energy consumption and environmental impacts. Waiting on the state to weigh in Council member David Marks, who introduced the moratorium bill along with Council Chair Mike Ertel, said the extension allows the county to wait for the state to weigh in on data centers. Maryland lawmakers could consider a statewide moratorium — New York and Texas have taken that step. If enacted, a move like that could extend Baltimore County’s pause beyond its current end in 2027. “We want to see what the Maryland General Assembly is going to do first, and we’ll act accordingly,” said Marks, an Upper Falls Republican. The data center issue is expected to draw significant attention when lawmakers return to Annapolis in January for the next legislative session. Gov. Wes Moore has recently signaled a greater willingness to support restrictions on the tech facilities, telling Punchbowl News last week that he would sign a statewide moratorium if one reached his desk. The governor also announced Wednesday morning that he has established a task force to help steer the state’s data center decision-making and created a dashboard for tracking projects across the state. A skeptical public A fierce grassroots backlash against data centers has erupted across the country, and Baltimore County is no exception. The planning board’s public hearings on data centers in May and September drew standing-room-only crowds and hours of public comment. Dozens also spoke out against data centers at the council’s Sept. 15 work session — among them environmental activists, faith leaders, community organizers and a high school student. Many data center opponents have said the county’s moratorium doesn’t go far enough and are pressing lawmakers to enact a permanent ban like the one in neighboring Harford County. Though a ban isn’t on the table in Baltimore County yet, the mounting uproar has at least turned data centers into a volatile election-year issue. With Tuesday’s move, lawmakers have approved a pause on the tech facilities for the second time in eight months.

artigo.texto: AUSTRALIA will support the Philippines’ renewable energy development, carbon market, and offshore wind industry through a P2-billion economic development grant over five years. “This is a program that has been developed jointly by the Australian government and the Philippine government to deliver better economic outcomes to boost infrastructure and to improve living standards in communities throughout the Philippines,” Australian Assistant Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade Matt Thistlethwaite told reporters in a briefing on Tuesday. Thistlethwaite said that renewable energy, the establishment of a carbon market, and the development of the offshore wind industry were among the priority areas discussed with Philippine government officials under the Promoting Growth, Resilience, Economic Stability and Sustainability in the Philippines (Progress) program. “We haven’t allocated funding to specific projects yet. We’re very much in the scoping phase,” he said. Thistlethwaite said the Australian government has already allocated the AU$45 million or P2 billion for the program, but individual projects will still have to be identified and approved through a partnership between the two countries. “That will rely on the requests from the Philippine government. This project is very much about providing support for the Philippines government to deliver on their priorities,” he said. Australia has appointed Boston Consulting Group as a partner that will work with Philippine government departments to develop the details of the projects and funding commitments over the five-year period. Thistlethwaite clarified that the grant should not be viewed as a single disbursement for already identified projects. “The individual projects will be determined by the Australian government in partnership with the Filipino government and the government departments,” he said. As projects are approved, Australia and the Philippines will announce them jointly. “At the moment, the funding has been allocated from the Australian Government. It’s now up to us to work together on providing that funding to individual projects,” Thistlethwaite said.

artigo.texto: Power U.S. Battery-Storage Sector Faces New Hurdles, Despite Growth Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $6 billion in battery-storage projects set to begin construction across the U.S. in the fourth quarter Released Thursday, September 24, 2026 Reports related to this article: Written by Will Ploch, Assistant Editor-in-Chief for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary Battery-storage capacity has grown substantially across the U.S. in recent years, but recent shifts in federal policy could slow the adoption. More than $6 billion worth of related projects are set to kick off in the fourth quarter. Another 67 GW by 2030? Battery energy-storage system (BESS) units have been helping to stabilize swaths of the U.S. power grid as far back as 2022, according to a recent report from the Rocky Mountain Institute (RMI). But the battery-storage sector continues to face headwinds, including an August order from President Donald Trump that hinders the adoption of foreign-produced bulk power components. Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $6 billion worth of battery-storage projects that are set to begin construction across the U.S. in the fourth quarter. "Since 2018, BESS capacity deployed in the U.S. has increased more than 40-fold, with much of this growth occurring in Arizona, California and Texas," RMI said in its report. "Looking ahead, federal interconnection and planning data indicates that roughly 67 gigawatts (GW) of battery-storage projects are planned to come online by 2030." RMI said this trend would make batteries "the second-largest source of new electric capacity after solar." According to Industrial Info Resources data, about $1.3 billion of the total investment in fourth-quarter BESS kickoffs is attributed to projects at solar power-generation facilities, including DTE Energy Company's addition of a BESS unit at its Fish Creek Solar Plant in Sheridan, Michigan. DTE is adding 132 megawatts (MW) of battery storage to its solar plant, which generates 132 MW from 320,000 photovoltaic (PV) panels provided by First Solar Incorporated. Industrial Info Resources offers more information on the Fish Creek project in its Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Power Plant and Project databases, where readers can find details--including construction schedules, investment values and necessary equipment--in a plant profile and project report. Public Service Company of New Mexico, a subsidiary of TXNM Energy Incorporated, is planning a 50-MW BESS unit at its Sunbelt Solar Plant in Waterflow, New Mexico, which is designed to generate 100 MW from 200,000 First Solar PV panels. Construction on both parts of the project is expected to run through the end of 2027. Readers can learn more in a plant profile and project report. By the Numbers - More than $6 billion: Total investment value of battery-storage projects set to kick off across the U.S. in the fourth quarter - 67 GW: Total capacity of battery-storage projects set to be brought online by 2030, according to RMI - About $1.3 billion: Total investment in fourth-quarter BESS kickoffs attributed to projects at solar-power facilities A Separate, Less Optimistic View Despite growing interest, the continued adoption of BESS units across the U.S. is facing a slowdown, after Trump signed an executive order in August that aims to prevent some foreign-made batteries, inverters and other components from being incorporated into the U.S. power grid. This creates a massive hurdle for domestic battery-storage developers, who sourced about 40% of their inverters installed in 2025 from companies based in China, according to Bloomberg. It is not yet known which individual projects will be affected by the order. RMI points to California as one of the states that benefits most from BESS adoption, as the technology has helped the state meet a substantial portion of its power demand during some of the most brutal heat waves from recent years. Among the projects in the state nearing construction is LS Power Group's Commerce Energy Storage project in Commerce, California, which is set to hold 250 MW using LG Chemical Limited's lithium-ion technology. The Commerce project is an example of stand-alone battery storage, which accounts for nearly $4 billion of the roughly $6 billion in fourth-quarter BESS kickoffs. Readers can learn more from a detailed plant profile and project report. The Industrial Info Resources GMI Project and Plant databases offer a full list of detailed reports for projects mentioned in this article, and a full list of related plant profiles. Industrial Info Resources also offers a full list of reports for battery-storage projects that are set to begin construction across the U.S. in the fourth quarter. Key Takeaways - Since 2018, BESS capacity deployed in the U.S. has increased more than 40-fold. - But the U.S. BESS market is reeling from an executive order that hinders the adoption of foreign-produced bulk power components. - It is not yet known which individual projects will be affected by the order. artigo.texto: Maryland is joining a wave of other Democratic-led states in regulating new data centers, calling on the facilities to offer community benefits and abide by environmental and transparency standards. Gov. Wes Moore (D) signed an executive order Wednesday creating a new data center accountability task force made up of members of his administration that will guide development across the state. Developers are also directed to follow energy consumption standards and engage with communities on economic benefits under a new framework outlining best practices, which the task force must apply to new projects in the pipeline. The order was partially a response to the Trump administration ârolling back critical safeguards giving Big Tech more room to determine their own destiny,â Moore said. A majority of Marylandâs counties had already temporarily paused data center development and petitioned state officials to act. âIf the federal government has decided that they want to just take away all the guardrails and just do giveaways to Big Tech because itâs part of the presidentâs personal portfolio, then that is not going to stand inside of the state of Maryland,â Moore said during a news conference. Moore joins a growing list of Democratic leaders who have signaled tougher enforcement on data centers as the facilities stoke residential anxiety. In neighboring Virginia, Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) last week called for a similarly broad framework to guide the industry in the state with the largest concentration of data centers in the US. Marylandâs executive order applies only to new data center development and to facilities with a projected electric demand of 25 megawatts or more, Moore said. It also bans nondisclosure agreements between developers and state agencies, calls for state agencies to develop community benefits guidance, and mandates that any project not have an outsize effect on ratepayers, a common refrain as residential energy bills rise. During the news conference, Moore also targeted an existing tax exemption for data centers and said he would work with state lawmakers in the coming legislative session to repeal that break. Wednesdayâs executive order wonât override communities that already have local bans on data centers in place, Moore said.

artigo.texto: Data centers and artificial intelligence may not rank among voters’ top concerns heading into the midterms, but growing anxiety over their effect on electricity bills and local communities is giving Democrats and allied groups an opening to connect the industry’s rapid expansion to the issue that has consistently dominated the campaign: the cost of living. The League of Conservation Voters Victory Fund, a Democratic-aligned super PAC, launched a $2 million digital ad campaign Tuesday targeting six Republican House incumbents over their support for H.R. 1 (known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill”), President Donald Trump’s signature tax-and-spending law. The group is seeking to link the lawmakers to tax benefits received by companies involved in the data center boom. The ads will target Reps. Juan Ciscomani of Arizona, Zach Nunn of Iowa, Brad Finstad of Minnesota, Tom Barrett of Michigan, Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin and Rob Wittman of Virginia. The ads will run through Election Day, with 46% of the buy going to connected television, 43% to YouTube and 10% to social media. All six districts are among those the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has identified as potential pickup opportunities in November, which the committee refers to as “red to blue” districts. The campaign represents an effort by the environmental group to capitalize on a political backlash that has increasingly followed proposed data centers across the country. Residents in communities facing new developments have raised concerns about electricity costs, water use, noise and strain on local power grids. The issue has drawn attention from both parties: The House overwhelmingly passed legislation last week directing state utility regulators to consider whether data centers and other large electricity users should shoulder infrastructure costs associated with their power demands. LCV Victory Fund is betting that those local concerns can be tied to the broader affordability debate. “These six districts have planned or operational data centers in their districts,” Sara Schreiber, senior vice president of LCV Victory Fund, told MS NOW. “All of these members voted for the $80 billion in tax breaks for these companies.” The ads use what the group describes as “a tongue-in-cheek ’90’s Infomercial style” to make that argument. For example, in the Michigan spot targeting Barrett (embedded above), a narrator asks viewers, “Is your neighborhood too quiet? Is your water too clean? Paying too little for electricity?” before accusing Barrett of taking “data center money” and supporting tax breaks benefiting the industry. Barrett, however, has also sought to position himself against unchecked data center development. In August, he introduced two bills that his office said were designed to preserve local control over whether data centers are built and to prevent the federal government from overriding local zoning decisions. Barrett said residents in mid-Michigan had raised concerns about the projects’ potential effects on utility bills, land and water. “People in mid-Michigan are tired of big corporations and politicians negotiating backroom deals to put data centers in our communities without hearing from the people who would be impacted the most,” Barrett wrote at the time. But even his decision to introduce the legislation underscores how the issue has gained political traction. The $80 billion figure cited by LCV Victory Fund requires some context. An August analysis by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, or ITEP, found that six large companies — Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, JPMorgan Chase and Nvidia — received a combined $83 billion in federal income tax breaks in 2025. However, ITEP’s analysis did not attribute all $83 billion to tax breaks specifically for data centers. ITEP describes itself as a “non-profit, non-partisan tax policy organization” that promotes “tax justice.”

artigo.texto: Nvidia’s new qualification programme for products and solutions that meet its reference design requirements includes three battery storage solutions. Graphics processing unit (GPU) manufacturer and global stock market darling Nvidia launched Nvidia DSX Ready, a programme for artificial intelligence (AI) factory builders, earlier this week (21 September). The idea is that organisations can identify products and solutions that have completed category-specific qualification requirements for building AI factory infrastructure under the Nvidia DSX programme. Nvidia DSX AI factories are co-designed as unified products which are optimised for lowest token cost and energy efficiency, according to the company. Battery energy storage systems (BESS) are one of two initial categories, along with cooling distribution units (CDUs). Nvidia has not yet indicated the number or types of other categories that will follow. The company did say DSX Ready will apply to factory design and operations across compute, networking, power, cooling, facilities and software. LG ES said its BESS met applicable DSX Ready requirements for AC energy storage solutions and can help customers bring power online faster while addressing the critical power management challenges of AI facilities, including AI load smoothing, voltage ride-through and power reliability enhancement. LG ES talks up domestic content advantage, Hitachi Energy touts power electronics LG ES head of energy storage system (ESS) battery division Chang Beom Kang said the selection “validates the strength and competitiveness of our BESS products.” The company talked up the competitive advantage it presently holds in the US as one of the first to market with domestic content BESS products, including lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells, which enable LG ES and its customers to avail of tax credit incentives. Hitachi Energy noted that its qualification includes its power conversion systems (PCS) and power plant controller (PPC), two capabilities the company enhanced with the acquisition of the Spanish power electronics manufacturer Eks Energy. Nvidia noted that passing the qualification does not replace site-level engineering or imply site-level stability. artigo.texto: 3 min leitura Greenvolt inicia construção de sistema de armazenamento de 600 MW na Polónia O projeto de Siedlce faz parte da carteira de armazenamento em baterias da Greenvolt, que totaliza atualmente 4,6 GW, dos quais cerca de 2,4 GW estão localizados na Polónia. 24 Set 2026 - 14:15 3 min leitura O Grupo Greenvolt iniciou a construção de um sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) com 600 MW de potência e 2,4 GWh de capacidade em Siedlce, na Polónia, através da Greenvolt Power. O projeto deverá entrar em operação comercial no final de 2027 e será, segundo a empresa, a maior instalação deste tipo no país. O projeto de Siedlce terá capacidade para armazenar eletricidade durante períodos de elevada produção de energia renovável e disponibilizá-la quando a procura aumentar, contribuindo para equilibrar a oferta e a procura de eletricidade e para integrar maior produção de origem eólica e solar no sistema elétrico polaco. “Com Siedlce, estamos mais uma vez a passar dos planos à concretização. O mais importante é construir ativos, criar valor real e reforçar as infraestruturas necessárias para integrar mais energia renovável no sistema. A Polónia é um mercado estratégico para nós e o armazenamento de energia em baterias está a assumir uma importância cada vez maior no nosso crescimento”, afirma João Manso Neto, CEO do Grupo Greenvolt, em comunicado. O projeto faz parte da carteira de armazenamento em baterias da Greenvolt, que totaliza atualmente 4,6 GW, dos quais cerca de 2,4 GW estão localizados na Polónia. O grupo desenvolve projetos de armazenamento de grande escala através da Greenvolt Power e soluções behind-the-meter para clientes comerciais e industriais, através da Greenvolt Next. Na Polónia, a empresa tem ainda outros dois projetos de armazenamento em desenvolvimento ou operação. Turośń Kościelna, com 200 MW de potência e 800 MWh de capacidade, entrou em operação em julho de 2026, enquanto Ełk, com a mesma dimensão, tem entrada em operação comercial prevista para o quarto trimestre deste ano. Quando os três projetos estiverem operacionais, Siedlce, Turośń Kościelna e Ełk representarão, em conjunto, 1 GW de potência e 4 GWh de capacidade de armazenamento. A BYD Energy Storage será responsável pelo fornecimento da tecnologia de baterias. O projeto contempla 210 contentores de baterias e 105 contentores de transformadores equipados com sistemas de conversão de energia, que permitem o fluxo de eletricidade entre as baterias e a rede.

artigo.texto: A sanção do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter, ocorrida em 15 de setembro de 2026, estabeleceu uma nova diretriz de incentivos fiscais para a instalação e ampliação de unidades de processamento de dados em território nacional. O avanço legislativo será o tema central da edição inaugural do Data Center World Brasil 2026, evento programado para ocorrer entre os dias 6 e 8 de outubro de 2026, no pavilhão do São Paulo Expo, na capital paulista, em realização simultânea ao Futurecom. O fórum reunirá executivos do setor de tecnologia, operadores de infraestrutura hyperscale, investidores institucionais e representantes do setor público para debater as condições necessárias para a conversão do novo marco tributário em ativos produtivos. O debate promovido durante a feira e congresso busca analisar a posição do país diante do crescimento da demanda global por capacidade computacional intensiva, impulsionada pelo desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial generativa. A programação do evento abrange discussões estratégicas fustigadas por exigências de descarbonização, acesso a linhas de crédito de longo prazo, capacidade de transmissão de energia e latência de rede. A iniciativa pretende delimitar como o mercado brasileiro se articulará para capturar investimentos internacionais em concorrência com outros hubs regionais da América Latina. Panorama do setor e gargalos regionais de infraestrutura A criação do Redata ocorre em um momento de transição acelerada na demanda global por centros de dados. Historicamente, os investimentos no ecossistema brasileiro de tecnologia da informação concentraram-se na região Sudeste, primariamente no estado de São Paulo, devido à proximidade dos grandes centros de consumo corporativo e dos pontos de troca de tráfego de internet. Contudo, a expansão das arquiteturas voltadas para inteligência artificial exige capacidades energéticas na escala de centenas de megawatts por projeto, pressionando a infraestrutura elétrica e os modelos tradicionais de licenciamento ambiental e urbano. O mercado latino-americano de infraestrutura digital atravessa um período de forte competição inter-regional. Países como Querétaro no México, Santiago e Valparaíso no Chile, e regiões metropolitanas na Colômbia vêm estruturando políticas ativas de atração de capital estrangeiro para instalações hyperscale. No Brasil, embora a matriz energética seja predominantemente renovável — fator de atratividade para corporações globais com metas rígidas de sustentabilidade —, o setor enfrenta entraves operacionais relevantes, tais como os custos elevados de equipamentos importados, a morosidade nos processos de conexão às redes de distribuição e transmissão de energia, e a complexidade na estruturação do capital de financiamento (CAPEX). A projeção de expansão global de capacidade computacional reflete o impacto das tecnologias emergentes sobre as necessidades de processamento, conforme demonstrado no levantamento a seguir: Estudos setoriais realizados pela McKinsey & Company indicam que a capacidade instalada global de data centers precisará praticamente triplicar até o final desta década para suportar as cargas de trabalho associadas aos modelos de linguagem de grande escala (LLMs) e aplicações analíticas avançadas. A transição de cargas tradicionais de armazenamento em nuvem para sistemas de alta densidade térmica e energética altera radicalmente os requisitos de engenharia, demandando novas soluções de refrigeração líquida, transformadores de alta potência e suprimento contínuo de energia limpa sem oscilações. Impactos econômicos, tributários e operacionais do marco regulatório O Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter foi desenhado para desonerar a aquisição de máquinas, servidores, sistemas de climatização de precisão e insumos de alta tecnologia, tanto nacionais quanto importados. A medida busca equiparar as condições de investimento brasileiras às de jurisdições concorrentes que oferecem isenções fiscais diretas. Entretanto, a fruição dos benefícios tributários do Redata está vinculada a contrapartidas estruturadas pelo governo federal, exigindo das empresas contempladas compromissos formais em três eixos centrais: - P&D e Inovação: Investimentos compulsórios em pesquisa e desenvolvimento tecnológico em parceria com instituições locais. - Sustentabilidade Operacional: Adoção de métricas de eficiência no uso de energia (PUE) e de água (WUE), com uso de fontes renováveis. - Atendimento ao Mercado Local: Garantia de disponibilidade de capacidade computacional dedicada ao ecossistema doméstico de tecnologia. A viabilização prática dos projetos de alta complexidade depende da integração da cadeia de suprimentos. Fabricantes de componentes eletrônicos, fornecedores de materiais elétricos, consultorias de engenharia e empresas de climatização precisam alinhar cronogramas de entrega para evitar a ociosidade do capital investido. Durante as atividades do Data Center World Brasil 2026, painéis específicos abordarão os gargalos de financiamento de longo prazo com a participação de entidades como o BNDES, o Ministério das Comunicações e a Brasscom, focando em mecanismos para mitigar riscos cambiais e otimizar a estrutura de capital de grandes obras de infraestrutura. A cadeia de valor necessária para erguer e operar um centro de dados de grande porte envolve especialidades que vão desde a distribuição de energia até o monitoramento ambiental contínuo. Empresas do ecossistema como Schneider Electric, Vertiv, Johnson Controls, Kingston Technology, Saint-Gobain, Vaisala, Termomecanica, Transformadores União e Mpt Fios e Cabos atuam diretamente no fornecimento de subsistemas críticos. A eficiência do setor depende da capacidade dessas companhias em integrar tecnologias de refrigeração sustentável, cabeamento estruturado e isolamento térmico às exigências normativas e climáticas do território brasileiro. artigo.texto: The U.S. energy storage market installed a record 5.4 GW/18.9 GWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS) in the second quarter of 2026, according to the latest U.S. Energy Storage Monitor released by the American Clean Power Association (ACP) and Wood Mackenzie. While installed power capacity declined 7% year-over-year (YoY), energy capacity increased 17% YoY, marking a new quarterly record. The growth was driven in part by a shift toward longer-duration storage systems and increased residential storage capacity. The national average duration of newly installed battery storage systems increased from 2.8 hours in Q2 2025 to 3.5 hours in Q2 2026, reflecting growing demand for storage to support resource adequacy. Utility-Scale Storage Accounts for Majority of Deployments The utility-scale segment installed 4.7 GW/17.6 GWh during Q2 2026, representing an 8% YoY decline in MW terms as some established markets experienced increasing saturation. However, utility-scale installations during the first half of 2026 were 5% higher YoY, indicating that full-year deployment could remain broadly comparable with 2025 levels. Average project duration continued to increase during the quarter, supported by a long-duration project in California developed to meet state requirements and utility-contracted storage projects deployed in Texas. Residential Storage Records Fourth-Largest Quarter The U.S. residential storage market installed 676 MW in Q2 2026, making it the fourth-largest quarter on record. Installations declined 15% quarter-over-quarter (QoQ) but increased 3% YoY. California, Texas, Puerto Rico, Arizona and Illinois accounted for 88% of residential storage capacity installed during Q2. All five markets recorded sequential declines, with Puerto Rico experiencing the largest absolute decrease, falling from 129 MW in Q1 to 73 MW in Q2. The national residential storage market is projected to contract by 4% in 2026, amid the elimination of certain tax credits, consumer uncertainty and challenges associated with the transition in third-party ownership models. CCI Storage Returns to Historical Deployment Levels The Community, Commercial and Industrial (CCI) segment installed 48 MW of storage during Q2 2026, returning to historical deployment levels following an elevated first quarter in California associated with the Net Energy Metering 2.0 grandfathering deadline. CCI installations declined 2% YoY, although stronger deployment in Hawaii, New Mexico and Texas helped offset the contraction. U.S. Storage Market Projected to Reach 207 GW by 2031 The U.S. energy storage market is projected to grow by more than 50% in MW terms over the next five years, reaching approximately 207 GW/715 GWh of cumulative installed capacity by 2031, according to the report. Utility-scale storage is expected to record an average annual growth rate of 8% through 2031, supported in part by increasing electricity demand from data centers. The CCI segment is projected to grow 27% between 2026 and 2031, with deployment expected to expand beyond California into emerging markets such as Maryland and Texas. The residential segment is expected to recover between 2027 and 2031, with an average annual growth rate of 9%. Wood Mackenzie said increasing data center development is strengthening the outlook for energy storage across market segments, particularly as large electricity consumers face grid-connection constraints. Virtual Power Plants Gain Importance The report also highlighted the expanding role of virtual power plants (VPPs) in the U.S. distributed storage market. VPPs are increasingly being positioned as a mechanism to support growing electricity demand while enabling residential and CCI storage assets to participate in broader grid services and electricity markets. Supply chain conditions, including potential trade restrictions, could create short-term bottlenecks for the storage industry. The utility-scale segment could experience slower growth during 2026 and 2027 as the market adjusts to these conditions. Growth is projected to resume from 2028, with utility-scale installations expected to expand at an average annual rate of 11% through 2031, supported by increasing domestic battery cell manufacturing capacity. Solar-Plus-Storage Attachment Rate Reaches 46% The national residential solar-plus-storage attachment rate reached 46% in Q2 2026, up from 41% in Q2 2025. Meanwhile, the share of hybrid utility-scale installations declined to 33% in Q2 2026, compared with 45% a year earlier, primarily due to a contraction in California. Utility-scale battery system prices also continued to decline. Average system prices fell 2% YoY to $916/kW in Q2 2026, according to the report. The continued decline in system costs, longer-duration deployments and growing electricity demand are expected to support the expansion of energy storage across the U.S. power market. artigo.texto: Low-Frequency Noise and Data Centers: What to Know Infrasound produced by data centers is increasingly scrutinized by communities, making proactive mitigation and transparent communication essential for operators. Most of the noise that frustrates neighbors around data centers is audible. But one important factor isn’t: infrasound – low-frequency acoustic energy that most people can’t actually hear, yet may perceive as pressure changes, vibrations, or even building rattle. As communities scrutinize new projects, understanding what infrasound is, where it comes from, and how to control it is increasingly important. What Is Infrasound? Infrasound refers to acoustic energy typically below 20 Hz, which sits beneath the usual range of human hearing. Although it’s often inaudible, people can sometimes sense infrasound indirectly – as subtle body pressure, vibration in nearby structures, or resonance that causes doors, windows, or fittings to buzz. Where Infrasound Comes From in Data Centers Infrasound arises from both natural and human-made sources. Ocean waves, storms, and seismic activity all produce low-frequency energy. In data centers, several systems can contribute: - Cooling towers and large axial fans can emit low-frequency sound waves that propagate beyond the site, especially under certain wind or atmospheric conditions. - Standby generators – through engines, exhaust systems, and enclosures – are common sources of low-frequency noise and infrasound during testing or outages. - Server fans primarily contribute mid- to high-frequency noise; however, in aggregate, they can also contribute to low-frequency hum through airflow paths and structural resonance. They are typically secondary sources compared to cooling plants and generators. Why Low-Frequency Noise Matters Most people can’t hear infrasound, and many ordinances address only audible sound. For these reasons, one might think that the data center industry has little reason to be concerned about high levels of infrasound. In reality, infrasound is increasingly part of debates about the impact of data centers on local communities, with residents complaining that low-frequency noise and infrasound produce headaches, nausea, anxiety, and other health problems. So far, most of these claims have not been fully validated. Measuring infrasound accurately requires specialized equipment, and few communities have conducted the assessments necessary to prove infrasound at high levels – let alone to prove that data centers are the source of the sound or that it’s causing health problems. Practical Ways to Reduce Infrasound Data center operators aiming to stay in the good graces of local communities (not to mention politicians and regulators) would do well to invest in strategies for mitigating infrasound emissions from their facilities, whether real or perceived. Many options are practical and not especially costly: - Regularly clean fans and other mechanical components. Keeping blades and heat exchange surfaces clean helps equipment run smoothly and can reduce low-frequency noise and infrasound generation. - Install larger fans operating at lower speeds where feasible. Larger-diameter fans running at lower speeds can produce less low-frequency energy than smaller fans at higher RPM for equivalent airflow. - Use anti-vibration pads and proper isolation mounts to decouple infrasound-producing equipment from floors, walls, and other structural components. Low-frequency energy travels efficiently through solids, so preventing direct contact can significantly reduce transmission. - Optimize enclosures, mufflers, and silencers. Properly sealed and tuned enclosures around generators and large fans reduce low-frequency output during operations and testing. - Minimize generator runtime. Rely on the grid for normal operations, schedule tests during daytime windows, and consider battery energy storage to reduce generator use. - Consider active noise control in constrained paths. It can help in specific, controlled scenarios, but is rarely practical at a facility scale or in open-air environments, especially at very low frequencies. Prioritize source control and isolation first. - Evaluate alternative cooling approaches. Liquid cooling can reduce reliance on high airflow and the associated fan noise, but pumps and related components should be mounted and isolated to avoid introducing new low-frequency paths. Engaging the Community with Data and Transparency Beyond engineering controls, measurement and communication matter. Operators will likely win more hearts and minds if they have an open conversation about low-frequency noise and infrasound – including what’s been measured and what’s being done – rather than suggesting that the issue lies solely in neighbors’ heads.

artigo.texto: Geely has introduced a new 2.2MW ultra-fast electric vehicle charging system that can charge compatible EVs from 10% to 70% in around 4.5 minutes. The technology places Geely among Chinese automakers competing to reduce EV charging times closer to conventional fuel refueling. Geely Smart Charge Delivers 2.25MW Output The new system, called Geely Smart Charge, combines megawatt-level charging hardware with artificial intelligence-based battery and thermal management technology. Geely claims the charger can deliver a peak output of 2,250kW (2.25MW) through a single charging gun. According to Geely’s testing, a Lynk & Co 10 equipped with the company’s latest battery technology achieved a peak charging rate of 1,093kW. The vehicle charged from 10% to 70% in approximately 4.5 minutes and reached 97% charge in 8 minutes and 40 seconds. AI Helps Manage Battery Temperature Geely is using its Xingrui PowerMind energy model with the charging system to predict battery temperature changes and adjust charging power in real time. Managing heat is one of the biggest challenges with megawatt-level charging because extremely high charging speeds can increase battery temperatures and affect performance. The AI-based system is designed to keep the battery within safe thermal limits while maintaining higher charging speeds. New Aegis Golden Brick Battery Technology Alongside the charger, Geely also introduced its latest Aegis Golden Brick ultra-short blade battery technology. The company’s higher-performance 12C battery is used in vehicles such as the Lynk & Co 10 and Zeekr 001, while the 6C battery is being introduced in the upgraded Geely Galaxy E5. The 6C battery can charge from 10% to 70% in around 8 minutes and 25 seconds. However, the fastest 4.5-minute charging figure applies only to vehicles equipped with the higher-rate battery technology and compatible charging hardware. Geely Challenges BYD in EV Charging Race China’s electric vehicle market is increasingly shifting competition from driving range to charging speed. BYD has already introduced its own fast-charging technology, which can charge compatible vehicles from 10% to 97% in around nine minutes. Geely’s latest charging system enters the same competition, as automakers attempt to make EV charging stops comparable to traditional fuel stops. Geely executive Zhang Dewang said charging speeds are approaching physical limits, meaning future improvements may become smaller as battery and charging technologies advance. Charging Infrastructure Becomes the Next Challenge While ultra-fast charging technology is improving, widespread adoption depends on charging infrastructure. Vehicles capable of accepting megawatt-level charging require compatible charging stations to deliver those speeds in real-world conditions. Geely plans to expand its charging network in China, targeting more than 100,000 charging guns by the end of 2027, including over 50,000 Geely Smart Charge units. The company has also increased eligible battery warranties from eight years or 150,000 km to eight years or 200,000 km and plans to provide charging credits for buyers of compatible vehicles. Relevance for Pakistan Geely is preparing to enter Pakistan’s automotive market and plans to introduce electric vehicles, including the Geely EX5 SUV. The international version of the EX5 is based on the Galaxy E5 platform, which is among the vehicles receiving Geely’s newer 6C battery technology in China. However, local specifications for Pakistan, including battery technology and charging capability, have not been confirmed. The availability of high-speed charging infrastructure will also determine how much benefit Pakistani buyers can receive from future EV technologies. Geely’s Push Toward Faster EV Charging Geely’s 2.2MW charging system highlights the direction of China’s EV industry, where manufacturers are now focusing not only on increasing driving range but also reducing charging times. While the 4.5-minute charging claim applies to specific battery and hardware combinations, the wider challenge will be deploying enough infrastructure to make these speeds practical for everyday drivers. artigo.texto: The News Amazonâs chief sustainability officer said Tuesday the company needed to âdo betterâ on communicating the environmental impact of its vast data center buildout, amid growing opposition to the projects in the US and Europe. âThere is a lot of debate, backlash against data centers in this country right now, and one of the things that weâre doing is taking a look at what have we done well and where have we fallen down and what do we need to do better,â Kara Hurst told Semaforâs The Next Three Billion event in New York. âAnd so, weâre revising a number of our practices. Weâre calling for a lot more transparency and accountability because thatâs what people in these communities deserve. Weâre saying, âhold us accountable for our practices,ââ Hurst said. Amazonâs carbon footprint grew for the second year in a row in 2025, as the tech giant accelerated its data center buildout, investing $220 billion in capital expenditure in 2026 alone. But local opposition threatens to hinder tech giantsâ race to build, with data center projects worth some $68 billion delayed or blocked because of local opposition between April and June this year, according to Data Center Watch. Amazon is looking to publish more metrics tracking its environmental footprint such as the effectiveness of energy and water usage at sites, Hurst said, part of a wider effort to address concerns from environmentalists and communities. Communities where data centers are built should also get a âreturn on that investment,â Hurst said. âThey should get workforce development, they should get upskilling, they should get economic development.â Know More There is currently no national framework in the US requiring hyperscalers to report data centersâ environmental impact. But Hurst said that voluntary reporting has an advantage over mandated disclosure: It lets companies put data out, have scientists test whether the metrics hold up, and revise the methodology if they donât, rather than locking in a potentially flawed standard. âWhat we need is to publish data, information thatâs science-led, and to publish it quickly and to put it out there and say, âIs this the right methodology?ââ she said. The data center race has posed a dilemma for sustainability goals globally. An S&P Global assessment of data center companies globally found that just 15 of the 50 firms surveyed received a passing grade signaling that they would be low-carbon and climate-resilient by 2030. Amazon has set a goal to be net-zero carbon by 2040, but Hurst said the firm will likely see emissions rise in the near term as the data center buildout heats up. âWeâve said all along this is not going to be linear,â Hurst said.

artigo.texto: The two men hoping to represent South Whitehall in the Pennsylvania state Senate next year stood in line with residents Wednesday night to sound off about the proposed Project Atlas hyperscale data center across from Parkland High School. Incumbent Sen. Jarrett Coleman and his opponent in the race for the 16th Senate District, Lehigh County Controller Mark Pinsley, urged the South Whitehall Planning Commission to vote against the $8.9 million development that would be built on 410 acres of undeveloped land on North Cedar Crest Boulevard. Coleman, a Republican who has introduced legislation that would give local municipalities the option to place an 18-month moratorium on new and unapproved data center development applications, raised concerns about the data center’s strain on the power grid, cost to local rate payers and damage to infrastructure. “It poses risks to our utilities, environment and public safety. Risks more intensive than what this zoning was designed to allow, especially given the site’s proximity to Parkland High School,” Coleman said. Coleman warned the panel that the lithium ion batteries that data centers typically rely on could lead to a fire that the township’s volunteer fire departments are not equipped to handle. Turning to the developers, who made a brief presentation at the start of the meeting, the senator said: “No one wants you here, so I don’t know why you still want to be here,” prompting applause from the large crowd in the Parkland High School auditorium, where the meeting was held in anticipation of a large turnout. Pinsley, a South Whitehall resident, listed financial reasons for the data center to be denied. He noted that a study of electric costs in the county government administration building in Allentown showed that electric bills have increased 55% in four years, costing taxpayers approximately $1million. Pinsley said he called PPL to find out why the price was rising so steeply, and was told that it was the distribution cost. “They said it was in anticipation of the data centers. They are already hardening the grid for that,” he said. Pinsley urged Edged U.S., the company that is seeking to build the data center, to forgo the sales tax break on computer equipment that Gov. Josh Shapiro put in place in 2022 to attract technology firms to the Commonwealth. Finally, Pinsley addressed the applicants as the father of children who attended Parkland. “I don’t know whose bright idea it was to put a data center across the street from a high school, but you have never seen wrath like that of parents. I’m asking you kindly to leave,” he said. The two men made similar comments at a news conference before the meeting organized by the South Whitehall Civic Alliance, a community group raising money to fight the data center in court. Alliance member Greg Sussman raised concerns about how the project originated, pointing to records that showed that township officials were discussing a data center being built on the land back in 2025, shortly after the Planned Innovation, Research, and Technology (PIRT) Overlay District was created. A PPL substation open house was also pushed back until after the legal window to challenge the PIRT ordinance expired, Sussman said. “The practical effect is that residents learned the full infrastructure details only after our legal opportunity to challenge the ordinance had already closed,” Sussman said. He called for an independent accounting of the timeline and coordination between the township and the developer. The planning commission did not make a decision Wednesday. Edged officials said they have more information to present. The deadline for the project to be approved is Dec. 31.

artigo.texto: Columbia Borough Council hears residents’ concerns over data center regulations The Columbia Borough Council in Lancaster County held a meeting Tuesday night to discuss proposed regulations for data centers, drawing significant community input and concerns about data centers' potential impact. Residents seek stronger protections The meeting, which lasted from 7 p.m. to 9:30 p.m., covered about half of the ordinance, with council members planning another meeting to continue hearing public input. Approximately 40 to 50 residents attended to share their thoughts. "What protections do you have? I guess I'm saying for all of you to protect us," one attendee said. The council is working on rules for data centers in light industrial and industrial zones. Earlier this year, Columbia passed a zoning ordinance barring data centers from light business zones, but that ordinance still requires county approval. The new regulations aim to address issues such as where data centers can be located, their size, and their impact on the community and environment. Taylor Enterline, a Columbia resident and member of Lancaster Stands Up, said, "We really need, like, strict regulations in place, to protect ourselves from data centers. We know that in Pennsylvania, you legally can't, like, stop a data center. But we can make it really hard. And also put really strict regulations in place that protect us and our community, our environment, our animals, and our pockets." Enterline and other residents expressed concerns about the size, noise levels, power usage, heat output, and environmental impact of data centers. Council faces legal limits on zoning Council members reiterated that they cannot ban data centers entirely, as exclusionary zoning is prohibited. "We can't just say no data centers are allowed in Columbia," they said, explaining that at least one location must be available for potential development. Despite this limitation, council members assured residents that they are listening to their concerns and will use the proposed rules to address them as much as possible. When asked about the next meeting, council members said they have not yet set a date but hope to schedule it soon to avoid delays in implementing data center regulations.
