artigo.texto: Low administrative hurdles, a receptive market for clean energy and EU funding are among the reasons expert cite for the country's leading green energy role in the region. As Eastern Europe's power sector has taken a hit from a record drought, Bulgaria has benefitted from building out battery storage capacity alongside its rapid solar expansion. Around a hundred battery energy storage system (BESS) sites are now operating, most of them built in the past two years. The large-scale projects take advantage of former industrial sites and airfields or are integrated into existing power stations, including coal-fired plants. "The scale and speed of storage deployment in Bulgaria is unprecedented in a European context," Stavros Papathanassiou, a professor at the National Technical University of Athens, told the AFP news agency. Low administrative hurdles, a receptive market for clean energy and EU funding are among the reasons expert cite for the country's leading role in the region. The battery installations absorb surplus power from solar installations and feed it back into the grid when demand rises. That proved a boon when exceptionally low levels on the River Danube disrupted power generation at nuclear and hydroelectric plants in Eastern Europe, boosting demand for electricity imports. In July and August, Bulgaria, one of the EU's poorest countries, recorded net electricity exports of around 830 gigawatt-hours a month, more than twice the average in May and June. In July alone, Romania accounted for nearly half of Bulgaria's outward electricity transfers, valued at an estimated €74 million. Reducing coal reliance At Maritsa East 3, once Bulgaria's second-largest coal-fired power plant, the shift away from dependence on the fuel is visible on the ground. Built under communism with four generating units, the plant sharply reduced coal operations in 2024, repurposing existing grid infrastructure for a battery facility. "We could leverage the large connection to the grid. We decided to disconnect one coal unit and connect batteries," said Vassil Shtonov, head of Bulgaria operations for the British-based power company ContourGlobal. "Coal is out, battery is in. It was the right place at the right time," Shtonov told AFP, though he said Bulgaria should maintain a minimum coal-fired reserve for severe winters or disruptions to gas supplies. While Bulgaria accounted for about 9% of European battery-storage additions and about 2% of solar additions in 2025, it can "serve as a positive example for other European nations," said Lennart Herrmann at the Munich-based research and consulting firm FfE. "The right incentives...can enable a swift energy transition," he told AFP. The Bulgarian energy ministry said the country had around 5.7 gigawatts of operational battery-storage power capacity this month. That is equivalent, in power terms, to nearly a quarter of Bulgaria's installed power-generation capacity overall and more than five times neighbouring Romania's operational battery capacity. Businesses in Bulgaria have also signed contracts for nearly 14 gigawatt-hours of large‑scale storage, part of which has already come online. "The aim is for storage systems to find a sustainable role in the market," the ministry said, adding that it "must go hand in hand with other investments, such as in transmission and distribution grids." 'By chance' Nikola Gazdov, president of Bulgaria's Association for Production, Storage and Trading of Electricity, attributed the battery boom to a combination of factors rather than a crafted strategy. "Everything happened almost by chance," he told AFP. Solar and wind capacity has expanded rapidly across the region, but Bulgaria's renewables boom has been particularly solar-heavy, creating growing daytime surpluses. And in Bulgaria, large battery projects can be up and running in just nine to 18 months, much less than many solar or wind projects, Gazdov added. But battery storage technology has its limits. One is that grid connections with neighbouring countries are limited in the amount of current they can transport. Another is that current batteries can store power only for relatively short periods, "typically between one and six, sometimes up to eight hours," said Herrmann at FfE. So while they can support the grid in case of a temporary drop in power supply, they cannot replace a nuclear reactor that goes offline due to drought. And their success could ultimately reduce their own profitability, because when more BESS operators buy electricity when prices are low and sell it back at peak times, the gap between the two price periods will narrow.

artigo.texto: Sedgwick County unveils draft regulations for data centers amid community pushback WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH) - Sedgwick County planners and community members met Thursday to discuss proposed regulations for commercial data centers as local leaders work to establish permanent zoning rules before a temporary development pause expires. Sedgwick County paused data center development earlier this year to allow officials time to evaluate the industry’s footprint and draft standards that protect local resources. On Thursday, planners presented the first public draft of the regulatory framework. “We are taking the appropriate time to establish draft regulations that work for all of Sedgwick County and work for the City of Wichita,” said Justin Constantino, prinicpal planner for the Metropolitan Area Planning Department. Balancing Economic Growth and Neighborhood Concerns Officials spent more than two hours reading and discussing the initial draft before opening the floor to public comment. Residents attended the meeting to submit an alternative draft of regulations, urging planners to take a stricter approach to potential noise, utility strain, and environmental impact. Mike Betzen, a Sedgwick County resident who spoke during the hearing, emphasized that neighbors are not trying to block technological growth entirely, but rather want safeguards against massive developments. “We’re not saying, ‘not in our backyard,’ but if you’re gonna do it, you better understand the risk,” Betzen said. “These are issues everybody’s seeing around the nation. Which provides merit, because it’s not just an isolated thing. It’s everywhere. You’re seeing the same issues, whether it’s energy, power, water, buildings, the size, the construction phase. They’re all the same issues. So let’s do it right, and do it up front.” Betzen noted specific concerns regarding massive “hyperscaler” facilities, arguing they may be ill-suited for the area’s power grid and water infrastructure. “They may not be appropriate for Sedgwick County. And that’s what we’re saying. Smaller ones, done correctly. Limit the size, make sure you’ve got the things in place,” Betzen said. He also raised concerns about decommissioning plans: “They said, leave the building there. Well, I wouldn’t ever want to have a 25-, 30-acre building left there.” Next Steps for the Moratorium Planning officials said the proposed guidelines remain fluid and will incorporate additional feedback from residents and local leaders. “Again, just really early in the process. So, we’re working through this draft document right now,” Constantino said. “What’s in there currently is subject to change based on the feedback that we receive from the planning commissioners, the county commissioners and members of the public.” The planning committee is scheduled to reconvene in two weeks to continue reviewing revisions. A formal public hearing on the proposed regulations is set for Nov. 12. If the Metropolitan Area Planning Department recommends approval and the Sedgwick County Board of Commissioners approves them, the permanent rules could take effect in December before the county’s current moratorium expires. artigo.texto: Buffalo, N.Y. (WBEN) - Last week, the Buffalo Common Council were presented a resolution from North District Councilman Joe Golombek that was seek a two-year moratorium on any potential new data center or crypto mining facility across the city limits. During Tuesday's Community Development Committee meeting, the city lawmakers hosted a public hearing regarding the moratorium, where nearly a dozen people made up of community members and advocates spoke in support of the moratorium. After hearing from the public, many of the Council members also spoke in support of the measure. According to Golombek, who spoke with WGRZ's Nate Benson after the meeting, he expects the moratorium to pass at the next general Common Council meeting this coming Tuesday. Golombek also told Benson once the measure is passed, a commission will be formed that will address appropriate zoning and regulations for any city data centers. Buffalo Mayor Sean Ryan says his office had been working on a one-year moratorium as an Executive Order, but pulled it back when New York Gov. Kathy Hochul issued an Executive Order for a one-year moratorium across the state. "Now the Council has a two-year moratorium that differs significantly from the state's, so we're going to take a look at that," said Ryan on Thursday. "We all know what the enemy is. The enemy is big data centers coming in and buying land. But we have to make sure that we don't inadvertently sweep up Roswell Park's computers, M&T Bank's computers, Kaleida's computers, the University at Buffalo. So we're going to be checking with all these institutions that have rather large computer storage facilities to make sure this somehow doesn't affect them." As more-and-more municipalities continue to explore moratoriums on data centers and residents voice their concerns, utility companies like National Grid can understand the concerns. "We don't have any data centers here that are driving demand to levels where we would need to be super concerned about. The data center phenomenon really hasn't hit yet, but that's not to say we don't get inquiries," said Ken Kujawa, regional director at National Grid. "Data centers are looking all the time, they're looking to find where they can locate, where they can identify locations where the capacity exists to meet their loads." Kujawa says the data centers do pose some challenges for utility companies, because they are larger electric loads than what they normally see on their system. "With data centers, the issue is they're large consumers of electricity, so each case has to be looked at individually, in terms of the amount of electricity they're going to consume and also where they're going to locate, to make sure that the infrastructure is at that location to be able to serve them," Kujawa said with WBEN. "And if it's not and we have to build additional facilities to serve them, then that data center or that large load customer has the responsibility to pay for that." Kujawa knows well that ratepayers don't want to see their energy bills go up, and it's something all utility companies need to be cognizant of. He believes the state's guidelines that will be established during the one-year moratorium will help set the stage for much of what happens going forward. "Gov. Hochul created the moratorium through her Executive Order, the state's going to take a step back and create the rules of engagement for data centers. And, obviously, there's going to be a lot of focus on electricity. So I think we just have to wait to see what comes out of that, and then once we find out where the governor is going to land, then I think we'll be in a better position to talk about it in more detail," Kujawa said. He adds the guidelines the state establishes for data centers as a result of the moratorium will put utility companies in a better position to be able to figure out how to work with data centers across their franchise area. "We think that there's an opportunity for the potential for large loads like data centers to actually be able to create a revenue stream for utility companies to be able to fund future infrastructure investments," Kujawa noted. "So if we all do this right, we think there's a way that data centers can actually be beneficial when it comes to how utilities work with them and, looking down the road, have them help us fund investments that are needed in our infrastructure, not just to serve them but also our larger customer base." artigo.texto: New proposed Colleton County data center campus draws residents’ questions COLLETON COUNTY, S.C. (WCSC) — What’s going to happen if a data center development is built in Colleton County? It’s a $6 billion question that’s fueling a debate between protecting the rural environment or the potential economic boost it could bring to the county. The Colleton County Economic Alliance hosted a data center information session for local residents to answer questions about a new 1,000-megawatt data center development. “I came in prepared with about six pages of printouts with questions,” Nancy Thomas, a local resident of Colleton County, said. Residents wished this information had come sooner, just one week after the county passed its new digital infrastructure overlay district. The Rhodes Technology Park is a data center campus spanning more than 1,200 acres, with 10 data centers and two substations. “This is a single-user large hyperscale campus. We do not yet know who the user may be. You know, the Microsofts of the world, the Metas of the world, the Oracles of the world, will be a user occupying this entire facility,” Ken Loeber, a partner with Eagle Rock Partners, said. The project is west of I-95 off Mount Carmel Road, inside the new overlay district. Developers say it will meet a 65-decibel noise limit, use a closed-loop, non-evaporative cooling system and include proper buffers to mitigate impacts. “It sits behind a treed buffer because of the height of the trees. It really is $6 billion off of Mount Carmel Road that no one will be able to see,” Loeber said. Project leaders say that investment will create 500 permanent jobs and more than 1,000 construction jobs over five to seven years. “You’re talking $95 to 105,000 a year. That’s double our median household income,” Brantley Strickland, executive director of the Colleton County Economic Alliance, said. Loeber says 30% of the jobs would be network and IT engineers, about 30% would be in facility management, 30% would be in security and 10% would be administrative jobs. “We had a great meeting on Thursday of last week with some of the local contractors, people in the contracting community. And they said, ‘Look, we realize we’re not a large enough general contractor to run a $6 billion project, but I can certainly put up lights and I can certainly do other things. How do I as a Colleton County business owner or a laborer, how do I make sure that I’m prepared to be able to do that work when it occurs?’” Loeber said. A development agreement is also being finalized. It would fund road improvements near the property, create a contractor-training program so local residents can take part in construction and even invest in the future of STEM. Residents now have answers to questions about the proposed benefits. “What about a training program for local young people? They’re going to have a training program connected with the schools. That’s a plus,” Thomas said. Project leaders say the development will not cause rate increases for local residents and it is not tied to the Canady Gas Plant project. “Electric cooperatives of South Carolina have entered into an agreement that none of this transmission cost is going to be passed on to the residential customers. In fact, you may even see your residential rates go down because of that improved grid and the stability of that and sharing that fixed cost,” Strickland said. “We are paying for all the off-site transmission infrastructure as we should,” Loeber said. “The new gas plant is going to power South Carolina. We are taking power off the South Carolina grid, but there are many other ways that the grid in South Carolina is funded. We are not here because of the Canady’s plant. We didn’t follow it. It’s not being built for us,” Loeber said. And the county says the projected tax revenue from this project could be transformational. “We feel like this is our opportunity to kind of make that next step into the future and do something really great for our citizens. The ability to provide better county services; maybe people’s property taxes will even go down. We can pay teachers better, we can pay deputies better,” Strickland said. “Year four, you’re passing that $100 million a year threshold, so you know that would be huge. That’s more than doubling the county budget.” Eagle Rock Partners says, at its core, the facility’s purpose is simple. “Have electrons come in and knowledge come out. And that knowledge can be used in a host of different ways. Having that here where it’s controlled and regulated and American, I think is comforting,” Loeber said. Project leaders say construction is expected to begin around 2028 or 2029 as they finalize their energy and transmission study with Santee Cooper. Copyright 2026 WCSC. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - Energy storage systems supplied 13% to 19% of total generation at capacity factors, on par with gas-fired peaker plants when supply was at its tightest on California’s grid in 2024, avoiding more than $29 million in peak energy costs, RMI said in an analysis released earlier this month. - The following year, energy storage systems supplied 6% to 9% of generation during the Electric Reliability Council of Texas grid’s tightest hours, RMI said. - But an ERCOT rule change in December 2025 dampened energy storage systems’ ancillary services participation, adding $3.6 million to ERCOT wholesale pricing over just 24 hours and underscoring batteries’ role in maintaining cost-effective grid stability, RMI said. The nonprofit energy think tank’s forecast for 30% annual growth in battery deployment over the next five years is based on a projection made by London-based energy consultancy Wood Mackenzie in 2024, when the Biden-era Inflation Reduction Act was still in full effect. Earlier this year, Wood Mackenzie dialed back its five-year forecast for utility-scale battery deployments to 16%. Wood Mackenzie’s most recent forecast, released today, sees utility-scale deployment flatlining in 2026 and growing just 8% through 2031. Analysts say President Trump’s August executive order restricting deployment of foreign-produced bulk power components layers new challenges for the industry on top of existing headwinds like import tariffs and unfavorable tax treatment of systems reliant on parts tied to China. RMI’s report finds already-deployed batteries were helping to stabilize major U.S. grids as far back as 2022. At the peak of a record-breaking heat wave that year, 3.4 GW of grid batteries met 6% of California’s energy needs and “materially strengthened the system’s ability to maintain reserve margins,” RMI said, citing an ICF analysis. During a less intense heat wave two years earlier, when it had less than 1 GW of grid-connected battery capacity, California saw rolling blackouts despite a demand peak roughly 10% lower, according to the report. RMI found utility-scale energy storage systems provide significant financial benefits to host communities as well. Its review of project agreements in California, Massachusetts, Nevada and Texas put the average annual gross tax contribution around $6,600/MW, with some contributing more than $10,000/MW. RMI said a 250 MW/500 MWh battery installation that came online in February will provide about $46 million in revenue over 20 years for the town of Medway, Massachusetts. And even after factoring in partial state property tax abatements, the 400-MW Purple Sage Energy Center will deliver $3.4 million in payments to local governments in Nevada each year, the group said. RMI used the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s CO-Benefits Risk Assessment Health Impacts Screening and Mapping Tool to determine that Suffolk County, New York, could avoid $5.3 million in annual health costs by transitioning its 500-MW Port Jefferson peaker to battery storage. artigo.texto: SALT LAKE CITY — A new poll shows the majority of Americans, and even more than a majority in Utah, oppose an artificial data center in their neighborhoods. The poll was conducted by our partners at the Deseret News and the Hinckley Institute of Politics. Their results show most people oppose building these data centers, even if they promise to bring jobs and economic growth to their area. Nationwide, 26% of the people surveyed said building data centers is necessary for the U.S. to compete with China. Nearly 60% of Americans said that protecting communities from the effects of nearby data centers is more important that keeping up with China. Fifteen percent of those polled said they were not sure. In Utah, 67% of people polled said they prefer to keep their neighborhoods the way they are when compared to putting a data center there.

artigo.texto: LEBANON, OH — The Warren County Board of County Commissioners is considering a temporary moratorium on data center developments following a work session discussion on Tuesday, September 22, 2026. The proposed pause aims to give county officials time to study the potential impact these large-scale facilities could have on the local electrical grid, water supply, and zoning regulations. Ray Drafft, the Warren County Director of Building and Zoning, presented an informational brief to Commissioners Shannon Jones, Tom Grossmann, and Dave Young regarding the different scales of data centers. He noted that while smaller co-location facilities currently operate within municipal areas like Lebanon and Deerfield Township, the county’s current rural zoning code does not contain specific regulations or definitions for larger "hyperscale" facilities. Assistant Prosecutor Bruce McGary clarified that under the county's existing framework, any immediate application would have to be evaluated against "same or similar" land uses, which has previously created regulatory challenges with other utility-scale projects. Utility and Environmental Considerations A primary focus of the work session was the resource consumption associated with data center cooling and operations. Drafft informed the board that data center designs vary, with some utilizing open-loop evaporation systems that consume significant amounts of water, while others use closed-loop recycling systems. To better understand local capacity, county officials are awaiting the results of a Southwest Ohio water sustainability study currently being conducted by the Ohio EPA and the Ohio-Kentucky-Indiana Regional Council of Governments (OKI), which is scheduled for release in November 2026. Commissioners also raised questions regarding the long-term effects on local infrastructure, residential utility rates, and continuous noise levels from facility cooling fans. Zoning Options and Community Feedback Drafft outlined three potential regulatory pathways for the county moving forward: - Conditional Use: Allowing facilities via Board of Zoning Appeals approval with uniform use standards. - Site Plan Review: Requiring administrative review and public hearings directly before the Board of County Commissioners. - Data Center Floating Zone (Option 3): Establishing a specific "DC" zoning classification that would require a formal rezoning process, legislative discretion by the commissioners, and potential township voter referendums. Turtle Creek Township Trustee Jonathan Sams spoke during the public portion of the meeting, expressing support for a cautious approach. Sams noted that portions of Turtle Creek Township sit above a sensitive aquifer and suggested forming a multi-jurisdictional task force to evaluate the broader economic, tax, and infrastructure burdens of these projects. Next Steps The commissioners expressed a consensus that implementing a temporary moratorium would be a practical step while data continues to be gathered. Commissioner Shannon Jones noted that a pause would allow the county to plan appropriately and develop clear standards rather than leaving development to chance. The board directed the prosecutor’s office to draft a formal moratorium resolution. Once the draft is prepared, the county will schedule and advertise a public hearing to allow residents to comment before any official restrictions are voted into place. artigo.texto: Data Centers Gubernatorial Candidates Split on Data Center Policy in 2026 September 18, 2026 | Morgan Scarboro September 24, 2026 | Kim Miller Key Takeaways: Residents in 28 localities across six states will consider data center ballot measures in the upcoming November elections. These measures propose bans or moratoriums on data center construction, while others seek to make existing restrictions more permanent and have the potential to put residents at odds with local officials. In Emporia, voters will decide whether to prohibit the construction, installation, operation, and maintenance of “high impact data centers” in all zoning districts. The measure defines these facilities as data centers with a peak electrical load exceeding 10 MW or a daily water draw exceeding 100,000 gallons. The thresholds are notably lower than those used in many recent proposals targeting larger data center developments. The measure has also prompted litigation. City officials sought judicial review over whether the proposed ordinance is a proper subject for the citizen-initiative process. A court ordered the question placed on the November ballot, but legal questions concerning the measure remain pending. If voters approve the ordinance, it cannot take effect until those issues are resolved or a court otherwise permits implementation. In El Dorado, voters will consider a similar proposal prohibiting high-impact data centers, but adds a provision allowing the moratorium to remain in effect for ten years, and stipulates that only another vote could repeal or amend the moratorium. The proposal would also prohibit certain battery energy storage systems due to concerns about fire. El Dorado officials also sought judicial review of the citizen-initiated proposal. In August, the district court determined that the proposed ordinance concerned a legislative function of municipal government and could proceed through the citizen-initiative process, clearing the way for the measure to appear on the November ballot. High Impact Data Center A high impact data center, as defined in the Kansas ballot measures, is a facility with a peak electrical load exceeding 10 megawatts or a daily water draw exceeding 100,000 gallons. These thresholds are lower than those used in many other proposals and are intended to target larger-scale data center developments. In Bloomington, voters will decide whether to impose a moratorium on large scale data centers in the city. The ballot measure is proceeding despite a six-month moratorium passed by the City Council earlier this year. The ballot measure does not specify the length of the moratorium. One resident who spoke in support of the ballot measure stated that he wanted to ensure that officials “on the county level and on the state level understand that the people in this community do not want data centers here that are unregulated, that don’t have any guardrails.” Elsewhere in Illinois, voters will have the chance to weigh in on new data center development. Voters in four cities in Madison County will consider advisory measures asking whether local officials should permit the construction and operation of new data centers. Nine measures ask voters whether data centers should be prohibited based on their projected electrical demand, while three jurisdictions will consider outright prohibitions on data center construction regardless of electrical demand. These ballot measures are another flashpoint in growing skepticism towards data centers in Ohio, where at least 125 data center moratoriums are currently in effect. Local jurisdictions across the country have considered or implemented data center moratoriums, frequently with the goal of studying the impact that data centers will have on their community. The November ballot measures give residents an opportunity to weigh in directly on whether data center development should proceed in their communities at all. In some jurisdictions, voters will decide whether their concerns can be addressed through limits based on electricity demand while in others, voters will consider prohibiting new data centers regardless of energy needs. In Edgewater, Florida, voters will decide whether to amend the city's charter to prohibit the permitting, construction, expansion, or operation of new data centers within city limits. Voters will consider this ballot measure following the enactment of a data center ban by the Edgewater City Council earlier this month. Council members stated that they enacted the ban to prevent a data center from being approved before the November election. The ballot measure is moving forward despite the council's action, as proponents argue that a future city council could reconsider the prohibition and that amending the city charter would provide a more durable restriction on future data center development. There has been speculation that opposition to data centers will play a substantial role in the midterm elections. Some voters have stated that opposition to data centers in their community is their primary concern this election, causing some to consider voting for candidates they may not otherwise support, however, recent polling suggests that concerns about data centers and AI are not a big concern for many voters. artigo.texto: O sistema de armazenamento de energia (ESS) da DoGo Power, que forma redes inteligentes, foi lançado e está pronto para encomendas globais. XANGAI, 22 de setembro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A DoGo Power realizou o evento "Formando o Futuro da Energia" - Estratégia e Lançamento de Novos Produtos, lançando globalmente sua estratégia "Orientada a Cenários + Formação de Redes + IA", juntamente com soluções inteligentes de armazenamento de energia para formação de redes para cenários comerciais e industriais (C&I) de grande e médio porte e em escala de serviços públicos. Robin Zhu, fundador e CEO da DoGo Power, afirmou: "Após uma rápida expansão em escala, o setor de armazenamento de energia entrou em uma fase de desenvolvimento de alta qualidade." A adaptação de cenários, a formação de redes e a IA tornaram-se elementos essenciais da competitividade. O armazenamento de energia precisa deixar de ser uma "unidade de custo" e se tornar uma "unidade criadora de valor". A DoGo Power concentra-se no armazenamento de energia em escala de rede para formação de redes elétricas, com o objetivo de ser líder em tecnologia de ponta para o novo tipo de sistema de energia. Buscamos cooperar com parceiros globais para fomentar um novo crescimento industrial através da inovação tecnológica." A DoGo Power estabeleceu três centros de P&D e dois centros de simulação e testes na China, reunindo 19 grupos de especialistas interdisciplinares liderados por doutores, com mais de 60% da equipe dedicada à P&D. Seus três centros de produção globais oferecem uma capacidade de produção de 10 GWh na primeira fase. Apoiada por uma rede de vendas e serviços que abrange mais de 30 países e regiões, a DoGo evoluiu da exportação de produtos para a operação localizada. Orientação estratégica: Da industrialização da energia renovável à transformação das indústrias tradicionais pelas energias renováveis. A DoGo Power identifica um caminho de evolução em quatro estágios para um novo tipo de sistema de energia: 1-Expansão de P&D, da indústria e das tecnologias, 2-Formação de Grade para Estabilização, 3-IA para Maior Receita e 4-Integração Inteligente Holística. O setor encontra-se atualmente na Fase 2. Com base nisso, a DoGo desenvolve uma solução para a Etapa 3 e implementa negócios globais rumo à Etapa 4 sob dois pilares principais: - Definição de soluções baseada em cenários reais de clientes, desafios práticos e valor comercial mensurável. - A plataforma tecnológica 4S, desenvolvida internamente, impulsionada duplamente pela formação de redes e pela IA, possibilita um sistema de energia definido por algoritmo. Integrando EMS, PMS, PCS e BMS, a plataforma 4S constrói estações de armazenamento de energia inteligentes capazes de análise, otimização, tomada de decisões e atualização iterativa. Com o respaldo dessa base técnica, a DoGo fornece soluções em escala de rede adequadas para diversos cenários, requisitos de múltiplas energias e múltiplas escalas temporais em todo o mundo. Soluções de Novos Produtos Baseadas em Cenários Duas soluções emblemáticas de sistemas de armazenamento de energia (ESS) para formação de redes inteligentes foram lançadas para cenários comerciais e industriais (C&I) e de grande escala para concessionárias de serviços públicos. 1.Solução C&I Smart GFM ESS Adotando um design compacto do tipo "1 ESS substitui 8 gabinetes", esta unidade de 3 metros consolida as funções de seis gabinetes ESS de 260 kWh+, um gabinete combinador, um gabinete on/off-grid e um transformador de isolamento. Isso reduz o CAPEX inicial em 1,2 centavos de dólar por Wh, diminui a ocupação de terras em 35% e encurta a entrega do projeto em 5 a 7 dias. Com suporte para acesso a múltiplas fontes, como painéis fotovoltaicos, geradores a diesel, pontos de recarga, rede elétrica e sistemas de gerenciamento, o sistema permite a comutação perfeita entre conexão e desconexão da rede em ≤20ms, atendendo de forma confiável cargas sensíveis e de alta potência e concretizando o conceito de "1 contêiner equivale a 1 microrrede". A capacidade de dimensionamento flexível suporta a implantação mista de diferentes séries e a compatibilidade com inversores de terceiros para maximizar a utilização dos ativos existentes. 2.Solução de armazenamento de energia GFM inteligente em escala de utilidade pública Desenvolvido para projetos com terrenos complexos e restrições de transporte, o contêiner pesa menos de 22 toneladas, dobrando as rotas de transporte viáveis em comparação com os contêineres convencionais de 20 pés e reduzindo os custos de logística marítima e terrestre. Seu design sem cabos elimina a necessidade de escavações e montagem de cabos no local, com o pré-comissionamento completo do sistema realizado na fábrica. Aproveitando a arquitetura dinâmica de taxa C, os clientes podem começar com uma implementação de duração de 2 horas para controlar o CAPEX e expandir por meio de gabinetes de expansão de data center para ajustar suavemente as taxas C e as durações de backup para corresponder aos modelos de negócios em evolução. Grade‑Formando o Núcleo: Arquitetura de Coordenação de 3 Camadas Para equilibrar a estabilidade do sistema e os benefícios econômicos, a DoGo Power adota uma arquitetura de 3 camadas: - Camada de controle formadora de grade estável inferior: Atende às demandas de estabilidade em nível de milissegundos, incluindo a resposta inercial. - Camada intermediária de controle de coordenação eficiente: Executa funções de nível de centenas de milissegundos, como regulação secundária de frequência e tensão e partida a frio rápida. - Camada superior de despacho de otimização inteligente: Oferece previsão e otimização globais para maximizar os retornos econômicos em condições de operação estáveis. A arquitetura permite que os sistemas de armazenamento ofereçam suporte à estabilidade e regulação flexível nos lados da geração, da rede e da carga. artigo.texto: A infraestrutura para inteligência artificial ganhou destaque nos programas de governo de importantes nomes da política nacional. Figuras como Lula, Flávio Bolsonaro, Ronaldo Caiado, Romeu Zema e Renan Santos concordam sobre a urgência de ampliar a capacidade computacional, embora apresentem visões distintas sobre o papel estatal, incentivos e regras ambientais. Diferenças nas propostas dos candidatos As estratégias variam conforme o grupo político. O plano de Lula vincula os servidores à autonomia tecnológica, sugerindo supercomputadores e serviços de nuvem controlados por instituições brasileiras, além de impor critérios rigorosos de eficiência energética e uso de recursos hídricos. Por outro lado, Ronaldo Caiado condiciona benefícios tributários a metas socioambientais e tecnológicas. Já Flávio Bolsonaro e Romeu Zema focam na captação de recursos privados, priorizando energia acessível e desregulamentação para atrair as empresas. Enquanto Renan Santos aposta em zonas econômicas voltadas à inovação, Augusto Cury enxerga a tecnologia como um pilar estratégico de Estado, embora sem detalhar medidas específicas para a instalação dessas estruturas físicas. Desafios na busca por autonomia digital Especialistas apontam que a simples multiplicação de servidores no território nacional não assegura autonomia. “Você pode ser um quintal para data centers de outros, que simplesmente vão absorver os seus recursos naturais e energéticos”, afirma Luca Belli, professor da Fundação Getulio Vargas. Para o meio acadêmico, o ideal seria envolver universidades, centros de pesquisa e governos locais no processo. Além disso, existe uma forte dependência externa em relação a fornecedores de chips avançados e serviços de computação em nuvem, dominados por poucas corporações estrangeiras. Impactos na infraestrutura e o avanço do Redata O consumo massivo de eletricidade e água para refrigeração e funcionamento contínuo dessas instalações preocupa entidades de defesa do consumidor, como o Idec, que cobra rigor nas regras de localização e estudos de impacto. Enquanto o debate político ocorre, o Congresso já movimenta pautas econômicas para o setor. O Senado aprovou recentemente o Redata, programa que concede isenções bilionárias de tributos como IPI, PIS/Cofins e imposto de importação para o setor, exigindo em contrapartida o uso de energia limpa e eficiência hídrica. O cenário internacional também impõe desafios geopolíticos complexos para o país, dividindo atenções entre potências globais. Sobre esse aspecto, a ministra da Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação, Luciana Santos, pontuou em entrevista à Folha de S.Paulo: “Os Estados Unidos ameaçam cessar o fornecimento a quem fizer negócios nessas áreas mais críticas com a China.” Dessa forma, o futuro digital brasileiro depende não apenas do volume de investimentos atraídos, mas da capacidade de reter tecnologia, gerar empregos qualificados e proteger os recursos naturais essenciais para a população.

artigo.texto: Data Center developer holds community meeting on potential Sulphur Springs project HOPKINS COUNTY, Texas (KLTV) - Residents of an East Texas community met tonight hoping to learn more about a potential project in their backyard. CyrusOne , a data center developer, held a community meeting regarding a potential data center just outside Sulphur Springs City Limits. The project would sit on the old Thermo mine. Residents will got chance to ask the developer questions at the Hopkins County Civic Center on Thursday evening. The property was previously under development by another company, MSB Global. They are no longer involved in the project after ongoing legal battles involving the land. The project, which Cyrus One says “could ultimately include multiple data center buildings developed over time” is still under consideration and is not a done deal. “We are committed to having a conversation with the community before we fully scope that out with the City of Sulphur Springs,” said Katy Hancock with CyrusOne. The project could bring a $2.6 billion investment to the community and 30 to 40 permanent jobs per data center building. There could be over a thousand construction jobs for a multi-year construction period. The data center would be self-powered using natural gas, but grid connection could be a possibility as the campus grows. The company says they would pay for any infrastructure upgrades. Each building would use around a thousand gallons of water a day. According to the EPA, an average family of four uses about 400 gallons of water a day at home. Several residents raised concerns about potential noise pollution. “There are times we can hear Interstate 30, and it’s four miles away, said one resident. ”Please tell me how you are going to mitigate sound when we can hear Interstate 30." While the scope of the project isn’t determined, the company said the center would emit the noise level of a typical conversation. The land for the project is tied up in ongoing legal battles. The former landowner is suing the City of Sulphur Springs and the former developer. They allege the City went against the terms of the land deed, which said they couldn’t have means of power generation. “If we don’t find a solution, and the solution has to be through the litigation process,” said Gene Alessandrini with CyrusOne, “That would just push the data project out.” A judge has ruled that the land can’t have means of power generation while lawyers prepare for trial, which is set for next year. The company says they will return for another meeting before any announcements are made. Copyright 2026 KLTV. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: CASPER, Wyo. — Concerns and skepticism surrounding the impacts of the planned Prometheus Hyperscale data center project, as well as data centers more broadly, took center stage Wednesday at a forum hosted by the Wyoming Outdoor Council. The Prometheus Hyperscale Data Center is a proposed $500 million, 1.5-gigawatt campus situated on 940 acres of Falls Ranch property south of Interstate 25 between Casper and Glenrock, entirely within Natrona County. Project representatives say the facility is being designed to generate its own electricity on-site without drawing power from the public utility grid. Jocelyn Wulf, the data center policy manager for the council, said on Wednesday that while data centers have existed for several decades, the difference of recent developments is one of scale. She contrasted traditional facilities that draw five to 10 megawatts of power with hyperscale developments that consume hundreds of megawatts or gigawatts, pointing to Google’s Project Tembo in Cheyenne which currently uses 2.7 gigawatts and is designed to scale up to 10 gigawatts. Focusing on environmental impacts, Wulf pointed to water, air and energy as three of the resources most impacted by data centers. Of the three, Wulf said concerns regarding water are the most prevalent in communities throughout the country, as well as in Wyoming specifically. “This is probably the single biggest concern I hear from people when data centers come up in the conversation,” she said. “And it’s a really valid concern. I think as we all know, Wyoming is a semi-arid state. Water is a really critical and precious resource here.” Wulf said there has actually been positive momentum in data centers’ usage of water, as hyperscale developments are increasingly adopting closed-loop cooling systems that recirculate water and chemical coolant mixtures that significantly reduce direct water consumption. Previously, she said, data centers would consume thousands of gallons daily, if not more. However, she added that concerns surrounding water still remain. Wulf said a lack of mandatory public reporting creates blind spots regarding wastewater discharge, which can contain dangerous chemical coolants, citing an incident in Cheyenne where a contractor released wastewater containing harmful bacteria into the city’s municipal system. Wulf also noted that co-located natural gas power plants required to supply continuous electricity to large facilities can consume tens to hundreds of millions of gallons of water daily. “While the facilities themselves might not be using so much water, we really still need to look at the power generation side of the conversation,” she said. Worries over water impacts were also shared by several attendees, with multiple residents pointing to the planned facility’s proximity to the North Platte River. After the meeting, Wulf said it’s difficult to predict what the impact to the river will be. “I think we would have to be really careful and very cognizant of how Prometheus is dealing with its water discharge to make sure that it does not affect such a delicate ecosystem as the North Platte negatively,” she told Oil City News. Natural gas plants also factor into environmental questions surrounding data centers’ impacts on air quality, Wulf said. Expanded energy production — particularly from co-located natural gas plants — increases greenhouse gas emissions. And because the facilities require 24/7 power, they utilize backup diesel generators that release pollutants like nitrogen oxides and particulates. And because hyperscale data centers require what Wulf said are “orders of magnitude” more energy than older data centers, grid connections require expensive infrastructure upgrades, including new substations and power lines. To ensure safe and responsible data center development, the WOC is advocating for changes to the state’s regulatory framework. Wulf said that while Wyoming’s Industrial Siting Act requires comprehensive environmental and economic evaluations, developers can bypass state review by siting facilities within city or county industrial parks. That exemption shifts evaluation responsibilities to local county commissions, which she said may have limited capacity for extensive technical reviews. “When the ISA is bypassed, that burden for comprehensive, rigorous state agency review now falls onto the shoulders of local governments who, despite their best intentions, may have a little bit more limited capacity for federal review,” she said. Local resident Marc Nogle suggested the state establish a commission to regulate data centers to address the concern. “I think the state or somebody has to set up a separate entity that regulates these data centers,” Nogle said. “There’s way too much stuff that nobody understands, and there’s been no transparency, no information. And they come to Wyoming because [they thing] we’re hillbillies and they can get away with it.” Wulf, meanwhile, attributed developer interest in Wyoming to low energy costs, available land and state sales tax exemptions on computational equipment. To protect areas where data centers are planned, Wulf said the WOC is advocating for community benefit agreements that commit developers to a set of guarantees. As an example, she pointed to one in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, where the local government required daily water use caps, local hiring, renewable energy use, money reinvested into the area and more. “I know that lots of communities in Wyoming struggle with things like stormwater infrastructure. So that’s an example of what could be asked for by communities around Wyoming,” she told Oil City News. In an effort to ensure transparency, the WOC has started a petition that would look to create enforceable standards, require transparency and disclosure of impacts, close loopholes, improve funding for state regulators and more. artigo.texto: Maryland governor signs executive order establishing new framework for data center development ANNAPOLIS, Md. - Maryland Gov. Wes Moore has signed an executive order creating strict guardrails for transparent and accountable data center development and announced plans to work with the General Assembly to repeal the state’s 2020 Data Center Sales and Use Tax Exemption. The order establishes a Maryland Data Center Task Force to protect ratepayers, the environment and local communities. The framework sets one standard, one review process and one public record for any proposed data center of 25 megawatts or more. Projects will be evaluated on five principles: ratepayer and grid protection, economic benefits for Marylanders, community voice, environmental protections, and transparency and accountability. RELATED: Wes Moore holds nearly 48-to-1 cash advantage over Dan Cox in Maryland rematch The task force will review each project, publish rules, maintain the public Data Center Dashboard, support local governments and coordinate with neighboring states. Members will come from multiple state agencies, including Energy, Commerce, Labor, Environment, Natural Resources, Agriculture and Planning. Each project will receive a public determination of Aligned, Conditionally Aligned or Not Aligned. The executive order also creates a Data Center Dashboard, updated monthly, that will serve as the state’s public record of data center development. It will list project locations, developers, parent companies, anchor tenants, projected power demand and water use, requested state actions, determinations, commitments and annual reports. The Source: Information in this article comes from The Office of Governor Wes Moore and previous FOX 5 reporting.

artigo.texto: Nova Scotia Power has inaugurated three 50MW/200MWh battery energy storage systems (BESS) in Bridgewater, Waverley and White Rock, now Atlantic Canada’s largest battery storage facilities. The Government of Canada invested CA$109 million (US$79 million) for pre-development work, installation and grid modernisation upgrades tied to the projects, part of Natural Resources Canada’s Electricity Predevelopment Program. The Canada Infrastructure Bank (CIB), a federal Crown corporation that provides debt financing for infrastructure projects, provided a further CA$138.2 million loan. Nova Scotia Power, the province’s monopoly electric utility, expects the combined 150MW/600MWh portfolio to support the province’s shift away from coal-fired generation and strengthen grid reliability during peak-demand periods and outages. The Canada Infrastructure Bank said the arrangement marks the first clean energy project backed by its Indigenous Equity Initiative. Vivek Sood, president and CEO of Nova Scotia Power, said the completion of all three sites reflected years of planning, engineering and community engagement. “These projects strengthen the reliability of the electricity system for our customers while enabling the continued growth of renewable energy across the province,” Sood said. Crystal Nicholas, president and general manager of the WMA, said the equity structure gives Mi’kmaw communities a direct stake in the province’s energy transition. “Inclusion in such projects opens pathways toward economic reconciliation and ensures that traditional Indigenous values are considered in major project development,” Nicholas said. Nova Scotia Utility and Review Board regulators approved the three-site portfolio in 2024, following amendments the province made to its Electricity Act in 2023 specifically to accelerate energy storage deployment. Those amendments allowed Nova Scotia Power to run competitive solicitations to procure battery storage resources, a legislative change that paved the way for the Bridgewater, Waverley and White Rock sites to proceed to construction. Nova Scotia has estimated it will need between 300MW and 400MW of energy storage by 2030 to help meet its target of 80% renewable energy and a full coal phase-out by that date. In 2022, more than 70% of the province’s electricity still came from coal, natural gas and other fossil fuels, with renewables, including hydro, wind, tidal and solar, contributing around 23%. Nova Scotia already hosts more than 300 commercial wind turbines, including five wind farms that are majority-owned by Mi’kmaw communities, and Chinese wind turbine manufacturer Envision Energy has separately signed a partnership agreement to explore a 300MW hybrid wind-plus-storage project near Sydney, Nova Scotia. Provincial utilities across Canada are moving on battery storage through different procurement models Nova Scotia’s approach, a utility-led build supported by direct federal investment and an Indigenous equity structure, sits alongside distinct battery storage strategies emerging in other provinces. In Ontario, the Independent Electricity System Operator’s (IESO) Long-Term 1 and Long-Term 2 procurement rounds have driven the country’s largest battery contracting activity to date, including the 250MW/1,000MWh Napanee BESS, developed by a joint venture between Ameresco and Atura Power, which began commercial operations in May 2026 roughly five weeks ahead of schedule and under its CA$600 million budget. Ontario’s storage build-out has been driven partly by the scheduled 2026 closure of the 2,100MW Pickering Nuclear station. Trade association Energy Storage Canada has recommended the province establish a dedicated procurement track for behind-the-meter and distribution-connected battery storage, arguing that existing compensation structures undervalue the grid services smaller, faster-to-deploy battery assets can already provide. British Columbia is taking a more centralised approach. BC Hydro, the province’s Crown-owned utility, is advancing what it describes as the first major battery storage project in the province, a facility of at least 100MW planned for a site near Duncan on Vancouver Island, which the utility intends to own and operate directly rather than procure through a long-term contract with a private developer. BC Hydro has identified up to 500MW of potential battery storage capacity across the province under its Powering Growth plan. Federally, the Nova Scotia investment is part of the government’s broader CA$4.5 billion Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program, which supports grid modernisation, storage and renewables deployment across every Canadian region, and follows the government’s May 2026 launch of a national strategy aimed at doubling the country’s grid capacity by 2050.

artigo.texto: Aprovação de regras para data centers deve destravar investimentos no RN A aprovação, pelo Conselho Estadual do Meio Ambiente (Conema), de regras para a instalação de data centers vai ajudar a destravar investimentos, gerar emprego e renda, além de trazer segurança jurídica para o Rio Grande do Norte A aprovação, pelo Conselho Estadual do Meio Ambiente (Conema), de regras para a instalação de data centers vai ajudar a destravar investimentos, gerar emprego e renda, além de trazer segurança jurídica para o Rio Grande do Norte. É o que avaliam segmentos que representam a indústria de energias renováveis do estado ouvidos pela TRIBUNA DO NORTE. A minuta de resolução deve ser publicada no Diário Oficial do Estado ainda esta semana. O documento aprovado pelo conselho na última segunda-feira (21) estabelece diretrizes, critérios e procedimentos para o licenciamento ambiental dos data centers no RN. A medida cria, pela primeira vez, um regramento específico para a atividade, permitindo ao Instituto de Desenvolvimento Sustentável e Meio Ambiente do RN (Idema) iniciar o licenciamento de projetos. Darlan Santos, presidente do Centro de Estratégias em Recursos Naturais e Energia (Cerne), avalia que a aprovação da minuta “é um passo decisivo, necessário e positivo”, sendo a previsibilidade regulatória o principal ativo para atração de investimentos. “A clara diferenciação entre sistemas de refrigeração fechados e abertos demonstra maturidade técnica na análise socioambiental, indicando a preocupação dos recursos hídricos do estado, enquanto desburocratiza projetos de menor impacto hídrico por meio do Relatório Ambiental Simplificado”, diz. Segundo Williman Oliveira, presidente da Associação Potiguar de Energias Renováveis (APER), a medida vai acelerar as discussões em torno do tema e ajudar a gerar emprego e renda no estado. “Temos urgentemente que oferecer essa oportunidade aos investidores, uma vez que tivermos com as normas e leis que tragam a segurança jurídica para os investimentos”, disse. A resolução representa um avanço, mas, ainda assim, cercado de desafios, na avaliação do presidente da APER. “É preciso prestar a infraestrutura em paralelo à legislação favorável para o desenvolvimento de data centers do RN, o que é um desafio”, explica. O presidente da Federação das Indústrias do RN, Roberto Serquiz, disse reconhecer a posição do Governo do Estado, “que compreendeu a importância dessa agenda e fez valer a qualidade técnica do órgão ambiental, com a participação decisiva dos diretores e secretários ligados ao desenvolvimento sustentável”. Segundo Roberto Serquiz, a resolução avançou mesmo diante da resistência de setores que historicamente se recusam a reconhecer que é possível e necessário aliar proteção ambiental e desenvolvimento. “Agora torcemos para que nossos parlamentares também avancem na aprovação da Política Ambiental que está em pauta, incorporando esses conceitos e ajudando o RN a recuperar sua capacidade competitiva”, falou. Empreendimentos serão classificados em categorias De acordo com o Idema, a resolução cria uma regulamentação estadual para a atividade e padroniza os procedimentos administrativos, técnicos e ambientais aplicáveis aos empreendimentos. Os data centers são instalações destinadas ao processamento, armazenamento e comunicação de dados, reunindo estruturas como fornecimento de energia, refrigeração, segurança, conectividade e servidores, além da infraestrutura de distribuição de energia. Um dos principais critérios para o enquadramento dos projetos será a capacidade elétrica instalada. Os empreendimentos serão classificados em cinco categorias: micro, com até 20 MW; pequeno, acima de 20 MW até 50 MW; médio, acima de 50 MW até 100 MW; grande, acima de 100 MW até 500 MW; e excepcional, acima de 500 MW. A potência considerada inclui os equipamentos de tecnologia da informação e os sistemas de refrigeração. A modalidade de licenciamento e os estudos ambientais exigidos também devem variar conforme o porte e o sistema de refrigeração adotado. Nos sistemas fechados, a água utilizada no resfriamento dos equipamentos circula dentro de um circuito e é reaproveitada, sem necessidade de reposição constante em grandes volumes. Já os sistemas abertos, que utilizam torres de refrigeração, podem resultar em consumo hídrico maior. Segundo o diretor-geral do Idema, Werner Farkatt, a proposta foi amplamente discutida com o objetivo de garantir segurança jurídica, técnica e ambiental ao licenciamento da atividade. “Um dos principais pontos de atenção foi a diferenciação entre sistemas fechados e abertos de refrigeração, especialmente em relação ao consumo de água e à escassez hídrica no semiárido”, disse. “A resolução estabelece um licenciamento mais simplificado para sistemas fechados, enquanto os empreendimentos de grande e excepcional porte e com sistemas abertos estarão sujeitos a estudos ambientais mais complexos. A aprovação pelo Conema fortalece a segurança jurídica e cria condições para análise dos processos sem comprometer a proteção ambiental”, considerou Werner Farkatt, em seguida. O presidente Darlan Santos, do Cerne, explicou que esses empreendimentos podem estimular a hibridização de parques, com projetos que combinam eólica e solar no mesmo ponto de conexão para mitigar a variabilidade ao longo das 24 horas do dia; atrair investimentos em baterias de grande porte (Sistema de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias, ou BESS, na sigla em inglês); e reduzir o impacto do curtailment (cortes de geração impostos ao setor renovável). Ainda segundo o presidente do Cerne, a oferta de energia renovável do RN é suficiente para atender à demanda de grandes data centers sem pressionar o sistema elétrico. “A oferta de energia é abundante. O RN gera substancialmente mais do que consome, exportando a maior parte de sua produção renovável para o restante do país. artigo.texto: NYSERDA lança 8 projetos de armazenamento de energia em larga escala e 13 projetos renováveis em Nova York A New York State Energy Research and Development Authority está lançando oito novos projetos de armazenamento de energia em larga escala e 13 projetos de energia renovável de grande porte em Nova York, segundo a NYSERDA. Juntos, os projetos devem entregar 1,7 GW de novos recursos energéticos de grande porte, apoiar mais de 1.000 empregos que sustentam famílias e atrair mais de US$ 3,7 bilhões em investimento privado. A presidente e CEO da NYSERDA, Doreen M. Harris, afirmou que os projetos recém-contratados impulsionam o crescimento da energia limpa, mais que dobram o armazenamento em escala de concessionária atualmente em operação no estado e se encaixam na estratégia energética abrangente de Nova York, que contempla todas as fontes. Ela acrescentou que os projetos devem ajudar a reduzir custos para os consumidores e, ao mesmo tempo, melhorar a confiabilidade da rede. Os projetos foram apresentados por meio da chamada de Armazenamento de Energia em Larga Escala da NYSERDA e da chamada de 2025 do Padrão de Energia Renovável Tier 1. Espera-se que gerem mais de US$ 127 milhões em atividade econômica em comunidades desfavorecidas, conforme definidas pelo Climate Justice Working Group. Portfólio de Armazenamento Uma vez em operação, os oito projetos contratados de armazenamento de energia em larga escala acrescentarão 950 MW de nova capacidade de armazenamento. O portfólio abrange a cidade de Nova York, Long Island, o Vale do Hudson e o oeste de Nova York. Os projetos foram escolhidos em um processo de seleção que recebeu propostas de 46 projetos, totalizando cerca de 6 GW de capacidade. As durações contratadas variam de quatro a oito horas, e espera-se que os projetos proporcionem benefícios de confiabilidade à rede elétrica do estado. No oeste de Nova York, os projetos são o Lighthouse Energy Storage, no condado de Chautauqua, e o Zenobe Burns, no condado de Allegany. O Eastwater Energy Storage será localizado na região dos Finger Lakes. O KCE NY 5 está previsto para o Vale do Hudson. O Blue Spruce Storage e o Palladium Storage, ambos no condado do Bronx, atenderão a cidade de Nova York. O Holtsville e o KCE NY 37 ficarão em Long Island. Os pagamentos previstos nos contratos só começarão quando os projetos entrarem em operação comercial, após a obtenção de todas as licenças e aprovações locais. Os projetos contratados usarão tecnologia de íons de lítio e, como todos os projetos de armazenamento apoiados pela NYSERDA, têm exigência contratual de atender aos novos códigos de segurança de armazenamento que entraram em vigor em 1º de janeiro de 2026. A NYSERDA planeja emitir sua segunda Solicitação Anual de Propostas para Armazenamento de Energia em Larga Escala até o fim do ano, com a meta de contratar 3 GW em projetos de armazenamento ao longo de três chamadas. Projetos Renováveis Os 13 projetos contratados de energia renovável de grande porte totalizarão mais de 719 MW de capacidade, o suficiente para abastecer mais de 230.000 residências de Nova York anualmente após a conclusão. Os projetos solares incluem o Flint Mine Solar, o Hecate Greene 1 e 2, o Greens Corners Solar Park e o Rich Road Solar Energy Center. Todos os projetos devem entrar em serviço até o fim de 2030, conforme exigido pela Ordem de Armazenamento de Energia da New York Public Service Commission de 2024.

artigo.texto: U.S. energy storage market posts record number in Q2 2026, report says Data analysis firm Wood Mackenzie has good news for the American energy storage sector in its latest U.S. Energy Storage Monitor report, as the market installed a record 18.9 GWh in Q2 2026. Even as installed power fell 7% year over year, Wood Mackenzie’s research finds that longer duration storage in utility-scale and residential storage systems drove the sector further than ever. The wattage itself went down slightly, as the company’s research notes, but wattage-hours exploded, up 17% year over year from Q2 2025. In a practical sense, that means the national average’s energy storage duration went from 2.8 hours to 3.5 hours thanks to installations from Q2 2026. “Battery storage is one of the most important tools we have to meet growing electricity demand,” says John Hensley, SVP of markets and policy analysis at American Clean Power. “Storage can be deployed quickly, strengthens reliability, and helps the grid make better use of both existing and new generation. With a strong pipeline and continued technology improvements, the outlook for storage remains exceptionally strong.” The implications of this data are far-reaching across the American energy industry, Wood Mackenzie officials say. Storage has become a trend in the solar and energy sector over the past few years. Now, that trend has its guiding star: AI data centers. “Data center buildout strengthens the U.S. storage outlook across all sectors. Storage can provide needed capacity faster, cheaper and more reliably than gas alone,” says Allison Feeney, research analyst at Wood Mackenzie. “As hyperscalers increasingly face grid-connection bottlenecks, utility-scale storage will enable speed to power for data centers.” As data centers continue to drive the storage market forward, the numbers tell a promising story for 2026. By the numbers Much of the AI data center-related came from the American utility-scale storage segment, according to Wood Mackenzie’s data. Comparing Q2 2025 to Q2 2026, the segment went down in pure wattage, installing just under 4.7 GW in Q2 2026 — good for an 8% drop in installation. However, the wattage-hours of the utility-scale segment moved up 16% from 2025 to 2026, as the segment installed more than 17.6 GWh in Q2 2026. The commercial and industrial sector of the storage market remained largely stagnant year over year, Wood Mackenzie’s data says. The segment remained practically unchanged, installing 49 MW in Q2 2025 and 48 MW in Q2 2026. Additionally, the wattage-hour numbers stayed consistent, going from 104 MWh in Q2 2025, to 103 MWh in Q2 2026. But perhaps the most promising figure from the storage segment in Q2 2026 was the residential segment. Looking at the year over year numbers, Wood Mackenzie’s research states that the residential storage market was the only segment of the three to see an uptick in wattage itself, installing 676 MW for a 3% increase over Q2 2025. The biggest swing in favor of the residential storage segment came from wattage-hour installation, Wood Mackenzie says. Going from 791 MW installed in Q2 2025, to nearly 1.2 GW in Q2 2026, the sector saw a 48% increase year over year. A promising forecast Looking forward, Wood Mackenzie representatives estimate that the American solar market will reach 207 GW / 715 GWh by 2031. Thanks to continued utility electrification, data center buildout, and the potential reinstatement of the Biden-era Solar For All program, the market is well-positioned for growth through the end of the decade. With a 21% jump in wattage-hour installation from 2025 to 2026, the market should continue to expand as it enables large load growth, the data company states. While the utility-scale sector could stagnate in 2027 as it adjusts to new supply chain dynamics, 2028 and beyond is expected to be a growth period for the market as a whole. Additionally, the market is receiving some help from an unexpected source: electric vehicles. “The slowdown in EV demand has become an unexpected tailwind for storage,” says Allison Weis, Wood Mackenzie’s global head of energy storage. “Manufacturers are repurposing idle EV cell capacity, accelerating the domestic supply base just as trade policy makes it most valuable.” In total, Wood Mackenzie officials say the U.S. energy storage market could add more than 130 GW / 534 GWh, in the utility-scale segment alone, between 2026 and 2031. The commercial and industrial segment is equally rosy with an expectation of 29% growth between 2026 and 2031. While the national residential storage market will likely drop slightly before the end of the 2026, that downgrade represents a mild hiccup in an otherwise bullish prediction.

artigo.texto: The lithium battery fire was reported around 11:40 a.m. near a solar panel field on the northeast side of the facility in the 3200 block of Wheeler Avenue. Crews from the La Verne Fire Department and Los Angeles County Fire Department responded. One employee suffered minor injuries and was taken to a local hospital, according to La Verne Fire Department Battalion Chief Mark Savage. Shortly after 3 p.m., the L.A. County Fire Department said the fire had been knocked down. AIR7 video shows firefighters dousing the flames with water. La Verne fire crews were still monitoring the scene and mopping up, noting that there was still a risk, with more lithium batteries at the site. By Tuesday evening, no flare-ups had been reported, and crews were using a drone to monitor the batteries. Firefighters estimate there are fewer than 20 lithium batteries in the storage facility. "These things do not like any kind of additional heat, and the understanding is, there is something going on with that bank now that it is reacting to the previous heat that it was exposed to," said Batt. Chief Mark Savage. "So we are monitoring closely. We have reinitiated cooling measures for that battery bank now. But it's one of those things that, once it gets started, it's extremely difficult to stop, if not impossible to stop." The fire prompted evacuation orders and warnings near Bonita Avenue and Wheeler Avenue and a shelter-in-place for the surrounding residential neighborhood. Click here to see if you are in an impacted area. Some evacuation orders were later downgraded to warnings. By early Tuesday evening, firefighters said the orders were only impacting the approximately 185 properties closest to the facility. La Verne police said shopping centers along Wheeler Avenue north of Foothill Boulevard were evacuated as a precaution. Grace Miller Elementary School, located just east of the facility, was under a shelter-in-place order, and Holly Oak Street south of the campus was closed to traffic. Savage said students appeared to be released from the school while firefighters battled the blaze. Parents told Eyewitness News that Ramona Middle School and Bonita High School were also affected. Holy Name of Mary School, Damien High School and the University of La Verne were evacuated. The university said all classes were canceled until further notice. Eyewitness News spoke to Ramona Middle School parents who arrived to pick up their kids. By the time most parents arrived, it was already the school's normal pick-up time. "They're blocking off Wheeler, so it makes it a little hectic but scary at the same time, so we're just here getting the kids out of safety," said parent Irene Flores. "We got it on our phones, the emergency message to evacuate our facility. So might as well come get the kids, make sure they're safe," said parent Jason Wagner. "In La Verne, we've never seen these kind of things." The Metropolitan Water District said its water supply was not affected by the fire. The cause of the fire is still under investigation. Savage said nothing like this has happened there before, but it's raising concerns for neighbors who had no clue that the water treatment plant housed massive battery banks with the potential to catch fire. If you're wondering if you live near a facility that houses potentially dangerous or hazardous items, you can find out. Back in May, 7 On Your Side did an investigation and we shared the Environmental Protection Agency's interactive map, where you can learn about the enforcement and compliance history of facilities near you. City News Service contributed to this report.

artigo.texto: Paolla Oliveira é a nova rainha de bateria da Imperatriz Leopoldinense Atriz retorna ao Carnaval carioca à frente dos ritmistas da Swing da Leopoldina, comandada por Mestre Lolo; a coroação acontece no dia 17 de outubro A atriz Paolla Oliveira, 44, é a nova rainha de bateria da escola de samba Imperatriz Leopoldinense para o Carnaval de 2027. O anúncio aconteceu nesta quarta-feira (23) pela agremiação de Ramos. Segundo comunicado, o convite foi feito pela presidente Cátia Drumond, e sua coroação está marcada para o próximo dia 17 de outubro. "É com muita alegria e honra que a nossa escola recebe a Paolla como rainha de bateria. Tenho certeza que ela chega para somar ao nosso time, aos nossos ritmistas e principalmente à comunidade de Ramos e toda Zona da Leopoldina, que está ansiosa para abraçar e reverenciar sua nova majestade. Que ela seja muito bem-vinda e claro, muito feliz conosco", afirmou Catia. Em 2025, Paolla fez seu último desfile à frente da bateria da Grande Rio. Ao anunciar a decisão, a atriz disse que a escolha estava sendo difícil, mas que precisava "pensar em redistribuir sua atenção" em outras áreas da vida, como, por exemplo, a parte pessoal. Após um ano longe da folia, Oliveira volta para reinar diante dos ritmistas comandados pelo mestre Lolo. "O Carnaval vive em mim, vocês sabem. E a vida tem essa beleza do inesperado, onde a gente percebe que pode ainda ter muita coisa bonita para viver, sem nunca perder de vista tudo o que já foi vivido", disse à imprensa. "Estou muito feliz de estar aqui, de coração aberto e para começar mais uma história no carnaval. Chego com muito respeito, vontade de estar perto, conhecer, aprender e viver mais uma vez essa experiência rica e coletiva. Tem frio na barriga, claro, mas tem também uma alegria enorme por tudo que está começando", acrescentou. Com o enredo “A Memória do Rei e o Sumiço de Dona Júlia”, idealizado pelo carnavalesco Leandro Vieira, a Imperatriz Leopoldinense será a quarta escola a desfilar na Marquês de Sapucaí, fechando a segunda-feira de Carnaval, 8 de fevereiro, em busca do 10º título de sua história.

artigo.texto: PHOENIX — Count data centers as another issue that deeply divides Attorney General Kris Mayes and her Republican opponent, Senate President Warren Petersen. Moderators at Wednesday night’s Clean Elections debate asked the Mayes’ call for a temporary halt on new data centers. “Do we want to be the data center capital of the world?” Mayes said. “The vast majority of Arizonans that I come across say ‘absolutely not,’ and they want to have a say.” But Petersen said a moratorium is not needed. “Kris Mayes has a philosophy of just shutting everything down, whether it's housing or data centers, or whatever it is, and that increases the cost of everything,” he said. Do you have a concern in your community or a news tip? We want to hear from you! Connect with us: share@abc15.com Mayes says the state needs to come up with a strategy for the facilities given cuts to the state’s share of Colorado River water and pending utility rate hikes. “We need a pause so that we can get our hands around this situation,” she told reporters after Wednesday’s debate. Mayes said she’s working on a plan for a new approval process that would allow communities to vote on data center projects and create a commission to review proposed data centers like the Arizona Power Plant and Transmission Line Siting Committee does for energy projects. The proposals would then go to either the governor or attorney general, she said. “These data centers are being plunked right in the middle of neighborhoods,” Mayes said during the debate. “Can you imagine if one of these hyperscale data centers came into your neighborhood with no notice, with no vote by the community?” But Petersen said data centers are sorely needed. “If you like your tech and your phone and your computer and the stuff you can use that for, you probably think data centers are important,” he said. He pointed to three major issues: location, power and water. Like Mayes, he said local communities should decide if they want data centers. “Maybe it's a heavy industrial location or some place where the community says ... we're OK with this,” he said. But he said the facilities can address the electricity and water concerns. “Data centers need to generate their own power,” he said. “And there's a water concern, and data centers, again, need to be responsible for their water, whether that means recycling it or making sure that they have brought their own water supplies.”

Limited (CATL) World's largest battery manufacturer Several large-scale battery energy storage system developments across Central and Eastern Europe have reached completion, financing or supplier milestones, according to Energy-Storage.news. The activity spans Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary and Poland and involves companies including Greenvolt, Renovatio, CATL, Renalfa, MOL Group, Tavion, MetaWealth, Enexus and Longi. The announcements arrive shortly before the Energy Storage Summit Central and Eastern Europe 2026, scheduled for 6-7 October in Warsaw, Poland. Construction is underway on a 918MWh battery energy storage project in Romania, described as one of the country's largest. Independent power producer Greenvolt owns the project, Renovatio Solar is providing engineering, procurement and construction services, and CATL is supplying the battery technology. The project is expected to be completed within 12 months. Developer and EPC firm Enexus will deploy 50MWh of battery storage from solar photovoltaic manufacturer Longi across two solar-plus-storage projects in Romania. The two battery projects, sized at 15MWh and 35MWh, are located in Dambovita County and represent the first storage collaboration between the companies, which have previously worked together on solar PV projects. Longi entered the battery storage sector recently through its acquisition of system integrator PotisEdge late last year. Real estate investment platform MetaWealth has completed a EUR19 million financing structure for its first battery storage project, a 50MW/100MWh facility also in Romania. The structure comprises EUR10 million from CEC bank, EUR5.5 million from the founding Topolinski family and EUR3.5 million from its securitisation and bond platform. Renalfa IPP has completed the repowering and hybridisation of its Devnya PV plant in Northeastern Bulgaria. The company increased the plant's capacity from 5MWp to 65MWp and added a battery storage system totalling 60MW/165MWh. Solarpro served as the EPC contractor. According to a speaker at the Energy Storage Summit Central and Eastern Europe, Bulgaria is now the most battery-heavy electricity market in the world. Industrial firm MOL Group has completed a 37.4MWp solar and 20MW/40MWh battery storage project in Hungary called Algyo. According to head of communications Ambrus Halasz, the project benefited from funds under Hungary's EU-backed capital expenditure grant scheme for storage. Battery storage owner-operator Tavion has raised EUR50 million, equivalent to US$57 million, through a fundraise and debt raise. The proceeds will go towards completing three projects in Poland with a combined capacity of 69MW. Leitmotif and Oberon Capital led the fundraise, which totalled EUR34 million. Construction will start on the first two projects this month. They form part of a 184MW portfolio Tavion intends to deploy in Poland.
