artigo.texto: Colleton County residents raise concerns over proposed data center, power plant projects COLLETON COUNTY, S.C. (WCIV) — Two major projects proposed for Colleton County — a data center near the ACE Basin and a power plant tied to a pipeline near the Edisto River — are drawing questions and concern from residents as representatives begin outlining plans that could break ground in the next few years. Residents were invited to two separate public presentations, where officials and project representatives fielded questions about potential environmental and economic impacts. “The pipeline and the plant they want to build on the Edisto River, it’s not just going to impact this area with the air pollution and water pollution. It’s going to impact us in Charleston County as well,” said Juliana Tuihri, a North Charleston resident. READ MORE | "Colleton County leaders OK zoning changes to allow data centers farther north." Christopher Stout, bureau chief for the S.C. Coastal Management DES, said his agency organized an availability session because of community interest in the proposed Cenedy plant. “We know there’s a lot of interest in the community about the Cenedy plant and so what we’ve pulled together is earlier this evening was kind of an availability session,” Stout said. The other presentation focused on a controversial data center proposed near the ACE Basin. Ken Lober of Eagle Rock Partners said the meeting was intended to provide information and answer questions. “We’re here to inform. And to be able to answer any questions people have, you know this is for a project we do with Colleton county, not in Colleton county,” Lober said. READ MORE | "Colleton County erupts as residents clash with developers over controversial data center." Lober said the data center would use roughly the same amount of water as a local car wash and would provide hundreds of high-paying jobs. If built, the project would bring $6 billion into the county, according to the information presented. Brantley Strickland, executive director of the Colleton County Economic Alliance, said the project could have long-term effects for residents. “A transformational for families and truly something that could impact everyone in the county. We’re talking from a tax revenue standpoint. Perhaps even the opportunity for your property taxes to go down one of these days,” Strickland said. About eight minutes down the road, S.C. Environmental Services held a public hearing on plans to build a massive power plant. Stout said an initial land service permit would cover early site preparations, with additional development expected later. “This initial land service permit is just for some initial site preparations. And we know there is going to be a lot more build-out that comes with that so we know it’ll be a lot further down the road before anything is finished,” Stout said. READ MORE | "South Carolina emerges as one of top states for data centers, local skepticism persists." Stout said there is no connection between the data center and the power plant. Still, some residents said they are troubled by the prospect of either project moving forward. “The ACE basin is the last greatest place on earth. At what point do we lose it?” one resident said. S.C. Environmental Services said there is no exact date for when construction could begin. Representatives for the data center said they hope to complete construction by 2030.

artigo.texto: Gov. Wes Moore laid out a data center policy plan Wednesday aimed at protecting Marylanders’ wallets and the environment, even as he steered clear of the statewide pauses enacted by some other state executives. Moore’s proposal, made by executive order, outlines uniform standards for reviewing data centers, establishes a task force within the governor’s office to help steer the state’s data center decision-making, and creates a dashboard for tracking projects across the state. Moore also pledged to work with lawmakers to repeal a broad tax exemption for data centers, approved by the General Assembly in 2020. According to a recent report from the watchdog group Good Jobs First, that exemption cost Maryland $22 million in forgone revenues in 2026 alone. The announcement comes as concerns about data center growth and the artificial intelligence industry they power have become a top political issue across Maryland and the country while federal officials have yet to take action. “By signing this executive order, we are establishing clear safeguards to ensure Marylanders do not foot the bill, our people benefit, community voices are heard, and our environment is protected — all while centering transparency and accountability throughout the process,” Moore said in a statement on the order. Moore, a Democrat, made data centers part of his plan to boost Maryland’s economy and reduce the state’s reliance on jobs in the federal government, healthcare and education. Moore has cautioned against giving data center companies “free rein” to write their own rules and has urged local say-so over projects. Still, many data center critics hope to keep the massive server farms out of Maryland for good, and Moore’s plan stops short of the statewide pause that some advocates have called for. The announcement comes days after Moore told political news site Punchbowl that if the legislature approves a statewide moratorium or ban, he will “absolutely” sign it. The General Assembly instituted guardrails for data center developers earlier this year, but since then calls for a pause have grown louder, and lawmakers are expected to weigh various moratorium bills in the upcoming session. For some local leaders, large data center developments promise jobs and property tax windfalls, but others have already moved to slow new data center expansion. Counties from the deep-blue Washington, D.C., suburbs to the conservative Eastern Shore have enacted data center moratoriums of varying lengths, while Republican-led Harford County approved the state’s first indefinite ban in June. Wednesday’s executive order also comes as governors across the country have raced to outline stricter data center policies in recent months. Some of those governors have enacted sweeping development stoppages: In July, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a one-year pause on hyperscale data centers. And on Tuesday, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott paused reviews of all data center permits. Others have chosen a softer approach. Last week, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger issued an executive order aimed at tightening policies around data center development, while California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a slate of bills cracking down on the industry’s usage of land, water and energy. Unlike those two states, which each house hundreds of data centers, the industry remains in its infancy in Maryland. Frederick County has the state’s only approved hyperscale project. On Tuesday, Moore announced a series of proposals to regulate the artificial intelligence industry in the state as existential fears over unbridled AI have compounded data center anxieties.

artigo.texto: Greenvolt investe 300 milhões de euros em projeto de armazenamento de energia na Polónia A empresa liderada por João Manso Neto iniciou a construção de um projeto de armazenamento de energia em baterias na Polónia com um investimento superior a 300 milhões de euros. A Greenvolt iniciou a construção de um projeto de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) na Polónia com um investimento superior a 300 milhões de euros, disse esta quinta-feira a empresa à Lusa. Escolha o ECO como fonte preferida no Google A infraestrutura a ser construída na cidade de Siedlce, terá 600 MW de potência e 2,4 GWh de capacidade de armazenamento, o que segundo a Greenvolt trará “uma maior flexibilidade ao sistema elétrico polaco, armazenando eletricidade durante períodos de elevada produção de energia renovável e disponibilizando-a quando a procura aumenta”. “Com Siedlce, estamos mais uma vez a passar dos planos à concretização, o mais importante é construir ativos, criar valor real e reforçar as infraestruturas necessárias para integrar mais energia renovável no sistema. A Polónia é um mercado estratégico para nós e o armazenamento de energia em baterias está a assumir uma importância cada vez maior no nosso crescimento”, afirmou o presidente executivo do grupo, João Manso Neto, citado em comunicado. As baterias serão fornecidas pela BYD Energy Storage, sendo que a infraestrutura contempla 210 contentores de baterias e 105 contentores de transformadores equipados com sistemas de conversão de energia, permitindo o fluxo de eletricidade entre as baterias e a rede. Este não é o único projeto polaco na carteira da empresa, tendo Turosn Koscielna, com 200 MW/800 MWh entrado em operação em julho de 2026, enquanto Elk, também com 200 MW/800 MWh, deverá entrar em operação comercial no quarto trimestre deste ano. Quando os três projetos estiverem operacionais, disponibilizarão, em conjunto, 1 GW de potência e 4 GWh de capacidade de armazenamento. artigo.texto: As data centers expand across Arizona, experts weigh water concerns and evolving technology YUMA, AZ (AZFamily) — As communities across Arizona weigh the economic benefits of tech expansion against drought concerns, local leaders and residents are increasingly asking whether the desert state has enough water to sustain massive data centers. While some municipalities have pushed the pause button on new developments, water policy experts say the feasibility of these sprawling facilities depends heavily on location, local resource availability and community priorities. Sarah Porter, director of the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University, said water consumption varies significantly depending on the design and operational needs of each site. “From data center to data center, the amount of water that is used is quite variable depending on the size of the facility and the kind of technology that’s used for cooling,” Porter said. A decade ago, data centers relied on heavy water usage to keep high-powered servers and processors from overheating. However, technological shifts are beginning to curb that demand, including new computer chips designed to operate safely at higher temperatures. “The other (factor) is that many data centers are now deploying cooling technologies that use a lot less water,” Porter said. Arizona currently has between 100 and 115 operating data centers, with roughly 86 additional projects either planned or under construction statewide. Securing approval for new builds has become increasingly rigorous. Before developers can break ground, they must comply with municipal water ordinances and rigorous resource standards, such as programs modeled around the state’s Assured Water Supply rules. Under these frameworks, cities and utilities must ensure they have sufficient water in their portfolios to satisfy a 100-year supply commitment without depleting resources meant for surrounding residents. Despite ongoing cuts along the shrinking Colorado River and broader desert water challenges, Porter noted that data centers alone are unlikely to destabilize Arizona’s long-term supply, provided strict local oversight and advanced conservation planning remain front and center. artigo.texto: A Evos, empresa do Grupo Interjato especializada em conectividade e segurança no transporte de dados, está ampliando sua infraestrutura de fibra óptica no Rio Grande do Norte para atender ao crescimento da demanda por conectividade de alta capacidade e resiliência associada a datacenters, supercomputação e aplicações de Inteligência Artificial. CONTEÚDO RELACIONADO – Redata pode favorecer data center de IA ligado à estratégia de soberania digital do governo Atualmente, a empresa possui 1.441 quilômetros de fibra óptica no Rio Grande do Norte e está implantando 410 quilômetros de rede subterrânea, modelo que reduz a exposição da infraestrutura a ocorrências em redes aéreas e aumenta a proteção das rotas físicas. Para os próximos seis meses, estão planejados mais 245 quilômetros de fibra, expansão que permitirá à Evos chegar a Fortaleza (CE) com infraestrutura própria. Com as duas etapas, a malha da companhia passará dos 2,1 mil quilômetros de fibra óptica. O movimento ocorre em um momento de expansão da infraestrutura computacional no estado. Em agosto, o Governo Federal anunciou a implantação, no Parque Científico e Tecnológico Augusto Severo (PAX), em Macaíba, de um novo supercomputador de alto desempenho voltado à Inteligência Artificial. Conduzido tecnicamente pelo Laboratório Nacional de Computação Científica (LNCC/MCTI), o projeto integra o Plano Brasileiro de Inteligência Artificial (PBIA) e deverá ampliar a capacidade nacional para desenvolvimento, treinamento e utilização de modelos avançados de IA. Para a Evos, a chegada de uma infraestrutura computacional desse porte evidencia uma nova categoria de demanda para o Rio Grande do Norte: além de energia e capacidade computacional, operações críticas de IA e data centers dependem de redes de alta capacidade, disponibilidade, redundância e diversidade física de rotas. A infraestrutura da empresa foi concebida para permitir interconexão com múltiplos carriers e rotas fisicamente distintas, reduzindo pontos únicos de falha e ampliando a resiliência necessária a operações que precisam permanecer disponíveis de forma contínua. Segundo Erich Rodrigues, CEO do Grupo Interjato, o anúncio do supercomputador eleva o patamar da discussão sobre infraestrutura digital no estado. “O Rio Grande do Norte começa a reunir componentes que podem colocá-lo em uma nova posição no mapa da infraestrutura digital brasileira. Energia renovável é uma vantagem importante, mas aplicações críticas de Inteligência Artificial precisam também de conectividade de alta capacidade, redundância e rotas fisicamente independentes. É nessa camada que estamos investindo”, afirma. O estado possui mais de 98% de sua potência instalada de geração elétrica proveniente de fontes renováveis, principalmente eólica e solar. Na avaliação do Grupo Interjato, essa disponibilidade cria uma vantagem competitiva para projetos de infraestrutura digital intensivos em energia, desde que acompanhada por avanços em transmissão elétrica, conectividade, licenciamento e segurança operacional. A expansão da Evos faz parte dessa estratégia. Além de reforçar a infraestrutura dentro do Rio Grande do Norte, a chegada a Fortaleza por fibra própria amplia as alternativas de conexão interestadual e aproxima a rede de um dos principais pontos de conectividade internacional do país. “Nossa visão é contribuir para que o Rio Grande do Norte transforme sua vantagem energética em uma vantagem também digital. Para isso, não basta ter geração de energia ou terrenos disponíveis. É preciso construir uma infraestrutura capaz de dar previsibilidade e segurança a quem pretende instalar operações críticas no estado. A nossa contribuição é entregar a camada de conectividade necessária para que esses projetos possam operar e crescer”, acrescenta Rodrigues. A expansão anunciada é a primeira etapa de uma estratégia da Evos direcionada a infraestruturas digitais de missão crítica. A companhia pretende aprofundar, nos próximos meses, iniciativas envolvendo diversidade de rotas, interconexão com carriers, redundância, conectividade interestadual e atendimento às novas demandas de data centers e computação de alto desempenho. A Evos é uma empresa do Grupo Interjato especializada em conectividade, SD-WAN e segurança no transporte de dados para empresas privadas e instituições públicas. Integra um grupo com mais de 30 anos de atuação em tecnologia e conectividade e possui certificações ISO/IEC 20000 e ISO/IEC 27001. artigo.texto: Resumo Uma vez operando, os data centers podem injetar R$ 7,3 bilhões no Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) do Ceará e contribuir com a criação de até 112,3 mil empregos no Estado, segundo estudo do Observatório da Indústria, ligado à Federação das Indústrias do Ceará (Fiec). A estimativa foi apresentada nesta quinta-feira, 24, pelo economista-chefe do Observatório, Guilherme Muchale, no Proenergia Summit 2026, evento do setor de energia que ocorre no Centro de Eventos do Ceará. Confira os assuntos econômicos no Ceará, no Brasil e no Mundo Vale lembrar que o PIB consolidado dos estados é calculado pelo Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE) e publicado com uma defasagem de dois anos. Ou seja, o dado oficial mais recente para o PIB cearense é o de 2023, quando o indicador foi de R$ 232,2 bilhões. Tomando esse número como base, os projetos de data centers poderiam elevar sozinhos o PIB estadual em 3,1%. Nas projeções apresentadas por Muchale, são ofertados cenários de atividade econômica tanto durante a construção dos complexos quanto durante seu efetivo funcionamento no Estado. De acordo com ele, o levantamento utilizou dados do Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE 2035), além de referências acadêmicas e premissas do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata). "Por se tratar de um estudo preliminar, o cenário considera 2,7 Gigawatt (GW) de capacidade de data centers, conforme o PDE 2035, e premissas de eficiência energética e hídrica mais restritivas do que o Redata, dado que as informações dos investimentos no Ceará indicam práticas mais sustentáveis do que estipulado na regulamentação", apontou o economista. Muchale ressaltou ainda que a apresentação não estabelece uma tarifa específica de energia, nem detalha individualmente a disponibilidade futura da infraestrutura elétrica, além de não fixar cronograma anual exato de operação total. Acompanhe mais notícias de Economia no Linkedin do O POVO Durante a construção, projeta-se uma injeção de R$ 44,8 bilhões ao PIB cearense, um impacto estimado de 27,4%. Além disso, calculam um total de 176,2 mil empregos sustentados durante as obras. Conforme o economista, dada a magnitude dos investimentos, as ocupações "tendem a se distribuir ao longo dos anos, acompanhando o avanço da infraestrutura". "Na implantação, além do setor de construção, haverá forte demanda para produtos locais ou atração de investimentos ligados à toda a cadeia construtiva, de material e equipamentos elétricos, metalmecânico, mineral e serviços de apoio à construção", destacou. Já para o primeiro ano de funcionamento, a entidade calcula impacto de 4,5% no PIB, considerando as próprias projeções sob o PIB do Estado. No funcionamento dos complexos de processamento de dados, a Fiec projeta 551 empregos diretos. [SHORT_CODE_RECOMENDATION_COLUMNIST_6ab5d0566a337] O cálculo considera também 111,7 mil empregos sustentados na cadeia dos data centers, o que resulta em 112,3 mil ocupações totais como efeito de sua operação no Estado. Muchale detalhou que essa distribuição ocorre porque os data centers são empreendimentos intensivos em capital e infraestrutura, mas com operação direta que requer menos mão de obra. "Fazendo com que parcela relevante do impacto sobre o emprego ocorra nos serviços e fornecedores demandados pela operação." Siga o canal de Economia no WhatsApp para ficar bem informado "Na operação, além dos serviços demandados pelos Data Centers, como manutenção da infraestrutura, rede e conectividade, refrigeração, energia e pessoal de operação, o Ceará se posicionará com firmeza para atrair serviços de alto valor agregado, como Fintechs, serviços de nuvem, IA e cibersegurança, mídia, jogos e outros setores da economia criativa, bem como parte da indústria de equipamentos elétricos e de refrigeração", reforçou. Outro ponto citado no estudo é que as projeções do PDE posicionam o Ceará como o 3º maior polo do Brasil, atrás apenas de São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro. Para o especialista, o dado reforça os diferenciais competitivos do Estado na atração desses complexos. Nesse contexto, Joaquim Rolim, gerente de Desenvolvimento Sustentável da Fiec, ressaltou que o crescimento do Estado vai ao encontro ao cenário global. Veja dicas rápidas sobre Educação Financeira no Dei Valor "O setor está em forte expansão no mundo. Em 2025, os data centers representavam cerca de 2% do consumo mundial de energia, participação que deve dobrar até 2030", afirmou. O consumo no País, dessa forma, de acordo com Rolim, deve saltar de 1,6% em 2025 para mais de 5% em 2030, com o Nordeste ganhando força no mercado nacional e o Ceará na liderança regional. "No mundo todo se buscam formas mais eficientes e sustentáveis para o projeto e operação dos data centers. O Nordeste brasileiro e especialmente o Ceará têm todas as condições para atender esses requisitos. Com os investimentos que já começam a se concretizar, estarão contribuindo fortemente para o desenvolvimento econômico e social da região", concluiu o gestor. Muchale e Rolim participaram do painel "Data Centers, Infraestrutura & Negócios". O debate contou ainda com Luis Carlos Fontes, superintendente de engenharia da Omnia; Rafael Theodoro Alves, consultor técnico da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE); Hugo Figueiredo, presidente da Empresa de Tecnologia da Informação do Ceará (Etice); e Giselle Viveros, da Enel Comercializadora. artigo.texto: Additional experts will arrive and evaluate an identical lithium battery storage unit Thursday that is adjacent to one that caught fire Tuesday at a Metropolitan Water District facility in La Verne and prompted an evacuation order for more than 500 homes. The original fire broke out around 11:40 a.m. Tuesday in the storage unit at the facility at 3201 Wheeler Ave. As La Verne and Los Angeles County Fire Department personnel responded to the scene, there was a small explosion in the battery unit, La Verne Fire Department Battalion Chief Mark Savage said. Due to the hazardous nature of lithium batteries, fire crews sprayed the area with water to prevent the flames from spreading. Evacuation orders and warnings were issued in the areas around the facility. La Verne police said shopping centers along Wheeler Avenue north of Foothill Boulevard were evacuated as a precaution. By about 2:30 p.m. Tuesday, the fire activity had diminished significantly, but a hazard remained, Savage said. He said one civilian was injured in a fall and taken to a hospital. The injury was not severe, Savage said. A short time later, some evacuation orders were downgraded to warnings, while others were reduced to advisories for residents to remain alert. An evacuation order remained in place in the immediate vicinity of the facility. Crews monitored the situation overnight Tuesday into Wednesday. Savage said a second battery storage unit adjacent to the one that burned began smoking and making popping sounds Tuesday evening due to heat exposure from the original fire. By about 7 a.m. Wednesday, the temperature inside had jumped about 20 degrees to around 90 degrees, Savage said. “It was in the low 70s at midnight,” he said. “It’s now approaching the 90s and it’s not that warm here yet.” La Verne Fire Department Chief Brandon Coatney, speaking at a news conference at fire department headquarters Wednesday morning, said cooling measures had resumed as a result. “We did have a spike in the temperature this morning, so we’ve initiated cooling measures on the second battery system,” he said. Those cooling measures primarily involved streams of water being sprayed on both battery units. On Wednesday afternoon, crews again shut off those streams to see if the units had cooled, but temperatures again spiked upward in both units, Coatney said. As a result, crews resumed spraying water on the units. Evacuation orders in the immediate vicinity of the facility remained in place Thursday and are expected to stay in effect until further notice. The additional experts will arrive sometime on Thursday to evaluate the battery units and the cause of the fire, according to a statement from the city of La Verne. The batteries cannot be approached and dismantled until conditions allow, the city said. Once the batteries are de-energized and no longer producing heat or hazardous vapors, they will be transported to a hazardous waste unit and the area will be investigated. Nearby Grace Elementary School was closed Wednesday and will remain shuttered Thursday. Pelota Park is also closed until further notice. The fire also prompted the closure of the University of La Verne on Tuesday, but it was reopened on Wednesday. Overnight parking restrictions will not be enforced throughout the city of La Verne until Friday at 5 a.m. to adjust for evacuated residents staying at other locations in the city. Both the battery storage unit that caught fire and the one being monitored Wednesday are 8 feet wide, 8 feet high and 20 feet long, Savage said. “The original battery bank, that fire has subsided. There’s no active fire there,” Savage said. As for the second unit, it was exposed to fire and around 5:30 p.m. Tuesday crews heard pops and saw puffs of smoke and saw that a door jamb had been blown ajar. “The concern is that behavior is going to continue,” he said. Air quality monitoring was showing no sign of dangerous toxins, Savage said.. The area under the evacuation order is bounded by Moreno Avenue to the west, Foothill Boulevard to the north, B Street to the east and Paseo Drive, Winterhaven Drive and Kendrick Drive to the south, according to a statement posted on La Verne’s website. Residents within the area are ordered to remain evacuated until further notice and residents with nowhere to go are encouraged to call the La Verne Police Department Watch Commander at 909-596-1913. An emergency shelter was set up at the La Verne Community Center. The MWD issued a statement saying the fire occurred “at a battery energy storage system near a solar panel field on the northeast side at the La Verne facility, which also houses the Weymouth Water Treatment Plant. The safety of Metropolitan’s water supply is not affected.” Residents can receive updates from the social media pages of the La Verne fire and police departments or at laverneca.gov/736/METROPOLITAN-WATER-DISTRICT—SEPTEMBER-. The MWD is a regional water wholesaler that distributes water to agencies throughout Southern California, serving millions of customers. Officials said that water remains safe to drink in La Verne and in areas served by the Metropolitan Water District of Southern California, including Los Angeles, Orange, Riverside and San Bernardino counties.

artigo.texto: Nevada data center growth drives approval of temporary gas plants The Public Utilities Commission of Nevada has approved two temporary natural gas plants to power two data centers in northern Nevada. The PUC on Sept. 17 approved Fleet Data Centers’ applications for two temporary, natural gas-fueled power plants for two data centers in northern Nevada. Fleet is a subsidiary of Tract Capital, a Denver-based digital infrastructure company, who filed applications for the natural gas-powered generating plants in April for its South Valley and Peru Ridge data centers. “This temporary power system is required because data center growth is outpacing NV Energy’s ability to supply power in new areas,” Fleet said in its application. The company said growth in the Tahoe-Reno Industrial Center is outpacing the speed at which NV Energy can build permanent infrastructure for large loads such as data centers. Tract Capital said in a statement to the Review-Journal that it appreciates the commission’s decision and careful review of its applications. According to Tract, the plants will come at no cost to Nevada residents and provide economic benefits to Storey County. “We appreciate the Commission and its staff for their consideration and look forward to continuing to work with state and local stakeholders as Fleet continues to invest in Northern Nevada,” said Tract in the statement. NV Energy didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The TRIC is a 107,000-acre industrial park larger than the size of Detroit located in northern Nevada’s Storey County. The majority of the estimated 70 planned data centers in Nevada from Nevada Legislative Counsel Bureau are clustered in the area. In its recent Integrated Resource Plan filing, which provides a roadmap of load growth for the next approximately 20 years, NV Energy said data centers will drive a dramatic shift in Nevada’s energy landscape, growing from 5 percent of electricity sales today to 64 percent by 2046. NV Energy’s existing and approved systemwide generating capacity through 2050 is roughly 10 gigawatts. If projected data center demand materializes, the systemwide generating capacity needed to serve projected demand could exceed 20 gigawatts by 2050. Planned northern Nevada power plants The South Valley power plant will be on 37.4 acres at 8990 USA Parkway in Sparks with a 144 megawatt generating capacity. The Peru Ridge generating plant will be located on 23.4 acres in the TRIC near Peru Drive in Reno with a 218 MW generating capacity. Both of them will be used to power the associated South Valley and Peru Ridge data centers in northern Nevada, totalling over 2,000 acres and 1,445 MW. The power plants are slated to start construction in early 2027, take around six months to erect and be operational for two to three years. Both will be located on previously disturbed land, already graded for the associated data centers. PUC Commissioner Randy Brown said “no permit will be issued without proper state agency oversight.” Multiple permits, including a Storey County building permit and air permit, must be obtained before construction can start. The approval did not come without pushback. There was around two hours of public comment during the meeting expressing criticism on the power plants. In public comment, Elizabeth Bree Kasper called the proposed natural gas power plants “destructive” to northern Nevada’s air quality, water resources and “climate future.” “Calling these massive natural gas facilities ‘temporary’ is a bureaucratic fiction,” said Kasper. “You cannot build hundreds of megawatts of fossil fuel infrastructure without permanent destructive impacts.” Mary Levinson, a retired chemical engineer and physician, said she believes the commission “does not value the environment nearly as much as it values development. “The commission concludes that ‘the need for the facility balances any adverse effect on the environment,’” said Levinson, reading from a PUC filing. “But who really needs this facility? Certainly not Nevadans.” Tract Capital is a major data center player in the state. In February, its South Valley data center was granted $23.35 million in tax abatements. It is anticipated to create 14 jobs with an hourly wage of $54.29 within five years; make $300 million in capital equipment investment in the first five years of operation and generate $45,743,902 in new taxes over 10 years. Bloomberg reported that the South Valley data center will be leased by major chip manufacturer Nvidia, although both companies declined to comment on the matter. Tract Capital has five data centers “owned and in development” in northern Nevada, totalling 12,390 acres. Contact Emerson Drewes at edrewes@reviewjournal.com. Follow @EmersonDrewes on X.

artigo.texto: Data centers drawing 25 megawatts or more of electricity are no longer allowed on Allegheny County-owned property. County Council voted unanimously Tuesday to prohibit the construction, operation or establishment of large-scale data centers — and the infrastructure built specifically to support them — on county-owned land and in county-owned buildings. The measure does not restrict data centers on privately owned property, leaving those land-use decisions to individual municipalities. The ordinance had broad support ahead of Tuesday’s votes, with council’s Sustainability and Green Initiatives Committee unanimously advancing it last week. Sponsors of the bill include President Michelle Naccarati-Chapkis, D-Plum; Dan Grzybek, D-Bethel Park; Kathleen Madonna-Emmerling, D-Moon; Lissa Geiger Shulman, D-Hampton; Pat Catena, D-Carnegie; Paul Klein, D-Pittsburgh; Jordan Botta, D-Bloomfield; and at-large members Bethany Hallam, D-North Side, and Alex Rose, I-Squirrel Hill. On Tuesday, Rose, who chairs the Sustainability and Green Initiatives Committee, explained to the council that the committee adopted an amendment to help avoid accidentally banning servers from “existing on Allegheny property” and avoid unintended impacts on facilities such as county server operations and the 911 center. Under the bill, infrastructure associated with data centers, including generators, utility lines, cooling water and wastewater treatment facilities, water-holding facilities, pump stations, water towers and other environmental controls are prohibited. Also, county property can no longer be used for data center ancillary use or secondary structures such as administrative, logistical, fiber optic, storage and security buildings or structures. The council opted not to impose a countywide land-use ban because, under Pennsylvania law, zoning and land-use decisions involving private property are made by individual municipalities rather than the county. Private developers could still potentially propose a data center in a municipality subject to that municipality’s zoning and other applicable laws. Some municipalities in Allegheny County already host existing smaller data centers or have larger projects proposed. In Springdale, a major planned data center would stand 75 feet tall and stretch over 652,000 square feet. Several boroughs and townships, including East Deer, Oakmont, Tarentum, Upper Burrell, Murrysville and Gilpin, have adopted or are in the process of implementing ordinances similar to the county in an effort to regulate data center development.

artigo.texto: LA VERNE, Calif. (KABC) -- Hazardous materials crews were monitoring rising temperatures Wednesday in a battery storage unit near a solar farm at a Metropolitan Water District facility in La Verne adjacent to an identical unit that caught fire and burned a day earlier. The storage unit being monitored began smoking and making popping sounds Tuesday evening due to heat exposure from the original fire and by about 7 a.m. Wednesday, the temperature inside had jumped about 20 degrees to around 90 degrees, La Verne Fire Department Battalion Chief Mark Savage confirmed. "It was in the low 70s at midnight," he said. "It's now approaching the 90s and it's not that warm here yet." The lithium battery fire was reported around Tuesday morning near a solar panel field on the northeast side of the facility, prompting evacuation orders and warnings near Bonita Avenue and Wheeler Avenue and a shelter-in-place for the surrounding residential neighborhood. Some evacuation orders were later downgraded to warnings. Grace Elementary School was to remain closed Wednesday. The school was placed under a shelter-in-place order Tuesday as was Bonita High School as crews worked to contain the blaze. The fire prompted the closure of the University of La Verne. The university announced it will reopen Wednesday. An evacuation order for the immediate vicinity of the MWD facility remained in effect Wednesday. La Verne fire crews were still monitoring the scene and mopping up, noting that there was still a risk, with more lithium batteries at the site. Both the battery storage unit that caught fire and the one being monitored today is 8 feet wide, 8 feet high and 20 feet long, Savage said. The original fire was put out Tuesday night, but a drone was being used to monitor the temperature in both units, he said. "The original battery bank, that fire has subsided. There's no active fire there," Savage said. As for the second unit, it was exposed to fire and around 5:30 p.m. Tuesday crews heard pops and saw puffs of smoke and saw that a door jamb had been blown ajar. "The concern is that behavior is going to continue,'' which would require the same cooling measures employed Tuesday. Air quality monitoring is showing no sign of dangerous toxins, Savage said. The Metropolitan Water District said its water supply was not affected by the fire. Meanwhile, the cause of the fire is still under investigation. Savage said nothing like this has happened there before, but it's raising concerns for neighbors who had no clue that the water treatment plant housed massive battery banks with the potential to catch fire. If you're wondering if you live near a facility that houses potentially dangerous or hazardous items, you can find out. Back in May, 7 On Your Side did an investigation and we shared the Environmental Protection Agency's interactive map, where you can learn about the enforcement and compliance history of facilities near you. City News Service contributed to this report.

artigo.texto: O avanço da inteligência artificial e da computação em nuvem está acelerando a construção de data centers no Brasil e aumentando a pressão por energia, conectividade e infraestrutura capaz de sustentar cargas computacionais cada vez maiores. O país concentra 71% da capacidade de data centers atualmente em construção na América Latina e cerca de 48% da capacidade instalada em operação na região. A expansão ocorre em meio ao crescimento das aplicações de inteligência artificial, dos serviços em nuvem, do comércio eletrônico, dos bancos digitais, do streaming e de sistemas corporativos que dependem do processamento permanente de grandes volumes de informações. A infraestrutura necessária para treinar e executar modelos de IA também elevou a importância dos data centers de alta capacidade, especialmente aqueles preparados para operar servidores e aceleradores computacionais com elevado consumo de energia. O mercado latino-americano de data centers encerrou 2025 com 1.105 MW de capacidade instalada. Somente no segmento de colocation, foram entregues 184 MW de nova capacidade durante o ano, enquanto o inventário regional cresceu 20%. Considerando projetos de colocation e hyperscale, 42% da capacidade em construção já estava pré-contratada, indicando que parte relevante da nova infraestrutura chega ao mercado com demanda previamente estabelecida. Nesse cenário, os data centers passaram a ocupar uma posição crítica na infraestrutura digital. Uma interrupção pode afetar desde plataformas financeiras e serviços de nuvem até sistemas públicos, operações industriais e aplicações de inteligência artificial. Por isso, os projetos dependem de redundância elétrica, sistemas de refrigeração, conectividade por diferentes rotas, automação, segurança física e mecanismos de prevenção e combate a incêndios. O crescimento da IA adiciona uma camada de complexidade a essa infraestrutura. Servidores destinados ao processamento de modelos avançados podem operar com densidades energéticas muito superiores às de ambientes computacionais tradicionais, aumentando as exigências sobre distribuição elétrica e refrigeração. Isso faz com que a disponibilidade de energia em grande escala se torne um dos principais fatores para a localização e expansão dos novos empreendimentos. O Brasil tem como vantagem uma matriz elétrica com participação relevante de fontes renováveis, principalmente hidrelétrica, eólica e solar. Essa característica pode favorecer projetos que buscam reduzir a emissão associada ao consumo de energia, mas não elimina um dos principais desafios do setor: garantir fornecimento contínuo, estável e em grande volume para instalações que precisam funcionar 24 horas por dia. Além da geração de energia, a expansão dos data centers depende da capacidade das redes de transmissão e distribuição, da disponibilidade de terrenos conectados à infraestrutura elétrica, do acesso a redes de fibra óptica e da existência de profissionais especializados. Projetos desse tipo também precisam combinar sistemas elétricos, climatização, telecomunicações, automação e segurança dentro de uma mesma arquitetura. Segundo Marco Alberto Silva, cofundador e CEO do Grupo Engemon, os diferentes sistemas precisam ser planejados de forma integrada para reduzir riscos de indisponibilidade. Na avaliação do executivo, energia, climatização, conectividade, automação, segurança e prevenção de incêndios não podem ser tratados de forma isolada em instalações que operam continuamente. Apesar de concentrar quase metade da capacidade instalada da América Latina e a maior parcela dos projetos em construção, o Brasil ainda disputa espaço em uma indústria global marcada por investimentos elevados e pela corrida para ampliar a infraestrutura destinada à inteligência artificial. A disponibilidade de energia, a expansão das redes elétricas e de telecomunicações, a formação de profissionais e a previsibilidade regulatória e tributária deverão influenciar a velocidade desse crescimento nos próximos anos. A tendência é que a pressão continue aumentando à medida que modelos de inteligência artificial generativa exigem mais capacidade computacional e empresas transferem novas cargas de trabalho para a nuvem. Nesse contexto, a expansão dos data centers deixa de ser apenas uma questão de armazenamento de dados e passa a fazer parte da infraestrutura necessária para sustentar o avanço da inteligência artificial e da economia digital no país.

artigo.texto: Publicidade Montadoras chinesas voltaram a registrar forte crescimento nas vendas na Europa no mês passado, ampliando participação no mercado enquanto rivais europeias enfrentam dificuldades para manter competitividade. Os emplacamentos de modelos da BYD – indicador de vendas – mais que dobraram na comparação anual e chegaram a 26.007 unidades no conjunto formado por União Europeia (UE), Reino Unido, Islândia, Liechtenstein, Noruega e Suíça, segundo a Associação Europeia de Fabricantes de Automóveis (ACEA, na sigla em inglês). Nos últimos anos, BYD e outras marcas chinesas vêm ganhando espaço na região apoiadas em linhas de veículos relativamente mais baratas, pressionando fabricantes locais. A SAIC Motor teve alta de 32% nos registros, para 21.214 unidades, enquanto a Leapmotor mais do que triplicou para 7.630 veículos. Em contraste, a alemã Volkswagen registrou queda de 3,6%, para 210.818 unidades, e a Renault recuou 4,4%, para 71.906. Agosto costuma ser um mês fraco para emplacamentos na Europa por causa das férias de verão do Hemisfério Norte, quando muitas concessionárias fecham. Ainda assim, a diferença no ritmo de crescimento entre chinesas e europeias indica que BYD e pares seguem avançando, mesmo que grupos europeus ainda vendam mais em números absolutos. Várias montadoras europeias revisaram portfólios e reconheceram baixas contábeis por desvalorização de ativos nos últimos anos, frequentemente apontando a concorrência chinesa como uma das principais razões. Na semana passada, a Volkswagen cortou uma meta importante de rentabilidade após indicar cerca de US$ 11,5 bilhões em baixas contábeis relacionadas à participação na Porsche, além de citar condições difíceis de mercado e reestruturação. A empresa também aprovou recentemente um plano para dobrar cortes de empregos para 100 mil, em meio a tarifas nos EUA, aumento de custos e concorrência chinesa. A Porsche informou no fim de julho que reduzirá 5.000 vagas, citando queda de vendas na China, tarifas americanas e uma aposta antecipada em veículos elétricos. Continua depois da publicidade No mercado, os emplacamentos de veículos 100% elétricos a bateria cresceram 52% na Europa no mês passado. Híbridos avançaram 3,4% e híbridos plug-in, 13,5%. A Tesla registrou alta de 4% nos emplacamentos em agosto, para 15.430 unidades, desacelerando em relação aos ganhos de dois dígitos dos meses anteriores; na UE isoladamente, a alta foi de quase 53%. A ACEA informou que os registros de automóveis de passeio subiram 5,3% na Europa como um todo e 4,5% na União Europeia, com alta de 2,6% na Alemanha, 7,4% na França e 3,2% na Itália. Fonte: Dow Jones Newswires. *Conteúdo traduzido com auxílio de Inteligência Artificial, revisado e editado pela Redação do Broadcast, sistema de notícias em tempo real do Grupo Estado. artigo.texto: Solex Energy revela plano de INR 40 bilhões para expansão de células solares e armazenamento em baterias A Solex Energy Ltd. divulgou informações adicionais sobre sua estratégia de ampliar as operações além da produção de módulos solares e dos serviços de engenharia, aquisição e construção, avançando para a fabricação de células solares e sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias. Em maio, a empresa firmou um memorando de entendimento com o governo de Gujarat abrangendo 5 GW de capacidade de fabricação de células solares e 10 GWh de capacidade de armazenamento de energia em baterias. Em sua 12ª Assembleia Geral Anual, a Solex apresentou um cronograma para a expansão, com meta de 2,2 GW de capacidade de células solares até o ano fiscal de 2028 e 5,2 GW no início do ano fiscal de 2029. A empresa também pretende construir 10 GWh de capacidade de montagem de baterias e contêineres, com a fase inicial de 5 GWh prevista para o ano fiscal de 2029. Essa expansão faz parte de um programa de investimento de aproximadamente INR 40 bilhões, equivalentes a US$ 418,2 milhões, abrangendo do ano fiscal de 2027 ao ano fiscal de 2030. A Solex caracterizou esse programa como o maior de sua história corporativa. No ano fiscal de 2026, a Solex registrou receita de INR 16,21 bilhões, um aumento de 143,9% em relação ao ano anterior. O Ebitda ficou em INR 1,87 bilhão, enquanto o lucro após impostos somou INR 983 milhões. A empresa informou que sua carteira de pedidos supera INR 34 bilhões. Chetan Shah, presidente do conselho e diretor-gerente da Solex Energy, afirmou que o foco da empresa está em construir, a partir da Índia, uma plataforma de energia integrada, orientada por tecnologia e globalmente competitiva, com resiliência para crescer em diferentes ciclos e disciplina para criar valor duradouro. A Solex indicou que o planejado ingresso na fabricação de células solares lhe dará maior controle sobre qualidade, custos e cadeias de suprimentos, ao mesmo tempo que amplia seu papel no setor de fabricação solar doméstica da Índia. O armazenamento de energia representa outra área de foco da expansão. A empresa prevê que a demanda por geração renovável combinada com armazenamento aumentará junto com o consumo de eletricidade proveniente da mobilidade elétrica, da eletrificação industrial, da inteligência artificial e dos data centers. A Solex pretende alcançar receita superior a INR 45 bilhões até o ano fiscal de 2028. A empresa também busca crescimento internacional por meio de planos para a Solex Europe e a Solex USA. A Solex ampliou recentemente seu roteiro tecnológico por meio de uma parceria com a alemã ISC Konstanz, concentrando-se no avanço de tecnologias de células solares de alta eficiência. A colaboração abrange esforços para modernizar linhas de células TOPCon e desenvolver tecnologias de contato traseiro e tandem de próxima geração. Em outubro de 2025, os parceiros apresentaram um conceito de módulo solar de contato traseiro que utiliza tecnologia do tipo n, com eficiência de até 24,6% e potência de 665 W, com produção comercial prevista para o ano fiscal de 2027.

artigo.texto: Mercado global de servidores rack para data center: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de servidores rack para data center até 2035: demanda de IA e hiperescala impulsiona o crescimento Resumo De acordo com o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de servidores rack para data center, o mercado entra em 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compras mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de servidores rack para data center entra em uma década de transformação, à medida que compradores de hiperescala e corporativos redirecionam os gastos com infraestrutura para cargas de trabalho de IA, aprendizado de máquina e virtualização densa. Os servidores rack, blocos modulares dos data centers modernos, estão sendo redesenhados em torno de desempenho por watt, eficiência térmica e custo total de propriedade, e não apenas de capacidade bruta de processamento. Este relatório analisa o mercado de 2012 a 2025 e projeta sua evolução até 2035, abrangendo a arquitetura da demanda, a dinâmica da cadeia de suprimentos, a lógica de preços e o posicionamento competitivo. O mercado está se dividindo em segmentos otimizados para hiperescala e para empresas, cada um com modelos de compra e requisitos técnicos distintos. A escala de fabricação liderada por ODM compete com a integração e o valor de software liderados por OEM, enquanto ciclos de qualificação e listas de fornecedores aprovados criam barreiras significativas à entrada. A demanda é cada vez mais moldada por arquiteturas específicas para cargas de trabalho, incluindo IA/ML, HPC e infraestrutura componível, o que exige colaboração mais profunda entre fabricantes de componentes, integradores e usuários finais. Geograficamente, a produção se concentra em polos industriais importantes, enquanto o design e a inovação permanecem em clusters especializados de P&D, expondo as cadeias de suprimentos a riscos geopolíticos e comerciais. O horizonte de previsão até 2035 destaca tanto oportunidades quanto restrições, incluindo escassez de componentes, disponibilidade de energia e mudanças de padrões. Este estudo oferece uma visão estruturada e comercialmente fundamentada para fabricantes de componentes, fornecedores de sistemas, equipes de OEM e ODM, distribuidores, investidores e novos entrantes estratégicos que buscam navegar pelo mercado em evolução de servidores rack para data center. O cenário-base para o mercado de servidores rack para data center até 2035 pressupõe expansão contínua da geração global de dados, da adoção de nuvem e da demanda de processamento impulsionada por IA. Espera-se que os operadores de hiperescala continuem sendo o maior pool de demanda, embora os segmentos corporativo e de colocation contribuam com crescimento relevante à medida que os ciclos de renovação se aceleram e as implantações próximas à borda se expandem. A projeção indica crescimento a uma taxa composta anual de 8,2% entre 2026 e 2035, alcançando um índice de mercado de 220 em 2035 (2025=100). Esse cenário-base incorpora melhorias moderadas na resiliência da cadeia de suprimentos, alívio gradual das restrições de componentes e progresso constante nos padrões de eficiência energética. No entanto, as perspectivas não estão isentas de obstáculos: a disponibilidade de energia nos principais polos de data centers, as tensões comerciais geopolíticas e os longos ciclos de qualificação podem conter o crescimento em regiões ou segmentos específicos. O mercado também passa por mudanças arquitetônicas, com os servidores rack sendo cada vez mais projetados como elementos componíveis e definidos por software, em vez de nós autônomos. Isso favorece fornecedores com forte capacidade de integração de software, gestão térmica e suporte ao ciclo de vida. A pressão sobre os preços permanece intensa nos contratos de hiperescala, enquanto os compradores corporativos priorizam confiabilidade, segurança e suporte do fornecedor. O cenário-base não considera uma grande recessão global e assume um ambiente regulatório estável para a soberania de dados, embora sejam esperadas divergências regionais. No geral, o mercado está preparado para um crescimento robusto, porém desigual, com a IA e a computação acelerada atuando como principal motor de demanda até 2035. artigo.texto: DINWIDDIE COUNTY, Va— Dinwiddie County families confronted the project team behind a proposed data center Tuesday night, demanding answers about a development they say could erase the county's rural character. What was supposed to be an open house with TRACT — the project team over Haven Oak Technology Park, the proposed data center near White Oak Road and Claiborne Road quickly became a public hearing as Dinwiddie families came with questions but were not happy with the outcome. Many attendees voiced frustration over the lack of answers from the project team. "I think there was a lot of stuff that they told us we can't answer that. We have to check into that. We're not certain about that. Well, if you can't answer the questions, why did you come?" said longtime Dinwiddie resident Jeannie Schelin. Chantelle Lands, who opposes the data center said the development threatens what makes the area unique. "When we take a very beautiful rural area and convert it into an emerging technology park, we're then losing all of our rural character, and that's concerning," Lands said. A portion of the property lies within the White Oak Road Battlefield, raising concerns about the fate of historic land, along with wildlife, water, noise, and electricity demand. Those concerns led state leaders to press TRACT on who controls what gets built and how it operates. State Delegate Kimberly Pope Adams (D-Dinwiddie) questioned the project team directly. "How can you give us any promises when you are not the operator?" Pope Adams said. TRACT pushed back on concerns about backup generators, saying they would only operate during emergencies, with testing limited under the proposed conditions. The project team also shared that the data center is expected to bring 12,000 construction jobs. "We heard your concerns, and we made a technology change to this. So again, all data centers aren't equal," a TRACT representative said. However, families say they are still in the dark because there is no disclosed future operator at this stage. "We really don't know what the outcome is going to be. We really don't know what the rules are going to be," Lands said. The proposal is still in the early stages. The application is still under review by the planning department, and then Dinwiddie elected officials will have to vote. This is a developing story, so check back with WTVR.com for updates. artigo.texto: Hazardous materials crews were monitoring rising temperatures Wednesday in a battery storage unit near a solar farm at a Metropolitan Water District facility in La Verne adjacent to an identical unit that caught fire and burned a day earlier. The storage unit being monitored began smoking and making popping sounds Tuesday evening due to heat exposure from the original fire, and by about 7 a.m. Wednesday, the temperature inside had jumped about 20 degrees to around 90 degrees, La Verne Fire Department Battalion Chief Mark Savage told City News Service. “It was in the low 70s at midnight,” he said. “It’s now approaching the 90s and it’s not that warm here yet.” La Verne Fire Department Chief Brandon Coatney, speaking at a news conference at fire department headquarters Wednesday morning, said cooling measures had resumed as a result. “We did have a spike in the temperature this morning, so we’ve initiated cooling measures on the second battery system,” he said. Nearby Grace Elementary School was closed Wednesday. The school was placed under a shelter-in-place order Tuesday as was Bonita High School as crews worked to contain the blaze. The fire also prompted the closure of the University of La Verne on Tuesday, but it was reopened on Wednesday. An evacuation order for the immediate vicinity of the MWD facility remained in effect Wednesday. The fire broke out around 11:40 a.m. Tuesday at the facility at 3201 Wheeler Ave., Savage said. As La Verne and Los Angeles County Fire Department personnel responded to the scene, there was a small explosion in the battery unit, Savage said. Due to the hazardous nature of lithium batteries, fire crews sprayed the area with water to prevent the flames from spreading. Evacuation orders and warnings were issued in the areas around the facility. La Verne police said shopping centers along Wheeler Avenue north of Foothill Boulevard were evacuated as a precaution. At about 12:50 p.m., the Los Angeles County Fire Department announced the fire was a hazardous materials incident and an evacuation order was issued “for everyone near Wheeler and Bonita Avenue.” “Gather family and LEAVE NOW,” the fire department advised on social media. “Your safety is in danger if you stay. Use caution while evacuating. Follow instructions from emergency personnel.” By about 2:30 p.m., the fire activity had diminished significantly, but a hazard remained, Savage said. He said one civilian was injured in a fall and taken to a hospital. The injury was not severe, Savage said. A short time later, some evacuation orders were downgraded to warnings, while others were reduced to advisories for residents to remain alert. An evacuation order remained in place in the immediate vicinity of the facility. Both the battery storage unit that caught fire and the one being monitored Wednesday are 8 feet wide, 8 feet high and 20 feet long, Savage said. The original fire was put out Tuesday night, but a drone was being used to monitor the temperature in both units, he said. “The original battery bank, that fire has subsided. There’s no active fire there,” Savage said. As for the second unit, it was exposed to fire and around 5:30 p.m. Tuesday crews heard pops and saw puffs of smoke and saw that a door jamb had been blown ajar. “The concern is that behavior is going to continue,” which would require the same cooling measures employed Tuesday. Air quality monitoring was showing no sign of dangerous toxins, Savage said.. The area under the evacuation order is bounded by Moreno Avenue to the west, Foothill Boulevard to the north, B Street to the east and Paseo Drive, Winterhaven Drive and Kendrick Drive to the south, according to a statement posted on La Verne’s website. Residents within the area are ordered to remain evacuated until further notice and residents with nowhere to go are encouraged to call the La Verne Police Department Watch Commander at 909-596-1913. An emergency shelter has been set up at the La Verne Community Center. The MWD issued a statement saying the fire occurred “at a battery energy storage system near a solar panel field on the northeast side at the La Verne facility, which also houses the Weymouth Water Treatment Plant. The safety of Metropolitan’s water supply is not affected.” Residents can receive updates from the social media pages of the La Verne fire and police departments or at laverneca.gov/736/METROPOLITAN-WATER-DISTRICT—SEPTEMBER-. The MWD is a regional water wholesaler that distributes water to agencies throughout Southern California, serving millions of customers.

artigo.texto: Bolloré Logistics Major player in ESD-safe container solutions According to the latest IndexBox report on the global ESD Storage Containers market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global ESD storage containers market is entering a phase of sustained expansion, with demand projected to accelerate through 2035 as electronics manufacturing and battery production capacity scale up worldwide. ESD storage containers—including conductive and dissipative bins, totes, shelving inserts, cabinets, and custom handling solutions—are essential for protecting sensitive components from electrostatic discharge during storage, transport, and assembly. The market is underpinned by the rapid build-out of battery gigafactories, renewable energy integration projects, and data-center infrastructure, all of which require stringent static-control protocols. Between 2026 and 2035, the market is forecast to grow at a compound annual growth rate of 6.2%, reaching a market index of 182 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook reflects not only new capacity additions but also shortening replacement cycles and rising adoption of premium, high-temperature-rated containers. While supply remains concentrated in Asia and Europe, import-dependent regions face lead-time and cost pressures, prompting strategic inventory adjustments. The report provides a data-driven view of market size, demand drivers, supply chain dynamics, and competitive positioning to support procurement, investment, and strategic planning. The baseline scenario for the global ESD storage containers market anticipates steady growth from 2026 to 2035, with a compound annual growth rate of 6.2%. This projection assumes continued expansion in battery gigafactory construction, particularly in Asia-Pacific, North America, and Europe, alongside sustained demand from electronics assembly and data-center backup systems. The market index is expected to reach 182 by 2035, up from 100 in 2025. Growth will be supported by tightening ESD control standards, such as ANSI/ESD S20.20 and IEC 61340, which compel manufacturers to upgrade or replace storage infrastructure. Replacement demand, driven by wear from repeated cleaning and chemical exposure, is set to contribute an increasing share of annual sales, rising from roughly 35% in 2025 to over 45% by 2035. Regionally, Asia-Pacific will remain the largest consumer, while North America and Europe see accelerated adoption of smart, RFID-enabled containers. Supply constraints, including raw material price volatility and lengthy supplier qualification cycles, may temper growth slightly but are unlikely to derail the overall upward trajectory. The baseline scenario does not assume disruptive regulatory changes or major economic recessions. Battery manufacturing is the largest and fastest-growing end-use sector for ESD storage containers, driven by the global build-out of gigafactories. In this segment, ESD bins, totes, and shelving are used to store and transport battery cells, modules, and packs, where electrostatic discharge can damage sensitive electronics and create safety hazards. As battery production volumes surge through 2035, demand for high-temperature-rated and chemically resistant containers will rise sharply. Key demand-side indicators include gigafactory capacity announcements, battery production volumes, and adoption of automation in material handling. The segment is also seeing a shift toward RFID-enabled containers for inventory tracking, which improves traceability and reduces downtime. Replacement demand is significant, as containers degrade from repeated exposure to electrolytes and cleaning agents. Major companies in this sector include Tesla, Panasonic, LG Energy Solution, CATL, and Samsung SDI. Current trend: Rapid growth. Major trends: Shift toward high-temperature and chemically resistant ESD containers, Integration of RFID and IoT for real-time inventory management, Increasing automation in battery assembly lines requiring standardized containers, and Growing focus on sustainability, driving demand for recyclable ESD materials. Representative participants: Tesla, Panasonic, LG Energy Solution, CATL, and Samsung SDI. Electronics manufacturing remains a cornerstone of ESD storage container demand, encompassing the production of semiconductors, printed circuit boards, consumer electronics, and automotive electronics. In these environments, ESD containers protect sensitive components during assembly, testing, and storage. The ongoing miniaturization of electronic components and the rise of 5G, IoT, and automotive electronics are increasing the sensitivity to electrostatic discharge, thereby driving demand for more sophisticated ESD storage solutions. Demand-side indicators include semiconductor fab construction, PCB production volumes, and automotive electronics content per vehicle. Through 2035, the segment will see growing adoption of conductive and dissipative containers with enhanced cleanliness properties to prevent particle contamination. Replacement cycles are relatively stable but are shortening in high-mix, high-volume facilities. Major companies include Intel, Samsung Electronics, TSMC, Foxconn, and Texas Instruments. Current trend: Steady growth. Major trends: Increasing sensitivity of components driving demand for advanced ESD materials, Growth in automotive electronics and 5G infrastructure, Adoption of lean manufacturing practices requiring efficient storage solutions, and Rising demand for cleanroom-compatible ESD containers. Representative participants: Intel, Samsung Electronics, TSMC, Foxconn, and Texas Instruments. Data centers and IT infrastructure represent a growing end-use sector for ESD storage containers, as the proliferation of cloud computing, AI, and edge data centers drives demand for servers, networking equipment, and storage devices. artigo.texto: The late Fred Rogers, creator and host of “Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood,” once recalled that “When I was a boy and I would see scary things in the news, my mother would say to me, ‘Look for the helpers. You will always find people who are helping.’” Filmmaker Bess O’Brien has plenty of experience in “looking for the helpers.” For the past three decades, she has made award-winning documentaries about Vermont’s social ills and the people whose lives they consume. Her 2003 film Here Today and 2013’s The Hungry Heart highlighted the devastating consequences of heroin and prescription pill addiction, respectively, for everyday Vermonters. All of Me (2016) focused on young women and men trapped in the downward spiral of eating disorders. And her 2024 documentary, Just Getting By, profiled Vermonters struggling with food and housing insecurity. While various types of “helpers” often feature in O’Brien’s work, in her latest project she spotlights the helpers themselves. The idea struck in November 2024, when the Barnet filmmaker had completed a statewide tour of Just Getting By and Donald Trump was reelected president. “The next four years are going to be hell,” O’Brien remembers thinking. “I was feeling the doom of where our country was going.” For the benefit of her own mental health and that of viewers, O’Brien said, she decided her next movie wouldn’t be another deep dive into Vermonters’ pain and misery. Instead, she wanted to highlight people who are doing good deeds, bridging cultural divides, building community and bringing joy to others. “I wanted to be shooting a film and have a smile on my face the entire time,” she said. The result is Every Day: Big and Small, O’Brien’s love letter to the state of Vermont, which begins a screening tour on Friday, September 25. Unlike her previous documentaries, this one has no central characters or narrative, instead resembling a collection of short stories. Its 18 vignettes were shot around the state, capturing fly-on-the-wall moments when people came together, helped each other out, or just gathered to be themselves and have fun. One major impetus for the film was the catastrophic, back-to-back floods of July 2023 and 2024, stories of which bookend the film. Every Day: Big and Small is dedicated to the memory of Dylan Kempton, the 33-year-old Peacham man who died on July 10, 2024, when floodwaters swept him away in an off-road vehicle. The 90-minute documentary begins at the Peacham property of Jenny and John Mackenzie, schoolteachers who lost their home and most of their possessions in the July 2024 flood. In the midst of this devastation, the flood also delivered an unexpected gift: a deep connection to their neighbors. “It’s a weird dichotomy,” John says in the film. “I’d lost everything, but I hadn’t lost anything. It was extraordinary.” The outpouring of community support during the floods, as people mucked out their neighbors’ basements, delivered food, cared for others’ pets and stored personal belongings, became an aha moment for other Vermonters, too. “But guess what?” O’Brien said. “This is happening all around us every day. We just don’t notice it.” Every Day: Big and Small features a visit to Amy’s Armoire in Barre, which sells and gives away children’s clothes, furniture and other youth items, from cribs to prom dresses, to people in need. Less like a thrift store than a community center, Amy’s Armoire offers its clients a sense of comfort and security. One man in the film, who started going there for his kids after his release from prison, says tearfully, “It’s not just what [Amy’s Armoire] gives me. It’s emotionally so warming. I haven’t had anyone like that in my world.” O’Brien also spent time at the Patricia A. Hannaford Career Center in Middlebury, where a group of young women preparing to graduate from a local high school discuss plans for the future. After sharing some prom pictures shot on a hay wagon — “No tractor oil on my prom dress this year!” one of the girls exclaims — many express a desire to return to Vermont after college and work on their families’ farms. From there, the film moves to Swanton, where another group of young women is building a single-engine airplane as part of a Habitat for Aviation project. O’Brien also drops in on a teen center in St. Johnsbury; a Movement for Parkinson’s dance class in South Burlington; a Pride rally in Barre; a drag show at the Elks Lodge in Rutland; and a small military museum in Danville, set up in an aluminum trailer by 15-year-old Luke Morrison, who is obsessed with U.S. military veterans and their memorabilia. Every Day: Big and Small has a minimalist, almost ethereal feel: O’Brien provides no narration or on-screen text to inform viewers where they are or who is speaking. While the effect is slightly disorienting at first, the filmmaker offers enough aural and visual cues to allow viewers to quickly grasp the sentiments she captures. In an interview, O’Brien described the film as a visual journey across Vermont in an almost dreamlike state, without the intrusion of textual information every few minutes. It’s not until the closing credits that the viewer learns who these people are and with which businesses and organizations they’re affiliated. The film is less about telling a story than creating a mood, she added. Once the viewer catches on, the transitions — from a kids’ yoga class at Wolcott Elementary School to a men’s group for domestic violence offenders in St. Johnsbury to four-wheel drivers gunning their engines at Goss’s Mud Bog in Barnet — feel seamless. Some of the vignettes could have been expanded into stand-alone documentaries, O’Brien noted. One features the High Horses Center for Equine-Assisted Services in Sharon, where we meet Gayle Smith, 78, a retired Army nurse who served in a MASH unit in South Vietnam. artigo.texto: What restrictions could the Hillsboro City Council place on data centers in October? Published 5:30 am Wednesday, September 23, 2026 Months after Hillsboro staff approved a wave of data center tax break applications that sparked backlash and demands for changes to city code, city leaders could cement the city’s first permanent restrictions on where facilities may be built. While Hillsboro is under a temporary moratorium that blocks new data center proposals and development until Nov. 24, the Hillsboro City Council will consider the first phase of potential changes to the city’s development code during a public hearing Tuesday, Oct. 6. The amendments would narrow where standalone data centers are allowed, establish acreage caps, require public hearings for proposed facilities and prevent data centers from operating within 1,000 feet of schools. Recommended by the Hillsboro Planning Commission in September, the proposal would also establish new regulations for battery energy storage systems, which Hillsboro’s development code does not currently address as a specific land use. The changes would be the first step in a two-phase approach intended to put immediate protections in place while giving the city more time to study additional requirements, according to city staff. A second phase, planned for winter and spring 2027, would address building heights, buffers, green-building requirements and other environmental protections. Where data centers could be built Data centers are currently allowed in all of Hillsboro’s industrial zones, as well as the Commercial-General zone and three mixed-use zones. Under the proposed changes, standalone data centers would be allowed only as primary uses in the Industrial Park and Industrial Sanctuary zones, both of which are largely concentrated in North Hillsboro around the Hillsboro Airport and industrial areas along Northeast Evergreen Road and Brookwood Parkway. The amendments would cap standalone data center development at 215 total acres in the Industrial Park zone and 310 acres in the Industrial Sanctuary zone. According to the city, about 203 acres in the Industrial Park zone and 293 acres in the Industrial Sanctuary zone have already been approved for data center development. That would leave room for about 12 additional acres of standalone data centers in the Industrial Park zone and 17 acres in the Industrial Sanctuary zone. Separate limits would remain in place for the Jackson East area, where existing rules allow up to 62 acres of standalone data centers in the Jackson East-South area and 21 acres in the Jackson East-North area. Standalone data centers would remain prohibited in the Meek subarea, though accessory facilities could be allowed. Other restrictions on data centers Beyond limiting where facilities can be built, the proposed amendments would prohibit data centers within 1,000 feet of public or private schools serving primarily children under 18. The distance would be measured between property lines. The changes would also establish a formal definition of data centers, covering facilities that store, process or transmit digital information — including those used for artificial intelligence. Businesses with ordinary server rooms would not automatically be classified as data centers. Companies could still operate data centers to support their own operations, but they could not lease computing services to outside customers. Those accessory facilities would be limited to 25% of a property’s acreage or 30% of its floor area, whichever is less. New data centers would additionally face greater public scrutiny. Under the proposal, new facilities — including projects converting existing buildings or accessory operations into standalone data centers — would undergo a development review requiring a public hearing rather than approval through an administrative review by city staff. That decision could then be appealed to the city council. The amendments would establish separate rules for battery energy storage systems, which store electricity for later use. Facilities built primarily for energy storage would be limited to 12 acres per site and require conditional use approval in designated industrial zones. Battery systems installed to support another operation, such as a data center, would generally be limited to 30% of the property’s acreage. A long-awaited change Pressure for changes to Hillsboro’s development code has been mounting for months, following news that the city received 17 enterprise zone tax exemption applications from eight entities ahead of a statewide moratorium on new data center incentives. Fifteen of those applications were ultimately approved, according to the city’s updated figures, spanning seven companies and nine sites. But the approvals have also landed Hillsboro and Washington County in court. A lawsuit filed in June by a coalition that includes land use advocates and Hillsboro City Councilor Kipperlyn Sinclair seeks to overturn the tax breaks, alleging officials exceeded their authority and failed to follow required public notice procedures. The Hillsboro City Council has since moved to restrict both tax incentives and development. On July 21, councilors approved a 180-day pause on new Strategic Investment Program applications for standalone data centers, while requiring applications involving accessory data centers to go before the council for a public hearing. Less than a week later, councilors unanimously adopted a 120-day moratorium on new or expanded data centers and battery energy storage facilities proposed as primary uses. The temporary ban took effect July 27 and is scheduled to expire Nov. 24 unless extended. But several proposed data centers had already entered the city’s development pipeline before the moratorium took effect. artigo.texto: Anne Arundel County is backing away from a proposed ban on new data centers and instead considering a temporary pause on new development while officials decide how to regulate the facilities. The County Council unanimously approved an amendment to Bill 63-26 that would replace the proposed ban with a moratorium lasting until January 31, 2028, or until the county adopts comprehensive data center legislation, whichever comes first. During the moratorium, the county would establish a work group to study data center development and recommend regulations to the county executive and council. The group would consider issues including energy and water use, utility infrastructure, climate and environmental impacts, air quality, noise and economic development. Projects already in the development process would generally be allowed to continue. The amendment also includes future phases of existing data centers on adjacent or adjoining properties. The original bill drew concerns from residents about the potential impact of data centers on electricity demand, water use, noise and the environment. Others argued a countywide ban could hurt Anne Arundel County's technology and cybersecurity sector, particularly around Fort Meade, NSA and U.S. Cyber Command. Microsoft, which is developing a data center campus at Annapolis Junction Business Park, testified against the original ban. A company representative said Microsoft has completed two buildings at the site and plans additional phases. The company said it supports data center regulations and a work group but wants existing campuses to continue development. The amendment also calls for repealing a personal property tax assessment reduction for data storage centers. The County Council approved the amendment 7-0. The amended bill is scheduled to come back before the council on October 5. This is a developing story, so check back with WMAR2News.com for updates.
