artigo.texto: Data center triggers a small-town makeover as big cities fight to keep them out WASHINGTON (WBFF) — For decades, Quincy, Washington, was known for exporting sweet corn and potatoes. Now, the small town’s biggest export is computing power, a shift residents and local leaders credit largely to Microsoft’s data center campus built there 20 years ago. Since the company began developing the campus, Quincy — a town of about 9,000 — has seen major changes that supporters say have strengthened the local economy and improved public services. “It's changed it for the better and our poverty level has dropped immensely,” Quincy resident Nick Konen said. ALSO READ | Gov. Moore's data center guardrails put politics, tax breaks and local concerns in focus Local leaders said the data center helped expand the job base and drove property values higher, fueling new construction and public investment. “New schools, new fire station, new police station, city hall," Mike Stetner, whose watched his small business grow from three employees to 200 over the past two decades, said. A new high school was built, along with a 550-seat auditorium. The principal said the impact has been visible in the classroom: “They've seen our schools dramatically improve. They’ve seen our programs improve." Health care infrastructure also changed. A new medical center replaced an older hospital, and a representative described the facility’s capabilities: “We’re a 24-7 level four trauma emergency room. We are 100% confident that if we had not had an assessed value by the data centers we could not have done this.” Supporters also said the growth came with little impact on utility rates. Residents in Quincy currently pay 6.2 cents per kilowatt hour — about half the current rates in Baltimore City. In Maryland, Kelly Schulz, CEO of the Maryland Tech Council, said data centers have been misrepresented and argued that communities can see significant upside. “The community benefits can be very vast,” Schulz said. “There are very positive stories across the country, but they’re not amplified in the way the negative impacts are out there.” ALSO READ | Baltimore County Council unanimously extends data center moratorium for another year Researchers at Georgia Tech said larger cities typically have more to gain from data centers than smaller communities because they tend to have stronger infrastructure. “They have better infrastructure. They have better fiber network. They have more suitable tenants,” researcher Daniel Yue said. Still, Schulz said communities that treat data centers as a negotiating opportunity stand to benefit the most. “Those communities that look at this as an opportunity to negotiate what they want out of these data centers and how it can benefit their constituencies, they’re the ones who will win at the end of the day,” Schulz said.

artigo.texto: Switch data center proposal heads to North Las Vegas review as Nye fight continues LAS VEGAS (KSNV) — Two major data center proposals are moving in very different directions in Southern Nevada, with a new project now under review in North Las Vegas while a separate plan in Nye County faces a legal fight after the county approved a ban. In North Las Vegas, Switch is proposing a new data center at the Apex Industrial Park near Apex Power Parkway and U.S. 93. Switch has operated data centers in Southern Nevada for more than 25 years and has recently emphasized design changes it says address common concerns about data centers, including energy use and water consumption. In a media release, Switch said its data center designs have been “100-percent renewable for the past decade.” The company said that includes generating power with solar panels and conserving water used for cooling. Switch also said, “Zero water consumption - no water is consumed in our closed-loop EVO data center designs since 2022.” In its letter of intent to the city, Switch proposed Phase 1 of the project to include two data center buildings, a fire pump house and several other buildings on 175 acres. It is still early in the process, and it is not yet clear how the proposal will be received at North Las Vegas City Hall. District 1 City Councilman Isaac Barron, who has called for economic diversification at Apex, pointed to the city’s recently enacted Apex Act and its role in oversight of development. “This will allow us to oversee this permitting process, especially for things of the nature of infrastructure that will be driving, of course, development there for the next 20 to 30 years,” Barron said. In Nye County, the Manse Technology Campus proposal is further along in the development process but stalled after the Nye County Commission approved a data center ban several weeks ago. The legal team representing Manse said the company initially complied with Nye County zoning laws and made substantial investments in the project. The legal team said that investment was later disregarded and that rules were changed “to reach backward.” Manse Technology issued a statement Manse Technology Campus proceeded with its data center project because Nye County’s zoning laws permitted it. Because our project complied with Nye County’s zoning, we made substantial investments toward the project and acted in lockstep with Nye County’s consistent positive guidance throughout the development process. Nye County then adopted Ordinance No. 631, disregarding our substantial investments in reliance on existing zoning, changing the rules after the fact and writing the change to reach backward. Earlier this month, we filed a petition asking the court to review questions that should be of concern to everyone. We are asking the Court to confirm that when Nye County adopted the ordinance it did not keep faith with firmly established principles, which mandate that an ordinance must be lawfully adopted, applied, and uphold a principle that protects every landowner here: you should be able to rely on your property's zoning, the county's guidance, and the county's own process when you invest. If your zoning can be undone at any time, then property rights become property privilege, and that should concern every property owner in Nye County. We take residents' concerns about water, noise and the character of the valley seriously, and know they can be addressed through clear, enforceable standards written into a binding agreement that Nye County can enforce. We remain optimistic that with the right structure and continued dialogue, we can build something with Nye County residents and officials that minimizes the impacts on this valley and delivers real, long-term benefits.” Manse’s legal team is asking Nye County District Court to confirm the county commission did not act in good faith, arguing that if zoning can be undone at any time, “property rights become property privilege.” The legal team also said it remains optimistic it can build a data center in Nye County that minimizes impacts and delivers long-term benefits. Nye County Commissioner Ian Bayne, who represents District 3, said the zoning was done improperly because a moratorium was in place. “So one of the things that would happen in court possibly is to go and ask that attorney if they were aware of a moratorium and why they would move forward in defiance, in open defiance of a moratorium,” Bayne said. “That’s pretty problematic.” Legal action involving the Manse Technology Campus and any timeline for the proposed Switch data center at Apex remain under review.

artigo.texto: A massive fire in California forced the evacuation of hundreds of homes. The danger isn’t the flames themselves, but the lithium batteries stored at the Metropolitan Water District of Southern California in La Verne. The fire started Tuesday in a battery energy storage system near a solar panel field, KTLA reported. They were used to help power the water plant instead of relying on the electrical grid. KNBC reported that the fire was out, but the batteries were still dangerously hot and could explode, officials explained on Wednesday. It isn’t known how long the batteries will take to cool down. Firefighters used water on a storage unit to cool them and monitored temperatures with drones, KTLA said. They are trying to prevent what KTLA said was a “thermal runaway, where rising temperatures trigger a chemical reaction that can spread among battery cells. Once it starts, it cannot be stopped, the Los Angeles Times said. “The all-clear is going to be a long process,” La Verne Fire Chief Brandon Coatney said. “It’s going to involve de-energizing batteries.” Even if they don’t explode, they could produce smoke that could release hazardous vapors into the air. As of Wednesday, there were no indications of hazardous substances in the air. Water also did not appear to be affected, the Los Angeles Times reported. The cause of the initial fire is under investigation. ©2026 Cox Media Group

artigo.texto: Data centers impulsionam o crescimento do armazenamento em baterias nos EUA em todos os segmentos, informa a Wood Mackenzie A construção de data centers está melhorando as perspectivas para os sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias nos EUA em todos os segmentos de mercado, segundo a empresa de pesquisa de mercado Wood Mackenzie. A Wood Mackenzie publicou em 23 de setembro seu relatório US Energy Storage Monitor do terceiro trimestre de 2026, projetando que as instalações de armazenamento de energia nos EUA crescerão mais de 50% em termos de megawatts nos próximos cinco anos, com os baixos custos levando o armazenamento a novas regiões e aplicações. Volumes trimestrais recordes apesar de potências menores O mercado de BESS dos EUA instalou um recorde de 5,4GW/18,9GWh no segundo trimestre de 2026, mesmo com a potência instalada recuando 7% em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior. Sistemas residenciais e de escala utilitária com maior duração impulsionaram a expansão em termos de energia, enquanto as instalações de potência enfraqueceram. Os projetos de escala utilitária responderam por 4,7GW/17,6GWh no trimestre, uma queda de 8% ano a ano na capacidade em megawatts, à medida que os principais mercados caminham para a saturação. O segmento de escala comunitária e comercial e industrial implantou 48MW, voltando a volumes normais após o que a empresa descreveu como um primeiro trimestre excepcional na Califórnia, ligado ao encerramento do direito adquirido do programa de medição líquida conhecido como NEM 2.0. As instalações residenciais registraram o terceiro declínio trimestral consecutivo, caindo 15%, para 676MW, atribuído à eliminação gradual dos créditos fiscais, à incerteza do consumidor e a complicações decorrentes da transição para a propriedade por terceiros. Estimativas concorrentes Os números totais do segundo trimestre nos EUA da Wood Mackenzie são um pouco inferiores aos divulgados semanas antes pelo US Energy Storage Market Outlook, um relatório concorrente da associação setorial Solar Energy Industries Association e da empresa de pesquisa Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Esse relatório apontou implantações de 6,7GW/20,2GWh no segundo trimestre de 2026 em todos os segmentos entre março e o fim de junho. Previsões por segmento Espera-se que o armazenamento de escala utilitária cresça a uma taxa média anual de 8% nos próximos cinco anos, impulsionado pela necessidade de equilibrar o aumento das grandes cargas e da geração renovável. As durações dos projetos continuaram a se alongar no segundo trimestre com a implantação de um projeto de armazenamento de energia de longa duração na Califórnia, construído para atender a mandatos estaduais, ao lado de ativos contratados por concessionárias no Texas. Em junho, a REV Renewables e sua controladora LS Power, desenvolvedora e investidora do setor de energia dos EUA, colocaram em operação o primeiro BESS com duração de 8 horas da Califórnia, a instalação Tumbleweed Energy Storage, no condado de Kern. Projeta-se que o segmento comercial e industrial cresça 27% entre 2026 e 2031, à medida que a implantação se espalha para além da Califórnia, chegando a mercados emergentes como Maryland e Texas. A expansão no Havaí, no Novo México e no Texas compensou em parte o declínio geral, enquanto Nova York e Massachusetts permaneceram entre os mercados mais fortes do segmento. Neste mês, o Departamento de Recursos Energéticos de Massachusetts anunciou que distribuiria cerca de US$ 40 milhões a 36 projetos de BESS por meio de seu Advancing Massachusetts Power Energy Storage Grant Programme. Prevê-se que o armazenamento residencial caia 4% em 2026 antes de voltar a crescer de 2027 a 2031, com expansão média anual de 9% nesse período. Principais mercados e recursos distribuídos Os cinco maiores mercados, Califórnia, Texas, Porto Rico, Arizona e Illinois, responderam por 88% da capacidade de armazenamento instalada no segundo trimestre, embora todos os cinco tenham registrado quedas trimestre a trimestre. Porto Rico teve a maior contração absoluta, recuando de 129MW no primeiro trimestre para 73MW no segundo. A empresa de recursos energéticos distribuídos Sunrun e a Tesla anunciaram recentemente que o BESS residencial na Califórnia descarregou mais de 580MW de potência de pico para a rede do estado na noite de 9 de setembro, por meio de uma usina virtual conjunta. Em julho, a FranklinWH Energy Storage, fabricante de gestão de energia residencial e BESS da região da Baía de São Francisco, disse ter sido selecionada para participar de dois programas de usinas virtuais no Texas. Em abril, o Puerto Rico Energy Bureau aprovou uma moção da Tesla, da Sunrun e da instaladora de solar residencial SunStrong Management para inscrever automaticamente participantes em um programa de recursos de capacidade de emergência criado pelo Conselho Diretor da Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority. A startup de armazenamento de energia residencial Base Power, que em agosto anunciou um financiamento Série D de US$ 1 bilhão com valuation pós-money de US$ 13 bilhões, expandiu-se para Illinois em junho, instalando BESS para clientes da concessionária ComEd. Data centers e restrições da rede O relatório da Wood Mackenzie afirma que a expansão dos data centers eleva as perspectivas de armazenamento nos EUA em todos os segmentos, observando que o armazenamento pode fornecer a capacidade necessária de forma mais rápida, mais barata e mais confiável do que apenas o gás. À medida que as hyperscalers enfrentam cada vez mais restrições de conexão à rede, o armazenamento de escala utilitária ajudará os data centers a obter energia mais cedo, seja por meio de implantação no local para gerenciar as cargas dos ativos, seja no nível do sistema para atender aos requisitos evolutivos da rede. artigo.texto: ADM stock falls 1.3 percent as carbon plans meet grain risks Published on 09/23/2026 at 15:26 | Editorial responsibility: Rafael Müller, Editor-in-Chief AD HOC NEWS ADM stock (ISIN US0394831020) closed at USD 82.30 on the NYSE on September 22, 2026, down 1.3 percent from the previous close. The stock remained inside a 52-week range of USD 55.58 to USD 88.75, leaving the latest close USD 6.45 below the annual high. Carbon market plan adds a new angle ADM announced plans on September 21, 2026, to enter the voluntary carbon market through credits from its corn processing facility in Columbus, Nebraska. According to ESG Dive, the facility has estimated annual carbon capture capacity of more than 800,000 tons, with planned credit issuance over 15 years after certification and verification. The initiative broadens ADM's earnings narrative beyond agricultural processing, but it does not yet provide a reported revenue contribution. The immediate financial test remains the company's operating performance in its most recent reported quarter. Q2 earnings beat consensus ADM reported second-quarter 2026 earnings of USD 1.84 per share, according to MarketBeat. That result exceeded the USD 1.49 consensus estimate by USD 0.35, while quarterly revenue increased 7.2 percent year over year. The earnings comparison is the clearest quantified support for the stock's valuation. At the same time, ADM's consensus rating remains Hold, with an average price target of USD 79.67, below the September 22 close of USD 82.30, according to MarketBeat. Grain flows remain the counterfactor As 247WallSt reported on September 22, 2026, ADM and Bunge had posted strong second-quarter results and raised full-year guidance. The same market context identified biofuel policy and grain flows as important variables for the agribusiness sector. That mix explains the tension in the shares: second-quarter EPS beat estimates by USD 0.35, yet the stock finished below its 52-week high and the consensus target stood USD 2.63 below the latest close. For investors, the carbon project is a longer-duration opportunity, while grain markets and policy remain nearer-term earnings drivers. artigo.texto: Local leaders in Tucson and Cedar Rapids share different approaches to one of the country’s fastest-growing development issues WASHINGTON — As demand for Artificial Intelligence (AI) and cloud computing drives rapid data center development across the country, local governments are confronting complex decisions about water and energy use, infrastructure, economic development and community impact. More than 3,000 data centers currently operate in the United States, and more than half of the world’s hyperscale or AI data centers are located here. NLC research has found that at least 120 communities have adopted moratoria on data centers and 60 have passed new zoning regulations this year. In a new episode of the National League of Cities’ CitiesSpeak podcast, Kate Stoll, project director at the American Association for the Advancement of Science Center for Scientific Evidence in Public Issues; Tucson, Ariz. Councilmember Nikki Lee; and Cedar Rapids, Iowa Mayor Tiffany O’Donnell examine the choices communities face as data center proposals expand nationwide. What Local Leaders Should Know The Scale of a Project Matters Data centers vary significantly in their demand for local resources. Stoll explains that a 100-megawatt hyperscale facility can use roughly as much electricity as 80,000 U.S. households, while a large facility’s peak water use can reach between one and eight million gallons per day. She recommends that communities evaluate energy, water, air quality, infrastructure costs, jobs and tax revenue before making development decisions. NLC and the AAAS EPI Center developed the Key Questions to Ask When Considering a Data Center in Your Community resource to help local leaders evaluate these considerations and better understand the potential benefits and impacts of proposed projects. “These are questions you could ask of data center developers to get a real handle on what will be the impacts of the data centers, what will be the positive benefits, what will be the drawbacks, with the ultimate goal of bringing more clarity and transparency for communities so that they can make informed decisions for their communities.” — Kate Stoll, Project Director, AAAS EPI Center Tucson Chose Stronger Guardrails After Rejecting a Hyperscale Proposal After significant community concern contributed to the city’s decision not to move forward with annexation for the proposed $3.6 billion Project Blue, Tucson spent nearly a year developing new regulations with input from a 13-member technical advisory committee and the public. Councilmember Lee says the process reinforced the importance of considering the full system of water, energy, infrastructure and environmental impacts, and engaging residents early. “You really have to look at the whole system and not just, for example, water. What does the water meter at the site say? We have to look at the whole picture on what resources are actually necessary to power and operate these facilities.” — Councilmember Nikki Lee, Tucson, Ariz. Cedar Rapids Has Taken a Different Path The city is welcoming two hyperscale facilities after years of planning and due diligence around infrastructure capacity. Mayor O’Donnell says development agreements are expected to generate significant property tax revenue and include investments in water, wastewater and other infrastructure, as well as community betterment funding. “Ask for what you need, know what you need. Do your due diligence, good relationships and communicate with the public. The public has to know all that’s going on if you want the project to have any shot at being successful.” — Mayor Tiffany O’Donnell, Cedar Rapids, Iowa The conversation underscores that there is no single approach to data center development for every community. Local leaders are weighing different economic opportunities, infrastructure capacities, environmental considerations and resident concerns as they determine what, and under what conditions, makes sense locally. Listen to the full conversation, also available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube. About CitiesSpeak Each episode of NLC’s podcast, CitiesSpeak with Clarence Anthony, dives into a critical issue facing local leaders today, featuring conversations with elected leaders and policy experts from across the country. The podcast is a relaxed and entertaining resource for local policymakers looking for ideas and information to bring back to their communities. The podcast is hosted by NLC CEO and Executive Director Clarence Anthony, who previously served as mayor of South Bay, Florida, for more than two decades. New episodes of CitiesSpeak are available on all major podcasting platforms and on YouTube. If you have feedback for the show or ideas for future guests, email us. Happy listening!

artigo.texto: Firefighters continued pouring water on two lithium-ion battery storage units at a Metropolitan Water District facility in La Verne on Wednesday afternoon after temperatures spiked when crews twice tried to stop cooling them, authorities said. One section of the battery unit that initially caught fire Tuesday climbed to about 300 degrees during an afternoon test, La Verne Fire Chief Brandon Coatney said. The adjacent unit, which had been exposed to heat from the original fire, also experienced another temperature increase. Los Angeles County Fire Health Hazmat Capt. Ernie Hernandez said the second unit reached about 112 degrees. Officials had been closely monitoring that second unit throughout the day. Its temperature had risen from about 70 degrees to about 90 degrees as of 7 a.m., La Verne Fire Department Battalion Chief Mark Savage said. Crews resumed flowing water onto both units and were able to keep temperatures and smoke production under control, Coatney said. Hernandez said low levels of gases typical of battery fires were being detected immediately around the units, but monitoring at the perimeter of the facility and outside it showed no detections. “Nothing’s leaving the property,” Hernandez said. Water samples from the site had also been sent to a laboratory, though results were still pending Wednesday afternoon, he said. Officials said they were not concerned about a large explosion but warned that an uncontrolled increase in fire activity could produce a hazardous smoke plume. “We’re not worried about an explosion,” Coatney said. “We would have a plume of smoke that would travel through the city.” Coatney said the worst-case scenario would be for the fire to grow beyond what firefighters’ hose streams could control, allowing smoke and hazardous vapors to move through nearby neighborhoods with the prevailing winds. The evacuation zones were being maintained to keep residents out of the potential path of such a plume, he said. The best-case scenario, Coatney said, would be for crews to keep the batteries controlled as the remaining material consumes itself without a hazardous release. Evacuation orders remained in place for about 500 homes Wednesday, and officials said residents could remain displaced for days. La Verne police Capt. Travis Tibbetts said the evacuation area was bounded generally by Moreno Avenue on the west, Foothill Boulevard on the north and B Street on the east, extending south to the property line of the Metropolitan facility and the north side of Pelota Park. Police officers were going door to door throughout the evacuation area Wednesday, Tibbetts said. About half of the homes officers had checked appeared to be empty, while roughly a quarter of the residents contacted were leaving or preparing to leave. About 20% told officers they planned to remain. “We would like those residents to leave,” Tibbetts said. “If smoke should be up in the air and is traveling through the air, our police officers are not going to be able to get out of the car and tell you to leave.” Officials could not say exactly when residents would be allowed to return. “I would definitely say it’s going to be days,” Coatney said. The evacuation orders could be lifted once the batteries stop producing heat and hazardous vapors at levels that concern officials, Coatney said. Work at the site would continue afterward as crews fully de-energize the lithium-ion batteries and prepare them to be transported to a hazardous-materials facility for disposal. Grace Miller Elementary School, which is just outside the evacuation zone, will remain closed Thursday, Tibbetts said. Pelota Park also remained closed to sporting activities. The two battery energy storage systems are housed in steel containers about 12 feet long, 8 feet wide and 9 feet high, Metropolitan Water District Assistant General Manager Shane Chapman said. Each container holds several batteries stacked and wired together. The systems were installed within the past 18 months and put into service in June, Chapman said. They store energy generated by nearby solar panels so it can later be returned to the electrical system. The cause of Tuesday’s initial fire remained under investigation. Chapman said experts were being brought in to evaluate the systems once conditions were safe enough for them to enter the area. Both units have been taken out of service, and Metropolitan has not decided whether they will ever return to operation at the site, Chapman said. “Given the experience we’re going through here, my own opinion at this point, it’s not worth it,” Chapman said when asked about operating the battery systems in an urban environment. Crews began monitoring the second storage unit after it began smoking and making popping sounds on Tuesday evening due to the heat exposure from the original fire, which was reported about 11:40 a.m. Tuesday at the facility at 3201 Wheeler Avenue, authorities said. Judy Jeevarajan, vice president and scientific advisor at UL Research Institutes, has worked in battery safety for more than 25 years and previously led battery safety and advanced technology work at NASA’s Johnson Space Center. Jeevarajan said the behavior of a lithium-ion battery fire depends heavily on the size of the battery system and how much heat is generated. Heat from one cell can spread to others and trigger thermal runaway, a self-sustaining reaction that can continue even after the visible fire appears to be under control. “It all depends on how much heat is generated,” Jeevarajan said. She said water is generally the most effective suppressant because firefighters need to cool the cells themselves, not just the exterior of the battery system. artigo.texto: Residents get another chance to shape Fayetteville's data center rules Fayetteville will host three community sessions Sept. 30 to hear feedback from residents on the proposed Unified Development Ordinance amendments for data centers, according to a news release from the city Sept. 23. Residents will have the opportunity to voice their concerns on topics such as water, electricity, emissions, setbacks, appearance and noise. City staff will listen and record comments from residents. The information gathered during the sessions will help inform the city's proposed amendments. Sessions will be held in Fayetteville at: - College Lakes Recreation Center, 4945 Rosehill Road: 10 a.m.- noon - Massey Hill Recreation Center, 1612 Camden Road: 2–4 p.m. - Cliffdale Recreation Center, 6404 Cliffdale Road: 6–8 p.m. The city has had contentious public hearings on data centers marked by protests and multiple removals from City Hall. On Aug. 10, the City Council voted to send the proposed data center regulations back to staff for revisions, with an updated ordinance expected to return for public review at a special meeting in October. Cumberland County held similar sessions in August, as part of its six-month moratorium process. The county used the public input to help draft its data center ordinance. The ordinance will be presented to the Cumberland County Board of Commissioners for approval later this year. Residents who cannot attend the community sessions can share feedback through an online form on the city’s website: FayettevilleNC.gov/UDOAmendments. Coral Aponte is the government watchdog reporter. Reach her at caponte@usatodayco.com.

artigo.texto: Note: Welcome To RCBJ’s “Your Voices” Column, an occasional column prompted by readers’ commentary. If you have something to say, in a well-reasoned essay of 500 to 700 words, email the editor at ttraster@rcbizjournal.com 120 Moratoriums Across 40 Counties Have Been Imposed; 13 Jurisdictions Have Restricted All Battery Storage Projects, Regardless of Size. By Malaquias Encarnacion Orangetown recently passed a local law establishing a temporary moratorium on the approval, construction, and installation of both battery energy storage systems and data centers. The decision to group these two technologies under a single moratorium was not accidental. It reflects a growing recognition that the siting debates around battery storage and data centers share the same root cause: local planning boards are being asked to evaluate complex energy infrastructure applications without the technical tools to do so. I run a firm that specializes in permitting battery energy storage systems, and we track every BESS moratorium enacted in New York. The statewide count now exceeds 120 moratoriums across more than 40 counties. Thirteen jurisdictions have gone further, restricting all battery storage regardless of project size. In June alone, four new moratoriums were enacted. The Hudson Valley has been one of the most active regions. These moratoriums are not irrational. The concerns driving them are legitimate. Lithium-ion battery fires produce toxic gases. Thermal runaway, the cascading failure mode that can cause a single battery cell to ignite its neighbors, is a real engineering challenge. Communities near proposed projects want to know what happens if something goes wrong, and they deserve a clear answer before construction begins. The problem is that a moratorium does not provide that answer. It defers the question. What actually resolves the siting question is a set of technically grounded local standards that give planning boards a framework for evaluating applications on their merits. These tools already exist. National fire codes, specifically NFPA 855, establish safety requirements for energy storage installations including spacing, ventilation, fire suppression, and explosion prevention. UL 9540A, a standardized test protocol, generates the data that determines how far a battery system must be placed from occupied buildings and property lines. A Hazard Mitigation Analysis, prepared by a licensed fire protection engineer, translates that test data into a site-specific safety plan. And an Emergency Response Plan, coordinated with the local fire department before a permit is issued, ensures that first responders know exactly what they are dealing with. When a community adopts a siting ordinance built on these standards, the planning board gains the ability to approve projects that meet the bar and deny projects that do not. That is a more durable outcome than a moratorium, which expires, gets extended, and eventually forces the same conversation the community was trying to avoid. Rockland County sits at a particularly interesting intersection. The DataBank expansion in Orangeburg has already triggered a positive SEQRA declaration requiring a full Environmental Impact Statement. Governor Hochul signed an executive order imposing a one-year statewide moratorium on large data centers consuming more than 50 megawatts. And the communities surrounding Rockland, in Orange, Ulster, Dutchess, and Sullivan Counties, are navigating their own BESS moratoriums and siting debates simultaneously. The convergence is not a coincidence. Data centers and battery storage are increasingly co-located because battery systems can absorb the grid impact that would otherwise require expensive transmission upgrades. That means the siting debates will continue to overlap. Communities that develop a coherent local framework for evaluating energy infrastructure, one grounded in fire science rather than arbitrary setback distances, will be better positioned to distinguish between projects that belong and projects that do not. I am not arguing that every proposed battery storage project should be approved. I am arguing that planning boards should have the technical basis to make that determination rather than defaulting to a blanket prohibition that treats all projects, and all technologies, the same way. For communities interested in what a technically grounded BESS siting framework looks like in practice, we maintain a permitting guide that walks through the process from fire code compliance through local approval. The data is publicly available. The tools exist. The question is whether local governments will use them. Malaquias Encarnacion is the Managing Director of Carina Energy, a firm specializing in the permitting and development of utility-scale battery energy storage systems. He can be reached at contact@carina.energy

artigo.texto: Lula, Flávio Bolsonaro, Ronaldo Caiado, Romeu Zema e Renan Santos defendem expansão dos data centers, enquanto propostas divergem sobre incentivos, energia, investimentos e tecnologia nacional. Em 2026, os data centers ganharam espaço nos planos dos principais candidatos à Presidência da República. Lula, Flávio Bolsonaro, Ronaldo Caiado, Romeu Zema e Renan Santos apresentam propostas para ampliar essa infraestrutura, considerada necessária para armazenar dados, oferecer serviços digitais e executar sistemas de inteligência artificial. O interesse pelo setor ocorre enquanto o Brasil tenta aumentar sua capacidade computacional e atrair investimentos ligados à IA. Embora exista convergência sobre a expansão, os programas apresentam diferenças sobre participação estatal, incentivos fiscais, investimentos estrangeiros, transferência tecnológica e exigências ambientais. Augusto Cury também dedica parte de seu programa à inteligência artificial e à robótica. Seu plano, porém, trata a IA como infraestrutura estratégica de Estado sem apresentar uma proposta específica para construir ou ampliar data centers. - Meta prepara óculos inteligentes sem câmera após críticas sobre gravações, mantém inteligência artificial e tenta reduzir preocupações com privacidade nos dispositivos vestíveis - Grok deixa de ser apenas chatbot nos carros da Tesla, passa a controlar funções físicas e prepara novo recurso para enviar mensagens usando linguagem natural - Plataforma lança cursos gratuitos de inteligência artificial com certificado, ensina a criar prompts e automatizar tarefas e prepara novas formações para profissionais em setembro - Novo robô humanoide Digit 5 trabalha até 20 horas por dia, levanta cerca de 23 kg e recupera carga em apenas 9 minutos para atuar lado a lado com humanos em fábricas, armazéns e operações logísticas industriais Supercomputador de R$ 1 bilhão anunciado no Rio Grande do Norte colocou capacidade computacional no centro da estratégia brasileira para inteligência artificial Em 20 de agosto de 2026, Lula anunciou em Macaíba, no Rio Grande do Norte, um supercomputador para inteligência artificial com investimento estimado em R$ 1 bilhão. O governo também anunciou outra estrutura de computação avançada no Rio de Janeiro, em parceria com empresas chinesas. Os projetos fazem parte da estratégia para ampliar a capacidade computacional disponível no Brasil, recurso necessário para treinar e operar sistemas de inteligência artificial. No programa eleitoral, essa expansão aparece relacionada diretamente à ideia de soberania digital. O plano de Lula prevê infraestrutura computacional nacional, serviços de nuvem e supercomputadores desenvolvidos ou operados por instituições brasileiras. A expansão também seria acompanhada por eficiência energética, fontes renováveis, avaliação dos impactos elétricos e hídricos e contrapartidas de conteúdo local. Caiado, Flávio Bolsonaro, Zema e Renan Santos também defendem data centers, mas apresentam caminhos diferentes para atrair investimentos ao Brasil Ronaldo Caiado defende incentivos tributários condicionados a exigências ambientais, tecnológicas e sociais. Seu programa menciona energia renovável, eficiência hídrica, geração de empregos, qualificação profissional e investimentos necessários para ampliar a rede elétrica. Flávio Bolsonaro e Romeu Zema apresentam uma abordagem mais direcionada à atração de capital privado. Os dois relacionam a expansão dos data centers à disponibilidade brasileira de energia competitiva e a um ambiente regulatório e tributário capaz de atrair empresas de tecnologia. O programa de Flávio propõe transformar o Brasil em um polo global de data centers sustentáveis, aproveitando a matriz elétrica renovável. Zema pretende usar a disponibilidade de energia limpa e competitiva para atrair setores intensivos em eletricidade, incluindo inteligência artificial e data centers. Renan Santos defende incentivos para instalação dessas estruturas e concentra parte da estratégia no Nordeste. Seu programa propõe zonas econômicas especiais para inteligência artificial, com regras próprias envolvendo energia, impostos e regulação. Construir data centers no Brasil não significa conquistar automaticamente soberania digital, segundo especialistas que acompanham o avanço dessa infraestrutura A presença física dos servidores no território brasileiro não garante, por si só, independência tecnológica. Luca Belli, professor da Fundação Getulio Vargas e coordenador do Centro de Tecnologia e Sociedade, afirma que o resultado depende da forma como esses empreendimentos são integrados à economia nacional. Belli defende que a instalação dessas estruturas seja associada a universidades, laboratórios, startups e governos locais. Essa conexão permitiria formar pesquisadores, desenvolver empresas e estimular transferência de tecnologia, em vez de limitar os benefícios ao investimento inicial e aos empregos da construção. A preocupação também envolve a concentração internacional da tecnologia. A computação em nuvem é dominada por um grupo reduzido de empresas americanas, enquanto a fabricação de chips avançados permanece concentrada. Para Belli, soberania digital significa manter escolhas e reduzir dependências difíceis de substituir. Disputa tecnológica entre Estados Unidos e China aumenta importância dos fornecedores escolhidos para sustentar inteligência artificial no Brasil A expansão brasileira ocorre em meio à corrida tecnológica entre Estados Unidos e China. Em julho de 2026, o Brasil assinou o acordo para criação da Waico, Organização Mundial de Cooperação em Inteligência Artificial, criada em Xangai com participação de 29 países. A organização pretende estimular cooperação científica, formação profissional, compartilhamento de infraestrutura, desenvolvimento de modelos abertos e padrões de governança para inteligência artificial. artigo.texto: Seneca Lake power plant in Yates County converting to AI data center, sparks calls for moratorium TORREY, N.Y. — A petition is calling for a moratorium on new AI data centers in the Town of Torrey in Yates County as Greenidge Generation transitions to artificial intelligence operations under a new name, Vulcan Infrastructure and Power. News10NBC’s Garrett Chan reports the former Greenidge power plant has already transformed once, from a coal-fired plant to cryptocurrency mining. Now, a nonprofit environmental group is pushing for more town oversight as another transformation looms. “So the transition has already begun,” said Yvonne Taylor, vice president of Seneca Lake Guardian. “Some estimates are saying that they are already 30% artificial intelligence data center. And they’re just waiting that, you know, they’re in the queue among other, you know, AI companies in New York to get additional power,” Taylor said. Taylor started a petition urging the Torrey Town Board to consider a moratorium on new development or expansion of AI data centers. She says the governor’s moratorium does not apply to Greenidge because of its permits with the DEC. “The thing is with the Greenwich or the Vulcan facility is it doesn’t stop at the town of Torrey’s borders,” Taylor said. “What happens in Torrey will have an impact on the entire region’s electricity bills, our environment, our climate, our thriving agriculture and tourism industry,” she said. Town Supervisor Peter Martini said a moratorium isn’t necessary right now. The town hasn’t received a formal proposal from Vulcan. “If things accelerated and we felt like we weren’t adequately prepared, we may be able to do something,” Martini said. “But if you do a moratorium for one project, you cannot do that legally because it’s just like trying to shut down a single entity as opposed to blocking any of the development,” said Martini. Taylor said the petition has gotten more than a thousand signatures. She’s planning a community forum on the issue for Oct. 13 in Torrey. News10NBC reached out to Vulcan Infrastructure and Power for their thoughts on the petition. They have not responded. Statement from Greenidge Generation The statement below is from Dale Irwin, the president of Greenidge Generation: “Permitted emissions, water use, noise and any local considerations are not impacted in any way — we will continue providing critical power to the local electricity grid and meet the terms of our historic emissions reduction agreement with NY State, while powering the data center we’ve operated at the site since 2020. We’re simply pivoting what the data center computers will be used for, from using computing power for cryptocurrency to high-performance computing.”

artigo.texto: A small town hall in Michigan found itself with inboxes full of vitriolic emails and voicemails from people all over the country this summer. Town leaders were told, in message after message, they were traitors, liars, and thieves who should rot in hell. Their family members were ugly. They were monsters. They should be gutted like pigs and dismembered. If heaven is real, one caller said, the leaders of Tyrone Township wouldn’t be going there. The messages suggested town leaders had sold out their community’s future to data center developers and would destroy the local environment. But township leaders say they had no data center in development, and had a moratorium in place that applied to such projects. “It has definitely been a roller coaster,” township supervisor Greg Carnes told Scripps News Group. “It’s making public officials and township employees fearful, because of the mob mentality.” The trouble started when a video clip from one of their public meetings caught fire online, showing Carnes and other officials refusing to answer if they had signed non-disclosure agreements with any developer. Carnes said he refused in an attempt to keep order in the meeting and avoid turning the public comment period into a question-and-answer session. When asked by Scripps News Group if anything could have been done differently to avoid the backlash, Carnes answered, “I guess we could have all answered the question, and said no, we haven’t signed NDAs.” Data center debates in communities like Tyrone Township and across the country are boiling over into arrests and perceived threats, sometimes fueled by online misinformation and misunderstandings, other times fueled simply by strong community opposition to real proposals. Scripps News Group gathered police reports, videos, emails, and voicemail recordings from across the country, documenting the data center backlash. People on all sides of the debate say they feel feel targeted, and experts worry threats of political violence may continue to escalate if citizens feel their questions are not being answered by the people in power. Government and business leaders report threats Scripps News Group found examples all over the country of local government leaders expressing fear for their safety because of the data center backlash. In Michigan’s Saline Township, the treasurer tearfully announced her resignation at a public meeting, citing threats over a new data center being built in the community. “You all deserve premature early death for what you’re doing, building a data center,” one caller said in a voicemail obtained by Scripps News Group. Two Illinois men were arrested, in separate incidents, and charged with making threats on Facebook while expressing their opposition to local proposals. In Indianapolis, councilman Ron Gibson said he awoke in April to find bullet holes in his door and a note at his front porch that said, “No data centers,” after he publicly supported a proposed project. No one has been arrested for the incident. Local elected leaders are especially vulnerable to potential political violence around this issue, said Yannick Veilleux-Lepage, a Canadian researcher and professor who studies terrorism and recently wrote about the potential for increased anti-AI violence. In some communities, government and business leaders have reported being threatened even when there is no data center project planned. In California, Mt. Shasta police said in June city leaders received threats of violence because of a “rumored data center” the city had “no interest in pursuing.” Elsewhere in California, Mario Crncic, a construction company owner, became a target because people mistakenly believed his crew was building a data center in Cathedral City. In fact, he says, they were working on a housing tract. “I started getting calls at two o’clock, three o’clock in the morning, cussing me out… one guy said he hopes my wife gets raped for what I’m doing to the public, and for what I’m doing to the environment,” Crncic said. Cathedral City officials have said there are no plans to construct a data center there. Citizens arrested while participating in public meetings Experts are also warning about the implications of another troubling trend around the data center debate: citizens trying to speak out about proposals and being removed from public meetings by police. Video from Emporia, Kansas of a local teacher being carried out of a city commission meeting by police drew outrage online. Police removed the teacher for clapping from the audience after others spoke. Commission members had warned the audience to stay quiet and avoid disruptions. After the incident, Emporia city leaders began holding subsequent meetings virtually, and recently released dozens of examples from the onslaught of messages they’ve received in the wake of the clapping incident. “The communications range from questions and criticism to profanity and violent and threatening language,” city manager Trey Cocking said. Veilleux-Lepage said it’s a problem when people begin to believe their voices will not be heard by their elected leaders. “When I see somebody in a council meeting clapping enthusiastically and being arrested, I look at this as a failure,” Veilleux-Lepage said. “Once you start abolishing the legitimate means for grievances to be heard, people resort to political violence.” “I think a lot of the grievances and a lot of the skepticism toward data centers or rapid deployment of AI are entirely grounded, and they’re valid criticism,” he said. He said his work is “a plea on both sides” for how future unrest may be avoided. Veilleux-Lepage said local activists should guard against fringe members who may resort to violence, and law enforcement and community leaders should be careful not to shut down voices of community opposition. “It’s very important that they make a very clear distinction between people that are AI skeptics, people that don’t want a data center in their communi

According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Flywheel Energy Storage market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global flywheel energy storage market is entering a phase of renewed relevance as grid operators and industrial users seek high-power, high-cyclicity solutions that complement electrochemical batteries. Flywheel energy storage systems (FESS) store electricity as rotational kinetic energy in a spinning mass, offering rapid response, long cycle life, and minimal degradation. These characteristics make them particularly suited to frequency regulation, uninterruptible power supply (UPS) for data centers, railway regenerative braking, and microgrid stabilization. Between 2026 and 2035, demand is expected to accelerate as renewable energy penetration rises, grid inertia declines, and ancillary service markets increasingly value fast-responding resources. While the overall installed base remains smaller than that of lithium-ion batteries, the flywheel segment is carving out defensible niches where cycle life and power density outweigh energy density. This report provides a data-driven outlook on market size, segmentation, supply chain dynamics, and regional demand patterns, with a forecast horizon to 2035. It is intended for manufacturers, integrators, investors, and advisors seeking a consistent analytical view of the flywheel energy storage landscape. The baseline scenario for the world flywheel energy storage market from 2026 to 2035 assumes continued policy support for grid resilience, steady renewable capacity additions, and gradual cost reductions in composite rotors and magnetic bearing systems. Under this scenario, the market is projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 5.8%, reaching a market index of 176 by 2035 (2025 = 100). Growth is not uniform across applications: frequency regulation and data center UPS remain the largest and most mature segments, while railway regenerative braking and microgrid stabilization show higher growth rates from a smaller base. The baseline assumes no major technological breakthroughs that would dramatically alter cost structures, but it does incorporate incremental improvements in power electronics and system integration. Supply chain constraints for high-strength composites and rare-earth magnets represent a moderate risk, though diversification efforts are underway. Regionally, Asia-Pacific is expected to remain the largest market by share, driven by grid infrastructure investments in China and India, while North America and Europe see steady growth supported by ancillary service market reforms. The outlook is cautiously optimistic, with flywheels maintaining a specialized but essential role in the broader energy storage ecosystem. Frequency regulation remains the largest application for flywheel energy storage systems. Grid operators require fast-responding resources to maintain frequency within narrow bands as variable renewable generation displaces synchronous thermal plants. Flywheels excel in this role because they can inject and absorb power within milliseconds and sustain hundreds of thousands of cycles with minimal degradation. Currently, flywheel farms provide regulation services in competitive markets such as PJM in the United States and parts of Europe. Through 2035, demand will be driven by the continued retirement of coal and nuclear baseload plants, which reduces system inertia, and by the growth of solar and wind capacity. Key demand-side indicators include the share of renewables in the generation mix, the frequency of grid disturbances, and the compensation mechanisms for fast frequency response. As battery costs decline, flywheels will compete primarily on cycle life and response speed, maintaining a specialized but resilient position in high-duty-cycle regulation markets. Current trend: Steady growth as renewable penetration increases. Major trends: Increasing renewable share reduces grid inertia, boosting demand for fast frequency response, Ancillary service markets increasingly value speed and accuracy, favoring flywheel technology, Hybrid flywheel-battery systems emerge to combine power and energy capabilities, Retirement of synchronous generators creates inertia gaps that flywheels can partially fill, and Regulatory reforms in North America and Europe expand compensation for fast-responding resources. Representative participants: Beacon Power, Temporal Power, Amber Kinetics, Stornetic, and ABB. Flywheel-based UPS systems provide ride-through power for data centers, hospitals, and industrial facilities, bridging the gap between power interruption and generator startup. Unlike batteries, flywheels offer high power density, rapid recharge, and long service life with minimal maintenance, making them attractive for mission-critical operations. Currently, adoption is concentrated in large data centers and financial trading facilities where power quality is paramount. Through 2035, demand will be supported by the exponential growth of cloud computing, AI workloads, and edge data centers, all of which require reliable backup power. Demand-side indicators include data center construction spending, uptime requirements, and the frequency of grid disturbances. However, competition from lithium-ion UPS systems is intense, and flywheels will likely retain a niche in high-cycle, short-duration backup applications where battery replacement costs are prohibitive. Hybrid solutions combining flywheels with batteries are expected to gain traction. Current trend: Moderate growth driven by data center expansion. artigo.texto: UK energy industry regulator Ofgem said it is minded to approve the introduction of a financial commitment for BESS in an attempt to reduce the oversupply of the projects awaiting a grid connection. There is about 90GW of battery energy storage (BESS) capacity either operational or in the reformed connections queue, almost three times the 29GW that the government is targeting as part of its Clean Power 2030 target. The Oversubscribed Technologies Commitment Fee (OTCF) would require projects to demonstrate a minimum level of financial commitment starting at £3,000 per MW and rising to a maximum £25,000 per MW if the queue remains significantly oversubscribed. Ofgem said that while battery storage has a “vital role” to play in a clean energy system, the scale of the queue “makes it difficult to know which projects are genuinely likely to be built”. This was the issue with the broader grid connection queue before it was reformed to follow a ‘first ready, first connected’ process. artigo.texto: A Getmax completa 30 anos de atuação em um mercado que mudou profundamente desde a criação da empresa. Com sede em Porto Alegre (RS), a companhia é especializada na revenda de equipamentos de informática, softwares e soluções de infraestrutura para o setor corporativo e mantém mais de 300 clientes ativos no Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina, Paraná e São Paulo. Entre os clientes estão empresas como Embraer, Petrobras, Panvel, Yara Fertilizantes, Lojas Lebes, Altus Sistemas de Automação, Hyundai Elevadores e Viação Ouro e Prata. A empresa trabalha com um portfólio que reúne fabricantes como Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft, Cisco, Fortinet, APC, Aruba, Intelbras, Samsung, LG, Seagate, Kingston, Zebra e Honeywell, entre outras marcas. A estratégia permite atender desde estações de trabalho e notebooks até servidores, redes, segurança, armazenamento, comunicação e infraestrutura para ambientes corporativos. A evolução da Getmax acompanha a transformação do próprio mercado. Se há três décadas a informatização das empresas estava concentrada na aquisição de computadores, periféricos e servidores, hoje a tecnologia está diretamente ligada à produtividade, continuidade operacional, Segurança e competitividade. Computação em Nuvem, Inteligência Artificial, Automação e crescimento dos volumes de Dados passaram a exigir uma infraestrutura mais integrada. “Quando começamos, a necessidade das empresas era muito mais concentrada em equipamentos. Hoje, a conversa com o cliente é completamente diferente. Ele quer entender como a tecnologia pode melhorar a operação, reduzir riscos e gerar eficiência. O equipamento continua sendo importante, mas ele é parte de uma solução muito maior”, afirma Frederico Braga, diretor Comercial da Getmax. O movimento ocorre em um mercado brasileiro de TI que ganhou escala nos últimos anos. Segundo Dados da ABES/IDC citados no estudo utilizado pela empresa, os investimentos brasileiros em tecnologia da informação chegaram a US$ 58,6 bilhões em 2024, crescimento de 17,6% sobre o ano anterior. O Brasil respondeu por 34,7% dos investimentos de TI da América Latina. Para Frederico, a mudança mais importante está no comportamento do comprador corporativo. “O cliente está mais informado, mais exigente e muito mais preocupado com integração. Ele não quer simplesmente comprar um computador, um servidor ou um firewall. Quer saber como aquela tecnologia vai conversar com o restante da infraestrutura e como poderá acompanhar o crescimento da empresa”, diz. Inteligência Artificial muda a infraestrutura A chegada da Inteligência Artificial acrescenta uma nova camada de complexidade ao mercado. Sistemas de IA demandam maior capacidade de processamento, armazenamento, Conectividade e Segurança, aumentando a necessidade de modernização da infraestrutura corporativa. Segundo o levantamento citado no estudo, 90% das grandes empresas brasileiras já utilizavam IA em pelo menos um caso de uso. “A Inteligência Artificial está mudando a conversa dentro das empresas. Antes se discutia muito a aquisição de equipamentos. Agora se discute capacidade de processamento, Dados, Segurança, Conectividade e onde essa infraestrutura vai estar. A IA acaba puxando uma série de investimentos que muitas vezes o usuário final nem percebe”, afirma Fredrico. Essa mudança também altera o papel das revendas. Para a Getmax, a oportunidade está em combinar diferentes fabricantes e tecnologias de acordo com a necessidade de cada cliente, em vez de atuar apenas como Canal de venda. “Nosso papel é entender o problema do cliente e encontrar a combinação de tecnologias que faça sentido para aquela operação. Temos parceiros muito fortes em hardware, software, redes e Segurança, e isso nos permite montar soluções diferentes conforme o perfil e o nível de exigência de cada empresa”, explica o diretor. Data Centers ampliam o mercado A expansão dos Data Centers abre outra frente de crescimento para o ecossistema de tecnologia. Segundo os Dados reunidos no material da empresa, o Brasil recebeu 106 MW de nova capacidade de Data Centers no primeiro semestre de 2026, com previsão de mais 134 MW até o final do ano e investimentos estimados em aproximadamente US$ 8 bilhões. O avanço desses ambientes movimenta uma Cadeia que vai muito além da construção dos próprios Data Centers. Servidores, armazenamento, switches, roteadores, sistemas de Segurança, monitoramento, Conectividade, energia, UPS, refrigeração e softwares de gerenciamento passam a fazer parte de uma demanda crescente. “O crescimento dos Data Centers é muito relevante porque cria uma cadeia inteira de oportunidades. artigo.texto: Barrett Helps Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Increase Transparency, Ban Data Centers NDAs Washington, D.C. — Today, Congressmen Tom Barrett (MI-07), Greg Landsman (OH-01), and Jamie Raskin (MD-08) introduced the No Secrets for Data Centers Act to prohibit non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) by government officials to conceal details of data center projects from the public. The bipartisan bill, which applies to federal, state, and local officials, builds on the No Data Center NDAs Act Barrett introduced last month to prohibit members of Congress from signing NDAs to hide data center details. The legislation comes as government officials are increasingly signing NDAs with data center developers, keeping local residents in the dark about how the projects could affect natural resources and electric rates. “Local residents must have the final say about data centers in their communities, and that means they need to know all the facts so they can make an informed decision,” Barrett said. “The recent surge in NDAs is keeping people in the dark about how a data center might affect their land, their water, and their electric bills — until it’s too late. Blocking these confidentiality agreements is an important step in our fight to increase transparency and protect citizens’ right to decide what is best for their community.” “Big Tech needs to be transparent about these deals, not force local officials to sign NDAs and keep secrets from their communities,” said Landsman. “That means no more NDAs. Transparency can’t just be a promise – it needs to be law.” “The American people have a right to know how data centers being built in their communities will affect local utilities, the local environment, and the local economy, and who will be responsible if and when things go wrong,” said Raskin. “Yet throughout the country, local officials are blocked from discussing these projects with their constituents because of the Non-Disclosure Agreements Big Tech companies are imposing to cloak these projects in secrecy. I’m proud to introduce this bill with Rep. Landsman to ban these corporate gag orders and make sure no public official is stifled in their most fundamental duty: answering to the people they represent and protecting their interests.” The new bill also comes the week after Barrett and the U.S. House of Representatives approved the Ratepayer Protection Act to require large-load energy customers, such as data centers, to cover the full costs of increased grid capacity. Background The No Secrets for Data Centers Act would prohibit and invalidate NDAs signed by government officials to conceal details of data center projects. NDAs have gained attention in Michigan in recent years, with many federal, state, and local officials signing secrecy deals about a variety of proposed corporate projects. The bill would also prohibit data center operators from receiving government incentives if the conditions include entering an agreement to keep information about the project confidential. Michigan currently prevents disclosure of details about data centers receiving targeted tax incentives, and other states have adopted similar confidentiality provisions. Barrett has been a leader on reining in government overreach and increasing transparency and accountability for artificial intelligence and data centers. He voted against Michigan’s corporate welfare for data centers when he was a state lawmaker, and he’s introduced or co-sponsored the following bills in Congress: - The Protecting Local Control of Data Centers Act (H.R. 10119) to prohibit federal agencies from overriding local land-use, zoning, siting, or permitting authority related to data centers. - The No Data Center NDAs Act (H.R. 10118) would prohibit members of Congress from signing non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) about data centers, including any information about possible locations or how much water or energy a facility is expected to consume. - The Doctors Not AI Act (H.R. 10210), introduced by Barrett and Landsman, to ensure that artificial intelligence cannot make or dictate health insurance coverage decisions involving medical judgment. - The Children Harmed by AI Technology (CHAT) Act (H.R. 7218) to require AI chatbots to implement age verification measures to protect minors. The bill requires parental consent for minors using chatbots, bans chatbots from engaging in sexually explicit communications with minors, and requires chatbots to notify a minor’s parent if the minor’s chat shows signs of suicidal ideation. - The AI Threat Output and Monitoring Incident Containment Act (H.R. 9965) to test advanced AI systems to prevent risks to nuclear safety. - The Human Authority over Autonomous Weapons Act (H.R. 9729) to ensure that no autonomous or artificial intelligence-enabled weapon system used by the United States military can carry out an intentionally lethal strike without meaningful human oversight or a human decision-maker in the loop. - The VA Claims AI Accountability Act (H.R. 10418) to require VA employees — not AI — to make the final decisions for approval of disability claims or benefits. The bill also strengthens oversight and accountability for the VA’s digital benefits system. - The VA AI Transparency Act (H.R. 10417) to require the VA to disclose to every veteran any use of AI by the VA, including in claims processing and customer service chats. artigo.texto: A Greenvolt arrancou com a construção de um sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) de 600 MW / 2,4 GWh em Siedlce, na Polónia, um projeto que será o maior deste tipo no país e um dos maiores da Europa. A entrada em operação comercial está prevista para o final de 2027. O projeto está a ser desenvolvido pela Greenvolt Power, área de negócio do grupo dedicada às energias renováveis de grande escala, e representa mais um passo na expansão da empresa no mercado europeu de armazenamento de energia. Com 4,6 GW de projetos BESS em carteira, dos quais cerca de 2,4 GW estão localizados na Polónia, a Greenvolt tem vindo a reforçar esta área como uma das componentes da sua estratégia de crescimento. “Com Siedlce, estamos mais uma vez a passar dos planos à concretização. O mais importante é construir ativos, criar valor real e reforçar as infraestruturas necessárias para integrar mais energia renovável no sistema. A Polónia é um mercado estratégico para nós e o armazenamento de energia em baterias está a assumir uma importância cada vez maior no nosso crescimento”, afirmou João Manso Neto, CEO do Grupo Greenvolt. Com 600 MW de potência e 2,4 GWh de capacidade de armazenamento, a instalação permitirá armazenar eletricidade em períodos de elevada produção renovável e disponibilizá-la quando a procura aumentar. O objetivo é aumentar a flexibilidade da rede elétrica polaca e facilitar a integração de produção proveniente de fontes eólica e solar. Siedlce junta-se a outros projetos de armazenamento da Greenvolt Power na Polónia. Turośń Kościelna, com 200 MW / 800 MWh, entrou em operação em julho de 2026, enquanto Ełk, também com 200 MW / 800 MWh, tem entrada em operação comercial prevista para o quarto trimestre deste ano. Quando os três projetos estiverem em funcionamento, representarão, em conjunto, 1 GW de potência e 4 GWh de capacidade de armazenamento. “Estamos agora a avançar com Siedlce para a fase de construção, com os acordos de fornecimento das baterias e de ligação à rede já estabelecidos. A experiência que adquirimos com Turośń Kościelna e Ełk proporciona-nos uma base sólida para concretizar um projeto desta dimensão, e a nossa prioridade é manter este ritmo e colocar Siedlce em operação até ao final de 2027”, afirmou Weronika Nowak, CEO da Greenvolt Power. A tecnologia de baterias será fornecida pela BYD Energy Storage. O projeto contará com 210 contentores de baterias e 105 contentores de transformadores equipados com sistemas de conversão de energia, que permitem o fluxo de eletricidade entre as baterias e a rede. Na construção das infraestruturas elétricas, a Greenvolt Power está a trabalhar com a empresa de engenharia e construção P&Q e com a ONDE, empresa de energias renováveis e empreiteiro.

Changes to traditional tax equity structures and growing geopolitical tensions are fundamentally reshaping how renewable energy projects secure financing in the US, according to Nathan Picarsic, co-founder of Horizon Advisory, a geopolitical and supply chain risk intelligence provider. Picarsic outlines how legislative changes enabling tax credit transferability have opened up renewable energy financing to a much broader pool of capital allocators, whilst mounting US-China tensions are forcing developers to reassess their supply chain strategies. Transferability expands capital access The introduction of tax credit transferability created what Picarsic describes as a “secondary tranche” in renewable energy financing, allowing a more diverse set of capital allocators to participate in the market beyond traditional tax equity investors from major banks. This allows projects that might previously have struggled to secure financing to move forward, whilst creating a more risk-adjusted investment universe. Domestic content versus speed to market Developers now face a complex trade-off between navigating regulatory hurdles to gain domestic content tax credits versus importing components to accelerate project timelines. Picarsic characterised this as “a new type of consideration, a new challenge” for the market. “Developers are ultimately looking at economic return,” he says. “There’s the timeline on which they need to deliver a project and generate liquidity for their upstream capital formation.” Many developers are currently in a “sit and wait situation” seeking maximum certainty before proceeding, though some are moving forward where the economic delta between domestic and imported components justifies faster execution. However, Picarsic suggests the political and regulatory environment is pushing towards models that support domestic manufacturing capacity, pointing to challenges in the data centre space as an early signal of these political realities. “There’s both leadership in US government as well as popular support on economic development, but a certain type of economic development,” he says. “People need electrification to deliver all sorts of common goods that people want across the country, and we need to decrease emissions in all sorts of ways and in all sorts of places across the country.” Credit expiry timelines versus policy direction With solar investment tax credits (ITCs) set to expire at the end of 2027 and storage credits running to 2033, developers face strategic decisions about capital allocation sequencing. Picarsic identifies a current rush to lock in anything that can be safe harboured or imported and put into service as quickly as possible, independent of credit expiry dates. However, he argues that credit timelines are less important than the underlying bipartisan policy push towards stronger domestic and allied supply chains for critical infrastructure. “Investors, developers, suppliers who understand and build their businesses around that logic are likely the ones that are going to win out by the time we’re to 2037. There’s a capex story that you’ll see playing out toward that trajectory that is a little bit indifferent toward the 2027 or 2033 deadlines,” he says. FCC inverter ban and implementation challenges Regarding the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) 28 July equipment bans targeting Chinese inverters and other components, Picarsic emphasises that implementation details will prove critical. He suggestes successful models would pair bans with white lists or approved vendor lists, where suppliers clearly documenting their supply chains and firmware can guarantee compliance upfront, lessening the burden on broader markets dependent on cost-competitive inputs. “You end up in some place where domestic and some whitelisted set of things can substitute for where risks exist,” he says. Picarsic notes that subnational regulations may carry as much or more weight than federal import bans, pointing to authorities already on the books in Texas’s ERCOT market that could be leveraged to accomplish or supersede the scope of potential FCC bans. “That’s the space that I would look for the actual pacing of timing enforcement,” he notes. “It might be from state, local authorities that have their own set of regulatory approaches and legal authorities.” Long-term US-China trajectory On the broader question of how the US-China relationship might evolve, Picarsic—who serves as a Senior Fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington think tank known for its hawkish foreign policy positions—offeres a notably pessimistic outlook on bilateral relations. artigo.texto: Twenty-six Energy Prism containerized storage units will store solar-generated electricity at an oil and gas production site in northern China, marking EnerVenue’s first commercial multi-megawatt-hour order. EnerVenue has signed its first multi-megawatt-hour commercial order. Twenty-six Energy Prism containerized storage units, with a combined capacity of 11 MWh, will be installed at an oilfield in northern China, where they will store electricity generated by an onsite solar array and supply it back to the operation. The first three units ship in December 2026 and the remaining twenty-three follow in March 2027. The order was placed by a major Chinese oil and gas producer for one of its established production sites. Further details of the project, including the end user, will be shared as the installation progresses. Oil and gas sites are among the most safety-conscious industrial environments in the world, and any equipment installed on them has to satisfy the operator’s fire and process safety requirements before its performance or its cost is considered. That requirement was the deciding factor in the choice of battery. Henning Rath, Chief Executive Officer of EnerVenue, said “An oil and gas producer does not put new technology on a working site unless it is completely satisfied that the safety case is sound, and this customer examined everything before choosing us. It is a perfect location to deploy a large scale project.” “A battery designed to run for thirty years is a piece of infrastructure, and infrastructure gets judged on how it performs across its whole life rather than on the day it is delivered. We built the Aqueous Metal Cell for customers who think about it that way, and it’s very satisfying to see such huge demand for our product.” EnerVenue’s Aqueous Metal Cell carries zero risk of fire from thermal runaway. Its electrolyte is water based and non-flammable, it contains no lithium, and it has passed UL 9540A, the industry’s standard test for battery fire propagation, with no fire propagation at cell level. Dr Majid Keshavarz, Chief Technology Officer of EnerVenue, said: “While thermal runaway is generally defined as a self-accelerating sequence of exothermic reactions, the AMC chemistry does not produce the same progression of events that leads to ignition, fire, explosion, or propagation to adjacent cells. That is a property of the chemistry itself, and it is what allows this battery to go onto sites with the strictest fire safety requirements.” Rahul Mehta, Chief Revenue Officer of EnerVenue, said “Oil and gas operators are among the world’s most demanding buyers of industrial equipment, and fire safety is non-negotiable. We are proud that our first multi-megawatt-hour order has come from a customer that rigorously evaluated our technology on precisely this critical requirement. This order demonstrates growing demand for energy storage designed not only for exceptional fire safety, but also for reliable performance over decades. That combination of safety and long operating life is the value EnerVenue brings, and the conversation we want to advance across every market we serve.” The project pairs solar generation with battery storage on an operating oilfield, shifting daytime solar output into the hours when the site draws power. The Energy Prism units will be built from EnerVenue’s fourth-generation Aqueous Metal Cell and delivered as complete containerized systems, ready to connect to the site’s power conversion equipment. EnerVenue’s first Aqueous Metal Cell installation, a 150 kWh system integrating onsite renewable generation with electric bus charging, has been operating at Jintan in Changzhou since November 2025. The Northern China project is the company’s first commercial contract at multi-megawatt-hour scale. The cells for the project will come from EnerVenue’s new high volume manufacturing line in Changzhou, Jiangsu, which opens on Thursday 24 September. The factory will produce 250 MWh of Aqueous Metal Cells a year in its first phase, which is around 300 cells a day at full automation, with production ramping to 1 GWh in 2027 and multi-gigawatt-hour scale by 2028 as capacity expands. It is the first facility in the world to produce the Aqueous Metal Cell at scale. EnerVenue will also be unveiling its full range of products at the factory launch on 24th September. Energy Core, at 30 kWh, is designed for distributed and remote sites. Energy Cube, at 108 kWh, is designed for in-building and data centre use. Energy Rack, at 150 kWh, is designed for commercial, industrial and grid-connected work. Energy Prism brings the same cells to utility and heavy industrial sites. All four are built on one chemistry. The Aqueous Metal Cell is a water-based metal battery built on nickel-hydrogen chemistry. The same chemistry powered the Hubble Space Telescope and the International Space Station for decades, and EnerVenue re-engineered it with low-cost materials for use on Earth. The cell is designed for 30,000 charge cycles, equivalent to up to three cycles a day for thirty years, compared with a typical lithium-ion figure of 8,000 to 10,000 cycles, and it requires no scheduled augmentation across that life. A lithium-ion installation is typically replaced or augmented every seven to ten years. Over the life of a project that changes the economics. An Aqueous Metal Cell installation needs no augmentation, no active cooling and, where local codes allow, no fire suppression system, so the auxiliary equipment that usually adds cost and complexity to a storage site is largely absent, and the levelized cost of the energy it stores over thirty years falls accordingly. The cell uses no lithium and no rare earths. Its bulk materials are steel, nickel, glass-fiber composite and a water-based electrolyte, and the nickel and steel can be recovered and reused at end of life.
