artigo.texto: Compressed air energy storage holds much promise for large-scale, long-duration energy storage (LDES), but so far has struggled to really get off the ground outside of China. Will Hydrostor’s iteration on the technology finally take it to large-scale, commercially viable deployments? CAES and A-CAES technology explained Compressed air energy technology that delivers mechanical power has been around since the 19th century. Compressed air energy storage (CAES) is relatively newer, with the first utility-scale CAES project opening in 1978 at Huntorf in Germany. There have been other CAES projects commissioned since, with the largest to date coming online in Jiangsu Province, China. The Huai’an Salt Cavern CAES project in China has a 600MW power output and a 2,400MWh storage capacity. Even though there are multiple CAES projects live, they are hard to deploy. Hydrostor has been developing a new type of CAES called advanced CAES (A-CAES), that they will hope will make CAES easier to deploy. CAES works by pressurising and directing air into a storage medium. When there is an excess of electricity, be it from the grid or from renewable generation, the electricity is used to compress air. This air is then compressed in a cavern underground and acts as the stored energy (instead of traditional electrochemical stored energy). The heat captured during the compression process is released to the surrounding atmosphere. When the demand for energy is high, the compressed air is expanded and released through a natural gas combustion heating system to drive a turbine generator that produces electricity. A-CAES still compresses air to store energy and releases it via a heating medium, but the technology captures the heat generated during the charging process instead of venting it to the atmosphere. This heat is stored in overground thermal storage tanks and used as the fuel in the discharge heating process, eliminating the need for natural gas. The air in A-CAES is stored slightly differently to CAES. Where CAES stores energy in natural rock salt caverns, A-CAES can store air in different hard rock caverns that have been artificially made into the rock body. Inside these caverns, a water head is used to enhance land density and maintain the system at a constant pressure. When it’s time to discharge the energy, the water head weight is released, and the cavern is flooded with water. This pushes the air to the surface, and it is recombined with the stored heat, expanded, and sent through the turbine to create electricity. When it’s time to charge, the introduction of compressed air to the cavern displaces the water upwards into a surface reservoir (ready for release again when there’s a need to discharge). In essence, the water acts as a kind of piston. So, while the technologies are similar in principle, they actual everyday function is different. The cavern in A-CAES maintains a moderate pressure of 75bar, and the installation of one these systems require a one-time fill of water to create the water head. This requires 150 cubic meters per MWh. For a 500MW, 8-hour A-CAES system, this is about 50 Olympic sized swimming pools worth of water. The other main difference is the cavern itself. CAES uses natural rock salt caverns whereas A-CAES requires the excavation of a cavern at a suitable geological site. Controlled detonations between 0-2,000ft provides the initial 4-foot diameter shaft down to the cavern, which eventually becomes the air shaft. A cavern is then excavated using mining equipment and a second 8-foot diameter shaft is made using a raise bore process back to the surface to act as the water shaft. Why CAES is difficult to deploy The invention of the newer A-CAES process has been driven by the inherent difficulty of developing CAES. Yes, there are some in use, including some that have been around for a long time, but there are also many projects that have been cancelled and companies that have folded because it has been too difficult. For example, Corre Energy developed CAES and has already been liquidated and Bedrock Energy has recently had its 382MW/3,056MWh CAES project in Huron County, Ontario, Canada rejected because it was planned to cover over 100 acres of ‘productive farmland’. There are various technical, economic, and social challenges facing companies looking to deploy CAES. One of the main challenges is a low round-trip efficiency (RTE), as the RTE is often as low as 40% because the majority of the heat produced during air compression is lost. This could make CAES a lot less favourable for grid operators, especially when they have a much lower RTE than BESS. There’s also the challenge of integrating and synchronising CAES technology with the power grid, as the power grid requires assets to be synchronised at specific grid frequency and voltage levels—and it requires a lot of extra ancillary equipment, such as grid-tied inverters, sensors, and smart controllers to connect CAES to the grid. CAES also has slow ramp rates which makes it unsuitable for some energy deployment scenarios that require quicker and more responsive deployment of energy. The last major technical hurdle is that CAES require specific geological structures, such as salt domes, depleted aquifers, and hard rock caverns. These formations are not available everywhere, which limits where the energy storage systems can be sited. A-CAES

artigo.texto: RWE has taken a final investment decision (FID) on 400MW/1.1GWh BESS in the Netherlands with construction to start in due course, while Giga Storage has started building its 2.8GWh Green Turtle project in Belgium. Both are set to be commissioned in early 2028. RWE to build congestion-relieving BESS in Netherlands Power firm RWE has taken FID on the 2.75-hour battery energy storage system (BESS) to be built at the Moerdijk power station site, it said yesterday (21 September). Commissioning is planned for the second quarter of 2028, and it will contribute to the system integration of the 795MW OranjeWind offshore project, which is a joint venture between RWE and TotalEnergies. The BESS will comprise 208 lithium-ion containers (a little over 5MWh each) Mark Lentjes, regional director of grid operator TenneT Southern Netherland said the BESS would act as a congestion reliever. It will do this via ‘steering agreements’ with TenneT, whereby it will be dispatched to relieve congestion in the Noord-Brabant region. That means that space can be created on the grid for parties on the waiting list. Other projects have been given ‘time-dependent transport rights’ (TDTR), similar to a flexible connection agreement (FCA) in Germany The Moerdijk benefits from a location close to the 150,000V high-voltage substation at Moerdijk-Noord, where it will help to alleviate the regional bottleneck, which in turn has an impact on congestion across the whole region, Lentjes said. The project can also provide advanced grid services such as instantaneous reserve (inertia). RWE is highly active in BESS in the Netherlands, its home country of Germany as well as the US and Australia, see all coverage of it here. Giga Storage starts building Belgium’s largest BESS project BESS owner-operator Giga Storage has launched construction on its Green Turtle project, a 700MW/2,800MWh system, one of the largest in Europe. Announced last week (17 September), the start of construction comes a few months after financing was secured and a letter of intent (LOI) was agreed with Tesla to supply the project. Tesla will provide 640 of its lithium iron phosphate-based (LFP) Megapack 3 BESS units under a full EPC wrap contract, while civil works are being carried out by Stadbader Contractors. We did a deep-dive on the Megapack 3 product in a recent ESN Premium article. Commissioning is scheduled for March 2028. Preparatory earthworks and roadworks commenced in mid-August and now the batteries, cabling, and high-voltage installations will begin. Like RWE’s Dutch project, Green Turtle benefits from close proximity to a high-voltage line, the 380kV Van Eyck-Gramme line. Grid operator Elia is building a new high-voltage substation at the site to accommodate the project. Giga Storage, owned by investor InfraVia since 2024, is based in the Netherlands and also is active there, recently launching construction on a 1.2GWh BESS there last year, and it is also building a 1.4GWh one in Germany.

artigo.texto: Hiring for long-term manufacturing roles starting at $23 per hour RACINE, Wis., Sept. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Modine (NYSE: MOD), a diversified global leader in thermal management technology and solutions, today announced ongoing hiring efforts in southeastern Wisconsin to fill up to 300 positions to support its rapidly growing data center cooling business. The state-of-the-art manufacturing facility at 3303 W. Oakwood Road, Franklin, WI, will host a walk-in hiring fair on Thursday, September 24, to fill these positions across both first and second shifts. The hiring expansion comes amid growing demand for energy-efficient cooling solutions that support the rapidly expanding U.S. data center market. In September 2025, Modine opened a new 153,000-square-foot plant in Franklin, dedicated to manufacturing Airedale™ data center cooling systems. The additional workforce will help ramp up production to meet increasing demand for cooling solutions that optimize data center performance and sustainability. "In 2025, our expansion into Franklin was fueled by customer interest in the advanced thermal management solutions our team builds to cool data centers in the U.S.," said Karen Sutherland, Vice President of Human Resources for Data Centers, Americas at Modine. "We're now at a point where we need a larger, committed workforce that wants to help serve the growing needs of our customers. We provide on-the-job training, with no prior manufacturing experience required for most entry-level positions." The Franklin expansion is part of a broader investment announced by Modine in July 2025 to increase U.S. manufacturing capacity for Airedale data center cooling products across facilities in Franklin, WI; Grand Prairie, TX; Grenada, MS; and Jefferson City, MO. Franklin Facility Hiring Fair Open on September 24 Modine will host a hiring fair Thursday, Sept. 24, from 4–7 p.m. at its Franklin facility, 3303 W. Oakwood Road. The company will have HR professionals and leaders onsite to discuss open positions and conduct on-the-spot interviews. Candidates are encouraged to register in advance using this form: Airedale - Walk-In Interview Event – Form, and walk-ins are welcome. Modine has first and second shift openings, with production assembler positions starting at $23 and an additional $1-per-hour premium for second shift. New employees are eligible to receive health insurance and other benefits beginning on their first day. Modine will continue to hire in the coming months until open roles are filled and will also be promoting the openings through a billboard advertising campaign throughout the Milwaukee area. Below are links to assembler positions posted on Modine's website. Assembler - Assembler Job Details | Modine Manufacturing Company For more information, visit https://airedale.com/careers. About Modine For more than 100 years, Modine has solved the toughest thermal management challenges for mission-critical applications. Our purpose of Engineering a Cleaner, Healthier World™ means we are always evolving our portfolio of technologies to provide the latest heating, cooling, and ventilation solutions. Through the hard work of more than 11,000 employees worldwide, our Climate Solutions and Performance Technologies segments advance our purpose with systems that improve air quality, reduce energy and water consumption, lower harmful emissions, enable cleaner running vehicles, and use environmentally friendly refrigerants. Modine is a global company headquartered in Racine, Wisconsin (U.S.), with operations in North America, South America, Europe, and Asia. For more information about Modine, visit modine.com. Contact: Media Relations Ashley Conley [email protected] Investor Relations: Kathleen Powers [email protected] SOURCE Modine

artigo.texto: Greenvolt Power Starts 600MW/2.4GWh Siedlce BESS in Poland, as CEE Storage Construction Accelerates Greenvolt Power, an independent power producer, has broken ground on its Siedlce battery storage venture in Poland, one of a series of large-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) developments advancing to the construction phase across Central and Eastern Europe and the Baltics. The Siedlce facility is planned at 600MW/2.4GWh, with commercial operations targeted for the close of 2027. Once finished, it is set to rank as Poland's biggest BESS and among the largest such projects in Europe. P&Q, an engineering and construction company, and ONDE, a renewable energy contractor and developer, are handling construction. Siedlce follows Greenvolt Power's 200MW/800MWh Turosn Koscielna project, which began commercial operations in July, while the equally sized Nowa Wies Elcka project is due to come online in Q4 2026. The three projects, amounting to 1GW/4GWh in total, all carry capacity market contracts. Greenvolt secured the biggest portion of BESS awards in Poland's 2023 capacity market auction, some of which it has since divested. The capacity market, with its 17 years of contracted revenue, underpins the business case for large-scale BESS in Poland. BYD, an EV and BESS firm, supplies all three projects, with the Siedlce deal announced in June. In separate news reported a day earlier, Greenvolt began construction at a 918MWh BESS in Romania. Also in Poland, GS EU Fund SCSp, managed by investment manager Gore Street Capital, has purchased the 40MW/160MWh Wolborz BESS. The project holds a capacity market contract beginning in 2030 and is expected to start operations in Q1 2028. The seller was not named. Alicja Kowalewska-Montford, managing director at Gore Street, said the company's attention is now on constructing and delivering the Wolborz project, and that it is cultivating ties with local counterparties, including EPC and other contractors, as it expands its footprint in Poland. The Irish transaction between the two Gore Street funds provoked objections from certain shareholders, who recently sought a wind-down and asset sale of the GSF fund due to underperformance. The company narrowly defeated that proposal in a vote last week. DS1, an energy infrastructure firm, has entered an EPC agreement and started construction on a 140MW/327MWh BESS in Ayltus, Lithuania. The project is being built alongside BLEnergy, an Israel-headquartered energy services and construction company, at a new 330kV substation. The pair had previously collaborated on a 30MW/60MWh project in Lithuania supplied by CATL, though scant details were given about the Ayltus project. High ancillary service prices currently propel the Baltic region's energy storage market, while longer durations beyond one or two hours signal a move toward energy trading and other uses. Taaleri Energia, a Finland-headquartered clean energy IPP, has put money into a 192MW/420MWh BESS in Estonia via its SolarWind III Fund. The SolarWind III Fund, a co-investor in SolarWind III Fund, and KJK Fund III, a fund managed by KJK Capital, jointly own the project. Construction will begin in September 2026, and the BESS is expected to be fully operational by November 2027. Developer Evecon and French IPP Corsica Sole developed the project, and the two are also deploying projects to own and operate together in the region. Local contractor Smartecon will build it, with LG Energy Solution supplying the BESS and European-made inverters coming from Power Electronics. Taaleri has previously deployed projects in its home market of Finland. The flurry of activity precedes the Energy Storage Summit Central and Eastern Europe 2026, set for 6-7 October in Warsaw, Poland. - 1. artigo.texto: Lithium-ion battery fire keeps hundreds of homes under evacuation orders for second day - Click here to listen to this article - Share via See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred Approximately 200 homes remain under evacuation orders in La Verne on Wednesday as fire crews continued to work to stabilize lithium-ion batteries burning inside a Metropolitan Water District of Southern California facility, authorities said. The incident was first reported at 11:40 a.m. Tuesday following a “minor explosion” and ensuing fire in one of two battery storage systems located at the Wheeler Avenue facility, according to La Verne Fire Chief Brandon Coatney. Lithium-ion battery fires can emit toxic smoke harmful to humans. Thus far, air quality monitoring has not detected any hazardous battery components in the vapor coming off of the burning batteries, according to Ernie Hernandez of the L.A. County Fire Department’s hazardous materials team. However, as a precautionary measure, residents living in the immediate area surrounding the facility are asked to remain away until further notice. Grace Miller Elementary School remains closed Wednesday due to its proximity to the incident. The fire started at a battery energy storage system near a solar panel field on the northeast side of the facility, which houses Weymouth Water Treatment Plant, according to the water district. One civilian was injured at the outset of the incident and transported to a hospital for treatment, according to La Verne Fire Department Battalion Chief Mark Savage. Almost two years after a massive battery fire south of Santa Cruz displaced 1,200 people and smoldered for days, the same facility is burning again. “The safety of Metropolitan’s water supply is not affected,” according to a district statement. “We are supporting our first responders as they take the appropriate steps to help ensure the health and safety of residents, employees and others in the affected area.” Residents living near Wheeler and Bonita avenues were ordered to evacuate around 12:30 p.m. Tuesday, while shelter-in-place orders were issued at nearby schools, according to the La Verne Police Department. An evacuation shelter has opened at La Verne Community Center, 3680 D St. After assessing safety conditions around the hazardous blaze, crews were able to use water to start cooling the batteries, enabling them to significantly reduce the risk to the public posed by the fire. “Later in the day, we were able to get that first battery storage system to a relatively stable point, to where it was not putting off any hazardous plume and the heat signature had gone down quite a bit,” Coatney said at a Wednesday morning news conference. Most evacuation orders were downgraded to warnings shortly before 3 p.m. Tuesday, while orders in the immediate area surrounding the facility remain in place. A map of areas affected by evacuation orders and warnings can be found here. Lithium-ion battery fires are challenging to combat, as excessive heat inside the battery creates a self-sustaining chemical reaction called thermal runaway that can easily spread to adjacent batteries. On Tuesday evening, fire crews determined that an adjacent second battery storage system had also suffered some damage and the battery packs were entering thermal runaway, Coatney said. Once thermal runaway starts, the process cannot be stopped, and batteries will burn for hours. In the case of large, multiple-battery fires, they can burn for days while releasing toxic gases such as hydrogen fluoride, hydrogen chloride, carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide. “We immediately deployed our air monitors, checking for all battery components coming off that fluid, that smoke,” said Hernandez at Wednesday’s news conference. “I am happy to report we got non-detects.” Crews continued to use water to cool the second battery storage system Wednesday morning.

artigo.texto: Samsung SDI Major supplier to automotive & electronics According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Plastic Battery Containers market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global plastic battery containers market is a critical enabler of the energy transition, providing essential protection, thermal management, and structural integrity for battery cells and modules in electric vehicles (EVs) and stationary energy storage systems (ESS). As battery deployment accelerates worldwide, demand for plastic containers is bifurcating into high-volume, cost-optimized solutions for EV platforms and highly engineered, safety-focused solutions for ESS. The market is transitioning from passive enclosures to integrated functional subsystems, with suppliers increasingly responsible for thermal management, fire retardancy, and electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding. This evolution elevates qualification burdens and locks in strategic supplier partnerships. Between 2026 and 2035, the market is forecast to grow at a robust pace, supported by platform standardization, cell-to-pack designs, and regulatory mandates for battery safety and recyclability. Asia-Pacific remains the dominant production and consumption hub, but regionalization of battery supply chains is fostering growth in North America and Europe. Key challenges include raw material price volatility, competition from metal enclosures, and divergent global safety standards. This report provides a comprehensive analysis of market size, segmentation, competitive dynamics, and strategic imperatives for stakeholders across the value chain. The baseline scenario for the global plastic battery containers market anticipates sustained expansion from 2026 to 2035, underpinned by accelerating EV adoption and the rapid build-out of grid-scale battery storage. Demand will be driven by automotive OEMs scaling electric platforms and ESS integrators deploying containers for renewable energy integration and grid resilience. The market will increasingly favor large-format, modular designs that accommodate multiple cell chemistries and simplify assembly. Material innovation will focus on flame-retardant engineering plastics and composites that meet stringent safety standards such as UL 9540A and IEC 62619. Supply chains will regionalize to mitigate geopolitical and logistical risks, with local production gaining importance in North America and Europe. Pricing pressure will persist in the EV segment, while ESS applications command premiums for reliability and certification. Competitive advantage will hinge on early supplier involvement in platform design, in-house tooling, and advanced quality control. The market index is projected to reach 245 by 2035 (2025=100), reflecting a compound annual growth rate of 9.4%. This outlook assumes no major technological disruptions or extreme regulatory shifts, but acknowledges potential upside from faster-than-expected ESS deployment and downside from material substitution or economic slowdowns. The EV sector is the largest and fastest-growing end-use market for plastic battery containers, driven by the global shift to electric mobility. Plastic containers are essential for protecting battery cells and modules, providing thermal insulation, and reducing weight to extend driving range. As automakers transition to dedicated EV platforms and cell-to-pack designs, demand is increasing for large-format, modular containers that can accommodate various cell chemistries and simplify assembly. Key demand indicators include EV production volumes, battery pack energy density, and the adoption of 800V architectures requiring enhanced thermal management. Through 2035, the EV segment will continue to dominate, but growth rates will moderate as markets mature. Innovations in flame-retardant plastics and composite materials will be critical to meet safety standards and consumer expectations. The trend toward localizing battery production in North America and Europe will create new opportunities for regional container suppliers, while cost pressures will drive automation and material efficiency. Current trend: Growing. Major trends: Shift to cell-to-pack and cell-to-chassis designs reducing component count and driving larger, integrated containers, Increasing use of engineering plastics with high flame retardancy and thermal conductivity, Platform standardization by OEMs to reduce costs and accelerate model rollouts, Regionalization of EV supply chains with local battery gigafactories, and Growing demand for lightweight containers to improve vehicle range. Representative participants: SABIC, BASF, Covestro, Lanxess, and DuPont. Stationary energy storage systems (ESS) for grid support, renewable integration, and backup power represent the second-largest and most technically demanding end-use sector for plastic battery containers. Unlike EV applications, ESS containers must prioritize safety, longevity, and reliability over weight, often requiring enhanced fire resistance and thermal management to meet stringent standards like UL 9540A. artigo.texto: What restrictions could the Hillsboro City Council place on data centers in October? Published 5:30 am Wednesday, September 23, 2026 Months after Hillsboro staff approved a wave of data center tax break applications that sparked backlash and demands for changes to city code, city leaders could cement the city’s first permanent restrictions on where facilities may be built. While Hillsboro is under a temporary moratorium that blocks new data center proposals and development until Nov. 24, the Hillsboro City Council will consider the first phase of potential changes to the city’s development code during a public hearing Tuesday, Oct. 6. The amendments would narrow where standalone data centers are allowed, establish acreage caps, require public hearings for proposed facilities and prevent data centers from operating within 1,000 feet of schools. Recommended by the Hillsboro Planning Commission in September, the proposal would also establish new regulations for battery energy storage systems, which Hillsboro’s development code does not currently address as a specific land use. The changes would be the first step in a two-phase approach intended to put immediate protections in place while giving the city more time to study additional requirements, according to city staff. A second phase, planned for winter and spring 2027, would address building heights, buffers, green-building requirements and other environmental protections. Where data centers could be built Data centers are currently allowed in all of Hillsboro’s industrial zones, as well as the Commercial-General zone and three mixed-use zones. Under the proposed changes, standalone data centers would be allowed only as primary uses in the Industrial Park and Industrial Sanctuary zones, both of which are largely concentrated in North Hillsboro around the Hillsboro Airport and industrial areas along Northeast Evergreen Road and Brookwood Parkway. The amendments would cap standalone data center development at 215 total acres in the Industrial Park zone and 310 acres in the Industrial Sanctuary zone. According to the city, about 203 acres in the Industrial Park zone and 293 acres in the Industrial Sanctuary zone have already been approved for data center development. That would leave room for about 12 additional acres of standalone data centers in the Industrial Park zone and 17 acres in the Industrial Sanctuary zone. Separate limits would remain in place for the Jackson East area, where existing rules allow up to 62 acres of standalone data centers in the Jackson East-South area and 21 acres in the Jackson East-North area. Standalone data centers would remain prohibited in the Meek subarea, though accessory facilities could be allowed. Other restrictions on data centers Beyond limiting where facilities can be built, the proposed amendments would prohibit data centers within 1,000 feet of public or private schools serving primarily children under 18. The distance would be measured between property lines. The changes would also establish a formal definition of data centers, covering facilities that store, process or transmit digital information — including those used for artificial intelligence. Businesses with ordinary server rooms would not automatically be classified as data centers. Companies could still operate data centers to support their own operations, but they could not lease computing services to outside customers. Those accessory facilities would be limited to 25% of a property’s acreage or 30% of its floor area, whichever is less. New data centers would additionally face greater public scrutiny. Under the proposal, new facilities — including projects converting existing buildings or accessory operations into standalone data centers — would undergo a development review requiring a public hearing rather than approval through an administrative review by city staff. That decision could then be appealed to the city council. The amendments would establish separate rules for battery energy storage systems, which store electricity for later use. Facilities built primarily for energy storage would be limited to 12 acres per site and require conditional use approval in designated industrial zones. Battery systems installed to support another operation, such as a data center, would generally be limited to 30% of the property’s acreage. A long-awaited change Pressure for changes to Hillsboro’s development code has been mounting for months, following news that the city received 17 enterprise zone tax exemption applications from eight entities ahead of a statewide moratorium on new data center incentives. Fifteen of those applications were ultimately approved, according to the city’s updated figures, spanning seven companies and nine sites. But the approvals have also landed Hillsboro and Washington County in court. A lawsuit filed in June by a coalition that includes land use advocates and Hillsboro City Councilor Kipperlyn Sinclair seeks to overturn the tax breaks, alleging officials exceeded their authority and failed to follow required public notice procedures. The Hillsboro City Council has since moved to restrict both tax incentives and development. On July 21, councilors approved a 180-day pause on new Strategic Investment Program applications for standalone data centers, while requiring applications involving accessory data centers to go before the council for a public hearing. Less than a week later, councilors unanimously adopted a 120-day moratorium on new or expanded data centers and battery energy storage facilities proposed as primary uses. The temporary ban took effect July 27 and is scheduled to expire Nov. 24 unless extended. But several proposed data centers had already entered the city’s development pipeline before the moratorium took effect. artigo.texto: Com a criação do primeiro leilão de reserva de capacidade focado em baterias no Brasil, a TTS Energia prepara estratégias para oferecer serviços de engenharia e construção. A empresa quer se tornar parceira dos projetos vencedores, utilizando sua experiência em usinas solares e sistemas de armazenamento para garantir que as novas instalações funcionem com segurança e eficiência. Setembro de 2026 A TTS Energia, empresa especializada em construir usinas solares e outros ativos de energia renovável, está expandindo suas atividades no setor de armazenamento de energia. A empresa vê uma grande oportunidade no primeiro Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade focado em tecnologia de baterias (LRCAP-BESS) no Brasil. Com experiência em projetos que unem armazenamento, geração solar e controle de energia, a TTS se prepara para atuar em um mercado que cresceu muito, com mais de 6 mil projetos cadastrados, somando quase 300 gigawatts (GW) de potência. Essa movimentação reforça o objetivo da TTS de ser parceira tecnológica e de engenharia para as empresas que participarão do leilão. A companhia se prepara para firmar acordos com investidores, desenvolvedores e outros participantes para ajudar nos estudos de viabilidade, na engenharia, na integração, na implantação e na operação dos empreendimentos que avançarem no LRCAP-BESS. - Mais de 6 mil projetos de baterias foram cadastrados para o leilão LRCAP-BESS. - Os projetos somam quase 300 gigawatts (GW) de capacidade instalada. - A TTS já instalou um sistema de baterias na sede da CorSolar, em São Paulo. - Um microrrede off-grid foi criada com usina solar, gerador e baterias no agronegócio. - Desde 2019, a empresa já realizou mais de 620 empreendimentos no país. A expectativa é que o mercado de armazenamento evolua rapidamente nos próximos anos. Os empreendedores precisarão de parceiros com experiência em integração de sistemas, engenharia elétrica, implantação e operação de ativos de energia. É exatamente esse papel que queremos desempenhar, afirma Jacques Hulshof, CEO da TTS Energia. Experiência prática em armazenamento A empresa já possui experiência prática com diferentes configurações de armazenamento. Em junho deste ano, a TTS implantou um sistema BESS no centro de distribuição da CorSolar, em São Paulo. O projeto contemplou desde o desenvolvimento do projeto executivo até a implantação completa, incluindo engenharia e construção, e foi executado em um mês. A solução foi dimensionada para operar com load shifting, armazenando energia em períodos de menor custo para utilização nos horários de maior tarifa. A companhia também participou do desenvolvimento e implementação de uma microrrede off-grid em uma propriedade de agronegócio, formada por uma usina fotovoltaica de 3 MWp, um grupo gerador de 2,6 MVA e um sistema BESS de 630 kVA e 1,26 MWh. O projeto utiliza um sistema de gerenciamento de energia (EMS) para coordenar geração, armazenamento e consumo, garantindo maior autonomia e confiabilidade operacional. A experiência acumulada em projetos de energia é uma das bases para a nossa estratégia no novo mercado. Atuamos desde 2019 no desenvolvimento, implantação e operação de projetos, com mais de 620 empreendimentos realizados e mais de 360 MWp em operação, informa Hulshof. Engenharia e integração serão decisivas Na avaliação do CEO da TTS Energia, o grande volume de projetos cadastrados para o LRCAP-BESS demonstra o potencial do mercado, mas existe uma distância significativa entre registrar um empreendimento e colocá-lo efetivamente em operação. A próxima etapa deverá selecionar projetos com maior maturidade técnica, viabilidade de conexão, estrutura financeira, fornecedores e capacidade de execução, comenta. A competitividade de um projeto BESS, portanto, não será determinada apenas pelo preço das baterias. Localização e disponibilidade de conexão, CAPEX, eficiência global do sistema, degradação das baterias, disponibilidade, garantias, estratégia de reposição de módulos, custos de operação e manutenção e confiabilidade dos fornecedores estarão entre os fatores relevantes, acrescenta. Segundo o executivo, também haverá uma exigência elevada de integração entre diferentes equipamentos e sistemas. Baterias, PCS, EMS, transformadores, sistemas auxiliares, proteção, automação, comunicação e SCADA precisam funcionar de forma coordenada e atender aos requisitos de conexão e operação do sistema elétrico. Um projeto BESS precisa ser analisado como uma solução completa. A bateria é apenas um dos componentes de uma planta que envolve conversão de energia, gerenciamento, proteção, comunicação, transformação e conexão. É nessa integração que a engenharia passa a ter um papel decisivo para garantir desempenho, segurança e confiabilidade ao longo da vida útil do empreendimento, explica Hulshof. A TTS Energia pretende, assim, aproveitar a abertura desse novo ciclo para ampliar sua atuação em armazenamento, combinando a experiência acumulada em engenharia, construção e operação de ativos de energia com novas competências e parcerias tecnológicas. A estratégia vai além de participar apenas das oportunidades associadas ao LRCAP-BESS. A proposta é atuar de forma consistente na expansão de um mercado em que as baterias devem ganhar espaço na gestão da energia, na segurança operacional e na integração das fontes renováveis, conclui.

artigo.texto: O MPF reafirma seu papel na proteção de comunidades tradicionais no mercado de carbono. O procurador Felipe Moura Palha destacou essa missão em seminário realizado pelo CNMP. A atuação do MPF é fundamentada pela Lei nº 15.042/2024, relacionada ao comércio de emissões de gases. O MPF realiza consultas prévias obrigatórias para proteger direitos humanos e culturais. Limitar a atuação do MPF para interesses econômicos é considerado inconstitucional. Desde 2007, o MPF fornece diretrizes em um manual para seus membros. Destacam-se a proteção de comunidades e a necessidade de consultas prévias justas. O seminário foi realizado em parceria com a Abrampa, discutindo a nova legislação ambiental. O Ministério Público Federal (MPF) reafirmou sua atuação essencial na proteção dos direitos de comunidades tradicionais no contexto do mercado de carbono. Em 17 de outubro, em Brasília, o procurador Felipe Moura Palha destacou a missão do MPF em preservar a vida e a autonomia desses povos durante um seminário no Conselho Nacional do Ministério Público (CNMP). Palha, representante das Câmaras de Populações Indígenas e Comunidades Tradicionais (6CCR) e de Meio Ambiente e Patrimônio Cultural (4CCR), afirmou que a participação do MPF é mandatária pela Lei nº 15.042/2024, que criou o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa. Ele sustentou que o MPF é vital em consultas prévias obrigatórias para projetos nos territórios tradicionais, sempre visando resguardar direitos humanos e culturais. Segundo o procurador, qualquer tentativa de limitar a atuação do MPF para favorecer interesses econômicos seria inconstitucional. Com quase duas décadas de experiência, desde 2007, o MPF lançou um manual abrangente que traz diretrizes para fortalecer essa proteção. Este documento é um guia para membros do MPF em todo o país. Palha chamou a atenção para a necessidade de consultas prévias justas, direito de recusa das comunidades, proteção absoluta a povos isolados e eficácia climática real. Ele defendeu um diálogo transparente para evitar conflitos, mas reconheceu a necessidade de ações judiciais quando necessário. O seminário, realizado em parceria com a Associação Brasileira dos Membros do Ministério Público de Meio Ambiente (Abrampa), discutiu os impactos e a regulamentação da nova legislação ambiental.

artigo.texto: The Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (MERC) has proposed a revised regulatory framework aimed at accelerating the integration of renewable energy and energy storage systems across Maharashtra. the draft signals a shift towards treating storage as an independent and increasingly important component of the state’s power system. The draft Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (MERC) (Battery Energy Storage System) Regulations, 2026 cover the planning, procurement, development, ownership, operation, scheduling, dispatch, metering and commercial settlement of BESS across the state. The framework applies to generators, transmission and distribution utilities, standalone BESS developers, open-access consumers, captive projects and renewable energy developers. One of the most significant proposals is the recognition of standalone BESS as a distinct asset class. Such projects would be permitted to participate in applications ranging from energy arbitrage and energy banking to ancillary services, demand management, renewable energy optimisation and electricity market participation. The draft also establishes clearer entry thresholds. Standalone BESS would require a minimum capacity of 5 MW for inter-state transmission connectivity and 1 MW for distribution connectivity, with a minimum duration of two hours. Aggregation of smaller systems could be enabled through a designated “Lead ESS”. Importantly, the proposed framework could improve the economics of storage. Electricity drawn for intermediate storage would be exempt from certain transmission, distribution demand, wheeling and surcharge-related charges, provided the stored electricity is subsequently consumed within Maharashtra. At the same time, BESS operators would face significantly greater grid discipline, including separate injection and drawal metering, scheduling, energy accounting, deviation settlement, telemetry, cybersecurity and safety requirements. Overall, the draft marks an important move towards creating a structured market for storage, positioning BESS not merely as an adjunct to renewable generation, but as a dispatchable grid asset capable of providing multiple power-system services. The proposed framework has been released for public consultation as the state looks to manage rising electricity demand alongside increasing solar and wind generation. The commission said demand is also growing from major cities and data centres, which require reliable round-the-clock renewable power. Boost For RE Sources Maharashtra is targeting 50% of its electricity demand from renewable sources by 2030 under initiatives including Mukhyamantri Saur Krishiwahini Yojana 2.0. Renewable generation in the state has increased by 25% over the past year, with solar generation growing 36% and wind generation by 12%, according to the press release. The Maharashtra Renewable Energy and Energy Storage Policy 2035-36 further targets 65% of electricity demand from renewable sources by 2036. It also envisages meeting at least 10% of demand through energy storage technologies such as battery energy storage systems and pumped hydro, requiring 100 GW of renewable capacity and 100 GWh of storage. Long Term Pathway The framework also proposes a long-term pathway for Renewable Purchase Obligation and Energy Storage Obligation, along with related amendments to the State Grid Code. MERC said the proposed changes are expected to facilitate additional solar, wind and storage capacity while strengthening grid reliability and promoting a fair allocation of network and system service costs. The framework also seeks to protect existing contracts under the prevailing regulatory regime, while giving eligible consumers and project developers the option to migrate to the proposed framework. MERC has invited comments and suggestions from consumers, industry stakeholders, renewable energy developers, utilities, experts and members of the public. Stakeholders have 21 days to submit their views, with the deadline set for October 12, 2026. Counter-submissions can be made until October 15.

artigo.texto: CLARKSVILLE, TN (CLARKSVILLE NOW) – A public hearing will play a part in the submission process for any future data centers proposed in Montgomery County under a new set of requirements being studied by the Regional Planning Commission. The RPC shared the additional information Tuesday as they discussed the update to zoning regulations that aims to make sure any future data centers have restrictions on water use, electricity use and noise. No data centers are currently proposed in Montgomery County. Google has operated a large data center here since 2019. Checklist for data center proposals RPC Director Jeff Tyndall previously told Clarksville Now the Montgomery County Building and Codes Department proposed the update to the RPC because data centers are not currently addressed in county or city zoning. “If this is well received, we can probably do something similar for the city,” Tyndall said at Tuesday’s RPC meeting. “We’ve added a definition for data centers; it’ll be permitted on review use in M-1 or M-2 (zoning classifications). Then the review will have seven checklists if you will.” He said that list includes the site must be on a minimum of 10 acres, but not greater than 100 acres; setbacks for all zones, with the exception of M-1 or M-2, is 100 feet; a noise plan must be submitted showing the location extent of noise that would leave the property boundary; plus, a letter or study must be shown in regard to the water supply. “If it’s getting water from a municipal source, we’d want a letter from the municipal source stating that they can or cannot service it,” Tyndall said. “If they are going to draw it from a surface water source, then we would want a study showing that the surface water can accommodate that.” He also said feedback will likely be needed from TDEC or the EPA. Tyndall said for in regard to electricity and the natural gas supply, the RPC also wants data centers to submit written statements from the TVA and local utility providers. Data centers responsible for infrastructure improvements Tyndall said the owner/operator of any proposed or expanded data center project will be responsible for the cost of all infrastructure improvements necessary to provide utility services to the facility, which is in accordance with state law. “It goes on to say that the utilities cannot then pass along those costs to the ratepayers,” he said. “I’m glad the state did that this past year. That’s a fairly new law that they put in to protect everybody.” | MORE: Proposed zoning update would restrict future data centers on water, electric, noise Proposed data centers would require public hearing Tyndall said any future proposed data center projects would have to go before the Board of Zoning Appeals before making their way to the Planning Commission since it is permitted on review. “The BZA would have to make sure they are meeting all seven of those items, as well as holding their own public hearing for the use before it comes to the Planning Commission,” he said. During public comments on Tuesday, no one spoke in favor or against the zoning update, which was approved with one commissioner voting against. The zoning update will now go before the Montgomery County Commission. RPC’s informal meeting: discussion over constant noise At the RPC’s informal meeting on Friday, Tyndall told commissioners he met with the Land Regulation Advisory Committee last week on the subject of data centers. “We originally came in with about a 500-foot setback from the data centers. They said, if you have a 500-foot-long by 500-foot-deep setback, you’re wasting 10 acres just to have a setback,” Tyndall said on Friday. “The biggest complaint about data centers is the constant noise 24 hours a day. So, instead of a setback, we would require when they go to the Board of Zoning Appeals. … They have to have a noise plan showing that they do not exceed more than 3 decibels over the ambient noise of the area or 55 decibels at the adjoining property lines.” Tyndall said that applies to properties that are not M-1 or M-2. “Industry against industry, you could be noisy, obviously,” he said. Appropriate grading, landscaping and site layout can also help reduce noise, Tyndall said. “Any future data centers could build berms; they could put the compressors behind the building, or they could put them under a roof. There are things you can do to cut down on noise,” he said. Zoning update to deter ‘hyper-scale’ centers Tyndall said the requirement that any data center site be a minimum of 10 acres, but not greater than 100 acres, should deter any “hyper-scale” center from developing in Montgomery County. “Honestly, after Google’s done building and Google has their last building in front of you, they don’t plan on doing any more, and this community can’t support any more.” Patricia Galarza-Grillasca contributed to this report. | NEWS TIPS: Do you have a local news tip? artigo.texto: European Commission Proposes Energy Efficiency Rating for Data Centers The European Commission has put forward a proposal for a European Union rating scheme to help ensure energy efficiency and minimize resource wastage and emissions at data centers. Concurrently it launched a public consultation on minimum energy efficiency standards for data centers across the 27-member bloc. "In addition to using more energy, an increase of data centers could put extra pressure on electricity grids and the use of natural resources, such as water, and contribute to increase carbon emissions", the Commission said in an online statement. "To limit these impacts, it is essential that data centers are highly energy- and water-efficient and sustainably integrated in the energy system". Covering data centers that exceed 500 kilowatts of capacity, the rating scheme would measure the actual use of energy and water resources. "It will also cover data centers' contribution to the grid such as the reuse of waste heat, the addition of clean energy generation capacities as well as flexibility", the Commission said. "A striking example: reusing around half of all waste heat from European data centers is the equivalent of the total heating demand of four million households in Europe. "Sustainable, flexible and well-designed data centers that can adjust their electricity use to the grids conditions can help lower the overall cost of the electricity system, improve grid stability and integrate more renewable energy". Ratings would be issued by means of electronic labels. Labels would be issued to data centers starting August 2027, valid for one year, according to the delegated regulation published by the Commission. The rating scheme builds on Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364, which already implemented a reporting scheme for data center operators. "The thresholds for each indicator have been set based on analysis of the data submitted by data center operators during the first reporting period and assessment of existing legislation, initiatives, benchmarks and standards", the new proposal document says. "The selected indicators and thresholds will be reviewed and may be revised in the future to accommodate technological progress, improve the effectiveness of the scheme and strive for higher sustainability standards", the proposal says. "This regulation is part of an ongoing effort of simplification and harmonization across EU policies. By leveraging already reported data, it makes sure that no additional burden is put on member states and data center operators", it says. "The rating scheme is intended to harmonize approaches across EU member states and will be used to assess the sustainability of data centers in other EU legislation, including in the Cloud and AI Development Act. It has also been considered in the review of the Climate and Environmental Delegated Acts under the Taxonomy Regulation", it says. Crafted after public consultation, the new delegated regulation is now subject to a two-month scrutiny period by the European Parliament and the European Council before taking effect. Additionally the Commission said it is "following up to the declaration of intent signed in June 2026, working with data center operators, grid operators, energy providers and public authorities towards a tripartite agreement on data centers in the second half of the year". The consultation on minimum energy standards for data centers ends December. "Tripling our data center capacity cannot mean tripling the pressure on our grids, our water and our energy bills. That starts with transparency, rating large data centers depending on their impact on our energy system", said Teresa Ribera, Commission executive vice president for a clean, just and competitive transition. "Efficient, flexible, powered by additional clean energy and reusing waste heat, this is how data centers become an asset for EU's energy transition". On June 3 the Commission proposed the Cloud and AI Development Act, which aims to triple the EU's "data center capacity" over the next five to seven years. artigo.texto: Energy Vault Holdings has acquired a portfolio of U.S. battery energy storage projects from Goshe Energy Storage, adding more than 2.3 gigawatts of development capacity across 15 projects to its Asset Vault platform. The transaction includes 350 megawatts of ready-to-build projects that are expected to generate approximately $30 million in combined annual run-rate EBITDA once operational. Energy Vault has also secured a credit facility commitment of up to $40 million from S2G Investments to support the portfolio’s development, construction, and operations. The acquisition expands Energy Vault’s strategy of developing, financing, owning, and operating energy storage infrastructure capable of generating recurring revenue over the long term. The acquired portfolio includes two ready-to-build projects with capacities of 150 megawatts and 200 megawatts, respectively. Both projects are expected to reach commercial operations in the first quarter of 2028. Once operational, Energy Vault expects them to contribute approximately $30 million in combined annual run-rate EBITDA. The remaining projects provide additional development opportunities as Energy Vault expands its owned infrastructure portfolio across the United States. The acquisition also brings an experienced development team from Goshe Energy Storage into Energy Vault. The incoming professionals have more than 75 years of combined experience in renewable energy development, battery energy storage project management, and financial services. Goshe, headquartered in Boulder, Colorado, has focused on acquiring and advancing late-stage battery storage projects through financing, construction, and commercial operation. Its development activities include projects in ERCOT, the Texas electricity market, where battery storage has become an increasingly important component of the power system. The integration of Goshe’s personnel and projects is intended to strengthen Energy Vault’s ability to identify development opportunities, complete construction, and operate large-scale battery storage assets. The up to $40 million credit facility from S2G Investments represents a continuation of S2G’s existing strategic relationship with Goshe. The financing will support the acquired portfolio as Energy Vault moves projects through development and construction toward commercial operations. Financial terms of the portfolio acquisition were not disclosed. Energy Vault’s Asset Vault platform focuses on the ownership and operation of energy storage and AI infrastructure rather than relying exclusively on revenue from developing and selling technology. The company combines project development with engineering, procurement, construction, and ongoing services to generate revenue throughout an infrastructure asset’s lifecycle. Following the Goshe acquisition, Energy Vault now expects its Asset Vault platform to generate more than $200 million in annualized EBITDA based on its projected exit run rate at the end of 2028. That projection applies to the broader Asset Vault platform, rather than solely to the newly acquired projects, and remains dependent on development, financing, construction, and operational milestones. Energy Vault’s existing global portfolio of owned assets includes more than 1.75 gigawatts of energy and AI digital infrastructure in operation or under construction. The company is also expanding into modular data center infrastructure, including powered-land and powered-shell developments intended to support growing electricity demand from AI and high-performance computing facilities. The acquisition of Goshe’s portfolio increases Energy Vault’s U.S. battery storage development pipeline while adding projects that could contribute recurring earnings as they enter service. KEY QUOTES: “This portfolio fits squarely within Energy Vault’s strategy of acquiring late-stage, de-risked development projects that can be moved efficiently toward construction and operation. The team has a track record of originating and advancing high-quality BESS projects, and we’re glad to have them join us as we continue to scale our owned-asset portfolio across U.S. markets.” Cory Magnuson, President of Asset Vault “Joining Energy Vault allows our team to continue the work we started – developing and delivering the storage projects the grid needs – with the backing of a large, vertically integrated and global platform. We’re pleased that S2G will continue as a financing partner through this transition, and we look forward to seeing this portfolio through to construction and operation as part of Energy Vault’s platform.” Bailey McCallum, CEO of Goshe Energy Storage “Goshe’s team has built a high-quality, late-stage development portfolio across some of the fastest-growing battery storage markets around the globe. This acquisition adds meaningful scale to our Energy Vault pipeline and brings in a group of experienced developers who know how to advance projects efficiently and effectively. It reinforces our strategy of building a long-term, owned-asset platform that generates predictable, recurring value for our shareholders.” Robert Piconi, Chairman and CEO of Energy Vault

artigo.texto: Governor Wes Moore signed an executive order establishing a new State review process for large data center projects, with local approvals, ratepayer protections, infrastructure impacts, and community engagement built into the framework. The order applies to data centers that require at least 25 megawatts of power at peak, including expansions that add 25 megawatts, as well as projects that qualify as large load customers under State law. It takes effect when a covered project seeks a State permit, incentive, letter of support, or other discretionary State action. The order creates the Maryland Data Center Accountability Task Force within the Governor’s Office. It directs the group to review projects against five principles: ratepayer and grid protection, economic benefits for Marylanders, community voice, environmental protections, and transparency and accountability. For counties, the framework preserves an important distinction between State support and local land-use authority. A project denied a required local approval cannot receive an “Aligned” or “Conditionally Aligned” determination, while projects that do not meet the framework must secure local land-use approvals and demonstrate consistency with the local plan before State review moves forward. That structure reflects several priorities counties have raised throughout the data center debate: preserving local land-use authority, protecting ratepayers and taxpayers, and keeping host jurisdictions at the center of decisions that affect local infrastructure and communities. The Task Force must notify the host jurisdiction during its initial review and consider local and public comments before issuing one of three determinations: Aligned, Conditionally Aligned, or Not Aligned. Developers can also enter into a public Statement of Commitments outlining specific obligations and deadlines. Projects that receive an Aligned or Conditionally Aligned determination can access a coordinated State review pathway and remain eligible for State incentives and other support. Projects that do not meet the framework lose access to that coordinated process, State incentives, agency assistance, and letters of support. However, the order does not create a new legal barrier to permits otherwise available under State law. The framework also requires developers to address how they will supply new power without increasing costs for other customers and pay for necessary grid upgrades. The review will also consider jobs and wages, local hiring, water use, air emissions, stormwater impacts, community benefits agreements, and whether a project fits local zoning and planning. The order creates a public Data Center Dashboard showing each project’s location, owner, power and water use, State requests, Task Force determination, commitments, and annual reports. State agencies also may not sign, renew, or extend nondisclosure agreements with data center developers. The Maryland Department of Planning will also develop guidance for counties and municipalities, including model zoning, suggested community investment levels per megawatt, and model agreement terms. The order directs the Department to develop that guidance with MACo, MML, labor, community groups, and the Office of People’s Counsel. Governor Moore also announced plans to work with the General Assembly during the 2027 legislative session to repeal the State sales and use tax exemption for qualifying data center equipment. The order builds on the governor’s earlier data center framework, which called for projects seeking State support to cover their own power costs, hire local workers, and engage local governments and communities. Stay tuned to Conduit Street for more information.

artigo.texto: Pindamonhangaba recebe neste sábado (26) um seminário regional para discutir a implantação de um data center de grande porte no município e os possíveis impactos do empreendimento sobre os recursos naturais e a população do Vale do Paraíba. O encontro, intitulado “A nuvem tem endereço – Data centers e a defesa das águas e da vida no Vale do Paraíba”, será realizado das 14h às 18h, na sede do Sindicato dos Metalúrgicos, no Centro. A participação é gratuita, mas exige inscrição prévia pelo site anuvemtemendereco.com. O debate é organizado pela Rede Agroflorestal do Vale do Paraíba após o anúncio da implantação do projeto RiverHook Village, que prevê um data center de hiperescala em uma área com mais de 500 mil metros quadrados em Pindamonhangaba. A programação reunirá lideranças, pesquisadores e ativistas ambientais do Vale do Paraíba e de outros estados. Participam representantes de localidades como Caucaia (CE), Uberlândia (MG) e Eldorado do Sul (RS). Entre os temas previstos estão o consumo e a disponibilidade de água, possíveis impactos sobre o abastecimento, demanda de energia elétrica, eventuais quedas de energia nas proximidades, poluição sonora, geração de empregos e a legislação relacionada à instalação de grandes data centers. Segundo a Rede Agroflorestal, o município já enfrenta dificuldades relacionadas ao abastecimento de água e ainda não teria sido apresentado publicamente um estudo sobre os possíveis impactos do empreendimento para a população. O seminário também terá participação de entidades e coletivos ligados às áreas ambiental e de defesa do consumidor. A atividade conta com apoio da Semana Sustentável, iniciativa do Instituto de Defesa de Consumidores, além do Sindicato dos Metalúrgicos, do coletivo Mulheres pelo Clima – Vale do Paraíba e do coletivo Subverta. artigo.texto: Startup EnerVenue Wins First Major Battery Storage Deal in China (Bloomberg) -- Battery-storage startup EnerVenue Holdings has signed its first major commercial contract with a Chinese oil and gas producer, marking a key step in scaling its nickel-hydrogen technology. The US company will install 11 megawatt-hours of storage capacity at an oil field in northern China, Chief Executive Officer Henning Rath said in an interview with Bloomberg Television. He declined to disclose the customer’s identify and value of the contract. EnerVenue’s batteries use nickel-hydrogen cells with a water-based electrolyte and are designed for 30,000 charge cycles. The technology is similar to the aqueous metal cells that powered the Hubble Space Telescope and the International Space Station for decades. EnerVenue has redesigned the battery with low-cost materials for wider use. China’s energy-storage demand has surged in recent years as a rapid deployment of renewables increased the need for grid flexibility. The country is expected to add 223 gigawatt-hours of storage this year, 21% more than in 2025, according to BloombergNEF. The cells will be produced in the company’s new factory in Changzhou, eastern China, with an initial capacity of 250 megawatt-hours. The plant will start operations on Sept. 24 and its capacity will be increased to 1 gigawatt-hour in 2027, Rath said. EnerVenue is pursuing more deals, including in the Middle East and Canada. “We see right now really huge demand, especially in countries in the Middle East where we have very high temperatures,” Rath said, adding that the technology has no fire risk and can withstand high temperatures, making it suitable for mines and oil fields. Founded in 2020 by Stanford professor Yi Cui, Fremont, California-based EnerVenue has raised more than $700 million so far, part of which has funded the Changzhou factory. ©2026 Bloomberg L.P.

artigo.texto: Power Quality: The Conversation Data Centers Can't Afford to Ignore Uptime and cooling performance both depend on something that is often overlooked during the data system design process: power quality. In this podcast, "Power Quality: The Conversation Data Centers Can't Afford to Ignore," we talk with a Power Quality expert about harmonic distortion in data centers — what it is, how it is created, and how poor power quality impacts data center cooling, uptime and performance. We will also dig into solutions engineers can employ to mitigate poor power quality in their data center. Power quality deserves a seat at the table alongside the metrics data center operators already obsess over — availability, PUE, and thermal performance. Total Harmonic Distortion, or THD, gives engineers a real, measurable way to gauge the health of their electrical system, turning power quality from an abstract concern into something concrete that can be monitored, benchmarked, and acted on. This discussion will focus on where harmonics actually come from — and it's something of a paradox. Many of the same components installed specifically to make data centers more efficient, such as variable frequency drives and EC fans, are also responsible for generating the harmonic distortion that undermines power quality. Understanding which specific equipment, in which specific areas of a facility, pose the greatest risk to power quality, gives engineers a practical way to identify where problems are most likely to originate. Once data center engineers understand the source of harmonics, we’ll dig into the interdependency between power quality and thermal cooling in data centers. Clean, stable power is required to cool a facility properly, and proper cooling is required to run a data center efficiently — the two don't operate independently, one relies on the other. When harmonics go unmanaged excess heat accelerates equipment wear, protective devices trip unexpectedly, cooling systems degrade, and thermal throttling sets in. Left unaddressed, the result is unplanned downtime — the very outcome every data center is designed to avoid. The physical layout of a facility matters too. "Grey space" and "white space" — the mechanical/support areas and the core IT data hall, respectively — each present different harmonic challenges and require different mitigation approaches. There isn't one single location in a data center where power quality can be fixed once and for all; effective mitigation means evaluating the facility as a whole, rather than searching for a single point of resolution. Finally we’ll explore solutions available for engineers to help mitigate harmonics in data centers. One of the primary solutions we will focus on will be active harmonic filters. Active harmonic filters continuously monitor power quality of the system and make real-time corrections to mitigate harmonics. Where these filters are installed matters as much as the technology itself, and getting placement right has a direct impact on effectiveness. We’ll also discuss how engineers can take a hands-on approach to maintaining power quality by calculating their own harmonic distortion levels to determine how much filtering capacity they actually need — turning an otherwise theoretical challenge into something they can size, plan for, and solve. Ultimately, this podcast makes the case that power quality deserves the same level of design attention as uptime and cooling — because in reality, all three are connected. Whether you're a data center engineer, facility owner, or simply responsible for keeping systems running reliably, understanding harmonic distortion isn't a peripheral concern. It's foundational to how well a data center performs. Sponsored by:

artigo.texto: Pune-based Rechargion Energy has deployed its first 1 kWh locally made sodium-ion battery at CII’s Godrej Green Business Centre in Hyderabad. The company announced this during the Energy Efficiency Summit 2026. Rechargion Energy deploys its first 1 kWh locally made sodium-ion battery A rooftop solar installation at the Green Business Centre charges Rechargion’s 1 kWh sodium-ion battery, which then supplies power directly to an outdoor display. The setup acts as a standalone system, eliminating any need for conventional power transmission. It avoids a DC-to-AC conversion before electricity reaches the connected load. Rechargion claims that this configuration can reduce losses associated with transmission and power conversion. It also demonstrates how distributed renewable generation and storage can work together at the point of consumption. The Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) is Rechargion’s first customer for the commercially deployed 1 kWh battery. The Hyderabad facility serves as CII’s centre for green practices and businesses, working across areas including energy management, renewable energy, green buildings, and cleaner production. Established in 2004, the centre has become an important platform for demonstrating green technologies and sustainable business practices. Also read: Bengaluru-based Vishwatronix develops Pinaka, a 5 kg remote weapon station for quadruped robots About Rechargion Rechargion was founded in 2021, emerging from the research ecosystem of CSIR–National Chemical Laboratory (NCL). Its founders include husband-and-wife researchers Dr Vilas Shelke and Dr Manjusha Shelke, along with Dr John Raymond Normanton. The company’s origins are closely linked to NCL’s research ecosystem. In October 2021, Rechargion signed a technology-transfer agreement with Venture Center of NCL for technologies emerging from Manjusha Shelke’s laboratories. Its stated objective has been to translate advanced battery research into commercially relevant energy-storage products, with sodium-ion technology at the centre of that effort. Rechargion is betting on sodium as an alternative to lithium for applications where cost, resource availability, safety and domestic manufacturing are important considerations. Sodium is considerably more abundant than lithium, and the company argues that sodium-ion chemistry can reduce dependence on imported lithium, nickel and cobalt. Its proprietary technology uses a hard-carbon anode and a symmetrical aluminium-aluminium current-collector structure, which can provide advantages including faster charging, improved thermal stability, wider operating temperatures and long cycle life. In June 2024, Rechargion announced the inauguration of India’s first dedicated sodium-ion cell fabrication pilot plant. By August 2025, the company said its sodium-ion cells became the first in India to pass ARAI validation testing against IEC 62660/IS 16893 safety standards. The company’s product portfolio includes sodium-ion cells such as the NaBh10, NaBh06 and NaBh02, with different dimensions and capacities. By pairing rooftop solar, locally manufactured sodium-ion storage and a direct DC load, Rechargion is taking a practical route toward decentralised energy systems. "‘Self-Reliance’ for energy needs is rapidly becoming essential for many countries," says Rechargion Energy. "A domestic supply chain for all raw materials amalgamated with our end-to-end battery cell manufacturing make our Na-ion technology ideal for India, which is capable of being replicated worldwide."

artigo.texto: Tesla Cybercab battery: in-house nickel cathode from Gigafactory Texas Tesla has assembled the first Cybercab using cathode material produced in-house. The official Robotaxi account said the car used material from Tesla's own cathode facility, while Elon Musk clarified that it was a nickel cathode made directly at Gigafactory Texas. The development adds an important detail to the Cybercab program, whose production Tesla has already started in Austin. The company is bringing another key and costly lithium-ion battery component inside its own manufacturing chain instead of buying finished cathode material from outside suppliers. In August, Tesla North America said the Austin facility had become the first large-scale cathode-material manufacturing operation in North America and was part of the 4680 cell production chain. That does not, however, confirm that the Cybercab shown here uses 4680 cells: Tesla did not identify the cell format in the new statement. There is also no confirmation of any change to the vehicle's specifications. Tesla did not disclose the cathode chemistry beyond Musk's description of a nickel cathode, nor did it reveal the Cybercab's battery capacity, cell cost, driving range or savings versus purchased material. For now, this is primarily a manufacturing-localization milestone rather than the announcement of a new battery. Gigafactory Texas already combines several major Tesla processes. Vehicles are built at the same site, and now Tesla's own cathode material has made its way directly into a completed Cybercab. For Tesla, that reduces the number of outside links between material production and the finished vehicle and could provide more control over costs and supply. The economic effect cannot yet be measured, because Tesla has disclosed neither how much in-house cathode material was used for the Cybercab nor the actual reduction in battery cost. artigo.texto: Maryland is the latest state to clamp down on artificial intelligence (AI) and data centers this week, with Gov. Wes Moore announcing a series of new guardrails. On Tuesday, Moore announced a framework "for the responsible development, deployment, and regulation" of AI in the state, aiming to protect Maryland workers from the dangers of the technology while preparing them to "thrive alongside it." Stream NBC4 newscasts for free right here, right now. Then on Wednesday, Moore signed an executive order calling on state lawmakers to limit tax exemptions for data centers. "We are establishing clear safeguards to ensure Marylanders do not foot the bill, our people benefit, community voices are heard, and our environment is protected," Moore said of the data center guidelines in a press release. Power companies BGE, Delmarva Power and Pepco also expressed support for the order, saying in a statement, in part, "As demand from large energy users increases, it can drive up supply costs across the region - costs that are ultimately borne by customers. That’s why we have long supported a simple principle: large new energy users should pay for the infrastructure needed to serve them, rather than shifting those costs to families and existing businesses." Here's what to know about the new regulations in both areas. Moore's AI framework The Maryland AI framework has three "guiding principles," all three of which prioritize humans over the technology: "Protecting our people," "centering our workers" and "keeping our kids safe." Each of those principles categorizes more specific goals and concerns the framework will address. They include plans to: - Recommend laws to regulate AI companies when it comes to safety, worker protections, public reporting and more. - Establish a "Right of Publicity" so each individual owns their own likeness, so people do not need to prove harm to get relief if their face is used by a generative AI model. - Prohibit the use of AI to discriminate in housing, specifically by banning tenant-screening tools that rely on discriminatory algorithms and banning landlords' use of non-public shared pricing platforms. - Ensure financial, housing and labor regulators in Maryland are informing state residents that "existing civil rights, consumer protection, housing, and lending laws already reach AI-driven decisions." - Issue state workplace guidance to explain how existing discrimination law applies when AI is involved. - Create worker protections so that AI is not used to track and prevent labor organizing or used in ways that worsen systemic biases. - Engage with unions to stay aware of how AI is affecting Maryland workers. - Provide training on AI as it evolves, and provide opportunities for workers to learn skills in other in-demand fields as AI affects job availability. - Strengthening chatbot protections to protect young people. - Curb addictive, AI-based social media and chatbot design. - Require schools to implement protocols for any AI tools students use and ensure all AI tools have demonstrated learning outcomes. - Prepare students to make ethical choices around AI as they move through the world. The rapid advancement of AI — and the warnings of doomsday scenarios from industry executives — has caused worldwide alarm in recent weeks. Some of that alarm comes from concerns the technology will advance beyond human understanding, or fears that bad actors will use powerful technology to harm others. Others are more concerned about economic effects as companies invest in AI tools over human workers, or about negative mental health effects on young people. Moore referenced inaction at the federal level in response to such concerns as part of his motivation for the state-level AI and data center policies in Maryland. "In the absence of federal guardrails around this rapidly developing technology, Governor Moore’s AI principles are grounded in safeguards to mitigate the risks of AI, while ensuring the technology serves the people of Maryland," a second press release about the framework said. Moore's data center regulations Wednesday's executive order on data centers outlines specific standards for new developments in the state. Any large data center, defined as one "that covers 25 megawatts or more," will be judged on five principles: - Ratepayer and grid protection - Economic benefits for Marylanders - Community voice - Environmental protections - Transparency and accountability "Projects will receive a written, public determination from the task force: Aligned, Conditionally Aligned, or Not Aligned," the release about Moore's executive order says. Data centers automatically enter the review process as soon as they ask for permits or incentives. A task force created by the order is charged with performing those reviews and recommending future protections. Maryland will also create a public website with a record of data center projects and actions in Maryland so residents are not surprised by construction in their neighborhoods. Finally, the executive order asks the Maryland General Assembly to a tax exemption for data centers that was originally enacted in 2020. AI's rapid growth since 2022 has caused a parallel boom in data center construction, which has left residents in some areas of the U.S. frustrated as they see growing environmental effects and instability in the power supply. Those frustrations have led states from Virginia to Texas to implement new regulations on data centers to demand accountability and, in some cases, reverse the incentives that led to such rapid growth. "By signing this executive order, we are establishing clear safeguards to ensure Marylanders do not foot the bill, our people benefit, community voices are heard, and our environment is protected — all while centering transparency and accountability throughout the process," Moore said of data centers.
